# Tolkovy Typikon <a id="tolkovy-typikon-of-mikhail-skaballanovich-kyiv-19101915"></a>
## Explanatory Exposition of the Typikon with an Historical Introduction
**Compiled by Mikhail Skaballanovich**

*(Kyiv Pechersk Lavra / Moscow: First Issue, 1910)*  
*(Frontispiece emblem: The Great Indiction / Liturgical Paschal Cycle Wheel: "Круг миротворный") (Editorial Annotation & Master Table of Contents)*

### Annotation

The text of the *Tolkovy Typikon* contains Greek citations with full diacritics and requires a complete Unicode font containing this Unicode range (such as Arial Unicode MS, Palatino Linotype). In curly brackets of the form `{p. NN}` is indicated the page numbering of the original, marked at the beginning of each page according to the edition: *Tolkovy Typikon: Explanatory Exposition of the Typikon with an Historical Introduction*, Sretensky Monastery Publishing House, Moscow, 2004.

The source text of Chapter 1 is taken with the kind permission of Fr. Vladimir Shin from the repository `http://www.orthlib.ru/other/skaballanovich/index.html`.

The text represents the first part of the *Tolkovy Typikon*, comprising Chapter 1 of the work of M. Skaballanovich.

# VOLUME I: THE HISTORICAL INVESTIGATION OF THE TYPIKON (Ancient, Byzantine, Rus'-Ukrainian, and Western Typika)

## Introductory Chapter

## History of the Liturgical Typikon

### From the Author

*(Orig. p. 6)*  
History is the best teacher, and the most profound interpretation of the Typikon will be its historical interpretation. Having in view from the very outset to provide the Typikon chiefly with an historical explanation, the author initially intended to present the latter in the form of exclusively detailed notes upon individual points and particulars of the Typikon. But were the work to be reduced merely to this, such an exposition could scarcely be termed historical, insofar as history is something integral and unified. Therefore, the author deemed it best to unite those historical explanations of the Typikon that could be joined together into a single large chapter, so that in the examination and analysis of the Typikon itself—without repeating what has already been stated in this latter chapter, and confining oneself merely to cross-references—one might dwell solely upon minor details. Thus, the interpretation of the Typikon in its very foundations and essential features is already presented to the reader in this "Introductory Chapter." This is neither a preface to the *Tolkovy Typikon* nor a mere introduction; it is its most fundamental and essential part. The author trusts that it is worthy of its honorable title as a "chapter" of the Typikon, albeit only an introductory one. The author is confident that whoever possesses the inclination or patience (either of which will depend not only upon one's interest in liturgical worship, but also upon the extent of the reader's general knowledge of church history)—whoever possesses the patience or inclination to read through this "chapter" will have the veil removed from before many mysteries and enigmas of the Typikon. Such a reader will perceive that the Typikon is already half and in its main substance explained, and will look to the subsequent contents of the book for the explanation of such particulars as, for example, why at Vespers the Augmented and Supplicatory Ectenias are appointed after the Entrance and reiterate the petitions of the Great Ectenia, or why at the Ninth Hour during Great Lent only three prostrations are appointed. Yet answers to such questions must be sought in the future installment of our work by one who reads this present installment attentively, unless this reading itself prepares him for the independent resolution of such perplexities.

The author does not fear that the scholarly character of the book will hinder its comprehension on the part of anyone interested in the ecclesiastical Typikon and *(Orig. p. 7)* studying it. A journalistic article may present, by its abundance of foreign loanwords and specialized terminology, far greater obstacles to understanding than the straightforward exposition of the present volume, which endeavors nevertheless not to sacrifice scientific scholarly objectives in the least, as befits a science that does not seek access merely to the broad masses.

*(Orig. p. 8)*  

### A. The Liturgical Typikon Prior to the Appearance of Its Complete Manuscripts
#### (1st–8th Centuries)

Inasmuch as our liturgical Typikon takes as its task the adaptation of church services to the sacred commemorations of the day, its compilation—which was naturally mental and conceptual at first, rather than written—must have begun with the very emergence of sacred commemorations within Christianity. The appearance of the first sacred commemorations dates back to apostolic times, when there unquestionably existed already a liturgical celebration at least of the day of the Resurrection (the Lord's Day / Sunday). Thus, it is no exaggeration to state that the first lines of our ecclesiastical Typikon, which set forth precisely the order of Sunday worship, were conceived by the holy Apostles themselves. It is not surprising, therefore, that ancient Russian scribes called the Typikon an "inspired book" [^2]. Its compilation began in those ages when there existed in Christianity a spiritual elevation of life that made possible the emergence of divinely inspired scriptures.

The formation of our divine services, which began in the apostolic age, reached its conclusion, one might say, only by the sixteenth century, when its Typikon acquired fully its contemporary form. And certainly, the value of this Typikon cannot be diminished by the circumstance that a millennium and a half was required for its creation. Rather the reverse: thanks to such an extended period of development of our liturgical Typikon, the Church of diverse epochs was able to take part in this development, and each of these epochs possessed its own strength and beauty and reflected them upon our centuries-old Typikon. And not only did the Church of different eras create the present Typikon, but also the Church of diverse localities and lands; consequently, it was wrought by the Church not merely Apostolic, but Catholic (*Soborna*) *(Orig. p. 9)* both in space and in time. From the pages of the Typikon there breathes the tender spirit of ancient ecclesiastical life, now of pious Constantinople, now of ascetic Egypt and the Thebaid. If, moreover, one takes into account the multitude of Old Testament material that has entered into our divine worship, in the moments of the latter we spiritually relive even sacred biblical antiquity, and "walk in unity of mind" in the Church of the Patriarchs and Prophets.

Being the conciliar creation of the Church, the liturgical Typikon was nonetheless elaborated preeminently by her most worthy sons alone. Its immediate authors were men who had no other life than prayer and fasting, for whom the sweetness of divine worship permitted them to partake of food but once every five days and to sleep only standing or sitting, who brought their all-night vigils to completion in churches locked and set ablaze from without by pagans—men whose martyr blood was at times mingled with the Eucharistic Blood. The pages of the Typikon compiled by them could not fail to be drenched with tears of compunction and the God-offered blood of confession, which cannot fail to be felt therein and to impart to the book a spirit of singular sanctity and purity. Herein lies the secret of the profound influence of Orthodox divine worship upon the soul: he who participates in it absorbs the influence of the Church of all ages in the persons of her finest powers and lives the life of the entire Church. This influence emanates not only from the poetry and music of the service, but also from its very architectonics—from these fortyfold repetitions of **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Господи, помилуй*), silent bows and prostrations intruding as lengthy pauses into chanting and reading, from the antiphonal manner of singing, and the like. The Typikon is concerned precisely with the architectonics and aesthetics of divine worship. In particular, among the array of ascetics, the currently authoritative Typikon attributes its compilation to Saint Sabas—more precisely, "that of the holy Lavra of our venerable and God-bearing Father Sabas in Jerusalem." This is the monastery not far from Jerusalem in the rugged Judean wilderness, founded in the fifth century by Saint Sabas the Sanctified. What share of participation belongs to this venerable father in the elaboration of the present Typikon cannot yet be determined in the present state of scholarly sources. In any case, the homeland of the present Typikon is Palestine and its wildernesses cultivated by ascetic labors. The creators of our ecclesiastical Typikon were, consequently, nurtured by that very wilderness which nurtured Elijah and John the Baptist, and which prepared the Savior Himself for His public ministry. Here the very air was saturated with sacred memories. Nearby were the greatest holy places of the Christian world—Jerusalem with the Sepulchre of the Lord and the Church of the Resurrection, where prayer of its own accord grew more fervent, and where, according to the testimony of a Western female pilgrim of the fourth century (Silvia of Aquitaine [Egeria]), when the Gospels of the Passion were read, "all the people raised such a cry and lamentation that there was no one who was not moved to tears at that hour" [^3].

*(Orig. p. 10)*  

### Old Testament Jewish Divine Worship

In order to form a proper conception of the origin of Christian divine worship and its ritual order, one must not forget that the Apostles and the most eminent members of the primitive Church were Jews; and though their faith and hope were no longer Old Testament, but new, their prayer and divine worship could not depart far from the Jewish forms of that day. Divine worship and ritual are conservative by their very nature; here sanctity is measured by antiquity... The religious enthusiasm that seized the Apostles and the other disciples of Christ after the Resurrection of Christ is manifested in the fact that they spent whole days in the Temple ("they were continually in the temple") [^4], which Christ had come to abolish, where, of course, praising and blessing ("praising and blessing") God was possible in Jewish ritual forms. If we direct our attention to these forms, it will become evident to us what influence they exerted upon the subsequent development of Christian divine worship.

### Old Testament Temple Worship

Although the essence of Hebrew Temple worship consisted of sacrifices, a musical and vocal element always entered into it to such an extent that Temple worship seemed almost entirely transformed into music and singing [^5], while the latter was regarded as a special kind of votive offering alongside material sacrifices [^6].

#### The Order of Sacrificial Psalmody

Instituted by Moses only for feast days and especially solemn sacrifices [^7], their accompaniment by the sound of trumpets [^8] became an adjunct of the daily morning and evening sacrifice and developed into an elaborate order of liturgical *(Orig. p. 11)* chanting and music [^9]. By the altar stood a choir of Levites with musical instruments, and two priests with trumpets. As soon as the sacrificial animal was laid upon the wood, the Levitical choir commenced the chanting of the psalm to musical accompaniment, so that the sacrifice was consumed amid the sounds of this chanting and music.

The chanting of the psalm at the daily sacrifice began properly with the libation of wine upon the sacrifice, because chanting is possible only in gladness of heart, and wine, said the rabbis, "cheereth God and man" [^10]. During chanting, the psalm was divided into three sections by fairly prolonged pauses; at these pauses the chanting and music fell silent, and only the sound of the trumpet rang forth. Concluding the third section of the psalm, the Levites raised the pitch [^11], and this served as a signal for the priests to sound their trumpets. At these solemn pauses in the psalm the people fell prostrate, worshipping the Lord. Thus the sound of the sacred trumpets was heard three times on ordinary days during sacrifice. (On the eve of the Sabbath they sounded the trumpets twice more before this: the first time to cease labor, and the second time to separate the weekday from the Sabbath). Upon the completion of the psalm the people exclaimed: **"Amen. Alleluia"** [^12].

Upon the burning of the sacrifice and the conclusion of the psalm, the officiating priest, standing upon the steps of the Temple vestibule (*Ulam*), imparted the blessing to the people, who thereupon fell prostrate, especially if the high priest himself had offered the sacrifice and imparted the blessing [^13].

#### Daily and Festive Psalms: Canticles of the Sabbath

For the daily sacrifice, a proper psalm was appointed for each day of the week: on the Sabbath, Psalm 91 [92]; on Sunday, Psalm 23 [24]; Monday, Psalm 47 [48]; Tuesday, Psalm 81 [82]; Wednesday, Psalm 93 [94]; Thursday, Psalm 80 [81]; Friday, Psalm 92 [93] [^14].

*(Orig. p. 12)*  
On especially important occasions proper psalms were chanted, and the psalm was sung not by the Levites alone, but the entire congregation participated in its singing, taking up the refrains at the ends of the verses. For this purpose certain psalms are structured in such a manner that each verse or section concludes with one and the same refrain (for example, Psalm 135 [136], where every verse has the refrain **"For His mercy endureth forever"** [*Яко в век милость Его*]; while for a series of psalms, 105–106 [106–107], 112–118 [113–119], 134–135 [135–136], **"Alleluia"** served as such a refrain). In the Bible several instances are indicated where such psalms were sung with the participation of the people, and in all these cases reference is made, apparently, to one and the same psalms—134 and 135 [135 and 136] [^15]. These psalms were suited for divine worship among the Jews, as among the early Christians, also because they are directly directed against idolatry [^16].

On the Sabbath, at the time of offering the special Sabbath sacrifice, the Canticle of Moses was sung: **"Give ear, O heaven"** (*Вонми, небо*; Deut. 32:1–43)—a one-sixth part of it on each Sabbath in succession—at the morning sacrifice; while at the evening sacrifice was sung **"I will sing unto the Lord"** (*Поим Господеви*; Exod. 15:1–19). (Hence is understood the passage in the Apocalypse [^17] where it is said that the saints, entering into eternal Sabbath-rest, sing the Song of Moses) [^18].

On the feasts of Pascha and Pentecost they chanted the Lesser or Egyptian Hallel, that is, Psalms 113–118 [114–119], which were considered especially rich in content, since they glorify the Exodus from Egypt. At the Feast of Tabernacles (*Sukkot*) was sung the Great Hallel, consisting, according to differing opinions of the rabbis, of Psalms 117–135 [118–136], or 119–133 [120–134] (the Gradual Psalms / Psalms of Ascents), or 134–136 [135–137] [^19]. Verses of one of these psalms—the 117th [118th]—entered into our typikal **"God is the Lord"** (*Бог Господь*). (According to ancient Typika, **"God is the Lord"** was appointed only on feast days) [^20]. After the model of the Gradual Psalms are composed our Gradual Antiphons (*anabathmoi*), which formerly replaced our present Polyeleos (according to ancient Typika, these latter were indeed sung with the verses of these psalms) [^21].

#### Significance and Character of Old Testament Temple Singing

For the singing of the psalms at divine worship, David set apart 4,000 singers and musicians out of all the 38,000 Levites [^22]; from that time there was formed among the Hebrews a kind of hereditary caste of singers, preserved even after the Babylonian Captivity [^23]. A strict specialization was introduced into it: the descendants of Jeduthun and Asaph played upon stringed instruments, the choir of Heman upon percussion instruments, while the sons of Korah were, apparently, the vocalists [^24]. Although the psalms were sung to musical accompaniment, judging by their titles, certain psalms were intended exclusively or *(Orig. p. 13)* preeminently for vocal singing—namely, those superscribed *shir*, *ᾠδή*, "song" / "canticle"; others for instrumental music—namely, those superscribed *mizmor*, *μέλος*, *ψαλμός*, "psalm." Sometimes these superscriptions are combined, now the first being placed first, now the second; such psalms must have been designated for singing at first with the voice, and then with music, or vice versa. In general, however, vocal singing in the Old Testament Temple was deemed more important than instrumental music. In the thought of the Talmud, the glorification of God in the Temple was to be expressed chiefly by a loud voice, whereas instrumental music was admitted only out of necessity [^25], "inasmuch as instruments supported the voices and singing of the Levites" [^26]. Membership in the Levitical order was requisite only for the singers; any Israelite, if known as an adept in music, could present himself at the Temple with his instrument and join the band of musicians, but no kinship with the priests conferred the right to sing vocally with the singers: this was the sacred prerogative of the Levites alone. The instrumental musicians were termed "vexers of the Levites," because (according to Maimonides' exposition) by their playing they drowned out the beauty of the Levitical song [^27]. In such relation as instrumental music stood to vocal singing, in like relation stood the playing of trumpets to instrumental music: it constituted the exclusive prerogative of the priests and was forbidden to the Levites. Levitical women also participated in Temple music and singing [^28].

The singing of psalms in Old Testament divine worship was distinguished by that simplicity characteristic of all antiquity; it was, of course, unisonous (like our ancient Russian and contemporary Old Believer chant), to which an indication is also found in the Bible ("and they were as one, the trumpeters and singers, making one sound to be heard") [^29]. Thus Hebrew music, calculated not for variety but for acoustic power, had a thundering and piercing character. The Talmud states that when they played in the Temple, it was heard as far as Samaria [^30]. Clement of Alexandria compares Hebrew music with Greek, specifically with the Dorian mode [^31], which formed the basis of our Tone 1. In any case, the singing was diatonic, not enharmonic or chromatic [^32]. High voices were perhaps termed *alamoth*, "after the manner of maidens" (soprano), as certain psalms are superscribed (Slavonic: *o taynykh*, "concerning secrets"); low voices—*sheminith*, "upon the eighth" (octave, Slavonic: *o osmey*); the former tones expressed joy, and the latter sorrow: for the most part, psalms with the first superscription are of a joyful character (for example, Ps. 45 [46]), while the latter are mournful (for example, Ps. 6, **"O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine anger"** [*Господи, да не яростию Твоею обличиши мене*], and Ps. 12 [13], **"How long, O Lord"** [*(Orig. p. 14)* *Доколе, Господи*]). The Psalms of Ascents (Gradual Psalms) must have united all tones within themselves, beginning from the lowest and concluding with a loud *forte* [^33].

#### Lamps and Incense

Concurrently with the daily morning and evening sacrifice in the first court of the Temple, its outer court, the other two divisions of the Temple—the Sanctuary (Holy Place) and the Holy of Holies—were not left without divine worship, though the service here was reverently silent. In the Holy Place in the morning, the high priest or priest performed the preparation (Heb. *hetiv*, properly "adorning / trimming," Slav. *ustroyayet*) of the lamps [^34] for their evening kindling, and in the evening their actual kindling for the entire night [^35]. It is possible that from this Christian Vespers received the title of "lucernarium" service, *λυχνικόν* (*lychnikon*, a name applied to it already by fourth-century monuments) [^36]. At the same time, the burning of sweet incense took place upon the Altar of Incense, which stood directly before the veil of the Holy of Holies and therefore belonged rather to the latter than to the Holy Place [^37]. Occurring thus in the holiest precinct of the Temple, this offering of incense was accounted as much a sacrifice as the bloody sacrifice [^38]. From this, perhaps, our Matins and Vespers received the offering of incense at their beginning.

#### Rites of the Feast of Tabernacles (*Sukkot*)

We do not dwell upon the Hebrew festivals, which are sufficiently known to everyone. We note only certain rites of the Feast of Tabernacles. On this feast the entire altar was adorned with greenery, and the rite of the drawing of water took place. The Temple was not locked in the evening as usual, but the people remained therein through the entire night; and to the music of the Levites, with singing and with burning torches in hand, four men performed sacred dances. Moreover, the Temple court was illuminated by lamps set aloft in such numbers that they were said to illuminate all the courtyards of Jerusalem [^39].

We have set forth the order of Old Testament Temple worship with attention directed to those parts of it which, in our opinion, could have exerted an influence upon our divine services. From the exposition presented, the degree of this affinity is sufficiently manifest.

Upon the dispersion of Christians from Jerusalem and upon the destruction of the Temple, the majestic sacred music of the Temple and the Levitical choirs must have resounded in the ears of the faithful for far too long a time for this not to have left its imprint upon the elaboration of Christian divine worship.

*(Orig. p. 15)*  

### Synagogal Worship

Synagogal worship likewise could not fail to exert a certain influence upon the development of Christian divine services. Synagogal worship was closely related to that of the Temple. In the Temple itself, upon its outer court, there was a synagogue, in which the divine worship celebrated in the Temple was merely supplemented. Devoid of bloody sacrifices and of all the intricate ceremonial of the Mosaic Law, synagogal worship, far more than that of the Temple, was distinguished by a spiritual, verbal (rational) character, and therefore stood closer to Christian worship [^40].

Divine worship in the synagogue, as now, was celebrated not daily, but only on Saturdays (the Sabbath), on great feasts (such as Pascha, Pentecost, Tabernacles, and Purim), on the Day of Atonement (*Yom Kippur*), and other fasts. Very early there were joined to these days Monday and Thursday [^41], simply, perhaps, as market days in ancient Jerusalem. In addition to morning and evening worship, corresponding to the morning and evening sacrifice, the synagogue early introduced also a day (midday / noon) service. In this they may have had in view the ancient Hebrew custom of praying three times a day, mentioned by David and observed by Daniel and his companions in captivity [^42].

The synagogue was originally and in its concept rather a religious-educational institution than a liturgical one. But since in cities distant from Jerusalem (and in the Babylonian Captivity, where its inception may be sought) it was the sole place where religious consolation could be obtained, almost from its very emergence prayer began to be joined to the reading and exposition of Scripture; and already by the time of the Maccabees the synagogue possessed a very complex liturgical ritual [^43]. During the earthly life of the Savior and the Apostles, this ritual must have possessed an appearance quite close to contemporary synagogal worship. On the basis of investigations into this question (beginning with the twelfth-century rabbi Maimonides) [^44], one may delineate in ancient and contemporary synagogal worship approximately those components that must trace back to the first century after Christ.

Synagogal worship consists of: 1) introductory verses, psalms, and two prayers; 2) the recitation of the *Shema* (confession of faith) with its surrounding benedictions; 3) a series (from 7 to 18) of "Benedictions" or prayers of the *Shemoneh Esreh*; 4) the reading of the Law (except at the midday service); 5) the reading of the Prophets (at the morning Sabbath and festival services); 6) the concluding priestly blessing.

*(Orig. p. 16)*  

#### Introductory Psalms and Prayers

Divine worship in the synagogue now begins with introductory verses from the Psalms, whole psalms (akin to our introductory / preparatory psalms), and prayers (in one of which occur the words: "I will bow down and fall prostrate and bend the knee"). Psalms predominantly of an alleluiatic character are employed (perhaps because the very word *alleluia* may be regarded as an address of the reader to the congregation with an invitation to praise the Lord). The verses of the psalm are appointed to be read or chanted in recitative by one individual, while the congregation repeats either the same verse, or the first verse of the psalm, or responds to it with the refrain "alleluia" and others [^45]. All of this is regarded merely as preparation for divine worship. In different epochs the introductory part of synagogal worship assumed diverse forms, and concerning its degree of antiquity nothing definitive can be asserted.

Proper divine worship commences with the officiant (the *sheliach tzibbur*, cantor) approaching the ark of the scrolls and reciting the *Kaddish* and *Barechu* prayers, which contain the glorification of the divine Name and begin with the words: "May Thy name be magnified and sanctified" [^46], "Bless ye the Lord Who is blessed" [^47]. The congregation responds to these prayers: "Amen. May His great Name be blessed forever and unto eternity."

#### The Shema

Then follows the reading of the so-called *Shema*, akin to our Creed [^48], consisting of the following three sections of Scripture: Deuteronomy 6:4–9; 11:13–21; and Numbers 15:37–41 (the first section begins "Hear," Heb. *Shema*, whence also the title).

*(Orig. p. 17)*  
The *Shema* is preceded and concluded by proper prayers [^49]. In the prayers of the *Shema*, God is glorified for the creation of light and the Angels and for the election of Israel, and a petition is contained that God would extend His mercy to the descendants of the holy Forefathers and turn them toward the fulfillment of the commandments [^50]. The *Shema* with its prayers is now read by a single reader, and the congregation responds to the prayers with "Amen." Every Jew, with the exception of women, children, and slaves, is obligated to recite the *Shema* with its prayers even outside the synagogue, morning and evening [^51], yet without that prayer which contains the doxology of the Seraphim: "Holy, holy..." The *Shema* is one of the most ancient parts of synagogal worship. The contents of its prayers are reported by Flavius Josephus, who attributes them to the time of Moses [^52]. An allusion to the *Shema* is found with great probability in the question of the Savior to the scribe, a man learned in the Law: **"How readest thou?"** (*Како чтеши?*) [^53]; the scribe responds to this question with the words of Deuteronomy contained in the *Shema*; perhaps the question of Christ was understood by the scribe not in reference to the entire contents of the Law, but in reference to that reading which was termed reading *par excellence*, that is, to the reading of the *Shema*.

#### The Benedictions: Shemoneh Esreh

The reading of the *Shema* is followed by the prayers termed "Benedictions" (*Tefillah*) or *Shemoneh Esreh*, which signifies "Eighteen," because these prayers number eighteen (now properly nineteen), although they are never read in such full number. The first three of these prayers glorify the omnipotence and goodness of God; the last two contain thanksgiving for the divine mercy and a general supplication for the blessing of God; while the remaining prayers contain diverse particular petitions: for the conversion of Israel to repentance, forgiveness, deliverance from evil, health, the fertility of the earth, the ingathering of dispersed Israel, the restoration of the kingdom, the destruction of heretics (*minim*), the reward of the righteous, the rebuilding of Jerusalem, the sending of the Messiah, the hearing of prayer, and the restoration of sacrifice [^54]. The "Benedictions" are stamped with the character of profound antiquity [^55], and are distinguished *(Orig. p. 18)* by deep religious sentiment [^56]. Every Jew, without those exceptions that apply to the *Shema*, is obligated to recite the *Shemoneh Esreh* three times a day: morning, noon, and evening [^57]. Among the eighteen "Benedictions," it is appointed to read them at the weekday divine service; whereas on the Sabbath and feasts, of the eighteen Benedictions only seven are recited: the first three, one middle prayer corresponding to the day, and the final three; on the New Year (*Rosh Hashanah*), the lesser of the feasts, nine benedictions were recited; and on fasts, to the eighteen Benedictions six more are added, so that in all twenty-four are obtained [^58]. On feast days, a proper "additional" prayer (*musaf*) [^59] is joined to the Benedictions, and furthermore, certain modifications and insertions (*havdalah*) are made in the text of the Benedictions, for example: "Blessed art Thou, O Lord, Who sanctifiest such-and-such feast"; or, for example, on the Day of Atonement the customary address to God is replaced by the address "King of Justice"; in rainy seasons to the divine Name is added "Who sendest down the rain," and in the summer season "Who bringest down the dew" [^60]. Following the Benedictions ensues the reading of Holy Scripture.

#### Reading of the Law and the Prophets
As stated, the chief purpose of the synagogue in its original concept was not prayer, but the reading of Holy Scripture. Thanks to the synagogue, Judaism, and following it Christianity, came to regard the reading of Holy Scripture as an integral part of divine worship, a species of prayer. From the Scriptures in the synagogue, there was always read preeminently the Law of Moses, the Pentateuch, which was read straight through (originally once every 3 or 3.5 years, across half of a sabbatical cycle of years [^61], *(Orig. p. 19)* and subsequently every single year), for which purpose the Pentateuch was divided into small sections termed *parashah* (section). As regards the other two parts of the Hebrew Bible—the Prophets (*Nevi'im*) and the Hagiographa (*Ketuvim*)—the former were not read in their entirety, but in excerpts, while the Hagiographa were read only infrequently. The reading from the Prophets was selected each time by the reader himself [^62], specifically such that it corresponded to the reading from the Law [^63], disclosing and elucidating it; consequently, it stood in relation to the first reading just as in our rite the Epistle (*Apostol*) stands to the Gospel [^64]. The reading from the Prophets was called *haftarah*, "dismissal reading," inasmuch as it occurred at the conclusion of the service. The cycle of readings commenced on the Sabbath following the Feast of Tabernacles. On feast days, not the ordinary *parashot* and *haftarot* were read, but those corresponding to the sacred commemorations: for example, at Pascha from Leviticus 23; at Pentecost, Deuteronomy 15:9–13; at the New Year, Leviticus 23:25; on the Day of Atonement, Leviticus 16; at Tabernacles, Numbers 29:12–39; on the second Sabbath prior to Pascha, concerning the water of purification; and on the final Sabbath, concerning the preparation of the paschal lamb [^65]. The great feasts possessed readings also from the Hagiographa (the *Megilloth*): at Pascha the Song of Songs was read; at Pentecost, Ruth; at Tabernacles, Ecclesiastes; at Purim, Esther; on the fast of the Ninth of Av (July/August) in commemoration of the burning of Jerusalem, Lamentations. At weekday services only the Law was read. Following the reading of each verse and even phrase there ensued translation (targum) and exposition, turning not infrequently into an entire homily. Holy Scripture in the synagogue could be read by any man, excluding a slave and one with a speech impediment.

Yet it was required that the first section be read by a priest (*kohen*), and the second by a Levite, if such were present in the synagogue. Before the beginning of the reading, the first reader exclaimed: "Bless ye the Lord," to which the congregation responded with a general blessing of the Lord, while the reader added a blessing for the bestowal of the Law, to which the congregation answered "Amen." Prior to the reading of the Prophets the blessing was not so elaborate: it consisted of a single formula pronounced by the reader with the response "Amen." The reading likewise concluded with a blessing and the *Kaddish* prayer.

Divine worship in the synagogue concluded with the blessing (*Birkat Kohanim*), which was imparted by all the priests together, if any were present; but if not, the formula of blessing was recited by the synagogal minister (*hazzan* / *sheliach tzibbur*).

In synagogal worship, chanting no longer occupied so large a place as in that of the Temple. Nonetheless, the character of synagogal chanting could not fail to exert an influence upon our own.

#### Synagogal Singing
One cannot judge of ancient synagogal singing by contemporary singing in the synagogue. When Christianity became the dominant religion, numerous restrictions were imposed everywhere upon the Jewish cultus; even where this cultus was tolerated, as for example in Italy, the chanting of psalms was positively forbidden *(Orig. p. 20)* in synagogues; this prohibition was confirmed at numerous synods of the Western Church. Its consequence was the introduction into the synagogues of so-called cantillation, representing an intermediate form between reading and chanting: it is a loud recitation in which certain syllables are more or less prolonged. However, there are certain grounds for tracing cantillation back even to the era of the Temple. In any case, the contemporary synagogal singing of psalms must retain certain traces of antiquity, the spirit of which breathes from it. Cantillation in the synagogue recalls the chanting of psalms in the Roman Church, with the distinction that the latter employs diverse psalm tones (*toni psalmorum*), whereas cantillation is uniform for Sabbaths and feasts and resembles the fifth tone of Roman Catholic Gregorian psalmody—whence it was surmised that Catholic psalmody passed into the Christian Church through the Apostles from the Temple of Jerusalem. Traces of antiquity were preserved also in another genre of synagogal chant, approaching still closer to recitation: namely, the very reading of the Law and the Prophets with musical accentuation (*te'amim* / cantillation tropes), the marks of which are identical with grammatical punctuation marks (of which there are twenty-seven in the Hebrew language); musical accentuation varies according to the contents of the books: the Pentateuch, according to the characterization of the rabbis, must have sounds that are gentle yet low; the Prophets, sounds high and menacing; Proverbs, persuasive and insinuating; the Song of Songs, lively and joyful; Ecclesiastes, serious and solemn [^66].

#### External Signs of Prayer in the Synagogue

Among the external bodily signs that accompanied divine worship and prayer, there were in use in the synagogue the bowing of the head and the bending of the torso at the waist (*metania*). During fasts they prostrated themselves upon the floor in cruciform posture. During divine worship they sat for the most part, standing only for the Benedictions (*Shemoneh Esreh*) [^67].

Such was that divine worship in which the Apostles and the first Christians were nurtured, and upon the foundation of which they fashioned their new service of God in Spirit and in Truth.

The delineated depiction of synagogal worship demonstrates that its influence upon Christian divine services pertained to diverse minor particulars, partially to structural order and material elements, but not to spirit and essential content. Christianity introduced into divine worship such intimacy with the Godhead and such hope as the synagogue could not even conceive. There, one may say, was the shadow, but here the very archetype of communion with God [^68].

*(Orig. p. 21)*  

### Worship of the Therapeutae
Scholars discover points of contact between Christian divine worship and the worship of the Therapeutae. The Therapeutae—according to recent investigations [^69]—were a circle of ascetically minded Alexandrian Jewish legal scholars, touched by Platonic philosophy and striving (like Philo, who so deeply sympathized with them) toward the spiritualization of Judaism. This could not fail to draw them near to Christianity, which explains why the church historian Eusebius regarded them as disciples of the Evangelist Mark [^70].

#### All-Night Vigils and Banquets of the Therapeutae
Philo enthusiastically describes both the ascetic life of the Therapeutae and their liturgical assemblies—"all-night vigils" (*pannychides*), as Eusebius terms them—which were joined to a common banquet. The liturgical assembly among the Therapeutae commenced with a discourse by the president concerning some passage of Holy Scripture or another question.

"Then the president ariseth and chanteth a hymn to the glory of God [^71], either newly composed by himself, or borrowed from one of the ancient poets, who left behind many hymns appointed for execution during libations and sacrifices upon the altar (psalms?), for singing at tables and choral dances. After the president, the others likewise chant hymns in order, in due decency amid profound silence and universal attention [^72], except in those cases when it is necessary to sing the verse-terminations (*akroteleutia*) [^73] or refrains (*ephymnia*) [^74]. When each hath concluded his hymn [^75], the youths bring in the table, upon which is set the most holy (*panagestaton*) nourishment: leavened bread with salt and hyssop, after the likeness of the showbread. After the supper they celebrate the sacred all-night vigil (*pannychida*). The all-night vigil is celebrated in the following manner."

#### Singing of the Therapeutae
"They all arise together, and in the midst of the banquet hall first form two choirs: one of men and one of women; as leader and precentor in each choir *(Orig. p. 22)* is chosen the most venerable and skilled singer. Thus do they sing hymns composed in honor of God in diverse meters and melodies, now in unison, now in antiphonal harmony (*ἀνтифώνοις ἁрμονίαις*), in the latter case gesturing with their hands and dancing (*ἐпоρχούμενοι*), inspiredly performing (*ἐпиθειάζοντες*) melodies now processional (*prosodia*) [^76], now stationary (*stasima*), executing the necessary strophes and antistrophes. Then, when the company of men and the company of women separately have enjoyed all this, having become intoxicated, as it were at bacchic revels, with this God-beloved wine, they unite and form a single choir [^77], in imitation of that choir established of old at the Red Sea in thanksgiving for the wonders wrought there... Seeing and experiencing a wonder surpassing all imagination and description, wrought for them beyond expectation, then the Hebrews, seized with divine inspiration, men and women together forming a single choir, sang songs of thanksgiving to God the Savior, Moses the Prophet leading the men, and Miriam the Prophetess the women [^78]. It is of this very choir that the choir of the Therapeutae and Therapeutides forms the most exact copy, when to the deep (*barys*) [^79] voice of the men responds the shrill, high (*oxys*) voice of the women in resounding (*antechois*) and antiphonal melodies, which produces a truly harmonious and musical symphony" [^80].

Thus the Therapeutae significantly expanded and developed the musical element of synagogal worship, which had been so negligible there. Along this same path Christian divine worship likewise proceeded. To the hypophonic and epiphonic chanting of the synagogue, the Therapeutae added antiphonal singing [^81].

*(Orig. p. 23)*  

## 1st Century: Apostolic Worship

### Worship according to the Acts of the Apostles
According to the author of the Acts of the Apostles, the first newly converted Christians in Jerusalem continued steadfastly in the apostles' doctrine, in fellowship, in the breaking of bread, and in prayers [^82]. Their entire day was, as it were, a continuous liturgical worship, which consisted first and foremost in "the apostles' doctrine" (*ἐν τῇ διδαχῇ τῶν ἀпоστόλων* [^83]), that is, in their narratives concerning the life and preaching of the Savior, which subsequently formed the contents of the written Gospels, and in the instructions of the Apostles themselves, later set down in writing by several of them in their Epistles. To this teaching, which possessed a singular sweetness thanks to the freshness of events and the vividness of recollections, was joined the intimate fellowship (*koinonia*) of the believers among themselves, reaching even to their constant inseparability one from another and to the community of goods, but manifesting itself with particular radiance and reaching its zenith in the breaking of bread. By the breaking of bread is understood the Eucharist [^84] celebrated at common meals. These meals, on the basis of the Savior's commandment: **"This do in remembrance of Me,"** without doubt received a liturgical significance from the very beginning: they contained the commemoration of the Lord's death and the acknowledgement of the sacrificial value of that death, while also serving as the expression of inner *(Orig. p. 24)* communion of the disciples among themselves. Nonetheless, these meals originally did not possess an exclusively liturgical significance, but served in primitive Christian times also for the satisfaction of the natural need for nourishment [^85]. Alongside the breaking of bread the author of Acts places prayers. The plural form—prayers—points to diverse prayers, which could be in part new Christian prayers unbound by fixed formula, and in part psalms and prayers customary among the Jews [^86].

This general picture of Christian life at that time, which by virtue of the singular character of that life constitutes simultaneously a picture of divine worship, the author of Acts presents more vividly when he adds: and they, continuing daily with one accord in the temple, and breaking bread from house to house, did eat their meat with gladness and singleness of heart, praising God [^87]. Here the divine worship of the primitive Christians is presented in two forms: on the one hand, they participate in the Jewish, Old Testament worship of the Temple and what must have been the synagogue situated within its precincts; on the other hand, they possess as a supplement to it their own domestic worship. That the first Christians visited the Temple and participated in its divine services was entirely natural. In this case they were doing nothing other than that which Christ Himself had done. It was precisely in the Temple that He taught the people, and zeal for it even consumed Him [^88]. Following the Ascension of Christ and until Pentecost, the Apostles went daily to the Temple [^89], and after Pentecost we see them very frequently within it [^90]. True, Christians now recognized only a prefigurative, typological significance in many things that previously were regarded as essential; yet the prayers, sacrifices, and liturgical rites of the Old Testament spoke to their souls no less now that they had come to know their true spiritual meaning [^91].

It was precisely upon the soil of this Old Testament piety of the first Christians that a distinct Christian divine worship had to develop. Already within the Temple itself, during its ordinary services, Christians inwardly celebrated another worship of their own, as the author of Acts indicates in another passage: they were all with one accord in Solomon's porch; and of the rest durst no man join himself to them, but the people magnified them [^92]. In the Temple Christians kept themselves distinct from the Jews, many of whom involuntarily held them in reverence, yet feared openly to join them. In the vast courts of the Temple, Christians chose for themselves the most secluded and remote area—the portico stretching along the outer eastern wall of the Temple *(Orig. p. 25)* precinct (on the inner side, of course, of that wall [^93]), situated thus within the Court of the Gentiles [^94].

Nevertheless, when present in the Old Testament Temple, Christians could participate only in the worship celebrated there, which could no longer fully satisfy them and was inherently insufficient. Their own, and at the same time genuine, divine worship they could hold (resuming our interrupted examination of Acts 2:46) only "from house to house" (*καт᾿ οἴκους*), celebrating it now in one, now in another Christian home (for example, that of Mary the mother of Mark, of Joseph, of Nicodemus [^95], or the Upper Room of Zion [^96]). Here alone could Christians celebrate that breaking of bread of which the Book of Acts repeatedly speaks, and which, as we noted, serves as the designation of common meals possessing a Eucharistic character. Following the example of the Savior's Supper, these were evening meals. In the cycle of daily and day-long prayers, this was their final sublime moment, the culminating summit in which was consummated the prayerful fervor that had mounted throughout the entire day. By virtue of this, the very partaking of food among Christians took place always "in jubilant exultation" (*agalliasei*). The uniting at the meal of the poor with the rich stripped it of all envy and imparted to it also "singleness of heart." This meal, like the entire day of the Christians of that time, was wholly prayerful, with the praising of God: praising (*ainountes*) God—perhaps an allusion to sacred hymns [^97].

Thus was laid the foundation of the agapae, or love-feasts, which existed in the Christian Church until the fourth century, even after the Eucharist had separated from them and was transferred to the morning or midday, upon the foundation of which arose our contemporary Vespers with its blessing of loaves (*artoklasia*). As in the Old Testament religion, the evening was initially regarded in Christianity as the most sacred and prayerful part of the day (it being remembered that days began with the evening), to which the most solemn service was assigned; just as in the Old Testament Temple the "evening sacrifice" [^98] was more sacred and more solemn than the morning sacrifice (with the lighting of the lamps), so too our contemporary Vespers, which took the place of the ancient Eucharist and agape, approaches closest in its structure to the most sacred service of all—the Divine Liturgy; it consists primarily of ectenias, possesses *(Orig. p. 26)* only a single Introductory Psalm, has no canon, yet can possess the most complete readings from Holy Scripture, not only the Gospel, but also the Epistle. Thus, already in apostolic times and in living connection with the Old Testament cultus, was laid the foundation of one of our contemporary daily offices with all its distinctive structure.

Yet the Eucharist with the agape was only, as observed, the highest consummation of the daily apostolic worship, which, although day-long, could not after all be completely continuous. Like Jewish divine worship, apostolic worship likewise probably consisted of three daily services: in addition to the evening service—the principal one—there was a morning and a midday service. In this same Book of Acts we find clear indications of precisely a threefold number of daily prayers or services during apostolic times. Thus on Pentecost the Apostles with the believers gathered for prayer in the morning around the third hour (by our reckoning, 9:00 a.m.) [^99], approximately the hour of the morning sacrifice in the Temple; the Apostle Peter offered prayer at his lodging around the sixth hour (12:00 noon) [^100]; and the Apostles Peter and John went up to the Temple at the hour of prayer, being the ninth hour [^101], the hour of the evening sacrifice.

### Constituent Elements of Apostolic Worship
Thus the Book of Acts provides indications—albeit fragmentary—concerning the divine worship of apostolic times, yet of such a nature that from them one may form a judgment in general outlines regarding both the composition and, still more, the character of this worship. To be sure, regarding the composition of the service, the data of the Book of Acts do not present everything in the desired clarity. Concerning the four essential constituent parts of divine worship—prayer, chanting, the reading of Holy Scripture, and homiletic instruction—one can assert on the basis of the Book of Acts only that all these existed during apostolic divine worship, yet it remains unknown in what precise form they existed.

Thus, concerning prayers, not only are no liturgical formulas reported, but it is not even stated what their specific content was. Concerning the prayers of that era one can judge only by a few specimens cited in the Book of Acts [^102]; yet these are all prayers on special occasions. One may suppose, although nowhere in the New Testament is there an explicit statement to this effect, that in the divine worship of that time there began already to be employed, in accordance with the commandment of the Savior, the Lord's Prayer: a monument of the early second century, *The Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* (*Didache*), prescribes its recitation three times a day [^103], that is, precisely as many times as, according to the data cited above, there could have been prayer gatherings during the course of a day in apostolic times. The Apostle Paul in one passage [^104] apparently indicates the genres of prayer of that era: supplications (*deeseis*, from *deomai*, "I need"—*(Orig. p. 27)* the general generic concept of prayer as the expression of our helplessness before God), prayers (*proseuchai*—prayer directed toward God), intercessions (*enteuxeis*, from *entygchano*, "I approach / attain someone"—intercessory prayer on behalf of others), and thanksgivings (*eucharistiai*) [^105].

Concerning chanting in apostolic worship, the Apostle Paul speaks more definitively than the Book of Acts. In two passages of his Epistles he distinguishes three genres of sacred songs in use at that time: psalms, hymns, and spiritual songs (*ᾠδαὶ πνευματικαί*) [^106]. By psalms it is most natural to understand the Old Testament psalms, the extensive liturgical use of which among the Christians of that time is attested also by the expression of the Apostle James: **"Is any merry? let him sing psalms"** (*psalleto*) [^107], as well as by the more frequent quotation of the Psalter in comparison with other Old Testament books by the Apostles [^108]. Yet inasmuch as psalms are represented in the Apostle Paul as the result of a special inspiration ("be filled with the Spirit; speaking to yourselves in psalms... spiritual"), one may understand also psalms of the singers' own composition [^109]. By hymns ("lauds") there is no ground to understand the so-called biblical canticles: the Septuagint renders with *hymnos* many Hebrew titles of psalms: *shir*, *tefillah*; by hymns the Apostle probably denotes songs of a preeminently laudatory character [^110] in distinction from prayerful ones and others of general content designated by the word songs (*odai*), singling out the former from the latter as their finest part: according to St. John Chrysostom, "hymns are a holier thing than psalms, for the angelic hosts sing hymns (*hymnousi*), and do not sing psalms" [^111]. The evangelical canticles of Zechariah, of the Mother of God, and of Symeon the God-Receiver present "fine examples of how, in close connection with Old Testament types, the Christian spirit wrought new canticles" [^112].

Nowhere in the apostolic Epistles is mention made of the reading of Old Testament scriptures at the divine worship of that era; yet this may be presumed in view of the fact that the preaching of the Apostles was grounded entirely upon the Law and the Prophets, and the latter the Apostle Paul designates alongside the Apostles as the foundation of the Church [^113]. Concerning the reading of New Testament scriptures during divine worship testimony is offered by: the injunction of the Apostle Paul in the Epistle to the Thessalonians that this epistle be read unto all the holy brethren [^114], which could most conveniently be carried out at a liturgical gathering; the injunction *(Orig. p. 28)* to the Colossians to exchange epistles with the Church of the Laodiceans [^115]; and likewise the existence, according to the testimony of the Evangelist Luke, by his time of many written records concerning the life of the Savior [^116].

As regards the homily (preaching), in apostolic divine worship, in accordance with the needs of that era and owing to the undeveloped state of other liturgical elements, it occupied an exceptionally prominent place; in the picture of divine worship provided by the Book of Acts, "doctrine" is placed first; the Apostle James had already to contend with talkative, self-appointed preachers [^117]; and the Apostle Paul regards teaching as the paramount duty of the bishop and presbyter [^118].

### Development of Apostolic Worship
Still less can be said on the basis of the New Testament writings regarding the sequential order in which these constituent parts followed upon one another during the divine worship of that time. It is possible that, at least in the initial stages and within the Jerusalem Church, among Jewish-Christians divine worship possessed an ordo close to that of the synagogue. The Apostle James not only designates the place of Christian assembly a "synagogue," but also points to certain customs within it characteristic exclusively of the latter: **"For if there come unto your assembly [into your synagogue, *εἰς τὴν συναγωγήν*, Slav. *в сонмище*] a man with a gold ring, in goodly apparel, and there come in also a poor man in vile raiment; and ye have respect to him that weareth the gay clothing, and say unto him, Sit thou here in a good place; and say to the poor, Stand thou there, or sit here under my footstool: are ye not then partial in yourselves?"** [^119]. Here is the customary scene of a synagogue furnished with benches, with armchair seats in front for dignitaries, and with the distribution of worshippers according to their legal status in society [^120]. Even the Apostle Paul designates prayer by the synagogal term "blessing" [^121].

Yet if in the initial stages of church life, and especially in the Jewish-Christian Jerusalem community, divine worship in general could recall *(Orig. p. 29)* to mind that of the Temple and synagogue, nonetheless with the passage of time and in Gentile-Christian churches—and especially following the persecutions of the Church by the Jews and the dispersal of the Apostles from Jerusalem—this affinity could not fail to diminish. It is characteristic that the Apostle Paul designates liturgical assemblies no longer as *συναγωγή*, but as *ἐκκλησία*, the Church [^122]. In general, the New Testament writings following Acts, and especially the Pauline Epistles, clearly indicate that apostolic worship after the aforementioned events entered into the second stage of its historical development in comparison with that at which it is depicted by the Book of Acts and, in part, the Epistle of the Apostle James.

### Worship according to 1 Corinthians
This stage is characterized by two marks, apparently disparate, yet between which a connection can be discovered. The first is the degeneration of the institution of the agapae; the second is the development of spiritual gifts (charisms) and their extensive employment during divine worship. Concerning both matters the First Epistle to the Corinthians speaks in detail. Chapters 10–14 of this epistle are devoted entirely to the regularization of Corinthian divine worship, and provide a full and distinct picture of that form of worship which it assumed among Gentile-Christians in the middle of the apostolic period. This entire extensive section of the epistle falls into two parts, the first of which regulates the more external, bodily (in the broadest sense of the word) dimension of worship (chapters 10 and 11), while the second, as its very opening demonstrates—**"Now concerning spiritual gifts, brethren, I would not have you ignorant"**—does the same with the spiritual dimension of worship, its intellectual and pneumatological content [^123].

In the former respect, the Apostle directs attention to the disregard manifested at the Lord's Supper (*kyriakon deipnon*) [^124] toward its most sacred act: the communion of the Body and Blood of Christ. Certain Corinthian Christians came to the "Lord's Supper" with the intent to eat and drink; and inasmuch as at these suppers the poor were fed from the oblations that were offered, the wealthy participants endeavored to sate themselves as quickly as possible from their own offerings, lest the poor leave them hungry. The Eucharist for such participants of the "supper" occupied second place. Concerning such unworthy conduct at the "Lord's Supper" the Apostle Jude likewise complains, mentioning "spots in your feasts of charity" (*сквернители в любвах*) [^125]. In his writing, therefore, the love-feasts are already designated by this very name—*ἀγάπαι*—which indicates a further step in their historical development. At the same time, the conduct of the baser Christians toward them is branded with a more forceful term—*spilades*, blemishes / sunken reefs (which can signify also hidden rocks upon which an institution such as the agape might suffer shipwreck) [^126]. Such conduct toward *(Orig. p. 30)* the agapae was undoubtedly the consequence of pagan habits among newly converted Christians, who carried over into them the customs of Greco-Roman *eranoi* (potluck club banquets) and *symposia* (common drinking parties). The Apostle Paul with bitterness and indignation admonishes such participants in Christian suppers to eat at home, so as not to defile the table of the Lord by greed. Thus, already in this youthful period of their existence, the agapae bore within themselves the seeds of the separation of the Eucharist from them, and subsequently the abolition of their entire material aspect, as offering occasion for such abuses; in other words, even then they were close to being transformed from a supper into Vespers.

Following the instructions in the First Epistle to the Corinthians regarding the external aspect of the agapae and of divine worship in general, the Apostle proceeds to the internal, spiritual dimension of the latter (chapters 12–14), and here paints for us a magnificent picture of that divine worship which was possible only then and never again—a divine worship truly accomplished by the Holy Spirit Himself, not only through unutterable groanings in human hearts, but also through His outward manifestation in a whole array of diverse spiritual gifts (*πνευματικὰ χαρίσματα*), inasmuch as "the grace of the Holy Spirit in the primitive church poured forth like a sea" [^127].

### Celebrants of Apostolic Worship

Prior to speaking regarding the employment of these gifts during divine worship, the Apostle enumerates them and their bearers ("And God hath set some in the church, first apostles, secondarily prophets, thirdly teachers...") [^128], thus presenting the latter as the celebrants of divine worship [^129]. This list of these liturgists alone can sufficiently characterize the divine worship of that time.

These were: 1) *Apostles*. Thus were designated not only the twelve closest disciples of the Lord, but also other persons who felt within themselves a calling from the Holy Spirit to preach the Gospel among unbelievers, and who must have been or*(Orig. p. 31)*dained unto this by the Church in a manner similar to that which was done, according to the Book of Acts, with Barnabas and Saul (through the laying on of hands of the charismatic persons of the Church) [^130]. Their purpose was the foundation of new churches; having accomplished this, they departed unto other places unenlightened by the Gospel, only visiting for a brief time the churches founded by them and existing churches in general for their confirmation [^131]. According to a monument of the second century, the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*, true apostles—who consequently existed also at that time—could be distinguished from false ones precisely by the fact that they did not remain in a single church for more than one, or at most two days, and took nothing from the community except bread in an amount necessary until the place of their next lodging [^132] (complete disinterestedness). The instructions given in the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* regarding false apostles [^133] demonstrate that in the second century this ministry was already close to cessation.

2) *Prophets*—persons capable of special revelations from God regarding the future [^134] and the secret thoughts of man [^135], that is, capable of "speaking in the Spirit" (a requirement not demanded of apostles), and who occupied themselves not with missionary work, but with preaching in already existing churches. The Book of Acts names the following prophets: Barnabas, Judas, Silas, and the four daughters of Philip the Deacon [^136]. A model of a prophet of the post-apostolic era is Hermas, the author of *The Shepherd*. The Apostle Paul insisted upon the broadest participation of prophets in divine worship [^137]. Prophets particularly astonished people during divine worship by their gift of exposing the secret thoughts of those present [^138]. This ministry enjoyed scarcely less reverence than the apostolic: "Prophets are your chief priests," says the *Teaching of the Twelve* [^139]. And according to the satire of Lucian (second century), the prophet among the Christians was a "thiasarch," the leader of sacred offerings [^140]. Unto prophets the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* permits at the Liturgy "to give thanks (*eucharistein*) as much as they will" [^141], whereas for ordinary celebrants of the Liturgy prayer formulas had already begun to be established. According to the same monument, a prophet "in the Spirit" could "appoint a table," that is, require the celebration of an agape on an unappointed day. It was forbidden to test or judge a prophet speaking in the Spirit; even a prophet who teaches not to do what he himself does was not to be judged, because *(Orig. p. 32)* he has his judgment with God [^142]. The *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* reveals already many abuses in this charismatic ministry; nonetheless, the prophetic ministry existed somewhat longer than the apostolic [^143]. St. Irenaeus († 202) still heard prophets [^144]. In connection with prophecy the Apostle Paul places the gift of the discernment of spirits—receptivity toward prophecy, the ability to penetrate into the prophetic state and distinguish true prophecy from false in one or in diverse persons, to distinguish pure seizure by the Spirit of God from the impure admixtures of natural human or demonic excitements [^145]. Such discernment was necessary so that on account of false prophecies true prophecy might not be suspected: **"Despise not prophesyings; prove all things; hold fast that which is good"** [^146]; **"Believe not every spirit, but try the spirits whether they are of God"** [^147].

3) In the Epistle to the Ephesians, the Apostle Paul, in enumerating charismatic ministries, places *evangelists* after apostles and prophets, before pastors and teachers. If by them are not to be understood evangelists in the contemporary sense—three of whom by this time had become known through their Gospels—it is difficult to say what ministry is meant. Perhaps these were the closest assistants of the Apostles in preaching the Gospel. Thus Timothy is also termed an evangelist [^148].

4) *Teachers*, in whose case "there was joined unto revelation the labor of personal penetration into divine truths" [^149], on which account teachers could assume this title according to their own personal judgment [^150], as is evident from the admonition of the Apostle James: **"My brethren, be not many masters [teachers]"** [^151]. In the gift of teaching the Apostle Paul distinguishes two kinds: the *word of wisdom* (charismatic eloquence) and the *word of knowledge*; by the former is perhaps meant practical or holistic, general, more subjective knowledge, while by the latter is meant theoretical, detailed, objective knowledge [^152]. The charismatic ministry of teaching was preserved also in the post-apostolic era down to the third century inclusive. In Origen there are frequent mentions of "ecclesiastical teachers," "persons who among us (in Alexandria) wisely fulfilled the office of teacher, and they are placed alongside presbyters" [^153]. Dionysius of Alexandria (second half of the third century) in an epistle states that he convoked "presbyters and teachers" of the surrounding vil*(Orig. p. 33)*lages. And upon teachers (*didaskaloi*) of the post-apostolic era people looked as upon especially graced persons: St. Ignatius the God-Bearer and Dionysius of Alexandria caution that they write not as authoritative teachers [^154].

All these extraordinary ministries (apostleship, prophecy, and teaching, joining here also the following—the gift of wonderworking; see below) were not limited unto any single local church, but extended unto the whole Church, and were not so localized as the ecclesiastical hierarchy. The apostles, prophets, and teachers, who moved from one place to another and enjoyed high esteem in all communities, explain to us how diverse churches possessed among themselves so much in common in order and life, even though they were organized with complete autonomy [^155]. By their liturgical activity one may explain the affinity of liturgical forms in diverse churches which we observe in the third and fourth centuries.

Continuing the enumeration of charismatic ministries in the Church, the Apostle, after teaching with its gifts, names as a charismatic gift: 5) *Faith*—faith, as the nearest definition of this gift in other passages demonstrates, that works wonders, that "mother of signs," according to Chrysostom, the accomplishress of that which is beyond human powers. This charismatic gift, according to the Apostle, divides into the gift of healings and of powers [^156] ("powers"—wonders in general). According to St. John Chrysostom, he that possessed the gift of healings was able only to help the sick, but he who received the "operation of powers" was able also to punish [^157], as, for example, the Apostle Peter punished Ananias and Sapphira. The gift of wonderworking in apostolic times was a rather frequent phenomenon: the Apostle Paul indicates its presence also in the Galatian Church: **"He therefore that ministereth to you the Spirit, and worketh miracles [powers] among you, doeth He it by the works of the law, or by the hearing of faith?"** [^158]. Origen was a witness of many healings [^159]. A particular species of this gift was perpetuated in the Church by the Mystery of Holy Anointing (*Euchelaion*) [^160]. This charism must have provided the foundation for the establishment in the early Church of the office of exorcists, who adjured evil spirits (as the causers of diseases), and for the introduction into church services (not only the Liturgy, but also Vespers and Matins) of special prayers over the possessed (*energoumenoi*) or tempest-tossed (*cheimazomenoi*—that is, by unclean spirits).

*(Orig. p. 34)*  
6) The gifts of *helps* (*antilēpseis*) and *governments* (*kybernēseis*), which pertained to the permanent and local church hierarchy (the former to deacons with their care for the poor and the sick, the latter to presbyters and bishops). This ministry was not inferior to those enumerated above in general, yet during divine worship those extraordinary gifts and their bearers stepped into the foreground. Even in the second century a prophet was permitted at the Liturgy to improvise the Eucharistic prayer [^161], whereas a bishop and a presbyter were required to adhere to an established pattern. The *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*, where these rules are given, in general lets it be seen that in its era (the beginning of the second century) the pastoral ministry had begun to replace the extraordinary ministries—apostolic, prophetic, and teaching. "Appoint (*cheirotonēsate*) [^162] therefore for yourselves," the monument exhorts, "bishops and deacons; for they also minister (*leitourgousi*) unto you the ministry (*leitourgian*) of prophets and teachers. Therefore despise them not, for they are your honorable men along with the prophets and teachers" [^163]. A passage testifying, moreover, unto what broad and honorable position in the celebration of divine worship (*leitourgian*) [^164] was occupied by prophets and teachers.

7) and 8) The most extraordinary for our time, yet frequent in apostolic times, were the gifts of tongues and the interpretation of them.

### The Gift of Tongues according to Acts and 1 Corinthians in Apostolic Worship

The gift of tongues (glossolalia) was first imparted unto the Apostles, and perhaps unto the other believers, on the Day of Pentecost at the descent upon them of the Holy Spirit. This gift manifested itself in a certain extraordinarily inspired speech (in some measure recalling the speech of a person in a state of intoxication) ("to speak, to utter," *lalein, apophtheggesthai*) "of the wonderful works of God" "with other tongues" (*heterais glōssais*), such that listeners of fifteen nationalities heard from the mouths of the Apostles their own native dialect (*dialektos*) [^165]. The Spirit of the Lord, encompassing within Himself humanity in its nations and languages, and bearing within Himself the power of uniting them, produced in the innermost foundations of the soul an instantaneous removal of the national boundaries of language that most sharply divide humanity, symbolically prefiguring this future gracious unity of mankind.

A similar gift was imparted in the apostolic Church repeatedly after Baptism. Thus the gift of tongues was received by Cornelius and his household after Baptism, and by the disciples of John the Baptist through the laying on of hands of the Apostle Paul [^166]. It is not insignificant that the most powerful echo of the great wonder of Pentecost is found by us in so central and prominent a Gentile-Christian church as the Corinthian [^167]. In the Corinthian church this miraculous gift *(Orig. p. 35)* received the broadest employment during divine worship. It manifested itself, apparently, only at liturgical gatherings, "in the churches" [^168].

The content of the speech of the Corinthian glossolalists was prayer [^169], of a predominantly laudatory and somewhat mystical character [^170]. The tongue in which the glossolalist spoke was incomprehensible unto those present [^171], and, apparently, not entirely comprehensible unto the glossolalist himself (though his "spirit prayed" at that time, his "understanding was unfruitful") [^172], for which reason the speech of the glossolalist required interpretation [^173]; yet the interpretation of his speech likewise required a special gift of the Holy Spirit [^174], which the glossolalist was far from always possessing [^175]. Speaking with tongues was a coveted gift ("I would that ye all spake with tongues"), edifying the glossolalist [^176]; the degree of this gift depended upon the moral stature of the possessor, which is why, for example, the Apostle Paul possessed it more than all the Corinthians [^177].

#### Diverse Conceptions of the Gift of Tongues
Such are the biblical data concerning the gift of tongues. By them the question is not resolved whether the gift of tongues was always identical, and in what the Corinthian glossolalia, which received so broad an employment during divine worship, actually consisted. The Holy Fathers inclined toward the opinion that the gift of tongues in Corinth, and in general in all instances where an account of its manifestation is given (that is, in the two other mentioned instances), was identical with the glossolalia of Pentecost—that is, that all glossolalists received the ability to speak in existing foreign languages. Thus thought Saints Justin, Irenaeus, Cyril of Jerusalem, John Chrysostom, Gregory the Theologian, and Augustine, as well as Tertullian and Origen [^178]. Against such a conception it is objected that for the Corinthian Christians there was no necessity of speaking in foreign languages such as existed on the day of the first Christian Pentecost; that tongues are not here termed "other"; that the word often stands in the singular and is not glossed as in Acts by *dialektos*; and that the Savior promised unto believers speaking with "new" *(Orig. p. 36)* tongues, and not foreign ones. Others [^179] see in the speech of the glossolalists a primitive tongue, a composite language containing elements or rudiments of diverse historical languages (a rudimentary language) and serving as a type for the universality of Christianity; the ground for this conception is the use of *glōssa* in descriptions of the gift of tongues sometimes in the singular. Yet the singular can signify some single one of existing languages—a sense confirmed also by the absence of the article before it. On the ground that *glōssa* or *glōssēma* among classical authors signifies a provincial, archaic, or unusual word (an idiom) requiring explanation (a gloss) [^180], it was thought that the language of the glossolalists consisted precisely of such words [^181]: now archaisms, now neologisms, now foreign expressions. Yet the New Testament knows no such use of the word *glōssa*; such speech is no higher than ordinary speech, and in any case presents no extraordinary miraculous phenomenon. It is thought further that the speech of the glossolalists consisted of inarticulate sounds (it is compared by the Apostle Paul with the sounds of a trumpet) [^182] or a scarcely audible prayerful whisper [^183] (1 Cor. 14:2: **"For he that speaketh in an unknown tongue speaketh not unto men, but unto God: for no man understandeth [heareth] him"**), or, conversely, of ecstatic exclamations and fragmentary doxologies (the speech of a glossolalist is called for the most part not *logos*, a word, the instrument of thought, but only *glōssa*, a tongue, sound in itself) [^184]. Yet the Apostle explicitly states that glossolalists pronounced "words," albeit "unintelligible"; he compares them with high-sounding cymbals and trumpets.

This latter comparison, repeatedly employed by the Apostle, gave occasion to understand glossolalia in the sense of some special kind of chanting. All the terms employed by the Apostle Paul concerning glossolalia can bear also a musical sense. *Glōssa* was the name given to the body of a flute [^185]; by "kinds" (*genē*) ("kinds of tongues") classical authors [^186] designated diatonic, chromatic, and enharmonic melodies, and in such an application this word is more natural than when applied to languages, which the ancients did not know how to classify; *hermēneuein*, "to explain," is used among classical authors also of musical interpretation [^187]; in the expression **"and yet shew I unto you a more excellent way"** [^188], "way" (*hodos*) and "more excellent" (*kath' hyperbolēn*) likewise served as musical terms: the former signified the transition from one set of tones to another, while *hyperbolaion* was the name given *(Orig. p. 37)* to the tetrachord upon the fifth, highest string of the cithara [^189]. Of course, all these terms, besides their musical sense, can have also an ordinary meaning. Yet the persistent comparison of glossolalia with music and an entire array of terms that can have application unto the latter give cause for reflection. Significant also is the expression *apophtheggesthai*, "to utter / give vocal sound," regarding the glossolalia at Pentecost [^190]; according to the opinion of St. Irenaeus, the Apostles on the Day of Pentecost "sang in all tongues a hymn unto God" [^191]. One must also take into account the extensive use of singing in antiquity. Prior to the invention of letters, laws were chanted so that they would not be forgotten [^192]. All this gave occasion unto certain scholars to see in glossolalia singing [^193]. Against such a conception of the gift of tongues—in the sense of singing (hymnographic)—argues, apparently, the fact that regarding this gift the verb "to speak" (*lalein*) is persistently used. Yet, not to mention that this verb is used by the Apostle Paul concerning the execution during divine worship of psalms, hymns, and songs [^194], this objection vanishes if the singing was recitative [^195], as singing in its simplest form in the primitive Church with its as yet undeveloped liturgical forms could naturally be. Even Bl. Augustine says of the singing of his own time that the voice of the chanters resembled accentuated speech rather than singing [^196].

### Essence and Peculiarity of the Gift of Tongues

As we see, all the expounded explanations for the gift of tongues admit of objections against themselves, yet at the same time each of them possesses one or another serious foundation in the text of the New Testament.

All these explanations are reconcilable with one another, and it is possible that each of them points to an actual feature in this extraordinary phenomenon. The diversity of expressions of the Apostle Paul himself regarding the gift of tongues commands attention: "a tongue," "tongues," "kinds of tongues," "to speak with a tongue" or "with tongues," "to speak words in a tongue," "to pray with a tongue," "to have a tongue," "to sing," "to pray," "to bless," "to give thanks in the spirit," "in the spirit to speak mysteries," "to speak not unto men, but unto God" [^197]. This alone demonstrates that the gift of tongues could "infinitely diversify itself" [^198] in its manifestations. In order to judge correctly concerning the character of these manifestations, one must pay attention to the place assigned by the Apostle unto this gift among other *(Orig. p. 38)* spiritual gifts. In his classification of such gifts, the Apostle Paul singles out the gift of tongues with the gift of their interpretation into a distinct category:

arranging spiritual gifts according to the degree of benefit that they bring not unto an individual believer, but unto the whole Church, the Apostle in the first place sets the gifts of the intellect (teaching, prophecy), in the second place the gifts of the will (wonderworking, pastoral ministry), and in the last, evidently as manifestations of feeling—the gift of tongues [^199]. Consequently, speaking with tongues was the expression of a vivid inner movement and animation of those who for the first time felt themselves free from condemnation and experienced the unutterable joy inevitably bound up with the first (fresh) consciousness of divine sonship [^200].
