In Palestine, Rome, Pontus, Gaul, and Greece councils convened and pronounced in favor of the Roman practice. Pope Victor (c. 196) threatened the Asiatics with excommunication. The aforementioned epistle of St. Irenaeus had as its very purpose to reconcile the contending parties. Apparently the dispute continued down unto the Council of Nicaea, which adopted the Roman practice as universal. The Council of Antioch (341 [cited in the original text as 333]) excommunicates from the Church those **"who celebrate Pascha together with the Jews"** [^330]. The custom of fasting [misprinted in Russian text as *prostit'sya*, "to take leave," for *postit'sya*, "to fast"] at Pascha is rebuked even by St. John Chrysostom [^331].

### Wednesday and Friday

In the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* (*Didache*) we find an injunction regarding the fast of Wednesday and Friday: **"Let not your fasts be with the hypocrites"** (that is, the Jews, specifically the Pharisees), **"for they fast on the second and fifth days of the week; but fast ye on the fourth and the preparation day [Wednesday and Friday]"** [^332]. *The Shepherd* of Hermas mentions a fast bearing the designation of "station" (*statio*) [^333]. Since later writers designate by this name perhaps Wednesday and Friday [^334], this passage of Hermas is regarded as the most ancient witness unto these weekly fasts. It is remarkable that the *Didache* makes no mention of Pascha and its fast.

*(Orig. p. 68)*

### Pentecost

In a fragment from the writings of St. Irenaeus [^335] we find mention of the celebration in his time (that is, at the end of the 2nd century) of Pentecost, during which, as on Pascha and Sunday, they did not bend the knee. All other feasts in honor of the Savior took their rise later (the most ancient of them being Theophany / Epiphany in the 3rd century).

### Commemorations of Martyrs

From the 2nd century we possess the first notices concerning the liturgical veneration of martyrs. The most ancient of such accounts is found in the martyrdom acts of St. Ignatius (107 or 115): **"having spent several days beside his tomb in the singing of hymns, the Christians resolved also in the future to hymn his life and passion, and at his memory to glorify the Lord Jesus"** [^336]. Eusebius cites the epistle of the Church of Smyrna unto the Church of Philomelium (in Asia Minor) on the occasion of the martyric demise of St. Polycarp († 167); therein it is related that the proconsul, on the counsel of the Jews, burned the body of Polycarp, lest it become an object of worship for the Christians; **"but we gathered up his bones... and laid them where it was fitting; thither, so soon as it may be possible, we shall assemble with jubilation and joy, and the Lord will permit us to celebrate the day of his martyric nativity (*genethlion* [γενέθλιον])"**. Remarkable is this perspective upon the demise of a martyr as his birthday (*dies natalis* / *natalitiae*). This view was the reason why the ecclesiastical year, even in subsequent times, possessed no birthdays of saints whatever, with the exception of the Savior, the Mother of God, and John the Baptist; and why even these birthdays, not excluding the Nativity of Christ, began to be celebrated comparatively late. The cited passages speak of the celebration of martyrs' commemorations in general terms, without showing wherein this celebration consisted. Yet a number of other martyrdom acts demonstrate that the latter consisted primarily in the holding of agapes (whenever possible, at the sites of their martyrdom), which were styled *agapae natalitiae* [^337]. In certain of these acts there is mention of their being read aloud over the tombs of the martyrs on the day of their commemoration; for which reason unto the very lives and passions of the martyrs there was subsequently assigned the designation *legenda* [^338] ("things to be read") in the West, and in the East "Prologues" (introductory readings for divine service) and "Synaxaria" (readings at solemn assemblies) [^339].

The commemorations of martyrs were probably only lo- *(Orig. p. 69)* -cal, and not universal across the Church. Yet certain martyrs, through the circumstances of their sufferings, acquired widespread renown and became venerated, in all likelihood, even beyond the boundaries of their homeland; such were, for example, St. Ignatius the God-Bearer, who prior unto His passion accomplished, as it were, a triumphal progress throughout all the Christian regions of the Roman Empire, and St. Polycarp of Smyrna, of whom the Smyrneans in the epistle on His demise testify that he is especially honored among the martyrs and known even unto the pagans of many places [^340]. In general there were martyrs whose tortures caused the entire Christian world of that time to shudder, rendering them, perhaps, universally venerated. The commemorations of such martyrs were close, even in the 2nd century, unto becoming universal for the whole Church. Thus the commemorations of martyrs are the oldest feasts in the Church in honor of saints. Following the example of the martyrs, commemorations of the Apostles also began to be venerated. Yet concerning such apostolic commemorations from the 2nd century no records exist.
*(Orig. p. 70)*

## III Century

### Sources

Notices concerning the divine worship of this century are scattered, first of all, in the writings of ecclesiastical authors of that era; such are: Clement of Alexandria († 217), *Stromata* and *Paedagogus*; Tertullian († 220), *Apology*, *De Oratione*, *De Jejuniis*, and others; Minucius Felix, *Octavius* (early 3rd cent.); Origen († 265 [254]), *Contra Celsum*, *De Oratione*; St. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage († 257 [258]). Accurate accounts of the worship of this century could also reach the ecclesiastical historians of the 4th and 5th centuries—Eusebius, Socrates, Sozomen—as well as other writers of that period, namely the Holy Fathers (SS. John Chrysostom, Basil the Great, Blessed Augustine and Theodoret).

Yet perhaps the most important source for the history of 3rd-century divine worship is the series of canonical monuments of this era, now subjected by Western scholars unto the most detailed and thorough analysis. This analysis, however, has not yet succeeded in firmly establishing the chronology of these monuments so as to permit their dating unto the 3rd century with certainty. We refer unto a series of monuments which, together with the *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* (*Didache*, a monument almost certainly of the 2nd cent.), formed the foundation of the so-called *Apostolic Constitutions* [^341].

### The Apostolic Constitutions as a Redaction of III-Century Canonical Monuments

This monument, which attributes itself unto the Apostles and unto St. Clement of Rome, manifestly betrays a non-apostolic origin: therein are encountered such strange and non-Orthodox notions as, for example, the comparison of bishop, presbyter, and deaconess unto God the Father, the Son of God, and the Holy Spirit [^342], or the granting unto the deaconess of the right to baptize women [^343]. Nevertheless, in many portions of the monument and in its general tone there resounds a profound antiquity: from it there breathes palpably the spirit of the 3rd century—the spirit of the rigorism of that day, the immediacy of religious feeling; furthermore, in the *Apostolic Constitutions* there is mention, as of an existing *(Orig. p. 71)* and frequent phenomenon, of confessorship under persecution, of certain spiritual gifts and ministries of the apostolic era and the 2nd century; it is characterized by the complete unsettledness and embryonic state of theological terminology, and the like. Nonetheless, in places the *Apostolic Constitutions* bear the marks of the hierarchical and liturgical order of the 4th century (the offices of subdeacon, and doorkeeper of the church; there is mentioned the feast of the Nativity of Christ, which appeared in the East at the end of the 4th cent.). At all events, the *Apostolic Constitutions* could not have originated later than the beginning of the 5th century: they contain no echoes of the Nestorian and Eutychian controversies [^344]. Their author reveals himself to be a Syrian (using Syrian names of the months), and in his theological (christological) views a Semi-Arian or Apollinarian [^345]. This latter circumstance, together with the aforementioned strange ideas of the monument, was the reason why the Council in Trullo, notwithstanding the familiarity of this work in certain parts at least unto ancient Fathers (for instance, St. Epiphanius) and the enduring respect for it in the East, resolved not to recognize for it the same authority as for the *85 Canons of the Holy Apostles*, and decreed concerning it:

**"Forasmuch as in these canons"** (that is, the Apostolic Canons) [^346] **"it is commanded us to receive the Constitutions of the same Holy Apostles transmitted through Clement, into which long ago heterodox persons, unto the injury of the Church, introduced certain spurious matters foreign unto piety, which have darkened for us the fair beauty of divine teaching, we have prudently rejected such Constitutions of Clement for the edification and protection of the most Christian flock, by no means admitting the offspring of heretical falsehood, nor mingling them with the pure and perfect apostolic teaching"** [^347].

Scholars long ago directed attention unto the heterogeneous and multitemporal origin of the *Apostolic Constitutions* in their various parts. Gradually it became possible to discover the ancient sources of this compilation. In 1854 P. de Lagarde published the *Syriac Didascalia* (which had become known unto scholars even earlier) and demonstrated that it corresponds unto the Greek text cited by St. Epiphanius, which had previously been considered a borrowing from the *Apostolic Constitutions*, proving thereby that the first six books of the *Constitutions* represent a redaction of this *Didascalia* in its non-extant Greek original. Scholars unanimously date the *Didascalia* unto the 3rd century—some unto its first half, others unto the second [^348]. The *Teaching of the Twelve Apostles* (*Didache*, *(Orig. p. 72)* 2nd cent.), discovered by Bryennios in 1883, proved to be the source of the first part of Book VII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*. As regards Book VIII of the *Constitutions*, its first two chapters probably represent a reworked version of the lost treatise of St. Hippolytus of Rome, *On Spiritual Gifts* (*De charismatibus*), while the remaining portion of the book (with the exception of chapters 35–39, which set forth the order of Vespers and Matins and are not found in all manuscripts of the *Apostolic Constitutions*) is closely related unto the three following ancient monuments: 1) *The Testament of Our Lord Jesus Christ* (*Testamentum Domini nostri Jesu Christi*), discovered in a Syriac manuscript by the Roman Catholic Patriarch of Antioch, Rahmani, and published by him with a Latin translation in 1899 [^349]; 2) *The Canons of Hippolytus*, preserved in Arabic and published in Latin translation by Haneberg in 1870 and by Achelis in 1891 [^350]; 3) *The Ecclesiastical Canons of the Holy Apostles*, or *The Egyptian Canons*, *The Egyptian Church Order*—a monument preserved in Greek, Ethiopic, Coptic, and Arabic recensions, published in Ethiopic with a Latin translation by Ludolf in 1691, in Coptic with an English translation by Tattam in 1848, and by De Lagarde (without translation) in 1883, and in the Greek recension by Bickell in 1856 [1843] (the Arabic text remaining unpublished [^351]). All these monuments are in places so close unto one another and unto Book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions* that between them there cannot fail to exist a genetic dependency. Yet in defining this dependency, and consequently the comparative antiquity and date of origin of these liturgically critical monuments, scholars diverge. Achelis regards the *Canons of Hippolytus* as the most ancient of these monuments (not counting the *Testamentum*, which was not yet known unto him), assigning them unto the time of Tertullian, the first quarter or half of the 3rd century; the *Egyptian Canons*, according to Achelis, are a redaction thereof, and Book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions* is a redaction of the *Egyptian Canons*. Rahmani considers the most ancient to be, naturally, the *Testamentum* discovered by himself, assigning it unto the end of the 2nd century; the *Egyptian Canons*, in his view, are a rework of the *Testamentum*, while the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Apostolic Constitutions* are two parallel redactions of the *Egyptian Canons*. Funk regards Book VIII of the *Apostolic Constitutions* as the oldest of the three monuments, dating it, like the others, unto the 4th century; in its shorter recension (the so-called *Epitome*) he sees an extract from this book, and in the *Egyptian Constitutions* and the *Canons of Hippolytus* an abridged reworking of this extract, while in the *Testamentum* a redaction of one of these latter monuments, dating the *Testamentum* unto the beginning of the 5th century.

*(Orig. p. 73)*

### The Testament (Testamentum) of Our Lord Jesus Christ

In view of the richness of liturgical material in these monuments, especially in the *Testamentum*, it is by no means indifferent for the liturgist whether this latter monument must be assigned unto the 2nd or 5th century, and likewise whether the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Constitutions* are older than the *Apostolic Constitutions*, that is, whether they may be referred unto the 3rd century. Therefore, the polemic between Funk and Rahmani [^352] possesses great importance for us. Funk refutes all of Rahmani's arguments in favor of the origin of the *Testamentum* in the 2nd century, yet not all of his objections are equally forceful, and in any event they are not capable of removing this monument and those related unto it not only unto the 5th century, but, in our opinion, even beyond the end of the 3rd century.

In the *Testamentum*: 1) mention is made not only of confessors and martyrs, but of catechumens who are bound in chains and condemned unto death prior unto baptism; 2) no mention is made of the division of catechumens into classes, concerning which St. Gregory of Neocaesarea (233–270) already speaks; 3) nothing is said concerning the imposition of the Gospel Book upon the head of a bishop being consecrated—a custom that arose in the 3rd century; 4) the reader is sometimes placed above the deacon, whereas the epistle of Pope Cornelius unto Fabian [Fabius] of Antioch in 251 places him even below the subdeacon; 5) the creed consists solely of questions put unto the person being baptized prior unto immersion in water, and in these questions nothing is said of the resurrection of the body, which, as a great mystery, is imparted only unto the newly baptized; the sign of the cross is likewise regarded as a mystery (*arcanum*); 6) soldiers receiving baptism are required to renounce military service, in place of which the *Apostolic Constitutions* require only that which John the Baptist demanded according unto the Gospel of Luke 3:14; 7) mention is made of three spiritual gifts (*charismata*) as continuing to exist in the Church: the gifts of healing, knowledge, and tongues, whereas the *Egyptian Canons* know only the gift of healing, and the *Apostolic Constitutions* at this point mention merely exorcists [^353]. Certain of these arguments Funk does not refute, selecting for refutation others that are less cogent. Against these latter he makes, for instance, such objections: 4) in the hierarchy of ecclesiastical offices there was not yet uniformity; in Syria the reader might rank higher, while in Rome the subdeacon did; 6) the demand made of soldiers in the *Testamentum* is milder (!); 7) the mention of spiritual gifts is a survival from ancient writings utilized by the compiler of the *Testamentum*; and indeed even later there were individuals in the Church who considered themselves charismatics [^354].

Leaving it unto the reader to judge of the strength of these objections, we shall point out further the following indicators which do not permit dating the *Testamentum* later than the end of the 3rd century or the very beginning of the 4th: the cycle of feasts in it consists solely of Pascha, Saturday, Sunday, Epiphany, and Pentecost [^355]; *(Orig. p. 74)* there is no feast of the Nativity of Christ, whereas it exists in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, which arose in the same Syria [^356]; no mention is made of feasts in honor of the Apostles and the Protomartyr Stephen, which are present in the *Constitutions*; the Quadragesima (Forty Days' Fast) is spoken of only in connection with baptism, as a fast preparatory unto the latter [^357]. From a comparison of the liturgical practice of the *Testamentum* with the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons* we shall become convinced that the former monument frequently presents a less complex liturgical practice in comparison with the two latter, which according unto all indications and the virtually unanimous consensus of researchers date no later than the beginning of the 4th century.

On the other hand, to consider the *Testamentum* (with Rahmani) older than the second half of the 3rd century is precluded by the presence therein of the feast of Epiphany, which had its beginning in the 3rd century, and of the Quadragesima, the earliest mentions of which we find in writers only of the second half of the 3rd century. Nor does the plan of the Christian church building provided by the *Testamentum* allow this, wherein there are already present such components as a solea, a veil [curtain], three entrances, a diaconicon, a baptistery, an annex (nave / vestibule?) for catechumens, a chamber for recording those who offer gifts, and a gazophylakion (treasury). Certain of these elements undoubtedly arose at the close of the 3rd century, during the period of relative respite from persecutions (let us recall the church at Nicomedia). Moreover, even in the catacomb churches (crypts) of St. Agnes (in the Roman catacombs) and of St. Januarius (in Naples) there exist compartments for catechumens, traces of pillars whereon a curtain could hang, and a diaconicon. In an underground Cappadocian church there is a secret room which could serve both for hiding from persecution [^358] and as a treasury. A treasury attached unto a church is mentioned also by St. Justin Martyr and Tertullian [^359].

Certain features in that description of the church building given by the *Testamentum* bear the stamp of greater antiquity than the church plan in the *Apostolic Constitutions*. Thus the *Testamentum* does not demand of the church a basilican form, as do the *Apostolic Constitutions*; it indicates the ambo/pulpit for the reader near the altar, and not in the midst of the nave; it assigns for the bishop, presbyters, and widows special chambers within the church itself, which presupposes a church within an ordinary house; and it says nothing concerning the consecration of a church, which is known already unto St. Ephrem the Syrian (4th cent.) and the author writing under the name of St. Dionysius the Areopagite (c. 5th cent.) [^360].

Thus nothing in the content of the *Testamentum* prevents assigning it at least unto the end of the 3rd century. In any event, among the enumerated canonical monuments, the *Didascalia* is undoubtedly of the 3rd century, the *Testamentum* is almost certainly of the 3rd century, the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons* are probably of the 3rd century, while the *Apostolic Constitutions* stand close unto the 3rd century and have preserved in large measure its *(Orig. p. 75)* liturgical practice. The picture of divine worship afforded by them will in many respects corroborate this conclusion.

### The Agape in the III Century

The agape at the beginning of the 3rd century continues to occupy the chief place among ecclesiastical services after the Eucharist, although it already begins to lose its significance in favor of Matins, and by the end of the 3rd century becomes a secondary and infrequent service. Almost every one of the 3rd-century writers and every one of the described canonical monuments of this century contains discourse concerning the agape. Here are the testimonies concerning it in approximate chronological order. Each of them points out a new feature in the ritual of the agape, and taken together they provide an exceedingly complete picture of this unique service in the century of its greatest flourishing.

### The Agape according to Clement of Alexandria

Clement of Alexandria, rising up in his *Paedagogus* against immoderation at the agapes, first of all elucidates their profound internal meaning and significance. It is "a beautiful, saving institution of the Logos... The agapes are in truth celestial food, a banquet of the Word (*hestiasis logikē*, ἑστίασις λογικὴ)... And if thou lovest the Lord thy God and thy neighbor, then this festive and blessed celebration, having the properties of the heavenly, taketh place already as it were in the heavens... The agapes are a pure undertaking worthy of God, and their purpose is mutual assistance. The joys of the suppers of love, owing unto the participation in them of many, act upon love in a revivifying manner; they are a foretaste of eternal joy... That one must participate in the agapes in precisely this manner is revealed from the fact that herein we partake of the food (*brōsis*, βρῶσις) of Christ" [^361]. These passages, seemingly, speak in favor of the fact that the Eucharist continued to be joined with the agape [^362].

At the same time, the learned Alexandrian hath left us important information concerning the external aspect of the agapes as well. He provideth nearly a complete list of the dishes customary at the agapes. "Certain persons dare," saith Clement, "with insolent tongue to bestow the name of agapes upon certain petty feasts (*deipnaria*, δειπνάρια), reeking of roasted fat (*knissēs*, κνίσσης) and broths (*zōmōn*, ζωμῶν), reducing them unto wine, pots, and soups." "The most grievous of all falls is when unfading love (*agapē*, ἀγάπη), this inhabitant and child of heaven, is cast down from heaven unto the earth into soups." In contrast unto such a composition of the meal at the agape, Clement requireth for it the simplest dishes: "onions [or bulbs] (*bolboi*, βολβοὶ—perhaps also in a generic sense: garden plants with bulbous heads), olives (*elaiai*, ἐλαῖαι), various greens (*lachanōn enia*, λαχάνων ἔνια), milk, cheese, and likewise fruits (*ta te hōraia*, τὰ τε ὡραῖα), various boiled fruit decoctions (*hepsēmada*, ἐψήμαδα) [^363]—without broths; if, however, it be necessary, boiled meat (*kreōs*, κρέως) may be added." Under meat *(Orig. p. 76)* Clement understandeth fish (otherwise he would contradict his own previous rebukes), since he immediately citeth the Gospel narrative of how the disciples offered fish unto the risen Savior [^364]. "Furthermore, those dining with the Logos cannot deprive themselves of genuine dessert (*tragēmatōn*, τραγημάτων). In a word, of dishes at the agape there ought to be the most necessary, which may be consumed at once without fire, as well as those which are most readily at hand (*epei kai hetoimotera*, ἐπεὶ καὶ ἑτοιμότερα), and then also cheaper." Recalling the passage in Proverbs: "Better is a dish of greens (*lachanon*, λάχανον) with love, than a fatted calf with hatred" [^365], Clement qualifieth this by noting that he doth not consider this simplicity of dishes to be anything essential in the agape, but rather—love: "greens (*lachanon*, λάχανον) [^366] are not the agape, but meals (*deipna*, δεῖπνα) received with love" [^367]. In one passage Clement seemingly calleth the agapes *potos* [πότος] (in an unblameworthy sense) and speaketh of "drinking together" (*sumpinomen*, συμπίνομεν) at them with "hymning and glorifying God" [^368].

In rich and effeminate Alexandria, as is evident, they attempted to surround the agapes with special splendor and turn them into veritable luxurious banquets. Such figures as Clement of Alexandria energetically contended against these tendencies and openly declared agapes with meat dishes to be ordinary suppers. They demanded the observance of the former strict practice regarding meals at the agapes—a practice indications whereof we encountered in the 2nd century, that is, the consumption at the agapes of exclusively plant-based, and in extreme cases fish, food. Here, consequently, is the germ of the later fasting diet in the Christian Church. At the same time, Clement's inventory of dishes at the agape explaineth unto us why at present at Vespers during the blessing of the loaves (Litiya/artoklasia), which is undoubtedly a ritual remnant of the agape, there is blessed not bread alone, but wine, wheat, and oil, although the latter two products are not consumed in church and generally remain unused. In antiquity these products went toward the meal of the agape.

### The Agape according to Tertullian

Unto the relative luxury of the agapes Tertullian likewise pointeth, whose testimony can speak of the practice of the Roman and Carthaginian Churches, as Clement's doth of Alexandria. Tertullian, moreover, giveth a valuable indication concerning the order and rite of the agape. "Our supper (*coena*)," saith Tertullian, "fully justifieth its name *agapē* [ἀγάπη], which is employed by the Greeks to signify love (*dilectio*). Whatever our suppers may cost, our outlay is incurred in the name of piety on behalf of the indigent. They recline at table (*discumbitur*) not before they have tasted (*praegustetur*) of prayer unto God; they eat as much as is needed to satisfy hunger; and they drink as much as is profitable for the modest; *(Orig. p. 77)* they satisfy themselves as those who remember that even during the night (*per noctem*) they must pray unto God; they converse (*fabulantur*) knowing that the Lord heareth all. After the washing of hands (*post aquam manualem*) and the lighting of lamps (*et lumina*), each person is called forth into the midst to sing (*canere*) unto God either from Holy Scripture or from his own mind [or genius] (*ingenio*). From this it is already evident how each hath drunk. The supper endeth, as it began, with prayer. Then they depart as though they had conducted not a supper, but a lesson of moral discipline (*disciplinam*)" [^369]. Tertullian, as we see, could still boast before the pagans of complete good order at the agapes, which the Apostle Paul had so greatly desired and which in Alexandria and other cities had begun to decline once more. The agape presenteth in Tertullian a moving picture of eating unto the glory of God, with constant thought of God. However, Tertullian, as an apologist, might somewhat idealize. At the same time, the agape in Tertullian already receiveth a rather complex rite, with details that are not mentioned in the 2nd century. It is preceded, seemingly, by a prayer of no small duration. After the meal followed the washing of hands, which in this epoch was a customary rite before prayer [^370] (continuing to be preserved among us even now in the order of the Liturgy); consequently, the prayer portion of the agape began properly after the eating thereof. Inasmuch as the agape was celebrated in the evening, this prayer portion thereof fell upon twilight and night, for which reason the necessity for lamps arose. The example of Old Testament divine worship, as we have seen above [^371], could impart a special sacred (sacramental) significance unto the lighting of lamps at the agape, which other monuments of the 3rd century likewise note [^372].

The spiritual, prayerful side of the agape, according unto Tertullian's testimony, bore a hymnographic character, wherein nearly each of those present took part in singing by turn. The songs employed were as much biblical as of Christian composition, seemingly even improvised. (Even now Vespers is among us a more hymnographic service than Matins). Tertullian saith nothing concerning the Eucharist either in this description of the agape or in his preceding description of the morning service, naturally because this was not required by the aims of his apology.

### The Agape according to Minucius Felix and Origen

Among other writers of that period, *Minucius Felix*, a younger contemporary of Tertullian, mentioneth the agapes: "Our assemblies," saith a Christian unto a pagan in his work *Octavius*, "are distinguished not only by chastity, but also by solemnity; at them we do not surrender ourselves unto surfeiting with food, we do not sweeten the feast with wine; mirth itself we temper *(Orig. p. 78)* with gravity, chaste discourse, and yet more chaste bodily demeanor" [^373].

*Origen* mentioneth only memorial agapes. "When their memory (of the departed) is celebrated, we summon the pious together with the priests, and equally with the clergy we entertain the faithful; herein we feed the poor and indigent, widows and orphans, so that our festivity may serve for the remembrance and repose of the soul whose memory is celebrated, and for us before the face of God may be a sweet-smelling savor" [^374]. The last words point unto the sacrificial character of these memorial agapes. Consequently, in Alexandria in the middle of the 3rd century the agape is still accompanied by the Eucharist. Not so in Carthage.

### The Agape according to Cyprian

In *St. Cyprian of Carthage* we find for the first time an indication of the separation of the Eucharist from the agape and its transferral unto the morning. Demonstrating the insufficiency for the Eucharist of water alone without wine against the custom of certain heretics (Ebionites, Marcionites, Encratites, etc.), St. Cyprian saith: "Some, perchance, beguile themselves with the thought that, although in the morning water alone is offered, yet in the evening, when we come unto the supper, we offer the mixed cup. But at the time of supper we cannot call together all the people, so as to celebrate the genuine reality of the mystery (*sacramenti veritatem*) in the presence of the whole brotherhood. True it is that the Lord offered the mixed cup not in the morning, but after supper. Is it therefore the case that we also ought to celebrate the Lord's supper (*dominicum*—others translate: 'the Lord's day') after supper, and offer the mingled cup unto those who are present at the assembly? But it behoved Christ to offer His sacrifice at evening, so that by the very time He might demonstrate the setting and evening of the world... We, however, celebrate the Resurrection of the Lord in the morning" [^375]. The reason for celebrating the Eucharist in the morning is thus purely external—physical inconvenience and the impossibility for the majority of the people of evening assemblies.

The agape is described by St. Cyprian, seemingly, in the following passage: "And as it is now a feast day and a season of leisure, let us pass all the remainder of the day, when the sun is tending toward the west, in joy; but suffer not thyself at table for even a single minute to remain without thanksgiving unto God. Let it resound with sober psalmody; and since thou hast a good memory and a tuneful voice, begin this singing thyself according unto custom. Ye wish to provide for your best friends the best entertainment; but if we listen unto spiritual songs and attend unto them spiritually, we shall find a pious gratification for the bodily ear" [^376]. As in Tertullian and Clement, the agape according unto this testimony is filled with singing (the germ of the hymnographic sequence). Perchance reading and prayer had departed from it altogether along with the Eucharist.

*(Orig. p. 79)*
A similar picture of the agapes is afforded likewise by the *Sibylline Oracles*, the citation whereof in the *Apostolic Constitutions* [^377] giveth right to assign them unto the 3rd century: "With bountiful agapes and broadly bestowing hands, with sweet psalms and God-pleasing aspirations unto Thee, the Immortal, we cry aloud and glorify Thee, the unfailing God and Father of all" [^378]. Here is an indication of the sacrificial and charitable character of the agapes, of the abundance of dishes at them (cf. Clement of Alexandria), of the high inspiration which they instilled, and of the predominance of hymnody, even as it were an allusion unto the hymn "O Gladsome Radiance" (*Phōs Hilaron*).

### The Agape according to the Testamentum Domini

Of the mentioned canonical monuments of the 3rd century, the agape is described by the *Testamentum Domini*, the *Canons of Hippolytus*, and the *Egyptian Canons*; the latter in both of their recensions—the Coptic (edited by De Lagarde) and the Ethiopic (edited by Ludolf)—not completely identically.

The *Testamentum* speaketh less than the others concerning the agape and presenteth the simplest picture thereof [^379]. In it regarding the agape there are given several particular directives with obscure terminology, presupposing its customary practice to be well known.

"At a dinner or meal they receive" (it is understood, presumably: "the fraction," the bread sanctified by prayer and fraction—in such manner as is described in detail in the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons*, see below) "those" (understood: first) "who are closest unto the pastor—likewise also regarding the blessing" (according unto Rahmani: *ad benedictionem*; presumably the cup with wine) [^380]. "The catechumen, however, receiveth not. Whosoever is an intimate or kinsman of a teacher of secular subjects" (pagan?), "is not admitted unto praise, and it is unlawful to eat with him merely on account of kinship and intimacy, lest he surrender unto the wolf that which is unutterable, and bring condemnation upon himself."

There follow next instructions for those who are invited with the bishop "into the house of a faithful man" (unto an invited agape), regarding moderation in food, drink, and in general concerning blameless behavior befitting "saints," so as not to grieve the host; it is advised to eat in such manner that there be remnants for those unto whom the host may wish to send them; not to take food before the elders; not to contend in conversations, but to eat in silence; one may speak only in response unto a question from the bishop; the speech of the latter must not be accompanied by tokens of applause [^381].

This rite of the agape the *Testamentum* giveth after the description of the Paschal service; but in expounding the rite, the author presupposeth its celebration at any time, and only most immediately hath Pascha in view; moreover, this description of the agape is preceded and concluded by directives regarding the Paschal service, *(Orig. p. 80)* which we shall utilize later. The relationship of the Eucharist unto the agape is unclear from the *Testamentum*. Yet judging from the fact that the *Testamentum* provideth a distinct order of the Liturgy with a separate portion for the catechumens and setteth forth this order after the morning service separately from the agapes, the monument clearly presupposeth a celebration of the Eucharist entirely separate from the agape.

### The Agape according to the Canons of Hippolytus and the Egyptian Canons

While being very brief and general in its description of the ordinary agape, the *Testamentum* dwelleth with affection upon the description of the Paschal agape, in no way giving it to be understood that such an agape—as we shall see, with the solemn lighting of lamps, with the singing of psalms and hymns alternating with prayers, with lengthy readings and homily, with the solemn dismissal of the faithful homeward and the continuation of the service throughout the entire night for certain persons—is celebrated at any other time than Pascha [^382]. The *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons*, on the contrary, saying nothing specifically concerning the Paschal agape, transfer much of the composition and ceremonies of the Paschal agape of the *Testamentum* unto the ordinary, or at least Sunday, agape. Furthermore, they depict more distinctly and clearly the central ceremony of the agape—the fraction of bread. According unto these monuments, the agape is likewise a service entirely distinct from the Eucharist. At least, it can be celebrated even without the Eucharist: this the monuments give to be understood by presupposing that the celebration of the agape is possible by the laity alone without the clergy [^383]. The agape is celebrated necessarily with the Eucharist only on Sunday and at memorials [^384]. In the latter case it is noted: "If there be an *anamnēsis* [ἀνάμνησις, memorial] for the departed, before they sit down (unto the meal of the agape), they receive the Mysteries; yet not on the first day" [^385] (not on Sunday, or on the first day after death?); thus the Eucharist in such a case was celebrated prior unto the agape; concerning the Sunday agape the very same thing seemingly is stated in the expression: "Obligatory" (an Arabic word translated by the editors into Latin as *necessaria*) "for the poor (for whom an agape is arranged by someone on the Lord's day) is the *eucharistia* [εὐχαριστία], which taketh place at the beginning of the liturgy" (an Arabic word translated by the editors into Latin as *missa*). As the essential rite of the agape there is considered the fraction of bread, which is performed even without the clergy, and consequently without the Eucharist. If a bishop be present at the agape, he offereth prayer over the bread, blesseth it (*signet*), and distributeth it (*distribuet*) among the participants [^386]; in the absence of a bishop a presbyter doth the same [^387]; "in the absence of a presbyter a deacon taketh his place in that which concerneth the prayer and fraction of bread, which he distributeth unto the guests; but unto a layman it is not fitting to bless the bread, but let him only *(Orig. p. 81)* break it, doing nothing besides this" [^388]. The bread having received such a blessing (or perchance fraction alone—the latter is unclear) is called the bread of blessing, *eulogia* [εὐλογία], or bread of exorcism, *exorkismou* [ἐξορκισμοῦ] [^389], as being purified (*purgatus*) by prayer. Unto this bread, as its very name already showeth, there is ascribed a special sanctity and miraculous efficacy, evidently a power against evil spirits (here is the primary source of the note in Chapter 2 of our Typikon concerning the virtue of the blessed loaves); in particular, the bread of exorcism is eaten at the beginning of the agape, "that God may preserve the agapes from the dread of the evil one, and that they may be safely exalted in peace" [^390]. Unto the catechumens, who are not admitted unto the agapes, there is nevertheless sent, by direction of the bishop [^391], the bread of exorcism [^392] (as also the cup) [^393], "that they may be joined unto the Church" [^394]. This primary rite of the agape—the fraction of bread with the blessing thereof and of the cup, and the partaking of them—is preceded in the *Canons of Hippolytus* by those ceremonies wherewith the *Testamentum* surroundeth only the Paschal agape: "If there be an agape or a supper be arranged by someone for the poor on the Lord's day (*kyriakē*, κυριακῇ), at the time of the lighting of the lamp, in the presence of the bishop the deacon ariseth for the lighting. The bishop then prayeth over them (the poor, participants of the agape) and over him who invited them (the host of the agape). And he dismisseth them, that they may go their ways before the falling of darkness. They read psalms before they disperse" [^395]. In the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons* there are given prescriptions similar unto the *Testamentum* concerning good order at the table of the agape, and its order concludeth with instructions regarding that which the widows (deaconesses) ought to do after the agape, recalling the instructions in the *Testamentum* for widows and virgins at the Paschal vigil, yet recalling them by their complete antithesis. There the widows remain after the Paschal agape for all-night prayer; here, according unto the *Canons of Hippolytus*: "If anyone desire to prepare for the widows [^396] a meal, let him take care that they have their meal and be dismissed before the sun goeth down [^397]. If, however, there be many of them, let him beware lest there be disorder, and let him not hinder them from dispersing before evening. Let each of them be given sufficient food and drink. But let them depart before night falleth" [^398]. Here those very widows who alone with the clergy and virgins celebrate in the *Testamentum* the Paschal *(Orig. p. 82)* all-night vigil after the agape are solicitously sent away unto their homes at the onset of evening, wherein the reason for such a requirement is likewise stated: disorders that arose, evidently, owing unto the former practice. There are yet in these monuments several new remarks regarding the agapes, in comparison with the *Testamentum*, characteristic of their history. Thus the monuments clearly give to be understood that intemperance and noisy behavior at the agape not infrequently "grieved" the benefactor—the host thereof [^399]—and for the prevention of these disorders the *Canons of Hippolytus* advise requesting the host of the agape to be present at it with his entire family [^400].

If the agape was celebrated together with the Eucharist, the latter preceded it. This all the canonical monuments under consideration clearly give to be understood by the fact that they require the reception of the Eucharist prior unto other food. The *Canons of Hippolytus*, however, require this especially on fast days [^401]. The *Testamentum*, on the other hand, speaketh of this, as we shall see, in connection with the Paschal service: "Let the faithful man ever strive to partake of the Eucharist prior unto the taking of food; then he shall unknowingly escape affliction" [^402]. This latter promise for the eating of the Eucharist prior unto food the *Egyptian Canons* give in a more concrete form: "Whosoever receiveth (the Eucharist) with faith, even if something deadly be given unto him, it shall not harm him" [^403]. The tone of these requirements showeth that the custom of such reception of the Eucharist was still recent and demanded special insistence for its firm establishment.

### Firstfruits as Material for the Agapes

Toward the provision of the agapes went firstfruits, which the faithful brought unto the clergy from their fruits and revenues. Such an ancient monument as the *Testamentum* placeth these firstfruits in dependence upon the good will of each person: "Whosoever desireth to bring fruits or the firstfruits of the harvest, let him bring them unto the bishop"; the bishop then blesses that which is brought and reads over it a special prayer; herein a remark is made: "Vegetables are not blessed, but the fruits of trees, and flowers—roses and lilies" [^404].

The *Egyptian Canons* and the *Canons of Hippolytus* already counsel bringing firstfruits, but principally for the blessing thereof by the bishop—the former less resolutely: "Let them endeavor to bring at all times unto the bishop the firstfruits," and the *Canons of Hippolytus*: "Whosoever hath firstfruits..., let him bring them" [^405]. As in the *Testamentum*, over the brought firstfruits there is read by the bishop (*Canons of Hippolytus*) or priest a special prayer, wherein thanksgiving is offered unto God for the fruits of the earth, and the blessing of God is invoked upon them and upon the bringer [^406]. In all three monuments no remark is made *(Orig. p. 83)* regarding the destination of these offerings; yet that they went, among other things, toward the agape, we shall see presently from the *Didascalia*. The catalog of offerings is fuller in the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons* than in the *Testamentum*. According unto the *Canons of Hippolytus*, besides tree fruits there are brought "the firstfruits of the garden (contrary unto the *Testamentum*) and of vineyards, oil, honey, wool, and the firstfruits of wages for labor" [^407]. According unto the *Egyptian Canons* it is yet more definite: "grapes, fig, apple, olive, pear, pomegranate, peach, cherry, almond"; herein it is remarked: "There are not blessed: lotus [^408], onion, garlic, melon, watermelon, cucumber, and other vegetables; if flowers be brought, rose and lily are accepted; of the rest permit not to accept; but for all that is eaten let them render thanksgiving and eat, glorifying God" [^409]. Behold the primary source of the present blessing of grapes and apples on the day of the Transfiguration. These firstfruits the *Didascalia* already converteth into direct tributes, increasing their amount, or at least accurately defining this amount: "Bring (O Church) tributes and tithes and firstfruits unto Christ, the true High Priest, and unto His Servants, as the tithe of salvation... When (the bishop) shall receive them, he will divide them equitably, because the bishop well knoweth those in need... The pastor's portion must be set apart and given unto him according unto custom, even if he be not present at the agape and at the gifts" [^410]. Consequently, a portion of the offerings went toward the provision of the (charitable) agape, while the remainder was divided between the clergy and the poor. The *Didascalia* accurately defineth what portion of the offerings each cleric ought to receive: a widow receiveth one portion, a deacon two, and the presiding hierarch two double portions. Concerning these distributions of offerings the *Apostolic Constitutions* likewise speak in almost the identical expressions as the *Didascalia*, adding that the cantor and the doorkeeper likewise receive one portion. These monuments, consequently, require firstfruits no longer for the blessing thereof, but for the maintenance of the clergy and in part (*Didascalia*) for the agapes, thereby establishing the decline of the institution of agapes.

### Matins according to Tertullian

All the more, therefore, in the 3rd century was a purely "verbal," "noetic" [spiritual] ministry unto God destined to advance forward at the expense of the agape. And inasmuch as the evening of the day was occupied by the divine worship of the agape, a ministry of this kind and character became attached unto the morning and developed into a rather prolonged morning divine service. With the decline of the agape, the morning divine service was bound to acquire an ever greater significance and predominance over the evening service. But inasmuch as the first half of the 3rd century was, so to say, the era of the greatest flourishing of the agape (writers of this first half of the 3rd century, and even canonical monuments of the end of the century, furnish the richest ritual for it), in the 3rd century the morning divine service was only just beginning to acquire such a position for itself, and only toward the end of this *(Orig. p. 84)* century did it already occupy in certain churches at least the first place after the Liturgy.

From the monuments of the 3rd century we possess only two accounts concerning the morning divine service. In the first account, belonging unto Tertullian, it is remarkable first of all that the writer, compelled for apologetic purposes to touch upon the divine worship of Christians, not only speaketh first of the morning service, but likewise assigneth unto it no less space than unto the agape. Nothing other than the morning service can be meant by the following words of Tertullian, immediately preceding his testimony concerning the agapes cited above:

"We form," saith Tertullian, "gatherings and assemblies (*coetus et congregationes*), so as to encircle God with common prayers, as it were with an army assembled into one place by hand (*manu facta*). And this force is acceptable unto God. We pray for the emperor, his servants (*ministris*), his authorities (*potestatibus*), for the postponement of the end of this age (*pro mora finis*) [^411]. We assemble for the reading (*commemoratione*) of the divine scriptures, if the circumstances of the times require admonition or reminder. With these sacred words we nourish our faith, animate our hope, support our confidence, even as we reinforce discipline by the inculcation of precepts (*disciplinam praeceptorum nihilominus inculcationibus densamus*); here also are divine exhortations (*exhortationes*), reprimands (*castigationes*), and censure (*censura*): this judgment proceedeth (*nam et judicatur*) with great solemnity (*pondere*), as among those assured of the presence of God; this is a supreme anticipation (*summum praejudicium*) of the future judgment, so that if anyone hath transgressed, he is banished from communication with us in prayer, assemblies (*conventus*), divine worship, and in all sacred intercourse (*commercii*)" [^412].

Not devoid of significance in this testimony is already the dual designation of the worship assemblies of Christians as *coetus* and *congregationes*. The latter, presumably, were more populous and solemn, and it is possible that by them Tertullian understandeth the agapes described by him further on, and by *coetus* in such a case the morning worship assemblies. The latter, according unto Tertullian, bear predominantly a prayerful-homiletic character in distinction from the agapes described further on with their sacramental-hymnographic character: whereas at the agapes the chief element was the meal and singing [^413], the morning divine service was composed of prayers, the reading of Holy Scripture, and homily. The constituent petitions of the prayer represent the germ of the present litanies, in particular the Great Litany (Litany of Peace). In the highest degree remarkable is the mention of a certain "judgment" during divine worship—perchance the excommunication of unworthy members after pub-*(Orig. p. 85)*-lic penance; this peculiar detail of divine worship somewhat recalleth Pliny's *sacramento se obstringere* [^414].

### Matins according to the Testamentum Domini

Among other monuments of the 3rd century, information concerning the morning divine service is found only in the *Testamentum of Our Lord Jesus Christ*. Here there is already given a complete and rather complex rite of Matins. Concerning the morning divine service under the title of "laudation at dawn" (*collaudatio aurorae*), the monument speaketh immediately after the Liturgy; whereas concerning the agape the monument speaketh, as we have seen, only in the order of the Paschal service. Consequently, by the epoch of the *Testamentum* (the end of the 3rd century) Matins had already assumed its present honorable position in the circle of daily services. It was the sole public service besides the Liturgy. All other worship gatherings at special, prayer hours of the day—the number of which, as we shall see, significantly increased in the 3rd century in comparison with the 2nd century—bore a private, non-obligatory character. Such, presumably, the agape had become as well.

#### Episcopal Matins of the Testamentum Domini

"At first dawn," prescribeth the *Testamentum*, "the bishop gathereth the people to celebrate the service until the very rising of the sun. For the first laudation at dawn, he, surrounded by the standing presbyters, deacons, and the rest (of the clergy), saith: **"Glory be to the Lord."** The people: **"It is meet and right."**"

Then in the monument there is placed with the heading "Glorification of the Dawn" (or laudation at dawn) a prayer for reading by the bishop, beginning with the words: **"It is meet and right for us to praise Thee, and to exalt Thee, and to confess unto Thee, O ineffable God, Who hast created all things."** In it morning praise is offered unto God, all-wise and most merciful, the Strengthener and Protector of our souls, and unto His Word, Who resteth with His saints, the uncreated Artificer, the Expounder of invisible and pure holy things, Who hath revealed unto us the mysteries of wisdom and promised the light of immortality; in the second section of the prayer, addressed at first likewise unto God the Father and His Son, our Creator and Redeemer, a petition is offered that the Son of God would grant the ability unceasingly to praise Him; in the third section of the prayer, addressed already solely unto the Son of God, He is glorified for various specific benefits, for instance, for help unto those sailing upon the sea, those imprisoned in dungeons, those tortured, those crucified upon the cross, and a petition is offered that He would grant us to walk in His commandments and visit in His mercy the small and the great, the prince and his people, the pastor and his flock. Unto each of the first two sections of the prayer the people respond: **"Thee we praise, Thee we bless, unto Thee we give thanks, O Lord, and we pray unto Thee, our God"** (*Tebya slavim, Tebya blagoslovim, Tebe ispoveduyemsya, Gospodi, i molimsya Tebe, Bozhe nash*) [^415]; and unto the last: *(Orig. p. 86)* **"Amen."** Then:

"They sing psalms and four songs: one from Moses, one from Solomon (perchance Psalm 71 [LXX 71 / MT 72], inscribed with the name of Solomon), and one from the prophets (that is, from the canticles of our present canon). Boys, two virgins, three deacons, and three presbyters sing (it is not indicated whether together, or alternately—antiphonally). And the doxology is pronounced by the bishop and presbyter in the following manner: **"The grace of our Lord be with you all."** The people say: **"And with thy spirit."** The priest saith: **"Let us praise our Lord."** The people: **"It is meet and right."** The priest: **"Let your hearts be lifted up."** The people: **"We lift them up unto the Lord."**"

— Then in the monument there followeth, under the title: "Final Doxology" (*collaudatio finalis*), a prayer in three parts; in the first God the Father is glorified for granting us light bodily and spiritual—faith—and for His continual benefits, and a petition is contained that the Lord would grant us unceasingly to glorify Him; in the second the Lord Jesus is glorified pre-eminently for His grace-filled operations within our souls; in the third, after the glorification of the "Holy Lord" for the blessing of redemption and reconciliation with the Father, there is contained a series of specific petitions unto Him: "help the orphans, have mercy upon the possessed who are tormented by unclean spirits and cleanse them; teach the unwise; convert those who err; set free those imprisoned in dungeons; and preserve us all." Unto the individual parts of the prayer the people respond in the same manner as in the preceding prayer (**"Thee we praise, Thee we bless..."**). At the conclusion of the prayer:

"the reader reads the prophets and the other (readings); the presbyter, however, or the deacon reads the Gospel; in conclusion the bishop or presbyter instructs in that which is proper and profitable. Then a prayer takes place and the catechumens receive the imposition of hands (it is understood: the catechumens are dismissed). The bishop instructs the people in that which constituteth the mystery. If, however, there be no bishop, the presbyter speaketh, that the faithful may know unto Whom they approach, and Who is their God and Father."

The monument setteth forth also the very text of this "mystical teaching," "mystagogy," comprising an exposition of the most important truths of doctrine: concerning the two natures in Christ, concerning the mystery of the Incarnation and redemption, concerning the victory of Christ over death and hades (in our present divine worship the Creed correspondeth unto this mystagogy). Unto the mystagogy the people respond: **"Amen."** "When the people have been instructed in the mystagogy, the Eucharist is offered. However, the mystagogy is not always imparted, but only at Pascha, on the Sabbath day, the Lord's day, and on the days of the Epiphany and Pentecost" [^416].
The remark that immediately after the mystagogy the Eucharist is offered demonstrateth that the expounded service is at the same time also the preparatory portion of the Liturgy, the Liturgy of the Catechumens. In it, as we see, there is both the prayer for the catechumens and that reading of Holy Scripture which as early as Justin Martyr formed part of this section of the Liturgy. For this reason, in setting forth in another place, above, the rite of the Eucharist, the *Testamentum* begins this rite directly with the offering of the Gifts and the prayer over them, without touching upon the preparatory portion of the Liturgy. This portion of the Liturgy in the *Testamentum* thus mergeth with Matins.
*(Orig. p. 87)*

#### The Proclamation of the Deacon (Deaconal Matins)

Yet it must be noted that the expounded order of Matins, wherewith the Liturgy of the Catechumens merged, is not complete: inasmuch as it is placed in the section concerning the duties of the bishop, it provideth only the prayers and exclamations of the bishop. In another section of the *Testamentum*, devoted unto the duties of the deacon, there is cited that which is there designated the "Proclamation of the Deacon" (*Proclamatio diaconi*), that is, a series of exclamations which the deacon makes during divine worship. At which divine service the deacon makes them is not stated; it is noted only that a part of them precedeth the prayer of the bishop or presbyter, while a part followeth after it. But these exclamations are distinct from those placed in the rite of the Eucharist and correspond unto the exclamations of the deacon at the Liturgy of the Catechumens in the *Apostolic Constitutions*. Consequently, approximately the same place in the order of divine service must they occupy according unto the present monument as well, that is, they must have entered into the composition of the morning divine service, which consisted of Matins in the proper sense (the laudation at dawn) and the preparatory portion of the Liturgy. This "Proclamation of the Deacon," which appeareth as it were an independent service (Matins) of the deacon—just as the *Testamentum* hath a distinct episcopal Matins, a distinct presbyteral Matins, and even a distinct "Matins of the widows"—consisteth of 12 preparatory exclamations, 22 petitions, and 1 concluding exclamation. The preparatory exclamations are: **"Let us stand. — Let each know his place. — Let the catechumens depart. — Watch, lest there be anyone impious, lest there be anyone slothful. — Watch, whosoever believeth not, let him depart. — With one accord let us pray. — Let there be no fornicator, let there be no angry person. — Whosoever is a slave of sin, let him depart. — Watch, as children of light let us make entreaty. — Let us pray unto the Lord God, our Savior Jesus Christ."** "Then, when the presbyter or bishop begins the prayer (it is not known which)"—the *Testamentum* continueth immediately—"the people pray and bend their knees. The deacon, however, speaketh thus." There follow 22 petitions in such form: "For such-and-such let us pray, that the Lord...". The 1st petition—concerning heavenly peace (the peace from on high); 2—concerning faith; 3—concerning concord; 4—concerning endurance; 5—concerning the apostles (concerning the granting of power to imitate them); 6—concerning the prophets; 7—concerning the confessors; 8—concerning the bishops; 9—concerning the presbyters; 10—concerning the deacons; 11—concerning the presbyters (again) [^417]; 12—concerning the subdeacons, readers, and deaconesses; 13—concerning the faithful laity; 14—concerning the catechumens; 15—concerning the kingdom; 16—concerning the supreme authorities; 17—concerning the whole world; 18—concerning those who sail and those who travel; 19—concerning the persecuted; 20—concerning the departed; 21—concerning the fallen; 22—concerning all of us. The series of petitions concludeth with a general exclamation: **"let us pray and beseech the Lord, that He may accept our prayers."** "Upon the completion of the exclamations of the deacon,"—the *Testamentum* continueth—"the bishop makes a sign with his hand, and the deacon saith: **"Let us arise in the Holy Spirit, that, having already become wise, we may increase in His Grace, glorifying ourselves in His name, being edified upon the foundation of the apostles, and praying let us pray, that the Lord may graciously *(Orig. p. 88)* accept our prayers."** The bishop then concludeth (makes the dismissal). The people say: **"Amen"**" [^418].

#### The Preparatory Portion of the Liturgy and Its Connection with Matins

Judging from the fact that the proclamation of the deacon dismisses the catechumens from the church, it is to be thought that this proclamation followed after the prayer for the catechumens, the laying on of hands upon them, and their dismissal, all of which took place after the readings and homily [^419] (prior unto the mystagogy). In the *Apostolic Constitutions* the mentioned litany of the *Testamentum* is made already a litany for the faithful, after the expulsion from church of the catechumens, the energumens, and those preparing for illumination [^420]; but in another place in the *Apostolic Constitutions* an analogous litany is placed even after the kiss of peace immediately before the very offering of the Eucharist [^421]. Other ancient liturgies have the same or an analogous litany. Thus, the Chaldean liturgy divideth such a litany into two parts, placing one part after the Gospel, and the other after the Creed; the Armenian liturgy hath one part of the litany before the reading, and the other after the Creed [^422]; finally, our Liturgy (of the Basilian-Chrysostomic recension) hath placed this litany (in abridged form) at the very beginning of the preparatory portion of the Liturgy, while after the readings it introduced another litany, no less solemn (the Augmented Litany); this was done also by analogy with the Liturgy in our Matins and Vespers.
Nor was the practice of readings identical in the 3rd century at the morning service which merged with the preparatory portion of the Liturgy. As we have seen, the *Testamentum* prescribeth for this service readings from the prophets and "the others," and thereafter the Gospel. The *Apostolic Constitutions* contain already a more complex and definite practice of readings: they indicate two Old Testament readings: from the Law and the Prophets, and two or three New Testament readings from the Acts, the Epistles, and the Gospels [^423]; the Syrian and Chaldean liturgies sometimes replace readings from Acts with readings from the Catholic Epistles; the Armenian hath one prophetic reading before the apostolic epistles; the Coptic and Ethiopic liturgies have no Old Testament readings, but before the Gospel have three readings from the New Testament in the following order: from the Pauline Epistles, the Catholic Epistles, and the Acts [^424]. From the mutual influence and combination of these types of practice there arose our present order, according unto which the Old Testament read-*(Orig. p. 89)*-ings are assigned exclusively unto Vespers, the New Testament ones unto the Liturgy, while Matins, as a service close in time unto the Liturgy, is left without readings, excepting occasionally the Gospel.
It should be noted that, excluding Tertullian, other monuments of the 3rd century, in speaking of the composition of the morning divine service, present the preparatory portion of the Liturgy, which in the *Testamentum* merged with Matins, in approximately the same form as the *Testamentum*. Thus, the Arabic *Didascalia* (that is, the Arabic translation of the *Testamentum* for the Coptic Church) speaketh of the preparatory portion of the Liturgy in the following two passages:

"the place for baptism ought to be at the side of the church, so that the catechumens who are in it may have the opportunity to listen unto the pericopes and spiritual hymns and psalms which are recited in the church" [^425].

The bishop
"begins to celebrate the liturgy according unto the order and precisely thus. First he offers thanksgiving, then, when all the people are seated, he makes for them an explanation of the word, that is, of the sacred books, and instructs them unto repentance (conversion), as is proper, and in the path of honesty. Then let there be uttered psalmody from the book of psalms, from their poets of maxims, from the wise men of grace; and all the people with understanding and fear listen unto this, and with a contrite heart follow this. Then the presbyters bring the bread and the cup of the Eucharist" [^426].

The preparatory portion of the Liturgy is presumably had in view likewise by Tertullian when he speaketh concerning a certain Montanist woman, that she "according as the scriptures are read, the psalms are sung, discourses are delivered, and prayers are offered up, receiveth ever new material for visions" [^427].

Making now a general survey of the morning divine service according unto the *Testamentum* and comparing this service with the account of Tertullian, we obtain the following picture. According unto the *Testamentum*, Matins consisteth of five principal parts: 1) two prayers of the bishop, 2) Old Testament psalms and canticles between them, 3) readings from Holy Scripture, 4) two homilies: one for all, including the catechumens, and one for the faithful alone, 5) solemn prayers between these homilies: one over the catechumens with the imposition of hands and their dismissal, and one for the faithful with the exclamations of the deacon and genuflection. This is consequently already a very complex rite, more complex even than Matins possesseth in certain monuments of the 4th century; yet this complexity oweth much unto the circumstance that the Liturgy was directly conjoined unto Matins, and its first portion merged therewith. Not everywhere even in the 3rd century did such a merger take place, and in the 4th and especially in the 5th century the majority of liturgies already possess a preparatory portion, the Liturgy of the Catechumens; consequently, this merger was a local phenomenon of that Church wherein the *Testamentum* arose (the Syrian), and perchance of certain others, and at all events a temporary phenomenon. Yet it is important as witness that into Matins certain elements began to be introduced from the Liturgy (as likewise into Vespers, owing unto the former connection of the Liturgy with the Agapes), for instance, prayers *(Orig. p. 90)* for the catechumens. — In the account of Tertullian the morning divine service appeareth shorter, but of the parts indicated by the *Testamentum* it lacketh only the canticles, which were perchance omitted by chance. The "judgment" whereof Tertullian speaketh involuntarily recalleth the exclamations of the deacon: **"let there be no fornicator..."**. These exclamations are presumably a ritual survival of the former excommunication of grave sinners, under the form of removal from the solemn worship assemblies. Thus, in the Matins of the Syrian Church of the 3rd century there was already given the germ both of the present prayers during the Six Psalms and at the end of Matins (the prayer of the bowing of heads), and of the present Six Psalms (psalms), and of the Great Litany, and of the canon (the canticles of Moses and the prophets), and of the Gospel.

#### Presbyteral or Daily Matins according to the Testamentum Domini

The presented order of the morning divine service according unto the *Testamentum* is properly its episcopal order. Apparently, it was celebrated only on feast days, since the *Testamentum* provideth also another order of this divine service, entitled: "Daily Doxology" (*collaudatio quotidiana*) and intended for celebration by a presbyter alone. This Matins could be performed even without the people, as is evident from the following preliminary remark unto it: "The daily doxology the presbyters recite in church, by themselves at the prescribed time." This daily doxology, that is, daily or priestly Matins, representeth an abridgment and modification of the first, solemn, festive episcopal Matins. It consisteth only of a single three-part prayer with an introductory exclamation: **"The grace of our Lord be with you all."** The people: **"And with thy spirit."** The priest: **"Praise ye the Lord."** The people: **"It is meet and right."** The priest reads a prayer addressed exclusively unto God the Father, the first part whereof containeth glorification for the general benefits of God and especially spiritual ones granted by redemption, the second—for redemption, and the last—for the specific benefits of God unto the suffering and unto the Church. The prayer is twice as short as the episcopal one, but coincideth with it at times in expressions. Unto each of its three sections the people respond with the same exclamations as at episcopal Matins. Therewith the divine service concludeth, but a remark is added: "if, however, anyone speaketh prophetic words (subjoineth a reading from the prophets), he receives a reward" [^428]. In this order of the morning divine service there is for the first time given the type of a daily service in distinction from a festal one. At the same time, this order is close unto the later type of the Hours and services homogeneous with them (the Midnight Office and Compline), consisting of a single prayer and a single reading, that too non-obligatory and Old Testament.

#### The Midnight Office and Matins of the Widows according to the Testamentum Domini

In assigning for every order of the clergy its own service, more specifically—its own Matins, the *Testamentum* provideth a special order of such Matins also for the widows, the chief *(Orig. p. 91)* representatives ("female presbyters," *presbyterae*) of female ecclesiastical ministry, and at the same time of the asceticism of that Church wherein this monument arose. The widow was here appointed unto this dignity by a special prayer of the bishop; in the hierarchical ladder she stands below the deacon and above the subdeacon and reader; she was bound unto continual prayerful solitude and was required to celebrate, especially on feast days, special services *at night* and *in the morning*, at dawn. These services the widows performed singly; but, remarketh the *Testamentum*, if the widow hath like-minded companions—virgins, it will be very good if they with her shall pray, so as to respond: **"Amen."** The service the widow could perform either at home or in church, but during the period of purification she was not permitted to approach the altar. Both services of the widows consist of a single prayer. In the "nocturnal doxology" the widow at first glorifieth the holy, blameless God of the forefathers, prophets, and apostles with all her soul, strength, and heart for His care over the poor and the weak and for that He hath deigned to make her His servant, and entreateth Him to strengthen her heart for perfection in the Holy Spirit and to restore unto them, the widows, youth for the edification of the Church; turning then unto the Son, the Word and Mind of the Father, and confessing all that He hath accomplished for our salvation, the widow entreateth Him to help the widows, to guide their thoughts in steadfast faith. The "morning doxology" is intended (by its heading) already "For the widows who enjoy the presidency at assemblies." The doxology is addressed unto God the Father, and after general glorification of His Providence and mercy includeth a prayer that He would perfect in His handmaid the spirit of counsel, piety, and right-mindedness, after which there followeth praise unto God Who hath removed from "our" (the widows') poverty all turmoil, discord, evil custom, doubt, fear, and weakness; praise unto God Who hath changed the manner of thought of the widows, correcting their thoughts for upright service unto Him [^429]. These "widows'" services recall our present cell "rules" by the simplicity and uniformity of their content. It is characteristic that they are prescribed only for female ascetics, and not for men. The *Testamentum*, as a monument which arose in Syria, can speak only concerning the practice of that Church. Yet if such complex rites of Matins existed in the 3rd century in one Church, then they were possible in any other as well.

#### Hours and Days of the Celebration of the Eucharist

The enumerated monuments of divine worship clearly demonstrate that at least by the end of the 3rd century the Eucharist was definitively transferred unto the morning, following immediately upon the morning divine service, which began with dawn. Such was the case not only in the homeland of the *Testamentum*—in Syria—but judging by the testimony of Tertullian in other Churches as well: "the sacrament of the Eucharist,"—saith he—"we receive in pre-dawn assemblies and from no other hands than the hands of the president" [^430]. It is possible *(Orig. p. 92)* that in certain places the former practice continued to hold sway—the evening celebration of the Eucharist; concerning such practice there is testimony not only from the first half of the 3rd century (Clement of Alexandria) [^431], but also from the second (Cyprian of Carthage [^432], the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons* [^433]),—yet by a strange coincidence these testimonies concern only Egypt, wherein the custom of the evening celebration of the Eucharist existed even down unto the times of the historian Socrates (5th cent.) [^434].
And with respect unto the days on which the Eucharist was celebrated, there was no complete uniformity across the Churches. The *Testamentum* makes it rather clear that the Eucharist was celebrated only on Saturdays, Sundays, and feast days, whereof there were three: Pascha, Pentecost, and the Epiphany [^435]. Unto these days, as we shall see subsequently, must be added also the commemorations of (local) martyrs. Such, consequently, was the situation in Syria in the second half of the 3rd century. But in Rome and Africa, apparently, daily celebration of the Eucharist took place. Tertullian, in explaining the Lord's Prayer, understandeth under the daily bread the Body of Christ, and remarketh: "Therefore, in asking for daily bread we ask for perpetuity (*perpetuitatem*) in Christ and indivisibility from His Body" [^436]. From this one may infer a daily celebration of the Eucharist, especially if one compareth these words with the interpretation of the 4th petition of the Lord's Prayer in St. Cyprian: "we ask that this bread be given unto us daily, so that we who are in Christ and daily receive from Him the Eucharist as the food of salvation, may not be deprived of heavenly bread and separated from Christ's Body, if we should be barred from communion upon the commission of some very grave sin" [^437]. Origen saith: "Christians eat each day the flesh of the Lamb, that is, the Flesh of the Word of God, they listen unto the scriptures, each day they receive Pascha, sacrificed for us, that is, Christ" [^438].

#### The Presanctified Gifts

Yet it is possible that in all these testimonies the discourse is not concerning the daily *celebration* of the Eucharist, but only concerning daily *communion*. From Tertullian we learn that there already existed at that time the custom of taking the Eucharistic gifts home for daily partaking of them. Tertullian presenteth unto a Christian woman also such an argument against marriage with a pagan: "will not (thy husband) notice that thou tastest of something secretly before supper? And when he knoweth that it is none other than bread, what will he think regarding thee in his ignorance?" [^439] St. Cyprian relateth that a woman who "attempted with unworthy (according unto other MSS.—'unclean') hands to open her coffer (*arcam suam*), wherein was preserved the holy *(Orig. p. 93)* thing of the Lord (*Domini sanctum*), was scorched by fire issuing forth therefrom" [^440]. It is possible that the reservation of the Gifts was occasioned at times by the desire not to break the fast by partaking of them, concerning which apprehension, as we shall see, Tertullian makes mention [^441]. In view of this very thing, presumably, there began to be employed in certain places the custom denounced by St. Cyprian of using at the morning Eucharist water instead of wine [^442]. All this prepared the idea of the Presanctified Liturgy.

#### The Hours of Prayer according to Writers of the 3rd Century

The morning divine service and the agape, with the addition unto one or the other of the Eucharist (the Liturgy), were, as we see, in the 3rd century, as in the 2nd and the 1st, not only the principal church services, but also the sole public services. And they did not exclude the existence of special private services performed by the clergy either alone, or with the participation of a few zealous believers, both in church and at home. The apostolic custom of sanctifying by prayer the three most significant and important hours during the course of the day was maintained, as we have seen, in the 2nd century as well, and passed into the 3rd century. In the 2nd century, this custom is witnessed only by the *Didache* (*Teaching of the Twelve Apostles*), without indicating which precise hours were sanctified by prayer. The testimonies of the 3rd century upon this question are both more frequent and more definite. It is evident that the custom of sanctifying by prayer certain hours of the day is now increasingly spreading and becoming established.

For *Clement of Alexandria*, the hours of prayer are a firmly established and widespread custom.

"If some assign (*taktai aponemousi*, τακταὶ ἀπονέμουσι) for prayer definite hours, as for example the 3rd, 6th, and 9th, the man endowed with knowledge (*ho gnōstikos*, ὁ γνωστικὸς) prayeth his whole life, striving by prayer to abide with God. He hath left behind, in short, all useless things, having attained unto that place where he hath received perfection, as one acting according unto love. Yet even the setting apart of three hours for honoring with equal prayers (*tais isais euchais tetimēmenas*, ταῖς ἴσαις εὐχαῖς τεтиμημένας) is universally recognized in view of the three blessed states of the saints" [^443].

Thus, upon the hours of prayer Clement looketh as upon a good means toward moral advancement, non-obligatory only for one who hath attained perfection and is capable of unceasing prayer. In another passage Clement speaketh of the 6th hour of the day as one wherein "there was manifested (*emphainei*, ἐμφαίνει) something of the economy of salvation—namely, man was made complete (*eteleiōthē*, ἐτελειώθη)" (there is meant, presumably, redemption [^444]).
*(Orig. p. 94)*
*Tertullian* speaketh concerning the hours of prayer in approximately the same spirit:

"As regards the time of prayer, the external observance even of certain hours will not be superfluous, those, I mean, generally known hours which mark out the intervals of the day: the 3rd, 6th, and 9th, which also in Scripture may be found indicated as more solemn hours (*solemniores*);"

having referred unto the descent of the Holy Spirit at the 3rd hour, and unto the prayers of the Apostles Peter and John at the 6th and 9th hours, Tertullian continueth:
