But apart from Pascha it is not permitted to fast those 3 hours of the night which are between Saturday and the first day of the week, since it is the night of the first day of the week [^549].

*(Orig. p. 120)*

##### 2. The Apostolic Constitutions

It is forbidden also to swear by idols and to utter their abominable names with the mouth, or to worship them and fear them"—and thereafter followeth a detailed development of these thoughts without the mention, corresponding unto the *Didascalia*, of prayers on the days of Pascha and of Pascha itself [^550].

*(Orig. p. 121)*

"Let there be preserved among you the fast of the Forty Days (Четыредесятница / Lent), containing the commemoration of the life and legislation of the Lord; and perform ye this fast before the Paschal fast. After these days, having completed the fast, begin ye the Holy Week of Pascha, fasting therein all of you with fear and trembling, praying in these days for those who are perishing [^551]. For the counsel against the Lord they undertook on the second day after the Sabbath (Monday) of the 1st month, called Xanthikos; and on the 3rd day after the Sabbath (Tuesday) they were occupied with deliberation; on the 4th day (Wednesday) they resolved to crucify Him (the history of Judas' betrayal and the disclosure of his design at the Mystical Supper is related in detail, being assigned unto the 5th day of the week; then the subsequent history of Christ's Passion is related) [^552]. He Himself commanded us to fast in these six days on account of the impiety and lawlessness of the Jews, enjoining us to mourn over them and weep for their destruction; for He Himself also shed tears over them, who knew not the time of their visitation. On Wednesday and Friday He commanded us to fast—on the former because then He was betrayed, and on the latter because then He suffered; and to break the fast He commanded us on the seventh day, when the cock croweth; and on Saturday itself He commanded to fast not because it is meet to fast on the Sabbath, when creation was finished, but because it is meet to fast on that Saturday alone wherein the Creator was yet beneath the earth. For the Jews seized the Lord on their very feast, that the word might be fulfilled which saith: 'They have set up their banners in the midst of their feast and knew not.' And so it is meet to mourn over them, because *(Orig. p. 122)* they believed not the Lord when He came, but rejected His teaching, having judged themselves unworthy of salvation [^553].

Therefore ye, brethren, redeemed by the blood of Christ, must observe (*poieisthai*, ποιεῖσθαι) the days of Pascha with exactness and with all diligence after the equinox, lest ye celebrate the commemoration of the one Passion twice in the year, but that ye may commemorate Him Who died once only once in the year, no longer observing to celebrate with the Jews; for we now have no communion with them, because they err even in the reckoning of time itself, deeming it correct, as having gone astray in all respects and departed from the truth. Do ye, however, with exactness observe the return of the equinox of the springtime, which takes place on the 22nd day of the 12th month, Dystros (March), watching unto the 21st moon, lest the 14th day of the moon fall upon some other week [^554], and lest, erring through ignorance, we should celebrate Pascha twice in a year, or lest we should celebrate the Resurrection of the Lord on another day than the Lord's day [^555]. On the Paschal days fast ye, beginning from Monday unto Friday and Saturday, 6 days, using for food only bread, salt, and herbs, and for drink—water; but from wine and meat abstain ye in these days of mourning, and not of festival. On Friday and Saturday fast ye completely, whoever is able, tasting nothing until the nocturnal cockcrow; and if anyone cannot fast two days together, let him observe at least Saturday. For the Lord speaketh concerning Himself in one place thus: 'When the bridegroom shall be taken away from them, then shall they fast in those days'; and He in these very days was taken from us by the falsely called Jews, and nailed unto the cross, and numbered among the lawless [^556]. *(Orig. p. 123)* For this reason we exhort you to fast in those days until evening, as we also fasted when He was taken from us. On the other days unto Friday let each eat at the 9th hour, or in the evening, or as each is able. On Saturday fast ye until cockcrow, watching and assembling together in church; abide ye the entire night in vigil, prayers, and supplications unto God, reading until cockcrow the Law, the Prophets, and the Psalms, and baptizing your catechumens; and having read the Gospel with fear and trembling, and having offered unto the people a discourse concerning that which pertaineth unto salvation, cease your mourning and pray unto God that Israel may turn and obtain a place of repentance and remission of impiety [^557].

These passages demonstrate above all that in that era there arose for the first time difficulties in determining the time of Christian Pascha and its relation unto the Jewish Passover; hitherto Christians, apparently, had always celebrated Pascha simultaneously with or immediately following the Jewish Passover; now they do not trust the Jewish reckoning of Passover and establish their own Paschalion [^558], in consequence of which Christian Pascha at times diverges significantly in time from the Jewish. This gives rise to the need for a preliminary determination of the date of Pascha, an endeavor in which in the 3rd century St. Hippolytus, Bishop of Portus (the harbor of Rome), and Dionysius, Bishop of Alexandria, were engaged [^559]. In the 4th century this question was definitively resolved by the Church in the decree to celebrate Pascha on the first Sunday after the full moon occurring on or after March 21 [^560]. The *Apostolic Constitutions*, apparently, already know such a decree.

*(Orig. p. 124)*

Furthermore, characteristic is the view of these canonical monuments regarding Pascha as a propitiatory fast for the Jews, alongside which the very commemoration of Christ's Passion seems to recede into the background.

Alongside this latter commemoration there already emerges (as became noticeable in Tertullian) as an element in the concept of the feast also the commemoration of Christ's Resurrection. Yet this element does not yet receive in these monuments equal status with the sorrowful element of the festival. The Paschal vigil according to the monuments appears dedicated to the Passion and death of Christ, and only its conclusion receives a joyful character—in honor of Christ's Resurrection. The present Church Typikon with striking fidelity reproduces the spirit of this practice, when the Paschal vigil is composed of Passion services (the Canon of Great and Holy Saturday) and Sunday services (Paschal Matins); these two halves of the Paschal vigil even in the present Typikon are regarded as completely equal in standing; this is evident from the fact that: (a) they are of equal duration; (b) upon the coincidence of the Annunciation with Pascha, the Canon of the Annunciation is sung not only at Paschal Matins, but also with the Canon of Great and Holy Saturday.

The examined canonical monuments of the 3rd century almost agree in defining the hour at which the Paschal fast is broken. According to the *Canons of Hippolytus* this is done at dawn; according to the *Didascalia*, at the third hour of the night; according to the *Apostolic Constitutions*, at cockcrow. Yet Dionysius of Alexandria observes that in his time there was no uniformity in this regard: "Those who hasten and arise before midnight, we rebuke as disdainful and intemperate; but those who defer and manfully persevere until the fourth watch itself, we receive as noble and patient in labors; while toward those who break the fast between these terms, according as they have purpose or strength, toward them we are not harsh" [^561].

#### Pascha According to the *Testamentum*

At the same stage of development is Pascha represented also by the *Testamentum of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, whose prescriptions concerning Pascha significantly supplement the information given by the examined monuments concerning it from the 3rd century. If from the latter we become acquainted only with the general character and spirit of the feast in that era, the *Testamentum* provides also its detailed ritual. Yet many passages in this section of the *Testamentum* are exceedingly obscure. The monument speaks of Pascha in connection with baptism. Having stated that the catechumens designated for baptism are exorcised from the day of their selection, the *Testamentum* continues:

"As the days *(Orig. p. 125)* of Pascha draw near, the bishop exorcises each one individually... On the fifth day of the final week (Great Thursday) they must wash themselves and anoint the head (with oil?)... On Friday and Saturday they fast. On Saturday a general exorcism before baptism is performed over all by the bishop. (Here occurs the above-cited remark concerning forty days of fasting). On the final Saturday they keep vigil by night (the faithful), when the catechumens are exorcised until midnight of that Saturday" [^562].

There follow descriptions of baptism, chrismation, and the reception of communion; and after a brief parenthetical observation concerning the order of charity (with which the Eucharist was customarily accompanied), the monument returns to the rites of Pascha:

"On the fifth day of the final week of Pascha (Great Thursday) bread and the cup are offered, and He Who suffered for the one who offered is Himself both the One Who is and the One Who approaches (an obscure expression, rendered by the Coptic-Arabic version: 'on the fifth day in the evening the priest offers bread and the cup mixed with water and wine, for the celebration of the mystery of Pascha; likewise he does also on Saturday'). A lamp is brought into the temple by the deacon, who says: **'The Grace of Our Lord be with you all'** (*«Благодать Господа нашего со всеми вами»*), and all the people respond: **'And with Thy spirit'** (*«И со духом Твоим»*). The boys recite spiritual psalms and hymns at the lighting of the lamp. All the people, chanting with harmonious voice, respond: **'Alleluia'** (*«Аллилуиа»*). And no one kneels until the speaker (the youth?) finishes. Exactly so also if a reading is read or a word of instruction is delivered. When, however, he utters the Name of the Lord or anything else (similar), as has been said, no one falls prostrate. The breaking of the Paschal fast takes place at midnight which follows Saturday. In Pentecost no one fasts and none bend their knees, for these are days of rest and joy. Those burdened with heavy labors rest somewhat during the days of Pentecost and the Great Day of the Lord. The bishop before offering the sacrifice pronounces in the established order that which is appointed for the sacrifice, while those clothed in white alternately with one another say: **'Alleluia'** (*«Аллилуиа»*)" [^563].

Further in the *Testamentum* there follow prescriptions concerning order at the agapes, the offering of firstfruits, memorial alms, the prayer of blessing over the loaves, again concerning firstfruits, and concerning prayer before taking food [^564]; immediately whereupon the monument continues:

"On the days of Pascha, especially the final ones—on Friday and Saturday—by day and by night [^565] there are as many prayers as hymns; the instruction is long, the readings diverse and frequent. Vigils and nocturnal matins are celebrated with beauty and solemnity. The deacons who walk among the women, lest any illicit young men be found among them, are assisted by the readers. Over this also the subdeacons preside. They do not permit the youth to sleep; for that night, preeminently that which follows Saturday, is an image of the Kingdom of Heaven. Those who labor and grow weary may become exhausted before midnight; (therefore) first the catechumens are dismissed, having received a blessing from the breaking of bread. The faithful, when they are dismissed, go in order and modestly unto their homes; and they do not abandon prayer even at their repasts. The priests, however, do not interrupt their service. The women depart, each following *(Orig. p. 126)* her husband (simultaneously with their husbands). The widows, however, remain until morning in the temple, receiving here also their sustenance. The virgins also remain in the temple, and the bishop provides them assistance and care, while the deacons minister unto them. The presbyters remain with the bishop until morning, praying and resting. Exactly so also do the newly baptized. The virgin betrothed, however, accompany their mothers and go home; this is more decorous. The bishop commands it to be proclaimed that no one taste anything until the sacrifice is offered and the body of the Church receives new nourishment. Then from the beginning of the evening those who are to be baptized are baptized after the first reading. If anyone, before he receives the Eucharistic communion, tastes anything, he becomes guilty, and the fast wherewith he fasted shall not be accounted unto him at all. Upon the catechumens, when they are dismissed, hands are laid. If any of the faithful remains away through sickness, the deacon carries unto him the sacrifice, that is, the Eucharistic communion. If a presbyter cannot come unto church, a presbyter carries unto him (the communion). If a woman is ill through pregnancy and cannot keep the fast of those two days, let her fast the second day, and let her take bread and water at the first hour; and if she cannot approach (unto communion in church), let a deaconess carry the communion unto her. Concerning those who are sick, let them inform the bishop, that he may visit them as far as possible; for hereby great consolation is afforded unto the sick" [^566].

So far as these unsystematic and frequently digressive prescriptions permit us to judge, the feast of Pascha according to the *Testamentum* possessed the following order. The sorrowful-joyful solemnity began on Great Thursday, when there was celebrated with special solemnity and special rites (the most important of which were the lighting of the lamp and the chanting of the Alleluia) the Eucharist, yet a kind of peculiar one, perhaps without communion, as may be suggested by the obscure expression: "He Who suffered (Christ) for the one who offered is Himself both the One Who is and the One Who approaches"; communion was perhaps not received in view of the fast. From that same day, apparently, genuflections were discontinued in view of Pascha and throughout the whole of Pentecost (just as today they are discontinued from Wednesday evening). Friday and Saturday were spent in the strictest fast and unceasing day and night services, performed, as the monument notes, with special magnificence, wherein there were exceptionally lengthy readings (*paroimiai*), yet they were interspersed with an equal number of hymns (cf. the present manner of reading the Old Testament lessons on Great and Holy Saturday). On Saturday, after a solemn exorcism, the catechumens were baptized. Marked by exceptional duration was the vigil in the night following Saturday. At this vigil or immediately following it, the Paschal Eucharist was celebrated, which—in view of the fact that it was prepared for by a two-day fast, and in view of the fact that during it the newly baptized received communion for the first time—acquired exceptional significance: it had to be tasted before the reception of any other food whatsoever, and was administered decisively to "the entire body of the Church," for which reason the Holy Gifts were sent out even to the absent and the sick. (This latter circumstance well explains *(Orig. p. 127)* the present Communion Verse (*Koinonikon*) at the Paschal Divine Liturgy: **"Receive the Body of Christ"** [*«Тело Христово приимите»*]).

#### Pentecost

In connection with Pascha, almost all writers and monuments of the 3rd century speak also of Pentecost, the first mention of which is found, as we have seen [^567], in a fragment of St. Irenaeus (2nd century). Here, however, one may observe that earlier writers, such as Tertullian, know Pentecost as the fifty-day interval of time that followed Pascha and was accounted as joyful days; whereas later writers, such as Origen, assign the name of Pentecost unto a single festival day. Proving the superiority of Christianity over paganism, Tertullian remarks: "Every pagan feast hath for itself one single day in the year; but for thee the resurrection is renewed every seven days; gather all pagan feasts together, arrange them in succession, and they will not be able to fill out Pentecost" [^568]. Discussing the most suitable time for baptism and pointing unto Pascha as the most solemn day for baptism, Tertullian adds: "An exceedingly significant interval of time for the administration of baptism is presented by Pentecost, when both the Risen Lord conversed among the disciples, and the grace of the Holy Spirit was given, and the hope of the Second Coming of the Lord shone forth; for then, upon His Ascension into heaven, the Angels said unto the Apostles that He would come in the same manner as He ascended into heaven—namely, (He will come) in Pentecost" [^569]. Having mentioned in another place the impermissibility of fasting and genuflection on Sunday, Tertullian adds: "with that same exemption (*immunitate*) we rejoice (*gaudemus*) from Pascha unto Pentecost" [^570]. Finally, in one passage Tertullian states that the "fifty days" from Pascha "we spend in all exultation" (*in omni exultatione*) [^571]. In Origen, on the other hand, the juxtaposition of Pentecost with Pascha and Friday presupposes for the former a single day of festival [^572]. The *Testamentum*, as we have seen, knows Pentecost both as a period and as a single-day feast with a solemn Liturgy equal unto that celebrated on Saturday, Sunday, Pascha, and Epiphany [^573]. Characteristic is the silence concerning Pentecost in the *Canons of Hippolytus* and the *Egyptian Canons*.

#### Epiphany (Theophany)

In the 3rd century the feast of the Baptism of the Lord, or Epiphany (Theophany), had its beginning. It is first mentioned by Clement of Alexandria [^574]. Speaking *(Orig. p. 128)* in the *Stromata* (*Miscellanies*) concerning various attempts and methods of establishing the chronology for the Incarnation and death of Christ, he remarks: "There are also those who, determining even more inquisitively not only the year, but also the day of the Nativity of our Savior, say that it occurred in the years of Augustus on the 25th day of Pachon (December or May); the followers of Basilides celebrate also the day of His Baptism, passing the entire preceding night in readings (*prodianyktereuontes anagnōsesi*, προδιανυκτερεύοντες ἀναγνώσεσι); they say that it occurred in the 15th year of Tiberius on the 15th of Tybi (January), while others say that it was on the 11th of the same month" [^575]. Consequently, in Alexandria in Clement's time the Orthodox did not yet possess this feast. It is possible that the Basilidians arrived earlier than the Orthodox at the idea of celebrating the day of the Baptism of the Lord and named it Epiphany (Theophany), since according to the view of these heretics Christ became the Son of God precisely from the time of His Baptism and the descent upon Him of the Holy Spirit. Among the Orthodox the feast could have been established in counteraction unto the heretical festival, and into it, of course, a different meaning was invested. The mention of Epiphany in the *Testamentum* [^576] demonstrates that in the 3rd century the feast obtained wide dissemination. Unto these specified three feasts was the Church year of the 3rd century restricted: the feast of the Nativity of Christ becomes known later [^577], in the 4th century; the Ascension in the 5th century [^578]; others still later.

#### Commemorations of Martyrs

The veneration of *martyrs* in the 3rd century bore the same local character as in the 2nd century. The monuments of the 3rd century do not mention a single universal feast of the whole Church in honor of any saint or martyr. Yet, of course, reverence for the martyrs grew and prepared the idea of universal ecclesiastical commemoration for certain among them. Such martyrs as St. Laurence († 258) must have appalled the entire Christian world by the tortures they endured. The level reached by the veneration of martyrs and saints in the 3rd century is well demonstrated by the interpolation of the passage of the Syriac *Didascalia* concerning martyrs in the *Apostolic Constitutions*:

##### The Syriac *Didascalia*
"Therefore, blessed are the martyrs and pure from all sins and temptations, and removed from every unrighteousness, as is spoken of Christ in Isaiah: 57:1–2" [^579].

##### The *Apostolic Constitutions*
"And concerning the martyrs we say unto you, that they should be held by you in all honor, as also by us (the Apostles) are honored the blessed James the Bishop and our holy fellow-minister Stephen" [^580].

*(Orig. p. 129)*

These are the only saints whose (universal) commemoration is mentioned by the *Apostolic Constitutions*; consequently in the era of the *Didascalia* there did not yet exist even in their honor a universal commemoration.

Apparently, in the 3rd century no overly sharp boundary was yet drawn between the commemoration of martyrs and the remembrance of the ordinary deceased. Tertullian says: "we make oblations (*oblationes*) for the deceased (*pro defunctis*) on the anniversary day of their suffering (*pro natalitiis annua die*)" [^581]. "We celebrate," says Origen, "the commemoration of the saints and of our parents; likewise do we honor the memory of friends who die in the faith, both rejoicing over their repose and entreating for ourselves a righteous end in the faith. When their commemoration is performed," an agape takes place [^582], "so that our celebration may serve for the remembrance and repose of the soul whose memory is kept, and for us before the face of God may be a sweet-smelling savor" [^583]. Here the commemoration includes not so much prayers for the repose of the departed as it is permeated by a firm and joyful assurance of such repose. In the *Didascalia*, however, the character of the commemoration is already closer unto our own: "Do ye, however, according unto the Gospel and according unto the power of the Holy Spirit, assembling in the cemeteries (*memoriis*), perform the reading of the Holy Scriptures, and send up unceasingly unto God *prayers*, and offer the Eucharist, received in the likeness of the royal Body of Christ, both in all assemblies and in the burying-places and at the passing of the dying" [^584].

Making a brief survey of that which was accomplished by the 3rd century in the domain of divine worship—more particularly for the future Church Typikon—we find that, in regard to liturgical orders, there was now developed for the first time, in certain churches at least, a rather complex order of *Matins*, in some respects coinciding with our present service, as well as the order of the *introductory part of the Liturgy* directly adjoining it. In comparison with the 2nd century, attention is drawn in these services unto: (a) the formulation of prayers; (b) the establishment of a definite order for the reading of Holy Scripture; (c) the selection of specific melodies for ecclesiastical use from among the series of existing Greek chants. As regards the evening service, it was reduced entirely unto the *agape*, for which, in some churches at least, there was likewise a precisely elaborated rite; yet regulation here extended unto the ceremonial aspect of the service (the breaking of bread and distribution of the cup), but not unto its internal content: prayers, hymns, and instructions at the agape (in contrast unto Matins and the Liturgy), apparently, were left entirely unto the discretion of the participants under the oversight of the president, who in the absence of a bishop or presbyter could be a deacon and even a layman, if the agape was not conjoined with the Eucharist. Yet the agape was a comparatively rare and occasional service (if only for the sole reason that it was by no means inexpensive). Usually, however, the *evening* was sanctified by the same kind of semi-private, semi-public prayer as the other notable hours of the day, the worship *(Orig. p. 130)* of which, although no less than the agape left unto the freedom of each, consisted in the majority of cases in the chanting of psalms with diverse refrains, predominantly with the Alleluia, and with the addition, presumably, of improvised prayers, which served, however, merely as an appendage unto the Lord's Prayer. As regards the *ecclesiastical year*, first of all the *feasts* are noticeably distinguished from weekdays; from among the days of the week *Saturday* begins to stand out in certain places; *Pascha* acquires for itself the most prominent, exceptional position in the calendar, altering also its former character—that of a fast in honor of Christ's Passion and death—unto a dual character of sorrow over them and joy over Christ's Resurrection. In quantitative terms, the Church year increases by only one feast in comparison with the 2nd century—*Epiphany (Theophany)*.

*(Orig. p. 131)*

### The 4th and 5th Centuries

The cessation of persecutions, the revivification of theology under the influence of the Christological controversies, and the flourishing of monasticism could not fail to exert the most salutary influence upon the development of divine worship in the 4th and 5th centuries. If already by the close of the 3rd century there was established in certain churches a firm and complex order—in addition to the Liturgy—also for the morning service as the most essential worship, then in the two subsequent centuries such an order was created for well-nigh the entire present cycle of daily offices. And although this order differed among individual churches, and unto subsequent times transmitted by no means everything from its composition, nevertheless by the beginning of the 6th century throughout the entire Christian East there was elaborated that rather uniform and stable type of divine worship—or more accurately, several such types—from whose modification and confluence by the beginning of the 9th century the present order of the daily cycle of worship was delineated in its essential features. At the same time, in these centuries—the 4th and 5th—there arose for the first time the Menologion (Calendar) of Saints, and the cycle of the Great Feasts expanded from the three or four of the preceding century unto almost their present number. Being the most fruitful in theology, with the most vigorous pulse of ecclesiastical life, these centuries were also the most creative in Church worship: it was fashioned now in the (immortal) foundations of its structure that have survived to this day, in its present form and schema, which the 6th through 8th centuries merely filled out with hymnographic content, and the 9th through 12th centuries polished unto aesthetic elegance.

#### The Abolition of the Agape

In the realm of liturgical orders, the 4th and 5th centuries were marked above all by *the abolition of the agape*.

The immediate cause of this abolition was the vast outward expansion of the Church, wherein there now appeared many unworthy members; among the latter the agape was transformed into that which it had once been for the Gentile-Christians of the days of the Apostles Paul and Jude who were insufficiently imbued with the ideals of the new faith; and whereas such Christians were then few, and they gradually rose unto worthy participation in the agape—this "banquet of the Word" (to use the expression of Clement of Alexandria)—in the 4th and 5th centuries such Christians, tares among the wheat of the Church, grew ever more numerous, and the Church was compelled to renounce for a long time, if not forever, this ancient and exalted institution of hers. Furthermore, the agape did not entirely harmonize with that ascetic spirit wherewith, under the influence of an asceticism full of youthful freshness and vigor, Christian worship now began to be permeated.

The first half of the 4th century already requires an apology for the agape and an artificial preservation of it. The Emperor Constantine the Great mentions "the exceedingly modest banquets (*sōphronestata de kai symposia*, σωφρονέстата δὲ καὶ συμπόσια) instituted in memory *(Orig. p. 132)* of the martyrs by many, out of a feeling of pity for the indigent and for the relief of strangers and the poor," and remarks: "whoever considers them superfluous thinks not according to divine and most sacred doctrine" [^585]. The Council of Gangra (c. 340 or later) anathematizes those "who despise those who make agapes in faith and gather the brethren in honor of the Lord, and will not take part in these invitations, on the ground that they esteem this matter of no account" [^586]. Yet how vital and useful an institution the agape still was is evident from the fact that the Emperor Julian considers it an institution well-nigh the most dangerous in Christianity for paganism: he says that just as those who traffic in children entice them onto ships with dainties, so also Christians "by the same method begin (in their seduction of the pagans) with what are called among them agapes, feasting, and ministry at tables; and both this institution and its very name (agape—love) mean much among them (*esti poly*, ἔστι πολύ); and both the one and the other have drawn men most of all into godlessness" (into Christianity) [^587].

From the second half of the 4th century we encounter for the first time restrictive measures in relation to agapes and a struggle against them by pastors of the Church. The Council of Laodicea (c. 360 or earlier) forbids both "to offer the oblation (the Eucharist) in private houses" [^588], which was conjoined with the agape, and "in places belonging to the Lord (*kyriakois*, κυριακοῖς) or in churches to hold so-called agapes and to eat in the house of the Lord and spread couches (*akoubita strōnnyein*, ἀκούβιта στρωννύειν)" [^589]. St. John Chrysostom († 407) reckons, apparently, with an already fading habit of his hearers regarding agapes. Insisting that the celebration in honor of the martyrs should be preeminently spiritual, consisting of a purely prayerful assembly in church, he adds: "Yet dost thou desire to take part also in a bodily table? It is permitted, upon the conclusion of the assembly, here beside the shrine of the martyrs, having reclined beneath a fig tree or a vine, both to give rest unto the body and to deliver the conscience from condemnation. The martyr, seen nearby, standing close at hand, and presiding over the table itself, will not permit pleasure to turn into sin" [^590]. Blessed Augustine relates concerning the Church of Milan in the episcopate of St. Ambrose († 397): "according to the custom of the African churches, my mother here also on the days of the commemoration of the saints brought offerings into the churches for the common meal from diverse meats; once, when she appeared with such offerings, she was stopped by the doorkeeper of the church, who told her that the bishop had forbidden such offerings" [^591]. And "everywhere," in Blessed Augustine's time, according to his testimony, "in the greater part of Italy and in all or most other churches, agapes either are not held at all, or, if instituted according to custom, were brought to an end and discontinued after the loving *(Orig. p. 133)* exhortation of the bishop" [^592]. Nevertheless in Africa the statutory prohibition of agapes took place more than half a century later than in Asia Minor. Only the Third Council of Carthage in 418 [419] decrees: "let bishops or presbyters feast not in church, unless during a journey out of necessity they have rest there; and unto the laity, as far as possible, let such banquets be forbidden" [^593]. In the West, however, the agape survived even longer. For the Council of Arles the agape was still something inseparable from the Eucharist or near unto it in sanctity: "Whoever by priestly authority is excommunicated from communion must not be invited unto the colloquy or banquet (*colloquio atque convivio*) [printed: *collquio atoqne convivio*] not only of clerics, but of the entire people" [^594]. The agape was first prohibited in the West by the Council of Auxerre in 584 [^595].

Of special importance was the abolition of the agape for the later liturgical Typikon—apart from the influence of its ritual upon the structure of Vespers—in the respect that it definitively established the custom of receiving the Eucharist before the taking of food. Already in the 3rd century this custom enjoyed universal dissemination; yet the opposite practice met with no censure either. The cause of this latter circumstance was that the agape, an evening service, was still frequently united with the Eucharist and maintained the view of it as physical no less than spiritual nourishment, not distinguishing the Eucharist sharply from food in general. Therefore we see that in the African churches, where the agape persisted longer than elsewhere, the custom of celebrating the Divine Liturgy in the morning before the midday meal took root later than in other places. According to Socrates (5th century), "the Egyptians neighboring upon Alexandria, and the inhabitants of the Thebaid, hold their religious assemblies on Saturday, but do not participate in the Holy Mysteries as is customary among Christians; but having dined and eaten all kinds of food, toward evening they partake of the Holy Gifts" [^596]. The tone of condemnation in which the historian speaks of this custom points unto a universal practice of another sort. Nevertheless this latter practice still required statutory measures for its confirmation and admitted of an exception: "The holy mysteries of the sacrifice," decrees the Third Council of Carthage (419), "must be celebrated by men in no other manner than upon condition that they have not eaten, with the exception of one day in the year, whereon" ...the Lord's Supper is celebrated" [^597].

*(Orig. p. 134)*

#### The Daily Office in the 4th and 5th Centuries

The abolition of the agape imparted unto the cycle of the daily offices a thoroughly spiritual, "noetic" character, depriving Christian worship of the last element that made it somewhat resemble the cultus both of the Old Testament and of natural religions.

Owing unto this abolition, the various daily offices could not fail to receive, at the outset at least, an approximately identical structure, which they retained throughout the course of the two centuries under consideration. Only the subsequent period in the history of divine worship (the 6th to 8th centuries) engaged in the differentiation of the daily offices from one another and gave unto each of them its own distinctive character.

At the present time we possess rather detailed information concerning the daily divine services of the 4th and 5th centuries from three different lands and parts of the Christian world of that day, each of which elaborated its liturgical ritual independently, although—owing unto the constant close communion of the churches—not without external influence. We have in view the liturgical data contained: (1) in the *Apostolic Constitutions*; (2) in the *Pilgrimage to the Holy Places* (*Peregrinatio ad Loca Sancta*) of the late 4th century, attributed unto Sylvia of Aquitaine; and (3) in the ancient monastic rules. The first monument, being, as we have seen, of Syrian origin [^598], acquaints us with the divine worship of the Syrian Church of the 4th and early 5th centuries; the second, with the divine worship of the Church of Jerusalem of the late 4th century; and the third, with the rule of prayer of the Egyptian and Palestinian ascetics of the beginning of the 5th century. The first two monuments present the type of cathedral-parochial church services for the laity; the last constitutes the first and most ancient typikon of monastic divine worship. Both types of church service could not fail to exert an influence upon the liturgical practice of the Laura of St. Sabbas the Sanctified—a disciple of the disciples of the Egyptian ascetics, who founded his monastery in immediate proximity unto Jerusalem—the founder of the present Church Typikon, whose activity belongs already unto the 6th century.

#### Vespers and Matins According to the *Apostolic Constitutions*

The *Apostolic Constitutions*—a monument, as we have seen, of diverse dates of origin—speak of morning and evening worship in three places: in Book II, and in the appendices to Books VII and VIII.

The first passage belongs unto the most ancient portions of the monument, specifically representing a redaction of the 3rd-century Syriac *Didascalia* made in the 4th to 5th centuries [^599]. The redaction in this instance expressed itself in the fact that unto the general exhortation of the *Didascalia* to pray frequently *(Orig. p. 135)* in church, the *Apostolic Constitutions* add the requirement of morning and evening public worship and appoint for each a specific psalm. (The additions of the *Constitutions* unto the *Didascalia* we print in italics).

"O bishop, command the people and exhort them to assemble constantly (*endelechizein*, ἐνδελεχίζειν) in church every day, morning and evening, and not to forsake the assembly (*synolon*, σύнолон), but to frequent it continually... that no one by his absence may maim the Church and sever into parts the Body of Christ. *Every day assemble ye morning and evening, chanting and praying in the churches* (*psallontes kai proseuchomenoi en tois kyriakois*, ψάλλοντες καὶ προσευχόμενοι ἐν τοῖς κυριακοῖς), *in the morning reciting* (*legontes*, λέγοντες) *Psalm 62, and in the evening Psalm 140*" [^600].

The first of these psalms (**"O God, My God, Unto Thee Do I Watch from the Dawn"** [*«Боже, Боже мой, к Тебе утренюю»*, Ps. 62]), which enters into the composition of our present Six Psalms (in third place), is appointed for morning worship from that same era by Pseudo-Athanasius in the treatise *On Virginity* (*De Virginitate*) [^601] and, as we shall see, by Chrysostom. The former adds: "and at daybreak (recite): **'Bless the Lord, All Ye Works of the Lord'**" (*«Благословите, вся дела Господня, Господа»*, that is, the Song of the Three Holy Children). Concerning the use of Psalm 62 at the morning service St. John Cassian speaks [^602], and somewhat later (at the beginning of the 6th century) St. Benedict [^603].

In the appendix unto Book VII of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, without any connection with what precedes, and in certain codices even without title, is placed a "morning prayer" (*proseuchē*, προσευχή), beginning with the words **"Glory to God in the Highest"** (*«Слава в вышних Богу»*) and almost verbatim identical with a portion of the present Great Doxology; then an "evening" (*hesperinos*, ἑσπερινός)—presumably an evening hymn—**"Praise the Lord, Ye Children"** (*«Хвалите, отроцы, Господа»*), close unto the present **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*«Сподоби Господи»*) with the **"Now Dismissest Thou"** (*«Ныне отпущаеши»*, *Nunc Dimittis*) in conclusion; and finally a "prayer at breakfast" (*euchē ep' aristō*, εὐχὴ ἐπ' ἀρίστῳ): **"Blessed Art Thou, O Lord, Who Dost Nourish Me from My Youth"** (*«Благословен еси, Господи, питаяй мя от юности моея»*), similar unto the prayer in the present Order of the Panagia [^604]. Of the first of these prayers (**"Glory to God in the Highest"**) Pseudo-Athanasius also makes mention [^605] and cites its beginning; it is likewise read in the Alexandrian Codex of Holy Scripture (5th century) and others as an appendix unto the Psalms, with slight variation from its present form. The last prayer in almost the same form as in the *Apostolic Constitutions* is cited by Pseudo-Athanasius [^606] and by St. John Chrysostom [^607].

Finally, in the appendix unto Book VIII, which is not present in all codices, the *Apostolic Constitutions* provide the order and even the text of evening and morning worship. The very structure of both is completely identical, yet the content, naturally, is different—adapted unto the time of day. Inasmuch as the *Apostolic Constitutions* attribute each *(Orig. p. 136)* of their sections unto one of the Twelve Apostles, so also the present section, which occupies the final place in the book and constitutes an appendix unto it, the monument attributes unto an Apostle, not however from among the Twelve, but the primate of the remaining (seventy) Apostles—James the Brother of the Lord. Inasmuch as this Apostle according to tradition was the first Bishop of the Church of Jerusalem, the placement of his name over the order of worship may suggest a Jerusalem origin for this order. Indeed, the descriptions of Jerusalem divine worship at the end of the 4th century in Sylvia of Aquitaine [^608] speak of a significant similarity between this practice and that one, well-nigh of an identity in the fundamental features of their structure.

"When evening cometh, thou, O bishop, gather the Church; and after the evening (*epilychnios*, ἐπιλύχνιος) psalm hath been recited (*rhēthēnai*, ῥηθῆναι), the deacon proclaims (*prosphōnēsei*, προσφωνήσει)—(that is, pronounces the appointed prayer petitions, corresponding unto the present litany)—for the catechumens, for the tempest-tossed (*cheimazomenoi*, χειмаζομένων) [^609], for those being illuminated, and for the penitents, as we have said above (that is, in the order of the Liturgy). And after their dismissal the deacon says: **'As Many as are of the Faithful, Let Us Pray to the Lord'** (*«Елицы вернии, помолимся Господу»*); and after he proclaims that which is contained in the first prayer (*ta tēs prōtēs euchēs*, τὰ τῆς πρώτης εὐχῆς, meaning the prayer of the deacon in the order of the Liturgy, corresponding unto the present Great Litany and close unto it), he says..."

There follows under the heading "Evening Proclamation" (*prosphōnēsis epilychnios*, προσφώνησις ἐπιλύχνιος) a series of petitions, close unto the present Litany of Supplication [^610], beginning: **"Save and Raise Us Up, O God: Having Arisen, Let Us Pray..."** (*«Спаси и возстави нас, Боже: вставши помолимся…»*), which points unto a preceding kneeling prayer [^611]. After the petitions (the Litany of Supplication) of the deacon there follows the prayer of the bishop, beginning: **"O God Without Beginning and Without End, Maker of All Things"**, which entreats God, Who created day and night, the dawn and the sun, and Who hath brought us through the day unto the beginning of night, to receive the evening thanksgiving, to grant us a peaceful evening and a sinless night, and to vouchsafe us eternal life (close unto the third part of the first kneeling prayer of Pentecost). After this there is pronounced by the bishop yet another prayer of the laying on of hands, preceded by the exclamation of the deacon: "Bow yourselves down for the laying on of hands"; this prayer entreats God, Who fashioned man, placed him at the head of earthly inhabitants, and established among men rulers (*archontes*, ἄρχοντες) and priests, to incline Himself unto those who have bowed the necks of their hearts unto Him, to manifest His face unto them, and to bless them through Christ.

The service concluded with the exclamation of the deacon: **"Depart in Peace"** (*«Изыдите в мире»*).

*(Orig. p. 137)*

Matins of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, being, as observed, of the same structure as Vespers, differs from it only in the content of the prayers. It begins with the "morning psalm," by which is understood, as is evident from what precedes, Psalm 62. The diaconal petitions at it (the Litany of Supplication) are adapted unto the morning (the words "evening" and "night" are replaced by "morning" and "day"; there are also other minor differences in the text of the petitions). The first prayer of the bishop for the faithful (after the departure of the catechumens, etc.), **"O God of Spirits and of All Flesh"**, entreats God, Who created the sun, moon, and stars, mercifully to look down upon us, to receive our morning thanksgivings, and to vouchsafe us eternal life for our fidelity unto Him ("for we have not stretched out our hands unto a strange god"). The second prayer, of the bowing of heads, **"O Eternal and True God"**, entreats God, Who art merciful unto thousands and myriads that love Him, the Friend of the humble and Protector of the poor, in Whom all things have need and Whom all things serve, to look upon those who have bowed their heads unto Him, to bless them with a spiritual blessing, to preserve them in piety and righteousness, and to vouchsafe them eternal life.

In comparison with the only complete order of the daily office from the 3rd century that has come down to us—namely, Matins in the *Testamentum of Our Lord Jesus Christ* [^612]—this order of worship, belonging unto approximately the same church, if not shorter and simpler, is, apparently, in no wise longer or more complex. Yet it must be taken into account that the present order almost exclusively (if we except the initial psalm, which could not fail to be mentioned) indicates the prayers of the sacred ministers at the service (like the present *Sluzhebnik*). It is incredible that throughout an entire Vespers or Matins not a single hymn of Christian composition was sung, if such hymns already in the 2nd century (according to Pliny) and even in the Apostolic age constituted the principal content of divine worship. The same *Apostolic Constitutions* above cite morning and evening hymns, but here they do not indicate a place for them in the order of Matins and Vespers. It is likewise scarcely probable that at an entire service only one single psalm was sung, as also that there were no readings of Holy Scripture or instruction. Thus, the order of Matins and Vespers given by the *Apostolic Constitutions*, being intentionally incomplete and restricting itself unto prayers alone, does not permit of a detailed comparison with the daily office of the 3rd century, for example in the *Testamentum*. Such a comparison is possible only with respect unto the prayers of the two liturgical orders. The prayers at the divine service of the *Apostolic Constitutions*, in comparison with the prayers of the *Testamentum*, are distinguished by a greater generality of content and, as it were, less warmth of feeling. Furthermore, noticeable is an intensification of the ceremonial aspect in the prayers: not to speak of an entire gradation of worshipers into classes—instead of the verbal blessing of the sacred minister (with the words: "The Grace of the Lord... be with you") in the *Testamentum*, the present monument introduces the laying on of hands by the bishop, applied in the *Testamentum* only unto the catechumens, imparting unto it a special significance, making it the focus and *(Orig. p. 138)* principal moment of the prayer. In the arrangement of the prayers in comparison with the *Testamentum*, one cannot fail to notice a greater regularity, proportion, and sequence. This arrangement closely approaches the present one: a portion of our Vespers, beginning with the Litany of Supplication, with respect unto the prayers of the sacred ministers is given here completely, having finished its development: unto the first prayer of the bishop following the "proclamation" of the deacon corresponds the present exclamation after the Litany of Supplication, which is a remnant of the former prayer here (which was later joined unto the seven prayers of the Lucernarium); after this exclamation there now follows among us, as in the *Apostolic Constitutions*, the prayer of the bowing of heads. But the most important step in comparison with the 3rd century is that Vespers receives an equal place in the rank of daily offices alongside Matins (a consequence of the abolition of the agape and the definitive transference of the Liturgy unto the morning).

#### The 4th-Century Jerusalem Liturgy According to the *Pilgrimage* Attributed to Sylvia

If the *Apostolic Constitutions* have preserved for us models of prayer at the daily office of the 4th and 5th centuries and therefore acquaint us with the inner content of the latter, the *Pilgrimage to the Holy Places* (*Peregrinatio ad Loca Sancta*), attributed unto Sylvia of Aquitaine [^613] and describing the divine worship of the Church of Jerusalem of the late 4th century, acquaints us with the outward structure and *(Orig. p. 139)* composition of divine worship of that same epoch and approximately of the same region or one neighboring that wherein the *Apostolic Constitutions* arose.

The pilgrim describes first the weekday services, then the Sunday services, and finally the festal services (the latter without beginning or end). But the fundamental structure of each of these kinds of divine services is the same; Sunday and festal worship differ from weekday worship more in the place of celebration than in composition. The cycle of the daily offices consists of Matins, the hours of Terce, Sext, and None, and Vespers (not counting the Divine Liturgy); yet of these Terce was celebrated only in the Great Fast, while Sext and None, apparently, were celebrated only on weekdays.

The divine worship described by the pilgrim is so closely bound in its structure unto the place of its celebration that for an understanding of her description a clear conception is necessary of all the temples unto which it is attached. Usually (excepting feasts) it is celebrated in three temples, built by Constantine the Great upon the site of the Crucifixion and Burial of Christ and constituting, perhaps, a single complex of edifices: (a) the Church of the Resurrection, called by the pilgrim directly the "Resurrection" (*Anastasis*); in it or beside it was the cave (*spelunca*) of the Sepulchre of the Lord, separated from the church by a lattice (*cancelli*) and constituting the sanctuary (altar) of this church; (b) the Church at the Cross (*ad Crucem*), that is, upon the site of the finding of the Cross of Christ or for its preservation; from the first church it was separated by a large courtyard, called "Before the Cross" (*ante Crucem*) [^614]; the place behind this church was called "Behind the Cross" (*post Crucem*), and here also (*post Crucem*) stood (c) the third, greater church (*ecclesia major*), called the Martyrium [^615], because it was situated upon Golgotha itself, the site of the "passion" (Crucifixion) of Christ [^616]. In these three churches the daily and Sunday divine services are celebrated, passing from one church unto another. Festal divine worship, moreover, proceeded in solemn litanies unto other churches of Jerusalem and its environs, such as: the church on Sion, upon the site of the house wherein the Savior appeared unto the Apostles after the Resurrection; the churches on the Mount of Olives (one over the cave wherein Christ customarily taught the Apostles, and another upon the site of the Ascension, called the Imbomon); the church in Gethsemane; the church near Bethany; and unto Bethlehem over the cave of the Nativity of Christ [^617].

*(Orig. p. 140)*

#### Matins and the Hours According to Sylvia

The daily divine worship of the Church of Jerusalem of that day, according unto the description of the pilgrim, consisted of Matins, Sext, None, and Vespers. Weekday Matins, not designated by this name nor indeed by any name in the pilgrim, was celebrated entirely in the Church of the Resurrection (*Anastasis*). It began by night, "before cockcrow"; but prior unto dawn there took place its less solemn part, celebrated without the bishop by the priests and deacons in course for the monastics and virgins (*monazontes et parthenae*), and also for the more zealous among the laity of both sexes (*et laici praeterea—viri aut mulieres*). This part of Matins (corresponding unto our Midnight Office and the portion of Matins prior unto the Kathisma hymns / Exaposteilarion) consisted of hymns, psalms, and "antiphons," wherein the chanting of psalms was responsorial, that is, with the whole people chanting the concluding words of each part or each verse of the psalm (*dicuntur ymni et psalmi responduntur, similiter et antiphonae*); the psalms and antiphons, the pilgrim observes in another place, at divine worship always corresponded in content unto the time of day; at Matins they were not the same as at Vespers and the Hours—"always so suitable, so meaningful (*rationabiles*), that they relate unto that which is being performed" [^618];

"at each hymn (*cata singulos ymnos*)," continues the pilgrim her description of Matins, "there is a prayer, which a presbyter pronounces. When dawn breaks, they begin the morning hymns; and behold, there arrives the bishop with the clergy, and immediately (differently from Vespers) he enters inside the cave (the cave of the Sepulchre of the Lord, which served as the altar) and from within the lattice (which separates the cave from the temple—corresponding unto the iconostasis) he first utters a prayer for all and commemorates the names of those whom he desires, and then (*sic*) blesses the catechumens; thereafter he utters a prayer and blesses the faithful; and upon the departure of the bishop from behind the lattice, all approach unto his hand, and he, having come forth, blesses each one individually; then already at daybreak the dismissal takes place (*fit missa*) [^619]. At the sixth hour (at noon) all likewise go down unto the Resurrection; psalms and antiphons are recited (*dicuntur*), until they notify the bishop: he likewise comes down and sits not (differently from Vespers), but immediately enters inside the lattice (as at *(Orig. p. 141)* Matins) into the Resurrection, that is, where he had been also in the morning, and from thence in like manner he first makes a prayer, then (*sic*) blesses the faithful, and when he comes forth from behind the lattice, all likewise approach unto his hand.—The same is done at the ninth hour as at the sixth" [^620].

Thereafter the pilgrim describes the last office of the day—Vespers. Thus the pilgrim does not speak of the celebration of the Liturgy on weekdays, unless the latter is designated by the words *missa fit* (on Sunday she does speak of it). The distinction between the church services in the description of the pilgrim does not stand forth at all: the hours of the day (Sext and None) possess, apparently, entirely the same composition as Matins (Vespers, as we shall see, was more complex than Matins); if this were indeed so, if the similarity of the services here ought not to be attributed unto the generality and imprecision of the description or unto insufficient observation, then the Jerusalem divine worship of this epoch resembled the later so-called chanted office (*asmatike akolouthia*) [^621], which imparted unto the hours, at least in certain instances (for example, in Passion Week or generally in the Great Fast), a structure identical with Matins and Vespers: with chanting, litanies, the reading of the Apostle and the Gospel, and the like. Yet the expression of the pilgrim concerning Sext does not permit, however, an entirely complete identification of its structure with Matins, since she does not mention (possibly on account of the brevity of the description) the hymns (*hymni*) and the prayers accompanying them at the hours; nor does the pilgrim mention a special prayer at the hours for the catechumens. The principal and central moment of each service is the prayer of the bishop inside the lattice in the very cave of the Sepulchre of the Lord (the altar of the temple) and, as it were, the blessing brought forth by him from thence unto the people. Thus that prayerful presence of the bishop at each of the sacred hours in the temple, which the 3rd-century monument *The Testamentum of Our Lord Jesus Christ* only desires [^622], here finds realization, although for this purpose the number of prayer hours is reduced.

#### Vespers According to Sylvia

A completely distinctive and the most solemn service in the course of the day in the Church of Jerusalem of the 4th century, according unto the testimony of the monument under consideration, was Vespers. This service was so solemn that it did not change its composition (and perhaps its content) even for Sunday and for the greatest feasts (only in Passion Week and on Pascha did Vespers differ from the weekday office in that it had a Gospel reading).

"At the tenth hour, which is called *licinicon* (read *lychnikon*, λυχνικόν), and which we call Vespers (*lucernare*), in like manner all gather in the Resurrection; all the lamps and tapers (*candelae et cerei*) are kindled, and there is made *(Orig. p. 142)* an immense (*infinitum*) light. And fire is not brought in from without, but is provided from the interior of the cave, that is, from behind the lattice, where day and night a lamp burns. The evening psalms and more prolonged antiphons (than at Matins or the Hours?) are sung (selected verses of the psalms?). Then they notify the bishop, who comes down and sits above (upon the cathedra); the presbyters also sit in their places (evidently for hearing the readings, which in later typika were called 'sitting above' or 'sitting below' [^623]). Hymns and antiphons are sung (not psalms, as previously). And when they have brought them unto an end (*ad ubi perducti fuerint*), the bishop arises and stands before the lattice; and one of the deacons commemorates all individually, as is customary; and when the deacon pronounces each one's name, there stand many boys (*pisinni*), who constantly respond: **'Kyrie eleison'**... their voices are multitudinous [^624]... The bishop pronounces a prayer and prays for all, after which all pray, both the faithful and the catechumens together. Then the deacon proclaims that each of the catechumens, as he stands (*quomodo stat*) [^625], should bow his head, and the bishop, standing, pronounces a blessing over the catechumens. Then a prayer is read, and the deacon again proclaims (*mittit vocem*) that each of the faithful, standing, should bow the head, and the bishop blesses the faithful, after which the dismissal takes place (*fit missa*) in the Resurrection; and all begin to approach unto the hand of the bishop. And after this, (going) from the Resurrection unto the Cross, they sing a hymn (*ymnus dicitur*); the bishop goes together with all the people. When they arrive (as is evident from what follows, at the courtyard 'Before the Cross'), first the bishop reads a prayer and blesses the faithful. After this the bishop and all the people go Behind the Cross (presumably the courtyard behind the Church of the Cross—by analogy with the preceding), where again the same is performed as Before the Cross (the conclusion of Vespers—for the third time). And in like manner they approach unto the hand of the bishop, as in the Resurrection; so do they both Before the Cross and Behind the Cross. Everywhere hang multitudinous huge glass lamps (*candelae vitreae ingentes plurimae*) and multitudinous candlesticks (*cereofala*), both before the Resurrection, and Before the Cross and Behind the Cross. All this concludes with twilight (*cum crebris*). Such a service (*operatio*) is celebrated daily throughout six days at the Cross and in the Resurrection" [^626].

Consequently, the distinction of Vespers from Ma*(Orig. p. 143)*tins, imparting unto it greater solemnity, was: (a) the sitting of the sacred ministers, that is, the readings at it (*paroimiai*); (b) the litany of the deacon; and (c) the Litiya unto the nearest sacred localities, at which the final most important prayers and rites of Vespers were repeated, as though Vespers were celebrated again in miniature. The *paroimiai* and the Litiya even today constitute the principal distinction of Vespers. The Litiya, characteristically designated by ancient Slavonic typika as the "departure" (*iskhozhdenie*) [^627], was evoked in the practice of this church, evidently, by the desire to pray in all the places marked by Christ's Passion, at the very site of the Crucifixion (for which reason on feasts it is directed also unto distant localities outside the city), and by the memories bound up with them to rekindle prayerful fervor. It is remarkable that the Litiya does not enter into the other church (into the Martyrium), but is performed before it and behind it (as today—in the narthex).

#### Sunday Worship According to Sylvia

Sunday Matins differed from the weekday office above all in that its first part, celebrated without the bishop, was conducted not in the Church of the Resurrection, which on that day was opened not earlier than cockcrow, but in the basilica beside this church. The bishop arrived for Matins not at dawn, as on weekdays, but with the first crowing of the cock. Only with his arrival was the Church of the Resurrection, abundantly illuminated, opened unto the people, and in it Matins began as it were anew (on weekdays the bishop merely continued or rather concluded it with his prayers); there were sung responsorially three psalms—the first by a presbyter, the second by a deacon, the third by a cleric, after each of which a prayer followed; at the third prayer the commemoration of all was made. Then censers were brought in, and the church was filled with fragrance; the bishop, entering behind the lattice, took the Gospel and from the doors (in the lattice) read of the Resurrection of the Lord. After the Gospel they went with hymns unto the Cross; there a psalm was sung, a prayer was read, the bishop blessed the people, and the dismissal took place (*missa fit*); the bishop went home, but the service continued: the monastics with the priests and deacons in course and with the more zealous among the faithful returned unto the Resurrection, where until dawn psalms and antiphons were sung with a prayer after each of them [^628]. That is, into Sunday Matins, in comparison with the weekday office, was introduced the reading of the Gospel and a Litiya.

"At daybreak in the Martyrium," continues the pilgrim, "all is performed according unto the custom observed everywhere on the Lord's Day," that is, there takes place, as is evident from her subsequent description, the Divine Liturgy (*missa*); inasmuch as it is preceded by the instruction of several presbyters and of the bishop, it is prolonged until the fourth or fifth hour (10:00–11:00 a.m. according unto our reckoning). After the Liturgy the monastics escort the bishop with songs unto the Church of the Resurrection, whither together with him enter only the faithful, without the catechumens; the bishop enters behind the lattice; thanksgiving is rendered (*aguntur gratiae*) unto God, there takes place the prayer of the bowing of heads, the blessing of the bishop from within the lattice, and all is *(Orig. p. 144)* concluded (*protrahitur missa*) at about the fifth or sixth hour (11:00 a.m.–12:00 noon). Vespers is celebrated daily (*item et ad lucernares similiter fit juxta consuetudinem cotidianam*) [^629]. Thus there were, apparently, no Hours on Sunday; as it were in their stead the Liturgy received at the conclusion a special supplementary part—a Litiya for the faithful alone (inasmuch as the catechumens did not remain until the end of the Liturgy).

The pilgrim notes the exceptional concourse of people at Sunday Matins and the contrition wherewith the people listened unto the Sunday Gospel [^630].

Comparing this liturgical practice with the practice of the *Apostolic Constitutions* and taking into account the intentional incompleteness noted above wherewith the latter is depicted, we find that the most important daily offices—Matins and Vespers—here and there possess a well-nigh literally identical structure. To speak of "psalms," "hymns," and "antiphons," as we have seen, lay outside the scope of the task of the *Apostolic Constitutions*; as regards the prayers of the sacred ministers, which constituted the second and most important part of Vespers and Matins, they follow in both monuments one and the same order, close unto our present one. The chief distinction of the Jerusalem practice (in the *Pilgrimage*) from the Syrian (in the *Apostolic Constitutions*) is that unto Matins was imparted less solemnity in comparison with Vespers (and this, presumably, was a novelty and a reform—cf. the *Testamentum*), for which reason in the former the diaconal litany is omitted, while unto the latter is added the Litiya, tripling the conclusion of Vespers. A difference purely incidental from a liturgical perspective is that the Church of Jerusalem did not know such an elaborate gradation in the ranks of worshipers as appears in the *Apostolic Constitutions* (catechumens, the tempest-tossed, those being illuminated, penitents), but divided them simply into full-fledged and non-full-fledged worshipers (catechumens and faithful); subsequent practice eliminated even this division from the order of Vespers and Matins. Far more significant is the difference of the Jerusalem typikon from the Syrian, or more precisely—a step forward of the former in comparison with the latter—namely, the adaptation of divine worship unto the feasts of the church year, concerning which both the *Testamentum* and the *Apostolic Constitutions* are silent (not counting Pascha). It is characteristic also that the *Apostolic Constitutions* begin the depiction of the liturgical order with Vespers, whereas the pilgrim begins with Matins. But the latter could speak here from her own, Roman-Western viewpoint: among Roman Catholics the church day begins even now in the morning. (Did not the pilgrim, who was by no means a profound observer of divine worship, overlook Vespers on the eve of feasts on account of this?).

*(Orig. p. 145)*

#### The Daily Office According to Other Writers of the 4th and 5th Centuries

The liturgical practice depicted by the two examined monuments—the *Apostolic Constitutions* and the *Pilgrimage* attributed unto Sylvia of Aquitaine—can hardly be restricted unto the confines of those two churches wherein these monuments originated. Even in the 3rd century we observed an astonishing similarity between the most distant churches in their liturgical orders. In the 4th and 5th centuries this similarity was bound to increase. Only now was opened the full possibility of close intercourse between the churches; this was the most flourishing period of Councils and of beginning centralization in ecclesiastical governance. That the first of the examined monuments traces its practice back unto the Apostles in itself speaks for its relative universality; the canonical portion of the *Apostolic Constitutions* reflected the norms of the general, universal law of that era; the same must be expected also from the liturgical sections of the monument. As regards the liturgical practice of the 4th-century Church of Jerusalem depicted in the *Pilgrimage* of Sylvia, to ascribe unto this practice a purely local significance is precluded by the exceptional position which this church has always occupied in the Christian world. Indeed, if we compare with the rich liturgical material provided by these two monuments the meager data concerning 4th- and 5th-century divine worship that can be met with in the writers of these centuries, we shall become convinced of the substantial agreement of the various churches in this aspect of their life; just as the picture of divine worship provided by the monuments will thereby receive some supplementation. From the writers of the 4th century we shall gather first the data concerning the days and hours of divine worship, then concerning its general structure and order, and finally concerning its constituent parts and elements: prayer, psalmody, readings, and instruction.

#### Number and Types of Services

In other churches as well there took place that daily celebration of divine worship which the *Apostolic Constitutions* require, and which the 4th-century *Pilgrimage* attests in the Church of Jerusalem. At least the morning and evening services were celebrated daily, if not in all churches, then in the more significant—episcopal—ones, and were attended punctually. St. John Chrysostom speaks concerning Psalm 140: "The Fathers established that this psalm be read every evening; consequently, one may say that everyone knows this psalm and they sing it at every age... every day they sing it, yet understand not its meaning" [^631]. In his exposition of 1 Timothy 2 St. Chrysostom remarks: "What means 'first of all' (that supplications be made...)? It means at the daily divine worship. And this the initiates of the mysteries know, how it takes place among us every day both evening and morning, how we offer prayers for the whole world, for kings, and for all that are in authority" [^632]. The Council of Agde (*Concilium Agathense*, in southern Gaul) of 506, canon 20, decrees: *(Orig. p. 146)* "The morning and evening hymns shall be sung on all days, and at the conclusion of the morning and evening Masses let the *capitella* (short readings) from the psalms be read, and let the people after the collect (*collecta*) prayer be dismissed by the bishop with a blessing" [^633].

Besides morning and evening, there were everywhere observed also the prayer hours established by the preceding centuries: the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours, the beginning, middle, and end (before dawn) of the night. These were likewise honored, if not by public divine worship, then by elaborate, definite prayer (a prayer rule), at least among ascetics and in monasteries. St. Basil the Great, unto the question: "What times are suitable for prayer?", replies: "...we must not neglect the times of prayer established in the brotherhoods, which (times) were chosen by us of necessity, since each of them in a particular manner calls to mind the blessings bestowed by God. Thus we must not neglect the morning, so that the first movements of the soul and mind may be consecrated unto God... so that we may not set the body in motion for labor until we fulfill that which was spoken: **'Unto Thee will I pray, O Lord; in the morning Thou shalt hear my voice'** [^634]... Then also at the Third Hour we must stand for prayer and gather the brethren, even if it should happen that each be occupied separately with his own work; calling to mind the gift of the Holy Spirit given at the Third Hour unto the Apostles, all must worship with one accord, so that they themselves may become worthy to receive sanctification and ask of the Spirit guidance and instruction unto profit, imitating him who said: **'Create in me a clean heart, O God, and renew a right spirit within me...'** [^635] At the Sixth Hour we deemed it necessary to pray in imitation of the saints who said: **'Evening, and morning, and at noon will I speak...'** [^636] Concerning the fact that the Ninth Hour is necessary unto us for prayer, this is handed down unto us by the Apostles themselves in the Book of Acts [^637]. And at the close of the day there are needed both thanksgiving for that which has been given us on this day... and confession of that which we failed to fulfill..., for which reason it is said: **'What ye say in your hearts, be penitent upon your beds'** [^638]. Again, at the onset of night we must entreat that our rest may be without stumbling and free from fantasies, reading at this hour the 90th Psalm. And that midnight also is needed unto us for prayer, this was handed down by Paul and Silas, as the narrative of the Acts relates [^639]; and the Psalmist says: **'At midnight I arose to give thanks unto Thee for the judgments of Thy righteousness'** [^640]. And again we must arise for prayer, anticipating the morning, that the day may not overtake us in slumber and upon our bed, according unto that which is said: **'Mine eyes have prevented the morning, that I might meditate on Thy words'** [^641]."

The significance which St. Basil possessed for the monasticism of his own and subsequent times renders *(Orig. p. 147)* it probable that the instructions imparted by him here concerning the honoring of each of the prayer hours were taken into account during the formation of the office for them: all the psalms from which he draws excerpts were incorporated into these services, just as in the prayer of Compline his expression is literally repeated. (Hence, perhaps, the ascription of his name unto the majority of prayers at the Hours and other services).

#### The Origin of the First Hour

According unto the testimony of St. John Cassian, for the first time in his day, and specifically in the monastery of Bethlehem, there was established a special "morning canonical office" (*matutinam canonicam functionem*) "at sunrise"—that is, the First Hour; however, the venerable father remarks, this service was not newly instituted, but was derived through the separation from the nocturnal vigils (*nocturnarum vigiliarum*), celebrated after cockcrow until dawn (Matins), of the final part following Psalm 150—namely, Psalms 50, 62, and 89 (which were assigned unto the First Hour). This service was established, according unto the words of John Cassian, in order to restrain the monks from prolonged sleep during the interval of time between the conclusion of the vigil (Matins) and the Third Hour [^642]. Thus, apparently, one must understand Cassian's somewhat obscure expression concerning this:

"The songs (*hymnos*, that is, psalms, as is evident from what follows) which in this country they adopted (*excepere*) for the morning office (the newly established one, that is, the First Hour), and which are hitherto likewise sung at the end of nocturnal vigils, which customarily conclude after cockcrow before dawn—that is, Psalm 148 and those following it; whereas Psalms 50, 62, and 89 were assigned (*deputatos*—allotted) for this new service, as we know. In Italy even now in all churches after the conclusion of the morning hymns Psalm 50 is sung, which undoubtedly was borrowed from no other source than this" [^643].

The incentive for establishing the new service according unto Cassian was the abuse of sleep on the part of certain monks after the night office: upon its conclusion they slept not merely until dawn, but until the next service, which was the Third Hour, making up with daytime slumber the hours spent in nocturnal prayer [^644].

#### Weekday Matins According to Basil the Great

As regards the order of daily services in the various churches of the 4th and 5th centuries, brief indications concerning it are provided also in the testimonies cited above, and these indications for the most part coincide with the detailed, although likewise incomplete, data concerning the order of Syrian-Jerusalem divine worship in the *Apostolic Constitutions* and the *Pilgrimage*. A detailed description of the morning service is provided by St. Basil the Great in his letter unto the clergy of Neocaesarea:

"The customs which have now become established in all the churches of God are uniform and harmonious. For among us the people from the night rise early (*ἐκ νυκτὸς γὰρ ὀρθρίζει*) in the house of prayer, in labor, sorrow, and tearful contrition confessing unto God; *(Orig. p. 148)* after which (*τελευταῖον*), having arisen (from their knees) from prayer, they stand for psalmody. And behold, dividing themselves into two parts, they sing alternately unto one another (*ἀντιψάλλουσιν ἀλλήλοις*)... Then in their turn, having entrusted one to begin the singing of the melody (*τοῦ μέλους*), the rest respond (*ὑπηχοῦσι*), and having thus passed the night in the variety of psalmody interspersed with prayers (*μεταξὺ προσευχόμενοι*), at the very break of day, all together (*κοινῇ*), as it were with one mouth and one heart, offer unto the Lord the psalm of confession, making repentance each with his own words" [^645].

At this Matins, beginning, like the Jerusalem office according unto the *Pilgrimage*, likewise before dawn and uniting consequently the Midnight Office and Matins, the psalms are sung, as at that one, now antiphonally, now responsorially, and alternate with prayers. In it our attention is arrested by the penitential tone, in connection wherewith stands some kind of (public or private?) confession of sins at the beginning of the service (corresponding unto our Six Psalms, which according unto the *Typikon* one must listen to "praying for our sins" [^646]) and a solitary penitential prayer at the end of the service (corresponding unto the present 12 prostrations with silent prayer). This is the first testimony concerning the use at Matins of Psalm 50 (cf. above in Cassian), which according unto the most ancient complete typika (for example, the Hagia Sophia Typikon of Constantinople of the 9th century) constitutes the most important central portion of Matins.

#### The Saturday Vigil According to Cassian

From among the days of the week in liturgical terms, besides Sunday, Saturday was significantly singled out, at least in certain localities. The morning service, which on other days also, as beginning in the depth of night, could be termed a vigil in the proper sense, began on the eve of Saturday from the evening (*ab vespera illuscente sabbato*) and continued "the whole night"; only shortly before Cassian was it shortened by the "elders" (*seniores*) for the winter season to such an extent that it concluded at the fourth crowing of the cock, so that during the remaining two hours before dawn it might be possible to sleep [^647]. The institution of this vigil John Cassian traces back unto the time of "apostolic preaching" and explains by the fact that when "our Lord and Saviour was crucified on the sixth day of the week, the disciples were so struck by His suffering that had just taken place that they spent that whole night in watchful vigil." "For the sake of the labor of the vigil" on the eve of Saturday, Cassian adds, "throughout all the Eastern churches there is not unjustly maintained on Saturday the relaxation of the fast" [^648]. It is remarkable withal that concerning a vigil on the eve of Sunday Cassian speaks not, although he dedicates a special chapter unto the question "wherein Sunday worship differs from the service of other days." Consequently, Sun*(Orig. p. 149)*day Matins (in the localities observed by Cassian) was so insignificantly longer than the weekday office, beginning only slightly earlier than it, as was the case in the Church of Jerusalem according unto the *Pilgrimage*. The Roman Catholic Church has preserved an echo of this practice, when it attaches the vigil not unto the feast itself, but unto the eve thereof. The Saturday vigil according unto Cassian has the following structure:

"first standing they chant (*concinuerunt*) three antiphons; then, sitting upon the ground or upon low stools, they execute responsorially (*respondent*) after a single singer (*uno modulante*) three psalms, unto which, however, the brethren in turn respond (*qui tamen singuli a singulis fratribus vicissim succedentibus sibi praebentur*) [^649]; and sitting in the same quiet posture they join unto all this three readings" [^650].
