The same was true among the Collyridians of the 4th century, among whom women celebrated sacred rites in honor of the Most Holy Virgin Mary, as also among the Cataphrygians [^875].

##### Acclamations and Rites Accompanying Preaching

Inasmuch as preaching, serving as an exposition of Holy Scripture and wholly grounded upon it, was likewise regarded, in some measure, as the word of God, so also was preaching framed with rites and acclamations almost identical unto the reading of Holy Scripture. Thus before the sermon the deacon invited those present unto silence and attention [^876], perhaps with the acclamation **"Let us attend"** (*Proschomen*). Before the instruction the preacher offered a prayer, presumably secretly [^877]. Before the instruction it was customary for the preacher to greet the people in the name of God [^878]. *(Orig. p. 179)* This greeting was usually expressed by the acclamations: **"Peace be unto you"** [^879] or: **"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, the love of God the Father, and the communion of the Holy Spirit be with you all,"** with the response **"And with thy spirit"** [^880]. The sermon began with diverse prayerful acclamations, for example, **"Blessed is God"** (*Eulogetos ho Theos*) [^881]. The conclusion of the sermon was ordinarily a doxology unto the Holy Trinity [^882].

As regards the bodily posture in which the sermon was delivered and heard, at least the bishop usually delivered the sermon seated upon his ambo [^883], which, perhaps, was a borrowing from the synagogue and was founded upon the example of the Savior [^884]. But in St. John Chrysostom indication is also made of the preacher standing [^885]. The hearers always stood. Blessed Augustine says: "that I may not detain you long, since I speak sitting, whereas it is difficult for you to stand..." [^886] And Constantine the Great refused to sit during the lengthy sermons of Eusebius of Caesarea [^887]. Augustine permitted only weak and infirm listeners to sit down [^888].

#### The Origin of Monasticism

Monasticism in the Church appeared much earlier than the 4th century. From her first days there was always within her something corresponding unto this institution. Not to speak of the great *(Orig. p. 180)* asceticism of John the Baptist, which properly opened the era of the New Testament, both the Savior and the Apostles presupposed and sanctioned ascetic dispositions in certain Christians [^889]. In the writers of the 2nd and 3rd centuries, indications increasingly occur concerning the existence in the Church of an entire class of persons who made continence the goal of their lives [^890]. In the 3rd century such ascetics already constitute entire communities. At least there is record of communities of virgins from this era; into one of such communities (*eis parthenona*) St. Anthony placed his only sister before withdrawing into the desert [^891]. The virgins also differed in their outward appearance and clothing from ordinary Christians [^892]. A series of 3rd-century writers occupy themselves with the question concerning them, writing epistles unto them and treatises concerning them, for the most part praising their continence [^893], yet at times also rebuking their shortcomings [^894]. From the 2nd century examples are likewise known of withdrawal for a more or less prolonged period into solitary places for ascetic purposes [^895], sometimes on account of external inducements, for example, owing to persecutions against Christians [^896], yet frequently solely for ascetic struggles of continence. The latter phenomenon is known at least in Egypt, where before St. Anthony hermits were not uncommon, yet they struggled near their own villages, so that "a monk did not yet know the great desert" [^897].

##### Anchoritism

All these anchorites and even their communities, both by reason of their small number and their little renown, and because they did not break definitively with the former way of life, exercised no influence upon the elaboration of divine worship. This influence on the part of asceticism began when, with the further development of the latter, certain of the anchorites attained universal *(Orig. p. 181)* ecclesiastical fame, when their way of life (*modus vivendi*) and prayerful labors began to evoke imitation among many.

###### St. Paul of Thebes

The first ascetic of this kind was St. Paul of Thebes, concerning whom it was revealed unto St. Anthony himself that the former was greater than he. An Egyptian by birth, having withdrawn into the desert [^898] at the age of 15 during one of the persecutions against Christians, fearing the betrayal of his brother-in-law, St. Paul lived there without ever leaving for about 100 years (he died at the age of 113 in the year 341, when St. Anthony was 90 years old), without seeing a human face; he lived in a cave near a spring beside which a date palm grew; its fruits served him for food, and from its fronds he made clothing for himself. St. Anthony discovered this ascetic only a few days before his death [^899]. Yet thereby everything was done that such a life should not pass without a profound influence upon the Church. Perhaps the significance of Anthony himself in the development of monasticism was merely broader and more noticeable. For the history of divine worship, it was important here that the ascetic completely renounced the consolation afforded by public divine worship and replaced it with his own prayer. Thereby was laid the foundation for the elaboration of a new type of divine worship.

###### St. Anthony

St. Anthony the Great († 356) withdrew into the desert now exclusively from ascetic motives and spent therein his entire 105-year life from his twentieth year. He settled at first in a tomb-cave near his native village in Lower Egypt near the city of Heraclea and the Thebaid desert on the western bank of the Nile, then in an abandoned fortress of the eastern desert (between the Nile and the Red Sea), and finally in the depths of that same desert upon a mountain, in a cell hewn into the rock, of the length and breadth of a man's stature [^900]. St. Anthony nourished himself at first only with bread and salt, which was brought unto him some twice a year [^901]; in old age, partly in order to spare the labor of those who brought him bread, he began to cultivate a fertile plot in the desert, and at the request of his disciples began to eat olives and oil; St. Anthony took food once a day at sunset, remaining without food for 2 days and more, up to 4 or 5 [^902], frequently spending an entire night without sleep; he slept upon the bare ground, *(Orig. p. 182)* sometimes upon a rush mat [^903]. Everyone was especially astonished (which enhanced the attractive power of his ascetic feats) that under such a life "his body preserved its former appearance, not grown heavy from lack of movement, nor wasted away from fasts" [^904].

The constant occupation of Saint Anthony was prayer and the contemplation of God, wherein at the beginning he had to endure a grievous struggle against the thoughts and phantoms (*phantasiai kai schematismoi*) that troubled him [^905]. Against the latter St. Anthony, knowing their ultimate source (the demons), struggled through the gracious power of Holy Scripture, which he, having decisively refused in childhood (notwithstanding his cultured origin) to learn letters, could not read, but remembered from the readings in church [^906]; he especially made use in this struggle of certain passages of the Psalms, for example Ps. 117:7: "The Lord is my helper, and I shall look down upon mine enemies"; Ps. 26:3: "Though an host should encamp against me, my heart shall not fear"; Ps. 67:2: "Let God arise, and let His enemies be scattered, and let them that hate Him flee from before His face." This in general bears witness unto the extensive use of the psalms by St. Anthony in prayer. Moreover, this circumstance from the life of St. Anthony and other ascetics may have contributed unto the appearance in the liturgical typikon of prokeimena, *versicula*, *capitula*, and the like, whereof the 4th and 5th centuries knew nothing as yet. Very early St. Anthony recognized the necessity of joining manual labor unto prayer, a thought which, being very important and new, according to tradition was inspired unto the venerable father by a special vision (occurring already at the second place of his ascetic labors)—of an angel in monastic habit, weaving a rope from palm leaves in the intervals between prayer [^907]. From that time until the end of his life he alternated prayer with the weaving of baskets and mats from palm leaves. In the account of the *Lausiac History* concerning the testing unto which St. Anthony subjected St. Paul the Simple before admitting him unto himself as a disciple, the prayerful and ascetic daily routine of St. Anthony himself is partly described. After the labor of St. Paul (at weaving rope) which continued until the ninth hour, St. Anthony, it seems, intended to offer him food; yet for the sake of testing he postponed this until sunset. Then

"Anthony brought and placed upon the table four dry loaves of bread, of some 6 ounces each, and moistened one for himself and three for him; then he began to chant a psalm that he knew, and having chanted it twelve times, he prayed as many times, in order in this also to *(Orig. p. 183)* test Paul (to prolong the time before eating). After 12 prayers Anthony said unto him: Go, eat. Forbidding him, however, thereafter to eat, the venerable father 'said unto him: Arise, pray, and lie down to sleep. At midnight Anthony awakened him unto prayer,' and continued to pray until the ninth hour of the day. After the meal, which took place late in the evening, Anthony read 12 prayers and chanted 12 psalms. After the prayer they slept a little during the first sleep; then they arose again and chanted psalms from midnight until the very day" [^908].

Thus in the prayer of St. Anthony a definite order (*taxis*) is observed both in relation to its hours and its quantity.

##### Subsequent Anchoritism

###### St. Sisoes the Great

Once having appeared, asceticism could not but develop and grow not only in extent, but also in degree and intensity. Indeed, the anchorites following Anthony the Great elaborate in detail and perfect unto the utmost limits the ascetic life and monasticism. If they do not surpass the first founders of monasticism, they evoke greater amazement by their ascetic feats, and consequently exercise an irresistible influence upon the entire structure of church life. These were living typika of fasting and prayer, whereof written typika were faint copies, and unto which in any event our Typikon owes more than unto all subsequent typika, ktetorial and otherwise. Of the incredible results which this younger generation of Egyptian ascetics achieved, an approximate idea may be given by certain traits from the life of St. Sisoes the Great († 429).

"A brother asked Sisoes why he, having left Scete (a monastery founded by the younger contemporaries of St. Anthony in the Thebaid desert), had settled here (in the desert). The elder replied: When Scete began to become populous, and I heard that Abba Anthony had fallen asleep, I arose and came unto this mountain; and finding this place tranquil, I settled here for a little time.—And is it long, abba, that thou hast lived here?—the brother asked.—72 years,—the elder replied" [^909]. "The disciple of Abba Sisoes often used to say: Abba, arise, let us eat. The elder would say: Have we not eaten yet, my son? We have not eaten, father, the disciple replied. Then the elder would say: If we have not eaten, let us eat" [^910]; yet they ate no more than once a day—in the evening. "They recounted concerning Abba Sisoes: he did not eat bread (but only raw herbs). On the feast of Pascha the brethren entreated him to share the meal with them. The elder said unto them: I can do one of two things: I will eat either bread or the dishes prepared by you. They said unto him: Eat only bread. And so he did" [^911]. "One father related concerning Sisoes: once, desiring to overcome sleep, he suspended himself from a cliff in a cave. An angel came, took him down, and forbade him to repeat this, lest he set an example for others" [^912]. "They recounted concerning Abba Poemen: When certain elders visited him *(Orig. p. 184)* and, speaking of the elders, mentioned Abba Sisoes, Poemen would say: Cease speaking of Abba Sisoes; for his deeds are beyond narration" [^913].

#### The Influence of the Egyptian Anchorites upon Monastic Typika

##### a) Fasting

In general, the life of the Egyptian ascetics of this era outlined an ideal for all aspects of the monastic order touched upon by written typika. Most of all, of course, was accomplished in regard to fasting. Spontaneously there became established certain norms, rules, minimal requirements—and very arduous ones—both as regards the kind of food for the ascetic, and concerning the time of its taking and the durations of fasting. Meat, of course, was unconditionally not used [^914], yet the tasting thereof in case of necessity was not accounted a transgression of the vow [^915]. Dairy products, it seems, were occasionally permitted [^916], fish— *(Orig. p. 185)* more frequently [^917]. Wine was in principle allowed [^918], but many did not drink it [^919] and in general nothing beside water [^920]. The ordinary food consisted, among the majority of the Egyptian anchorites, it seems, of bread alone with salt, with abstinence from all else [^921]; others for decades nourished *(Orig. p. 186)* themselves only with raw herbs, denying themselves even bread [^922]; but many permitted themselves in general any, provided it were the simplest, vegetable food, and even at times (for example, on feast days) oil [^923].

As regards the time of taking food, before the ninth hour (3 o'clock in the afternoon) they did not eat at all [^924]; but the most zealous ascetics could boast that *(Orig. p. 187)* "the sun had never seen them eating" [^925], and demanded of their disciples to take food not at the ninth hour, but in the evening [^926]. In regard to prolonged total abstinence from food, the norm for an accomplished ascetic was considered the taking of food every two days [^927]; this certain anchorites counseled also unto their disciples [^928]. Others tasted no food for 5 days [^929] or ate once a week [^930]. As exceptional cases, instances of total fasting for 40 days [^931] and more [^932] are recorded. Through long practice of such fasting certain anchorites attained, it seems, unto such a state that after two days of total abstinence they felt no hunger whatever [^933]. But with the passage of time asceticism nevertheless arrived at the conclusion that total abstinence for longer than one day, presumably as being not within the capacity of everyone, was dangerous, and they ceased to recommend it [^934].

*(Orig. p. 188)*
With such a fast, into which the entire life of an anchorite was turned, it was nevertheless recognized as necessary to honor the general fasts of the Church, to distinguish them from the series of ordinary fasts, and, of course, by an intensification of abstinence, although among certain anchorites there was, it seems, nowhere further to go in this regard. These were thus fasts of fasts. Before the Great Fast (*Tessarakoste*), St. Macarius of Alexandria, "having broken off a great quantity of palm branches (for manual labor), stood in a corner and throughout the entire Great Fast until Pascha itself took no bread, touched no water, bowed not his knees, sat not down, lay not down, and tasted nothing save a few leaves of dry cabbage; and these he ate only on Sundays, and that so that they might see that he was eating, and that he himself might not fall into conceit; and if ever he went forth from the cell for any necessity, he returned as quickly as possible again and took up his work; not opening his lips and speaking not a word, he stood in silence; his entire occupation consisted in prayer of the heart and in weaving the branches which were in his hands" [^935]. St. Paul the Great, the Galatian, "spent the entire Great Fast with a small measure of lentils and a jar of water, and remained in seclusion until the feast itself" [^936]. The ascetics also honored the fast of Wednesday and Friday. "It is not permissible," said St. Apollos of Hermopolis (early 5th c.), "to violate without absolute necessity (*nisi grandis aliqua necessitas fieret*) the universal (*katholikas*, *legitima*) fasts (of Wednesday and Friday), for on Wednesday the Savior was betrayed, and on Friday crucified; therefore, whosoever violates this fast, together with His enemies betrays and crucifies the Savior. If in the fast a brother come unto thee, having need of refreshment (according to Rufinus: and before the 9th hour wishes to be strengthened for the journey), set a table for him alone; yet if it please him not, constrain him not; for we all have a common tradition concerning the fast" [^937].

##### b) Sleep and Clothing

Having by their life composed the chapter on fasts for later monastic typika, the anchorites exercised influence upon these typika also through other aspects of their life, namely by their attitude toward sleep and clothing. Sleep the ascetics considered as dangerous an enemy unto them as the belly. Many of them slept no more than an hour in a day, and that not lying down, but seated [^938].

*(Orig. p. 189)*
The hermits wore clothing sometimes made of palm leaves, or by reason of decrepitude utterly unfit for use [^939]. It is superfluous to remark what an influence such practice exercised upon the daily schedule prescribed by monastic typika (the majority of services at night, certain typika, as we shall see, had services of the 12 "night hours") and upon the chapter in them "on garments and footwear."

##### c) Prayer

The anchorites of the 4th and 5th centuries laid the foundations also for the elaboration of the monastic rule of prayer and psalmody. Our Typikon specifically inherited from them the extensive use of the Psalter. "The love of psalmody gave birth to monasteries," says Blessed Augustine [^940]. The narratives of the life of the anchorites are replete with mentions of the Psalter and citations of it in their sayings. Very early among the ascetics special rules were established also for the prayerful application of the Psalter. The most ancient rule of this kind was probably the reading at one time of the entire Psalter as a day or night prayer.

"One elder came unto another; the latter, having cooked some lentils, said: Let us perform a small synaxis (*synaxin*)—and one of them read the entire Psalter, while the other recited from memory two of the major prophets. When morning came, the visiting elder departed; they had forgotten about food" [^941].

"Once Abba Serapion († ca. 358) was passing through an Egyptian village, and seeing a harlot standing by her chamber, said unto her: Await me this evening; I will come unto thee and spend the night with thee.—Very well, abba, the harlot replied. And so she prepared herself and spread the couch. In the evening the elder locked the door and said unto her: Wait a little; I must only fulfill our customary rule (*epeide nomon echomen, heos hou poieso auton*). And the elder began his synaxis (*tes synaxeos*). Having begun the Psalter, he offered at (*kata*) each psalm a prayer (*euchen*) for her, entreating God to grant her repentance and salvation,—and God heard the monk. The harlot stood trembling and praying beside the elder. When the elder had finished the entire Psalter, she fell upon the earth. The elder took the Apostle, read much from it, and concluded his synaxis (*synaxin*)" [^942].

This harlot subsequently surpassed *(Orig. p. 190)* in her fastings, it seems, all the anchorites (she ate not for more than 40 days). This incident is characteristic for the view maintained therein regarding the gracious power of a prayer rule. Gradually, it must be, they began to reduce so very large a "rule" (the entire Psalter). Perhaps a rule was also fulfilled by Heron (mentioned above), when walking with the author of the *Lausiac History* and others through the desert, on the way he "read 15 psalms (a tenth part of the Psalter), then the great psalm (118?), then the Epistle to the Hebrews, then Isaiah and part of Jeremiah the Prophet, then Luke the Evangelist and Proverbs" [^943]. Not infrequent are indications of the use among the anchorites of 12 psalms as a prayer rule. Two anchorites who had chosen St. Macarius of Egypt as their director, when he visited them and passed the night with them, on the following morning proposed unto him:

"Wilt thou that we chant (*balomen*, *recitemus*) twelve psalms?—Very well, I replied,"—relates Macarius concerning this. "Then the younger chanted (*psallei*) 5 psalms, and after (*apo*) every 6 verses chanted one alleluia (literally: every, *apo*, 6 verses and 1 alleluia). And at each verse a ray of fire issued from his mouth and ascended unto heaven. In like manner, when the elder opened his mouth for singing, there issued from it as it were a cord of fire and reached unto heaven. And I also recited (*eipon*) a little from memory" [^944].

When a Roman ascetic in the monastery (Scete) was visited by a certain great Egyptian ascetic, at the onset of evening "they read (*ebalon*) 12 psalms and lay down. They did the same also at night," and again lay down [^945]. The same ascetic thus describes his prayer rule: "instead of music and singing I read through (*lego*) 12 psalms (by day or in the evening); in like manner also at night, for the sins which I have committed, immediately after taking rest (*arti met' anapauseos*—after a short sleep?) I perform my little office (*poio ten mikran mou leitourgian*)" [^946]. Besides the psalms and Holy Scripture, brief prayers were employed, recited hundreds of times. Paul of Ferme (4th c.) performed 300 prayers in a day, of which he kept count by drawing pebbles from his bosom (the germ of prayer ropes); when, however, he heard that a certain virgin performed 700 prayers, his rule began to seem small unto him, and he turned for the resolution of his perplexity unto St. Macarius of Egypt; the latter replied: "Behold, for sixty years now I perform only the 100 prescribed prayers (*tetagmenas euchas*)" [^947]. An example of such a brief prayer is given in the instruction of St. Macarius unto those who asked him: "How ought one to pray?"

— "There is no need for verbosity, but one must lift up one's hands and say: Lord, as Thou wilt and as Thou knowest, have mercy. And if temptation assail: Lord, help!"

[^948] As a memorial of these brief anchoritic prayers there serveth among us the prayer **"Lord Jesus *(Orig. p. 191)* Christ"** (*Gospodi Iisuse Khriste*), which is appointed to be recited hundreds of times by the illiterate in place of omitted church services. As the perpetual fast among the desert-dwellers was intensified during periods of church fasts, so likewise was their customary prayer rule increased for feast days.

"They recounted concerning Abba Arsenius, that on Saturday evenings toward the Lord's Day he would stand with his back unto the sun, and lifting up his hands unto heaven, would pray until the sun began to shine in his face; after which he sat down" (a vigil truly all-night) [^949].

On Sundays, as likewise on Saturday, the anchorites customarily communicated. "The monks dwelling in the desert are burned by the venom of evil demons, and they wait with impatience for Saturday and Sunday to go unto the fountains of water, that is, to draw near unto the Body and Blood of the Lord, in order to cleanse themselves from the defilements of the wicked one" [^950]. For this purpose the anchorites went for the most part unto neighboring churches, notwithstanding their remoteness [^951]. "They recounted that Abba Sisoes of Thebes was accustomed to run in haste unto his cell at the conclusion of the church service, and they said: a demon is in him" [^952]. Concerning the communion of anchorites with reserved Gifts, St. Basil the Great saith: "all the hermits (*monazontes*) dwelling in the desert where there is no priest, keeping the communion in their dwelling, communicate themselves" [^953]. There are indications of the celebration of the Liturgy specifically for an anchorite in his cell by a presbyter. "They recounted concerning Abba Mark of Egypt: he lived for 30 years without ever going forth from his cell; unto him there customarily came a presbyter to celebrate for him the holy oblation (*poiein autōi tēn hagian prosphoran*)" [^954]. "Unto a certain anchorite there went a presbyter, celebrating for him the oblation of the Holy Mysteries (*tōn hagiōn mystēriōn tēn prosphoran*)" [^955].

##### The Anchoritic Typikon

Thus in regard both unto fasting and prayer or divine worship there gradually became established among the holy anchorites a more or less uniform practice, common rules, a single typikon. This will not appear surprising if one take into consideration that intimate and constant intercourse wherein the desert-dwellers stood with one another, not only within the bounds of Egypt, but also the Sinaitic and Palestinian ascetics with the Egyptian; they frequently visited one another for mutual edification, while those nearest lovingly cared for one another; among them here and there luminaries of asceticism arose, becoming centers of spiritual instruction for a wide surrounding region. The anchorites constituted a single corporation, as it were a single monastery with a gradually evolving typikon and a certain organization. Beginners and the young *(Orig. p. 192)* had directors, yet the authority of the latter was wholly grounded upon immeasurable moral superiority [^956]. This was the most extensive and excellent monastery that the earth had ever beheld.

#### Anchoritic Monasteries of Ancient Christian Egypt

St. Anthony relinquished his seclusion after thirty-five years, at the second place of his ascetic labors. "Acquaintances coming unto him, seeing that he did not permit them to enter within the fortification (the abandoned one wherein he struggled), not infrequently spent days and nights in the courtyard. But since many strove and desired to imitate his ascetic life, while certain of his acquaintances came and broke down and opened the door by force, Anthony came forth as an initiate of sacred mysteries and a God-bearer from a certain sanctuary." Following the healings performed on the spot and words of edification, the venerable father "persuaded many to choose the monastic life; thus in the mountains monasteries appeared; the desert was populated by monks who had forsaken their possessions... By the power of his marvelous word numerous monasteries arose" [^957]. By the term "monastery" (*monastērion*, from *monazō*, to dwell alone; *monastēs*, one dwelling solitary) there is designated here (in Athanasius' *Life of St. Anthony*) a cell-cottage [^958] or cave [^959], as is evident from the fact that the abandoned fortification wherein St. Anthony dwelt is likewise termed his "monastery" [^960], as is further evident from the remark that before St. Anthony "monasteries were few in Egypt" [^961], and from the comparison of a monastery with a tent [^962]. When St. Anthony withdrew unto the final site of his ascetic labors, there soon arose there likewise an entire colony of monastic cells; the neighboring mountains were covered with them, but these too soon became cramped for the imitators of St. Anthony, and the monks began to settle upon the other side of the Nile near the city of Arsinoë [^963]. "These monasteries in the mountains were like taberna-*(Orig. p. 193)*cles filled with divine choirs of psalmists, lovers of learning, fasters, men of prayer, who were gladdened by the hope of future blessings and engaged in handiwork to distribute alms" [^964]. In this description are indicated also the occupations of the monks in the "monasteries" of St. Anthony. In the monastery-cell the entire day of the monk was to pass. In it he was to remain as far as possible without going forth: "As a fish," said St. Anthony, "taken out of the water dieth, so likewise perisheth the fear of God in the heart of a monk if he vainly goeth forth from his cell" [^965]. In this seclusion or enclosure of the monk within his cell St. Anthony distinguished diverse degrees. Unto total enclosure, wherein he himself lived (which, moreover, was likewise not absolute), he considered capable and admitted only a few. Unto St. Paul the Simple he saith: "If thou desirest to be a monk, go unto a cenobitic monastery (*koinobion*), where there are many brethren who are able to bear with thy infirmities; for I dwell here alone"; only when Paul had endured a severe probation did St. Anthony prepare a cell for him some three or four furlongs (*stadia*) from his own [^966]. The majority of St. Anthony's disciples, while dwelling solitary in their cells, nonetheless maintained a certain communion with one another: "For instruction Scripture is sufficient," Anthony said unto his disciples, "yet it is fitting for us to comfort one another by faith and encourage one another with a word" [^967]. In what specifically and concretely the common life in the "monasteries" directed immediately by St. Anthony was expressed, the preserved accounts do not permit us to say. They make no mention of the monks' prayers, whether common or private [^968], nor of their food and measure of abstinence. There are indications only of a common meal [^969]. Yet the system of spiritual direction and communal governance emerges quite clearly in the accounts. Apparently the young monks were under the unflagging supervision of the senior and experienced ones. "A monk," said St. Anthony, "ought frankly to tell the elders how many steps he taketh, or how many drops he drinketh in his cell, lest in any way he err therein" [^970]. As the supreme director of spiritual life in the monasteries that sprang up beside the site of St. Anthony's ascetic labors, he himself, of course, was recognized. In the "monasteries" nearest unto his dwelling he "frequently discoursed" [^971] with the monks. One such discourse, which must be a typical one, uniting *(Orig. p. 194)* within itself the diverse instructions of the venerable father at different times (on the struggle with demons), is transmitted and described by St. Athanasius: "On a certain day he came forth, and all the monks gathered unto him, desiring to hear a word from him. Anthony then spoke unto them in the Egyptian tongue" [^972]. Sometimes the venerable father took part also in the common meal of the monks: "Not infrequently, when drawing near with many other monks to taste of food and calling to mind spiritual food, he refused to taste thereof and went far away from them, accounting it a shame for himself if others saw him eating. Yet by reason of the necessary requirement of the body he took food, but in solitude, and not infrequently also together with the brethren, being as much ashamed before them as hoping to offer them an edifying word for their profit" [^973]. The influence and authority of St. Anthony in his monasteries were wholly grounded upon his moral height. His customary designation among the monks was "the Great": "The Great hath spoken," "The Great hath done" [^974]. "And his countenance possessed a grave and extraordinary grace. Anthony received also from the Savior this gift: whenever the venerable father was surrounded by a multitude of monks, and anyone who had not known him previously desired to see him, the one wishing so, passing by the others, went straightway unto Anthony, as though drawn by his gaze" [^975].

Thus the monasteries of St. Anthony were of the anchoritic type, "serving as it were as a transitional stage from strict anchoritism unto a strict cenobitic community" [^976]. In them there were not only no written rules whatever [^977], but the order of life was not elaborated in detail; only the general spirit of this order was outlined. It is scarcely probable that in the monastic settlements, the monasteries (in the broad and later sense of the word) founded by St. Anthony, there were, beside St. Anthony himself, any general abbas or hegumens [^978]. *(Orig. p. 195)*

##### Nitria

Somewhat more complex in arrangement and closer unto cenobitic monasteries (*cenobia*) was a series of Egyptian monasteries founded during the lifetime of St. Anthony by his fellow-laborers or younger contemporaries. The most significant of these monasteries were Nitria, Scete, and Kellia (*The Cells*). The first was founded upon the Nitrian (*nitron*—natron, nitre) mountain (a desert plateau) south of Lake Mareotis, at a distance of 40 Roman miles (*millia*, 40,000 paces) from Alexandria. Of the Egyptian ascetics the first to settle here, and consequently the founder of this monastery, was St. Ammon, who began his solitary life in the 40th year of his age, passed about 20 years in the desert, and fell asleep prior unto St. Anthony (c. 350), with whom he had met [^979]. At the beginning of the 5th century there were up to 5,000 monks upon the Nitrian mountain [^980]; they lived in separate cell-dwellings (*tabernacula*), whereof there were up to 50 of diverse size; in some of these dwellings there lived more monks, in others fewer (*pauci*), and in yet others only one. The monks were under the direction of a single "father" (*sub uno patre posita*) [^981]. This direction belonged unto one of the eight presbyters who were attached unto the church of Nitria, and passed upon his death unto the next among them: "so long as the first presbyter liveth, the others celebrate not, judge not, and deliver no instructions, but only sit with him in silence." Corporal punishments (strokes of the scourge) were employed. The life of the monks was one of labor. The monastery possessed a well-ordered economy: in it were bakeries preparing bread not only for its own needs, but "likewise for the anchorites who had withdrawn into the inner desert, unto the number of 600"; there were their own physicians and apothecaries; wine was prepared not only for their own consumption, but also for sale; and there was a guest-house (*xenodochium*). In church they assembled only on Saturdays and Sundays. Yet daily, at least in the evening, divine service was celebrated in the cells: "upon the onset of evening one may stand and listen in each cell unto songs of praise and psalms chanted unto Christ, and prayers sent up unto the heavens; one would think that he had been caught up and transported unto heaven" [^982].

##### Kellia

At a distance of 10 Roman miles (*millia*) from Nitria was situated another remarkable monastery of ancient Christian Egypt—Kellia (*The Cells*). It was founded by Nitrian monks, lovers of complete solitude, and was of a purely anchoritic type. One of the first director-presbyters was St. Macarius of Alexandria († 494) [^983]. The monastery consisted of a multitude of solitary cells, the distance between which was such that from one cell it was *(Orig. p. 196)* not possible either to see another or to hear anything from thence [^984]. Some cells were so small that in them it was impossible to lie down stretched out unto one's full stature [^985]. The monks sat without leaving their cells; only on Saturday and Sunday did they assemble in church, and "there they looked upon one another as though returned from heaven"; if anyone was absent from this assembly, this was a sign of his illness, and the brethren visited him, supplying him with what was necessary for life [^986]. Some in the monastery led an even more reclusive life, not going forth from their cell for 40 days [^987]. On feast days a meal was likewise arranged in the church [^988]. The clothing of the monks differed somewhat from the ordinary local attire: "A certain father related that under Abba Isaac (5th c.) a brother came into the church in Kellia in a small cowl (*koukoulion*); the elder cast him out, saying: 'Here are monks, but thou art a layman; thou canst not be here'" [^989]. Like other Egyptian monasteries, the monks were buried here in that *leviton* (a tunic with short sleeves) and cowl wherein they had received the monastic habit and which in the course of life they put on only for communion of the Holy Mysteries [^990]. Concerning the height of the ascetic life in the monastery such an incident testifieth: once a bunch of fresh grapes was sent unto St. Macarius; although he then was very hungry, he sent the grapes unto a sick brother, the latter sent them unto another, and so the grapes made the round of the entire monastery and returned again unto the superior [^991]. Monophysitism penetrated into the monastery, and subsequently there were two churches therein: one for the Orthodox, and the other for the Monophysites [^992].

##### Scete

Almost the most significant of the Egyptian monasteries of that era was the so-called Scete (Coptic *Shiēt*—vast plain). Founded by St. Macarius the Great or of Egypt († 390) [^993], it was situated south of Kellia, still further into the depth of the Egyptian (Libyan) desert, at a distance of twenty-four hours' journey from Nitria; unto this place there was not even a road, but the way had to be directed by the courses of the stars. For life in such a wilderness, destitute of a sufficient quantity of water, an extraordinary strength of spirit was required [^994]. The governance of the monastery was con-*(Orig. p. 197)*centrated in the assembly of the brethren, which took place customarily in church under the presidency of the presbyter [^995]; at these assemblies theological questions were likewise decided [^996]. Minor matters of administration were concentrated in the hands of the presbyter; he, for example, had charge of the economic department of the monastery [^997], and in general occupied an honorable position among the brethren [^998]. (The first to be ordained unto the presbyterate in Scete was St. Macarius the Great) [^999]. Scete was renowned for fasting. The customary food of the brethren here was bread alone. Unto the question of John Cassian concerning the daily norm of food for a monk, the Scetic Abba Moses replied: "We know that concerning this matter our fathers frequently discoursed; and having examined diverse modes of abstinence, consisting in that some nourished themselves only with legumes (*leguminibus*), others only with herbs (*oleribus*) or fruits (*pomis*), they preferred unto them all the nourishment of bread alone, recognizing as the most suitable quantity thereof two small loaves (*paxinacia*), weighing both together about a pound (*libra* = 12 ounces or 24 *lota*)." Unto the remark of Cassian's companion that it would be too much to eat such bread all at once, Moses replied: "If you desire to experience the power of this determination, adhere steadfastly unto this measure, adding nothing cooked (*coctionis pulmentum*) either on Sunday or on Saturday, nor on the occasion of a visit of brethren; for by strengthening oneself with cooked food, one may not only be content with a smaller measure on the remaining days, but likewise without labor refrain for a long time from using any other food" [^1000]. Unto Germanus' question, what then is to be done if after taking food (bread) in the specified measure, that is, after the ninth hour, a guest visit the monk, unto whom it is necessary to offer a meal and share it with him, Moses adviseth: at the ninth hour (the customary time of taking food) eat only one of the two loaves, and leave the other until evening in case of a brother's visit; if he come, eat the loaf together with him; yet if not, then alone [^1001]. Any other food beside bread was considered in Scete an impermissible luxury.

"Once Abba Achillas (5th c.) in Scete came into the cell of Abba Isaiah and saw that he was eating. Upon his dish was water with salt (*halas*). The elder, observing that Abba Isaiah hid the dish behind a basket, asked him: 'Tell me, what didst thou eat?' Isaiah replied: 'Forgive me, abba: I was cutting branches, and the heat came on; I took a morsel with salt, yet my throat was dried up from the heat, and the morsel would not go down; therefore I was constrained to pour a little water into the salt, that I might be able to eat. But forgive me!' Then the elder said: 'Come, look upon Isaiah, how he suppeth broth (*zōmon*) in Scete! If thou desirest to sup broth, go unto Egypt'" [^1002].

Unto John Moschus and Sophronius (early 6th c.) Abba John of Petra said: "Believe my words: when I was yet a youth in Scete, one of the fathers fell ill of the spleen. In the four lavras of Scete they sought for a little vinegar and found none. Such poverty and abstinence were among them, and there were about 3,500 fathers there" [^1003]. Abba Benjamin, presbyter of *(Orig. p. 198)* Kellia († ca. 392), recounted (concerning his stay in Scete):

"When after the harvest we returned unto Scete, there was brought unto us an alms from Alexandria, for each an alabaster vessel of pure oil. Upon the onset of the following harvest, the brethren brought into the church whatever remained with them. I had not opened the vessel, but piercing it with a needle I tasted a little of the oil, and it was in my heart as though I had committed a great transgression. When however the brethren brought their vessels as they were, while mine was pierced, I was put to shame, as though convicted of fornication" [^1004].

The same abba recounted:

"We came in Scete unto a certain elder and wished to give him a little oil; yet he said unto us: Behold where the small vessel lieth which you brought me three years ago; as you placed it, so it hath remained" [^1005].

"At the time of first-fruits there was brought unto Scete a jar (*saitis*) of wine, that a cup might be distributed unto each of the brethren. When one brother desired to flee from this into a tholos (*tholos*—a round cottage), the tholos collapsed. Those gathered at the noise saw the brother prostrate and began to reproach him, saying: 'It hath rightly happened unto thee, vain one'; yet the abba defended him and said: 'Leave my son alone; he hath done a good deed; and as the Lord liveth, this tholos shall not be rebuilt in my days, that the world may understand that through a cup of wine a tholos collapsed in Scete'" [^1006].

Departures from this austere regime [^1007] were made for feast days, especially at the agape meals [^1008], yet reluctantly [^1009], and for guests [^1010]. *(Orig. p. 199)* The strictness of life in Scete began to decline already in the 4th century. According unto the testimony of Poemen (5th c.), "from the third Scetic generation and from the time of Abba Moses († 400) the brethren have made no new progress" [^1011]. In the words of the same Poemen, "Abba Isidore, presbyter of Scete, once spoke unto the assembly thus: 'Brethren, was it not for labor that we came unto this place? and now here there is no longer labor. Therefore, taking my sheepskin cloak (*melote*), I will go where there is labor, and there I shall find rest'" [^1012]. In the early 5th century the monastery was devastated by nomads, concerning which Abba Arsenius, having in view Alaric's sack of Rome in 410, said: "The world hath lost Rome, and the monks Scete" [^1013]. Scete continued, however, to exist even after this devastation. In the 6th century Monophysitism drew away the majority of the Scetic monks; today in the desert of Scete there is a Jacobite monastery [^1014].

##### Other Anchoritic Monasteries of Egypt

Beside these three most important monasteries, which possessed no written typikon but contributed unto its formation, in ancient Christian Egypt there arose yet another series of monasteries of the same type, which without doubt likewise exercised a certain influence upon the elaboration of later monastic rules. Thus upon Mount Pherme, south of Nitria on the way unto Scete, there lived up to 500 ascetics [^1015], among whom St. Paul was especially renowned, and who probably constituted a single community. Near Hermopolis (in the Thebaid) was the monastery of Apollos or Apollonius (according unto Rufinus), having about 500 brethren. A peculiarity of this monastery was the daily communion of the Eucharist at the ninth hour of the day: "After communion (sometimes, according unto Rufinus) they sat down to listen unto the instruction *(Orig. p. 200)* of Apollos, which continued until evening; then (according unto Rufinus; according unto Palladius—before the instruction, immediately after communion) they took food, after which some withdrew into the desert and there throughout the entire night recited Holy Scripture from memory, while others remained at the place of assembly and spent the whole night until dawn in hymns and praises (*laudibus*) unto God; and yet others, having descended from the mountain at the ninth hour (for communion) and received the Eucharist, straightway withdrew again, contenting themselves with spiritual food alone until the next ninth hour; and thus they acted (according unto Palladius—many of them) during many (*plurimos*) days. And amid such ascetic labors they had always such joy, gladness, and exultation (*exultatio*) as is impossible upon earth among ordinary men; among them was none gloomy or sorrowful; and if anyone appeared sorrowful, Abba Apollos immediately asked concerning the cause of his grief and revealed what was in the secret of each one's heart."

Apollos likewise instilled in all the thought of the necessity of daily communion for a monk [^1016].

Among other monasteries of presumably the same type were the monasteries of the Thebaid city of Oxyrhynchus. According unto Rufinus, in this city (which now presents sand-covered ruins) there were about 10,000 monks and about 20,000 virgins; ancient public edifices and temples were converted here into monasteries, and of the latter there were more than of private houses; under the influence of the monasteries the inhabitants of the city were distinguished by singular piety (possessing twelve churches beside the monastic ones) and by hospitality, especially toward itinerant monks [^1017]. Near the city of Heracleopolis there was the monastery of St. Isidore, distinguished by strict enclosure: the brethren had absolutely no communication with the world and admitted strangers no further than the guest-house at the gates; the monks of this monastery, as its porter-presbyter recounted unto Rufinus and Palladius, were "so holy that almost all were able to work miracles, and none of them was ever sick unto death; yet when the time of departure arrived for any of them, he, having beforehand announced this unto all, lay down and died" [^1018]. Near the city of Arsinoë was a series of monasteries with 10,000 monks under the direction of St. Serapion: "Through the brethren he gathered a multitude of provisions; for at the time of harvest all the monks brought unto him the grain products which they received in place of wages for reaping the neighboring fields, and all this the abba used for the relief of the poor, so that none suffered want in the vicinity; bread was sent unto the poor even as far as Alexandria; this, moreover, was done also by other monasteries of Egypt" [^1019]. It is possible that of the same semi-cenobitic type were the monasteries near Alexandria, wherein the author of the *Lausiac History* lived for about three years, and wherein he reckons about 2,000 "exceedingly great, zealous, and valiant men" [^1020]. *(Orig. p. 201)*

#### St. Pachomius and His Monasteries

St. Pachomius († 348) marked an epoch in the development of monasticism in that he founded the first cenobium (*koinos bios*—common life), a strictly cenobitic monastery, and gave it a written typikon. A native of Upper Egypt—a region considerably distant from Lower Egypt (the sphere of life and activity of the first Egyptian anchorites and the majority of the above-named monasteries), and differing from it in climate (being more torrid)—a pagan by birth, who embraced Christianity under the captivating power of Christian virtues, St. Pachomius initially secluded himself in an abandoned temple of Serapis, cultivating vegetables and palm trees and deriving thence sustenance not only for himself, but likewise for the poor; after three years Pachomius went unto the renowned anchorite of that region, Palamon, around whom a community of monks had already arisen; since few were able to endure that way of life which Palamon demanded of his disciples, the latter began to turn Pachomius away from him also, pointing out unto him the arduousness of the impending ascetic feats:

"We always watch through half of the night, meditating upon the word of God; very frequently from evening until morning we twist ropes, in order to combat sleep and furnish ourselves with what is necessary for the support of the body; whatever remaineth over beyond our need we give unto the poor. We know not what it meaneth to eat oil or anything cooked or to drink wine; in summer we fast daily until evening, and in winter for two and three days together. The rule of common prayers [^1021] among us is to pray 60 times by day and 60 times by night, beside those prayers which we offer at every moment and whereof we know no count."

After several days of testing Pachomius, Palamon clothed him in monastic garments, girded him with the monastic belt, and began to accustom him especially unto night prayers and vigils. Upon the death of Palamon, Pachomius settled in the deserted village of Tabennisi ("palm of Isis") [^1022], concerning which he had received a revelation while Palamon was yet living, that a great monastery would arise here. Thither came unto him his brother John, who soon died, and then gradually around him a monastery arose. Initially it consisted, beside Pachomius, of three men. But soon the renown of Pachomius attracted unto him anchorites well known in Egypt (for example, St. Cornelius). With his monks the venerable father built and maintained a church in a neighboring village, and when up to 100 brethren had gathered, he built also a church within the monastery, whereon Saturdays the monks attended divine service in the village church, while on Sundays a presbyter came unto the monastery and celebrated the Liturgy here. Holy orders Pachomius himself did not receive, nor did he permit others in his monastery to receive them, to prevent pride. The monastery consisted of several houses, in each of which there was a superior and an assistant ("second"); the monks engaged in diverse crafts, especially the plaiting of rush mats; all this afforded the monastery considerable means, but, of course, the monies received went for common needs *(Orig. p. 202)* and charity (being at the disposal of a special steward); among the monks, moreover, were such as could not distinguish gold from silver (having entered the monastery with their parents). The principal director of the monastery, of course, was Pachomius himself, and the principal instrument of governance in his hands was discourse with the monks. Beside private discourses, St. Pachomius delivered three general instructions in the course of the week: one on Saturday and two on Sunday. On Wednesday and Friday the house superiors delivered instructions unto their monks. Food on non-fasting days consisted of cheese, eggs [^1023], cooked vegetables, and broth made from them; on Wednesdays and Fridays many ate nothing at all; others tasted food once in two days. All ate not more than once a day—some at the 6th hour, others at the 7th, 8th, 9th, 10th, 11th, or in the evening with the appearance of the stars. Such a picture of life in the Tabennesiote monastery is given by the *Lives* of St. Pachomius, preserved in diverse recensions—Greek, Latin, Coptic (in two dialects—Memphitic and Thebaic), Ethiopic, and Arabic; the greater part of this information is found in the Coptic *Life*, preserved in a 10th-century manuscript [^1024]. With this picture the description of Rufinus and Palladius fully agreeth. This description pertaineth unto that time when in Tabennisi there were already about 3,000 monks and they were governed by St. Ammon (end of the 4th c.): "the monks took food with their faces covered, casting their eyes down, that they might not see how a brother sitting near was eating; at table all kept such strict silence that it seemed as though one were in the desert; they sat down at table only for appearance' sake, in order to conceal their asceticism; once or twice they would raise their hand unto their mouth, taking bread or olives or whatever else was offered at table, and having tasted of each dish a single time, therewith were content; others, having eaten a little bread, touched nothing further; while others contented themselves with only three spoonfuls of gruel (*zōmou*)" [^1025]. During the Forty Days' Fast (Great Lent) the Tabennesiot monks, according unto the words of Palladius, did not partake of cooked food; moreover, certain ones then took upon themselves yet special ascetic labors: some took food in the evening, others after five days, while others stood all night at prayer and during the day sat at handiwork [^1026].

When the sister of St. Pachomius, Mary, came unto him, he, refusing to see her, advised her through the gatekeeper to settle in solitude at a considerable distance from Tabennisi, on the other side of the Nile, where he built a dwelling for her; around the latter there soon arose a convent of women with the same order of life as in the monastery of men; the nuns prepared woolen garments for the latter and in return received from thence the means of subsistence. When the ever increasing number of monks in Tabennisi rendered the monastery cramped, *(Orig. p. 203)* St. Pachomius founded another monastery not far off in the locality of Pbow (Faou), and thereafter yet seven monasteries. Over all of them St. Pachomius had direction, having settled in Pbow. The venerable father frequently visited the monasteries. In Pbow the monks of the other monasteries assembled twice a year—at Pascha and in the autumn, when they rendered an account of their labors unto the steward (*oikonomos*). Here they baptized catechumens during the Forty Days' Fast. When many Greeks began to enter the monastery (originally there were only Copts in them), Theodore, a former reader of the church of Alexandria, was appointed intermediary (interpreter) in their relations with the superior and likewise their head. Prior unto his death St. Pachomius proposed unto the brethren to choose a successor for him, and when they left this choice unto him, he appointed as hegumen the aged Petronius, who fell asleep after a month and appointed Orsisius (Horsiesius) as his successor; as assistant of the latter in the governance of the numerous monasteries of St. Pachomius and as superior of Pbow there was appointed St. Theodore the Consecrated († 368, prior unto Orsisius), who founded not far from Pbow a convent of women [^1027].

##### The Internal Order of the Pachomian Monasteries

Such were the external aspect and history of the Pachomian monasteries. The internal organization imparted by St. Pachomius unto his monasteries diverged considerably from the entire order of life both of anchoritism and of the above-enumerated Lower Egyptian monasteries of anchoritic type. The foundation here was authority, regimentation, and punishment (penance), principles that the anchorites in their spiritual direction refused to employ, while the anchoritic monasteries applied them only in the most restricted measure. Obedience now became the primary monastic virtue and is praised ever more insistently in ascetic literature [^1028]. When the cooks, during the absence of St. Pachomius, ceased preparing cooked broth on Saturdays and Sundays, contrary unto the typikon, seeing that the majority of the brethren did not eat it, and employed their free time in the fabrication of mats (the chief earnings of the monastery), St. Pachomius (upon the complaint of a certain monk concerning the deprivation of cooked food) ordered 500 mats woven through such economy to be burned. Unto a brother who had woven two mats instead of one in a day, St. Pachomius ordered him to bring them into church and ask forgiveness and prayers of the brethren, to sit without going forth in his cell upon bread and salt, and daily to weave two mats. Uncorrected monks St. Pachomius expelled from the monastery, and in certain years there were many such expulsions. Two suicides in the convent of women St. Pachomius forbade to be commemorated in prayers, or to celebrate the Liturgy for them, or to distribute alms, while all the sisters, for failing to prevent the deed, he excommunicated from communion *(Orig. p. 204)* for seven years [^1029]. The novelty or distinctiveness of such principles in the monastic life of that era will become evident from comparing them with the following facts from anchoritic practice:

"A brother asked Abba Sisoes: 'Give me an instruction.' The elder said: 'Why compellest thou me to speak vain words? Do what thou seest in me'" [^1030].

"A brother came once unto Abba Theodore of Pherme and remained with him three days, asking an instruction of him; yet the abba answered him not, and the brother departed sorrowful" [^1031].

"A certain sinning brother was cast out by the presbyter (hegumen) from the church; Abba Bessarion arose and went out together with him, saying: 'I too am a sinner'" [^1032].

St. Anthony twice sent back a monk expelled from a cenobium unto that same cenobium and thereby constrained them to receive him back [^1033].

"Once in Scete a brother fell into sin. The brethren, having assembled (Scete, as we have seen, was governed by an assembly of the brethren), sent for Abba (the hermit) Moses, yet he did not wish to go. Then the presbyter sent unto him with these words: 'Come, the assembly awaiteth thee.' The abba, arising, took a damaged basket, filled it with sand, and thus departed. The brethren, coming forth to meet him, ask him: 'What meaneth this, father?' The elder replied unto them: 'These are my sins pouring out behind me, yet I see them not, and I have come now to judge the sins of another.' The brethren, hearing this, said nothing further unto the (sinning) brother, but forgave him" [^1034].

A similar thing did Abba Pior in Scete on the occasion of such a judicial assembly of the brethren: he carried about the monastery a full sack of sand upon his shoulders in token of his own sins and a little sand in a basket before him in token of the sins of the fallen brother [^1035].

"There dwelt in a cenobium a certain hermit, Timothy by name. Rumor reached the superior that a brother had undergone temptation, and he asked Timothy: 'What is to be done with the fallen brother?' The hermit counseled him to expel him. When however they had expelled the brother, the temptation that had been with him befell Timothy also" [^1036].

It is not surprising that in St. Pachomius, in view of such divergence of the principles adopted by him for his cenobium from general ascetic practice, doubt sometimes arose as to their correctness; yet behold how it was resolved by one of the pillars of anchoritism. St. Macarius of Alexandria (presbyter of Kellia) "came unto Abba Pachomius of Tabennisi. Pachomius asked him: 'If the brethren observe not order, is it good to instruct them?' Abba Macarius replied unto him: 'Instruct and strictly judge thy subordinates, yet of strangers judge no one'" [^1037]. The work of Pachomius, according unto tradition, received approbation—already after his death—likewise from the head of anchoritism, *(Orig. p. 205)* St. Anthony [^1038]. Unto the Tabennesiots who visited him St. Anthony spoke concerning Pachomius: "Pachomius hath rendered a great service unto the Lord, uniting all these hosts and subordinating them unto a single rule in the work of serving the Lord. Before him a certain man, named Aut, began this service, but because his intention proceeded not from the depth of his heart, he did not receive this grace" [^1039]. The order of life in the Pachomian monastery, however much it differed from other monasteries in strictness and regimentation, was nonetheless not excessively harsh. It was calculated not only for ascetics of lofty strength of spirit and body, like anchoritism, but likewise for average and even feeble powers. When St. Macarius of Alexandria entered the Tabennesiot monastery secretly, he straightway so far surpassed all in ascetic labors that the brethren began to murmur against the superior for receiving him into the monastery: "From whence hast thou brought unto us this incorporeal man unto our condemnation? Either cast him out from hence, or all of us, be it known unto thee, this very day will depart from thee" [^1040]. It is not surprising that in the Pachomian monasteries there was no lack of monks, and they rapidly overflowed; at the falling asleep of St. Pachomius all the monks in the monasteries founded by him were numbered at up to 7,000 [^1041].

##### The Typikon Given by the Angel

Unto such a spirit of the Pachomian cenobium fully correspondeth that typikon which, according unto tradition, was given unto St. Pachomius by an Angel who appeared unto him with a bronze tablet [^1042]. These rules, defining in general the life in the cenobium in a lenient spirit, afford much place for private asceticism [^1043]. *(Orig. p. 206)* Build separate cells within a single structure [^1044], and in each of them let three monks dwell [^1045], having a common meal. Let them sleep not lying down, but upon sloping seats [^1046]. Clothing: a linen tunic without sleeves (*leviton*) and upon the shoulders a white goatskin (*melote*) [^1047], without which they must neither take food nor sleep; yet for communion let them take it off [^1048], untie the girdle [^1049], and draw near only in the *leviton* and cowl (*koukoulion*); upon their heads let them wear cowls [^1050] with embroidered crosses of purple color [^1051]. Divide the brethren into 24 ranks according unto the number of the letters of the Greek alphabet, so that unto each rank its own letter be assigned, beginning from *alpha* and *beta* in order, so that if the superior need to ask concerning anyone, he may ask: 'How fareth the rank of *alpha*?' or 'How fareth the rank of *beta*?' [^1052]. Therewith designate the least cunning and simpler ones by the letter *iota* (ι), and the insubordinate and intractable of disposition mark with the letter *xi* (ξ) [^1053], expressing in this manner by the very form of the letter the property of the inclinations, morals, and life of each. These signs shall be understandable only unto the spiritual [^1054]. A stranger from another monastery is not to be admitted unto the common meal [^1055]. One coming unto the monastery is not to be received prior unto three years of probation [^1056]; yet after the passing of three years, if he show capacity for higher ascetic labors [^1057], let him be received into the monastery [^1058]. At table eat with covered head, leaning down toward the dish and not looking about [^1059]. It is appointed to pray 12 times by day, 12 times in the evening, 12 times at night, and 3 times at the 9th hour of the day; at each prayer it is appointed to recite a psalm [^1060]. When the great Pachomius said unto this that the prayers were few, the Angel replied: "I have ordained it thus that the weak also without burden may fulfill this rule; for the perfect have no need of a law; they, abiding in their cells, spend their entire life in the contemplation of God [^1061]. A typikon I have given unto those whose mind *(Orig. p. 207)* is not yet mature, that they, even as insubordinate slaves out of fear of their master, may fulfill the common rule of life and attain freedom of spirit" [^1062].

In such form is this typikon transmitted in Palladius (in the *Lausiac History*), Sozomen, Dionysius Exiguus, and in the Arabic *Life of St. Pachomius*. There are no grounds to doubt the historical existence of such a typikon of St. Pachomius, although in it, seemingly, not all is authentic or accurately transmitted. In any case the transmitted rules bear the stamp of high antiquity, reflecting in themselves a still living connection with the old anchoritism [^1063]. Such in particular are the liturgical rules of this typikon. Characteristic is the prescription to celebrate at the 9th hour 3 prayers: this calleth to mind that prayer office which already in Tertullian was joined with the 9th hour [^1064]. Distinctive is the determination of prayers for the day, evening, and night at 12 prayers each [^1065]. This number of prayers, as also the typikon in general, according unto tradition, passed unto St. Pachomius from an Angel, whereas according unto another tradition, transmitted by Cassian [^1066], in Egypt it was appointed to celebrate 12 psalms at the evening and night offices likewise by the direction of an Angel, who appeared at a council of the fathers purposely deliberating upon this matter *(Orig. p. 208)* [^1067]. The prescription of the Angel in the Pachomian typikon to preface each meal by a prayer with a psalm evidently hath in view that meal which was joined with the communion of the Holy Mysteries or followed after it [^1068].

In the rules of the Angel almost all the most important aspects of monastic life are touched upon (food, sleep, clothing, reception into the monastery, its governance), yet they restrict themselves concerning each of them unto the most general and principled rules, without entering into particulars. In them there are no traces of the division of the monks by "houses" or of offices, except that of the abba, although in the *Lives* of Pachomius all this is presupposed. Therefore the rules of the Angel may be recognized as the initial sketch of the typikon given by St. Pachomius unto his monastery. Concerning divine worship they define the number of prayers, yet give no order (*ordo*) for them; evidently the *ordo* was left unto the personal discretion of each or unto custom. Concerning the Liturgy and the Hours, except the 9th, the rules make no mention whatever. Yet in the rules mention is made of "communion," which had to take place, evidently, at the Liturgy. The Liturgy could be celebrated on Saturdays and Sundays, when, according unto the words of the *Lives* of Pachomius, a priest came unto the monastery or the brethren went unto the neighboring church. Yet for other days the rules of the Angel make no mention of the Liturgy; in place of it they appoint 12 day prayers. According unto the testimony of St. John *(Orig. p. 209)* Cassian, who observed the life of the Egyptian monasteries at the end of the 4th century, in them public services were celebrated only twice a day—in the evening and at night: "throughout all Egypt and the Thebaid the number of psalms for the evening and night assemblies is determined at twelve" [^1069]. The day offices (except the Liturgy on Saturday and Sunday) Cassian regardeth as a later innovation, permitted originally in Palestine and Mesopotamia, and from thence passing over into Egypt. Thus the Pachomian Typikon of the Angel appointed prayers for precisely those offices which were then celebrated in Egypt (evening, night, and the 9th Hour), and instead of the weekday Liturgy introduced "day prayers." Since in the cenobia of Pachomius there was no priest, and the rules forbade the monks to aspire unto the priesthood, the absence of a daily Liturgy in them was wholly natural. This circumstance indeed constrained the Pachomian monasteries, which desired to remain secluded in the monastery without a presbyter [^1070], to introduce special services, more uniform, yet, of course, no less prolonged.

If these services could appear small ("the prayers are few," Pachomius objecteth unto the Angel), it was solely by comparison with the prayer rule of the anchorites, who, like Abba Palamon, prayed 60 times by day and 60 times by night [^1071].

##### The Rules of St. Pachomius in Later Recensions

The rules of the Angel could satisfy the monastery only in the initial stages of its existence. With the growth of the monastery and the multiplication of monasteries, a more detailed regimentation of life was required. The *Lives* of St. Pachomius testify that he gave unto his monasteries a detailed written typikon, which was read unto the brethren and learned by them by heart [^1072]. Yet one cannot say the same concerning another, more extensive collection of Pachomian rules. This *(Orig. p. 210)* collection is known today in three recensions. 1) The *Rules* (*Regula*) of St. Pachomius, translated into Latin by Blessed Jerome [^1073] (ca. 404) for the Latin monks of the Pachomian monastery in Canopus near Alexandria. In these rules detailed prescriptions concerning monastic life are given, yet there are few features of similarity with the picture of life in Tabennisi as it is depicted in the *Lives* of the originators of the cenobium. In general the *Rules* of Blessed Jerome represent not so much the original typikon of Tabennisi as its later codification, formed in the course of the 4th century under the influence of local needs of diverse Pachomian monasteries. Unto this testifieth already the fact that these *Rules* mention neither the letters of the Angel nor the 12 prayers, so firmly attested concerning Tabennisi both by the *Lives* [^1074] and by the *Lausiac History*. 2) Another recension of the *Rules* of St. Pachomius, likewise preserved in Latin translation, containeth the same rules, yet arranged in a different order and set forth more clearly than in Blessed Jerome [^1075]. 3) The briefest recension of the *Rules* containeth only 50 of them, the rules being brief (especially in the beginning) and destitute of later accretions; in tone and spirit they produce the impression of great antiquity [^1076]. Yet indubitable authenticity belongeth only unto those rules that are attested by the *Lives* of St. Pachomius and ancient church historians (Rufinus, Palladius, Sozomen).

###### The Rules of St. Pachomius Translated by Blessed Jerome

This recension falleth into 194 rules (*praecepta*), which are prefaced further by 16 rules (*praecepta et instituta*), 18 rules (*praecepta atque judicia*), and 11 rules (*praecepta ac leges*). All this was translated by Blessed Jerome from a Greek translation from the Coptic original, so that Blessed Jerome translated no longer from the original, but from a translation made by the monks of the Alexandrian monastery from the Egyptian language into Greek. The rules are set forth without system [^1077]. They are provided by Blessed Jerome with a brief preface wherein he giveth a general sketch of life in the Pachomian monasteries and explaineth the motives for his translation.

"In every Pachomian monastery," remarketh Blessed Jerome in the preface unto the translation of the *Rules*, "there is a father (abba), a steward (*oeconomus*), weekly servers (*hebdomadarii*), ministers, and housemasters (*praepositi*) separately for each house; in a house there dwell 40 or more or fewer brethren, obeying a single superior; while in a monastery there are 30 or 40 houses, which are united into three or four classes (*tribus*), so that those working at the same craft constitute one class." The abba of the monastery himself was chosen by the brethren or appointed by his predecessor; he possessed supreme authority in the monastery, yet shared it with the assembly of the elders and the steward; he appointed the housemasters (Rule 159), assigned labors unto the brethren according unto their abilities (Rule 49), transferred brethren from house to house (Rule 83), permitted leaves of absence from the monastery (Rules 52, 93), judged offenders, and confirmed the penances *(Orig. p. 211)* imposed by the housemasters (Rules 147, 151, 164). The deputy of the abba was the second after him (*secundus*), whose duties are not more closely defined in the rules [^1078]. The housemaster (*praepositus domus*) exercised immediate supervision over the monks of his house, who without his permission dared undertake nothing (Rule 157), even walking about the monastery (Rules 84, 52), or going into the cell of a brother (Rule 127); he received and distributed materials for labors, demanded an accounting thereof, and himself rendered it (Rules 26, 146, 123). Each housemaster had an assistant (*secundus*), who took his place during his absence or illness and had charge of domestic affairs (Rules 66, 70, 95). The financial administration in the monastery rested upon the steward, who had an assistant—the dispenser (*dispensator*). The rules afford a complete picture of monastic discipline. They define in detail the relation of the monk unto the property of the monastery, which was to be guarded as sacred (Rules 148, 149), and the rules of conduct of the brethren during prayer (Rule 49). Among the brethren each everywhere occupied a place according unto the time of his entrance into the monastery (Rule 1). Furthermore, the newly entered monk had to learn by heart the prayers and rules of the monastery (Rules 139, 140); for this purpose there came unto him at the 3rd, 6th, and 9th hours a senior monk, and standing before him, repeated the words after him (Rule 139); finally the novice had to learn by heart at least the Psalter and the New Testament (Rule 140). The entire life of the monk passed under constant surveillance and the strictest obedience; the slightest infraction of the rules was not left without punishment, penance. The degrees of penance were diverse—beginning from the admonition of a senior (Rules 102, 148, etc.) and ending with expulsion from the monastery; the most customary penances were standing while others sat (Rules 8, 22, 31, etc.), standing without girdle with bowed head or hands lowered (Rule 9, etc.); corporal punishments were likewise employed (for theft—Rule 149). Infraction of the rules was prevented also by this: that none of the brethren had the right to remain alone in the cell without the housemaster or the senior over the weekly labor *(Orig. p. 212)* (Rules 88, 107), while outside the monastery a monk had to go unconditionally with another monk appointed by the father of the monastery and obliged to keep watch over him (Rules 62, 63). The *Rules* regulate in detail also the labors of the monks. Concerning the weaving of mats, whereof the *Lives* speak so frequently, the *Rules* speak almost exclusively, scarcely touching upon other crafts; they define in detail how many mats a monk had to weave in a day (Rules 12, 26, 27, 74, 145–147, 177). They went unto labors outside the monastery as well—to cut reeds, gather firewood, herbs for pickling, and dates (Rule 78). And at these labors the monks were under the constant direction of the experienced (Rules 116, 145, 68, 134). As regards clothing and footwear, beside the tunic (*leviton*), sheepskin (*melote*), and cowl (*koukoulion*) mentioned in the Typikon of the Angel, the *Rules* mention the humeral scapular (*paramand*), a short mantle, sandals, and a staff (preface and Rule 81); of tunics it was appointed to have two, of which one was without sleeves, as well as cowls and sheepskins (Rule 91); the mantle was put on only for church; sandals were removed upon entering the church and refectory (Rule 101). Each of these articles the monk used with the knowledge and permission of the housemaster; washing garments was permitted only on designated days by direction of the housemaster (Rules 67–73). Food was distributed by direction of the housemaster (Rule 23). The customary food consisted of bread, cheese, vegetables, and cooked herbs (*pulmentum*), olives, dried dates, small salted fish, and sauce (*liquamen*) made of a special kind of herbs salted with vinegar (Rule 80); upon departing from the monastery the brethren received bread, salted olives, and cheese (Rule 80). Food was prepared twice a day—at dinner and supper; bread was distributed in the cells, each time for three days (Rules 37–40). Any other food was forbidden to be eaten even on journeys and at relatives' houses (Rules 46, 54). Wine and fish were permitted only unto the sick (Rule 45). "Whosoever desireth not to go unto the refectory (for the sake of abstinence), receiveth into his cell only bread, water, and salt for one day or for two days" (Rule 37). Beside the appointed hours of the meal, it was forbidden to taste food (Rule 75). At night before dawn (upon awakening) it was forbidden to drink water (Rule 87). "On other days (beside Wednesday and Friday, when they fasted until evening) some take food at midday, others in the evening, while others content themselves with food taken once *(Orig. p. 213)* at dinner or supper... Sitting at table, none ought to look upon others, but casting his eyes down unto his plate, meditate upon God or listen as the reader readeth something from Scripture" (Rule 36). One arriving late, conversing, or laughing at table was subjected unto penance (Rules 31, 33). Upon departing from the refectory the monk had to go straightway unto his cell, without stopping for conversation with another (Rule 34).

With prayer and divine worship the *Rules* do not occupy themselves specifically, mentioning them only in passing. Concerning the so-called "day prayers" it is observed that they were celebrated at midday (Rule 24). In addition, the *Rules* mention morning prayer at the hour of dawn (Rule 20) and six evening prayers (Rules 34, 121, 125), yet these must be evening domestic prayers in each house; in place of Vespers in an open place in the Typikon of the Angel, as we have seen, 12 prayers were appointed, or according unto others only 6. At the conclusion of morning prayer in each house the brethren discussed what the housemaster had said (Rule 20). If prayer was celebrated in church, the time for assembling in church and going forth unto it was signaled by the striking of the semantron (*klepalo*) by the weekly server with the blessing of the abba (Rule 24); this weekly server watched also over order in church (Rule 143). At the signal of the semantron the brethren went forth from their cells, whispering or repeating something by heart from Scripture and meditating upon it (Rule 3). For the singing of psalms in church each was called forth according unto rank and sang no more than one psalm; whosoever stumbled in singing bore penance (Rules 13, 14, 17, 127). Mention is made of readings (from Scripture) at prayers (Rule 13). Under penalty of penance it was forbidden at church and domestic prayers to laugh, converse, whisper, cough, yawn, and the like (Rules 7, 121), as well as to look upon others, how anyone prayeth (Rule 7). To bend the knees (for prayer following the chanting of a psalm) was necessary only after the weekly server standing in front and chanting, and the signal to rise from one's knees was given by the abba striking his hand upon the floor (Rule 6). Whosoever arrived late at church for one prayer by day or for three by night (Rules 9, 10), and at domestic prayers indifferently by day or by night, whosoever arrived late for one prayer (Rule 121), was subjected unto penance. Whether a monk were upon a journey, in the field, or in a boat, or at labor outside the monastery, alone or with others, or whether all were at labor outside the monastery, all hours of prayer and psalmody had to be observed there as well (Rules 142, 189).
