"On the Lord's Day, when the Sacrifice is offered, none of the weekly servers ought to be absent, so that in turn they may respond (chant antiphonally) unto the one who chanteth" (Rule 17), and the singing was then begun (chanting the antiphon first) by the senior (Rule 18)—the abba or the housemaster.

*(Orig. p. 214)*
### Egyptian Cenobia According unto Blessed Jerome

As we see, the *Rules* attest a significant development of the principles laid down by St. Pachomius as the foundation of his coenobitic life, and struggle against that natural decline of ascetical life in monasteries which inevitably setteth in with their external expansion. Approximately the same order of life and the same phenomena were observed in other Egyptian cenobia, insofar as we may judge from: a) the accounts concerning them in the works of Blessed Jerome, and b) the detailed description thereof in St. John Cassian.

"The first condition," saith Blessed Jerome, who observed the Egyptian coenobites in the 380s, "among them is to obey the seniors. They are divided into tens and hundreds, so that over nine men the tenth is the leader; while the centenary hath under him ten deans (*decani*). They dwell separately, yet in interconnected cells. Until the ninth hour, as is appointed, no one goeth unto another, save perhaps unto the aforementioned deans; so that if anyone be troubled by thoughts, he receiveth counsel from them. After the ninth hour they come together, chant psalms, and read the Scriptures according unto custom. Upon the conclusion of the prayers, when all are seated, he whom they call father, standing in their midst, begins an instruction. During his discourse such silence reigneth that no one dareth look upon another, no one dareth even cough. Praise unto the speaker is expressed in the weeping of the hearers. Tears roll softly down their cheeks, and grief doth not break forth even into a groan. But when he begins to proclaim things to come, concerning the Kingdom of Christ, concerning future beatitude and glory, thou wilt see all with a subdued sigh and eyes lifted up toward heaven, saying within themselves: **"Who will give me wings like a dove, and I will fly away and be at rest?"** (*Кто дастъ ми крилѣ, яко голубинѣ, и полещу и почию*, Ps. 54:7 [LXX; 55:6 MT]). Thereupon the assembly is concluded, and each decade with its senior goeth unto table, whereat by weekly turns they also serve. During the meal there is no noise whatsoever; no one speaketh. They feed upon bread and vegetables seasoned with salt alone. Wine is drunk only by the aged, for whom the meal is often shared with youths, in order to sustain the advanced age of the former and not retard the beginning fast of the latter. Then they rise together and, having chanted a hymn, disperse unto their dwellings; here until evening each talketh with his companions, saying: 'Have ye seen such-and-such an one? How much grace is in him, how much quietness? What a humble gait!' If they behold one who is weak, they comfort him; if one burning with love for God, they spur that brother onward unto ascetical labor. And since at night, over and above the common prayers, each still keepeth vigil in his sleeping chamber, they go around all the cells and, applying their ear, diligently ascertain what is taking place. If they notice anyone being slothful, they do not rebuke him; but pretending as though they know not, they visit him more frequently, and at first rather entreat than compel him to pray. The daily labors are so arranged: whatever is done under a dean is reported unto the steward, who himself also every month with great trembling rendereth account unto the common father. He likewise tasteth the food, how it hath been prepared; and since it is not permitted for anyone to say: 'I have neither undergarment nor outer cloak, nor a bed woven of reeds,' he arrangeth all things so that no one may lack what is needful for him. If anyone falleth *(Orig. p. 215)* sick, he is transferred unto a spacious chamber, and the elders minister unto him with such zeal that he doth not even think of urban comforts or a mother's care. Sundays are devoted solely unto prayer and reading; indeed, the coenobites do the very same at all times upon concluding their labors. Daily something is read from Scripture. Fasting is uniform throughout the entire year, save for the Holy Forty Days, during which alone it is appointed to live more strictly. From Pentecost onward, suppers are exchanged for midday dinners, so as thereby to preserve church tradition and not burden the stomach with a twofold taking of food." [^1079]

### Egyptian Cenobia According unto St. John Cassian

St. John Cassian († 435), for some time a monk of the Bethlehem monastery, undertook from thence a journey unto Egypt to become acquainted with the life of the hermits and monasteries there, spending the years 390–400 in those regions. After the pattern of the Egyptian monasteries he founded in Marseilles both a male and a female monastery, and in 417, at the request of Castor, Bishop of Apt, who had established a similar monastery in his own diocese, he described in his work *De Institutis Coenobiorum* (*On the Institutes of Cenobia*) the life of Egyptian cenobia, supplementing this information subsequently in the *Conferences of the Fathers* (*Collationes Patrum*). The structure of coenobitic life observed by St. Cassian in Egypt, however close it may be unto the Pachomian *Rules* in the recension of Blessed Jerome and unto the latter's observations, readily revealeth a further stage of development, a more precise definition of certain details, especially in regard unto prayer and divine worship. At the same time, Cassian makes us acquainted also with the practice of other contemporary monasteries, especially Western ones.

It is characteristic that St. Cassian begins his description of cenobia with monastic garments: such significance was already ascribed unto them. This description, beside detailed indications of the form of each garment—testifying that this form was already firmly established (close unto the present day)—speaketh also of the symbolic meaning of the vesture. The latter is noted also by Sozomen. [^1080] Concerning reception into a monastery, St. Cassian supplementeth the data of the Pachomian *Rules* with the following particulars: he who desireth to enter the monastery is kept for ten days before the gates, where he, "prostrating himself upon his knees before all passing brethren, being intentionally rebuffed and despised by all as one seeking to enter the monastery not out of piety, but out of necessity, being moreover assailed with insults and reproaches, affordeth proof of his perseverance." He who hath been accepted stands "in the midst of the assembly of the brethren, putteth off his own garments, and by the hands of the abba is clothed in monastic attire." [^1081] Penances, it would seem, were imposed more frequently and more strictly; the customary penance was: "when all the brethren are assembled for prayer, the offender, lying prostrate upon the earth, entreateth forgiveness and remaineth in his position until the service is concluded and *(Orig. p. 216)* the abba biddeth him rise from the floor." [^1082] The weekly turn of service (*hebdomada*), saith Cassian, not only in Egypt but throughout the entire East in monasteries, endeth upon Sunday evening following the psalmody appointed before retiring unto sleep. [^1083] Concerning the refectory, St. Cassian noteth the distinction of Egyptian cenobia from others in that here the strictest silence was observed at table, whereas in other places there had been adopted the custom—which St. Cassian deriveth from Cappadocia (from St. Basil the Great?)—of reading at table "something sacred." [^1084]

### Divine Worship in Egyptian Cenobia According unto Cassian

Yet, as observed, prayer and divine worship receive in the description of St. Cassian the most elaborate practice by comparison with the *Rules* of St. Pachomius, being accorded also the greatest amount of space in his work (two books out of four). In this regard St. Cassian noteth first of all a great diversity and mutability in the practice (*diversos typos ac regulas*) of diverse monasteries—doubtless pre-eminently Western ones—unto which he, by way of reproach unto them, contrasteth the uniformity and antiquity of the Egyptian practice of psalmody and prayer. Pausing first upon the "night prayers and psalmody" (unto which the entire second book of *De Institutis Coenobiorum* is devoted), St. Cassian saith that "among some it is appointed to recite (*dici*) twenty or thirty psalms, and that antiphonally and unto diverse melodies (*et hos ipsos antiphonarum protelatos melodiis et adjunctione quarundam modulationum*); others have attempted to surpass even this number; among some there are eighteen psalms; thus in diverse places we see a diverse rule (*canonem*) established. Unto others also, in regard unto the daytime offices of prayer (*orationum officiis*)—that is, the third, sixth, and ninth hours—it seemed that in performing within them obsequies unto the Lord (*in quibus haec Domino redduntur obsequia*), the number of psalms and prayers ought to correspond unto the number of the hour, whereas others appoint six psalms unto each daytime assembly (*conventibus*). Therefore I consider it necessary to bring forward the ancient patristic ordinance which unto this day is observed by the servants of God throughout all Egypt." [^1085] "Throughout all Egypt and the Thebaid... a single, lawful rule (*modum*) of prayer is kept at evening assemblies or nocturnal vigils." [^1086] "Both at evening and at nocturnal solemnities (*solemnitatibus*) they chant twelve psalms, yet so that they are followed each time by two readings, one from the Old and one from the New Testament. This order, established in antiquity, hath remained inviolable through so many centuries across all the monasteries of those regions for this reason: that, as the elders affirm, it was established not by human contrivance, but was brought from on high unto the fathers by an Angel." [^1087] "Once the Egyptian fathers *(Orig. p. 217)* assembled to determine what measure of psalmody in the daily worship ought to be observed by the entire body of the brotherhood... In this gathering each, according unto his own zeal and mindful not of the infirmity of others, proposed to enact as law what he deemed easily practicable; each thought to establish a vast number of psalms, some forty, some sixty, while others, not content even with this number, deemed that even more than that should be appointed. While there was thus among them a holy disagreement of pious disputation concerning the liturgical rule (*religionis regula*), the hour of the evening office overtook them in the midst of this most sacred investigation. In this service, when they desired to perform the daily order of prayers, someone arose, stepped forth into the midst, and began to chant (*cantaturum*) psalms before the Lord. All, sitting—as is the custom in the lands of Egypt unto this day—listened... And he, having chanted eleven psalms in an even recitation (*parili pronunciatione cantasset*) without interruption, verse after verse, dividing them only with intermediate prayers, and concluding with the twelfth with the refrain Alleluia (*sub alleluia responsione*), suddenly vanished from before the eyes of all, and thereby brought an end unto the service (*caeremoniis*), as well as unto the dispute." [^1088] "Therefore the venerable council of the fathers... decreed to observe this number in assemblies both evening and nocturnal, annexing unto them two readings, one from the Old and the other from the New Testament. This they added as their own tradition, as it were of supererogation (*extraordinarias*), only for those who desire it. On Saturday and Sunday, however, both readings are taken from the New Testament, one from the Apostle and the other from the Gospel, which they do likewise throughout all the days of Pentecost." [^1089] "The aforesaid prayers they begin and perform in such wise that, having finished a psalm, they do not immediately bend the knees, as do some among us in this country... But before bending the knees, they pray for a brief space, and spend more time upon this standing (than upon the kneeling). After this, having fallen prostrate for a very brief moment, as though only to render adoration unto the Divine Goodness, they rise very swiftly and, lifting up their hands on high, again plunge more intensely into prayer, in the same manner as they prayed while standing previously. [^1090] And that which we behold in this country—namely, that a psalm should be chanted by one alone, and at its end all standing should chant aloud (*concinant cum clamore*): **"Glory be to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit"**—nowhere have we seen throughout the entire East; but there, amidst universal silence, by him who chanteth the psalm, upon its conclusion, prayer is begun. With this same glorification of the Trinity an antiphon is there customarily concluded." [^1091] Prayer "they prescribe to conclude with a swift end (*celeri fine concludi*), lest by lingering upon it an influx of saliva or phlegm should interrupt the course (*excessum*) of our prayer... For this reason they account it more profitable there to make prayers brief, yet as frequent as possible. [^1092] For this reason also the very psalms which *(Orig. p. 218)* they chant (*decantant*) in the assembly, they perform not without intermission, but divide them into two or three sections (*intercisionibus*), according unto the number of verses, with intermediate prayers... And this likewise is strictly observed among them: that with the response of Alleluia only those psalms are recited (*dicatur*) which have Alleluia in their title. The chanting of the twelve specified psalms they divide among themselves in such wise that if there be two brethren, they chant six psalms each; if three, four each; if four, three each. Therefore, however great a multitude of brethren be gathered in church, never are more than four brethren appointed to chant in the assembly. [^1093] This instituted number of twelve psalms they perform in a restful posture of body, so that when those customary offices are celebrated in assemblies (*congregationum solemnitates*), with the exception of him who riseth up to recite the psalms in the midst, all sit upon low benches (*sedilibus humilibus*)..., for by fasts and day-and-night labors they so exhaust their body that, were it not for this relief, they would not be able to hear even this number of psalms while standing... When the canonical psalmody appointed by rule (*orationum canonicarum functiones*) is ended, each, returning unto his cell—wherein it is permitted to dwell alone or with one other...—again zealously performeth the debt of prayer, as it were his own private sacrifice; while to sleep no one any longer permitteth himself, until with the appearance of daylight, following upon nocturnal work and meditation, daily labor succeedeth." [^1094]

St. Cassian noteth also the exactitude with which the hours of nocturnal services were observed in Egyptian cenobia: "Although daily habit causeth one to awaken at an appointed hour, he unto whom is entrusted the summoning unto liturgical assemblies or the care of the offices, nevertheless diligently and frequently observeth the course of the stars, and not otherwise than having accurately determined the time appointed for the assembly calleth the brethren unto the work of prayer." [^1095]

As regards the daytime offices—that is, the third, sixth, and ninth hours—they were not celebrated in the Egyptian cenobia of St. Cassian's time.

"These services, which the semantron (*klepalo*) compelleth (*admonitione compulsoris*) us to celebrate at appointed hours with certain intervals, are performed among them spontaneously (*spontanee celebrantur*) without interruption throughout the entire course of the day together with handiwork. For being constantly occupied by day with handiwork in their cells, yet in such wise that they never omit meditation upon the psalms or other Scriptures, and at every moment mingling therewith prayers and supplications, they spend the whole time of the day, as it turns out, in prayer, whereas we perform them at appointed hours. Therefore, with the exception of evening and nocturnal assemblies (*congregationibus*), there is among them by day no common service (*publica solemnitas*), save on Saturday and Sunday, whereon at the third hour they assemble for the reception of Holy Communion." [^1096]

*(Orig. p. 219)*
Thus St. Cassian affordeth a complete picture of Egyptian coenobitic worship of his time, the entire order thereof. In what measure it differed from the divine worship of the time of St. Pachomius and his successors, it is difficult to judge in view of the incompleteness wherewith the latter is described in the *Rule* of St. Pachomius (from the Angel) and his *Rules*. Proximity in time (several decades separate that practice from this one) doth not yet guarantee complete identity between the two, because, as St. Cassian himself giveth to understand, that was a time of rapid and energetic creation of specifically monastic divine worship. It is characteristic that in St. Pachomius the essence of worship is placed in "prayers," whereas in St. Cassian it is placed in "psalms." Remarkable also is the strong hesitation that occurred regarding the number of psalms for a service: the tendency toward the greatest possible number of them (sixty and more)—clearly presupposing the eremitic practice of chanting the entire Psalter at one sitting—confronteth the Pachomian principle of moderation here, as in all things (in fasting and labor), and the number twelve requireth a special new heavenly sanction. Remarkable, furthermore, is how everything elaborated hitherto by the secular churches is eliminated from monastic worship: not only litanies and prayers of fixed models—which was natural, since for them a member of the hierarchy was considered necessary [^1097]—but also psalms adapted unto the hour of worship: for Vespers Psalm 140, for Matins Psalm 62; [^1098] at divine worship the Psalter was chanted simply in sequence, and unto this the entire service was reduced. [^1099] Thereby the foundation was laid for the later *kathismata*.

### The Attitude of Egyptian Monasticism toward Church Hymnody

With such a character of divine worship, there could not possibly correspond unto it that already abundant hymnographic material which in the IV–V centuries continuously and vigorously grew across all churches, especially such centers of cultured Christianity as Jerusalem, Alexandria, and Constantinople. The following incidents illustrate the attitude of contemporary monasticism toward this element of divine worship. According unto a *Patericon* of one recension and the narrative of Nikon of the Black Mountain, Abba Pambo († after 386), a Nitrian hermit, sent his disciple unto Alexandria; having no shelter there, the latter spent the night in the narthex of the Church of St. Mark and, listening unto the church services, became fascinated with the troparia. When he returned unto the elder, the latter perceived confusion in him and inquired as unto the cause. The disciple saith: 'Carelessly, father, do we spend our life in the desert, knowing neither canons [^1100] nor troparia.' *(Orig. p. 220)* The elder answered him: 'Woe unto us, child! The days are near when monks will abandon the solid food spoken by the Holy Spirit (Scripture, and among other things the psalms) and will take to songs and musical tones (*ᾄσματα καὶ ἤχους*). What compunction or tears can come from troparia? What compunction will a monk have when, standing in church or cell, he lifteth up his voice like an ox? If we stand before God, we ought to stand in great compunction, not in mockery. Monks did not depart from the world to mock before God, to melodize (*μελῳδοῦσι*) songs, to modulate (*ῥυθμίζουσι*) tones, to wave their hands, and stamp their feet; but we ought with much fear and trembling, with tears and sighs, with reverence and compunction, in a meek and humble voice to offer prayers unto God. But I say unto thee, child, that days will come when Christians will corrupt the books of the Holy Gospels and the holy Apostles, composing troparia and Hellenic discourses.' [^1101] A similar judgment is placed upon the lips of another, somewhat later, Egyptian hermit. When the Persians devastated Cappadocia at the end of the IV and beginning of the V century, a monk from thence named Paul departed unto Constantinople, then unto Alexandria, and finally settled in the Nitrian desert with a certain hermit. But soon he appeared before the hegumen of the monastery and requested of him a separate cell, since he could not dwell with the elder, who observed no office (*ἀκολουθίαν*) and no order, neither monastic nor secular. Having mentioned the elder's deviations from Cappadocian customs regarding feasts and fasts, the monk addeth: 'Yet what is worst of all, he doth not permit the chanting of canons and troparia, which constituteth the customary psalmody among all.' The hegumen, persuading the monk to return unto the elder, remarketh: 'As for the chanting of troparia and canons and the employment of musical melodies (*καὶ ἤхους μελίζειν*), this is suitable for secular priests and worldly people, to attract the folk into churches; but for monks who dwell far from worldly clamor, such things are not profitable, but often harmful; for as an angler catcheth fish with a hook and worm, so the devil by the bait of troparia and singing casteth one into the pit of vainglory, human inventions, thirst for pleasure, and finally fornication; in truth, far away from the monk who desireth to be saved let all melodious chanting be!' [^1102] However negative the attitude of monasticism toward secular worship appeareth in these narratives, nevertheless they contain both a clear indication that such an attitude obtained solely in Egyptian monasteries situated under the direct influence of the hermits, and a glimmer of awareness that such a state of affairs could not be enduring.

Indeed, no sooner did monasticism step beyond the borders of Egypt than this attitude substantially changed, and monastic divine worship acquired a form closer unto that of the world. Such a reconciliation took place first, it would seem, in Palestine.

*(Orig. p. 221)*
### Palestinian Monasteries. St. Hilarion

Unto Palestine ascetical life was transplanted from Egypt by a disciple of St. Anthony the Great, St. Hilarion († 381). A native of the environs of Gaza in southern Palestine, which was in constant communication with Egypt, Hilarion, while studying under a grammarian in Alexandria, beheld there Anthony who was already renowned, [^1103] dwelt several years with him, yet at fifteen years of age (in 306) returned unto his homeland, having received from St. Anthony as a blessing his leather girdle, [^1104] and settled in the desert not far from Gaza. His dwelling was a small hut resembling rather a tomb than a house [^1105]—of such dimensions that standing one had to bow one's head, and lying down to bend one's legs; [^1106] he nourished himself at first upon the roots of certain shrubs and wild herbs, partaking of food after three or four days, but later began to use bread and cooked vegetables, even with oil; never did he eat prior unto sunset. [^1107] In ascetical feats St. Hilarion surpassed even Anthony the Great: he possessed not two cloaks, but one, and the like. His prayer consisted chiefly of the chanting of psalms and the reading of Scripture, which he knew by heart. [^1108] After twenty-two years of solitude, the healing wrought by St. Hilarion upon the children of the Praetorian Prefect of the East began to draw crowds unto him, and around his cell there arose (ca. 328) a monastery of anchoritic type, entirely reminiscent of the Antonian monasteries; the cells stretched out like the tents of nomadic tribes across the entire expanse of the desert bordering upon Egypt. These St. Hilarion visited periodically accompanied by other monks (at times up unto two thousand), in order to bless the monks and impart unto them instructions for their life (*τύπον τῆς πολιτείας*). [^1109] After thirty years, a foreboding of Julian's persecution moved St. Hilarion to withdraw first into Egypt and then unto Cyprus, where he was ordained unto the priesthood by his disciple St. Epiphanius of Cyprus, and there died; his body was translated unto his monastery. During St. Hilarion's absence his monastery suffered devastation at the hands of the pagans, [^1110] from which it could not recover, and in the V century it is mentioned no more. [^1111] This was the sole purely anchoritic monastery in Palestine, and its fate demonstrated that Palestine was destined for a different type of monasticism than Egypt.

### The Lavras of St. Chariton

The foundation of the new type of monastery was laid by St. Chariton († in the second half of the IV century) the Confessor (doubtless in the last persecutions), former *(Orig. p. 222)* primate (*τά πρῶτα φέρων*) of the Church of Iconium. He founded a "lavra" (*λαύρα*, properly a narrow passage, alley) in the natural caves of a desolate mountain near Jerusalem, where hermits had lived even before him; in this monastery he arranged first of all (with money left behind by the robbers from whom he had been miraculously delivered) a church, consecrated by Macarius, Patriarch of Jerusalem. The structure of life in this "lavra," which received the name of Pharan, must have represented something intermediate between the liberty of anchoritic settlements and the detailed regulation of life in cenobia. [^1112] Desiring solitude, St. Chariton nevertheless soon left his lavra, having first given unto his disciples rules ("commanding all that is proper unto the monastic rank") regarding food, psalmody, and other aspects of life. Among these rules are known: counsel unto the monks to eat only once a day in the evening—bread, salt, and water; [^1113] the requirement of unceasing residence in the monastery, and hospitality; the governance of the monastery St. Chariton committed unto one of the monks with the consent of all. Yet at the new place of residence of St. Chariton (one day's journey from Pharan in the direction of Jericho near the Mountain of Temptation) there soon arose another lavra, which received the name of the Jerichoan Lavra (Douka). At the next place of St. Chariton's solitude, two hours south of Bethlehem, arose a third lavra, named the Souka or Old Lavra, which existed until the end of the VIII century. Before his death St. Chariton gave unto the assembled brethren "sacred commandments" (a typikon?). [^1114]

### The Lavra of St. Euthymius and the Coenobium of St. Theoctistus

The Palestinian monasteries, multiplying so rapidly, were not so isolated from one another as the Egyptian: in 428 we find at the head of them all a single "archimandrite," [^1115] Passarion the Great, appointed by the Patriarch of Jerusalem. Yet a closer unification of Palestinian monasteries became possible when among them arose a monastery which occupied naturally and spontaneously the foremost place among them. That was the Lavra of St. Euthymius the Great († 473). An Armenian by birth, broadly educated, St. Euthymius already in his native land in the rank of presbyter had oversight over several monasteries, but from the cares connected therewith departed in the twenty-ninth year of his life in 406 unto Palestine, entering at first the Lavra of Pharan. Customarily withdrawing with a fellow ascete like unto him, St. Theoctistus, from January 14 until Palm Sunday into the wilderness for ascetical solitude, St. Euthymius from one such absence returned no more unto Pharan, but founded with St. Theoctistus *(Orig. p. 223)* between Jericho and Jerusalem in a region of mild climate his own monastery—or more precisely, two of them: St. Theoctistus the "lower coenobium," and St. Euthymius the lavra, consecrated in 429 by Juvenal, Patriarch of Jerusalem; the lavra, having the same organization as Chariton's, thanks to the donations of Empress Eudokia and the attention which St. Euthymius devoted unto the labor of the monks, soon attained prosperity and at the same time became a higher school of ascetical endeavor for the Palestinian monasticism of that epoch: into it entered men from the Lower Coenobium and other monasteries of cenobitic structure, which had by that time gained significant expansion throughout the cities and wildernesses of Palestine. Unto his lavra St. Euthymius gave rules which touched upon diverse minutiae of daily life (for instance, on the observance of silence during divine worship and at meals), resembling in this the rules of St. Pachomius, yet apparently lacking penances. Deviations therefrom, according to tradition, were punished by God Himself through illnesses, from which St. Euthymius healed the afflicted. [^1116] In his views upon monasticism St. Euthymius must have adhered unto the Egyptian anchorites: it is known that in his life he strove to imitate St. Arsenius of Scetis, and with pleasure listened unto narratives concerning the Egyptian fathers from his own monks who had entered under him from the monasteries of those parts, such as Martyrius and Elias. [^1117] Consequently, in the arrangement of monastic life as well, St. Euthymius must have inclined toward the anchoritic type. Yet prior unto his death he foretold that his lavra would soon be converted into a cenobium, and gave unto his successor Elias instructions concerning the site and plan for this cenobium, as well as rules for it. Five years after the death of the venerable father, Patriarch Martyrius entrusted unto the deacon Fidus (unto whom the apparition of Euthymius repeated his instruction) the reconstruction of the lavra into a cenobium: the cells were demolished; upon the site of the burial of St. Euthymius was erected the building of the cenobium with a wall and tower; the former church was converted into a trapeza (refectory), and a new temple was built. [^1118] This narrative, so clearly distinguishing the concepts of lavra and cenobium, must also point in general unto a temporary decline of lavriote-celliotic life in Palestine after St. Euthymius and its suppression by cenobitic life. The former demanded leaders of powerful spirit, who were not to be found after the death of St. Euthymius. The emergence of such a figure as St. Sabbas the Sanctified (whose activity belongs rather unto the VI century and inaugurated a distinct epoch in the development of the liturgical Typikon) was required for this type of monastery to revive once again. With its conversion into a cenobium, the Lavra of St. Euthymius lost its significance and gradually became deserted. [^1119]

*(Orig. p. 224)*
### St. Gerasimus

Palestine of this period (V c.) possessed, apparently, purely anchoritic monasteries as well. Such must have been the monastery of St. Gerasimus († 475) on the Jordan, a native of Asia Minor who had received his ascetical training in the Thebaid desert. Nourishing themselves upon bread and water and occupying themselves with basket weaving, the monks of Gerasimus's monastery remained in reclusion within their cells six days a week, assembling only on Saturday and Sunday for the Liturgy. St. Gerasimus himself the Forty Days Fast spent entirely without food. He was renowned for his power over wild beasts ("whom the lion served"). [^1120]

### Origins and Characteristics of the Palestinian Typikon

As we see, the lives of all these founders of Palestinian monasticism speak very little concerning their purely liturgical activity. Nevertheless, it is beyond doubt that, having created a distinct type of monastic life, they could not fail to impress a distinctive mark upon the "prayer rule" of their monks. Tradition, although comparatively late, regards precisely the enumerated Palestinian abbas as the forebears of the Jerusalem Typikon. The most ancient among the manuscripts of this Typikon surviving unto the present day (XIII c.) admonish the hegumen:

> "unswervingly and immutably to observe the ecclesiastical sequence, order, and constitution (*καταστάσεως*), even as it hath been handed down unto us and enacted by the holy fathers who were before us in their holy monasteries and lavras, that is to say, by Euthymius the Great, Sabbas the Sanctified († 532), Theodosius the Coenobiarch († 529), Gerasimus of the Jordan, whom the wild beast served, Chariton the Confessor, and Cyriacus the Anchorite († 556); which Typikon Sophronius, great among the patriarchs († ca. 640), committed unto writing for subsequent generations. And when the barbarians burned the Lavra of the great Sabbas, and the written record made by blessed Sophronius fell victim unto the flames, all-wise John Damascene, like unto an industrious bee, once again delivered it unto his successors, and it is preserved even unto this day." [^1121]

The same thought is expressed by St. Symeon of Thessalonica (XV c.):

> "our divine father Sabbas set forth the Typikon, having received it from SS. Euthymius and Theoctistus, and they received it from those who were before them and from Chariton the Confessor. And when this Typikon (*διατύπωσις*), as is well known, was destroyed upon the devastation of that land by the barbarians, then our father among the saints Sophronius, Patriarch of the Holy City, laboriously set it forth, and after him our divine father John Damascene, experienced in theology, renewed and transcribed it." [^1122]

One may, of course, doubt all the particularities of this genealogy, especially if it intends to assert that the Jerusalem Typikon in the entire compass which it possessed in the XIII–XV centuries, and which is very close unto its present composition, proceeds from *(Orig. p. 225)* SS. Chariton, Euthymius, Theoctistus, and Gerasimus; yet at the foundation of this tradition, in order for it to arise at all, an historical kernel must have lain. The liturgical orders of the enumerated Palestinian lavras must have differed noticeably from the practice of other monasteries, corresponding unto their entire distinctive constitution. And St. John Cassian, who observed the life of Palestinian monasteries in the present epoch, as well as several other accounts concerning them from the same era, permit us not only to determine the general character of their divine worship at that time, but also to perceive what elements in it were held in common with the later and present Jerusalem Typikon. Having forewarned that in general the rules of Egyptian monasteries are impracticable in the West (in Gaul) "on account of the inclemency of the climate or on account of the difficulty and diversity of customs," and that he would replace their rules in his instructions on cenobitic life with "the rules of Palestinian or Mesopotamian monasteries," [^1123] St. Cassian observes with regard unto Palestinian divine worship as well that it tempers the "perfection and inimitable rigor (*rigorem*) of the Egyptian rules." [^1124] The most significant distinction of Palestinian monastic worship from that of Egypt, according to Cassian, was that in Palestine, as in Mesopotamia and throughout the entire East, the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours were celebrated at their appointed times, whereas in Egypt they were not celebrated at all, being replaced by unceasing prayer during handiwork in order not to detach the brethren therefrom; yet so as not to impede necessary labors, these "prayer offices" in Palestine "are celebrated in due moderation," and precisely with this in view "for each hour (only) three psalms are appointed." [^1125] This report of Cassian does not stand alone. "The abba of a certain monastery situated in Palestine reported unto blessed Epiphanius, Bishop of Cyprus († 403): by thy prayers we do not abandon our rule, but diligently perform it at the third, sixth, and ninth hour." [^1126] The inalienable obligation of the office of the Hours for all days of the year subsequently remained an enduring peculiarity of the Jerusalem Typikon (the Stoudite suppresses the Hours on feast days). On the part of the Palestinian monasteries there was both a strict fidelity unto ancient customs [^1127] and an unwillingness to depart far from the practice of secular churches. [^1128] Unto Palestine of that epoch the liturgical Hours owe also an enrichment of their structure—the emergence of the distinct office of the First Hour. [^1129]

### The Spoudaioi

In general, the unwillingness to sever entirely the bonds with the customary forms of divine worship consecrated by antiquity and preserved in secular *(Orig. p. 226)* churches may be recognized as a characteristic feature of Palestinian divine worship at that time. We see from the *Pilgrimage* of Silvia what an active part "monastics and virgins" took in the services of the Church of the Holy Resurrection (Anastasis): together with the presbyters they began the service prior unto the arrival of the bishop, and sometimes continued it after the bishop's departure, together with the most zealous among the laity. [^1130] It is possible that by virtue of this the monks of Jerusalem or of its environs (for the majority of the lavras enumerated above were situated near Jerusalem), or an offshoot thereof, received the name of the Spoudaioi (*οἱ σπουδαῖοι*, "the Zealous Ones"). Concerning the existence of monks bearing this designation in the Jerusalem of that era, there is testimony in the *Life of St. Sabbas the Sanctified* composed by Cyril of Scythopolis (VI c.): "Patriarch Elias (494–517) built a monastery near the episcopal residence and gathered into it the Spoudaioi of the Holy Resurrection, who hitherto had been dispersed across diverse places near the Tower of David, giving unto each of them a cell with every material provision." At this new monastery a church was arranged in the name of the Mother of God, named *ἡ Θεοτόκος τῶν σπουδαίων* (the Theotokos of the Spoudaioi). [^1131] Modeled upon the Jerusalem Spoudaioi, perhaps already in the V century, a monastery of the Spoudaioi was founded in Constantinople as well. [^1132] It is striking that according unto the Holy Sepulchre Typikon in a manuscript of 1122, portraying the practice of the IX century, the role of the Spoudaioi during divine worship in the Church of the Resurrection is entirely identical unto that in the *Pilgrimage* of Silvia: they celebrate the office in the "Resurrection" prior unto the arrival of the patriarch, after which they withdraw into their monastery to finish the service, while on Sunday the clerics of the Holy Sepulchre chant. [^1133] These monks could serve as mediators and unifiers between the purely monastic and the cathedral secular liturgical practice, and it is possible that their influence upon the shaping of the Jerusalem Typikon was exceedingly significant. [^1134]

Proximity unto secular liturgical practice did not, however, exert an adverse effect upon the prayerful zeal of Palestinian monasticism (as the very name of the *Spoudaioi* implies), nor did their greater contact with the world, in comparison with Egyptian monasticism, lower the level of their ascetical endeavor. The finest representatives of this monasticism astonish by their feats of prayer no less than those in Egypt. Thus St. Adolius, a monk of a certain Jerusalem monastery, "from eventide until the morning hour when the brethren gathered once again in the chapels (*εὐκτηρίοις*), stood upon the Mount of Olives, upon the hill of the Ascension whence Jesus ascended, chanting psalms and praying. And this he did at all times: whether snow fell, or rain, or hail, he remained motionless. Having fulfilled the customary prayer rule (*κανόна*), with a waking hammer (*τῷ ἐξυπνιασ*(Orig. p. 227)*τικῷ σφυρίῳ*) he knocked upon all the cells, summoning the brethren into the chapels for the morning doxology (*δοξολογίαν*), chanting at (*καθ᾽*) each cell one or two (*δεύτερον*) antiphons with them, and having prayed in this manner with them, withdrew before dawn into his cell." [^1135]

### Syrian-Mesopotamian Monasticism

Nor did the Syrian-Mesopotamian ascetical movement pass without influence upon our liturgical Typikon, which in character of course differs as greatly from Egyptian and Palestinian as these three lands differ in every respect, and whose spiritual experiences were utilized by the principal "Typikon-framers" of Byzantium and the West—St. Basil the Great and St. John Cassian. Undoubtedly, only an inadequate acquaintance with this monasticism on the part of St. Cassian, who had not visited Mesopotamia, permitted him to regard Mesopotamian asceticism alongside Palestinian as "more moderate" than Egyptian. [^1136] Yet precisely "the characteristic feature of the former is an austere mode of life; in this respect Syrian monasticism leaves behind it original Egyptian monasticism; in this measure of it was manifested the distinctive spirit of the Syrian with his ardent, fiery, impetuous character." [^1137] It invented the most arduous and bizarre forms of ascetical feats. Here ascetes lived in chambers smaller than the human stature, wherein one had ever to maintain a bent posture of body, [^1138] or on the contrary entirely beneath the open sky in summer and winter, [^1139] in huts without windows and doors, [^1140] in suspended and swaying circular *(Orig. p. 228)* cages; [^1141] Syria precisely invented also the ascetical feat of stylitism (St. Simeon Stylites, † 459). It is not surprising that in the matter of fasting as well Syrian monasticism surpassed other lands. Thus here existed a class of ascetes termed *boskoi* (*βοσκοὶ*, shepherds, or more precisely "grazers"), because "they made no use of bread, cooked food, or wine, and when the hour arrived to partake of food, each of them, taking a sickle, went forth to wander upon the mountain like unto a grazing beast, and nourished himself upon plants." [^1142] Nowhere did men attain unto such a degree of contrition (*compunctio*, *katanyxis*) as here. Concerning St. Domnina, Blessed Theodoret recounts: "often, having taken my right hand and applied it unto her eyes, Domnina released it so wet that it seemed as though the hand itself poured forth tears." [^1143] St. Ephrem the Syrian recounts concerning his fellow ascete Julian: "Throughout the entire service he stood, not daring to lift his eyes, as though before the very judgment seat of our Lord Jesus Christ. One day I said unto him: 'Who spoileth the books here? For where there was written "God," or "Lord," or "Jesus Christ," or "Savior," there the outlines of the letters have been effaced.' The blessed man replied unto me: 'I will hide nothing from thee... as I read, as soon as I discover the written name of my God, I bedew it with my tears.'" [^1144] St. Ephrem the Syrian himself prayed that God would temper contrition within him ("relieve me the waves of Thy grace," *«ослаби ми волны благодати Твоея»*). [^1145]

### Syrian-Mesopotamian Monastic Divine Worship

It is understandable that through all this was created the most fertile soil for the development of divine worship as well. In the majority of monasteries and monastic communities, which Syria and Mesopotamia in the IV–V centuries counted in vast numbers, divine worship, apparently, did not differ from that customary in secular churches. Even concerning the *boskoi*, Sozomen observes that they, "dwelling in the mountains, ever give glory unto God with prayers and hymns according to the ordinance of the Church (*κατὰ θεσμὸν τῆς ἐκκλησίας*)." [^1146] St. Publius, having founded a monastery near the city of Zeugma on the Euphrates, erected therein a church wherein he gathered the monks "at the beginning and at the close of the day to offer unto God the morning and evening doxology"; and because there were Syrians and Greeks in the monastery, they, "dividing into two sides within the church, performed the psalmody *(Orig. p. 229)* alternately, now in the one and now in the other tongue." [^1147] For the midnight service (Matins) the superior himself roused the brethren in certain monasteries. [^1148] Communities possessing no temple went daily in the morning and at eventide unto neighboring churches, as, for example, the female companions of St. Domnina. [^1149] Yet, of course, such divine worship was insufficient for the Syrian ascetes, and they supplemented it with their own, which consisted of an alternation of psalmody and prayer; it doth not appear that this alternation consisted, as in Egypt, in accompanying each psalm with a prayer; rather, after a certain quantity of psalms followed a lengthy prayer or a series thereof: concerning St. Marcian it is recounted that he "replaced prayer with psalmody, psalmody with prayer, and both the one and the other with reading of the Word of God"; [^1150] the same is said concerning St. Publius; [^1151] St. Abraham "performed at night by turns forty psalmodies, filling the intervals between them with twice as great a number of prayers." [^1152] St. Julian Saba in his monastery near Edessa "commanded the brethren to offer unto God common psalmody in the cell, and after dawn to withdraw two by two into the desert, and there, the one kneeling, to offer unto God due adoration, while the other, standing, chanted at that time fifteen Psalms of David; then changing positions: the second standing to chant, while the other, prostrate upon the earth, prayed"; [^1153] and this they did continually from morning until twilight; before sunset, having rested a little, coming from here and from there, from all directions they assembled in the cells and together chanted the evening hymn unto the Lord. [^1154] These reports demonstrate also that in the prayer rule, as among the Egyptian ascetes, a certain importance was attached unto the number of psalms, and that the number taken in this case was sacred (forty) or round (fifteen = one tenth of the Psalter); yet the twelve-psalm office so widely adopted in Egypt is not mentioned here. Apparently, more significance than in Egypt was attached unto bows and prostrations: in the cited report the bow is intensified unto prolonged prostration upon the earth. In other instances this intensification found expression in a great quantity of short metanoias: St. Simeon Stylites "performed prayer now motionlessly, now making bows; many of the visitors sought to count their number; once someone counted 1,244 of them, but then grew weary and ceased counting; when the elder made bows, his forehead approached unto the very tips of his toes; partaking of food once a week and even then in small measure, his hollow belly afforded his back the ability to bend easily." [^1155] No less than in Egypt were ecclesiastical feasts and fasts venerated. The anchorites dwelling near Carrhae (= Harran) gathered into that city on Pascha and on the feast day *(Orig. p. 230)* of the holy martyr Elpidius for divine worship. [^1156] SS. Marana and Cyra received female visitors only on the days of Pentecost. [^1157] St. Simeon Stylites "on the days of church feasts from sunset until its very rising stood the whole night through with hands uplifted unto heaven, forgetful of sleep and weariness." [^1158] He likewise passed the entirety of the Forty Days Fast without food, arriving at times by reason of this at a state of syncope. [^1159]

### The Typikon of St. Basil (Asia Minor Monasteries)

The monastic Typikon of St. Basil the Great, if it be comprised by his 55 "Rules Expounded at Length in Questions and Answers" and 313 "Rules Expounded Briefly in Questions and Answers," and his other ascetical writings (*Discourse on Ascetical Discipline*, three *Ascetical Discourses*, *Ascetical Constitutions for Those Laboring in Cenobia and Monasticism*, etc.), represents in itself not a codification of diverse minutiae of monastic life like unto the *Rules* of St. Pachomius, but a general theory of ascetical endeavor; for this reason it could not exert a detailed influence upon our Typikon. What was important in this Typikon was that it disregarded those minutiae and particularities of monastic governance unto which the *Rules* of St. Pachomius of the later recension attached so much weight. Perhaps by virtue of this trait the Typikon of St. Basil proved to correspond unto the spirit of Palestinian monasticism more than that of Pachomius: under Bishop John of Jerusalem (386–417) the Typikon of St. Basil was introduced into the Carmel monastery; [^1160] St. Theodosius the Coenobiarch († 529) "frequently offered unto the brethren instructions from the counsels of the great Basil, unsurpassed in ascetical feats and invincible in doctrines of truth," and especially loved to read unto the brethren the introduction unto the *Longer Rules*. [^1161] Yet the monastic Typikon of St. Basil provided by his designated writings is of too general a character to impart a definitive organization unto a monastery. In all likelihood, under the name of the Typikon of St. Basil was understood not only his ascetical writings, but also the organization which he imparted unto his own monasteries. When St. Basil resolved to begin an ascetical life, he "desired to find a brother who had chosen this manner of life" [^1162] to serve as a guide for himself. In the homeland of St. Basil in Cappadocia there were already not a few anchorites, but they were in constant communication with the world and lacked close communion among themselves (like the Egyptian anchorites); for this reason they did not satisfy the ideal of St. Basil, and he undertook a journey into Mesopotamia, Syria, Palestine, and Egypt in order to acquaint himself with genuine ascetical endeavor. Here he arrived at the conclusion that cenobitic *(Orig. p. 231)* monasticism leads more surely unto the goal than solitary eremitism—a thought which is unfolded throughout all his ascetical works. This thought he resolved to realize in practice as well. At first he founded a monastery upon the bank of the Iris River (in Pontus), near the city of Ibora, where a convent of his mother and sister already existed. Subsequently, "traversing the Pontic cities (for the contest against Arianism), he founded there many monastic communities." [^1163] Unto the first monastery he invited his friend St. Gregory the Theologian. In the epistles addressed unto him on this occasion he set forth his ideal of monastic life, developed by him only in greater detail later in the *Rules*. The day of the monk must begin with prayer:

> "the honoring of the Savior with songs and hymnody; then, when the sun hath fully shone forth, setting about works and having prayer everywhere present with oneself, it is needful to season one's labors with psalmody, as with salt." [^1164] "Prayer hath two forms: the first is doxology with humility of mind, and the second and lower is petition; therefore when praying do not immediately proceed unto petition, [^1165] lest otherwise thou show that thou prayest solely out of necessity." [^1166] Alongside prayer must go the readings and study of the divinely inspired Scriptures: "if prayers follow upon readings, then the soul, moved by love toward God, approacheth them more maturely and vigorously." [^1167]

Although, as observed, prayer according unto St. Basil must be unceasing, ever accompanying the labor of the monk as well, nevertheless certain hours of the day and night are worthy of distinct prayerful veneration; as such hours St. Basil designates: morning, the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours, the conclusion of the day (Vespers), the onset of night (Compline), and midnight, indicating wherein each of these hours is significant. [^1168] An especially propitious time for prayer Basil the Great considers midnight: "that for which the morning is employed by others serveth the ascetes of piety at midnight, because the nocturnal silence more than all else bestoweth freedom upon the soul, when neither eyes nor ears convey harmful sights or rumors unto the heart." [^1169] It is unknown what "prayer" at the designated hours Basil the Great hath in view: private or public. Communion Basil the Great counseled daily for all men, and even more so for monastics, with the Reserved Gifts. [^1170]

No small significance doth Basil the Great attach unto the outward appearance of the monk:

> "Unto a humble and contrite manner of thinking there correspond a sorrowful gaze cast down unto the ground and a disregard for outward appearance." [^1171] It is not advised to seat oneself beside an elder or superior, but rather lower down, nor to cross one leg over another when sitting. [^1172] "It is necessary that the tunic be gathered upon the body with a girdle; and the girdle must not lie higher than the loins, for this would be effeminate, nor be drawn so loosely that the tunic might flutter, for this *(Orig. p. 232)* would be frivolous. The gait must be neither slow, which would betray a spiritual slackness, nor yet swift and hurried, which would disclose frenzied agitations of the soul." [^1173] The necessity is demonstrated of using a girdle. [^1174] "In food, bread will satisfy necessity, water will satisfy thirst in a healthy man, and cooked preparations of seeds or legumes can sustain strength in the body for necessary requirements." [^1175] "The ascete must by no means strive after variety in foods, nor even under the pretext of abstinence demand an alteration of the offered provisions... On the contrary, even if for eating with bread salted fish be offered, which the holy fathers judged right to add unto foods in small quantity in lieu of any other condiment, mixing it into food consisting exclusively of water or greens, the ascete must not, under the pretext of a vainglorious, self-willed piety, refusing this as though it were flesh-meat, demand other provisions (though non-fish, yet more costly and choice); but without special attention unto this, dipping a morsel into the broth made from a small piece of salted fish, let him partake with all thanksgiving; for this small quantity of fish, cast into such a volume of water, or if it so happen, into a broth of seeds or legumes, will not constitute non-fasting food, but genuine and the most strict fasting food of an ascete." [^1176] "Nor ought one to abhor wine, if it be taken for healing, yet neither ought one to seek after it without need." [^1177] Prayers are prescribed prior unto partaking of food and after it, wherein the second "let it contain within itself both thanksgiving for that which hath been bestowed and petition for that which hath been promised." [^1178] "For the taking of food there must be appointed one definite hour, and that the same one throughout the course of a given period, [^1179] so that of the twenty-four hours in the day only that single one be expended for the body, while all the remaining hours the ascete would spend in noetic labor (*умном делании*). Sleep must be light, from which one can awake without difficulty and such as naturally followeth upon a small intake of food; it should intentionally be interrupted by concerns regarding weightier matters." [^1180]

Basil the Great likewise imparteth instructions concerning the governance of a monastery, concerning the oversight over the brethren on the part of the superior, and concerning the reception of postulants into the monastery; all these instructions are likewise of a general character and do not enter into such details as the Rule of St. Pachomius, touching only occasionally upon specific matters; for instance, it is advised "in the event of perplexities in the brotherhood to choose one brother, that he might either propose the doubts of certain ones unto the brotherhood for common deliberation, or bring them unto the knowledge of the superior." [^1181]

Alms in the monastery may be bestowed only by him unto whom "after trial the stewardship (*oeconomia*) hath been entrusted" (the steward / *oeconomus*); "whether a naked man make request, or a deceitful *(Orig. p. 233)* man, whether by reason of utter necessity or out of cupidity, once and for all it is declared that to bestow (alms) or to take (from monastic goods) is not permitted unto everyone, but unto that one alone... with the common consent of those who govern alongside him, and from surplus." [^1182]

### The Constantinopolitan Monasteries:

#### a) The Akoimetoi (Unsleeping Ones) and b) The Stoudios Monastery

The most immediate influence upon the development of divine worship must have been exerted by the monasteries of such great cities as Alexandria, [^1183] Jerusalem, Antioch, [^1184] Constantinople, and Rome. Above, the significance was noted which the monasteries of Jerusalem and its environs had in the history of divine worship, laying the foundation for a distinctive form of the ecclesiastical Typikon. An identical influence upon the latter could not fail to be exerted also by the monasteries of another comparable center of Christian life—Constantinople, which had only just become the capital of the entire world. Constantinople created a distinctive type of monastery and for a long time, until the first blows inflicted upon it by the Crusaders, became the lawgiver in the sphere of divine worship, both cathedral-parochial and monastic. Yet information on this subject from the epoch of the IV–V centuries is limited unto three brief accounts, which are nonetheless exceedingly characteristic and momentous.

St. Alexander founded first in Mesopotamia, then in Antioch, and finally ca. 420 AD in Constantinople, near the Church of St. Menas, a monastery which immediately attracted up to 300 monks of diverse nations (Romans, Greeks, and Syrians) by its distinctive organization: in it unceasing divine worship was instituted throughout the twenty-four hours of day and night, for which purpose the monks were divided into three (according unto others, into twenty-four) shifts. [^1185] Such an institution, on account of which the monastery received the flattering designation of the "Akoimetoi" (*ἀκοιμήτων*, the "Unsleeping Ones"), was clearly calculated to satisfy the religious needs both of all strata of the surrounding populace—who did not always have the same hour at their disposal for prayer—and of every individual at whatever time there might arise a need for common prayer, or an inclination and disposition toward it. It is not surprising that such a type of monastery immediately attained widespread expansion: the successor of St. Alexander in the hegumenate, St. Marcellus († 485), founded an identical monastery in Bithynia; [^1186] identical monasteries are mentioned in the V century in the Chalcedonian diocese and other places of the Greek empire. [^1187]

The Constantinopolitan community of the "Akoimetoi" acquired exceptional significance in view of the fact that it linked its destiny with the monastery that subsequently became the most renowned—the Stoudios Monastery. According unto the tradition preserved in the Stoudios Monastery and recorded in the *Life of St. Theodore *(Orig. p. 234)* the Studite* († 826, the *Life* was composed by a disciple of the venerable father, Michael the Studite, or by someone else in the X century [^1188]), "there came from the city of Rome a man of noble lineage and wealthy, by name Stoudios—which in our tongue would be Euprepios—who had already attained the rank of patrician and consul; having settled in our city (Constantinople), he founded this glorious church unto the great Forerunner," which was the principal church of the Stoudios Monastery. Among the twelve senators who migrated from Rome unto Constantinople with Emperor Constantine the Great, a certain Stoudios is mentioned. [^1189] Yet hardly was this Stoudios the founder of the monastery. The Byzantine chronicler Theophanes (IX c.) and after him Kedrenos (XII c.) place under the 6th year of Emperor Leo the Great (457–474), consequently under the year 463: "in the same year Stoudios also built the church of the Forerunner and settled in it (*ἐν αὐτῷ κατέστησε*) monks from the monastery of the Akoimetoi ('Unsleeping Ones')." [^1190] According unto Kodinos (XIV c.), "the patrician Stoudios founded under Emperor Leo Marcellus the Stoudios Monastery, endowed it with extensive estates, and settled in it 1,000 monks." [^1191] According unto the Suda (X c.), "the Stoudios Monastery, before being converted into a monastery, was a parish church." [^1192] These accounts leave no doubt, at least, that the community of the Akoimetoi which appeared in Constantinople in the V century entered into a close relationship with the Stoudios Monastery that arose at that same time.

#### c) The Constantinopolitan Spoudaioi

It is possible that in this same epoch there appeared in Constantinople also a community of Spoudaioi monks. In an ancient synaxarion (of Sirmond) under June 7 is indicated the "memory of our venerable fathers Anthimus the Presbyter and Stephen, of the (monastery of the) Spoudaioi, which is near Florentius'." [^1193] The latter name designates an almshouse founded under Emperor Arcadius (395–408) by a certain Florentius. [^1194] This Anthimus must be none other than the admirer mentioned in the *Life of St. Auxentius* († ca. 470), the Bithynian ascetic, concerning whom the biographer of St. Auxentius, his disciple (George), recounts that he, "being first a deacon and later a presbyter in Constantinople, adorned and improved psalmody, having arranged at the vigils two choirs—a male and a female *(Orig. p. 235)* choir"; these vigils St. Auxentius also loved to visit. [^1195] In that same epoch in Constantinople, Theodore Lector (VI c.) indicates as a champion of the Council of Chalcedon, a "composer of troparia," and an organizer of vigils, likewise a certain Anthimus; all these consequently represent one and the same person. If so, then Anthimus, the first Constantinopolitan hymnographer, may be recognized as the founder of the Constantinopolitan community of Spoudaioi frequently mentioned in later times. From these accounts the true character of this community is disclosed: the Spoudaioi set as their primary aim the arrangement of magnificent divine worship and were originally chanters rather than monks; [^1196] such a character was possessed also by the Jerusalem Spoudaioi (the zealous guardians of divine worship in the Church of the Resurrection) until Patriarch Elias formed a monastery out of them. A tradition bearing a legendary character assigns the foundation of the monastery of *Spoude* (*Σπουδή*) unto the reign of Emperor Leo the Isaurian (716–741). [^1197]

Concerning divine worship in these Constantinopolitan monasteries of the IV–V centuries nothing is known, but one may think that, separated from desert monasticism and called to satisfy the spiritual needs of the urban population as well, these monasteries, even more than those of Jerusalem, had to take into account the orders of secular churches, which had by that time become so well developed. This must especially be said concerning the community of the Spoudaioi.

### The Church Year in the IV–V Centuries

Having done so much for the development of the order of the daily church services, the IV–V centuries did no less in establishing the festal ritual. In this regard: a) the conception of the sanctity of the feast was elevated; b) the number of feasts and fasts was increased by not less than twofold; c) the foundation was laid for the universal ecclesiastical veneration of saints, that is to say, the annual menologion. Yet very little was accomplished at that time toward the formation of a specifically festal order of divine worship: a feast was distinguished only by more prolonged, frequent divine worship, while the content and composition of festal worship still differed little from the ordinary. To create a distinctive festal worship remained a task to be accomplished by the VI–VIII centuries.

### Sunday

At the foundation of feasts, as previously, lay the Sunday day (the Day of the Lord), and if the feast now came to be venerated more than before, this occurred first of all with Sunday. Here the Church was indebted in many respects unto the secular government, which guaranteed the rest and sanctity of Sunday by legislative means. The beginning was laid by Constantine the Great. According unto the testimony of Eusebius, he *(Orig. p. 236)* "appointed for prayer the Lord's Day. Therefore the emperor inspired all Roman subjects with a disposition on the days eponymous with the Savior (the Lord's days, that is to say, Sundays) to cease from their occupations, and in like manner to venerate Fridays, [^1198]—it seemeth, in commemoration of those events which on these days were accomplished by the common Savior. As for the Sunday day, sometimes called also the day of light and of the sun, he inclined all his soldiers unto the zealous observance thereof; and unto those among them who had become partakers of the divine faith, he gave on that day freedom from military service, so that without hindrance they might keep vigil in God's church and that no one might impede them at that time from offering their prayers. And unto the other soldiers, who had not yet received the divine law, he prescribed by a special statute on Sundays to assemble in open plazas in the suburbs of the city and there, at a given signal and all together, to uplift unto God a prayer memorized beforehand." [^1199] In 321 AD Constantine the Great issued an edict:

> "All judges, the urban populace, and artisans of every > manner in the venerable day of the sun let them rest. Only in villages may agricultural laborers freely and without hindrance work, since it frequently happeneth that on another day it may be less commodious to entrust grain unto the furrow or vines unto the trench, lest, losing the favorable opportunity, they be deprived of the bountiful season sent down by heavenly Providence." [^1200]

According unto an edict of Emperor Valentinian I (364–375), on Sunday "none of the Christians must be subjected unto the exaction of debts." [^1201] Emperor Theodosius the Great prohibited public spectacles on Sunday. [^1202] According unto an edict of 386 AD of Emperors Valentinian II and Theodosius the Great, on Sunday "the conduct of all lawsuits, the transaction of trade, and the execution of contracts must cease; there must be no judicial proceedings either through arbiters, or through appointed and elected judges"; violation of this law was punished as sacrilege (*sacrilegus*). [^1203] By an edict of Theodosius the Great of 389 AD the operation of this statute was extended unto Holy Week and Bright Week. [^1204] These laws, understandably, heightened the halo of sanctity surrounding the Sunday day; among church writers of this epoch counsels are heard unto Christians to take an example from the pagans and Jews in their reverent attitude toward feasts, [^1205] while the thought that for a Christian every day is a feast is expressed more rarely. [^1206] "The week hath seven days," said St. John Chrysostom; "these seven days God hath divided with us not *(Orig. p. 237)* in such a manner as to take more for Himself and give us less, nor even divided them equally—but He hath given thee six days, and reserved for Himself but one." [^1207] "Let us establish an immutable statute for ourselves, for our wives, and for our children, to dedicate one day in the week entirely unto listening and remembering that which we have heard (in church)." [^1208] By this the thought was advanced that properly the entire Sunday day must be consecrated unto divine worship. Everything worldly—labor as well as entertainment—profaneth it; the latter even more: according unto Blessed Augustine, on a feast day "it is better to plow than to dance." [^1209] Such views could only reinforce the ancient custom of especially solemn divine worship on Sundays. The Council of Sardica (347 AD) excommunicateth anyone "who, dwelling in a city, on three Lord's days during three weeks doth not attend the church assembly." [^1210] We have seen that in the Jerusalem Church Matins, which always began, as in other churches, [^1211] long before dawn (for which reason it is frequently called a nocturnal service, and among monks—*pannychis*, *vigilia* [^1212]), on Sunday commenced so deep in the night that it could be termed a vigil [^1213]). Thus it was in other churches as well. According unto Socrates and Sozomen, the Arians in Constantinople "on all significant feasts, as well as on the first and last day of the week (Socrates: 'on the feast days of each week, that is to say, on Saturday and Sunday'), assembled at night in the public porticoes, and dividing into choirs, chanted hymns in two choirs, adapting the refrains unto their doctrine; and in the morning, chanting them (the refrains) publicly, withdrew unto the appointed places and held church assemblies there." In opposition unto these Arian vigils, St. John Chrysostom "began to incite the people unto similar psalmody" (Socrates: "countering them with the psalmody of his own people, he commanded that the confessors of the Consubstantial Trinity should likewise exercise themselves in the singing of nocturnal hymns"); "the Orthodox assemblies soon became more numerous and magnificent" than the Arian ones, "inasmuch as they were preceded by silver crosses accompanied by burning lanterns" [^1214] (litany processions).

At this time also, apparently, there definitively took root in the Eastern churches the custom of commencing festal celebration from eventide. In the work of Pseudo-Athanasius, *Questions unto Antiochus the Duke*, the question is already posed: "Why did God prescribe for us to begin the Lord's Day from Saturday evening?" Having observed that "many now argue vehemently whether day should precede night or vice versa," and that the Law commanded the Jews to begin the Sabbath from the evening "lest they be able to say that Christ arose on the Sabbath," the author perceiveth the foundation for the Christian celebration of Sunday from the evening not in this prescription of the Law, but in the fact that "God brought the nations forth from the darkness *(Orig. p. 238)* of ignorance and from the shadow of the Law into the light of divine knowledge and the Gospel; for this reason He very expediently prescribed to begin the day of His Resurrection from eventide and to conclude it with the light; for it would be exceedingly unfitting and improper to begin the day of Christ—the true Lamp—from the light and conclude it at night and in darkness." [^1215] St. John Chrysostom saith: "Earthly celebrations often cease already in the middle of the day, whereas heavenly ones are not so—they continue unceasingly." [^1216]

### Saturday

Saturday, which laid claim in the III century as well unto an exceptional position in the ranks of the days of the week, [^1217] was now in diverse places in the East venerated almost equally with Sunday. The *Apostolic Constitutions* seem to make no distinction regarding celebration between these two days, considering the attendance of divine worship on Saturday just as obligatory for a Christian as on Sunday, [^1218] commanding "on every Sabbath, except one (Great and Holy Saturday), and on every Lord's Day, assembling together, rejoice," [^1219] to feast them ("Celebrate the Sabbath and the Lord's Day, for the former is the memorial of the creation, and the latter of the Resurrection"), [^1220]—finally, prohibiting work on Saturday: "I Peter and I Paul decree: let servants work five days, but on the Sabbath and on the Lord's Day let them attend church for the sake of instruction in piety; for the Sabbath, we have said, hath the figure of creation, and the Lord's Day—of the Resurrection." [^1221] And this occurred not solely in that Church where the *Apostolic Constitutions* arose. Socrates, as we have seen, regardeth Saturday and Sunday as the festal days of the week and giveth it to be understood that the divine worship on them was of equal solemnity in Constantinople. [^1222] Thus it was, besides Constantinople, in Antioch, Pontus, Cappadocia, Cyprus, and Egypt. [^1223] Yet, apparently, the celebration of Saturday for the most part was reduced unto the celebration of the Liturgy on that day, wherever it was not celebrated daily: "whereas all churches throughout the world celebrate the Mysteries on the Sabbath day of each week, the Alexandrians and Romans on the basis of a certain ancient tradition do not wish to do this; while the neighbors of the Alexandrians, the Egyptians and the inhabitants of the Thebaid, although they hold assemblies on Saturday, partake of the Mysteries after having dined in the evening." [^1224] This latter restriction is charac*(Orig. p. 239)*teristic, inasmuch as it showeth that on Saturday the Liturgy was not considered, after all, so indispensable as on Sunday, and being celebrated in the evening, pertained rather unto the Sunday day, perhaps even combining with the Sunday Eve Vespers, as with us on Paramonies (Eves). It is possible that in general Saturday was venerated not so much from Old Testament motives as on account of its significance in the life of the Savior, unto which Cassian clearly pointeth, [^1225] and as the eve of Sunday. [^1226] If so, then: a) its full festive observance in certain very few Churches, predominantly far-eastern ones (such as Antioch), must be regarded as an extreme, an excessive fervor [^1227] condemned by the Council of Laodicea: "Christians ought not to Judaize and rest (*σχολάζειν*) on the Sabbath, but must labor (*ἐργάζεσθαι*) on that day, and honor rather the Lord's Day, resting upon it if they can, as Christians; but if they be found Judaizing, let them be anathema from Christ"; [^1228] b) from this is likewise understandable the custom of fasting on Saturday that arose in this epoch among Western Christians, mentioned (disapprovingly) by Cassian: [^1229] the fast was an identical form of honoring Saturday as the day marked by Christ's burial, just as on the East was the Liturgy celebrated on that day.

### Wednesday and Friday

Of the remaining days of the week the more sacred, as previously, were Wednesday and Friday. At this time we first discover a rationale for the fast on these days: "Fast on Wednesday and Friday, for on Wednesday sentence was pronounced against the Lord, and on Friday because on it the Lord suffered death upon the cross under Pontius Pilate." [^1230] Concerning the fasting regimen on these days it is known only that the fast concluded at the ninth hour, that is to say, they did not eat until that hour; concerning the kind of food on these days nothing is known; judging by the comparison of these fasts with the Forty-Day Fast (Great Lent), [^1231] one may think that it was identical unto that in the Forty-Day Fast (see below). "This fast (of Wednesday and Friday)," saith St. Epiphanius of Cyprus, "is observed throughout the entire year and continueth until the ninth hour. The fifty days of Pentecost are excepted, when there occurreth neither genuflection nor fasting... It is equally unseemly to fast on Theophany, when our Lord was born in the flesh, even though it occur on a Wednesday or Friday." [^1232] Consequently, the fast of Wednesday and Friday was omitted during Pentecost and on the principal feasts. Of these two weekly fasts Friday was considered more important, as in the III century: [^1233] on Friday Constantine *(Orig. p. 240)* the Great released soldiers from duty and abolished judicial sessions on that day, just as on Sunday. [^1234] In addition unto fasting, these days were honored also by divine worship—in certain places with the Liturgy, [^1235] in others with a special service that replaced the Liturgy, without the Eucharist: "the Alexandrians on Wednesday and on the so-called day of preparation (*παρασκευήν*—Friday) read the Scriptures, and the teachers expound them; on these days all things are celebrated which are customary, except for the Mysteries." [^1236] Probably this service—the Liturgy without the Eucharist—gave origin unto the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, which in certain ancient monuments is ascribed unto St. Mark and the Apostle Peter who preached in Alexandria, as well as unto St. Athanasius the Great. [^1237]

### The Forty-Day Fast (Great Lent): Lengthening of the Pre-Paschal Fast

From the IV century we possess the first clear testimonies concerning the forty-day duration of the pre-Paschal fast, which consequently only at that time (at the end of the III century) became the Forty-Day Fast (*Quadragesima*, *Tessarakoste*) in the proper sense. The first such testimony belongeth unto the Council of Nicaea of 325 AD, which requireth that local synods take place: "one before the Forty-Day Fast, so that upon the cessation of all animosity a pure gift may be offered unto God, and the other around the autumn season." [^1238] According unto Eusebius of Caesarea, "we celebrate Pascha by taking upon ourselves a forty-day ascetical labor for preparation unto it"; "before Pascha for six weeks we fortify ourselves with a forty-day fast." [^1239] St. Athanasius the Great repeatedly mentioneth the Forty-Day Fast, among other places in his Festal Letter of 330 AD, [^1240] as doth also St. Cyril of Jerusalem († 386). [^1241] The Council of Laodicea ca. 360 AD speaketh of it, [^1242] as doth St. Epiphanius of Cyprus ca. 375 AD. [^1243] In the West testimonies concerning it begin later: the first in St. Ambrose of Milan († 397). [^1244]

Several passing remarks among writers of that era shed light upon the very process of the expansion of the former one-week pre-Paschal fast into a forty-day fast. Socrates saith: "The fast before Pascha is observed differently in different places: namely, in Rome before Pascha they fast continuously for three weeks, except on Saturday and the Lord's Day; while in Illyria, throughout all Greece and Alexandria they observe a fast of six weeks before Pascha and call it the Forty-Day Fast; while others begin to fast seven weeks before the feast." [^1245] A younger contemporary of Socrates, Sozomen, in his *Ecclesiastical History*, *(Orig. p. 241)* heavily dependent upon that of Socrates, repeateth this passage from the book of his predecessor, but with characteristic additions and modifications: "The so-called Forty-Day Fast preceding the feast of Pascha, wherein the people fast, some count as six weeks, for example, the Illyrians and the Christians dwelling in the West, all Libya, and Egypt with Palestine; others as seven, as the inhabitants of Constantinople and the surrounding regions as far as Phoenicia; during the course of these six or more weeks some fast for three weeks with intervals, others for three weeks consecutively before the feast, while yet others for only two, as, for example, the followers of Montanus." [^1246] Both testimonies belong unto that time (the V century) long before which a whole series of witnesses, as we have seen, establisheth the universal expansion of the Forty-Day Fast in the Christian world. Consequently even at that time the Forty-Day Fast not only was far from being definitively defined, but had not yet received universal recognition. In diverse places instead thereof there existed a fast occupying in duration precisely the middle between the ancient short pre-Paschal fast of one to six days and the Forty-Day Fast—namely, a twenty-day fast. In this regard it is characteristic that this latter kind of fast took place in the West, where, as we have seen, testimonies concerning the Forty-Day Fast are noticeably late in comparison with the East.
