The elder then added: 'O Son and Word of God (*+ Lord*), Jesus Christ, our God, have mercy upon us, and help, and save our souls!' And when we said 'Amen', we sat down. And I say unto the elder: 'Why, Abba, dost thou not preserve the order of the Catholic and Apostolic Church?' And the elder saith unto me: 'He that preserveth not the order of the Catholic and Apostolic Church, let him be anathema both in this age and in that which is to come!' And I say unto him: 'How then dost thou not recite (*+ from the night*) at the Vespers of the holy Sunday troparia at **"Lord, I have cried"**, nor a troparion at **"O Gladsome Light"** (*+ at **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"***), nor at the kanon **"God is the Lord"**, nor at the psalmody of the Sunday kathisma psalms, nor troparia at the Song of the Three Holy Children, nor at the Magnificat (*at the Gospel*) **"Let every breath"**, nor at the Doxology **"The Resurrection of the Savior"** (*+ which we praise*)?' Unto the inquiries of the visitors the elder replied that the reason for such departures from the general ecclesiastical Typikon in his prayer rule was his lack of any sacred orders. 'All that thou hast spoken is the office of reader and chanter, subdeacon and presbyter, and in general of those possessing ordination; whereas those not possessing the latter ought not to dare to perform this. For this very reason the ecclesiastical order appointeth the reader and the chanter, the subdeacons and the presbyters: the chanter, in order to sing and to lead off with singing and voice and chant, and "to guide the people in the **'Holy God'**, and the prokeimena, and the precenting, and the sanctuary hymns, and at the entrance of the Mysteries the Cherubic Hymn, and the Communion verses"; the reader, for the paroemias (proverbial), prophetic, and apostolic books; the subdeacons and deacons, to minister at the altar; and the presbyters, to celebrate the sacred mysteries, to accomplish the rites, and to baptize. I too will ask of you an 'ecclesiastical head' [capital question]: tell me, in the divine offices, evening supplications, night vigils, and morning services, who ought to precent and lead off the alleluia, the introits, the sessional hymns, the readings, and the antiphons?" We said unto him: "The readers, chanters, and subdeacons." The elder said: "Rightly have ye spoken. And on solemn feasts *(Orig. p. 296)* and on holy Sundays, who ought to begin **'God is the Lord'**, both at the beginning of the kanon, and in the intercalary canticles of the Three Children, and **'Let every breath'**, and in the doxologies **'The Resurrection of the Savior which we praise'**, and at the end of the kanon?" We said unto him: "This is the office of presbyters; in the ecclesiastical tradition we have received that this be proclaimed by the priests." Adding then that he in this manner doth not cast aside the ecclesiastical order, but on the contrary by his manner of action expresseth a singular reverence toward it, looking upon it as something analogous unto the heavenly hierarchy, the elder noteth in passing also (like the aforementioned Egyptian fathers) that "unto hesychasts and those weeping for their own sins, troparia are not fitting"; yet he repeateth that he singeth them not principally because, in his judgment, they usurp the priesthood, like King Uzziah and Uzzah (who upheld the falling Ark), who, lacking ordination, "proclaim the psalms with song and utterance, and the people at the ends of the verses respond with voice and melody, usurping the prokeimena and sanctuary precentings, and appointing themselves chanters, readers, and subdeacons."

This narrative affordeth us a conception simultaneously of three types of divine worship of that period: the Sinaitic eremitic—and monastic Sinai was the spiritual offspring of Egypt; the Palestinian monastic; and the cathedral-parish type. The first is described in all completeness of detail. Concerning the composition of the second, one may deduce from that which arouseth perplexity in the first on the part of the visitors: unto them it seemeth strange that there should be an absence of "troparia" at **"Lord, I have cried"** (stichera), at **"O Gladsome Light"** (the prokeimenon), at **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (the aposticha), as well as the absence of **"God is the Lord"** "at the beginning of the kanon" (of Matins), of Sunday sessional hymns, of intercalary hymns (*mesōdia*) at the 3rd and 6th canticles (sessional hymns or something similar), and furthermore the absence of troparia at the Biblical canticles—especially at the Song of the Three Children and the Magnificat (presently the 8th and 9th odes of the kanon), of **"Let every breath"**, and of the Sunday hymn (**"The Resurrection of the Savior which we praise"**) at the Doxology. In Palestinian and other monasteries, consequently, all this was already in existence. But the most valuable indications are afforded us by the narrative concerning the cathedral-parish, secular divine service—valuable in view of the fact that no other information concerning it hath survived from this era. According unto the narrative, this divine service was reduced principally unto singing: there were sung—and evidently unto artful and intricate melodies—a) psalms, b) prokeimena and verses corresponding unto them: alleluia, antiphons, **"God is the Lord"**, **"Let every breath"**, c) stichera, sessional hymns, and troparia. The chanting of all this was initiated before the altar by the chanter, who was followed by the people singing along on appointed verses. Festal divine service differed from weekday service both in composition (for example, by the fact that instead of **"God is the Lord"**, alleluia was sung) and in the celebrants: whereas on weekdays the chanting of the most important portions was initiated by the chanters, readers, and subdeacons, on feasts it was begun by the priests. The subdeacons appear chiefly in the role of chanters. Reading was almost analogous in performance unto chanting. All these are characteristics of the so-called Chanted Office (*asmatike akolouthia*), detailed orders of which have been preserved from the IX and subsequent centuries, whose essence consisted precisely in the solemn singing *(Orig. p. 297)* of psalms, antiphons, prokeimena, and similar short verses, in frequent prayers (broad participation of the presbyter in the divine service), and in the congregational execution of diverse refrains unto the psalms. This office, especially in the form in which it is presented by the present narrative, hath much in common with the Western liturgical worship of that era. One of the common features of both, as we shall see, was the paucity of hymns of Christian composition (the dominance of biblical material): throughout the entire divine service there would occur only one or two such hymns (troparia), or canticles. Yet the divine worship in the homeland of the actual narrators already stands upon the transition unto the later type (the present one): in it are found many hymns of the latter kind—stichera, sessional hymns, and troparia for the kanon.

### Kontakia and Kanons

As a transitional stage from the earlier chanted type of divine worship (with the predominance of psalms and their verses in the form of antiphons, etc.) unto the new type with the predominance of stichera, one must suppose the existence of the kontakarian system of divine worship. Unto the most ancient and solitary hymn at divine worship—the troparion, which expressed in brief the essence of the liturgical celebration and was sung as a refrain unto the verses of certain psalms (for example, Ps. 50, Ps. 117 [LXX], etc.)—they began to annex a similarly concise hymn, but executed already independently of the psalm and having following upon it a series of similar songs: the kontakion with a series of ikoi. The first creator of kontakia was a reader or chanter of St. Sophia in Constantinople, St. Romanus the Melodist (*ho Melodos*, † first half of the VI century). He composed kontakia and ikoi, in all probability, for all the most important feasts of his era (with great certainty one may ascribe unto him this composition for at least 15 feasts and commemorations of the year) [^1509]. The number of ikoi in St. Romanus for each feast vacillateth between 24 and 14. Consequently, this was a long series of hymns, which in the services of that time occupied the place of stichera and the kanon: in liturgical books containing stichera and the kanon, only a single kontakion and ikos are ever indicated, rather than such a long series thereof. Stichera and especially the kanon appeared already to replace the kontakarian services, and as one of the first creators of kanons one may recognize St. Andrew of Crete († ca. 712 AD).

### The Horologion of the VIII Century

More detailed information concerning the aforementioned third type of divine worship—cathedral-parish worship—from the era of the VI–VIII centuries doth not exist. Only from the IX century and subsequent centuries have offices come down unto us, yet already in conjunction with later accretions—for example, stichera and kanons—which cannot be isolated with scholarly certainty, and therefore a reliable conception of this type of divine worship for the present period cannot be formed. Nevertheless, the exposition of the Chanted Office (*asmatike akolouthia*) of the IX–XVI centuries will simultaneously *(Orig. p. 298)* afford us subsequently certain conjectural suppositions concerning the form which it possessed at this time.

Meanwhile, concerning Palestinian-monastic divine worship of the era under examination, information hath been preserved for its further course as well—from the VIII century. This is the Greek "Horologion according unto the Typikon of the Lavra of Our Holy Father Sabas" (*Hōrologion kata kanona tēs lauras...*) in a manuscript of the VIII–IX century [^1510]. The Horologion was intended for cell use; for which reason it doth not contain not only all parts of the service (for example, litanies, priestly exclamations), but even certain services, such as Matins. Apparently, in lieu of Matins there stands at the beginning of the Horologion the first kathisma. Then follow the services for the 1st hour of the day, the 3rd, 6th, and 9th, the service for Communion of the Presanctified Gifts (corresponding unto the Typika / *Izobrazitel'ny*), Vespers, and the service for the 1st hour of the night (corresponding unto Compline), upon which the Horologion breaketh off. The services are very close unto the present ones. Thus Vespers (*ta hesperina*) consisteth of Ps. 103, the 18th kathisma with 3 *Glorias*, Ps. 140 with **"Glory... Now and ever..."** at the end, **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Phos Hilaron / Svete Tikhiy*), the Alleluia with diverse verses for different days (at first verses from the present prokeimenon **"The Lord reigneth"** [*Kyrios ebasileusen / Gospod' votsarisia*]), **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** (*Kataxioson, Kyrie / Spodobi Gospodi*), **"Now lettest Thou"** (*Nyn apolyeis / Nyně otpushchayeshi*), and the Trisagion (*Sviatoe Trishchastie*). The service of each hour consisteth of psalms, the number of which is distinct for different hours: for the First—8; for the Third—7; for the Sixth—6; for the Ninth—4; the Alleluia with verses; the troparion (such as exists at present for each hour, excluding the 1st), before which and after which is written its conclusion, which must have served as its refrain; then the verse of the hour, such as exists at present (that is, for the 1st hour [the printed Russian edition has '10-го часа', an obvious misprint for the 1st hour]: **"Order my steps"** [*Stopy moia*], etc.) with the tripling of its first half (as at present at the 1st Hour in Great Lent); and finally—the Trisagion; consequently, that part of the hour following upon the Trisagion did not yet exist. The service for Communion (= the Typika / *Izobrazitel'ny*) consisteth of the Beatitudes with the refrain **"Remember us, O Lord, when Thou comest"** (*Pomiani nas, Gospodi, egda priideshi*), the **"Heavenly Choir"** (*Lik nebesnyi*), the Symbol of Faith (**"I believe"** [*Veruiu*]), **"Our Father"** (*Otche nash*), **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Gospodi pomiluy*) thrice, **"One is Holy"** (*Heis Hagios / Yedin sviat*), **"O taste and see"** (*Geusasthe kai idete / Vkusite i vidite*), Ps. 33—**"I will bless the Lord"** (*Blagoslovliu Gospoda*), prayers after Communion with the intermediate verse: **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"** (*Eiē to onoma Kyriou / Budi imia Gospodne*). The extant portion of Compline hath the following composition: **"Come, let us worship"** (*Priidite poklonimsia*), **"Having traversed the day, I glorify Thee"** (*Tēn hēmeran dielthōn / Den' preshed blagodariu Tia*), Pss. 4, 12, 26, **"Glory..."**, Pss. 30, 90, 6, **"Glory..."**, **"God is with us"** (*Meth' hēmōn ho Theos / S nami Bog*), the Alleluia with verses (for example, **"Look upon me and hear me, O Lord my God"** [*Prizri, uslyshi mia Gospodi Bozhe*]) and troparia changing according unto the days, **"Lord, have mercy"** thrice, and **"Deliver not unto the beasts the soul that doth praise Thee"** (*Ne predazhd' zverem dushu ispovedaiushchuiusia Tebe*).

## Non-Chalcedonian and Oriental Divine Services

During the period of the VI–VIII centuries, the daily office assumed its present form not only in the Orthodox Church, but also in the heretical communities that separated from Her during this time—the Nestorians, Monophysites, and Monothelites, as well as throughout the entire western half of the Christian world. Acquaintance with the liturgical rites of all these churches sheddeth much light upon the history of our divine worship, all the more so since in the period under consideration the latter *(Orig. p. 299)* possessed much that was similar across diverse churches, and in the less cultured lands of the East could be preserved more invariantly than our own.

### Nestorian Divine Service

The Nestorian divine service possesseth almost no invariable elements. Vespers and Matins begin with **"Glory to God in the highest"** (*thrice*) **"and on earth peace, good will among men"**, and **"Our Father"**; then follow the appointed kathismata (the Psalter is divided into 20 kathismata, while the 21st is constituted by the 2 Canticles of Moses) and the so-called "Tone of Matins", that is, according unto the appointed tone (of which there are only two) one of the 2 kathismata—the 12th (with Ps. 67) or the 21st, with hymns assigned unto it on feasts, and on weekdays with litanies and dismissal prayers—all according unto the tone. Besides this, every Matins hath also Ps. 50, while Sunday Matins hath a Six Psalms (*Hexapsalmos*) composed of Pss. 99, 90, 103 (vv. 1–16), 62, 149, and 150. At every service the Nicene Creed is recited [^1511]. Concerning the composition of the Hours we possess no information.

### Armenian Divine Service

The Armenians (Monophysites) possess the following daily offices: the Midnight Office (*Gisherayin Zham*), Dawn (*Aravotyan Zham* = Matins), Sunrise (*Arevagal*, 1st Hour), the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours (*Jashu Zham*), Vespers (*Erekoyan Zham*), Peace (*Khaghaghakan Zham* = Compline), and the Service before Sleep (*Hangstyan Zham* / Rest). The services begin and end with **"Our Father"**. The Midnight Office: **"O Lord, open Thou my lips"** (*Kyrie ta cheilē mou anoixeis / Gospodi ustne moi otverzeshi*) thrice; "Blessed is the consubstantial, undivided, and holy Trinity, the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages". Psalms: **"Lord, how are they increased"** (Ps. 3), **"O Lord God of my salvation"** (Ps. 87), **"Bless the Lord, O my soul"** (Ps. 102), **"Hear my prayer, O Lord, give ear unto my supplication"** (Ps. 142). At the end of the psalms, **"Glory..."**. A prayer beginning: "Having arisen from the rest of sleep, which God Who loveth mankind hath granted unto us..." Then an exhortation or instruction is read. After it, **"Lord, have mercy"** on weekdays 50 times, in Lent 100 times, on feasts 3 times. Prayer: "We give thanks unto Thee, O Lord our God..." Hymns (of Christian composition). The Gospel—on Sundays. A special prayer: "By the intercession of the Holy Mother of God, of St. John the Baptist, and of the saint whose day it is, grant unto us, O Almighty God..." (corresponding unto our prayer before the kanon: **"Save, O God, Thy people"** [*Spasi Bozhe liudi Tvoia*]). Two divisions or "kanons" of the Psalter (the Armenians divide the Psalter into 8 portions, corresponding unto our kathismata and termed *kanons* [Ganonk']). Four instructions corresponding unto the day, and after each the singing of a similar prayer in diverse tones. Hymn: "King of the Ages", and another according unto the day. A special supplication, reading of the Menology (*Chet'yi-Minei*). The 3rd, 4th, and 5th divisions of the Psalter. — The service of "Dawn": **"We were filled in the morning with Thy mercy"** (Ps. 89:14). Song of the Three Children. A hymn in honor of the saints. Prayer unto the Blessed Virgin. **"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** (*Velichit dusha moia*). Hymn unto the Blessed Virgin. The Canticle *(Orig. p. 300)* of Zacharias. Then followeth on Sundays only: a prayer in the nature of a litany composed of priestly exclamations "Let us pray unto the Lord for such-and-such or for such a person", with the congregational response "Unto the Lord let us pray". Prayer: "Thou art the King of the ages". Three verses from the psalms according unto the day. **"Blessed be the name of the Lord from henceforth and for evermore"** (*Budi imia Gospodne blagoslovenno ot nyne i do veka*). The Resurrection Gospel. A homily or instruction beginning: "Rejoicing with great joy over the tidings of the Resurrection of our Lord Jesus Christ..." and a brief prayer. On other days, after the Canticle of Zacharias, Ps. 50, an exhortation unto prayer through the intercession of the saints of the day, a laudatory hymn unto the saints, and a prayer with kneeling. After this variable portion, again the invariable: Psalm: **"Praise the Lord from the heavens"** (Ps. 148) with the 2 following (Pss. 149–150). Three verses in honor of God and the saints of the day. **"Glory to God in the highest"**. Two verses from the psalms according unto the day. A prayer chanted by three monks or clerics. Another prayer. The Trisagion. Psalm: **"Praise, O ye servants, the Lord"** (Ps. 112). On Sundays—the Gospel of the day. A canticle or hymn. Psalms: **"Give ear unto my words, O Lord"** (Ps. 5), **"I loved, because the Lord hath heard"** (Ps. 114), **"Out of the depths"** (Ps. 129), **"Save me, O God, by Thy name"** (Ps. 53). The two final verses of Ps. 85 (**"Shew me a token for good..."**). Supplications for diverse classes of people (= the Augmented Litany / *ekteneia*). Hymn. Instruction. Prayer. — Sunrise (the 1st Hour): **"Blessed be the name of the Lord for ever: His name endureth before the sun..."** and so forth unto the end of Ps. 71. **"Glory..."**. Prayer. Psalm—**"It is a good thing to give thanks unto the Lord"** (Ps. 91). Prayer. Psalms: **"O God, my God, unto Thee do I rise early"** (Ps. 62), **"A psalm is due unto Thee"** (Ps. 64). Prayer. In fasts—a special hymn. Psalms: **"O God, my God, look upon me"** (Ps. 21); Ps. 142 from the verse: **"Cause me to hear Thy lovingkindness in the morning"**; **"My heart is ready"** (Ps. 107); **"O God, attend unto my help"** (Ps. 69). The two final verses of Ps. 85. Instruction. Prayer. — The 3rd Hour: Prayer unto the Holy Spirit. Ps. 50. A Canticle (Biblical) and instruction. The 6th division of the Psalter. Prayer unto the Holy Spirit. Pss. 21 and 142:8 ff. (**"Cause me to hear Thy lovingkindness in the morning"**). **"Glory..."**. Instruction. Prayer. — The 6th Hour: Prayer unto God the Father. Ps. 50. Instruction, prayer. The 8th division of the Psalter. Ps. 40:1–4 (**"Blessed is he that considereth the poor and needy"**). **"Lord, who shall abide"** (Ps. 14). Instruction. Prayer. — The 9th Hour: Prayer unto the Son of God. Ps. 50. Instruction, prayer; psalms: **"I loved"** (Ps. 114), **"I believed"** (Ps. 115), **"Praise the Lord, all ye nations"** (Ps. 116). Canticle, instruction. — After the 9th Hour the Liturgy is celebrated. After it, or if there be none, then after the 9th Hour an additional special office (without name): Psalm according unto the day. Panegyric word unto the saint of the day. The Trisagion. The 8th division of the Psalter. Prayer, instruction. Several verses from the psalms. An extensive reading from the Prophets or the Apostle (such that an entire Epistle is read through). Alleluia twice. 3 verses from the psalms. Alleluia once. Gospel. **"I believe"** (*The Creed*). Instruction, prayer. — Vespers: **"As for me, I cried unto God, and the Lord saved me"**; **"Evening, and morning, and at noonday will I pray and cry aloud, and He shall hear my voice"** (Ps. 54:17–18)—and verses of proper composition. Psalm: **"Bow down Thine ear, O Lord"** (Ps. 85). **"Glory..."**. **"Glory to Thee, O Lord"**. Pss. 139–141. On Sundays, a litany of 33 petitions with the response "Unto the Lord let us pray". Prayer. The Trisagion. Psalm: **"I lifted up mine eyes unto the hills"** (Ps. 120). Canticle. Instruction. Prayer. Psalms: **"Lord, who shall abide"** (Ps. 14), **"Unto Thee have I lifted up mine eyes"** (Ps. 122), **"Save me, O God, by Thy name"** (Ps. 53). Instruction. Prayer. — Compline: **"O Lord God of my salvation, I have cried day and night before Thee. Let my prayer enter into Thy presence: incline Thine ear unto my *(Orig. p. 301)* supplication"** (Ps. 87:2–3). **"Glory..."**. Psalms: **"When I called"** (Ps. 4), **"O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine anger"** (Ps. 6), **"How long, O Lord?"** (Ps. 12), **"Preserve me, O Lord"** (Ps. 15), **"Hear the right, O Lord"** (Ps. 16), **"As the hart panteth"** (Ps. 41), **"O God, attend unto my help"** (Ps. 69). The two final verses of Ps. 85. **"Glory..."**. A lengthy hymn, imploring from God a peaceful night. Instruction. Prayer. **"The Lord is my light"** (Ps. 26). In fasts—a special hymn. Instruction. Prayer. — The Service before Sleep: Ps. 42:3–5 (**"Send forth Thy light and Thy truth..."**). **"Glory..."** with several verses. From Psalm 118, several of its sections. Ps. 35:1–4 (**"For with Thee is the fountain of life: in Thy light shall we see light..."**). From the Canticle of Habakkuk 3:18–19 (**"Yet will I rejoice in the Lord..."**). Psalms: **"Lord, who shall abide"** (Ps. 14), **"Unto Thee have I lifted up mine eyes"** (Ps. 122), **"Save me, O God, by Thy name"** (Ps. 53). Beginning of the Song of the Three Children down unto **"O all ye waters, bless the Lord"**. Ps. 150. **"Lord, now lettest Thou"** (*Nyn apolyeis / Nyně otpushchayeshi*). Ps. 137:7–8 (**"Though I walk in the midst of trouble..."**). Ps. 141:6–8 (**"I cried unto Thee, O Lord..."**). The Magnificat. The 2 final verses of Ps. 85. Prayer. Psalm: **"When I called"** (Ps. 4). Hymn. Gospel. Prayer [^1512]. The principal peculiarity of the Armenian divine worship, therefore, is that the Psalter is read through completely during the offices of each day.

### Divine Service of the Copts and Abyssinians

The daily office of the Copts (Monophysites) consisteth of Matins, the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours, Compline, Vespers, and the Midnight Office. The services begin: "In the name of the Father...", **"Glory to the Father..."**, **"Our Father"**, and the verse "We give thanks unto the Beneficent, the Merciful One", and each consisteth of an initial series of psalms, the Gospel, troparia, and prayers, with certain additions unto this composition for the more important services. Matins hath 19 psalms: 1–6, 8, 11, 12, 14, 15, 18, 24, 26, 62, 66, 69, 112, 142; the Gospel of John 1:1–16; a hymn similar unto our Doxology; the Symbol of Faith; a series of short prayer exclamations; and 2 prayers. Vespers hath 10 psalms: 129, 130, 131, 136, 137, 140, 141, 145, 146, 147; the Gospel of Luke 2:25–30 (concerning the Meeting of the Lord with the Canticle of Symeon the God-Receiver); the Trisagion; the Creed; **"Our Father"**; and 2 prayers. The Midnight Office—7 psalms: 3, 6, 69, 85, 116, 117, 118; the Gospel of Matthew 25—the parable of the 10 virgins; troparia: **"Behold, the Bridegroom cometh"** (*Se Zhenikh griadet*), **"That day"** (*Den' on*), **"An invincible bulwark"** (*Tebe neoborimuiu stenu*); the Trisagion; the Gospel of Luke 7:36 ff. concerning the woman who was a sinner; 3 troparia which are met with among us as penitential sessional hymns; the Gospel of Luke 12:35 ff. concerning the expectation of the Second Coming; penitential troparia; laudatory verses unto the Most Holy Theotokos **"Rejoice"**, resembling our Akathist; and a lengthy prayer. Conversely, Compline (celebrated prior unto Vespers) consisteth solely of psalms and the Gospel. At the Hours are almost all of our troparia and, for the most part, as at Compline, 12 psalms (at the 9th Hour—11) [^1513]. Consequently, for the majority of the services the system of 12 psalms is adopted—as we have seen, the distinctive characteristic of ancient Egyptian monastic worship. — In doctrine and ecclesiastical structure, *(Orig. p. 302)* the Abyssinian Christians, likewise Monophysites, are very close unto the Copts. The divine worship of the two differeth somewhat. Yet the divine worship of the Abyssinians, both contemporary and especially ancient, possessed several types, a complete conception of which is not yet accessible unto European scholarship—owing unto the fact that in Abyssinia liturgical books are in manuscript and only certain of them have been published in recent times. Among others, there hath been published also the Horologion of the Abyssinian Church [^1514], yet in the form which it received by the XIV century under Coptic and Greek influence [^1515]. The services in it are very close unto the Coptic, but more extensive than they, and in places approach our own more closely than the Coptic. The most important differences from the Coptic Horologion are that in lieu of Matins there are two services: the "prayer (service) at the 3rd hour of the night" and the "prayer at cockcrow"; the 1st Hour significantly differeth from the others and is close unto the concluding portion of our Matins; Compline followeth after Vespers, as with us. Besides this Horologion, in Abyssinia even at the present day horologia of other types are in use, in all probability more ancient. One of these horologia, presently in use in only a single Abyssinian monastery, presenteth services consisting entirely of metrical hymns in honor of the Holy Trinity, the Mother of God, and diverse choirs of saints (at Vespers venerable monastics are praised; at the 1st Hour, the Apostles, etc.) and a multitude of biblical and edifying readings, yet possessing no psalms whatever; in another, in use in certain monasteries, the services consist of psalms, priestly prayers, and biblical readings. It must be noted that the Abyssinians in general take a rather free approach toward the order of divine service, and, while observing its general structure (scheme), fill it with hymns from their diverse collections and with improvisations; for this reason hymnography at their services occupieth an overwhelming position. There exist immense collections of these hymns: the *Deggwa*, the *Psalter of Christ*, the *Psalter of the Virgin*; the hymns are for the most part in verse, some of them resembling our Akathists—presenting a series of praises (*malk'e*), sometimes addressed unto diverse parts of the saint's body and beginning with the word "peace" ("Peace unto thy head, which...", "Peace unto thy hands...") or "rejoice". These are the so-called "likenesses" (*effigies / portraits*); furthermore there are distinguished also antiphons—refrains unto psalms and biblical canticles, and the *wazema*—akin unto our stichera. The greatest stamp of antiquity among Abyssinian liturgical orders is borne by the All-Night Vigil set forth in the book *Me'eraf* ("chapters", that is, Typikon) and the *Deggwa*. Its composition is: Ps. 23 [LXX Ps. 23 / Masoretic Ps. 24] **"The earth is the Lord's"**, titled among the Abyssinians, like Ps. 103, "the beauty of creation"; Ps. 92 **"The Lord reigneth"**, and Ps. 140 with *wazema* (stichera). The psalms are separated by litanies; then follow the appointed section of the Psalter (it is divided into 10 decades), the evening prayer of the priest, paroemias from the Apostolic Epistles, the prokeimenon, and the Gospel. The morning prayers of the priest; (p. 337) the prayer **"Save, O God, Thy people"** (*Spasi Bozhe liudi Tvoia*); the morning Litiya (litany petitions); the Four Psalms: Pss. 62, 91, 5, 64; the appointed section of the Psalter: Ps. 50; the Biblical canticles with refrains from the *Wazema*—namely: the Prayer of Manasseh, the Canticles of the holy Habakkuk, of the Three *(Orig. p. 303)* Children, and of Zacharias; the Lauds (*Ainoi*) psalms with refrains; the Synaxarion (*Senkessar*); Theotokia; the Gospel; the reading of the "Miracles of Mary" (*Ta'amra Maryam*); the Song of Songs (in Lent); improvised or collected refrains (*mawwaddes*) for Sunday (the Great Doxology at the 1st Hour) [^1516].

### Maronite Divine Service

The Maronites (Monothelites) possess 7 daily services: the Midnight Office, Matins, the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours, Vespers, and Compline. They do not chant the entire Psalter (as neither do the Copts) either in a day or in a week, but only certain psalms; at the Midnight Office—Pss. 62, 14, 50, and 116; at the 3rd and 9th Hours—Ps. 50; at Vespers—Pss. 50, 140, 141, and from Ps. 118 vv. 105–112 (**"Thy law is a lamp unto my feet..."** [*Lucerna pedibus meis lex tua* / *"Svetil'nik nogama moima zakon Tvoi..."*]); at Compline—Pss. 50, 14, and 116. At the beginning and conclusion of each office: the Trisagion, **"Our Father"**, **"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"** (*Bogoroditse Devo, raduisia*), the Symbol of Faith (**"I believe"**), and one prayer: following the customary opening, a hymn is performed alternately with a psalm or a biblical canticle or some prayerful invocation, so that after a part of a hymn there follows a part of a psalm or canticle, and so forth, with the entire hymn in conclusion; thereafter prayers, biblical canticles, psalms, and hymns alternate with one another, so that after a prayer there follows a canticle, after it a hymn or psalm, and the like. The Midnight Office contains 16 prayers, 11 canticles, 6 hymns, 2 psalms, 1 responsory, and other prayerful exclamations. Matins has 11 prayers, 7 hymns, 7 canticles, 4 psalms, and 1 responsory; the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours—5 prayers, 3 or 2 canticles, and 1 psalm (the 6th Hour has no psalm). Vespers has 7 prayers, 2 hymns, 4 canticles, 4 psalms, and 1 responsory. Compline—5 prayers, 3 psalms, 2 hymns, and 2 canticles [^1517].

### Divine Worship of the Western Church

The development of Western divine worship took a different course, although at times it exhibited significant convergence with the Eastern. In the daily offices here, the fixed psalms adapted to the time of day soon disappeared, leaving only brief excerpts from them in the form of antiphons and responsories, which, thanks to the solemn manner of their performance (complex melodies and the special alternation of officiants during their chanting), occupied the most prominent position in the service; antiphons accompanied the chanting of the psalms, and responsories accompanied the readings. The psalms themselves, as also the liturgical readings, were selected not to suit the specific moment (the hour of the office or the commemorated event), but were recited in continuous cursus: the entire Psalter was chanted through in regular order at the services, just as the books read in divine worship were read consecutively; consequently, the whole essence of divine worship lay in the quantity of psalms and antiphons, readings and responsories; by this quantity the solemnity of the office was measured. Only for certain offices, namely for the final portion of Matins, the 1st Hour, and Compline, were there fixed psalms adapted to them; and the connection of an office to the celebrated event was expressed only by a single reading (for example, on Sunday one of *(Orig. p. 304)* the readings was the Gospel of the Resurrection). Thus, only the antiphons and responsories bore a relation to the specific liturgical moment. Yet almost the principal difference between Western and Eastern worship, both in this epoch and in the subsequent one (as partly also in the preceding), was the extremely restricted use of hymns of Christian composition. In some places there was even a movement in favor of entirely excluding hymns from the body of divine service. The Second Council of Braga (*Bracarensis*, in Spain) of 563 requires "that, apart from the psalms and canonical scriptures of the Old and New Testaments, no poetic composition (*nihil poetice compositum*) be sung in church, as the holy canons also command" (canon 12). But the Second Council of Tours [in Gaul] of 567 decrees:
"Although in the canon we possess only the Ambrosian hymns, nevertheless, since certain of the remaining ones are worthy of being sung in form, we willingly agree to accept, in addition to them, those whose authors' names are indicated in the margins" (canon 23).
The 1st [4th] Council of Toledo of 633 (canon 13) demonstrates thoroughly and persistently the legitimacy of hymns in divine service against those who reject them. In the Church of Lyons, hymns are sung only at Compline; likewise in Vienne, hymns are sung only at Compline, varying on different feasts [^1518].

### Western Cathedral-Parochial Divine Worship in the VI–VIII Centuries

As in the East, the entire task of developing divine worship was assumed by monasticism; therefore, information regarding cathedral-parochial worship is very sparse. The daily offices were the same as in the East; but the Midnight Office and Matins formed a single service, frequently termed *vigilia* (vigil) from its commencement in the deep of night; according to the divisions of the night, it was divided into several, for the most part three, *nocturni* (nocturns), followed by Matins in the strict sense, designated *matutinum* or *ad Laudes*. The Hours were not celebrated everywhere, so that on the part of Caesarius, Bishop of Arles (in Gaul, † 542), a special ordinance was required so that the clerics, besides Matins and Vespers, would celebrate in the Cathedral of St. Stephen in Arles the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours with their hymns [^1519]. Regarding the order and rite of parochial services, the following testimonies have been preserved. The night service or Matins, at least in certain localities, gradually began to be started later and later. Whereas Gregory of Tours in the VI century says of his contemporaries that they "arise at midnight to render thanksgiving unto the Lord" [^1520], in the VIII century Chrodegang (*Grodegangus*), Bishop of Metz, in his rules for canons permits them "in wintertime, that is, from the Kalends of November until Pascha, to arise at the 8th hour (= 2 o'clock) of the night, in order to sleep a little even after midnight and be more alert for the vigil" [^1521]; and Amalarius in the IX century, explaining the psalm verses at the night vigils that precede the readings, says: "The second verse: **"At midnight I arose"** (*"Polunoshchi vostakh"* / *Media nocte surgebam*); it indicates at what hour of the night one must arise; but since *(Orig. p. 305)* we neglect the time at which our fathers were accustomed to arise, we dare not lie, and we replace this verse with another: **"For Thou wilt light my lamp"** (*"Yako Ty esi prosveshchiaiai svetil'nik moi"* / *Quoniam tu illuminas lucernam meam*)" [^1522]. There is an indication regarding the structure of the night service in the acts of the Gallic Council of 499 against the Arians in the presence of Gundobad, King of the Burgundians. When the bishops celebrated a vigil at the tomb of St. Justus on his feast day,
"it came to pass that when the reader at night according to custom began the reading of Moses, he came upon the words: **"And I will harden his heart"**; then, when after the singing of the psalms he read from the Prophets, there occurred the words of the Lord to Isaiah: **"Go, and say unto this people: Hearing ye shall hear..."** When the psalms were sung again, and he (the reader) read from the Gospel, he came upon the words with which the Savior rebukes the unbelief of the Jews: **"Woe unto thee, Chorazin..."** When at last there was a reading from the Apostle, the following words were pronounced: **"Or despisest thou the riches of His goodness..."** This was noticed by all the bishops, and all recognized that these readings fell out by the will of God, so that it might be known that the king's heart was hardened" [^1523].
Regarding the number of psalms at the night service, which is not stated in this account, the Second Council of Tours (in Gaul) of 567 says:
"At Matins on feast days let 6 antiphons be expanded (*explicentur*), each with two psalms; throughout the whole of August let there be accelerated Matins (*manicationes*, from *mane*), because at that time there are feasts and masses of saints; in September, 7 antiphons with two psalms each; in October, 8 with 3 psalms; in November, 9 with 3; in December, 10 with 3; in January and February the same until Pascha (consequently, the greatest number of psalms at Matins was 30, and the smallest 12); but whoever recites fewer than 12 psalms, let him fast until evening, eating bread with water, and let him have no other nourishment on that day; and whoever neglects to do this latter, let him eat bread with water all week and fast every day until evening" (canon 18).
At the night service, a special independent position was occupied by its concluding portion, which fell at dawn (*ad Laudes*); it was celebrated with particular solemnity. Gregory of Tours recounts of Gallus of Arverna (Clermont) that, although in other places at dawn they sang only the Benediction (*Benedictio*—the Canticles of the Three Holy Children and of Zacharias, which begin with the verb "to bless" and are appointed now in the final part of Catholic Matins [^1524]), he concluded Matins having chanted Ps. 50, the Benediction, and performed the Alleluiaticum with a little chapter (*alleluiatico cum capitello*—a brief excerpt from the Old or New Testament)" (all this is appointed even today at *ad Laudes*). — Regarding the office of the 1st Hour in the Western Church of this epoch, it is known that confession of sins took place at it: "Before Ps. 50," says Chrodegang (*Grodegangus*), Bishop of Metz in the VIII century concerning the 1st Hour, "let them make confession one to another, saying: **"I confess unto the Lord and unto thee, brother, that I have sinned in thought, word, and deed; therefore I beseech thee, pray for me"**; and the other brother answers: **"May Almighty God have mercy upon thee, and forgive thee all thy sins, deliver *(Orig. p. 306)* thee from every evil, preserve thee in all good, and bring thee unto life everlasting"**" [^1525] (a similar confession exists in a different formula even today at the Roman Catholic 1st Hour; cf. among us the mutual forgiveness at the end of Compline and the Midnight Office). Following the 1st Hour in certain churches there was a distinct office—the *officium capituli* (chapter office), consisting of the reading of some canonical or pastoral rule (cf. among us the Catechesis of St. Theodore the Studite at the 2nd Hour) and the martyrology, followed by the verse: **"Precious in the sight of the Lord is the death of His saints"** (*"Chestna pred Gospodem smert' prepodobnykh Ego"* / Ps. 115:6; cf. our prokeimenon); on Sundays, Wednesdays, Fridays, and feast days of saints, the first reading was replaced by a homily [^1526]. Among the other offices there is mention of the 6th Hour and Vespers. The aforementioned Council of Tours states: "The patristic ordinances command that at the 6th hour 6 psalms with Alleluia be said, and at the 12th hour 12 psalms likewise with Alleluia" (canon 18). By the 12th hour must be understood, presumably, Vespers, since Compline could only have appeared after Vespers. The Council of Mérida (*Emeritensis*) in Spain of 606 requires that "as in other churches on feast days in the evening, after the bringing in of the light (*post lumen oblatum*), the *vespertinum* (evening psalm) is said before the *sonus* (sound), so let this be observed also by us in our churches" (canon 2). The obscure terms encountered here are well explained by the order of Vespers in the Mozarabic (Spanish) Breviary: "Whether on a feast day or an ordinary day, the hours (the reckoning of liturgical time) always begin with Vespers on the eve [^1527], and the beginning is made through the invocation of Jesus Christ with the preceding Lord's Prayer—through pronouncing in a low voice: **"Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison. Our Father"**. And in a loud voice: **"In the Name of the Lord Jesus Christ, light be with you"** [^1528], that is, light hath been brought in. Those present respond: **"Thanks be to God"** (*Deo gratias*). And the presbyter says: **"The Lord be always with you"**. Response: **"And with thy spirit"**. And the order of Vespers, whether a feast or not, proceeds as follows: first the psalm is said, that is, the *Vespertinum* (evening psalm) [^1529]; upon its conclusion the presbyter says: **"The Lord be with you"**. Response: **"And with thy spirit"**. Immediately the *sonus* is said, if it be a feast, seeing that a weekday hath no *sonus*, with the exception of Sunday, when it is said for the sake of solemnity. Such is the rule. And this *sonus* is: **"O come,** **let us rejoice unto the Lord..."** (*"Priidite, vozraduemsia Gospodevi..."* / *Venite, exsultemus Domino* [Ps. 94:1 / MT 95:1]) [^1530].
On Sundays the office was more solemn: according to the ancient rite of the churches of Cambrai (*Cameracensis*) and Arras (*Atrebatensis*), the Sunday vigil was to begin before midnight, the ringing for it with all the bells (*signa*), the church was to be illuminated abundantly, the readings and responsories were to be performed protractedly (*tractim*), the ninth reading was evangelical from patristic homilies and was read by the deacon, presbyter, or bishop in its entirety, unless dawn intervened; at the beginning of each of the three nocturns there was censing with 2 censers, which at the *(Orig. p. 307)* first nocturn were brought to the altar, at the second into the choir, and at the third to the people; the morning portion of the vigil was chanted still more slowly and in a higher pitch than the nocturns [^1531].

### Antiphons, Responsories, and Collects

For a complete conception of Western cathedral-parochial divine worship in the VI–VIII centuries, a few additional remarks must be made regarding the manner of performing antiphons and responsories, which occupied such an important place in it, as also concerning the rite of concluding the service, since even greater significance was attached to this conclusion of worship here than in the East. In the epoch under consideration, the term *antiphon* had already fully acquired that meaning which it bears in contemporary Roman Catholic worship, that is, the meaning of a brief verse before a psalm or series of psalms or after it—a verse taken for the most part from that very psalm, expressing its central theme or adapting the psalm to the feast. Today, however, the antiphon is chanted only once before or after the psalm, whereas in the period under consideration antiphons were sometimes chanted with every verse of the psalm. Thus the canons of the Church of St. Martin of Tours, according to the testimony of John the Monk in the Life of St. Odo (Abbot of Cluny, † 943), wishing to prolong the service until dawn, chanted the antiphons twice at every verse of the psalm. The same is evident from the fact that on the greatest feast days at Matins (*in Laudibus*) at the end of the Canticle of Zacharias, and at Vespers at the end of the Canticle of the Theotokos (Magnificat), the antiphon was repeated thrice: once before **"Glory to the Father..."**, a second time at **"Both now and ever..."** (*Sicut erat*), and a third time at the entire concluding verse (such chanting of the antiphon was termed *triumphare—ter fari*, to 'triple') [^1532]. In a manuscript antiphonary of the XI century, to every verse of the Canticle of the Theotokos there is assigned as an antiphon a verse from the Gospel of Matthew concerning the Resurrection of Christ. The chanting of the antiphon was begun (*impositio*), at a sign from the archdeacon, by particularly skilled cantors holding the rank of subdeacon, of whom there were 7 in the Roman Church: the first antiphon being intoned by the foremost of these subdeacons (*primicerius*), the second by the second-ranking (*secundicerius*), and so forth; only at Pascha did a deacon intone the antiphon to the Gospel [^1533]. (Cf. below the Asmatic Cursus / Sung Office and above the assessment of Abba Nilus of Sinai regarding cathedral divine worship). By *responsory* was meant, for the most part, a verse sung in connection with a reading (cf. our prokeimenon), specifically following the reading. This is a verse taken mostly from a psalm, expressing the fundamental thought of the lesson; today by responsory is properly understood the second half of such a verse, constituting the choir's response to its first half sung by the cantor or priest, which is termed the verse—*versus*, *versiculum*. Amalarius (IX century) notes the difference in the singing of the responsory between the Roman and Gallican churches: the Romans, upon finishing the verse, 'begin the responsory from the beginning,' that is, they answer the singing of the verse by repeating that same entire verse *(Orig. p. 308)* (as among us in chanting the prokeimenon the second time), whereas in Gaul 'from the final verse they make a responsory by means of its two parts, joining them into a single body' (as among us in chanting the prokeimenon the 3rd time); for this reason, for a responsory it was necessary to select a verse both parts of which would possess their own meaning, while their union would yield a new thought [^1534]. The responsory was chanted in a special place of the temple or in the midst of the choir, but not upon the ambo. The verse preceding the responsory was always chanted more softly than the latter (cf. among us the chanting of the verse unto the prokeimenon), out of apprehension that the voice might not suffice for the responsory: 'while at the repetition of the responsory they raise the voice with confidence, no longer fearing the verse' [^1535]. According to canon 17 of the Fourth Council of Toledo of 633, 'some at the end of the responsory do not say **"Glory to the Father..."** on the ground that it sometimes sounds unsuitable; but let there be such a distinction, that on joyful responsories **"Glory..."** should follow, while on mournful ones the beginning should be repeated' (cf. among us the Alleluia of Lenten Vespers without the **"Glory..."**). In the Arabic recension of the canons of the Council of Nicaea it is required to chant the responsories from memory, and not from a book [^1536] (cf. our canonarch). — A very important part of Matins and Vespers was constituted by their conclusion, the final, dismissive prayer, termed the *collecta*. It was pronounced by the highest-ranking cleric present at the service. The Council of Barcelona (*Barcinonensis*) of 540 prohibits 'presbyters in the presence of the bishop to conclude (*non colligant*) the prayers' (canon 5). This conclusion was always identical for different offices, and Agrestius accused Abbot Columbanus at the Council of Mâcon (*Matisconensis*, in Gaul) in 585 of having introduced different collects for different offices. In the Lateran Basilica the Lord's Prayer served as the collect (cf. among us at the end of Vespers and at the end of the Hours according to the Horologia of the VIII–IX centuries), but this was a peculiarity and, as it were, a privilege of this single church, in which an indication was seen of the primacy and dignity of the Roman Church. In the words of the Spanish Abbot Beatus of the VII century, 'upon the conclusion of the office one must not depart from the church before they say: **"In the Name of our Lord Jesus Christ, let us go in peace"**' [^1537].

### Western Monastic Divine Worship

We possess far more information concerning monastic divine worship in the West during the period under consideration. It differed in different monasteries (just as even now many Roman Catholic monasteries possess special liturgical Typika / rules). Several renowned abbots and bishops of this period left behind their rules for divine worship, which, albeit in varying degrees, influenced the development of the present Roman liturgical rite and exhibit in places interesting correspondences with our own Typikon. To these monastic rules, it would appear, Roman worship is primarily indebted for the elimination from the offices of the fixed psalms (for example, the morning psalms, *(Orig. p. 309)* the evening psalm) and their replacement by continuous divisions of the Psalter. The most important of these monastic rules is: 1) that of St. Benedict of Nursia († 543), founder of the famous monastery of Monte Cassino in southern Italy and of the order bearing his name, and generally the principal organizer of Western monasticism. In his *Rule* (*Regula*) he refers unto the rules of Basil the Great, the *Collationes* of St. Cassian, and at times reveals dependence upon the Pachomian rules [^1538]. 2) Benedict's rival in influence upon Western monasticism was Columbanus († 615), an Irishman [lit. *Scot*], founder of a series of monasteries first in Gaul, then in Italy; his monastic rules are entirely distinctive, rather severe (bearing the imprint of his northern origin), contain no references unto older rules, including that of Benedict, and were adopted in many monasteries prior unto the introduction of the Benedictine Rule. Further noted for their monastic rules were: 3) Caesarius, Bishop of Arles (*Arelatensis*, in Gaul, † 542), and his second successor in the see, 4) Aurelian; unto the former, besides the *Regula ad monachos*, is also attributed the *Regula ad virgines* (intended for the sister of Caesarius and the nuns living with her) with a more complex and detailed liturgical order than in the first *Rule*, which excites doubt concerning their authenticity; Aurelian's rules coincide in places with those of Columbanus; 5) Isidore, Bishop of Seville, † ca. 666; 6) Donatus, Bishop of Besançon (*Vesontionensis*) in northern Gaul [or *Vesontio*], † ca. 624 (*Regula ad virgines*); 7) Fructuosus, Bishop of Braga (*Bracarensis*) in Spain, † after 675; 8) an anonymous author, surnamed *Magister* of the VII century (*Regula Magistri*); and 9) two unknown abbots: the rule of one of them was published with the works of Blessed Augustine, that of the other with the rules of St. Benedict [^1539].

### The Night Office

The rule of psalmody is simplest in the last-named anonymous author:
'One must assemble for three daytime gatherings and for as many at night; at each daytime gathering one must chant 3 psalms, and at all the night gatherings 12, besides that office (*missam*) which is celebrated at sunrise; prayers must also be pronounced, as well as two readings, one from the Old Testament and one from the New at each of the night gatherings; at the gatherings on Saturday and Sunday the office must be celebrated until cockcrow' (canon 30).
For the night office, close unto this rule in simplicity was the order observed by Columbanus in many (up to 1,000) monasteries contemporary with him:
'There are certain catholics who have one and the same canonical number of 12 psalms for both short and long nights, and from this rule they take for each *(Orig. p. 310)* night watch 4 psalms: for the beginning of the night, for midnight or cockcrow, and for Matins...; but on the especially sacred (*reverentissimis*) nights of Saturday and Sunday this number (of psalms) is tripled, that is, there are 36 of them' (ch. 7).
It is remarkable how in both of these orders the system of 12 psalms is maintained, transferred from Egypt unto the West already by St. Cassian. Somewhat more complex, but closer than others unto these orders, is the night office in St. Benedict: in it the 12-psalm system is likewise maintained, but the 12 psalms are sharply divided into two sections of 6 psalms each (cf. among us the Six Psalms and the Praises / Lauds psalms at Matins); moreover, in St. Benedict the office receives all the accessories of cathedral-parochial worship: antiphons, responsories, and other verses; great significance is likewise attached unto the readings. The night office (*vigiliae*) according to the Rule of St. Benedict begins with the verses **"O God, come to my assistance"** (*"Bozhe, v pomoshch' moiu vonmi"* / *Deus in adjutorium meum intende*) and (is said, *dicitur*) **"O Lord, open Thou my lips"** (*"Gospodi, ustne moi otverzeshi"* / *Domine labia mea aperies*) thrice (today in reverse order and the second verse once; cf. among us); then Ps. 3 (cf. among us) with **"Glory to the Father..."**, and Ps. 94 [LXX 94 / MT 95] **"O come, let us rejoice unto the Lord"** (*Venite, exsultemus Domino* / *"Priidite, vozraduemsia Gospodevi"*; as today), chanted with antiphonal refrains (consequently melodically, as today) or simply (*certe decantandus*, presumably depending on the solemnity of the service), and an Ambrosian hymn (as today; not the *Te Deum*); all this forms the introductory part of the office, just as today. Next follow 6 psalms with antiphons; after they are pronounced (*dictis*) and the abbot's blessing is given, there are three readings from the Old and New Testaments or from commentaries upon them, with responsories between them, during which the brethren remain seated; they rise at the **"Glory..."** of the final responsory, which alone has it (**"Glory..."**; cf. among us at the kathismata). Another 6 psalms are sung, now with Alleluia, and after them a reading of the Apostle from memory (presumably being very brief, = *capitulum*), a verse, and the petition of the litany, that is, **"Kyrie eleison"** (cf. our Augmented Litany and Litiya), with which the vigil concludes. Thus is the night office celebrated from November until Pascha; in summer, however, it is abbreviated: instead of 3 readings there is one from the Old Testament with one responsory and one from the New Testament. On Sunday the vigil is considerably lengthened, first of all by virtue of the readings: there are 13 of them instead of the 4 or 2 on weekdays: after the first 6 psalms there are 4 readings (not 3 as on weekdays) with responsories, and after the second 6 psalms (sung with antiphons and not with Alleluia), likewise 4 readings (not 1 as on weekdays); furthermore, the vigil receives at the end a new part, as it were a third nocturn, the most solemn: after the second series of readings
'three canticles from the Prophets are sung (cf. our triodion / three-canticle ode), such as the abbot designates, with Alleluia; after the recitation of a verse and the abbot's blessing there are again 4 readings from the New Testament, then the hymn **"We praise Thee, O God"** (*Te Deum laudamus* / *"Tebe Boga khvalim"*), and the abbot reads from the Gospel with fear and trembling, during which all stand, and upon the conclusion of the reading respond: **"Amen"**; unto this the abbot adds: **"Praise becometh Thee"** (*"Tebe podobaiet khvala"*) and, having given the blessing, begins Matins' (chs. 9, 10, 11).
Other rules appoint for the night office fewer or more than 12 psalms, and moreover an unequal quantity of them for different seasons of the year. Thus Isidore appoints for the vigil only 6 psalms and canticles: namely,
'first must be recited (*recitandi*) three canonical (fixed?) psalms, then three masses of psalms *(Orig. p. 311)* (presumably psalms with readings; see below in Caesarius), the fourth (mass) of canticles, the fifth of Matins; on Sundays and feasts of martyrs, for the sake of solemnity, particular (*singulae*) masses are added' (ch. 7).
The first unknown author appoints 6, 5, or 4 psalms: 'The night prayers in November–February have 12 antiphons, 6 psalms, 3 readings; in March, April, September, and October, 10 antiphons, 5 psalms, 3 readings; in May–August, 8 antiphons, 4 psalms, 2 readings' (ch. 1). Caesarius of Arles: from Pascha until October, 18 psalms, 2 readings, a hymn, and a *capitellum* (short reading), and from October until Pascha unto this nocturn there is added yet another, likewise of 18 psalms, 2 readings, and a hymn [^1540]. The Sunday vigil is distinguished by the fact that the readings are from the Gospel: the 1st concerning the Resurrection, the 2nd of the day of the week [Sunday], the 3rd concerning the Resurrection, the 4th of the day. Similarly also Aurelian:
'Daily at nocturns first of all there is recited in direct mode (*directaneus*—by a single choir) **"Have mercy upon me, O God, according to Thy great mercy"** (*"Pomilui mia, Bozhe, po velitsei milosti Tvoei"* / Ps. 50 [LXX 50 / MT 51]); then 18 psalms, three small antiphons, two readings from the Apostle or the Prophets, (a hymn), and a *capitellum*; upon the completion of the nocturns say Matins; thus from Pascha until October; but from October one must join other nocturns: the Psalm **"Have mercy upon me, O God, have mercy upon me"** (*"Pomilui mia, Bozhe, pomilui mia"* / Ps. 56 [LXX 56 / MT 57]), 18 psalms, 2 readings from the Prophets or Solomon, a hymn... and then, since the nights grow longer, perform 3 masses (readings) from the book; after the first 2 readings, a prayer; after the third, an antiphon, a responsory, an antiphon, and again a reading (*capitellum*?).'
Columbanus, so far as one can understand the obscure text of his rule (ch. 7), for winter vigils (from the autumnal equinox until February) appoints 36 psalms with 12 antiphons, and for summer vigils 24 psalms with 8 antiphons; on Saturdays and Sundays from November until February, 75 psalms with 25 antiphons; from February until May this number is decreased each week by 2 psalms with 1 antiphon, so that at the beginning of May there are 36 psalms (on weekdays then only 24), and such a number remains for the Saturday and Sunday vigil until July; from that point it again increases weekly by 3 psalms, until by November it reaches once more 75 psalms. Similar unto Columbanus is Donatus, except that for weekdays he divides the year into two equal halves by the equinoxes, and for Saturdays and Sundays from February 1 gradually reduces the number of psalms from 60 to 36; from May until October, 36 psalms; this number by November *(Orig. p. 312)* increases unto 75 and remains such until February. Fructuosus is the first to divide the night office into three parts, as it is divided today in the Roman Catholic Church:
'Having arisen before midnight, let them recite (*recitent*) by choirs 12 (*duodenos*) psalms; having rested a little, at midnight let them celebrate the office at which 3 responsories are sung (consequently, probably readings as well) for 3 divisions of psalms, so that after the recitation of 3 psalms there follows one responsory, and thus with 3 responsories 12 psalms are sung; after midnight, if it be wintertime, all sit, and one, sitting in the midst, reads, while the abbot or superior in his discourse explains what is read unto those who do not understand, and in conclusion, having again sung 12 psalms, they go to sleep a little until Matins (*Laudes*)' (ch. 3).
Concerning Sunday vigils Fructuosus says nothing. According to the Master (*Magister*):
'at nocturns the abbot intones the opening verse (*apertionis*, that is, **"O Lord, open Thou my lips"** [*Domine, labia mea aperies*]), the responsory of prayer (judging by the Benedictine Rule, Ps. 94 [LXX 94 / MT 95]), then in winter 12 antiphons without Alleluia and a responsory (consequently, there must also be a reading) without Alleluia, as always in the course of the Psalter (*currente dumtaxat psalterio*); then another responsory now with Alleluia, so that there are 16 beginnings (*impositiones*: 2 at the beginning + 12 pss. + 2 resp.; according unto Martène—intonations), a reading of the Apostle, a reading of the Gospel, which the abbot always performs, and in his absence the provosts [praepositi] in turn; then a verse and *Rogus Dei* (prayer); at the end of each psalm a prayer (chs. 44, 33); on all Sundays, however, all antiphons and responsories are said with Alleluia until the nocturns of Monday, and they do not kneel' (ch. 45).

### Matins (Laudes) in Western Monasteries

Closely connected with the night office, although appearing as an independent office, was Matins (*matutinum*), called after its psalms **"Praise the Lord from the heavens"** and the following: *Laudes* or *ad Laudes* (= Praises / Lauds). According unto the Rule of St. Benedict, at Matins first of all there is recited (*dicatur*) Ps. 66 [LXX 66 / MT 67] without antiphons, slowly, so that all may arrive in time, and Ps. 40 [LXX 40 / MT 41], which is recited with antiphons, and on Sunday with Alleluia; then 2 psalms changing by the days of the week: on Monday Pss. 5 and 35 [LXX 35 / MT 36], on Tuesday Pss. 42 and 56 [LXX 56 / MT 57], on Wednesday Pss. 63 and 64 [LXX 64 / MT 65], on Thursday Pss. 87 and 89 [LXX 89 / MT 90], on Friday Pss. 75 and 81 [LXX 81 / MT 82], on Saturday Ps. 142 and the Canticle of Deuteronomy (cf. among us on Meatfare, Cheesefare, and Lazarus Saturdays), which is divided into two 'Glories'; on Sunday Ps. 117 [LXX 117 / MT 118] (cf. among us **"God is the Lord"**) and Ps. 62 [LXX 62 / MT 63]. Then a canticle from the Prophets proper unto each day, 'as the Roman Church sings' (see below), and on Sunday—*Benedictiones*, that is, the Canticle of the Three Holy Children and the *Laudes* (Praises psalms [Pss. 148–150]), a reading from the Apostle (on Sunday from the Apocalypse), a responsory from memory, an Ambrosian hymn (today: *Aeterne rerum conditor* ['Eternal Maker of all things']), a canticle from the Gospel (today the Canticle of Zechariah [*Benedictus*]; on Sunday, therefore, 5 biblical canticles: 3 at the vigil and 2 at Matins, the latter in the order of our canon), a litany, and the conclusion (chs. 12, 13). According unto Aurelian, on Matins: 'first a canticle (*canticum*) unto an antiphon, then in direct mode (*directaneum*) **"Judge me, O God"** (*"Sudi mi, Bozhe"* / Ps. 42 [LXX 42 / MT 43]); **"O God, my God, unto Thee I rise early"** (*"Bozhe, Bozhe moi, k Tebe utreniuio"* / Ps. 62 [LXX 62 / MT 63]); **"Praise the Lord, O my soul"** (*"Khvali, dushe moia, Gospoda"* / Ps. 145 [LXX 145 / MT 146]) *(Orig. p. 313)*; **"Praise ye the Lord, for a psalm is good"** (*"Khvalite Gospoda, iako blag psalom"* / Ps. 146 [LXX 146 / MT 147:1–11]); **"Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem"** (*"Pokhvali, Ierusalime, Gospoda"* / Ps. 147 [LXX 147 / MT 147:12–20]). Then: **"Praise the Lord from the heavens"** (*"Khvalite Gospoda s nebes"* / Ps. 148); **"Sing unto the Lord a new song"** (*"Vospoite Gospodevi pesn' novu"* / Ps. 149); **"Praise the Lord in His saints"** (*"Khvalite Gospoda vo sviatykh Ego"* / Ps. 150). At the antiphon say the hymn: *Splendor paternae gloriae* (**"Radiance of the Father's Glory"** / *"Siianie otecheskoi slavy"*); another: *Aeterne rerum conditor* (**"Eternal Maker of all things"** / *"Vechnyi sveta Tvorets"*); and a *capitellum*, *Kyrie eleison* 12 times alternately.'

Sunday and festal Matins begins according unto Aurelian with the psalm (*directaneum*) **"I will extol Thee, my God, O King"** (*"Voznesu Tia, Bozhe moi i Tsariu"* / Ps. 144 [LXX 144 / MT 145]); then Ps. 42; **"O God, my God, unto Thee I rise early"** (Ps. 62); and **"O give thanks unto the Lord"** (*"Ispovedaitesia Gospodevi"* / Ps. 104 or 117) with Alleluia; the praise psalms of weekday Matins with Alleluia, separated into two groups by the *Benedictio* (the Canticle of the Three Holy Children) and the Canticle of Zechariah (*Benedictus*) or of the Theotokos (*Magnificat*); an Ambrosian hymn; **"We praise Thee, O God"** (*Te Deum laudamus* / *"Tebe Boga khvalim"*); **"Glory to God in the highest"** (*Gloria in excelsis Deo* / *"Slava v vyshnikh Bogu"*); and a *capitellum*. Columbanus appoints for weekday Matins 12 psalms (in course), and for Saturday and Sunday—36. Other rubricists do not indicate a special Matins for Sunday and feasts and provide a briefer order for it. Thus according unto the 1st unknown author, at Matins are recited Pss. 3, 62, 6, and 88 with the appointed antiphons, verses, and responsories. According unto Fructuosus, 'at cockcrow the morning sacred ministry must be celebrated, reciting (*recitatis*) 3 psalms with the Praise (= the Lauds psalms) and its (?) Blessing' (canon 3). According unto the Master, 6 morning psalms must be recited at all seasons (of the year), 1 responsory, a verse (both to the reading), the reading of a *capitulum* (from the Old Testament or the Apostle) and the Gospel, which the abbot always pronounces, in conclusion *Rogus Dei* (ch. 35). Isidore only mentions Matins without indicating its composition. It is remarkable that Caesarius gives the order only for Sunday Matins, and makes no mention of weekday Matins: this leads unto the thought that originally Matins, as an office coinciding with the hour of the Resurrection of Christ, took place only on Sunday; unto this also testifies its exceptionally joyful tone. The *Rule for Monks* of Caesarius gives the following order for Sunday Matins: 'simply (*directaneo*): **"I will extol Thee, my God, O King"**; **"O give thanks"**; **"Let us sing unto the Lord"** (*Cantemus Domino* / *"Poim Gospodevi"*—the Canticle of Moses); **"Praise the Lord, O my soul"**; the *Benedictio*; **"Praise the Lord from the heavens"**; **"We praise Thee, O God"**; **"Glory to God in the highest"**; and a *capitellum*' (ch. 21). The *Rule for Virgins*: 'First say simply a small verse with an antiphon: **"Let us sing unto the Lord"** and all the morning (psalms?) with Alleluia' (§ 69).

### The Hours

For the Hours the majority of abbots appoint 3 psalms, rarely 6 (Caesarius, *Rule for Virgins* § 69) and 12. The order of the office varies among different abbots, and does not resemble the present Roman order, but departs from the latter in the direction of the Eastern rites. According unto St. Benedict, the office of the Hour begins with the verse: **"O God, come to my assistance"** (*"Bozhe, v pomoshch' moiu vonmi"* / *Deus in adjutorium meum intende*), a hymn, 3 psalms separately (*sigillatim*) and not under one 'Glory', a reading, a verse, **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Kyrie eleison*), and the dismissal. On Sunday at the Hours are sections of Ps. 118 (chs. 17 and 18). According unto Aurelian, at each Hour for monks there are 12 psalms, and for nuns 6; after the psalms a hymn (not before the psalms as in Benedict and today, but after them, like our troparion), 2 readings from the Old and New Testaments, a verse (*versiculum*; cf. among us **"Order my steps"**, etc.). *(Orig. p. 314)* According unto Columbanus, 'at each Hour there are appointed by the elders 3 psalms with the addition of intercalary verses: first for our sins, then for all the Christian people, for priests, for the other degrees of the clergy consecrated unto God (*plebis*), finally for those who give alms, for the peace of the churches, and in the end for enemies' (cf. among us at the end of the Midnight Office and Compline) (ch. 7).
According unto Isidore: 3 psalms, a responsory, readings from the Old and New Testaments, *Laudes* (?), a hymn, and a prayer (ch. 7). The 1st unknown author indicates at the Hours 'proper psalms, 2 antiphons, and 2 readings with their prayers.' Fructuosus and the 2nd unknown author speak only of the number of psalms: 3. According unto the Master, at each Hour there are 3 psalms, separate responsories, a reading of the Apostle, a reading of the Gospel by the abbot or provost, and *Rogus Dei* (ch. 35).

### Vespers

At Vespers (*vespera*, *lucernarium*) a varying quantity of psalms is appointed, but it is remarkable that some appoint for it alone, as among us, only one psalm; the general structure of the office for the most part resembles that of an Hour, at times completely coinciding with it. According unto St. Benedict: 4 psalms with antiphons, a reading with a responsory (cf. the Old Testament paremias), a hymn (cf. **"O Gladsome Light"**), a verse, a canticle from the Gospel (**"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** / *Magnificat*), a litany (cf. among us), the Lord's Prayer (cf. among us), and the dismissal; the psalms at Vespers are in course from 109 to 147 [LXX 109–147 / MT 110–147], with the exception of those which are employed at other offices (chs. 17, 18). According unto Aurelian, first a *directaneus* (one psalm chanted by the choir simply), then two antiphons, and a third with Alleluia, and a hymn. According unto the 1st unknown author: 1 psalm, 1 responsory, 3 antiphons, and 3 readings. In Columbanus Vespers apparently has the composition of a three-psalm Hour. According unto Isidore, first a *lucernarium* (an evening psalm?), 2 psalms, 1 responsory, *Laudes*, a hymn, and a prayer (ch. 7). In Fructuosus, in winter 6, and in summer 5 psalms with antiphons, the last with Alleluia, 1 responsory, a verse, a reading of the Apostle and the Gospel (the latter by the abbot, on Sunday with Alleluia), and *Rogus Dei* (chs. 36, 41).

### Compline

Compline (*completorium*) is not indicated by all authors. According unto St. Benedict: 3 psalms simply without antiphons, namely 4, 90 [LXX 90 / MT 91] (cf. among us), and 133 [LXX 133 / MT 134], a hymn, one reading, a verse, *Kyrie eleison*, the Blessing, and thereafter occur *missae* (night readings?) (chs. 17, 18). Aurelian gives two complines: the first under the name of the '12th Hour', consisting of 18 pss., an antiphon, a hymn, a reading, and a *capitellum*; the second under the name *completa*—consisting of a *directaneus*, Ps. 90, and 'the customary *caputella*'. Columbanus at the beginning of the night prescribes the chanting of 12 psalms. According unto Fructuosus, at the 1st hour of the night 6 prayers must be performed, then 10 psalms in common singing, and in conclusion *Laus* and *Benedictiones*; then they mutually forgive and ask each other for reconciliation (ch. 2; cf. among us). According unto the Master, at Compline are recited 3 psalms, a responsory, a reading of the Apostle and the Gospel, the abbot recites *Rogus Dei* and the concluding verse: **"Set, O Lord, a watch before my mouth"** (*"Polozhi, Gospodi, khranenie ustom moim"* / Ps. 140:3; cf. among us **"Let Thy mercy, O Lord, be upon us..."**), followed by mutual reconciliation and forgiveness (ch. 30). At all the daily offices in monasteries, as in cathedral and parish churches, genuflection (*oratio*) was observed, during which prayers were uttered silently (*silentio*) and only the concluding exclamation of the officiant was made aloud. On Sundays, however, and throughout the entire Pentecostarion genuflection was abolished: they prayed standing upright or bowing down (*inclinati*) (cf. among us) [St. Benedict, chs. 50, 20; Master, ch. 48]. In the Master, moreover, genuflection is abolished also from the Nativity of Christ until the Theophany.

### The Roman Rite

The monastic divine worship described above, established in its principal features by St. Benedict and propagated by his disciples, by virtue of the high excellence of his Rule and the influence of the Benedictine popes (St. Gregory I the Great and Gregory II), formed the foundation of the divine worship of the entire Roman Church, supplanting from it the earlier cathedral and parochial worship. In the present Roman Book of Hours or Breviary (*Breviarium*), the division of the daily offices established by St. Benedict is retained, namely the sevenfold division (according unto Ps. 118:164: **"Seven times a day have I praised Thee"**): Matins with nocturns (*matutinum*), Lauds (*Laudes*), Prime, Terce, Sext, None [the 1st, 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours], Vespers (*vesperae*), and Compline (*completorium*); after the model of the Benedictine Rule the entire Psalter is chanted in a week, being distributed among the offices thus: at nocturns 12 psalms on weekdays (from Pss. 20 to 108, divided across the 6 days of the week); at the daytime Hours—Ps. 118; at Vespers—psalms from 109 to 147 (with the exception of those employed at other offices); at Compline—Pss. 4, 30 (the first 6 verses), 90, and 133 (the second psalm was not used by Benedict). In its details, however, the present Roman order of daily offices received greater development than in the Rule of St. Benedict, for which reason we describe it as the highest point of development of Western worship in the period under consideration; all the more so since for this period it was ready in its essential features and identical in the Roman secular and monastic breviaries. *(Orig. p. 315)*
The offices customarily begin with Matins. Before it is appointed the customary opening: the Lord's Prayer (**"Our Father"**), the *Ave Maria* (**"Rejoice, O Virgin Theotokos"**), and the Symbol of Faith (**"I believe"**), recited silently (introduced no earlier than the 13th century). Matins itself begins with the invitatory verses: **"O Lord, open Thou my lips"** (once) and **"O God, come to my assistance"** with **"Glory... Both now..."** and Alleluia (in Great Lent: 'Praise be to Thee, O Lord, King of eternal glory'). Then Ps. 94 with the refrain (*invitatorium*) and a morning hymn (differing for different days). After it follow the nocturns. They are of 3 kinds: Sunday, festal, and ferial [weekday]. On Sunday there are 3 nocturns. At the 1st nocturn are sung 12 psalms with 3 antiphons divided into 3 sections of 4 psalms each; a psalm that doth not conclude with an antiphon has, as always, 'Glory' at the end. After the antiphon of the final psalm follows a verse, the Lord's Prayer, the 'absolution' (*absolutio*—a brief petition unto the Savior for the hearing of prayers and mercy with glorification of Him), the abbot's blessing, and 3 readings: from the Holy Scripture of the Old and New Testaments and the Doctors of the Church, with responsories between them, during which the brethren remain seated, rising only at the 'Glory' of the final responsory. At the 2nd nocturn—3 psalms (cf. the kathismata of our Matins), a verse, the Lord's Prayer, the *absolutio*, the blessing, and 3 readings from the lives of the saints or patristic writings with 3 responsories. At the 3rd nocturn—3 Old Testament canticles (the Canticle of Isaiah 33:2–10; 33:13–17; 35:1–10, or other similar canticles) with one antiphon, a verse, the Lord's Prayer, the *absolutio*, the blessing, 3 readings from the New Testament with interpretations of the holy fathers, and 3 responsories. Then the hymn **"We praise Thee, O God"** (*Te Deum laudamus* / *"Tebe Boga khvalim"*), at the singing of which all arise. On feasts there are likewise 3 nocturns, but at each of them there are not 4, but 3 psalms, and at the 3rd nocturn the readings are not from the New Testament, but from patristic homilies for the feast, and instead of the 3rd responsory the hymn **"We praise Thee, O God"** is sung. On weekdays there is one nocturn: 12 psalms are sung under 6 antiphons (2 psalms to an antiphon), a verse, the Lord's Prayer, the *absolutio*, the blessing, 3 readings from Holy Scripture with responsories, as at the 1st Sunday nocturn; the hymn *(Orig. p. 316)* **"We praise Thee, O God"** at weekday Matins is replaced by a responsory (as also on Sunday in Great Lent from the Sunday of Septuagesima). The tripartite division of Sunday nocturns symbolically points, according unto Bonaventure (Commentary on Ps. 76), unto natural, legal, and evangelical revelation, for which reason at the final nocturn the readings are exclusively from the New Testament. After Matins or the nocturns follows the office *ad Laudes* (Praises): after the verse **"O God, come to my assistance"**, the above-indicated psalms and the proper biblical canticle in course with antiphons, a *capitulum* (short reading) from the New Testament, a morning hymn with a responsory, the Canticle of Zechariah (*Benedictus*) with an antiphon, then the prayer proper unto the day (*propria*), the greeting—*salutatio* and *collecta*, general commemorations (*commemorationes*) of the saints, that is, the prayerful invocation of the Holy Virgin, righteous Joseph, the Apostles, the patron of the church, a supplication for peace and the repose of the departed (*commemorationes* are not always said); in conclusion the antiphon of the Holy Virgin. The 1st Hour begins with **"Our Father"**, the *Ave Maria*, the Creed, **"O God, come to my assistance"**; then a hymn, psalms with antiphons, on Sunday—the Athanasian Creed (*Quicunque vult*), a *capitulum* with a responsory, prayers—*preces* (*Kyrie eleison*, *Christe eleyson*, *Kyrie eleison*, **"Our Father"**, the Creed, and several penitential verses from the psalms; on great feasts these are omitted), confession (*confessio*)—of sins unto all the saints with the promise of forgiveness from God, concluding prayers with *Kyrie eleison* and other verses (collect), and the reading of the Martyrology. The 3rd, 6th, and 9th Hours each begin with **"Our Father"**, the *Ave Maria*, and **"O God, come to my assistance"**, followed by a hymn, 3 sections of Ps. 118, an antiphon, a *capitulum* with a responsory, and a collect. Vespers in its structure resembles *ad Laudes*; the customary opening is as at the Hours; 5 psalms with antiphons, a *capitulum*, a hymn with a responsory, the Canticle of the Theotokos (*Magnificat*) with an antiphon, and the prayer proper unto the day. Compline begins with a brief reading (1 Pet. 5:8) with a preceding blessing (a prayerful wish from God of a peaceful night and a perfect end) and a subsequent confession as at the 1st Hour, followed by the above-indicated psalms with antiphons, a hymn, a *capitulum* with a responsory, the Canticle of Simeon (*Nunc dimittis*) with an antiphon, prayers—*preces* with *Kyrie eleison*, resembling the prayers at the 1st Hour, a prayer, a blessing, an antiphon unto the Holy Virgin, concluding prayers, and at the end the customary opening of the offices: **"Our Father"**, the *Ave Maria*, and the Creed, which consequently links the end of the daily offices with their beginning [^1541].

### Other Western Liturgical Rites

In place of the Roman rite, certain Roman Catholic churches and monasteries maintain their own liturgical rites, which are not inferior unto, and at times even surpass, the Roman in antiquity, having consequently been developed in the 6th–8th centuries. Such in particular are the Milanese (Ambrosian) rite, attributed unto St. Ambrose and used in the churches of Milan; the Mozarabic rite (*mozarabs* or *mixtarabs*—a mixture of Spaniards with Arabs), attributed unto SS. Leander and Isidore, Spanish bishops of the 7th century, and used in certain monasteries *(Orig. p. 317)* of Spain; and the Gallican rite, attributed unto St. Irenaeus of Lyons and used in certain churches of Lyons.

### The Ambrosian Rite
