The *Diatyposis*, of these officials (beginning from the epistemonarch), does not indicate taxiarchs, but defines the duties of epistemonarchs as the *Hypotyposis* defines those of the taxiarchs: unto them it likewise assigns the first half of the overseers' duties—to dispatch unto church after the bell-ringing those who have tarried, adding that from those remaining (in their cells during the service) they demand an explanation, and if they remained there not by order and not of necessity, they urge them unto diligence with moderate penances; furthermore, the *Diatyposis* speaks of only a single overseer, who 'day and night making the rounds of the cells, workshops, and other places of the Lavra with due severity and appropriate penance, disperses those who indulge in chatter and unseasonable strolls'; finally, the *Diatyposis* likewise indicates the office of the doorkeeper (*porter / thyroros / θυρωρός*), who, having charge of the entrance into the church, demands from those who did not arrive before the beginning of the service an account of their tardiness, and forbids those who leave unseasonably from exiting after one or two occurrences. Concerning penances (*epitimias*), although the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* mention them repeatedly, they do not specify their types and degrees, *(Orig. p. 420)* silently referring thereby unto the specialized instructions concerning them by St. Theodore in the *Monastic Epitimias* [^1802] and the *Great Catechesis* (§§ 60, 69). In penances St. Theodore is exceedingly close unto Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople († 828 AD), in his *Penitential Canons* [^1803]; from Basil the Great St. Theodore is distinguished by granting less discretion unto superiors in assigning penances [^1804]. The degrees of penance under St. Theodore are: 1) excommunication (*aphorismos / ἀφορισμός*)—that is, exclusion for a certain time from communion with the brethren at meals, in prayer, and in work [^1805]; it is appointed under St. Theodore in 23 cases: for example, for theft, inciting the brethren against the superior, evasion of confession and Holy Communion, negligence in service duties, idle wandering through the monastery, concealment of others' misdeeds (inter alia, also for reciting from memory unto the brethren from a book that was being transcribed); 2) xerophagy (*dry-eating / xerophagia / ξηроφαγία*)—subsistence upon bread and water, probably for a single day each time, for less important omissions in duty, and for tardiness unto divine services; 3) prostrations (*metanoiai / μετάνοιαι*) in varying numbers in church or in the cell; 4) standing (*parastasis / παράστασις*) during meals or in church at the departure of the brethren (the latter in a bowed posture—for slight tardiness unto the service); if the former was assigned for breaking dishware, the guilty brother stood holding the potsherds.

Without speaking definitively of any of these types of penance, the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* indicate only one, but more severe form thereof—confinement in a special chamber (*aphoristeria / ἀφοριστηρία*) upon dry-eating for the insubordinate and stubborn, wherein the former observes that 'correction by means of scourges (*dia mastigon / διὰ μαστίγων*, cf. above, p. 195 concerning the Nitrian monastery in the 4th–5th centuries), which is suited unto laymen, is justly rejected by our holy fathers' (*Hypotyposis*, § 25). Upon the inefficacy of penances recourse was had to expulsion from the monastery (according unto the *Diatyposis*). Of offenses, the *Diatyposis* speaks with special indignation concerning theft: 'those who commit any theft whatsoever of the monastery's property deserve the death of Ananias and Sapphira; but whereas they died bodily, these inherit death of the soul with a curse' (§ 33). Of the internal life of the monastery, both documents touch upon the following aspects: He who seeks admission into the monastery must dwell for two to three weeks in the monastic guest-house (*xenodocheion*), becoming acquainted with the order and being instructed by the hegumen; after this 'catechesis', the candidate was introduced into the assembly of the brethren, made a prostration before them, and they prayed for him (*Hypotyposis*, § 24; *Diatyposis*, § 11). Complete poverty (*non-acquisitiveness / ne-styazhanie*) is required of the monks: they may not possess even their own furniture (*Diatyposis*, § 30). The greatest attention is accorded unto the divine services. Among the offices, the *Hypotyposis* specifies the hours only for the Liturgy on fast days: when the meal is at the 9th hour (= 3:00 PM), the Liturgy is at the 6th hour (12:00 noon); on non-fast days, at the 3rd hour (9:00 AM) (§ 27); according unto the *Diatyposis*, weekday Matins is at the 7th hour of the night (1:00 AM), Sunday Matins at the 6th (12:00 midnight), festal Matins at the beginning of the 5th (10:00 PM) (§ 7). In the Great Fast, the First Hour is appointed to be celebrated separately from Matins at dawn (*Hypoty*(Orig. p. 421)*posis*, § 14). It is forbidden to stand in church with staves and even to enter therein with them, or to use stools (*skamnia / σκαмνίοις*, *Diatyposis*, § 13) when kneeling. According unto the *Hypotyposis*, daily at the beginning of the 4th Ode of the Canon the hegumen departs from the choir and, sitting down, receives the brethren for confession; according unto the *Diatyposis*, he does this whenever he desires, and may entrust confession unto another (*Hypotyposis*, § 22; *Diatyposis*, § 29). On the eve of Palm Sunday at *Lord, I have cried*, the choirs were exchanged, evidently for the entire year: the right choir became the left and vice versa—naturally in view of the greater difficulty and greater quantity of chanting upon the right choir (for which reason this is treated in the chapter 'On Proportion in the Services', *Hypotyposis*, § 34). In the Great Fast an elderly (according unto the *Diatyposis*—a 'discreet') brother is designated, who from the 3rd hour (9:00 AM) makes the rounds of all the work-places, and in each, having made a metania, proclaims: 'Brethren and fathers, let us take heed unto ourselves, for we die, we die, we die'; according unto another manuscript, there is added: 'let us call to mind also the Kingdom of Heaven'; according unto the *Diatyposis*: 'concerning eternal torment'; according unto the *Diatyposis*, in response unto this the brethren 'cease work, arise, recite the Trisagion, and sit down again' (*Hypotyposis*, § 23; *Diatyposis*, § 9). In a special article 'On Proportion in the Services' both documents regulate manual labor and furnish the schedule for the monastic day. According unto the *Hypotyposis*, the brethren all engage in bodily labors from sunrise or after the chanting of the First Hour, when the hours are appointed, until the 6th hour (12:00 noon); from the 6th unto the 8th hour (12:00–2:00 PM) rest is appointed for the brethren, whether there is dinner or not; from the 8th hour (2:00 PM) until Vespers there is work again: after Vespers, 'each retires into solitude as he desires' (§ 33). The *Diatyposis* indicates days when there is no labor: these are the first and Great Week of the Fast and the week of Pascha (*Bright Week*), especially until Wednesday; other great feasts are likewise understood. The *Diatyposis* does not speak of midday rest, but occupies itself in detail with the table for those performing heavy labors—blacksmiths, muleteers, boatmen, carpenters, vinedressers, and bakers; unto these workers before the common meal there is given at the 3rd hour (9:00 AM) in the great fasts bread, and on minor fasts and ordinary days wine also, and at the refectory an additional cup (*krasobolion*) of wine is granted them; on days free from labor they are content with the common allotment (*Diatyposis*, §§ 25, 26). On feasts when there is no labor, reading of books from the monastic library is recommended unto the brethren; the *Diatyposis* gives general counsel concerning this, while the *Hypotyposis* defines also the order for distributing books: the librarian strikes the wooden semantron (*bilo*) once, the brethren proceed unto the library, there each receives a book, and before Vespers, again upon the stroke of the semantron, returns it (*Hypotyposis*, § 26; *Diatyposis*, § 28). Those who had not learned the Psalter by heart presented themselves for Matins only at the Canon upon the threefold stroke on the semantron by the canonarch, employing the beginning of Matins (the Kathismata) for the study of the Psalter (*Hypotyposis*, § 36). Both documents determine in detail the quality and quantity of clothing (see ch. 39 of the Typikon) and of food throughout the entire year, principally during fasts (see chs. 32 and 33 of the Typikon). Here a distinguishing feature of these documents, in comparison with the Jerusalem Typika, is the permission throughout the entire Pentecostarion, on great feasts occurring on Wednesday and Friday and during the minor Quadragesimas, as well as for the evening of Great and Holy Saturday, of cheese and eggs; for Great and Holy Saturday this permission is not granted *(Orig. p. 422)* by later manuscripts of the *Hypotyposis* (*Hypotyposis*, §§ 28, 29; *Diatyposis*, §§ 14–18). This chapter of the *Hypotyposis*, although it entered into the Studite-Alexis Typikon in a softened form, provoked great disputes in Russia during the 12th–13th centuries in view of its discrepancy with the ancient canons and the Jerusalem Typikon (see below). In both monuments, comportment at the refectory table is defined in agreement: "When the brethren assemble to dine (*Diatyposis*: 'at the sound of the bell,' *kodonos*), in their mouths must be a verse" (a prayerful verse, according unto later monuments: **"Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us"**); according unto the *Diatyposis*, likewise: "and when they rise from the table, until such time as, having departed into the narthex, they offer thanksgiving for that which they have eaten"; they sit at the tables nine men each (*Diatyposis*), according unto the direction of the overseer watching that there be no vacant places; they sit at the refectory in hoods (*koukoulia*; *Hypotyposis*); there is also a reading, "which (*Diatyposis*) is directed by the ecclesiarch, who takes care that whatever they did not manage to read in church should be read at the refectory and nothing should be omitted"; "the signal for the conclusion of the reading is the clatter of spoons cast simultaneously into the bowls at the final dish; likewise for the pouring of wine and the serving of courses a signal is given by means of a strike" (*Diatyposis*: by a bell; *Hypotyposis*, § 28; *Diatyposis*, § 14). Finally, the *Diatyposis* also provides for a brother's departure from the monastery, "if he has no spiritual peace in our lavra"; it must not be a clandestine flight, but must occur upon forewarning the 'spiritual guide,' "so that departure from the monastery may also take place with prayer and blessing, and not with prohibition, nor with a curse, nor with excommunication by the Holy Fathers" (§ 31).

### The Disciplinary Portion of the Holy Mountain Typikon

The Great Synaxarion of the Athonite Iviron Lavra of the 11th century (see above, p. 372, n. 4), the exemplar of Holy Mountain Typika, in its disciplinary portion represents an abridgment and slight modification of the *Diatyposis*; from it are retained here the sections concerning the hour of services, food, proportion in services, non-acquisitiveness, the order of leaving the monastery, imprisonment, clothing, and non-working days. The hours of service are appointed for Matins: throughout the year, weekday Matins is at the 8th hour (2:00 AM; an hour later than in the *Diatyposis*); on Sundays at the beginning of the 7th hour, and festal Matins at the beginning of the 5th hour (slightly later than in the *Diatyposis*); during the Twelve Holy Days [from the Nativity of Christ unto Theophany], Cheesefare Week, and the second days of the Great Feasts of the Lord, toward the beginning of the 9th hour (around 2:00 AM); in Great Lent, toward the beginning of the 6th hour (around 11:00 PM). Concerning fasts, the dispensation of the *Diatyposis* for cheese during Pentecost and for feasts occurring during multi-day fasts is abrogated, and this dispensation is preserved for feasts falling upon ordinary Wednesdays and Fridays. Unto those occupied with heavy labors during a fast, food is given at the 6th hour (not at the 3rd). Monks are forbidden to acquire money (concerning furniture nothing is said). Of the penances, imprisonment is preserved with the observation: "punishment by blows or other means appropriate in the world is condemned by our fathers, although in case of extreme necessity it is permissible to resort unto them also." In the event of a desire to leave the monastery, "the hegu-*(Orig. p. 423)*-men shall entrust the departing brother unto another hegumen, or undertake whatever other measures." Feast days are divided into non-working days for all, including laborers, and non-working days only for the brethren; unto the former, besides the Twelve Great Feasts, belong September 13 and 26; November 8 and 14; December 6, 9, and 26; January 1; April 23; May 8 and 24 (Symeon the Wonderworker); June 24 and 29; August 29; unto the latter: September 20; October 18, 23, and 26; November 1 and 13; December 4, 13, and 27; January 17, 20, and 25; February 17 and 24; March 9; June 8; July 1, 8, 20, and 27; August 31; the small number of 'secular' feasts (for the laborers) the *Synaxarion* explains by the small number of laborers in the monastery (only four) and their high wages [^1806].
*(Orig. p. 424)*

### The Disciplinary Portion of the Studite-Alexis Typikon

Upon the foundation of the *Hypotyposis*, the disciplinary portion was elaborated in the Studite-Alexis Typikon (11th–12th centuries), which was for so long the regulator of monastic life in Russia. But the primary source here underwent greater modifications than, for example, in the Iviron *Synaxarion*, and was significantly expanded: out of the 281 folios of the most ancient manuscript of this Typikon, the disciplinary portion occupies more than one third: 85 folios. Later manuscripts leave this portion of the Typikon unaltered. Of the officials of the *Hypotyposis*, taxiarchs and overseers are not mentioned; their duties, apparently, are transferred unto epistemonarchs, whose title is translated in Slavic as *khitretsyanachalnika* [^1807]; there were two of them (fol. 215). The first person after the hegumen was the oeconomus (*ikonom*); but in church, if the oeconomus lacked holy orders, the senior among the priests was considered first after the hegumen (fol. 266v). Next follow such 'servitors' (*sluzhbnitsi*): the *kutnik*—chief superintendent over the refectory (that which under St. Theodore was the cellarer and refectorian); "those who are senior on both sides of the church," that is, the two *khitretsyanachalnika*, although they (according unto another passage of the Typikon) are placed in church immediately after the hegumen and oeconomus (fol. 266); "the paramonarios—sacristan (*ssudokhranilnik*); the granary key-bearer; he who attends unto the sick (infirmarian); he who awakens (the awakener?) [^1808]; the church domestikos (= canonarch); the keeper of books; the cellarer (supervisor of clothing?), and the senior hospitaller." The hegumen discharges (and consequently appoints) all monastic officials (fols. 225v, 226). Obedience unto the hegumen must be the same as unto a military commander. Before speaking with him, or catching sight of him, they bow "greatly" (*"Monastic commandments of those living in a cenobium, that is to say, living together,"* fol. 216v). One of the chief duties of the hegumen is to instruct the monks more frequently, both all together and each individually (*"Concerning this, that monks should be frequently catechized,"* fol. 223). Financial affairs of the monastery the hegumen is advised to conduct with the knowledge and mediation of other monastic officials; money is to be kept in a chest sealed by him, the oeconomus, and the *kutnik* (fol. 226v). The order for the election of a hegumen is indicated: after the death of a hegumen, the brethren, "having performed common prayer and fasting for three days, fervently entreat the Godhead to appoint one who is worthy"; "thereafter, with the Holy Gospel lying before them, they elect whom they know"; the elected candidate must be not younger than 33 years of age, from among the tonsured monks of the monastery, and not those who en-*(Orig. p. 425)*-tered from another monastery, so as not to grieve the local brethren by the necessity "to be pastured by an outsider," and lest the hegumen destroy "the rule of our divine fathers Elias and Theodore"; it is also necessary to elect one who is "by no means partaker of marital intercourse" (neither a widower nor one who has abandoned a wife), lest "love for kindred" distract him from the monastery; it is recommended to elect from among the "consecrated" [priests] or "great schema-monks"; if the election is not unanimous, they elect three candidates and present them unto the Patriarch (*"Concerning hegumens,"* fols. 238v–241). Regarding the spirit of monastic governance itself, the founder wishes, as we have seen, that the principles of St. Theodore be observed here, which is why at the conclusion of the Typikon there is appended a translation (unfinished) of the Penitential of St. Theodore under the title *"Concerning the remnants of church canons"* (fol. 280). The Typikon devotes much space unto admission into the monastery. The establishment of the monastery is fixed at 40–50 or more monks, "besides those who are in the villages" (*"Concerning the number of monks,"* fol. 231v). Unknown persons must be tested for a year before admission; those from other monasteries are to be received only with good recommendations; priests and deacons from other monasteries are admitted unto celebrating only after three months upon learning all the customs of the monastery. It is forbidden to demand from incoming applicants a contribution unto the monastery (*"Concerning priests and deacons,"* fols. 232–234v). Those who make large contributions dare not claim any privileges in the monastery (*"Concerning offerings,"* fol. 234); to receive someone into the monastery upon such conditions is worse than contracting a loan. In case of a deficiency of funds in the monastery, it is better to pawn something or borrow from the patriarchate or its monastery (*"Concerning renunciation,"* fols. 235v–237). In connection with this, the Typikon likewise forbids burying anyone in the monastery, "even if he should give something on that account"; at this, the founder-patriarch observes that even for himself he prepared a tomb in the monastery not by his own will, but at the request of the monks; he himself had the desire to be buried in the Studite monastery, where as a youth he received tonsure and labored until the patriarchate itself (*"Concerning this, that no one should be buried in the monastery,"* fol. 237v). The founder wishes to make the monastery, after the model of the great ancient ones, as isolated from the world as possible: leaving the monastery is permitted only with the hegumen's permission; visitors are received initially only in the hospice, and are reported unto the hegumen for further directions. To oversee this, at the outer 'hospice' gates of the monastery there is one monk, and at the inner gates three, "from men aged, chaste, and borne witness by all"; they may alternate in attending divine services, and at their post it is recommended to read the Psalter and other soul-profiting books. Women are unconditionally forbidden entry into the monastery; permission is granted only unto the empress with a single maidservant; while for the ladies of her court, "as many of the women as follow after her," it is permitted to enter the monastery only through the "bath-house" (the bath or refuse) gates into the small church; and it is forbidden for all to meet the empress, but only the hegumen, oeconomus, protopresbyter, paramonarios, and other elders (*"Concerning hospices,"* fols. 229–231). During Great Lent, however, from Vespers of Cheesefare Sunday until Friday of the sixth week, the monastery was locked unconditionally, except in case of deliveries or dispatching someone, for which purpose *(Orig. p. 426)* they open the rear gates (*"How it is proper to lock the monastery during holy Great Lent,"* fol. 215v) [^1809]. With the aim of greater isolation from the world, the monastery was required to maintain within itself (as was practiced also by ancient monasteries of high ascetic discipline) such necessary institutions as an infirmary with a physician and pharmacy, and a special hospice for elderly monks, placed under the charge of eight elders, where the means for its maintenance by the monastery in food, firewood, oil, and candles are defined in detail; into this hospice Christ-loving laymen were also received at their own expense, where it is likewise determined in detail for what payment is taken from them—not forgetting payment for soap in the bath-house and "the washing of their garments by one of the neighboring women" (*"Concerning the infirm and the aged,"* fols. 241–244). The means of sustenance the monastery was obliged to acquire for itself chiefly through the labors of the monks; therefore no one in the monastery is exempt from manual labors, not even the hegumen. In particular, kneading dough was also performed by all in rotation, for which purpose the brethren are divided into three 'ranks' (*chiny*): the first is called ("styled") the rank of the hegumen, the second of the oeconomus, and the third of the *kutnik*; each of these supervisors had assistants: the hegumen the *kutnik*, the oeconomus the sub-oeconomus, and the *kutnik* the sub-*kutnik*; alongside them, one of the brethren (a specialist?) was placed at the head of each rank; his duty included calling to the kneading. Following the Six Psalms at the beginning of the kathismata, this brother, having naturally prepared everything in the bakehouse, entered the church and, having made a bow in the center, approached first on the right side of the temple, then on the left, each brother of his rank, and with a bow said: **"Lord, bless, unto the bakehouse"** (*Gospodi blagoslovi v peklnitsyu*); those summoned in this manner assembled before the Royal Doors and, together with that brother, at the conclusion of the first antiphon, approached the hegumen and bowed unto him to the ground; the caller said: **"Bless. Pray for us, holy father"**; the latter replied: **"God save you"**; in the bakehouse, part of them kneaded the dough, while part chanted "the Six Psalms, one canon, and the remainder of Matins"; upon conclusion of the work they return unto the church and chant with the rest, "and the first manages according to the readiness of the dough"; prosphora were kneaded by a single baker (*"Concerning kneading,"* fols. 227v–228). "Just as kneading the dough is established for the brethren themselves, so also burdens brought into the monastery from without, such as firewood or wine and the like, they themselves we command to carry up from the shore into the monastery, and no one out of pride ought to be ashamed of such labor, but before all others let the venerable father hegumen labor with zeal and joy, providing an example unto his spiritual children" (*"Concerning the carrying of heavy burdens,"* fol. 229) [^1810]. The Typikon exhor-*(Orig. p. 427)*-ts the monks to perform all commissions given them, especially oversight of labors outside the monastery (where work must have been executed chiefly by hired hands under the supervision of monks), with constant thought of the unslumbering eye and to fear, as the sin of Ananias and Sapphira or as sacrilege, any dishonesty (*"Concerning those sent upon obediences,"* fol. 219). In free time they may not assemble for conversations, nor enter the cell of another even under the pretext of study. Those wishing to study assemble for this in the 'refectory' after Matins. The hegumen takes care that each monk know the Psalter by heart and chant it in church according to the "living book of the soul," and not search for a book here and there (*"That it is not fitting for monks to congregate with one another,"* fols. 220–221). In connection with the external life of the monastery, the Typikon speaks *"Concerning monastic vesture"* (fols. 223v–224) in greater detail than the present Typikon (see ch. 39 of the Typikon), and concerning the bath-house: they go to it by tickets ("seals") from the hegumen, apparently once a month (the place is abraded in the manuscript), and the sick according unto the direction of the physician (fol. 225). Extensive sections of the Typikon under the headings: *"Chapters of the church rule, similar unto the first rule-book (that is, the rule concerning food) of various chapters extending into church service"* (fols. 245v–249), *"Concerning this, with what great attentiveness monks must stand at divine doxologies"* (fols. 249–250), *"Concerning the standing of monks in church"* (fol. 253), interspersed with purely liturgical paragraphs (concerning how to chant the triadika [Trinity hymns], concerning the number of kathismata at Matins, concerning the chanting of kathismata on Saturday, concerning the chanting of **"God of gods"** [Ps. 49:1], that is, the second antiphon of the 7th kathisma, and **"Praise the Lord"** [Ps. 148], that is, the third antiphon of the 20th kathisma, with special alleluiaria, concerning the refrains unto the Psalms of Praise and **"Lord, I have cried"**), these sections are dedicated unto the comportment of monks in church. Here, first of all, the time for Matins is defined: during Pentecost it begins at the start of the 9th hour (3:00 AM) [^1811]; from Pentecost unto Great Lent, as also on Sundays and Feasts of the Lord throughout the year, at the 7th hour (1:00 AM); on Monday through Thursday of Great Lent at half-past the 4th hour (9:30 PM); on Friday and Saturday of Great Lent at the beginning of the 7th hour (2:00 AM). Upon the arrival of the hour, the awakener (*ubuzhayay*) rises and goes first of all unto the cell of the hegumen, bows unto the ground, and says outside the door: **"Bless and pray for me, holy father"**; the latter replies from within: **"God save thee"**; then the awakener, still by the cell, proclaims very loudly: **"Bless, holy fathers"** (*Blagoslovite svyatii*), and repeats this likewise loudly, passing by all the cells. Meanwhile, the striking of the *klepalo* begins, first upon the "upper sounding-board (*bilo*) at the guestmaster's," then upon the great *bilo*, and finally upon the small *bilo* (fols. 246v–247). Upon entering the church they make a prostration before the Royal Doors, yet without approaching the icon screen for this purpose; he whose place is near the hegumen makes a prostration unto him also; unto the brethren no bow is made (fols. 253v–254). Matins begins in the narthex, and in winter (from the Exaltation) *(Orig. p. 428)* in the church. In the church the brethren stand along the walls, in front the priests in order of their ordination, next the deacons, and so forth; in front of all on the right side stands the hegumen, on the left the oeconomus. They are required to stand erect, vigilantly, feet together, hands joined beneath the mantle, not scratching themselves ("for if a flea, gnat, louse, or something else falls upon one, immediately to turn one's thought unto it and scratch, this one his head, that one his feet, and another some other part of his body, or thrusting hands inside one's garment, is not the conduct of a steadfast man, but of one exceedingly negligent and impatient," fols. 245v–249). Beginning the chanting, concluding it, and making a bow after it must take place simultaneously with the senior (fol. 254). It is indicated what character the chanting of the Six Psalms, the triadika, and **"God is the Lord"** must possess (see below, ch. 2 of the Typikon). The reader during the reading must have his head uncovered, and likewise during the refectory reading (fol. 213). From the epistemonarchs ("the elders of both sides") is required careful preservation from damage of liturgical books (to keep them under lock, not allowing them to be touched with bare fingers, nor wax to drip, nor to bespatter them with saliva; fol. 261). In particular, among the disciplinary-liturgical aspects of monastic life, the Typikon defines in detail the order of kissing after Compline (fol. 265), the order of the Exaltation of the Cross (fol. 261), the order of monastic burial (fol. 273v); it indicates when the brethren are to stand in church with candles: at the consecration (patronal feast) of the church or narthex, at the Theophany blessing of waters, on Palm Sunday, on Great and Holy Tuesday at the chanting of the stichera of the Holy Passions, and on Great Week (*"How many times monks will take candles,"* fols. 271v–273). It is appointed on Great and Holy Thursday to clean, and on Great and Holy Friday to wash the church, and it indicates at this how to illuminate it on Great and Holy Saturday and Pascha (*"Concerning church illumination,"* fols. 278–279; see below under "Great and Holy Saturday"). In close connection with divine services, Eastern Typika have always placed fasting, for which reason the Studite-Alexis Typikon begins its disciplinary portion with the section on fasts (*"The rule-book examining concerning the food and drink of monks..."* fols. 196–212) and defines the monastic table for the entire year with even greater detail than the present Typikon. In this regard, the Studite-Alexis Typikon first of all indicates the order at the refectory table, providing what was subsequently called the 'elevation of the Panagia' (*chin o panagii*) with a ritual no less complex than the present one, only instead of the Panagia (the prosphoron of the Mother of God) a dish with morsels of bread (*ukrukhi*) is elevated (fols. 196v–201); an observation is made concerning the order of dining for those who did not dine together with all—the cellarer and those who served (*"Concerning the second table,"* fol. 201), concerning the evening meal (*"Concerning Vespers [supper],* fol. 202), concerning reading at the refectory and attentiveness unto it, a prohibition against being dissatisfied with the food [^1812] (fols. 203–204), and, finally, a detailed distribution of foods for all fasts (fols. 205–211; see chaps. 32 and 33 of the Typikon). This chapter concludes with a special rite of the 'carol' (*kolyada*), that is, the performance by the chanters at the Paschal, Dormition, Nativity, and Theophany refectory meals of the troparion, kontakion, ikos, and hypakoe, after which there was handed unto the chanters by the hegumen a recompense—*(Orig. p. 429)* "a blessing according to tradition from the corner (*kut*)" [^1813] (*"Kolyada,"* fol. 211v). It is forbidden to keep food in the cell or utensils for preparing it; if a monk needs to offer food unto a visitor or guest of his, this may be done only at the common refectory table with permission of the hegumen (fols. 213–214). The section concerning the refectory concludes with the instruction *"how it is proper to kindle fire where they bake and in the kitchen"* (fol. 216): the cook enters the temple, bows thrice unto the ground "before the pure screens" (the iconostasis), and asks for fire from the sacristan; the latter dips a reed into the lamp and kindles it from the holy light [^1814]. In another place of the Typikon, the festal allowance of the monastery (naturally including visitors) is defined in figures: September 8, November 21, January 6, February 2, March 25—"of bread 3 *spudy* (an unknown dry measure), of wine 3 measures"; June 29, August 6, Ascension, Pentecost, and the Sunday of All Saints—of bread 3 *spudy*, of wine 2 measures; September 14 and December 6—of bread 3 *spudy* and of wine 1 measure; April 23—of bread 1 *spud* and of wine 1 measure; on the patronal feast days of the monastery, this allowance increased significantly: August 15—of bread 10 *spudy*, of wine 10 measures, of kolyva and wheat 4 *spudy*, of boiled grain (*sochivo*) 4 *spudy*, of water 2; November 11, on the feast of St. Theodore the Studite—of bread 6 *spudy*, of wine 8 measures, of kolyva 6 *spudy*, of *sochivo* 6 *spudy*; March 17, on the feast of St. Alexis—4 + 6 + 3 + 2; June 24—4 + 4 + 4 of kolyva; July 27—3 + 3 + 3 + 2 (*"Concerning distribution,"* fol. 244v).

### The Disciplinary Portion of Ancient Founder Typika

Not a little space is allotted unto the disciplinary side of monastic life by all the other extant founder (*ktitoral*) Typika as well. The majority of them even have exclusively such content, referring for liturgical practice unto other Typika (see above, pp. 362–363). But these Typika exerted no influence upon our present Typikon: not one of them is older than the Studite-Alexis Typikon, which was preserved in an immutable form in Russia until the introduction of the Jerusalem Typikon. Nevertheless, a comparison of these Typika with the Studite-Alexis Typikon can demonstrate the distinctive character of the latter and explain why precisely unto this Typikon fell such a broad and enduring sphere of operation. In none of the currently known founder Typika does the administrative section touch unto such a degree upon all aspects of monastic life as in the Studite-Alexis Typikon. They occupy themselves more with the auxiliary institutions of the monastery—hospitals, hospices—than with the internal life of the monastery. At times, noticeable deviations from the counsels of asceticism are also made. Thus, for example, the organization of the Pantokrator Monastery in Constantinople resembles rather the staff of Hagia Sophia in Constantinople than the great lavras of antiquity; here are the same ecclesiastical ranks, including even four women who clean the temple and correspond unto the 'myrrh-bearers' of Hagia Sophia and *(Orig. p. 430)* of the Church of the Resurrection [^1815]; menial labors fall upon four permanent persons, and not upon the whole brotherhood in rotation [^1816]. Remarkable is the peculiarity in the election of the hegumen presented by certain of these Typika: they elected three candidates and determined the final choice by lot, wherein parchments with the names of those elected were placed upon the holy table and prayer was offered that God might reveal the one who was worthy; a priest, an illiterate monk, or a boy drew the parchment from the holy table [^1817]. Remarkable likewise is the requirement of certain of these Typika, for example the Evergetis Typikon, that the Typikon should be read at the beginning of each month at the refectory.

### The Typikon of Empress Irene in Disciplinary Regard

Among these Typika, the Typikon of Empress Irene deserves attention as the first (and almost unique) experience of a female monastic rule. The difference from male rules consists in: a lighter fasting regimen: on Wednesday and Friday usually oil; daily not two, but two or three dishes; yet of wine not two or three cups, but one, with permission also for an addition at the discretion of the abbess; all sleep in one or two rooms, so that "all might be visible unto all"; meeting with male relatives is permitted only at the monastery gates in the presence of the abbess or a most honorable nun; no exception is made even for sick nuns, who are carried unto the gates upon stretchers. Priests must be monks and eunuchs. They likewise serve as oeconomoi of the monastery in view of the inconvenience for nuns of external relations outside the monastery. The officials are the same as under St. Theodore with minor additions and modifications: there is a 'granary mistress,' a 'wine-pourer,' two 'docheiariai' (one for financial accounting, the other supervising clothing), and two 'ergodotriai'—labor-givers, that is, supervisors of handiwork [^1818].
*(Orig. p. 431)*

### The Disciplinary Portion in the Jerusalem Typikon According to Georgian and Ancient Greek Manuscripts

In contrast unto the Studite Typika, the ancient Jerusalem Typika possess a very small disciplinary portion. In the most ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, for example, the Georgian Shiomghvime MS of the 13th century and the Greek MS of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection No. 35/491 of the 13th century, the disciplinary sections are inserted here and there among the liturgical material into the first general part of the Typikon, preceding the Menologion and the Triodion and setting forth the order of Sunday and weekday daily services, so that these sections not only do not form an independent part of the Typikon, but are scarcely noticeable within it; while the rules of comportment in church, which in the Studite Typika constitute the most prominent disciplinary section, are here for the most part situated within the order of the service itself, for example, the observation concerning silence during the Six Psalms, concerning the choir convergence. Thus the disciplinary portion proper in the mentioned two copies of the Jerusalem Typikon possesses the following uncomplicated composition. At the end of the exposition of the weekday service, such observations are made: "It is necessary to know that the monk appointed to chant the prokeimenon, following its intonation, bows unto the holy doors, then turns toward the west and stands with hands crossed upon his chest until the brethren recite the last verse; thereafter he bows and goes unto his place. If paroemias are appointed, he reads them also, as well as the Acts of the Apostles at the Vigil, and **\"God is the Lord\"**. He likewise intones **\"Let every breath\"** and the kontakion after the 6th ode of the canon. After the 9th ode the priest says: **\"Holy is the Lord our God\"** and the beginning of **\"Glory to God in the highest\"** at the Great Doxology. The aforementioned monk intones the prokeimena at the Divine Liturgy; he reads also the Epistle with the Alleluia, if he happens to know this. But if not, the ecclesiarch invites another who is skilled; after the prokeimenon, the two of them together make a bow. It is necessary to know that at Matins **\"God is the Lord...\"** and the Alleluia, and at the Divine Liturgy the prokeimena and the Epistle, we chant and read standing; during the reading of the Gospel, at the Cherubic Hymn, at the **\"Our Father...\"**, and at **\"Let our mouths be filled...\"**, we uncover our heads." During chanting it is forbidden to converse at the service, as well as to leave the church, but one must wait until a reading is offered; nor is it permitted to enter during the chanting of that choir in which someone stands, but to wait until the other choir begins to chant; having entered into his stasidion, he must bow unto the brethren. According unto the Greek MS, oversight of this is entrusted unto the ecclesiarch; while the Georgian MS demands here of the ecclesiarch oversight that no one stand without a partner, alone. The ecclesiarch must arrange that the brethren standing in the narthex allow no one into the temple, neither monk nor layman, "when the church is chanting, which is a sign of disorder" (later MSS: "but let them await the dismissal," that is, latecomers stand in the narthex until the end of the service). Next is indicated the order for the alternation of choirs during chanting: "The choir that began the psalmody (kathisma) at Vespers must begin it also at Matins; it begins the odes (canon) as well; from it also must be the chanter for the prokeimenon, **\"God is the Lord\"**, and the exapostilarion; at the Divine Liturgy *(Orig. p. 432)* (the same choir begins) the Typika [^1819], at Compline—**\"God is with us\"**, **\"All-Holy Lady Theotokos\"**, and **\"O Lord of hosts\"**; in holy and Great Lent the Hours are recited with psalmody thus: the choir that began at Matins **\"Praise the Lord\"** begins also the psalmody of the First Hour, that is, the Alleluia in Tone 6 (the tone of the troparion of the First Hour); at the Third Hour the other choir begins the Alleluia of the second kathisma in Tone 6; at the Sixth Hour the other choir begins the first Alleluia of Tone 2; while the monk who makes the beginning chants the prokeimenon of prophecy, reads the prophecies, and also performs the reading from the *Ladder* [of St. John Climacus]; at the Ninth Hour the other choir begins the first Alleluia of Tone 8; the same choir makes the beginning of the Beatitudes; while from Vespers onward there is again an alternation (of choirs)" [^1820]. The Typikon returns again unto discipline following the exposition of the service of the Hours and Mid-Hours: after the First Hour and its Mid-Hour, "those wishing to be saved do not leave the cell until the time of the church bell tolling (*chrousmatos*), but some occupy themselves with handiwork, others with reading, and others with psalmody with the knowledge of the superior; while the servers (*diakonetai*) attend unto (*scholazousi*) their service. It should be known that when we are present at church offices, the ecclesiarch directs (*tassei*) the right choir, while the epistemonarch directs the left." Next is cited the chapter concerning the awakener in the recension of the present Typikon (cf. the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis*) [^1821]. Finally, and this is already for the third time, the most ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon touch upon monastic discipline at the end of their first general part, before the Menologion; here an observation is made that at Compline "at Psalm 50 the candle-lighter (according unto the Georgian MS, the canonarch) gives water unto the brethren"—this in view of the fact that after Compline, as the last prayer of the day, partaking of any food is already forbidden on account of the morrow's Liturgy (on days of Vigils it is forbidden to drink water after partaking of the blessed bread and wine at Vespers); furthermore, it is required right here to conclude Compline before dark (*epiouses hemeras*, "while daylight yet remains"); after Compline "it is not permitted for monks to engage in conversations (*syntychias*) with one another, but each departs unto his cell, to occupy himself a little with the Trisagion which we have received (evidently, the cell rule, as is explicitly stated in the Georgian MS) and with reading, so that with attentiveness they may rise for Nocturns and the remaining office and church assembly (*synaxei*)" [^1822].

### The Disciplinary Portion According to Late Greek and Slavic Jerusalem Typika

This all too meager disciplinary material subsequent Greek manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon expand, chiefly by insertions from the *Hypotyposis*. Following the exposition of the daily cursus with the aforementioned *(Orig. p. 433)* disciplinary insertions, some of which are at times omitted (for example, in MS of the Moscow Synodal Library, Greek No. 391 of the 13th–14th centuries, the observation concerning the awakener is omitted), certain Greek MSS have the following sections: 1) an exhortation unto the superior not to despise that which is contained in the Typikon and not to spend much time outside the monastery, neglecting the souls entrusted unto him; especially not to leave the monastery during the three holy Forty-Day Fasts, and not to permit others to leave the monastery during this time; 2) an exhortation unto the brethren to care only for the heavenly, intensely to seek the kingdom of heaven, and to strive that all things be conducted among them in good order, especially in church, to preserve the mind unenticed by anything worldly, to go unto church at the first bell-ringing (*blagovest*), to stand there attentively from the very beginning; with particular reverence and attentiveness must one stand during the Six Psalms; entering into the church at that time is strictly forbidden; those unable to stand throughout it thus—the elderly and the sick—let them stand in the narthex; attentive, slow chanting with a meek, even, and clear voice is required; conversations are forbidden upon the cliroi, as well as at the refectory: at the latter it is likewise forbidden to look about or where one should not, for example, at how others eat; it is forbidden also to murmur against the quality of the food served [^1823]. Then, under the special title: "Of the Monastery of Stoudios," a series of disciplinary excerpts from the *Hypotyposis* is given: concerning the monastic officials, concerning confession unto the hegumen at the 4th ode of the canon, concerning an elder-brother appointed during the Forty-Day Fast to remind of death, concerning a two-to-three-week trial prior unto admission into the monastery, concerning the reading of books from the library on feast days, concerning the hour of the Divine Liturgy during fasts, concerning proportion in the services, concerning a penance for one who breaks dishware at the refectory, and concerning the quantity of clothing [^1824]. Following the exposition of the order of the Divine Liturgy, the aforementioned MSS of the Typikon contain two further disciplinary articles: concerning the three ranks of feasts from Nikon of the Black Mountain (see above, p. 408) and the following "Canons" (*κανόνες*) of Nicephorus, Patriarch of Constantinople: dispensation for an ailing monk during the Forty-Day Fast to take cooked food, oil, and wine; prohibition against traveling on Sunday except under necessity and constraint; prohibition against receiving Communion from a priest who does not fast on Wednesday and Friday; rejection of apocryphal books: the Apocalypses of Paul, Ezra, and Zosimas, the "Two Martyrdoms" of St. George, of Cyricus and Julitta, and the books of Macarius and Diadochus; permission for laboring monks during the Forty-Day Fast to eat bread at the 9th hour [3:00 PM] and to sup in the evening, with a prohibition against relaxing unto oil and wine under pretext of labor; permission for hired workmen to partake of food on non-fasting days from the 3rd hour [9:00 AM], and during fasts at the 6th hour [12:00 PM] (according unto the Holy Mountain Typikon, see above, p. 422). In Slavic copies of the Jerusalem Typikon, almost all these disciplinary rubrics disappear, at least as specialized sections; but in place of this, as we have seen, there appear in these Typika our present disciplinary excerpts from Nikon of the Black Mountain (in MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 329/384 of the 14th century, still in a separate gathering sewn unto the front; in later MSS, for example No. 678/386 of the 15th century, already in the very *(Orig. p. 434)* text: apparently, these excerpts were introduced into the Typikon by Athanasius of Vysotsk; see above, p. 375).

### The Markian Chapters

Thus, by the 13th–14th centuries, all the most essential parts of the Typikon had gradually taken shape: besides the fundamental Menologion-Triodion section, there was also the general liturgical section (the daily cycle of services) and the disciplinary section. Later than these parts, there entered into the Typikon as an independent and separate section yet another part: liturgical rubrics for the coincidence of fixed feasts with Sundays or movable feasts. In the most ancient Typika, these rubrics are very brief and indefinite, being provided in the Menologion under the corresponding days of the month. Thus, already in the Studite-Alexis Typikon under September 8, the observation is made that if it fall upon a Sunday, "the Sunday service is chanted first," and that one must act likewise if the memory of an apostle or evangelist fall upon a Sunday; of the details of the service, an instruction is given only regarding the troparia at the conclusion of Vespers and at the Divine Liturgy. Under March 25, the identical observation (in the Studite-Alexis Typikon) is very extensive; it provides for the coincidence of the Annunciation with an ordinary Saturday and Sunday, with Lazarus Saturday, Palm Sunday, all days of Holy Week, and with the Sunday and Monday of Holy Pascha, providing rubrics regarding all stichera, troparia, and canons. This exhausts the material in the Studite-Alexis Typikon corresponding unto the content of our present Markian Chapters. These observations are not inscribed here under the name of Mark. The identical form and scope are possessed by these observations in the Western Studite Typika and in the Evergetis Typikon; here too the name of Mark does not appear over them, which is particularly characteristic for the Western Studite Typika in view of their proximity unto the place of activity of Mark, Bishop of Otranto. The identical scope and form are possessed by the rubrics concerning the coincidence of fixed feasts with movable ones in the most ancient copies of the Jerusalem Typikon, the Greek MS of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection No. 35/491, and the Georgian Shiomghvime MS; here these rubrics are very close unto the Studite ones, with the exception, naturally, of the peculiarities of Jerusalem practice, and likewise do not bear the name of Mark. In later Greek copies of the Jerusalem Typikon, as already in MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 381 of the 13th–14th centuries, these rubrics are supplemented by marginal annotations, so that around the Annunciation the margins of several pages are covered with them. But in such an ancient copy of the Jerusalem Typikon as the Greek MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 456, probably of the 13th century, all observations of this kind are gathered into one place, divided into 95 chapters, and inscribed: "Compendium (*σύνταγμα*) of Mark, sinful hieromonk, compiled concerning the doubtful matters (*ἀποῤῥούμενα*) of the Typikon" (fol. 165). Thereafter, in the most ancient Slavic Typika, MSS of the Moscow Synodal Library Nos. 328/383 and 329/384 of the 14th century, there is an identical compendium of these observations with the heading (in the first): "Of Mark the sinful hieromonk concerning the omissions of the Typikon" (fol. 189). Subsequently, in many subsequent Slavic and Greek MSS, such a compendium is found with varying numbers of chapters and *(Orig. p. 435)* with an identical name in the inscription, for example: "Of the most sacred Mark of Hydrous [Otranto]," "Of Mark, most holy oeconomos," and the like. Unbound, as previously, unto the days of the month, these compendia, the attribution of which unto Mark, Bishop of Otranto of the 9th–10th centuries (see above, p. 413), rests solely upon the witness of these MSS of the Typikon, acquired here the capacity to expand significantly and to generalize their content—to provide rubrics for the coincidence with Sundays and movable feasts not only of individual feasts, but of entire classes thereof: such as a feast of Christ in general or of the Theotokos with a Sunday; the forefeast, afterfeast, or Apodosis of a Great Feast with a Sunday; a great (vigil-rank), polyeleos, or six-stichera saint with a Sunday, with a Saturday, and the like. This we observe already in the most ancient recensions of the Markian Chapters bearing his name (for example, the Greek Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 456 of the 13th century, and the Slavic Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 328/383 of the 14th century). In later Slavic manuscripts, as already in No. 678/386 of the 15th century, these compendia are divided into two parts: the first, containing general rubrics concerning feasts of the Lord and of the Theotokos and their forefeasts and afterfeasts on a Sunday, and concerning saints on Sunday and Saturday, is placed separately in the first general part of the Typikon setting forth the daily services, and the name of Mark is for the most part not inscribed over it; while the second, bearing the name of Mark, is distributed according unto the days of the months (that is, it assumes its original form). So it is likewise in our present Typikon, though the general part is abridged: treating only of saints on Sunday and Saturday. In yet later Slavic manuscripts from the 16th century onward, for example MSS of the Museum of the Kyiv Theological Academy Aa 194 and 196, rubrics are added concerning the coincidence of temple feasts with movable feasts (the "Temple Chapters" of our present Typikon). In Greek manuscripts, however, up unto the printed edition of the Greek Typikon, and within that printed edition itself, the Markian Chapters are placed in a single section, though they are subsequently repeated under the days of the months (in a shorter, more ancient recension), while the temple chapters are absent.

### Compendia of Brief Hymns in the Typikon and Similar Material

Yet even this is not all that entered into the composition of ancient Typika and enters into our present one. Already the most ancient Studite-Alexis Typikon in MS of the Moscow Synodal Typography Library No. 285/142/1206 of the 11th–12th centuries places upon its pages, alongside rubrical observations, also the most essential and most frequently employed brief hymns, such as: prokeimena, alleluiaria, kontakia, and troparia. Such material, in greater or lesser volume, enters likewise into all subsequent copies of the Typikon. Other sections of more or less related content also find their way into it: for example, notices concerning the lives of commemorated saints (in the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th–10th centuries), the order of the Divine Liturgy (MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 381), expositions of essential dogmas, and the Paschal Tables (in late Greek copies).

### The Architecture and Plan of the Typikon in its Historical Evolution

With the identical gradualness wherewith the content was composed and the volume of the Typikon grew, its plan also was elaborated. The simplest plan is found in the Typikon *(Orig. p. 436)* of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th–10th [printed: 9th–5th] centuries, which possesses only rubrical observations for various days of the year (of the Menologion and Triodion). But as prototypes of the plan of our present Typikon served the *Hypotyposis*, attributed unto St. Theodore the Studite, and its revision, the *Diatyposis* of St. Athanasius. Beginning with an exposition of the Paschal service (a special section entitled: "How we proceed in the assemblies of the holy and glorious three-day Resurrection"), these monuments present in the first place a series of purely liturgical, disconnected observations: concerning the services of Pentecost, the Fast of the Holy Apostles, and onward for the most essential fixed feasts and periods of the ecclesiastical year, followed by the Forty-Day Fast (a special section "Concerning the Holy Forty-Day Fast"); in the disciplinary part that follows, discussion treats first of the monastic officials, of comportment during divine services, and following several minor observations of a disciplinary character, the monuments proceed unto the monastic refectory table (in the sections "Concerning the quantity and quality of food and drink and concerning good order at tables," "Concerning the holy and great Forty-Day Fast," and "Concerning the Annunciation," the last paragraph being of more liturgical content), unto the labors of the monks ("Concerning proportion in services"), and unto their clothing ("Concerning the quantity of clothing, footwear, the arrangement of beds, and the like"—only in the *Hypotyposis*). The identical plan is preserved in general by the Studite-Alexis Typikon, which presents first the Triodion rubrics (from the Sunday of the Publican), then the Menologion (in MSS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 333/381 of the 14th century and No. 906/382 of the 15th century, the Menologion comes earlier—a later transposition, as demonstrated by the preface unto the Menologion in the second MS); the disciplinary part that follows initially seems likewise intended to follow the *Hypotyposis*, speaking first of the table; but subsequently it abandons a consistent plan, endeavoring merely to arrange subjects by some resemblance: as, for example, the paragraphs concerning monastic officials stand almost all side by side, as do the paragraphs concerning comportment during divine worship. The Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th–10th centuries initiated a different plan of Typika, placing the Menologion prior unto the Triodion. Such an arrangement is maintained by all the Western Studite Typika and the Evergetis Typikon. The Typikon of the Great Church and the Western Studite Typika do not possess a disciplinary section, but the Typika of the *Calabrian Recension* (of the Monastery of St. Nicholas of Casole) begin with a general liturgical section containing (in 28 chapters) instructions concerning various points of the daily cycle of worship: for example, concerning the chanting of **"God is the Lord"** and the Alleluia, concerning the bell-ringing, concerning the censing, concerning the kathismata at Matins and Vespers on simple days and on feasts, concerning the suspension of prostrations on certain days, concerning kathismata in fasts and collaterally concerning the table on ordinary days and during fasts, concerning the stichera at services—Sunday, weekday, and festal—concerning the canons at various services, concerning readings, and concerning Compline [^1825]. Similar chapters were found also in Typika of the Sicilian Recension, but situated between the Menologion and the Triodion [^1826]. The Evergetis Typikon, following the Menologion and Triodion portions, presents the order of Sunday Vigil and the Divine Liturgy, makes general observations concerning weekday *(Orig. p. 437)* services, provides the liturgical prokeimena, Sunday and weekday, the alleluia verses of Vespers, speaks of Saturday Vespers and the panikhida for the departed, of the comportment of the canonarch, of censing, and of entering and exiting the church during the service, and thereafter in a special "Prologue" presents the disciplinary part of the Typikon ("Exposition and Depiction of Life in the Monastery"). As it were a third epoch in the elaboration of the plan for the Typikon was created by the Jerusalem Typika, which, retaining the order of Constantinople and the Western Studite Typika in having the Triodion follow the Menologion, prefixed unto this "Synaxarion" and principal part of the Typikon a general liturgical and disciplinary part; wherein, in accordance with their chief distinctive feature—the Sunday Vigils—they began the Typikon precisely with the order of this Vigil and of Sunday services in general, continuing it with the order of weekday and Saturday services, at times also of festal services, and proceeding thereafter unto general rubrical observations, unto fasts, and in general unto the order of monastic life; while following the Synaxarion part there followed, so to speak, "appendices"—troparia, prokeimena, temple chapters, and the Paschal Tables. Yet this composition grew and became complicated gradually. The most ancient recension of the Jerusalem Typikon, represented by the Georgian Shiomghvime MS and the oldest Greek MSS of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection No. 491/35, and of the Moscow Synodal Library Nos. 456 and 381 (13th–14th centuries), contains the following sections: the order of Small Vespers (Greek only); the order of the All-Night Vigil; concerning the number of Vigils in the year (= Chapters 1 and 2 of our present Typikon); concerning the number of kathismata at Matins and Vespers of the entire year (= Chapter 17 of our present Typikon); the order of weekday Vespers and Matins (when Alleluia is chanted, = Chapter 9 of our present Typikon); the First Hour (with Alleluia); a series of minor observations of a liturgical-disciplinary character: concerning not chanting the Alleluia at Vespers on Sunday and Friday; what the canonarch intones at services and which verses the priest recites; what we chant standing and at what we uncover our heads (see above, p. 431); concerning the number and composition of stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**, that is, of weekday Vespers (always 6, and only from the Menaion; if there are 3 there, they are doubled) and at the Aposticha (always of the Octoechos according unto the tone) and concerning the union of choirs for chanting the latter; when the priest censes ("at **\"Lord, I have cried\"**, at the Six Psalms, at the 9th ode, at which we make prostrations unto the ground always, and at the Blameless [*Amomoi*] on all Saturdays and Sundays"); concerning the composition of stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** and at the Aposticha during the period of the Pentecostarion; concerning the manner of chanting the "Polyeleos" (that is, the 1st *Slava* of Kathisma 19), "The God of gods" (the 2nd *Slava* of Kathisma 7), and "Praise the Lord" (the 3rd *Slava* of Kathisma 20) at **"God is the Lord"** and Alleluia (a modification of the well-known article of the Studite Typikon—see above, pp. 365 and 376); prohibition against conversing, entering, and exiting during chanting; concerning the alternation of choirs (see above, p. 431) (in the Georgian MS here: concerning the canons of Matins of the entire week); a general observation concerning the Hours and Inter-Hours during the lesser Forty-Day Fasts and their distinctions from the Hours of the Great Fast; the order of the Inter-Hours (*mesoria*) of the Third, Sixth, and Ninth Hours and the method of joining them unto the Hours; the order of the Typika (*Izobrazitelnye*); an observation concerning the number of Alleluia days during the Nativity Fast; an observation concerning the number of prostrations at **"God is the Lord"** (only 3 upon entering the church: one before the altar and two unto the choirs, and at the dismissal three great prostrations; in the cell according unto desire); when the Inter-Hours are not chanted *(Orig. p. 438)* (only on days of Vigils and of saints with the Great Doxology); the Inter-Hour of the First Hour (in the cell); a series of disciplinary observations concerning comportment after the First Hour, concerning direction upon the right choir by the ecclesiarch and upon the left by the epistemonarch, and concerning the awakener (see above, p. 432); concerning the canons at Matins throughout the entire week (in Greek MSS, = Chapter 11 of our present Typikon); concerning the Saturday service with commemoration of a saint (that is, with **"God is the Lord"**, = Chapter 12 of our present Typikon)—wherein the observation is made that if the memory of an apostle or a great saint does not occur on Saturday, Alleluia is chanted; concerning the Saturday service with Alleluia (= Chapter 13 of our present Typikon; in the Georgian MS, articles concerning the Saturday service stand after the Menologion and Triodion); how the Gospels and their commentaries are read (= Chapter 10 of our present Typikon); when the Liturgies of Basil the Great, John Chrysostom, and the Presanctified are celebrated (presently the note "Behold" unto Chapter 10 of the Typikon); concerning the order of reading the Sunday Matins Gospels; concerning the chanting of the Theotokos Canon at Compline; and disciplinary observations concerning water at Compline and concerning comportment thereafter (see above, p. 432) [^1827]. Later Greek manuscripts somewhat revise and supplement the most ancient ones, but not in their plan. Herewith the Georgian and oldest Greek MSS conclude the first general part of the Typikon and proceed unto the Menologion and Triodion; but later Greek MSS, and even MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 381 of the 13th–14th centuries, contain prior unto the Menologion also the above-cited (on p. 433) disciplinary exhortations unto the superior to observe the Typikon, not to leave the monastery, especially during Forty-Day Fasts; the exhortation unto monks to seek the Kingdom of Heaven; rules concerning attentiveness in church, concerning the chanting of the Six Psalms and silence thereat; excerpts from the *Diatyposis*; the order of the Divine Liturgy for the deacon and chanters; the exclamations of the priest at Vespers and Matins; "How the priest must cense" (= Chapter 22 of our present Typikon); a table of feasts; the wheel of Matins Gospels; rubrics specifying when the reading of each evangelist begins and ends in the church year (and concerning liturgical leaps [*otstupki*]); and the canons of Patriarch Nicephorus [^1828]. Following the Menologion and Triodion, the most ancient manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon display great variation. The Georgian MS possesses here the aforementioned articles concerning the Saturday service with **"God is the Lord"** and with Alleluia, the Order of Orthodoxy, the exapostilaria of feasts, of the principal saints, and of the Triodion, the Paschal Tables, the kontakia of feasts and of the principal saints, and the troparia **"The Angelic Council..."** [^1829]. Among Greek MSS, the oldest, MS of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection No. 491/35, contains here the rubric of censing, liturgical prokeimena with alleluiaria for Sundays and weekdays, Sunday morning prokeimena, exapostilaria of the Octoechos, an exhortation to observe the Typikon, and general dismissal troparia unto the saints (fols. 172–175v, defective at the end). MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 456 of the 13th century has in this identical position the rubric of censing, identical prokeimena, an extract from the *Hypotyposis*, "Concerning the Lunar Cycle" (Paschal data), stichera chanted on feasts of the Lord and on days of great saints at the conclusion of Matins, Theotokia with Stavrotheotokia and Sessional Hymns, Cherubic Hymns, *(Orig. p. 439)* troparia following the Gospel at Psalm 50 in place of **"Through the intercessions of the Apostles..."**, Markian Chapters—63 in number, Sunday troparia and hypakoai of the 8 tones, kontakia of the Triodion and the most essential from the Menologion; in another hand: the Hours on the eve of the Nativity of Christ, Theophany, and Great and Holy Friday (the latter—only the beginnings of the psalms)—different from those in the regular sequential order of the Typikon (namely, of our modern type) (fols. 134–240). At the beginning of this MS is a supplementary gathering in another hand, wherein, among other items, tables of contents (*πίναξ*) of several collections with festal homilies and readings are placed (fols. 7–12); these tables of contents probably served for locating in the corresponding volumes the readings prescribed by the Typikon. MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 381 of the 13th–14th centuries, following the Menologion and Triodion, contains: troparia at Psalm 50 in place of **"Through the intercessions of the Apostles..."**, the Hours on eves, Theotokia at **"God is the Lord"** and at the end of Matins, Theotokion kontakia arranged by tones and days of the week, kontakia of feasts, of the most important saints, and of the Triodion, Sunday prokeimena for the Divine Liturgy and Matins, and weekday prokeimena, "The most wise... (unclear) paraphrase of the ikoi of the Most Holy Theotokos (that is, Her Akathist)," and the rite before the Divine Liturgy for priest and deacon (vesting prayers, proskomedia, censing of the temple) (fols. 177–199). Later Greek manuscripts contain among supplementary articles the following additional ones in comparison with the examined manuscripts: "The office of the leaven," *ζύμης* [^1830], "Concerning the elevation of the artos during Renewal [Bright] Week" (No. 380, fol. 260), and "Prayer for the blessing of grapes [fruits]" (No. 379, fol. 242).

### The Plan of the Greek Printed Editions of the Jerusalem Typikon

Beyond these supplementary articles, the development of the Jerusalem Typikon in its Greek copies did not advance, as shown by its printed editions of the 16th century, which not only lack any other articles beyond those provided by the described manuscripts, but even reduce the number of these articles, gravitating generally closer unto the ancient MSS. The printed editions of the Greek Jerusalem Typikon were produced in Venice: the first in 1545 [^1831], the second with slight additions (two new disciplinary articles) in 1577, and subsequent ones in 1603 and 1643 without alterations from 1577. The printed edition of the Greek Jerusalem Typikon is divided into 5 parts: general liturgical-disciplinary, the Menologion, *(Orig. p. 440)* the Triodion, Markian Chapters, and supplementary articles; but the editors divide the Typikon into two parts, assigning unto the first three a common numbering of 100 chapters, the Markian Chapters likewise 100, while the supplementary articles, unnumbered by chapters, they regard simply as an appendix. The first general liturgical-disciplinary part, divided into 10 chapters, constitutes an almost verbatim reproduction of the identical part of the most ancient Greek manuscripts, for example, MS of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov collection fols. 1–19, in comparison with which and other known Greek MSS there is here only one additional article—Chapter 7: "Concerning which canons are to be preferred": "It should be known that if the Menaion contains for the memory of any saint canons by various hymnographers, then if there is a canon of Kyr Cosmas, it is preferred; if there are canons of Kyr John and others, that of John is preferred, for he takes precedence over others; if of Kyr Theophanes and others, that of Kyr Theophanes is preferred, for he takes precedence over others; if of Kyr Joseph, it is preferred unto the remaining hymnographers. If there are no such (canons of Joseph), then that of Kyr John; if these are not found, then that of Kyr Theophanes. But above all of them, the canons of Kyr Joseph are preferred unto all the rest." (Thus canons of later hymnographers are preferred unto the most ancient). The Markian Chapters likewise possess the identical composition as in the most ancient Greek MSS, for example MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 456, but unto them are appended—evidently to obtain the number of 100 chapters—as Chapters 94–100 the chapters concerning the Saturday service with Alleluia, concerning weekday canons, the rubric of censing, prokeimena, and the rubric of their intonation by the reader. Supplementary articles: "Questions from canonical ordinances"—concerning food on great feasts falling during fasts (on the basis of the canons of the Holy Apostles, Theophilus of Alexandria, and others); "Epistle of Nicholas, Patriarch of Constantinople, unto Anastasius, Hegumen of Sinai," in verse; concerning the same subject and concerning the comportment of monks in general: "Of Anastasius, Bishop of Caesarea of Palestine, concerning the Fast of Artzivourion"; "Of the Holy Fathers in Antioch concerning the Great Week"—concerning the identical matter; from the *Apostolic Constitutions* V, 13 concerning feasts and fasts; "Canons of Peter and Paul" (apocryphal) concerning non-working days; "Concerning churches," that when divine worship is impossible within them, it must be performed in houses; concerning orderly singing in church according unto Canon 75 of the Trullan Council; days of fasting relaxation and its degrees; two other articles concerning the same; lives of the four Evangelists (from the *Synopsis* of St. Dorotheus of Tyre); the order of reading the Evangelists during the year; how one ought to believe; "Exhortatory chapters in maxims" (moral counsels); and the Paschal Tables.

### Composition and Plan of Slavic Manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon

The Slavic copies of the Jerusalem Typikon differ significantly in plan and composition from the currently known Greek MSS, expanding their content with new articles, the number of which usually increases with the chronological age of the manuscripts. The most ancient of such MSS of Russian provenance, MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 328/383 of the 14th century, possesses the following new articles in comparison with known Greek copies: the order of three kinds of Compline and Midnight Office, the order of the refectory table (the later "Office of the Panagia"); on the other hand, almost all the minor rubrics of the general liturgical-disciplinary portion of Greek MSS are omitted here, and of *(Orig. p. 441)* this part there is retained here only the order of the All-Night Vigil with an observation concerning how many Vigils occur in the year, and the order of weekday services—Vespers, Matins, and Hours with Inter-Hours; there are not even chapters concerning the Saturday service. Closer unto the Greek MSS is the Slavic MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 329/384 of the 14th century; it contains many of the supplementary articles of the Greek MSS, but retains no more than the first MS from the introductory liturgical-disciplinary part of Greek MSS. It possesses also new articles: not to mention a gathering sewn in front of it in another, probably later hand and of diverse content (prokeimena, Epistles and Gospels for various occasions, prayers, dismissals, the order for the kneading of bread), wherein are given disciplinary excerpts from Nikon of the Black Mountain comprising Chapters 32–47 of our present Typikon; in the primary MS, among the Markian Chapters placed here after the Menologion, there occur also such chapters: concerning a saint who has an entrance (Litiya) (from the Serbian Typikon), concerning the psalmody of the 1st Ode (**"Let us sing unto the Lord..."** [*Gospodevi poyem...*] = Chapter 18 of our present Typikon), concerning the singing of the **"More honorable..."** [*Chestneyshuyu...*] (= Chapter 31 of our present Typikon). Yet closer unto Greek MSS is the Slavic MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 332/385 of the end of the 14th century. Here is given in translation almost the entire introductory part of Greek MSS, and following it, prior unto the Menologion, a section of the Markian Chapters of general content (concerning feasts of the Theotokos on Sunday, etc.) with those chapters new in comparison with Greek MSS that are found in No. 329, and furthermore with the chapter "Concerning how candles are to be kindled" (= Chapter 25 of our present Typikon); then disciplinary excerpts from Nikon of the Black Mountain; following the Menologion and Triodion—common Epistles and Gospels for the saints for various occasions, Sunday readings, dismissals, the prayer for the kneading of bread, and the refrains at the 9th Ode. Here is already fully the plan, even the composition and volume, of our present Typikon; only the temple chapters are lacking. Close unto it is the Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 678/386 of the 15th century. It provides, among other matters, the order of the panikhida for the departed, and in connection therewith the order "for the libation" (*za prilivok*) at the refectory (that is, prayers with chanting upon the pouring of wine in honor of the departed, fol. 22v). Subsequent manuscripts introduce further new articles, few of which have been adopted into our present Typikon: for example, Moscow Synodal Library No. 336/388 of the beginning of the 16th century: "Concerning the curtain of the holy altar, when it is opened"; No. 337/389 of 1553: "Concerning temples for the entire year" (likewise No. 335/391 of the beginning of the 17th century: "The Temple Directive" [*Ukaz khramny*]). Not all such articles possessed an equally close relation unto the Typikon. Thus at times there was placed in the Typikon the entire Horologion (MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 331/387 of 1438), the Skete Typikon (see above, p. 393), instructions on how to serve "if anywhere there are no monthly Menaia" (No. 335/391, beginning of the 17th century, fol. 312), "A prayer over one frightened in sleep," a prayer "For a temple wherein a demon begins to dwell" (*ibid.*, fol. 562), "A prayer for deliverance from fornication" (No. 953/395 of the 17th century, fol. 279v), ascetical instructions of the Holy Fathers—Athanasius the Great, Macarius, Maximus the Confessor (*ibid.*, fols. 167, 177), and narratives of similar character ("Narrative concerning one tempted in sleep," *ibid.*, fol. 379v).

### Printed Editions of the Slavonic Jerusalem Typikon

The printed editions of the Slavonic Typikon in Russia necessarily took as their foundation the widespread Slavic manuscript copies; therefore, in the initial *(Orig. p. 442)* stages, as long as the deficiencies of the latter were not recognized, they were of the identical plan and composition. The first edition of the Slavonic Typikon in Russia was produced in 1610, with the blessing of Patriarch Hermogenes and with the counsel of the hierarchs of that time, by the *golovshchik* and *ustavshchik* of the Trinity-Sergius Lavra, Longin (Shishelev), upon the foundation of several manuscripts, though probably exclusively Russian-Slavic ones. It contains a general liturgical-disciplinary part—57 chapters; Markian Chapters—173; the rubric for services unto Slavonic-Russian saints, especially upon their coincidence with the Pentecostarion—25 chapters; temple chapters—46; the Menologion and the Triodion. The disciplinary part here is very extensive, but not everywhere systematic: many extracts from the Studite Typikon, and from the Holy Mountain Typikon according unto Nikon; one may say not a single disciplinary article from the Slavic copies was omitted; yet material entirely extraneous unto the Typikon (prayers from the Trebnik) is absent. On account of certain inaccuracies in the text, principally on account of discrepancies between the exclamations of prayers and their content (prayers addressed unto one Person of the Holy Trinity concluded with an exclamation addressed unto the entire Holy Trinity) and the addition in the prayer for the blessing of water unto the words "by the Holy Spirit" of "and by fire," this edition of the Typikon was condemned unto burning by Patriarch Philaret as heretical (several copies survived in the Moscow Typography Library and elsewhere), and a new edition was produced in 1633, somewhat more systematic and concise: certain articles of Russian origin were excluded, among others, from the Markian Chapters as well. This edition was likewise produced on the basis of Slavic manuscripts. It was reprinted in 1634 without alterations (only an error in pagination was corrected). (From this edition the Old Believer Typikon is printed presently). The subsequent edition under Patriarch Joasaph in 1641 restored much that had been excluded in 1633 and introduced certain corrections into the text. Close unto it is the edition of 1651 under Patriarch Joseph. Patriarch Nikon did not succeed in attending unto the correction of the Typikon. It was carried out under Patriarch Joachim, and the result thereof was the edition of 1682, wherein the Typikon received already its modern composition and volume.
