The correctors (*spravshchiki*) now for the first time turned unto Greek manuscripts, as well as unto ancient Slavonic ones; upon a single copy of the 1641 Typikon (in the Moscow Typography Library No. 1373) the notations of the correctors for printing have been preserved—annotations, cancellations, paste-overs—and, among other things, there are indicated (in an annotation above the Menologion) the sources for correction: "by decree of the most holy Patriarch with the hierarchs, it is commanded to follow in all things the Greek Typika and Menaia, and the corrected Slavic Horologion and the Anthologion (*Trefologion*, Festal Menaion) of the Lviv edition (in Lviv 1632 and approved by the 4 Eastern Patriarchs), unto the Slavonic Typika, and the Philaret Typikon (that is, the Typikon of 1633, as approximating closest in its brevity unto the Greek ones). There have been preserved traces of the labors of the correctors (*spravshchiki*) also upon certain manuscripts of the Typikon: for example, upon MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 321/393, where upon the colophon leaf it is stated explicitly: "begun to be printed... and finished and issued in the typography... in the year 1682" (there are marginal notes of correctors, though of an unknown date, also upon the MS of the identical library No. 337/389: for example, opposite the ikos for the departed: "concerning the alleluia, report whether once or thrice"; opposite the Beheading: "concerning fish, report, *(Orig. p. 443)* in the sequential order it is not indicated to eat"). The Typikon of 1682, in comparison with those immediately preceding, is significantly abbreviated; all articles of Russian provenance are excluded (for example, the rite of the veneration of the Shroud [*Plashchanytsia*]) and up to 50 commemorations of Russian saints, on account of their absence in Greek books; furthermore, this Typikon was harmonized with the text of other liturgical books recently corrected, in those places where it touches upon them—in the text of troparia, kontakia, and the opening words of stichera. In the disciplinary section, besides abbreviation, contradictions between individual articles were eliminated, especially concerning fasts; the article "from the canons of the Holy Fathers," which contradicted the Jerusalem Typikon, was excluded. In the liturgical sections, expressions favoring a twofold alleluia were eliminated; the rubric of censing was harmonized with the contemporary layout of the temple; the rubric concerning Lenten prostrations was set forth more clearly; **"Let my prayer arise"** (*Da ispravitsya*) at the Liturgy of the Annunciation was abolished; and the Sunday Gospel at the Nativity of the Theotokos falling upon a Sunday following the Great Doxology was cancelled [^1832]. The subsequent edition of the Typikon followed in 1695 under Patriarch Adrian: the alterations affected the Menologion, which was harmonized with the Menaia corrected under this Patriarch; of the number of Russian-Slavic saints excluded by the 1682 edition, about 12 commemorations were restored in the 1695 edition (for example, St. Andrew, Oct. 2; Great-Martyr George, Nov. 26; St. Arsenius of Tver, Mar. 2; the Tikhvin Icon, June 26; St. Philip of Moscow, July 3); but the commemorations placed in the 1682 Typikon of Euphrosynus of Pskov on May 14 (on account of the association with his name of the twofold alleluia) and Nicetas [Nikolai] Kachanov on July 27 were excluded. From 1695 onward, the Typikon is printed almost without alterations; there are introduced only commemorations of newly canonized saints [^1833].

### The Present-Day Greek Typikon

The Greek Church presently uses for cathedral and parish churches not the Jerusalem Typikon, but a special one, representing an adaptation of the Jerusalem Typikon unto the practice of the Studite tradition and even of Hagia Sophia (the Typikon of the Great Church). This practice, living for centuries as an unwritten tradition, found expression for itself in a printed edition of the Greek Typikon produced in Constantinople in 1828 by Constantine, Protopsaltes of the Great Church, under the title *Ecclesiastical Typikon according to the Order of the Great Church of Christ* (*Τυπικὸν ἐκκλησιαστικὸν κατὰ τὴν τάξιν τῆς τοῦ Χριστοῦ Μεγάλης Ἐκκλησίας*), reprinted several times (1851, 1868, 1884) and translated into the Slavic language for the Bulgarians by Hieromonk Neophytus of Rila. Being destined not for monasteries, unto which in the preface the right is acknowledged to be guided by former Typika [^1834], and differing from the Jerusalem Typikon chiefly by the absence of Vigils, *(Orig. p. 444)* this Typikon lacks likewise the monastic-disciplinary section. Its general section (in 6 octavo pages) consists of the order of Sunday services, the peculiarity of which is the reading of the Gospel after the 8th Ode of the canon, and the omission of the Hours (they are not mentioned in the Typikon and in practice are not read); of observations concerning the distinction therefrom of festal services; and of the time of celebrating the 3 different Liturgies; unto this are subjoined Canon 75 of the Trullan Council concerning decorum in chanting, Canon 15 of the Council of Laodicea permitting only canonical clerics to chant in church, and the prohibition of the Jerusalem Typikon against conversing in church. Peculiarities of the Menologion: the services of the Nativity of Christ and Theophany have no Great Compline, but consist solely of Matins with Litiya at the beginning; if the Annunciation occurs on Great and Holy Friday or Saturday, it is transferred unto Pascha, with the exception of monasteries (this was introduced by Patriarch Gregory VI in 1835–1840 in view of the rubrical difficulties in such a coincidence, wherewith parish priests were unable to cope); on September 29 occurs the local Greek commemoration of the Miracle of the Mother of God upon the Island of Corfu; Great-Martyr Catherine on November 25; Martyr Charalampus on February 10 and Martyr Euphemia on November 11 [July 11] have festal services (for the former, the Presanctified Liturgy even in the 1st week of Great Lent, except Monday). Peculiarities in the Triodion: in the 1st week the Great Canon is read at Compline following the Doxology, and at the end of Compline is the Gospel (a vestige of the Chanted Pannykhis); on the 1st Friday of Great Lent the Great Canon is chanted either at Small Compline before **"It is truly meet"** (*Dostoyno*), or at Matins, as among us; the Akathist is chanted at Small Compline before the 1st, and after the 3rd, 6th, and 9th Odes of the canon; the distribution of palms takes place at the Praises; the Shroud (*Plashchanytsia*) on Great and Holy Saturday is carried into the altar permanently after the Great Doxology at Matins; at Paschal Matins following **"Thy Resurrection, O Christ our Savior"** (*Voskreseniye Tvoye, Khriste Spase*) is read the Gospel of Matthew, chapter 28; the Homily of Chrysostom is read after the Prayer behind the Ambon; the Gospel at the Paschal Divine Liturgy is read ordinary [in the vernacular], and in diverse tongues at Vespers. Following the Triodion, there are in the Typikon supplementary articles: the order of the consecration of a church, the rite of the induction of the Patriarch into the Patriarchate, explanations of the titles for diverse ecclesiastical hymns and among them the names of the pieces of silver ("Concerning the 30 Pieces of Silver"), the hours of the bell-ringing for diverse services and the days of the Patriarch's celebration, marriage regulations, and the funeral rite.
*(Orig. p. 445)*

## Notes to Volume I: The Historical Investigation of the Typikon

### Notes to the Chapter: Old Testament Jewish Worship

1. Thus the earliest printed Typika designate themselves on their colophon leaves, ending with those published under Patriarch Joseph, as does the present Old Believer Typikon—of the Edinoverie edition.
2. *Peregrinatio ad loca sancta*, 34; *Pravoslavny Palestinsky Sbornik*, issue 20, p. 54.
3. Lk 24:53.
4. Pss 150; 149; 1:3.
5. Ps 21:23, 26 [LXX 21:22, 25]; Ps 49:14, 23 [LXX 49:14, 23 / MT 50:14, 23]. Cf. Heb 13:15.
6. Num 10:10.
7. Sacred trumpets likewise substituted among the Hebrews for our church bells: with them the people were summoned unto the tabernacle, and subsequently, in all probability, unto the temple; for this purpose there were at the tabernacle two silver trumpets; when both were sounded together, this was a summons for the entire assembly; the sound of a single trumpet—for the chieftains alone; for breaking camp they sounded an alarm (Num 10:1–7). The passage concerning this from the Book of Numbers is read in our Church and in the Roman Catholic Church at the blessing of bells. At the temple the number of trumpets reached up to 100 (1 Chron 15:24; 2 Chron 5:12; cf. Flavius Josephus, *Antiquities* III, 12, 6). The trumpets possessed exclusively a sacred use. They resembled horns wherewith muezzins presently summon Mohammedans unto prayer. Olesnitsky (A.), *Drevneevreyskaya muzyka i penie* [Ancient Hebrew Music and Chant], *Trudy Kievskoy Dukhovnoy Akademii* [Proceedings of the Kyiv Theological Academy], 1871, issue 11, p. 117.
8. 1 Chron 16:40, 41.
9. Judg 9:13. Talmud, *Arakhin*, *Gemara* 11.
10. Perhaps the passages of the psalms where such an elevation of tone and trumpet accompaniment were to occur are designated by the enigmatic term *selah*. This term is found in 39 psalms (for example, Pss 7, 21, 22 [LXX 7, 21, 22 / MT 7, 22, 23]) and the Canticle of Habakkuk; 16 psalms contain it once, 15 twice, 7 psalms and the Canticle of Habakkuk three times, and one psalm (Ps 88 [LXX 88 / MT 89]) four times. The LXX translate this term *διάψαλμα* (*diapsalma*); the Slavonic Bible omits it. The term, as well as its rendering in the LXX, has been explained variously (the most ancient explanation: "unto eternity"), but the majority inclines unto the view that it signifies the beginning of strophes or an alteration of voice and musical tone, and most likely an upward modulation thereof (Sommer, J., *Biblische Abhandlungen*, vol. I, Bonn, 1844, I: "Erklärung des Sela," pp. 1–84). It is likewise thought that *selah* signifies the place in a hymn where one choir was to pause and another repeat what had been chanted by the first, and that the word constitutes the initial letters of the words: *sor lema'alah hashir*—"return, chanter, unto the beginning" (Olesnitsky, *Drevneevreyskaya muzyka i penie*, *T.K.D.A.*, 1871, issue 12, p. 371).

"Blessings" (*berakhot*) are the usual designation for prayer and the most widely used prayer formula among the Hebrews. It is prescribed by the Talmud for all circumstances: "During rains and upon hearing good tidings, they recite: 'Blessed is the All-Good Benefactor'; upon hearing evil tidings: 'Blessed is the righteous Judge'; upon seeing a rainbow, they recite: 'Blessed is He Who is faithful unto His covenant'; at the sight of a Negro, a red-skinned man, an albino, a giant, and a dwarf, they recite: 'Blessed is He... Who diversifieth His creatures'; at the sight of a beautiful man or a beautiful tree, they say: 'Blessed is He... Who hath created in His world beautiful creatures'; at the sight of an idol, they recite: 'Blessed is the Long-Suffering One'" (*Berakhot* IX, 1).

Naturally, in the earliest times of Christianity there could have been introduced into the prayers a curse upon Jews converting unto Christianity, which subsequently was probably excluded and replaced by a general curse upon apostates and enemies of Judaism.

80. Unto such chanting in ancient temple practice, Psalm 146:7 [LXX 146:7 / MT 147:7] perhaps points: "Sing alternately," in Hebrew *'anu*, "respond," but in the Greek *ἐξάρξατε* (*exarxate*), Slavonic *nachnite* ("begin"); the expression can likewise be understood of the two other modes of chanting: epiphonic and hypophonic. The term *selah* is likewise understood in the sense of an indication of antiphonal singing. It is thought that antiphonal chanting was borrowed by the Hebrews from Egypt, where a song was divided between the priests and the people, between men and women, between children and adults. By such chanting the adoration of the golden calf was accompanied: descending from the mount and hearing the noise, Moses says: "It is not the voice of them that shout for mastery, neither is it the voice of them that cry for being overcome; but the noise of them that sing do I hear" (Ex 32:18); more literally from the Hebrew: it is not the alternating voices (*'anot*—answering) of the victors, nor the alternating voices of the vanquished, but alternating voices do I hear.—Philo sees the initial instance of antiphonal chanting in the Song of Moses after the crossing of the Red Sea. How far is this correct? The execution of this song is described thus in Exodus: "Then sang Moses and the children of Israel this song unto the Lord, and spake, saying: I will sing unto the Lord, for He hath triumphed gloriously..."; following the exposition of the song it is added: "And Miriam the prophetess, the sister of Aaron, took a timbrel [tambourine, drum, a dance musical instrument] in her hand; and all the women went out after her with timbrels and with dances [Hebrew *meholot*, dances; Greek *χορῶν*]; and Miriam answered them: Sing ye unto the Lord, for He hath triumphed gloriously; the horse and his rider hath He thrown into the sea" (Ex 14:31; 15:1, 20, 21). This description commentators understand variously (not in the sense of antiphonal chanting alone): according unto some, the men repeated immediately after Moses and according unto his melody each verse of the song, and then the identical verse was sung by the women (as among us the prokeimenon, troparion, and exapostilaria are chanted thrice); according unto others, the women sang one verse, the men another, etc., alternately; but far more directly follows from the context of the speech such an understanding, that after Moses the verse chanted by him was repeated by the men, while the women repeated constantly the single first verse, changing the first person "I will sing" into "Sing ye," as though inviting thereby their husbands to sing the hymn unto Jehovah more harmoniously; this all the more so, since clearly the words of the song could be heard only by those standing closer unto Moses. Olesnitsky, *Drevneevreyskaya muzyka i penie*, *Trudy K. D. Ak.*, 1871, issue 11, pp. 115–116. Our order of executing the canticle on Great and Holy Saturday is based upon this latter understanding. (Cf. likewise Keil, *Rukovodstvo k bibleyskoy arkheologii* [Manual of Biblical Archaeology], Russian translation, Kyiv, 1879, II, § 136).

3. The breaking of bread is the technical designation of the Eucharist in the New Testament: Acts 20:7; 1 Cor 10:16; 11:24. Therefore the Peshitta translates this expression here and in 20:7: "in the breaking of the Eucharist." Between the words "in communion" and "in the breaking of bread," certain codices lack "and," whereby the teaching of the Apostles and communion are separated as an independent pair alongside the other of the breaking of bread and prayers; the Vulgate, on the contrary, merges the second member with the third: *in communicatione fractionis panis*.

Melodic tropes are used even presently among the Greeks, South Slavs, and among our Old Believers and Russian Athonites. In the Monastery of St. Panteleimon on Mount Athos, owing unto melodic tropes, the chanting of the troparion **"Theotokos Virgin"** (*Bogoroditse Devo*) at Vespers extends for an entire hour. *Zametki poklonnika sv. gory* [Notes of a Pilgrim unto the Holy Mountain], Kyiv, 1864, pp. 32–33; Razumovsky, D., *Tserkovnoye peniye v Rossii* [Church Singing in Russia], issue 1, Moscow, 1867, pp. 108–109.

141. The gift of tongues is presented in the New Testament as such a miraculous, majestic, and soul-stirring phenomenon that it cannot in any wise be acknowledged as a phenomenon of the identical order with the glossolalia of Russian and foreign sectarians (Khlysts, Malevantsy, Irvingites, Mormons), which consists in an utterly meaningless combination of syllables and words (for example: *rentre fente rente fintrifunt, — trrr, tlim, tlim, dze*; Konovalov, D., "Religiozny ekstaz v russkom misticheskom sektantstve" [Religious Ecstasy in Russian Mystical Sectarianism], *Bogoslovsky Vestnik*, 1908, issue 4, pp. 738, 744) and constitutes a purely nervous phenomenon accompanied by convulsions (*ibid.*, issue 10, p. 200; issue 4, p. 754), whirling (issue 3, pp. 734, 755), and hysterical laughter and weeping (issue 4, p. 753). On a neurotic basis there may likewise appear in certain individuals speech in a foreign tongue heard by them at some prior time and absorbed unconsciously. Both phenomena were familiar likewise unto the ancient Christians, but were sharply distinguished by them from the gift of tongues communicated by the Holy Spirit; they were explained as the influence of evil spirits upon man. Eusebius cites the narrative of an ancient historian concerning the glossolalia of the Montanists: "A certain person named Montanus, they relate, from among the recent converts, through an excessive desire for primacy, fell under the influence of the adversary, and suddenly, having entered into a state of possession and frenzy, began to speak and utter strange sounds (*λαλεῖν καὶ ξεноφωνεῖν*), that is, he prophesied contrary unto the custom handed down from of old and preserved by succession in the Church... He [the devil] even raised up two women and filled them with a lying spirit, so that they also, like the aforementioned Montanus, spoke senselessly, inappropriately, and strangely" (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 16). According unto the account of Bl. Jerome, a certain Frankish official who had fallen under the dominion of a demon from childhood, in the presence of St. Hilarion, scarcely touching the ground with his feet and blushing exceedingly, began to speak in the Syriac and Greek languages, which were unknown unto him, with entirely correct pronunciation (*Life of St. Hilarion*, ch. 22). Among sectarians, both Russian and foreign, speaking in unknown foreign tongues has not been observed, but only the utterance of senseless sounds.

150. 1 Cor 14:16. "He that occupieth the room of the unlearned," Slavonic: *nevezhdy*, Greek: *ἰδιώτου*. An *ἰδιώτης* is a person not holding an official or leading position, or a layman / non-specialist: for example, ordinary citizens in distinction from the king (Herodotus II, 81, and elsewhere); the general public in distinction from the scholars of the philosophical school (Plutarch, *Symposiacs* I, 1); non-ecstatics and non-diviners in distinction from a visionary (Pausanias, *Description of Greece: Corinth* 13). In the LXX in Proverbs 6:8, as in Herodotus. In the Talmud—an ordinary man in distinction from a rabbi, craftsman, ruler, and the like. In agreement with all these meanings, the word here clearly signifies every member of the liturgical assembly in distinction from the one coming forward with a revelation, in this particular case with speaking in tongues. Consequently, the word does not stand in the sense of a casual visitor unto the assembly—for example, an unbeliever, as in verse 24, where the identical word appears—nor in the generic sense of an ignorant or uneducated person, still less in the modern colloquial sense of this word, which certain scholars likewise allowed, rendering it, for example, in German as *Idiot* (Binterim, A., *Die vorzüglichsten Denkwürdigkeiten der Christ-Katholischen Kirche*, IV, 1, Mainz, 1827, p. 319). "He that occupieth the room" indicates that the status of an *ἰδιώτης* is not permanent, but situational: all, except the one actively ministering during divine worship, are *ἰδιῶται*, and each becomes one at a given moment when he does not have a revelation (Zahn-Bachmann, pp. 420–421). Here, therefore, is already given a rather sharp division (more so than in the synagogue) of the worshipers into celebrants and laity, although this demarcation is not yet rigid, but fluid.

Recently in Russian literature the opinion was expressed that into the composition of the ancient veneration of martyrs in the 2nd–4th centuries there entered likewise religious dances (Konovalov, D., "Religiozny ekstaz v russkom misticheskom sektantstve" [Religious Ecstasy in Russian Mystical Sectarianism], *Bogoslovsky Vestnik*, 1907, issue 10, p. 351; 1908, issue 4, pp. 707–728). In the acts of the martyrs, which often conclude with a description of liturgical assemblies in honor of the martyrs, there is no mention of dances in their honor: to interpret the expression in the *Martyrdom of Polycarp* concerning the celebration of his memory "with gladness and joy — *ἀγαλλιάσει καὶ χαρᾷ*" as referring unto dance (Konovalov, p. 707) is arbitrary. Only a few monuments of the 3rd and 4th centuries speak of these dances as a local and tolerated phenomenon. Thus, according unto the testimony of St. Gregory of Nyssa, St. Gregory the Wonderworker (3rd century), yielding unto the inclinations of his flock and in order to divert them from pagan festivals, permitted modest dances (*τὶ μικρὸν ὑποκιρτᾷν*) in honor of the martyrs (*Homily on Ecclesiastes* 6). A 4th-century homily in memory of the martyr Polyeuktos († 259 in Armenia) invites: "according unto established custom let us exult [*χορεύσωмен*] in honor of the martyr" (Aubé, B., *Polyeucte dans l'histoire*, Paris, 1882, p. 79). There is pointed out likewise in St. Basil the Great the expression: "we dance with sacred dances [*ἐνθέоις χоρείαις*] at the tombs of the saints" (cited in Conybeare, F., *Philo: About the Contemplative Life*, p. 154, citing: Bas., t. 1, p. 512 B). In the Abyssinian liturgy down to the present day there has been preserved dancing at prayer services and cross processions, wherein priests also take a certain part (Turayev, B., "Abyssinia," *Pravoslavnaya bogoslovskaya entsiklopediya*, vol. I, St. Petersburg, 1899, col. 71). Orthodox Arabs in Jerusalem likewise permit it around the holy places (Muravyov, *Puteshestviye k svyatym mestam* [Journey unto the Holy Places], part 2, St. Petersburg, 1849, p. 124). Thus all these were religious excesses, taking place only in such enthusiastic regions as Asia Minor and Armenia, and not approved by the Church. St. John Chrysostom considers dancing to be a demonic affair (*Homily 48 on Matthew*). St. Gregory the Theologian advises dancing as David did, but understands the dancing of the latter in an allegorical sense (*Oration 5*). Bl. Augustine is indignant at former dances in the martyrium of St. Cyprian and before the very basilicas of the saints (*Sermon on the Day of the Martyr Cyprian* and *Sermon 215 [265]*). The Council of Carthage of 397, Canon 71, forbade "indecent dances (*ὀρχίσεις μυσαράς*), performed in holy places and even on the feast days of the blessed martyrs." The Council of Laodicea (at the end of the 4th century), Canon 53, forbids even at weddings bouncing or dancing (*βαλλίζειν ἢ ὄρχεσθαι*). In view of such an attitude toward religious dancing in the Church and such rarity of it among ancient Christians, one can hardly see a ritual remnant of it in the circular procession at baptism, marriage, and chirothesy (Konovalov, p. 723).

In the time of Tertullian men and women still kissed one another at prayer without distinction of sex: "what pagan will permit his wife to approach one or another of the brethren for a kiss?" (*To His Wife* II, 4). But in the *Apostolic Constitutions* men kiss men, and women women (VIII, 15). The intermediate link between the two practices is found in St. Ambrose: the deacon kisses the deaconess, and she kisses the women (*To Women*, Epistle 6).

174. It is customary to think that by "stations" in Tertullian and writers of that era the fast of Wednesday and Friday is meant. But Tertullian calls the three-week fast of the Montanists a "station" as well (*On Fasting*, ch. 19), and neither he nor other writers apply this term specifically unto either fast, but unto fasts in general. Hermas, unto the question of the Shepherd: "Why hast thou come hither [unto the mountain] so early?" answers: "Because, sir, I am keeping a station..." "And what is a station?" he asked. "That is, I am fasting, sir, said I" (*Shepherd of Hermas*, *Similitude* 5). Only the following passages from Tertullian might speak in favor of such a narrow meaning of the term "station": "we dedicate the fourth and the sixth day of the week unto stations" (*On Fasting* 19); concerning a Christian drawn into military service: "and stations he performs, or rather unto someone other than Christ, or on the Lord's Day, when [they are performed] in any case not unto Christ" (*On the Soldier's Crown* 11).

187. One cannot therefore, along with certain Western scholars, cast suspicion upon the authenticity of all mentions of the Forty Days Fast [the Holy Forties / *Tessarakoste*] that occur in 3rd-century monuments merely on the grounds that other monuments of that century do not yet know such a prolonged fast. Thus Achelis in his edition of the *Canons of Hippolytus* considers the word "40" in the above-cited passage of this monument to be a later interpolation (Achelis, *Die Canones Hippolyti*, p. 102). The testimonies of Origen are suspected on the grounds that Origen's commentary on the Book of Leviticus, where it is found, has reached us in the translation of Rufinus († 410). And Rufinus was a very free translator, which he not only admits, but repeatedly warns the reader of, for example, in the preface unto the translation of Origen's work *Περὶ ἀρχῶν* [*On First Principles*]. And in the afterword unto the translation of Origen's commentary on the Epistle unto the Romans he remarks concerning his work: "we supply what was spoken by Origen for the Church of his day not so much for purposes of explanation as for purposes of edification, as we did also in the homilies or discourses on Genesis and Exodus; and especially in the homilies on the Book of Leviticus, where what was spoken by him for beauty of style we render into plain language for clarity; this labor of supplying what is lacking we undertook so that the Latin reader might not be troubled by questions raised and left unresolved, as Origen is accustomed to do according unto the requirements of homiletic art." Once such principles were laid at the foundation of the translation, then, as the editor of Origen in Migne's *Patrologia* remarks, the reader can never be certain whether he is reading Origen or Rufinus. True, so wide a freedom of translation ought not to extend unto purely factual data in Origen, such as an indication of the existence in his day of the Forty Days Fast. But here one recalls Rufinus' translation of Irenaeus' words concerning a 40-hour fast... Furthermore, in Origen's expression concerning the Forties, "the days of the Forties consecrated unto fasting," attention is drawn unto the misplaced flowery style of the phrase, which does not match the simplicity of that which follows it: "we fast both on Wednesday and on Friday." Funk thinks that Origen was speaking here of the forty-day fast of the Savior (Funk, *Kirchengeschichtliche Abhandlungen und Untersuchungen*, vol. 1, Paderborn, 1897, p. 254).

11. Subsequently they were forbidden by the Council of Liège of 743 and the Council of Aachen of 846. Pope Eugene in 862 still complained of disorders at agapae. In the East as well, the Council in Trullo (692) was obliged to repeat against agapae the canon of the Council of Laodicea with the penalty: "Those who dare to do this, let them either cease or be excommunicated" (Canon 74). Agapae in connection with the Eucharist exist at the present day in Abyssinia; something similar unto them is found among the Herrnhuters and Methodists (Sokolov, *Agapai*, pp. 160–161).

25. These "tempest-tossed" in the rite of the Liturgy of the *Apostolic Constitutions* (VIII, 6) are more precisely named "those energized (*ἐνεργούμενοι*) by unclean spirits" [the possessed]. In the epoch of the monument, consequently, the phenomenon of "demonic possession" was of no small prevalence, unless prayers for the "energoumenoi" were already at that time such a relic of antiquity as prayers for the catechumens are today. Characteristic is the place occupied by this class of worshipers: between the catechumens and the illuminandi; the catechumens prior unto exorcism were likewise considered to be under the influence of unclean spirits, like all pagans.

29. The monument was discovered by the Italian archaeologist Gamurrini in 1884 in a Latin manuscript of ca. the 12th century belonging unto the Confraternity of St. Mary in Arezzo. The initial leaves of the work are lost, which is why neither the title of the work nor the name of the author has been preserved. In the margins of the manuscript, in two places in the corner, appear the letters *PE*, which are regarded as an abbreviation of the title. Indirect evidence in the work points unto the end of the 4th century as the time of the origin of the *Pilgrimage*: the Jerusalem edifices are described in such wise that the Constantinian structures can be recognized in them; mention is made of a recently built church in Edessa, which occurred in 372 under Emperor Valens; of the left bank of the Tigris belonging unto the Persians, which was ceded unto them by Emperor Jovian in 363; of the Thebaid ascetics (among them St. Anthony, † 356, and Pachomius, † 340); on the other hand, St. Jerome's translation of Holy Scripture is unknown unto the pilgrim, as is the decree of Pope Gelasius of 494 against reading apocrypha — the letter of Abgar, the *Acts of the Apostle Thomas*, and the *Acts of the Martyr Thecla*; nor are Justinian's constructions in Sinai and Constantinople mentioned. The pilgrim came unto the Holy Land *de extremis porro terris* (from the furthest ends of the earth); judging by her comparison of the Euphrates unto the Rhône (*Rhodanus*), she was presumably a native of Gaul; she is an educated and well-read woman; she travels as a noble personage — with a retinue; she is provided with a military escort; bishops meet and accompany her. In Palestine she spent three years, residing in Jerusalem and making excursions thence. Having returned unto Constantinople, she described her pilgrimage unto her "sisters" (fleshly sisters or nuns?). The identification of the pilgrim by some with Galla Placidia, daughter of Theodosius the Great, and by others with Silvia, sister of the Constantinopolitan prefect Rufinus (an Aquitanian), is rather arbitrary. The monument is, of course, of inestimable liturgical importance, but one cannot help regretting that it belongs unto a foreigner and a woman: the pilgrim observes only the ceremonies, the processions, how they approach to kiss the hand of the bishop, and the like, while concerning the content of divine worship she restricts herself unto the remarks: "psalms and hymns were sung," "prayers were read." Nevertheless, the order of divine worship is presented quite distinctly. The monument was published in *Pravoslavny Palestinsky Sbornik*, fascicle 20, 1889, from a transcript made directly from the manuscript itself, and provided with a Russian translation and preface (by Mr. Pomyalovsky), whence the present information concerning it is derived (pp. I–IX).

35. It is unknown whether *missa* signifies the dismissal or the Liturgy, which is designated by the pilgrim sometimes as *oblatio*, *offertur*, and rarely *sacramentum*. The designation *missa* was adopted for the Liturgy in the West either from the solemn formula of dismissal therein: "*Ite, missa est*," or from the fact that it is celebrated after the dismissal of the catechumens and forms the conclusion of long church services. If in the pilgrim's work *missa* signifies the Liturgy, then daily in the Church of Jerusalem two Liturgies were celebrated — one after Matins, and another after Vespers (on Passion Thursday and Great Saturday the pilgrim clearly indicates two Liturgies — *oblatio* — a morning and an evening one, but in different churches: *Pilgrimage* §§ 35, 38), inasmuch as the description of Vespers in the pilgrim's account likewise concludes with the words *missa fit* (the opinion concerning two Liturgies was expressed by Gamurrini, G., *S. Hilarii tractatus de mysteriis et hymni et S. Silviae Aquitanae peregrinatio*, Rome, 1887, pp. 77–78). If, however, *missa* here signifies the dismissal, then on weekdays there was no Liturgy (so thinks Waal, "Die Feste des Kirchenjahres zu Jerusalem gegen Ende des IV. Jahrhunderts," *Römische Quartalschrift für christliche Alterthumskunde und für Kirchengeschichte*, 1887, issue 4, p. 313; Krasnoseltsev, N., "Bogosluzheniye iyerusalimskoy tserkvi v kontse IV v." [Divine Worship of the Jerusalem Church at the End of the IV Century], *Pravoslavny Sobesednik*, 1888, issue 11, pp. 351, 359).

232. Concerning the acclamation **"Glory to Thee, O Lord"** before the reading of the Gospel, there are no reliable accounts from the fourth to fifth centuries. In the homily on the circus or hippodrome, formerly attributed to St. John Chrysostom, it is said: "When the deacon begins the cycle (*dromou*, δρόμου) of readings, we immediately stand up, acclaiming: **'Glory to Thee, O Lord.'**" In the Mozarabic Liturgy (the order of which has been preserved more or less unchanged from the sixth to seventh centuries), upon the announcement of the Prophecy and the Epistle the people respond: "Thanks be to God" (*Deo gratias*). In this manner, originally and in various places the acclamation **"Glory to Thee, O Lord"** or the like accompanied the reading of other scriptures as well, besides the Gospel. In the Mozarabic Liturgy and in the Rule of St. Benedict of the sixth century (ch. 11), after the reading of the Gospel the people pronounce "Amen", which, according to the explanation of other commentators, here bears the meaning: "may God grant us firmly to abide in the evangelical teaching" (Bingham, *Origines*, XIV, 82).

This collection of narratives concerning fourth-century ascetics, written by a friend of St. John Chrysostom to the imperial *praepositus sacri cubiculi* (chamberlain) Lausus, ca. 420, is one of the most precious and reliable documents on ancient monasticism. Very close to it in places is the *History of the Monks*, superscribed with the name of Rufinus, presbyter of Aquileia († 410), who was only the translator of this work by an unknown author; this monument is somewhat older than the preceding (402–404) and in places was incorporated into its composition.

330. *Lausiac History* 128 (145) and many others. St. Isidore († 491) said: "It is not so harmful for a man to eat meat as to be proud and puffed up" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Isidore 4). In other Christian lands abstinence from meat among monks was not as absolute as in Egypt; according to the words of St. Epiphanius, "some of them (the monks) abstain from all meats, both of four-footed beasts and of birds and of fish, and from eggs, and from cheese; others only from four-footed beasts and permit the consumption of birds and the rest; others abstain also from birds and use only cheese and fish; others do not partake even of fish, but only cheese; others do not eat cheese either" (*Exposition of the Faith* [*Expositio Fidei*], 23).

331. "It happened that certain fathers entered into the house of a Christ-loving man, among whom was also Abba Poemen. At table meat was set before them. All began to eat except Abba Poemen (fifth century). The elders, knowing his discretion, marvelled why he did not eat. When they arose from the table, they said to him: 'Thou art Poemen, yet what hast thou done!' The elder answered them: 'Pardon me, fathers. You ate, and no one was scandalized; but if I were to eat, many brethren coming to me would be scandalized and would begin saying: Poemen ate meat, why then should not we also eat?' And the elders marvelled at his discretion" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Poemen 170). The "fathers" who visited Theophilus, Archbishop of Alexandria, ate the veal offered to them; but when Theophilus, handing a piece of meat to the elder sitting next to him, said: "here is a good piece, eat it, abba", the elders said: "hitherto we have eaten vegetables; if this is meat, we will not eat"; and not one of them ate any more. (*The Ancient Paterikon Arranged by Chapters* IV, 75 [63]. This collection, close to the *Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, but somewhat later than it, is described by Patriarch Photius in his *Bibliotheca*, cod. 198, under the title *Book of Holy Men* [Ἀνδρῶν ἁγίων βίβλος, *Andrōn hagiōn biblos*]. It was translated into Latin in the sixth century by Pelagius and John, Roman deacons; the translation was published by H. Rosweyde, *De vitis et verbis seniorum*, Antwerp, 1628, and in Migne, *Patrologia Latina*, vol. 73, and has been preserved in Greek in an eleventh–twelfth-century manuscript of the Moscow Synodal Library, No. 782, and elsewhere. The Greek text in certain places differs from the Latin; from it a Russian translation was made, published by the Athonite St. Panteleimon Monastery, Moscow, 1891; the numeral in parentheses denotes the section according to the Latin text).

332. "Clerics forewarned Abba Simon (presumably of the fifth century, of Sinai): 'Abba, prepare thyself; a certain magistrate, having heard concerning thee, is coming to receive a blessing from thee.'—'Well, I will prepare myself,' said Simon. Putting on a *kenton* (a garment of multicoloured rags) and taking bread and cheese into his hands, the abba sat down by the doors and ate. The magistrate arrived with his retinue; seeing the elder, those who had arrived looked upon him with contempt, and said: 'Is this that hermit of whom we heard?' And they immediately departed" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Simon 2).

333. *Lausiac History* 128 (145), On Candida. St. Hor († ca. 390) and Athre tested each other's obedience by means of fish: at the wish of the latter, the former praised a spoiled boiled fish dish and declared a well-prepared fish to be bad (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Pistos).

334. "A brother asked Abba Xoi: 'If I drink three cups (*potēria*, ποτήρια) of wine, is it not too much?' The abba answered: 'If there is no devil, it is not too much'" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Xoi 1). "To Abba Xanthias, for the sake of his arduous ascetic struggle, they brought a little wine. A possessed man was brought to him. The demon began to revile the elder: 'To this wine-drinker have you brought me!' The elder did not wish to cast out the demon. But on account of his reviling, he said to him: 'I believe in Christ, that before I finish drinking this cup, thou shalt depart.' And no sooner had the elder begun to drink than the demon cried out: 'Thou burnest me, thou burnest me!' And before the elder had finished the cup, the demon departed through the operation of Christ's grace" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Xanthias 2). Even St. Sisoes did not refuse wine; but when they offered him a third cup, "the abba would not accept it and said: 'Desist, brother; or knowest thou not that there is a Satan?'" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Sisoes 8).

335. St. Hyperechios contrasts wine with meat: "It is better to eat meat and drink wine than through slander to devour the flesh of a brother" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Hyperechios 4; *Ancient Paterikon* IV, 59 [51]). When a glass of wine was brought to an elder at a festive meal, he said: "Take away from me this death" (*Ancient Paterikon* IV, 63 [53]). Peter of Pionia, a Sinaite ascetic of the fifth century, would not permit himself in old age even the slightest mingling of wine with water (*Ancient Paterikon* IV, 33 [35]). St. Paphnutius (fourth–fifth centuries), who had not drunk wine his whole life, when he drank it at the demand of a robber, thereby converted him to repentance along with his entire band (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Paphnutius 2). "Some related to Abba Poemen (fifth century) concerning a certain monk that he drank no wine; the elder answered: 'Wine is not a monastic thing at all'" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Poemen 10). St. Athanasius the Great, reproaching the monks, says: "We see bishops who drink no wine, and monks who drink" (*Epistle to Dracontius*).

336. *Lausiac History* 73 (86), and elsewhere. Water sometimes had to be gathered from dew, as with Onuphrius; *Veterum patrum analecta nova*, Venice, 1781, pp. 122–127.

337. Abba Agathon († 435) had two disciples who lived separately in the desert; one day he asked one of them: "How livest thou in thy cell?" He answered: "I fast until evening, then I eat two rusks (*paxamatia*, παξαμάτια)." The elder said to him: "Thy manner of life is good and not very difficult" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Agathon 20). St. Megethius of Sinai, a disciple of St. Sisoes and St. Poemen of Egypt, ate one loaf of bread every two days (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Megethius 2). Bread was for the most part barley bread—dry (hard biscuits, *paxamos*, πάξαμος), which can be preserved for half a year and is customarily consumed by the poor population of Egypt (St. Athanasius the Great, *Life of Anthony*, § 12); they ate it soaked in water (*Ancient Paterikon* IV, 68 [56]). Freshly baked bread, which could be had only by hermits living near villages or monasteries, was considered a luxury, and neighbours were invited to it as to a feast (*Ancient Paterikon* IV, 76 [64]). Cooked food, for the most part in the form of lentil porridge, was prepared only for guests (*Ancient Paterikon* IV, 68 [56], 69 [57]). One elder refused to eat porridge cooked from tree-buds (*myxaria*, μυξάρια) even during a severe hemorrhage (*Ancient Paterikon* IV, 77 [59]). Another "elder during an illness was visited by a brother, who prepared a cooked meal for him from his own offering and gave it to him to eat. The elder said to him: 'In truth, brother, I had forgotten that men have such consolation'" (*Ancient Paterikon* IV, 78 [66]). Concerning St. Isaac it was related that he ate his bread with ashes from the liturgical censer (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Isaac 6). St. Macarius of Alexandria († 394), "having heard that a certain monk partook of only one pound (12 ounces) of bread, resolved to imitate him: he broke up all his rusks and dropped them into a jar, making it a rule to eat no more than his hand could draw out. Cheerfully he recounted this to us (says the author of the *Lausiac History*): 'I would seize a good handful of pieces, but the narrow neck would not allow me to pull them out; my jar would not let me eat at all. For a full three years he struggled in such abstinence, eating four or five ounces of bread and drinking a corresponding amount of water" (*Lausiac History* 19).

338. Concerning St. Evagrius, deacon of Pontus († 399), it is related in the *Lausiac History*: "This blessed man said: 'From the time that I entered the desert (of Egypt), I have eaten no salad, no greens, no fresh herbs, no fruit of trees, no grapes; I have not washed my body, nor eaten meat, nor bread, nor drunk wine, nor anything prepared by fire, except certain raw vegetables and a small quantity of water. Finally, after he had lived in this manner for 16 years without partaking of cooked food, and when his body had grown weak and his stomach disordered, he felt the need of food prepared by fire, and began to eat bread; but even in the last two years he ate no cooked vegetables, unless it were cabbage and beans'" (*Lausiac History* 73 [86]). "St. Macarius of Alexandria resolved for seven years to taste nothing cooked by fire, but sustained himself solely on raw vegetables, or when it happened, on soaked beans; nothing else did he taste during those seven years; having fulfilled his vow, he nevertheless abandoned such a manner of life" (*Lausiac History* 19). Heron, a young Egyptian ascetic (a younger contemporary of Evagrius), who soon fell and repented only before his death, "often took food only once every three months, being content solely with Holy Communion of the Holy Mysteries, and if perchance a wild plant came his way" (*Lausiac History* 32 [30]).

339. St. Candida "did not consume the flesh of animals; she ate only fish, oil, and vegetables, and that only on feast days. But at all other times she was content with water mixed with vinegar, and dry bread" (*Lausiac History* 128 [145]). The above-mentioned St. Evagrius, prior to settling in the desert, lived for 14 years in the monastery of the Cells, and during all this time consumed one pound of bread a day, and in three months expended one sextarius (*xestēs*, ξέστης—one-sixth of a congius, a congius being equal to three jugs) of oil (*Lausiac History* 86 [73]). And St. Macarius in his three-year fast on bread alone expended one-sixth of a congius of oil (*Lausiac History* 19). St. Dorotheus ate six ounces of bread a day and a small bundle of herbs, and drank a little water (*Lausiac History* 2). St. Elias of Thebes in his old age ate three ounces of bread and three olives daily (*Lausiac History* 51 [46]). A certain virgin, after sixty years of enclosure, at the bidding of the local martyr Colluthus who appeared to her, came in the morning on the day of her death to a meal in his church, having taken into a basket some bread, an olive, and a few vegetables; and waiting until the ninth hour, the customary time for taking food, when no one was in the church, she partook of these viands there, returned home after praying to the martyr, and died that night (*Lausiac History* 123 [139]).

340. *Lausiac History* 123 (139) (see above). *Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Macarius of Egypt 32: two hermit brothers offer a meal to St. Macarius of Egypt who visited them only at the ninth hour; Silvanus 5: a visitor of St. Silvanus of Sinai expects at the ninth hour that he will be summoned to table. Cf. *Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Zeno 8. Among the hermits this was a general rule equally for fasting and non-fasting days. "A brother asked Abba Matois: 'What shall I do if on a fast day, or at dawn, a brother comes to me? This troubles me.' The elder answered him: 'If without qualm of conscience thou eatest with thy brother, thou doest well; but if thou art expecting no one to visit thee, and yet eatest—in that is thine own self-will'" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Matois 6). But in monasteries, especially in later coenobia, the taking of food not earlier than the ninth hour was made a rule only for fasting days: *Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Matois 5; *Ancient Paterikon* IX, 16, 12; X, 37 (30). The following passage from the *Ancient Paterikon* hardly argues in favour of earlier eating: "A certain brother hungered one morning and struggled with his thought so as not to eat until the third hour; when the third hour arrived, he resolved to endure until the sixth hour; when the sixth hour came, he soaked his bread, and having sat down to eat, he stood up again and said: 'I will endure until the ninth hour'; the ninth hour also came, and the elder, having made prayer, saw the power of the devil departing like smoke from his bosom; and so his hunger passed" (IV, 70 [58]). No more does the following incident concerning St. Sisoes argue for taking food on non-fasting days in the morning or during the day: he persuaded Adelphius, Bishop of Nicopolis, who visited him, along with his companions, to partake of food for the road in the morning. Now this occurred during a fast. When the meal was set before them, behold, brethren knocked at the door; Abba Sisoes said to his disciple: "Give them a little porridge, they are weary." "Leave it," Abba Adelphius said to him, "lest they say that Abba Sisoes eats from the morning" (in general, and all the more so during a fast?). It turned out that the brethren who knocked begged that Sisoes should not be forced to take food, lest he should subsequently exhaust himself with several days of fasting on account of it (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Sisoes 13).

St. Arsenius († 450) "passed the whole night in vigil, and when towards morning nature compelled him to sleep, he would say to sleep: 'Come hither, wicked servant', and having slept a little while sitting, he immediately arose" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Arsenius 14). He used to say that for a monk, if he is an ascetic, it is enough to sleep for one hour (*ibid.* 15). St. Bessarion († 466) "did not lie down upon his side for forty years, but slept sitting or standing" (*Sayings of the Holy Fathers*, Bessarion 8). "God is witness", recounts Palladius concerning St. Dorotheus of Thebes, "I never saw him stretch out his feet, or lie down to sleep upon a mat or upon a bed; all night long he would sit and plait ropes. And from his youth he lived in this way for sixty years; he never lay down to sleep, but only while working or at table would he close his eyes for a few minutes, so that a morsel would sometimes fall from his mouth while drowsing" (*Lausiac History* 2).

393. Written rules, however, have also come down to us under the name of St. Anthony. Benedict of Aniane (ninth century) cites them in his *Codex Regularum*; in a somewhat different recension they were discovered in an Arabic manuscript in the seventeenth century (both recensions are published in Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 40; Russian translation in *Khristianskoye Chteniye*, 1880, part 37). But the authenticity of these rules is questionable, because St. Athanasius and Bl. Jerome make no mention of them, and because written rules for monks would conflict with St. Anthony's general view of asceticism; moreover, the rules are permeated with an entirely different spirit from that of St. Anthony. They do not reflect the theological views of St. Anthony (demonology, polemics against the Arians); and they presuppose an order of monastic life far too complex for the era of Anthony: subordination to the superior, a church building, assemblies of the brethren, monastic lands, and a monastic habit endowed with symbolic significance, etc. The "Rules" represent a compilation of the monastic rules of St. Pachomius, Isaiah, and others, interwoven with the thoughts of St. Anthony. Lobachevsky, *St. Anthony*, pp. 168 ff.

423. Under such a mode of life, the absolute non-possessiveness in the monastery is not surprising: "A certain nobleman from some country brought with him much gold and asked the presbyter of Scetis to distribute it to the brethren. The presbyter said: 'The brethren have no need.' But since he urged the presbyter persistently, the latter placed the basket by the church doors and said: 'Whoever has need, let him take.' Yet no one approached it, and others paid no attention to it whatever. Then the presbyter said: 'God has accepted your alms; go and distribute it to the poor'" (*Ancient Paterikon* VI, 23 [19]).

For I have seen a brother who eats with you and drinks of the same cups with you, and his prayer ascends like fire unto heaven.'"

425. A brother asked Abba Sisoes (who had begun his ascetic life in Scetis): "What should I do? When I go to church, so often there is a love-feast, and they constrain me to stay." The elder said to him: "It is a difficult matter!" Abraham, his disciple, also asked him: "If it should happen that there is a love-feast on a Saturday or a Sunday and a brother drinks three cups (*potēria*, ποτήρια, that is, of wine), would that be too much?" The elder replied: "If Satan were not there, it would not be much" (*Ancient Paterikon* IV, 45 [37]).

426. Abba Serenus thus entertained Cassian and Germanus (ca. 390–400) in Scetis after the Sunday service: "In place of brine (*muria*, probably salted water, from *mare*, the sea), which was offered daily with the addition of a drop of oil, he prepared a little broth (*liquaminis*), pouring into it slightly more oil than usual; for that small amount of oil is added daily by each (a relaxation of the former regime?), not to provide any gratification to the palate, since so little is poured that it is scarcely enough—I do not say to lubricate—even to pass down the throat, but in order to suppress by this practice the vanity of the heart. Then he offered three olives each, seasoned with salt. After that he brought a small basket with parched chickpeas (*cicer frictum*), which they call dessert (*trogalia*), from which we took only six grains (*grana*) each, two plums (*mixaria*), and one dry fig (*caricas*); to take more than this number is considered reprehensible in that desert" (Cassian, *Conferences* VIII, 1).

430. P. Kazansky, *History of Orthodox Monasticism in the East*, part 2 (Moscow, 1865), p. 152. The structure of life in these three principal monasteries of ancient Christian Egypt was so simple that it could not be determined by a written rule. Therefore, on both external and internal grounds, one must recognize as spurious the rules for monks allegedly established by an assembly of four Nitrian and Scetiote fathers—Serapion, the two Macarii, and Paphnutius (Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 34, cols. 971–978), the collection of which is divided into four parts, each part being attributed to one of these fathers. The most characteristic of these rules: "Let there be one superior over all the brethren: let no one turn aside from his counsel and command, but let him obey him with joy as God Himself. In the church assembly, no one may begin the chanting of the psalms without the command of the superior; if the superior delays, let him be notified and act according to his direction. Those entering the monastery are to lie before the gates for a full week. From the first hour until the third, time is consecrated to God; from the third to the ninth, to labor. All things found in the monastery—vessels, tools, and the rest—are holy. A visiting cleric, even of inferior rank, begins the prayers at divine worship."

459. Sozomen: "The rules permitted each to eat and drink, to work and to fast or not to fast, as much as each was able; and upon those who ate more, it was commanded to impose heavier labors, but upon the ascetics, lighter ones." Dionysius: "Permit each to eat and drink according to his strength, and compel them to work according to the measure of their nourishment; forbid neither moderate eating nor fasting; assign heavier labors to the stronger and those who eat, and lighter ones to the weaker and those who practice abstinence." Arabic: "Permit each to eat and drink whatever he requires; do not hinder them from fasting, but leave this to their discretion; and give to those who are robust in body heavy and burdensome tasks, but to those who are frail and devout, light and unburdensome ones." In the Arabic this rule occupies the second place, while the first is concerning cells (which comes next in the Greek *Lausiac History*).

Arabic: "do not receive a brother coming from another monastery if he has acquired customs different from yours; but receive strangers, comfort them, and show mercy to the poor in a special place in your monastery, yet so as not to eat or drink with them."

476. Sozomen: "to pray twelve times every day, and as many in the evening and as many at night, and at the ninth hour three times; moreover, before partaking of food, to precede prayer by the chanting of a psalm." Dionysius: "the daytime prayers (*diurnae orationes*) must be twelve, and the evening twelve, and the nighttime twelve." Arabic: "let each of the brethren perform twelve prayers during the day; and at the evening hour, when they assemble to take food, let each of them perform three prayers before eating, and six before sleeping, and with every prayer a psalm. Let them sleep half the night, and let them spend the other half keeping vigil, for continuous prayer and the glorification of God."

477. Arabic: "these prayers are not too few for those who have spent but a short time in such a life, lest prayer become wearisome to them."

478. Dionysius: "abiding in their cells, they pray without ceasing." Arabic: "and I know that their days and nights will be employed in accordance with the laws of God."

479. Let us recall this practice as described on pp. 202–210, and we can see that each rule, as it were, lowers its individual requirements by several degrees. From this point of view, the rule concerning sleep will not appear petty either (see Troitsky, *Survey of the Sources for the Early History of Egyptian Monasticism*, p. 62); instead of sleeping in a standing or sitting posture, sleep in a reclining posture is permitted. Most singular appears the rule regarding the division of the monks into classes according to the number of letters in the Greek alphabet. This rule may be viewed as a distinctive poetic (with mystical coloring) depiction of the pastoral care of the superior of the monastery for the brethren.

480. See above, p. 139.

481. The Arabic recension of the rule specifies the number of prayers only in place of the Liturgy with its Hours ("daytime prayers"), the Ninth Hour ("before meals"), and Vespers ("before sleep"), assigning for each service a number of prayers proportional to its importance: 12, 6, 3; whereas it defines the nighttime service not by a quantity of prayers, but by their duration: half the night.

482. Cassian, *Institutes of the Coenobia* II, 7.

484. The not entirely clear expression concerning this latter "prayer" probably bears this meaning: if the meal on a given day is not communal, but separate for each "order" or class of monks, for each monastic house, then before it one psalm is chanted with prayer; but if it is communal, for several orders (houses), then as many psalms with prayer are chanted as there are such "orders" participating in the meal. In this manner the meal was preceded by a service not different in structure from other services; compare among us the Order of the Panagia; see the explanation of Typikon Chapter II, end.

According to Sozomen, the beginning of asceticism in Syria was established by a certain Aon, a contemporary of the Emperor Valens (364–370): "they say that this Aon in Syria, like Anthony in Egypt, before all men laid the foundation of strict philosophy" (*Ecclesiastical History* III, 14). But nowadays it is demonstrated that even earlier—prior to 325—St. James, Bishop of Nisibis, practiced asceticism here, and there even existed, apparently, entire monastic communities under the name "sons of the covenant". Hieromonk Anatoly, *On the Origin and Beginning of Syrian Monasticism*, in *Trudy Kievskoy Dukhovnoy Akademii* (1910), no. 4, p. 393.

554. Thus St. Baradatus "fashioned out of wood a small box disproportionate to his body, and lived in it constantly in a bent posture" (Bl. Theodoret, *A History of the Monks of Syria* [*Philotheos Historia*], ch. 27 [Ἡ φιλόθεος ἱστορία]; Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 82; Russian translation, St. Petersburg, 1853: the work consists of biographies of all the Syrian ascetics known to the author and contemporary with him [† 456]). Likewise St. Marcian (*ibid.* 3). St. Eusebius placed an iron chain around his neck and fastened it to a similar cincture around his waist, so that "being bent in this manner, he was constantly of necessity looking toward the earth" (*ibid.* 4).

555. St. James, a contemporary of Bl. Theodoret, "had neither hut nor tent, refused to use the shelter of a tree, but lived in a completely open field, where rain drenched him, snow covered him, frost froze him, and the sun burned him" (*ibid.* 21). So also lived many Syrian ascetics (*ibid.* 27).

556. St. Salaman (late fourth century) lived in a "refuge" without windows or entrance, into which one could crawl only beneath the wall, and he crept out of it once a year to make a provision of food (*ibid.* 19).

557. St. Thalalaeus, a contemporary of Bl. Theodoret, "made two wheels two cubits in diameter and fastened them together with planks separated from one another by considerable intervals; then, having fixed three long poles in the ground and joined their upper ends with planks, he suspended on them the aforementioned dwelling of two wheels and planks, and took up residence therein; and since the interior space of the dwelling has a height of only 2 cubits, and in width one, whereas the blessed man is very tall of stature, he sits there not in an upright posture, but constantly bent over and with his head inclined to his knees" (*ibid.* 28).

The author of *Historical Dissertation on the Fasts of the Orthodox Eastern Catholic Church* (Moscow, 1837) (Hieromonk Alexy Soloviev) suspects the testimonies of Socrates and Sozomen concerning the varying duration and timing of the pre-Paschal fast of inaccuracy and even of intentional distortion of the truth, explaining the latter by sympathy toward Novatianism: "they could not have been pleased with the positive ordinances of the Church; hence it certainly arose that it was deemed necessary intentionally and with effort to search out differences in the rites of the Church, and therein to mingle half-truth with truth or with falsehood" (p. 17). Yet of the Church's ordinances, a forty-day fast would least of all have displeased the Novatians, the Christian rigorists of that day.

681. Bingham, *Origines Ecclesiasticae*, XXI, 214. In confirmation of this, Bingham adduces the following accounts from Sozomen and Eusebius. To St. Spyridon of Trimythous "someone came from a journey during the Forty Days, when he was fasting with his household and ate food only on a designated day, while on the remaining days he went without nourishment. Seeing that the traveler was very weary, he said to his daughter: 'Wash this man’s feet and set food before him.' When the maiden answered that there was neither bread nor flour, since a store thereof by reason of the fast would have been superfluous, he first prayed and asked forgiveness, and then ordered his daughter to roast some pork that happened to be in the house. And when it was roasted, Spyridon, seating the traveler with himself, began to eat the meat set before them and urged the man to imitate him. When the latter, calling himself a Christian, refused, he added: 'All the less ought you to refuse, for the word of God (Tit. 1:15) hath declared: unto the pure all things are pure'" (Sozomen, *Ecclesiastical History* I, 11). To the martyr Attalus there was a revelation concerning his fellow-martyr Alcibiades, who ate nothing except bread and water, that he "was not doing well in not partaking of the creatures of God, and thereby giving an occasion of stumbling to others" (Eusebius, *Ecclesiastical History* V, 3).

754. Since the lunar year is 11 and 1/4 days shorter than the solar year, among those employing lunar reckoning (the Semites) an addition of an extra month to the year is made from time to time; to balance both reckonings it is necessary within 8 lunar years to make 3 intercalary months. The supplementary month among the Hebrews was attached to the last month of the year, Adar (corresponding to February), and was called "Veadar", "another Adar". But in that era such intercalations were not regulated and depended on the arbitrary discretion of influential rabbis. And if the intercalation was not made in timely fashion, Pascha fell before spring. In the Talmud there is preserved an epistle of Rabbi Gamaliel (the teacher of the Apostle Paul) to Babylon and Media: "We inform you that since the doves (for sacrifice) are still too tender and the lambs too young, and the time of Aviv (= Nisan, the first spring month) hath not yet arrived, we have, in agreement with our colleagues, deemed it necessary to add 30 days to the year" (Kellner, *Heortologie*, 34). For this reason a special announcement of the arrival of Passover was required every year. During the existence of the Sanhedrin, it dispatched special messengers annually throughout all Palestine with notification as to from which day the beginning of the month of Nisan was to be reckoned and upon which day Passover fell; and in order to make this known also to the Euphrates Jews, fires were kindled at the Nisan new moon upon the Mount of Olives and following it upon other mountains right up to Babylonia itself: V. Rybinsky, *On Pilgrimage to Jerusalem in Biblical Times*, in *Trudy Kievskoy Dukhovnoy Akademii* (1909), no. 11, p. 499.

793. For the feast on the 40th day after Pascha no mention is made of such a Gospel or in general of a celebration of the Ascension. It may be that the Ascension and the Descent of the Holy Spirit were celebrated together at Pentecost. In general these two feasts were not yet separated everywhere. Thus the Council of Elvira (305) decrees: "an erroneous custom must be corrected in accordance with the testimony of the Scriptures, and all must celebrate the day of Pentecost; otherwise whoever faileth to do so shall show himself to be the introducer of a new heresy" (Canon 43). An ancient *epitome* (abbreviated collection) of this Council renders this canon thus: "after Pascha let the 50th day be observed, and not the 40th" (Mansi, *Sacrorum Conciliorum Nova et Amplissima Collectio*, II, 13). Perhaps the Montanists, who thought that only in Montanus did the Holy Spirit first appear on earth, were opposed to the celebration of Pentecost: C. Hefele, *Conciliengeschichte* (Freiburg im Breisgau, 1855), I, 145.

816. The latest and most complete edition is in *Monumenta Germaniae Historica*, *Auctores Antiquissimi*, vol. IX, part 1, fasc. 1 (Berlin, 1891). The principal sections of the collection are: *Natales Caesarum* (birthdays of the Caesars), *Fasti Consulares* (official court calendar) for the year 354, the Paschalion of 312–358 continued by a later hand down to 410, the list of Roman prefects down to 354, *Depositio Episcoporum*—the death days of Roman bishops from 255 to 352, *Depositio Martyrum*—the burial days of Roman martyrs, and a calendar of pagan feasts written and artistically executed by Furius Dionysius Filocalus (according to catacomb inscriptions, the calligrapher of Pope Damasus). The collection, embellished also with many illustrations (portraits of Caesars, views of cities), probably constituted a reference manual for an imperial dignitary; it is preserved in a seventh–eighth century manuscript: Kellner, *Heortologie*, 92.

819. Differently Kellner, *Heortologie*, 99. Various explanations are given as to what caused the separation of the feast of the Nativity of Christ from the Theophany. It is thought that the cessation of martyrdom played a role here in part, allowing earthly life and its beginning to be valued more highly; perhaps there was a desire to counterpose the Christian feast to the pagan festivals commemorating the December solstice. In Rome the Saturnalia was celebrated on December 18–23; corresponding to the somber character of the god Saturn or Cronus (who devoured his own children), this was a mournful celebration accompanied by gladiatorial combats (St. Cyril of Alexandria, *Against Julian*, 4); after it followed the joyful festival of the "unconquered sun" (*Sol Invictus*), celebrated with particular splendor by Emperor Julian in honor of the rising sun and on the threshold of the new year, falling at the time when the solstice was already becoming noticeable to all (Emperor Julian, *Oration 4*). In the aforementioned Roman calendar of Filocalus under December 25 it is indicated: "*N(atalis) Invicti*"—"birth of the unconquered": "unconquered" was the customary epithet of the gods, especially fitting in relation to the newly dawning sun (it is possible, however, that the birthday of the reigning emperor was so named in this calendar, since in other months the calendar indicates the birthdays of the emperors—Smirnov, F. [Bishop Christopher], *The Origin and Significance of the Feast of the Nativity of Christ*, Kyiv, 1883 [printed: 1833], pp. 92 ff.)). In Alexandria on December 25 there was the pagan festival of the Kikellia; festivals also took place at that season in other countries. The conjecture has been expressed that the institution of the feast on December 25 may also have been influenced by the Jewish feast of the Dedication of the Temple (Hanukkah) on the 25th day of the month of Kislev (= December), to which indications are found in the prophets Haggai (2:15–18) and Zechariah (2:10; 8:14 [printed: (:, 14]; cf. John 10:22), and that moreover in connection with messianic prophecies (Smirnov, F., *ibid.*, pp. 59 ff.).—When the feast of the Nativity of Christ was assigned to December 25, that day came to be regarded as the day of the event itself. Prior to that, the question of the day of the Savior’s birth had been disputed. We have seen that Clement of Alexandria points out, apparently, three opinions existing in his time concerning the day of the Savior’s birth: some assigned it to the 25th of Pachon (an Egyptian month, = May 20), others to the 15th or [printed: "ио"] 11th of Tybi (January 10 or 6). Cf. above the opinion of St. Epiphanius of Cyprus. In the third–fourth century work *De Pascha computus* [printed: *cimputus*], ascribed to St. Cyprian, the day of the Nativity of Christ is held to be March 28, and in the inscription on the statue of St. Hippolytus of Rome—March 25. In the portion of the commentary of St. Hippolytus on the book of the prophet Daniel recently discovered by Georgiades (on Chalki), there is the remark: "The first manifestation of the Lord in the flesh, wherein He was born in Bethlehem, took place on December 25, in the 42nd year of Augustus, 5500 years from Adam; and He suffered on March 25, on a Friday, in the 18th year of Tiberius, in the consulate of Rufus and Rubellius"; but in other fragments of that same commentary (for example, in an ancient manuscript in the Chigi Library) and in the quotation of this passage by the Armenian bishop George dating from 714, the day of the month is not indicated here, nor is it required by the context of the commentary (Kellner, *Heortologie*, 98). Only in the fourth and fifth centuries did they begin decisively to defend the date of December 25 for the Nativity of Christ—St. Chrysostom (see below) and Blessed Augustine (*Sermons* 190, 1; 192, 3; 196, 1).

850. Under Roman law, earthly justice was fully satisfied by the death of the criminal, and his corpse was permitted to be given for burial to whoever requested it: *corpora animadversorum quibuslibet petentibus ad sepulturam danda sunt* (*Digesta* 48, tit. 24, no. 3), except in cases where this was dangerous to public tranquility; but this latter restriction was scarcely ever applied before Diocletian: Kellner, *Heortologie*, 131.

851. They were kept by a secretary (*notarius*, *commentariensis*, *exceptor*) of the proconsul or procurator, and in them were recorded the accusation, the interrogation, the depositions of witnesses under torture [printed: "пытки", misread by OCR as "пятки"], and the sentence. Copies of these acts could be obtained for a fee. Several such records have reached us in their authentic form; best known are the *Acta proconsularia Sancti Cypriani*, the renowned Bishop of Carthage († 258); commemoration August 31 (Ruinart, *Acta Martyrum*, II, 46, 47).

852. The oldest and most famous of such records (called for the most part *passiones*) is the Epistle of the Church of Lyons and Vienne to Asia Minor concerning their martyrs. *Passio Sanctae Perpetuae et Felicitatis* (African martyrs, † 203, commemoration February 1).

853. According to the account in the *Liber Pontificalis*, Pope St. Clement I (91–100) divided Rome into seven regions (perhaps corresponding to the fourteen administrative wards into which Augustus had divided Rome) and appointed for each region a Christian "notary" "who should diligently and zealously investigate in his area the deeds (*gesta*) of the martyrs," that is, all that took place with the martyrs in the prisons, at the tribunal, and at executions; Pope Fabian (236–251) subordinated these notaries to seven subdeacons, so that the latter might examine the acts drawn up by the former and present them for confirmation to the Pope, after which they were preserved in the ecclesiastical archive (*Liber Pontificalis*, ed. Duchesne, pp. 52, 65, 148). Particular care for the acts of the martyrs is also noted in Pope Anterus (235–236) (*ibid.*, pp. 95, 147). St. Cyprian, Bishop of Carthage, during the Decian and Valerian persecutions sent out priests and deacons across the province both to encourage the martyrs and to bury them, and likewise in order that they might record the names and the day of death of the martyrs for the celebration of their commemorations (St. Cyprian, *Epistle* 12, 2).

854. This calendar is frequently called Bucherian after the name of its editor, Aegidius Bucher (Gilles Bucher, Antwerp, 1633; so also in Archbishop Sergius, *Complete Menology of the East*, I, 40).

858. On the grounds that it contains a commemoration of "Arius, Presbyter of Alexandria" and Eusebius of Caesarea, and contains no commemorations of the Fathers of the Council of Nicaea, and that the calendar was compiled in a period and region where Arianism held sway, Western scholars almost unanimously regard it as Arian (Duchesne, Egli, Kellner). Against this it is objected (Bickell, Bolotov) that Arius here is a martyr, and such a martyr and presbyter existed in Alexandria; that there is no commemoration of Eusebius of Nicomedia (an Arian, whereas Eusebius of Caesarea was a semi-Arian); and that there is a commemoration of James of Nisibis, a participant in the Council of Nicaea (Bolotov, V., "Traces of the Ancient Calendars of Local Churches," *Khristianskoye Chteniye*, 1893, I, 177 ff.). In the calendar, apparently, some martyrs are entered several times; there are errors in the names of saints, for example, instead of Sixtus—Axitus, and especially in the names of cities; the greatest error, if only it be an error, is that by comparison with the pseudo-Hieronymian calendar the commemorations of June 8–30 have been transferred to the same dates of July (Kellner, *Heortologie*, 196 f.).

867. "With regard to hierarchs or holy hierarchs, it must with great probability be accepted that originally they were numbered among the saints or canonized in the same manner as martyrs, that is, *eo ipso* or by the very fact that they were hierarchs, and that later they began to be canonized in the same manner as ascetics, whom the Church recognized as saints not by reason of their belonging to a specific class, but because personally she deemed this or that one worthy of this recognition. Symeon of Thessalonica says that in Constantinople 'in the great Church of the Apostles, the bishops who had reposed from ancient times were laid within the sanctuary, like the relics of saints, for the sake of the grace of the divine priesthood' (*De ordine sepulturae*, cap. 364; Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 155, col. 677 [printed: *sepulrurae*]). Turning to the Greek calendar adopted among us, we find that the Patriarchs of Constantinople, beginning from the first, Metrophanes (315–325), down to Eustathius (1019–1025), are almost all numbered among the saints, with the exception of those among them who were heretics, certain of those among them who did not remain upon the throne until death, but in their lifetime abandoned it or were removed from it, and finally those among them who led a notoriously corrupt life; of the 74 Patriarchs of Constantinople down to 1025, 18 were heretics. Of the remaining 56—49 are saints (of the remainder, nothing is known of one, one abandoned the throne, two were removed, one occupied the throne dishonorably, two wavered between Orthodoxy and heresies). It is remarkable withal that the patriarchs of other cities in the present calendar are far from all included. This must be understood in the sense that when the individual calendars of each local church (diocese) were replaced by the general calendar of the whole Greek Church, the Patriarchs of Constantinople entered therein in the full number in which they were found in the local Constantinopolitan calendar, while the patriarchs and bishops of other churches entered according to a very limited selection, wherein the criterion served on the one hand by their greater or lesser ecclesiastical significance, and on the other by the greater or lesser renown of their personal holiness" (Golubinsky, E., *History of the Canonization of Saints in the Russian Church*, in *Readings in the Imperial Society of Russian History and Antiquities*, Moscow, 1903, pp. 16–18, 13, 377).

These fasts were a Christian transformation of the Roman pagan festivals associated with different seasons of the agricultural year: *feriae sementivae*—the feast of sowing; *feriae messis*—the feast of harvest; *feriae vindemiales*—the feast of the vintage. (For Christian antiquity, fast and feast were almost synonymous, for which reason the word *feriae* came to signify in the Roman Church first a fast, and later a weekday; in the Church of Jerusalem the Forty Days was called *heortae* [ἑορταί]—feasts: *Pilgrimage of Silvia*, § 27).

The name *Bessoi* (*βέσсоι*), who are mentioned by Cyril of Scythopolis also in the *Life of St. Sabas* (namely, that the Bessoi of the Jordan defended the Orthodox and the Laura of St. Sabas in Jerusalem), was borne by a Thracian tribe, many of whom lived in Palestine in the fifth and sixth centuries. Georgian scholars argue that this word is a corruption of *Iberes* (*ἰβῆρες*), Iberians, Georgians, who are indicated in the Laura of St. Sabas by the *Life* of the latter: Bishop Theodosius, *Monasteries of Palestine*, 101.

All these "Rules" in their parts concerning divine worship are adduced, at times in an explanatory paraphrase (especially unclear are the rules of Columbanus), in Martène, *De Antiquis Ecclesiae Ritibus*, III, 11 sq., and published in full in Migne, *Patrologia Latina*, vols. 66 (Benedict and both unknown ones: *Alia regula incerti auctoris* [printed: *anctoris*], cols. 996–998, and *Regula cujusdam patris*, cols. 987–994), 67 (Caesarius), 68 (Aurelian), 80 (Columbanus), 83 (Isidore), 87 (Donatus and Fructuosus), and 88 (*Magister*).

51. At the psalms "the lesser antiphons with their alleluiatics (*alleluiaticis*)..." "After Pascha until Pentecost on Fridays they refresh themselves (*reficiendum*) once, and after the 12th hour there take place six *missae*, that is, 18 readings must be recited by heart, and then 18 psalms, 3 antiphons; and after the nocturn there must be 3 *missae* from the book until daybreak." This obscure passage of Caesarius must prescribe, throughout the entire period of Pentecost on Friday evenings going into Saturday, especially long vigils from 6 p.m. on Friday without supper until the very dawn of Saturday (cf. in Cassian, above, p. 162), wherein the customary vigil of 18 psalms was preceded by 18 readings and followed by another 3 readings. All this is in *Regula ad virgines*, § 66. More briefly Caesarius describes the nocturnal service in *Regula ad monachos*: "The vigils from October until Pascha consist of two nocturns and three missae (readings): at one missa a brother reads three leaves and pray; he reads another three leaves and stands up; say an antiphon, a responsory, and another antiphon; and the antiphons are according to the order of the Psalter; at the first missa the reading is concerning the Resurrection, and during it all stand" (rule 21).
