Celebrating the Resurrection, we simultaneously perform the 'divine and all-honorable' festival of the Mother of God, and Sunday is dedicated, together with the Saviour, to the honoring of His Mother, just as other days of the week are dedicated to other saints. Occurring frequently, the celebration of Sunday cannot so completely absorb the prayerful attention of the believer as do rare feasts, such as the Twelve Great Feasts, the offices of which are therefore entirely occupied with the celebrated event (in those services there are therefore no Theotokia even at 'Both now'). Constituting the subject of independent glorification in the Sunday service alongside Her Son, the Mother of God in all the hymns dedicated to Her on Sunday is praised not in connection with the Resurrection (as, for example, in the Theotokia of the Paschal canon: **"Beholding Thy Son risen..."**), but from a gen*(Orig. p. 483)*eral point of view. So it is also in the present stichera. Specifically, the aposticha of Little Vespers now glorify the Mother of God, depicting a picture of the benefactions received by us through Her, now contain sorrowful, penitential supplications unto Her. At the same time, in the stichera of certain tones the first theme predominates, in others the second, but in the majority these themes alternate and are even combined within one and the same sticheron; the stichera of Tone 8 bear the most laudatory character (being composed of a series of 'Rejoice' acclamations); those of Tone 2 are the most sorrowful; at times (for example, Tone 5) the first sticheron is sorrowful, while the remainder are laudatory. The refrains to the stichera are those verses of Psalm 44 [LXX 44 / MT 45] that serve as refrains for the aposticha of the majority of feasts of the Mother of God (for example, the Nativity of the Theotokos): **"I shall remember Thy name..."** [v. 18 / MT 17]; **"Hear, O daughter, and see..."** [v. 11 / MT 10]; **"The rich among the people shall entreat Thy face..."** [v. 13 / MT 12]. As the sticheron at 'Glory... both now...', as in the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**, there serves a 'Dogmatikon', consequently, a sticheron of more exalted content than those preceding it, and devoid of mournful themes.

## Troparion, Litany, and Dismissal

Following the aposticha at Little Vespers there immediately follows **"Now lettest Thou Thy servant depart"** (*Ныне отпущаеши* / *Nunc dimittis*), the Trisagion with the **"Our Father"**, the Sunday troparion with its Theotokion, and an abbreviated augmented litany (termed the 'Little Augmented Litany') consisting of 4 petitions: the initial (introductory), the petition for the Reigning House (without specifying the objects of petition), for the Holy Synod and the local Ruling Hierarch; while all the remaining petitions of the augmented litany are united in the concise: **"Again we pray for all the brethren and for all Christians"** (which is why the petition for the Holy Synod is without the addition: 'and for all our brethren in Christ'). This litany occupies at Little Vespers the same place as the augmented litany at Daily Vespers, that is, the very end of the service, as its most solemn part. An identical litany and in the same position is found in the initial, 'Royal' section of Matins.

From thence it was borrowed into Little Vespers, since this portion of Matins, as we shall see, is more ancient than Little Vespers. In turn, into that portion of Matins the litany was borrowed, probably, from the ancient *pannychis* (*παννυχίς*), an office that preceded Matins and for the most part consisted of: Psalm 50 [LXX 50 / MT 51], the canon, the Trisagion, and this litany, like the present service before the Paschal Matins, where there is likewise such a litany.

Little Vespers concludes with a Little Dismissal, like the Hours, Compline, and Midnight Office, and with the Polychronion (*Mnogolietie*, **"The Most Pious, Autocratic..."**), as does every Vespers.

## Alterations in the Order from the Concurrence of Commemorations

The rich content of Little Vespers becomes still more varied when there coincides on Sunday any Great Feast or even a Medium (Polyeleos) feast. In that case the festal aposticha from Great Vespers, at which they cannot be chanted on account of the Sunday stichera, are transferred unto Little Vespers. Thus, if a Great Feast of the Mother of God *(Orig. p. 484)* or the Meeting of the Lord (*Hypapante*) coincides with Sunday, their aposticha can be heard only at Little Vespers.

In the case of such a concurrence (of a feast, or of a great or polyeleos saint) with Sunday, Little Vespers undergoes also a series of other alterations in its composition. These alterations concern the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**, the aposticha, and the troparion. At Little Vespers—though not on Sunday—there may even be a paremia (if the Meeting of the Lord coincides with Cheesefare Saturday). All these deviations of Sunday Little Vespers from its usual (set forth above) composition will be discussed in the rubrics for feasts whose concurrence with Sunday induces such alterations.

# THE EVENING REFECTORY

## Liturgical Character of the Refectory

According to the commandment of the Apostle: **"Whether therefore ye eat, or drink, or whatsoever ye do, do all to the glory of God"** [1 Cor. 10:31] [^1971], the Orthodox Church regards even the partaking of food as divine worship, in essence not differing from other church services. Therefore, among the rank of the latter, she possesses a special 'order' (*chin*), or church office of the refectory, which is why meals in monasteries are served in a church (a special refectory temple, *trapeznaya tserkov'*).

The view of the taking of food, or the refectory, as divine worship goes back to the Old Testament Church. There, one of the kinds of sacrifice, namely the so-called peace offering, concluded with a sacred meal from its remnants, which was held in the temple itself, in its outer court, where for this purpose there were special rooms, and even kitchens [^1972]. And among the early Christians, scarcely any meal was not Eucharistic [^1973].

## Two Meals

The Typikon of the Church (as also monastic practice in general) recognizes only two meals: the first after the Liturgy, and the second after Vespers (for fasting days, however—only one, after Vespers). The midday meal, as the principal one, has a more elaborate liturgical order, which, in view of the fact that it includes a special rite over the prosphora of the Mother of God (*Panagia*), is called the *Order of the Panagia* (*chin o panagii*). The order of the evening meal constitutes an abbreviation of this Order of the Panagia, the order of the midday meal.

*(Orig. p. 485)*
## The Order of the Evening Meal

Upon entering the refectory (it being presupposed—directly from church following Vespers), there is read ('we say') the verse from Psalm 21:27 [LXX 21:27 / MT 22:26]: **"The poor shall eat and be satisfied, and they shall praise the Lord (preeminently for being satisfied) that seek Him; their hearts shall live unto the ages of ages"** (*Ядят убозии и насытятся...*), that is, the soul is enlivened forever by the Lord, as the body is for a time by nourishment. By this prayer the attention of those approaching the refectory is directed toward spiritual food, and thanksgiving is offered unto the Lord for the granting of the refectory even prior to partaking thereof. (This verse replaces the reading of the entire Psalm 144 [LXX 144 / MT 145] with the **"Our Father"**, appointed at the beginning of the midday meal). After the verse, the blessing of the priest is requested in the customary manner: **"Glory... both now... Lord, have mercy"** (three times), **"Bless"** (in the same manner the priest's blessing is requested for leaving the temple before the dismissal). **"And the priest blesses the refectory"**; in what words is not specified here (in Chapter 1 of the Typikon), but is indicated in the order of the midday meal ('On the Panagia') in Chapter 2 of the Typikon: **"O Christ God, bless the food and drink of Thy servants..."** (for the conclusion see the Sequenced Psalter [*Sledovannaya Psaltir'*]: **"for holy art Thou always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen"**).

Concerning the meal itself, it is remarked: **"we partake lightly of that which is set before us, that we may not be weighed down for the vigil."** Thanksgiving after the refectory is offered unto the Most Holy Trinity by the Little Doxology (as also at the midday meal), and then unto the Most Holy Theotokos by the troparia **"Thy womb hath become a holy table"** (*Бысть чрево Твое святая трапеза*, in place of **"It is truly meet"** at the midday meal) and **"More honorable"** (*Честнейшую*). Then (in place of Ps. 121 [LXX 121 / MT 122]: **"I was glad when they said unto me"**, appointed at the midday meal) there is read an excerpt from Psalm 91:5 and Psalm 4:8–10 [LXX 91:5; 4:8–10 / MT 92:4; 4:7–8]: **"Thou hast made us glad, O Lord..."** (*Возвеселил ны еси Господи...*), containing the glorification of God for being satisfied and a prayerful hope for peaceful sleep. All the remaining prayers of the Order of the Panagia, even those not directly pertaining to the Panagia, are omitted in this brief order of the refectory (for example, the Trisagion with the **"Our Father"**, the prayer **"We thank Thee, O Christ our God"**, the troparia **"O God of our fathers"** and **"By the prayers, O Lord, of all the saints"**); and immediately after **"Thou hast made us glad, O Lord"** the priest's blessing for dismissal is requested in the customary manner: **"Glory... both now... Lord, have mercy"** (three times), **"Bless"**. The dismissal likewise differs from the Order of the Panagia: (in place of: **"Blessed is God Who showeth mercy and nourisheth us"**)—**"God is with us by His grace and love toward mankind, always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen"** (more suitable for nocturnal time; cf. at Great Compline **"God is with us"**). Thus, almost all the prayers of the evening refectory are distinct from the midday meal, but the very structure, the liturgical order of both is the same, excluding the rite of the elevation of the Panagia.

## History

In the earliest Typika, the order of the evening meal differed almost not at all from the midday meal; at it there likewise occurred the elevation of the dish *(Orig. p. 486)* with fragments (*ukrukhi*, corresponding to the Panagia). Thus in the Studite Typikon of Patriarch Athanasius of the 12th c. [^1974] and in the Typikon of the Pantokrator Monastery of 1136 [^1975]. The principal distinction of the evening refectory from the midday meal according to these Typika was that at the former, during the elevation of the fragments, there was proclaimed: **"Great is the name of the Holy Trinity"**, whereas at the latter: **"Most Holy Theotokos, help us."**

Yet already the Georgian Shiomgvime Typikon of Jerusalem type in a 13th-century manuscript possesses the order of the evening meal without the elevation of the Panagia.

'After Vespers they strike small bells (*kandya*?); the brethren gather quietly into the refectory and begin: **"The poor shall eat and be satisfied."** Arising, they say: **"The light of Thy countenance hath appeared upon us"** [Ps. 4:7 LXX / MT 4:6], and after **"Bless"** they depart unto their cells until Compline' [^1976].

The earliest Greek manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon (in Russia), Moscow Rumyantsev Museum, Sevastyanov Collection No. 491/35 of the 13th c., has no order for either the midday or the evening meal. The earliest Slavic Jerusalem Typikon, Moscow Synodal Library No. 328/383 of the 14th c., has for the evening meal an order identical with the present one, with the following differences: **"The poor shall eat..."** is said thrice; after the meal the superior: **"By the prayers of the holy fathers..."**; the brethren: **"Glory to the Father..."**, and the elevation of the Panagia takes place according to the order of the midday meal; the dismissal is not **"God is with us..."**, but **"By the prayers of the holy fathers..."** [^1977].

*(Orig. p. 487)*

---

# VOLUME II: EXPLANATORY EXPOSITION OF THE TYPIKON — PART II: THE ALL-NIGHT VIGIL (Typikon Chapter 2: Great Vespers, Matins, and First Hour)

## CHAPTER 2 OF THE TYPIKON: "THE ALL-NIGHT VIGIL"

## (Sunday Great Vespers and Matins, the Hours, the Liturgy, and the Order of the Panagia)

*(Orig. p. 488)*

# THE BELL-PEAL AND CENSING

## The Appointed Time for the Vigil

It is appointed to begin the Vigil 'a little after the setting of the sun.' According to the Eastern reckoning of time, this is the 1st hour of the night. Thus, the Vigil naturally begins with the onset of the night of the feast.

## Character of the Bell-Peal

The bell-peal (*blagovest*) for every Vigil is appointed first on the great bell, slowly and at length, and then on all the bells (not on 2 or 4, as for ferial services and minor feasts, see Chapter 9 of the Typikon): 'he strikes the great bell (*kampan*) slowly, chanting the Undefiled [Psalm 118 / MT 119] or saying Psalm 50 softly 12 times. And then entering, he kindles the lamps and prepares the censer. And having thus gone forth again, he strikes upon all the bells.' Thus, the peal is appointed to be performed in two stages with a small interval between the peal on one bell and the ringing of all, wherein the duration of the peal on one bell must be equal to the time in which one can chant Psalm 118 or Psalm 50 twelve times. The bell-peal for the Vigil on Great Feasts in the Typikon is described similarly to the Sunday peal, yet it is nevertheless indicated that it must be more solemn: more prolonged and upon larger bells (on the Nativity of Christ: 'there is a bell-peal and then a festal peal [*trezvon*] on all the bells'; on Theophany: 'they signal on the great [instrument] [^1978] and on all the heavy ones'; on Pascha: 'he strikes on the great [instrument] and strikes sufficiently', and then: 'he strikes on all the bells and heavy ones and strikes sufficiently') [^1979].

In the earliest manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon—the Greek Moscow Rumyantsev Museum, Sevastyanov Collection No. 491/35 of the 13th c. and the Georgian manuscript of the Shiomgvime Monastery of the 13th c.—the bell-peal for the Sunday Vigil is described thus:

'he strikes the heavy instruments slowly (*κρούει τὰς βαρέας σχολαίως*), chanting (*ψάλλων*) the Undefiled'; then upon kindling the lamps and preparing the censer 'he signals upon the great [semantron], then upon the iron (*σημαίνει τὸ μέγα εἶτα σίδηρ[ον])*', according to the first monument; 'first upon the iron semantron, then upon the great', according to the second monument [^1980].

According to the earliest Slavic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon, for example, Moscow Synodal Library No. 328/383:

'he strikes upon the great semantron (*bilo*), saying: **"Blessed are the undefiled"** [Ps. 118 LXX / MT 119] divided into 12 parts, or **"I believe in one God"** 12 times, striking once [upon each]' (that is, for each of the 12 parts of Psalm 118 or for each recitation of the Creed he strikes once, so that in all there will be 12 very slow strokes), 'and thus he rings frequently and finishes' (in conclusion he strikes more rapidly); 'thereafter he signals upon the iron' [^1981] (no interval between the ringings is appointed).

In subsequent manuscripts of the Jerusalem *(Orig. p. 489)* Typikon and in the present Old Believer Typikon:

'he strikes upon the great wood with a heavy stroke (Old Believer + obliquely) rarely... And having gone forth again he strikes upon the great semantron (not in all manuscripts) [^1982] and upon the iron' (or 'iron semantron-blade' [*zhelezno bil'tse*], 'iron small-semantron' [*zheleznoe klepal'tse*]).

The Sunday bell-peal according to ancient Typika does not differ from that of a Great Feast (even the Paschal peal).

## Prayer Accompanying the Bell-Peal

Regarding the bell-peal as a sacred liturgical action, the Typikon directs its performer to accompany it with prayerful reading or chanting. The peal for the Vigil is appointed to be accompanied by the chanting of the Undefiled, that is, Psalm 118 [LXX 118 / MT 119], or by reading Psalm 50 [LXX 50 / MT 51] twelve times. Psalm 118, the most compunctious of the psalms, constituted according to earlier Typika an indispensable component of Sunday Matins, for which reason the bell-peal is accompanied by its chanting. By this prescription of the Typikon there is simultaneously determined also the duration of the peal: chanting the 176 verses of Psalm 118 or the 21 verses of Psalm 50 twelve times requires no less than half an hour. Of the ferial services, it is appointed to accompany the peal for Matins with a single reading of Psalm 50 (in Chapter 9 of the Typikon). Accompanying the bell-peal with prayer, of course, has the purpose of imparting to it a grace-filled sanctification. The effect of the bell-peal upon the soul of a Christian resembles the effect of prayer and divine worship.

Accompanying the sounding of instruments with prayer is an ancient custom. According to the Rule of St. Pachomius the Great (4th c.): 'whosoever strikes the semantron before dinner or before prayer, must meditate upon something edifying' [^1983]. In the Life of St. Cyriacus the Anchorite, under whose spiritual guidance the presumptive author of the present Typikon (St. Sabbas the Sanctified) lived, it is related that, when striking the semantron before the beginning of the service, he did not conclude the ringing until he had recited the Undefiled. (This custom and the rubrical prescription arising from it testify also to how thoroughly the Psalter was known in antiquity; if certain monks made it their custom to recite the entire Psalter daily, knowledge of Psalm 118 by heart is not surprising). The earliest Typika of the 13th c., as we have seen, speak of chanting only the Undefiled during the peal. Later Typika of the 14th c. permit replacing the Undefiled with the Creed and Psalm 50, evidently as a consequence of the fact that knowing the Psalter by heart had become a rarer phenomenon.

## Meaning of the Censing

Immediately following the bell-peal there begins in the temple a part of the Vigil that may be called silent. It consists in the censing of the entire temple. The fact that this censing, which requires considerable time, is appointed to be performed entirely before the beginning of the service itself and in the presence of all who have gathered for it, who before it are invited to stand, as well as the detail with which this *(Orig. p. 490)* censing is described in the Typikon—all this makes of the censing as it were a distinct service, preceding the All-Night Vigil and preparing for it, just as the bell-peal also prepares for it. The preparation in the one case and the other is of a different nature, but thereby all the more comprehensive. The bell-peal prepares the faithful for the service by sounds—by music. The censing prepares us for the service by the 'odor of fragrance.' This bodily, external worship precedes spiritual, 'noetic' divine worship. Incense lifts the mind unto the throne of God, whither it ascends with our prayers. In all ages and among all nations the burning of sweet spices was regarded as the finest, purest material sacrifice unto God, and of all forms of material sacrifice accepted in natural religions, the Christian Church retained only this and a few others (oil, wine, bread). And in outward appearance nothing so recalls the grace-bearing breath of the Holy Spirit as the smoke of incense. Filled with such exalted symbolism, the censing greatly fosters the prayerful disposition of the faithful also by its purely physical effect upon man. Fragrances exert an elevating, stimulating influence upon our disposition. With this purpose the Typikon, for example, before the Paschal Vigil prescribes no longer simply a censing, but an extraordinary filling of the temple with fragrance from vessels set out with incenses.

In Hagia Sophia of Constantinople, at least before divine services attended by the Emperor, the filling of the temple with fragrances was performed from special apertures in the floor. In the *Book of the Pilgrim* (*Kniga Palomnik*) by Archbishop Anthony of Novgorod (12th c.), it is related thus concerning this:

'The church is paved with red marble, and beneath it is a *dopleko* (second floor), and men approach and passages are made through the marble. And when the emperor enters into that church, then they carry beneath much *xylaloe* (aloe) and frankincense (incense) and place them upon coals, and the fragrance issues through those passages into the church into the air' [^1984].

According to the Typikon of the Georgian Shiomgvime Monastery of the 13th c., the taper-lighter (*kandilovzhigatel'*) censes the church between the first and second bell-peal for the Vigil [^1985].

## Peculiarities of the Present Censing

### a) Its Celebrant

Inasmuch as the censing at the beginning of the Vigil is the first in the daily cycle of divine services, it is performed with special solemnity and is described with the same detail as in Chapter 22 of the Typikon, which is specifically dedicated to censing. Unto the beginning of the Vigil the censing (as also the exclamation **"Glory to the Holy..."**) was transferred from the beginning of Matins. Therefore, as there also, it is performed by the priest, and not by the deacon—in view of the exceptional importance of the moment. (Cf. the Polyeleos; at the Liturgy the deacon censes, because the priest is occupied with more important sacred actions).

The historical reason for performing this censing specifically by the priest is that Matins and Vespers were celebrated without that solemn*(Orig. p. 491)*ity with which the Liturgy was celebrated, and therefore without a deacon; and in monasteries there was not always a deacon present.

### b) The Candle at the Censing

Another peculiarity of the present censing, likewise common to it and the censing at the beginning of Matins and at the Polyeleos, is the bearing of a candle before the censing priest. At Vespers, as a service less solemn than Matins, the censing is performed without a candle; at the Liturgy, the censing recedes into the background before other, more sacred actions and is therefore performed with less solemnity, likewise without a candle.

The historical basis of this difference is that Matins, from the beginning of which the present censing was transferred unto the beginning of the Vigil, always began at night, before dawn, when walking through the temple and all its aisles was impossible without a lamp; Vespers and the Liturgy, on the other hand, were always celebrated by day.

Yet since the censing at the beginning of the Vigil, as also of Matins, must nevertheless not be as solemn as at the Polyeleos, it is prescribed that the lamp be borne at the censing not by the deacon, as at the Polyeleos, but by the paraecclesiarch or taper-lighter. However, further on in parentheses the Typikon notes that in cathedrals and parish churches 'the deacon performs this.' In the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra only at the beginning of Matins does a monk in a mantle bear the candle before the censing priest, whereas at the Vigil it is the deacon.

The historical basis for the rubrical requirement that the paraecclesiarch, and not the deacon, precede the censing priest with a candle is that the Vigil, owing to the absence of deacons, was celebrated for the most part by a priest alone. At the Polyeleos, however, it is otherwise, because the Polyeleos was introduced into the office when monasteries for the most part had deacons.

More particularly, the Typikon describes the censing before the Vigil in the following manner. After the bell-peal, the taper-lighter or paraecclesiarch lights a candle in a candlestick and sets it before the Royal Doors. In parish churches and in those monasteries where the deacon begins the All-Night Vigil with the priest, the candle is borne by the deacon, who bears it before the priest also during the censing of the sanctuary.

In the Greek Typikon of the Shiomgvime Monastery of the 13th c. there is no such note concerning the candle (the taper-lighter simply takes it in his hands before the exclamation). In manuscript Greek and Slavic Typika of the 13th–14th centuries it was indicated to place this candle or lamp in the midst of the church [^1986]. In Typika of the 15th and 16th centuries it is indicated to place it either 'right before the royal doors nearby' [^1987], or 'in the midst of the church right before the royal doors' [^1988]. So also in the first printed editions of the Typikon. By 'royal doors' were designated the principal doors from the narthex into the nave; they are consequently understood here as well, for which reason the candle standing before them turns out to be in the midst *(Orig. p. 492)* of the church. In the corrected copy of the Typikon for the 1672 edition, the words 'in the midst of the church' and 'nearby' were crossed out, and beginning with that edition are not inserted into the Typikon (in the Old Believer Typikon they are retained), evidently because by 'royal doors' men came to understand the holy doors of the altar screen.

## Vesting of the Sacred Ministers

Having set the candle, the paraecclesiarch makes a bow unto the priest whose turn of service it is, and the latter unto the superior; the priest, 'having stepped forth' (that is, having left his stasidion), makes three bows: before the holy doors (one) and unto both choirs (one each); during all this time the brethren sit; the priest, having entered the altar, puts on the epitrachelion, having kissed the cross upon it. In parish churches and monasteries where the priest begins the All-Night Vigil not with a paraecclesiarch, but with a deacon, this order is somewhat altered in practice. Customarily the priest and deacon who are to serve enter the altar after making the indicated bows, and there vest—the deacon in sticharion with orarion, the priest in epitrachelion and phelonion, concerning which the present Typikon remarks further on in parentheses.

The practice accepted today—the participation of the deacon in the celebration of Great Vespers at the Vigil from its very beginning—is no less ancient than that prescribed by the Typikon, according to which the paraecclesiarch takes the deacon's place. Only the former traces its origin from the customs of the ancient cathedral of Hagia Sophia ('the Great Church') in Constantinople, while the latter traces its origin from the Jerusalem Typikon. This is well seen from how these preparatory actions for the Vigil are represented in the *Diataxis* (*Διάταξις*) of Patriarch Philotheus of Constantinople (14th c.):

'When the time arrives, that is, of Great Vespers, the priest departs with the deacon, and they make bows (*μετανοίας*) toward the icon of the Master Christ, while all the brethren sit; likewise they make three bows toward the icon of the Theotokos, one toward the center (of the church), and one each toward the choirs; then they enter into the sanctuary; the deacon, having taken his sticharion with the orarion and bowed toward the east thrice, approaches the priest and says: **"Bless, Master, the sticharion with the orarion"**; the priest blesses them, saying: **"Blessed is our God always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages."** Then both put on their appointed vestments. This is now not so done, but the priest bows alone and alone puts on the epitrachelion and phelonion, and begins to cense with a reader or *eutaxias* [^1989], who holds the candlestick.'

According to the just observation of Goar [^1990], Patriarch Philotheus did not himself compose the order of sacred ministry (*Diataxis*) proposed by him, but only recorded the ancient order of Constantinople's Hagia Sophia. The observation 'this is now not so done' shows that by the time of Patriarch Philotheus this order was being displaced even from cathedral and *(Orig. p. 493)* parish churches by some other, evidently by the order from the practice of the Jerusalem Typikon that was spreading ever more widely at that time. In the point under consideration, as in others, the latter Typikon gives a less solemn and less complex order; even the bows before entering the altar are fewer according to the Jerusalem Typikon. (Note that according to the order of Philotheus no veneration of the holy doors is indicated).

## Censing of the Sanctuary

Having vested, the priest 'censes the holy table (altar) crosswise round about and the entire sanctuary, and having opened the holy doors, goes forth.' The holy doors are customarily opened before the beginning of the censing, which does not contradict the present direction, since the latter expression can signify in general: he goes forth through the open holy doors. 'Censes crosswise' is an echo of that practice of censing when the censer was without chains and it was convenient to form a cross with it; today the crosswise manner of censing is replaced by its threefold repetition.

## "Arise" or "Command"

Following the censing of the sanctuary, the taper-lighter, according to the direction of the Typikon, or the deacon, according to accepted practice, standing before the holy doors with candle in hand, proclaims in a loud voice: **"Arise!"** (*Возстаните!*). All arise. In the Greek Typikon and in our earlier Typika at this place there was appointed the exclamation not **"Arise!"**, but **"Command!"** (*Повелите!*). In the earliest manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon—the Georgian manuscript of the Shiomgvime Monastery: 'arise.' But in that competing with it in antiquity, Moscow Rumyantsev Museum, Sevastyanov Collection No. 491/35: *κελεύσατε*. So also in all Greek Typika of the 14th c. and the *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus. In manuscript Slavic Typika of the Moscow Synodal Library Nos. 328/383 and 329/384 of the 14th c.: *келепсаите* [*kelepsaite*]; in No. 332/385 of the 14th c.: *келепсаите, рекше встанете* ('kelepsaite, that is, arise'); in No. 678/386 of the 15th c. and others, and in the first printed editions, ending with the edition of Patriarch Joseph in 1641: *келепсаите; рекше по речи исъкуству повелите* ('kelepsaite; that is, artificially rendered, command'); that is, these Typika regarded *kelevsate* as an artificial expression for 'arise.' This latter remark is retained also in the present Old Believer Typikon. — *Κελεύσατε* (*Keleusate*), **"Command"**, an exclamation used according to the present Typikon at the ordination of a presbyter and deacon and at the Presanctified Liturgy before the words **"The light of Christ illumines all"**, entered into divine worship from the Byzantine court ceremonial. By this exclamation masters of ceremonies invited dignitaries at imperial receptions to enter into certain halls of the palace or to depart from them. In turn, into the Byzantine court the exclamation was borrowed from Roman practice: with the word *jubete* directors of public games addressed the consuls before opening them [^1991]. In all likelihood, in Byzantium as well a master of ceremonies in antiquity, only when addressing the emperor (or emperors, or the emperor with the empress), said "command" (*повелите*); the emperor, perhaps by a nod of the head *(Orig. p. 494)* or gesture of the hand, gave command, and the court dignitaries went forth from a given hall or entered into it. Yet, owing to the constant use of this word at exits/processions, it subsequently acquired the technical meaning of an invitation to go forth; it was pronounced in the absence of the emperor and was addressed not unto him, but unto such persons from whom the proclaimer not only does not seek permission, but himself invites them unto specific actions [^1992]. In the treatise *De cerimoniis aulae Byzantinae*, ascribed unto the Byzantine Emperor Constantine VII Porphyrogenitus (912–959) and definitively redacted no later than the beginning of the 11th century [^1993], this exclamation has the following instances of application. Upon the conclusion of an audience in the palace (morning or evening), the emperor said unto the papias (the supreme sacristan of the palace): "Go, make the dismissal"; the papias took the keys and jingled them (as a sign of dismissal), a silentiary (one of the masters of ceremonies) entered and said "command" (*повелите*), and the gathering dispersed; thus, here this exclamation is an invitation to disperse. Yet it did not always have such a meaning. On Sunday, after the Liturgy in the palace church, the highest dignitaries (*protospatharioi*), having received an invitation to dinner, went into one hall (the Lausiakos), while those who had not received an invitation went into another (the Justinian, that is, the Hall of Justinian), and there sat waiting for the dismissal; unto the latter (as though from the emperor himself) the master of ceremonies (silentiary) came forth, proclaimed "command" (*повелите*), and they departed. Then the acolyth, at a given sign from the masters of ceremonies, proclaimed, addressing the droungarios (commander of the guard): "command"—the latter bowed unto the masters of ceremonies and took his stand upon an elevation in the hall, as though forming an honor guard of the hall. The acolyth, standing at the door from the first hall (the Justinian) into the other (the Skyla), where the other court dignitaries gathered after the Liturgy, proclaimed unto the *magistroi* and patricians: "command" (*повелите*); they entered into the first hall and sat down. The acolyth said, addressing the lower officials (secretaries): "command, secretikoi" (*повелите, секретики*),—they likewise entered into the first hall and sat down. With the same exclamation the acolyth then invites the military officials from the second hall into the first. Then the list of those invited to the imperial dinner was read; the praepositus (supreme master of ceremonies) permits the dismissal to be made; the silentiary proclaims "command" (*повелите*), the uninvited disperse, while the invited remain for dinner. Thus, most frequently with the exclamation **"Command!"** (*повелите*) dignitaries were invited to pass from one hall into another [^1994]. The exclamation **"Command!"** (*повелите*) was also used at imperial processions [^1995]. Evidently, at the beginning of the All-Night Vigil this exclamation appeared in view of the usual presence of the emperor at it, and originally could have had the sense of seeking permission from the emperor to begin the service; yet the presented instances of its use permit us also to connect it with the procession of the *(Orig. p. 495)* priest forth from the sanctuary, after censing it, into the midst of the temple: the paraecclesiarch who utters the exclamation corresponds in this case to the court acolyth and, as it were, invites the priest to come forth from the sanctuary. In any case, this exclamation indicates the special solemnity of this moment and of this service (as of the others where it is used). It is characteristic that from the court ceremonial it penetrated even into purely monastic liturgical typika, such as the Jerusalem Typikon. Yet the noted hesitation of the ancient typika between the exclamations **"Command!"** (*повелите*) and **"Arise!"** (*возстаните*) may attest that the second was more ancient in a typikon of Jerusalem origin and was gradually displaced by the first, Constantinopolitan one. The Nikonian correctors, perhaps, had this in mind and wished to return unto the most ancient practice of the Jerusalem Typikon by adopting the reading **"Arise!"** (*возстаните*). In the present Greek Typikon, which follows Patriarch Philotheus in the order of the Vigil, it is *κελεύσατε* [*keleusate*] [^1996].

## Censing of the Nave

After the exclamation **"Arise!"** (*Возстаните!*), the censing of the middle part of the temple (the nave) begins. The priest censes first before the holy doors, then the icons on the right side of the iconostasis, then on the left, and finally the superior and both choirs according to rank (that is, first the right, and then the left); during this, the paraecclesiarch or deacon with a candle precedes the priest. While censing, the priest 'makes a slight bow'; his companion does the same. Since a censer without chains is presumed, a cross-wise censing is required: 'raising the censer straight (vertically) and across (transversely)'; today, as noted above, the cross-wise manner of censing is replaced by its threefold repetition. These directions of the chapter of the Typikon under consideration regarding the censing are somewhat supplemented in chapter 22. Thus, there it is noted that if the superior is not in the church, the icon at his place (above his stasidion) is censed. Concerning the censing of the choirs in chapter 22 of the Typikon, it is noted:

'He censes the entire right choir of the brethren twice, lifting up the censer before each straight and across, forming a cross (that is, a censing of each of the brethren individually is required); and when he has censed the entire choir and taken his stand directly in their midst, then he forms a cross with the censer toward the entire choir and makes a bow unto them decorously, unto all as one, and they all likewise make a bow unto him; similarly he censes also the left choir and all the brethren standing in the church.'

Concerning the manner of this latter censing of 'the brethren standing in the church,' a more precise indication is given by the note (the second 'Note well' [*zri*]) of chapter 2 concerning the Polyeleos; there it is said that after censing the choirs the priest 'censes passing through (that is, walking through the temple, and not from one place) all the standing people.' This observation evidently presumes the absence in the temple of other icons besides those on the iconostasis, and therefore does not speak of censing them. In practice, however, the priest, walking through the temple, censes not only the standing people, but prior to them also the icons of the middle part of the temple.

*(Orig. p. 496)*

According to St. Symeon of Thessalonica (15th c.),

'through the censing, which begins from the sanctuary (*ἱλαστήριον* / altar), is depicted the fragrant grace of the Spirit extending everywhere (*μεταδοτικήν*)' [^1997].

Among the ancient typika, the briefest observation concerning the censing of the middle part of the temple is given by the *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus:

'preceded by him (the *eutaxias*, corresponding unto the paraecclesiarch) with the candlestick, the priest censes the entire temple according to custom, having gone forth (starting from) from the (holy) doors' [^1998].

It is more complex in the Shiomgvime and Sevastyanov Typika (13th c.):

'having gone forth through the holy doors, *he censes there also cross-wise* (Sevastyanov instead of italics: "and having formed a cross with the censer opposite the sanctuary (*ἱλαστηρίου*, that is, the altar—into the open doors), he departs and censes"). Then *unto the chief* (absent in Sevastyanov) icon of the saint (that is, the patronal icon), likewise unto the hegumen (*τὸν καθηγούμενον*) and the choir *according to custom* (Sevastyanov: unto two choirs according to rank) preceded by the taper-lighter *with a lighted candle* (*τῆς λαμπάδος δηλονότι*); then he goes forth into the narthex...' [^1999].

Characteristic is the silence concerning other icons besides the patronal icon. Subsequent redactions replace this icon with icons in general; according to Slavic manuscripts of the 14th–15th centuries, 'he goes forth from the altar, preceded by a candle, and censes the holy doors cross-wise and the holy icons; thereafter he censes the hegumen thrice cross-wise or his place, and both choirs according to their rank; and he goes forth into the narthex' [^2000]. Subsequent redactions: '...the holy icons + which are on the right side and after them those which are on the left,' while omitting the remarks 'thrice' and 'or his place' [^2001].

The Old Believer Typikon restores the remark concerning the patronal icon:

'after the holy doors he censes the icon of the saint whose temple it is, likewise he censes in order the holy icons which are on the right side, and after them those which are on the left side' [^2002],

being in other respects like our own. Characteristic is the silence concerning the censing of the people, which is preserved also in the present Typikon (only in this chapter): in ancient monasteries all the brethren sang, forming two choirs.

## Censing of the Narthex

After the nave, the censing of the narthex is appointed; the narthex, as noted earlier, often yielded little in size unto the middle part of the temple and had to accommodate all the brethren in view of the fact that many services were celebrated here. In addition, the censing of the narthex is a remembrance of the ancient ecclesiastical institution of catechumens and penitents, who were not admitted into the temple itself. Finally, the censing of the narthex could have in view the departed who were buried here [^2003].

*(Orig. p. 497)*

The brief remark of the present chapter concerning the censing of the narthex: 'he goes forth also into the narthex and censes according to rank also the brethren being there'—is likewise supplemented in chapter 22 of the Typikon: the censing of the narthex, according to this chapter, begins with the priest 'forming a cross with the censer before the Beautiful Gates'—the principal doors from the narthex into the temple—just as the censing of the middle part of the temple began with a similar rite before the holy (royal) doors; 'then he censes on both sides the holy icons and all the brethren according to their rank; and finally, returning unto the Beautiful Gates, facing toward the west, he censes all cross-wise'—that is, a general censing of all is performed, as earlier each was censed individually ('according to rank').

The remark of the present chapter concerning the censing of the narthex is preserved unchanged in the Typikon from its most ancient manuscripts: *ἐξελθὼν δὲ εἰς τὸν νάρθηκα καὶ θυμιάσας καὶ ἐνταῦθα τοὺς ἀδελφοὺς κατὰ τάξιν ὑποστρέφει* ('and having gone forth into the narthex and censed also there the brethren according to rank, he returns') [^2004]. In the Shiomgvime manuscript 'brethren' is absent [^2005].

# THE OPENING EXCLAMATION

## "Bless, Master!" ("Lord, Bless")

After the censing of the narthex the priest, as the present chapter of the Typikon states, 'having returned again into the church and taken his stand in the midst of both choirs (before the holy doors?), signs a cross with the censer, facing toward the east,' that is, he censes a second time toward the open holy doors, returning for the conclusion of the censing unto its beginning, 'and proclaims in a loud voice: **"Lord, bless!"** (*Господи, благослови*).' [Note: In Byzantine Greek this is *Κύριε εὐλόγησον*, rendered in Slavonic as *Господи благослови* and commonly in liturgical English as **"Bless, Master!"**].

By this exclamation the priest asks a blessing for the beginning of the service from the superior; for this reason, if a deacon concelebrates with him, the latter pronounces this exclamation, asking thereby a blessing from the priest, as before the Liturgy with the exclamation: **"Bless, Master"** (*Владыко, благослови*) [^2006]; by a similar exclamation ("In the name of the Lord, Father, give the blessing" / *Именем Господним благослови, отче*) the reader asks the priest's blessing at the service of the Hours. (In these exclamations there is a certain gradation of address corresponding unto the importance of the service: master [*vladyko*], lord [*gospodi*], father [*otche*] [^2007]).

Concluding the censing, the priest censes a second time all the most important objects with which he began it: after the holy doors, the icons surrounding them, the superior (for the nave), and the holy table (for the sanctuary): 'and immediately he censes the icon of the Savior Christ and of the Theotokos, and the superior at his place, and having entered into the holy altar, and taken his stand before the holy table, he signs a cross with the censer thrice, and then *(Orig. p. 498)* proclaims: **"Glory to the Holy..."**' Thus, the entire censing must conclude, according to the Typikon, by the beginning of the All-Night Vigil, and take place without words and hymns, in reverent silence, concentrating thought upon itself.

This section in the present Typikon has likewise received a certain alteration in comparison with the ancient ones. According to these latter, the exclamation **"Lord, bless!"** (*Господи, благослови*) was pronounced by the priest upon entering from the narthex into the temple at the 'royal doors,' that is, at the principal doors from the narthex into the nave. Thus according to the Sevastyanov MS (13th c.):

after the censing of the narthex the priest *ὑποστρέφει καὶ εἰσελθὼν εἴσω τῆς βασιλικῆς πύλης χαράττει μετὰ τοῦ θυμιατοῦ σταυρὸν καὶ ἐκφωνεῖ μεγαλοφώνως: κύριε εὐλόγησον*—'returns (from the narthex into the temple) and, having entered within the royal doors, signs a cross with the censer and proclaims in a loud voice: **"Lord, bless!"**' [^2008].

According to Slavic typika of the 14th–15th centuries:

'and turning toward the royal doors, he censes cross-wise and proclaims...' [^2009].

Yet according to the order of Patriarch Philotheus it is indefinite:

'he enters through the Beautiful (*ὡραίων*) Doors and proclaims melodiously (*μετὰ μέλους*)' [^2010].

Likewise indefinite in the Shiomgvime manuscript:

'he enters into the church through the royal doors; having signed a cross with the censer, he proclaims in a loud voice...' [^2011].

Hence arises the ambiguity also of the present Typikon regarding the place where the exclamation is pronounced. The present redaction of this passage is found in manuscripts of the 16th century [^2012] and in the Old Believer Typikon [^2013].—Nor did the second part of this section remain without change, regarding the actions of the priest from the exclamation **"Lord, bless!"** (*Господи, благослови*) unto the exclamation **"Glory to the Holy..."** (*Слава Святей*). The simplest practice here is given by the Shiomgvime manuscript:

'afterwards he censes the hegumen or his place, enters into the altar, and takes his stand before the ciborium; having depicted a cross twice with the censer, on the third time he proclaims: **"Glory to the Holy..."**' [^2014].

The concluding censing here is performed only unto the hegumen, since the blessing for the exclamation (**"Lord, bless!"**) is asked of him. The Typikon of Patriarch Philotheus, instead of 'the hegumen,' has: 'again the holy icons' [^2015], and concerning the censing of the holy table simply: 'censing.' The Sevastyanov MS: 'the superior or his place, then the saint (*τὸν ἅγιον*),' that is, the icon; later Greek MSS (14th c.): 'the saint of the monastery' (*τὸν τῆς μονῆς ἅγιον*) [^2016]. Slavic MSS of the 14th–15th centuries in place of the latter: 'the festal icon.' Manuscripts of the 16th century and the Old Believer Typikon: 'he censes the hegumen at his place (Old Believer: or his place, if it happen that the hegumen be not there) and again the previously censed holy icons as before, and then the Saint whose temple it is'—thenceforth as in our practice [^2017].

*(Orig. p. 499)*

## "Glory to the Holy..."

As the initial priestly exclamation for the All-Night Vigil, there was chosen not the exclamation of Vespers, which occupies the first place in the Vigil, but that of Matins, as the more important service. This exclamation (in Greek: *Δόξα τῇ ἁγίᾳ καὶ ὁμοουσίῳ καὶ ζωοποιῷ καὶ ἀδιαιρέτῳ Τριάδι, πάντοτε, νῦν, καὶ ἀεί, καὶ εἰς τοὺς αἰῶνας τῶν αἰώνων, ἀμήν*—**"Glory to the Holy, Consubstantial, Life-Creating, and Undivided Trinity, always, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages, Amen"**), as was noted also above [^2018], glorifies God, although not from so general a point of view as the Vesperal exclamation (**"Blessed is our God"**), yet neither with such elevation and expressiveness as the Liturgical one (**"Blessed is the Kingdom"**); namely, it glorifies the Holy Trinity only in Her indivisibility and general action upon the world (not in the economy of grace, like the Liturgical exclamation),—according to the explanation of this exclamation in St. Symeon of Thessalonica: 'before every song theologizing concerning the Cause of all and Master, the God of all One in Trinity, and giving doxology unto Him and thus laying the beginning for the hymnody of Him Who is the beginning and end of all' [^2019].

The exclamation **"Glory to the Holy..."** must have arisen from the Evangelical verse **"Glory to God in the highest."** In the most ancient typika, Matins during the Forty Days' Fast (the worship of which in general bears upon itself many traces of primitive practice) does not have the exclamation **"Glory to the Holy..."**, but after the usual beginning with the exclamation **"Blessed is our God"** begins with **"Glory to God in the highest"** [^2020] (as in general in antiquity services sometimes lacked anything corresponding unto the present initial exclamations [^2021]). In its original form, the exclamation perhaps resembled the formula in the present rite for the consecration of temples and antimenses (which has, in all likelihood, a Constantinopolitan Hagia Sophia origin and has been preserved very stably since the 11th–12th centuries): "Glory to Thee, Holy Trinity, our God, unto the ages of ages" [^2022].

The present exclamation has its simplest form in the most ancient manuscript of the Studite Typikon of the Moscow Typographical Library of the 11th century in the order of Paschal Matins (in other places of this Typikon it is not cited): "Glory to the Consubstantial Trinity, always, now and ever" [^2023]. In a manuscript of the same Typikon of the 12th century there is already added:

*(Orig. p. 500)*

"Holy" [^2024]. In a subsequent redaction of the exclamation, represented by a series of manuscripts of the 12th–13th centuries, unto these two adjectives there is joined "Life-creating" [^2025]. Close to this, yet perhaps more ancient than it, judging by the expressed hypothesis regarding the very original form of the exclamation, is the following: "Glory to the Holy, Consubstantial, and Life-creating Trinity, our God, always..." [^2026]. The present form, apparently, is first found in Greek typika of the 13th century [^2027]. Attempts were also made to expand the exclamation beyond its present form. Thus, the most ancient Slavic manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon have after "Trinity" the addition: "To the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit" [^2028]. In St. Symeon of Thessalonica (15th c.), unto the four present adjectives there is added yet a fifth: "All-powerful" (*παντοδυνάμῳ*) [^2029]. Before "now" (*nyně*) there is sometimes present, sometimes absent "and" (*i*) [^2030]. *Ἀδιαιρέτῳ* [*Adiairetō*] in Slavic is translated sometimes as "Undivided" (*Нераздельней*), sometimes as "Indivisible" (*Неразделимей*); the first, apparently, is more ancient [^2031]; the second translation is more frequent [^2032] and was adopted by the Old Believer Typikon.

# THE INTRODUCTORY PSALM

## The Singing of "O Come, Let Us Worship"

Since the so-called "Usual Beginning" of church services was performed recently, before the Ninth Hour, and by its sorrowful-prayerful character would not correspond unto the solemn beginning of the All-Night Vigil, it here takes the shortened form of the verse **"O come, let us worship"** (*Приидите поклонимся*), which receives a rounding addition: **"O come, let us worship and fall down before Him."** This verse, with the responsive **"Amen"** preceding it, follows immediately upon the initial exclamation of the Vigil. Moreover, in view of the solemnity of the moment this verse is sung (concerning singing it is not explicitly stated, but this follows from the singing of the introductory psalm that is joined directly unto it, and is so done in practice), and it is sung not in the usual, but in an exceptional manner, as are also other most important prayers of the services—by the superior alone or by the ecclesiarch, and moreover with a gradual strengthening of the voice upon each of the three verses (to express the gradually enveloping prayerful inspiration):

'the superior (*ὁ προεστώς*) or ecclesiarch begins: **"Amen. O come, let us wor-** *(Orig. p. 501)* **ship..."** in a low voice (*χαμηλῇ καὶ ἡσύχῳ φωνῇ*). Then the second, somewhat higher (*εἶθ' οὕτως ἀνώτερον πρὸς ὀλίγον*): **"O come, let us worship..."** Again the third time in a higher voice thus (*πάλιν τὸ γ' ἀνωτέρᾳ φωνῇ οὕτως*): **"O come, let us worship..."** Then alone (*μόνον*): **"O come, let us worship..."** And immediately he begins in a higher voice (*ἀνωτέρᾳ φωνῇ*) in Tone 8: **"Bless the Lord, O my soul"** slowly and with sweet singing, the rest of the brethren singing along (*ἀργὰ καὶ μετὰ μελῶν, συμψαλλόντων καὶ τῶν λοιπῶν ἀδελφῶν*).'

Tone 8 for the singing of the introductory psalm was chosen as the most calmly solemn: as such, it is used predominantly for singing the concluding stichera; among the feasts it dominates on Pentecost and the Exaltation; in it also the Akathist is sung as a hymn of victory. However, Tone 8 for this psalm has not its usual chant (melody), but a special one, as indicated by the note 'with sweet singing.'

The development of the verse **"O come, let us worship"** unto its present form has been shown above. The rubric for singing it here was subject unto slight modifications. According unto the Shiomgvime [Typikon], **"Amen"** and **"O come, let us worship"** "we say with a loud voice," after which "the superior or the ecclesiarch begins with a quiet voice" Psalm 103. But according unto the most ancient Greek and Slavic [monuments], the superior (Slav. *igumen*) or the ecclesiarch begins with **"Amen,"** as in the present Typikon. Concerning the tone of voice for the verses, the most ancient Slavic [manuscripts] say nothing, but only for the psalm [they specify] in Slavic "with a great voice." The most ancient Greek [manuscript] (the Sevastyanov), however, indicates from the very beginning (from **"Amen"**) to speak (*λέγων*) loudly and with chanting (*μεγαλοφώνως καὶ μετὰ μέλους*); while concerning the psalm, the ancient Greek [witnesses] agree with the present, except that the Sevastyanov and the ancient Slavic omit here (for the psalm) "the superior" or "the *igumen*" and speak only of the ecclesiarch, the head of the church (*tserkvenachal'nik*). According unto the Order (*Diataxis*) of Patriarch Philotheus, the superior or an appointed monk chants (*ψάλλει*) the introductory psalm [^2033]. The Greek Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 381 (14th c.) completely coincides with the present rubric regarding the officiant of the verses and psalm and their tone of voice (though there is a difference in the text of the verses of **"O come, let us worship"** [^2034]). These prescriptions of the Typikon are observed in the Kyiv Caves Lavra, where **"Amen,"** **"O come, let us worship,"** and the beginning of Psalm 103 at the Vigil are chanted with gradual elevations of the voice as a solo bass (most often the choir regent).

## Character and Content of the Introductory Psalm

Psalm 103 [104 MT], with which Vespers begins, "and with it all the services of the day" [^2035], and which is therefore termed introductory (*προοιμιακός* / *prooimiakos*), expresses the feeling inspired by the evening (vv. 19, 20: **"The sun knoweth his going down. Thou appointedst darkness, and it was night"**) with its repose from labours and leisure [^2036]—a feeling of awe at the glory of God in nature, in creation, and in providence over it, which have been contemplated *(Orig. p. 502)* throughout the entire day [^2037]. In this psalm, parallel unto Psalm 102 [103 MT]—which depicts the glory of God not in nature, but in Israel, and His gracious rather than natural providence over it (for which reason it is used at the Liturgy)—in Psalm 103, in the words of St. Symeon of Thessalonica, "the Lord is blessed, narration is made concerning all His creation (*δημιουργίαν*), and thanksgiving is lifted up unto Him, since upon the completion of the day it is fitting to give thanks for all things" [^2038]. Among the series of homogeneous psalms that depict the glory of God in nature (such as Psalms 8 and 18 [19 MT]—the glory of God preeminently in the heavens; Psalm 64 [65 MT], **"A hymn becometh Thee, O God,"**—the divine goodness revealed in the fertility of the earth; Psalm 28 [29 MT], **"Bring unto the Lord, O ye sons of God,"**—the majesty of God in atmospheric phenomena), the present psalm [^2039] was chosen for Vespers, presumably on account of its singular fullness, as well as for its distinct delineation of the days of creation, the beginning of which, according unto the Book of Genesis, coincides with the evening [^2040]. In view of such exceptionality, sublimity of content, and propriety of the psalm in this place, Vespers—alone among all the daily services—possesses only this single psalm as its introductory psalm (even the Hours have three introductory psalms, and Matins has six).

Following both the order of the days of creation and the comparative hierarchy of the cosmic spheres in depicting the glory of God, the psalm successively depicts the glory of the Creator in the heavens, upon the earth, and in the watery realm, and thereupon His glory as the Provider. Representing God under the image of a mighty King, the psalm calls light His garment (the 1st day of creation), and the tent ("curtain")—the vault of heaven, which, notwithstanding its watery composition, serves as the immovable upper chamber of God; the clouds are the chariot of this King, and His messengers and ministers are the wind and fire (the 2nd day of creation). As regards the earth, what is astonishing first of all is its unshakably firm foundation, a foundation which is properly nothing other than its own gravity [^2041]; equally expressive of the majesty of the Creator is the manner in which it received its present surface: the water (the deep) that originally enveloped it, even covering the mountains (**"upon the mountains shall the waters stand"** [^2042]), fled as it were timidly into its reservoirs before the authoritative word of God (on the 3rd day of creation), and upon the earth the mountains rose up, while between them valleys were laid out; gathered now into their natural boundaries, the waters came fully to serve the purposes of Providence: they not only "give drink" unto the beasts [^2043] upon the earth (of which, as an example, the wild asses, onagers—the most timid of steppe animals—and the birds nesting *(Orig. p. 503)* upon the coastal crags [^2044] are named, as being equally in need of ready drink), but also foster the growth of food upon the earth for its inhabitants, for which reason God sends waters (in the form of rain) even upon the highest mountains. The psalmist enumerates the chief kinds of these divine creations of the second half of the 3rd day, dwelling upon those particularly beneficial unto man—wine, oil, and bread—and unto beasts; yet those beneficial unto the latter, in contrast unto the former, God Himself causes to grow without the cooperation of man (**"which Thou hast planted"**—hence their frequent grandeur, as the cedars) in His care for all His creatures, for each of which He prepared upon the earth—now fully ordered (on the 3rd day)—a dwelling suited unto its instincts: for birds, trees, and for certain of them, such as the heron (Greek *ἐρῳδιός*, in Hebrew: the stork, crane, etc.), and particularly tall trees ("leadeth them"—rising above all nests) [^2045]; for the wild roes ("harts"), the mountains; for the timid hares [conies], the crags. This convenient habitation for His creatures—the earth—God also illuminated in a corresponding manner (the 4th day of creation), wherein among the luminaries the moon is named first, as regulating the longer and sacred intervals of time; night is appointed preeminently for the activity of wild beasts, and the day for man. Having surveyed the earth in the entire fullness of the creations of God (**"the earth was filled with Thy creation"**), which sufficiently testify unto the majesty of the Creator (**"for—oh, how!—magnified are Thy works, O Lord; in wisdom hast Thou made them all"**), the psalmist descends lower, into the sea, and there finds an almost greater fullness of life, downright innumerable in its creeping things (the 5th day of creation), yet more grandiose (**"this dragon"** [leviathan], Hebrew *leviathan*, sea monsters), which nonetheless is subdued by the power of God (**"which Thou hast made to play therein"**) even in the hands of man, who boldly navigates the waters filled with such inhabitants. Now the psalmist dwells generally upon the living inhabitants of the earth (the 6th day), who exist solely because God feeds them (Providence); their entire essence consists in the spirit that animates them, and this spirit is entirely in the hands of God: He takes it away at the death of a creature and returns it at birth, whereby—through this life in death and after death—the face of the earth is ever renewed (most immediately, the reference must be unto autumn and spring). The psalmist would desire that the glory of the Creator be preserved unto the ages; God indeed, as an artist, rejoices in His work (cf. in Genesis the divine approval of each day of creation); yet at times the earth also provokes the wrathful gaze of God, which shakes and sets it on fire (earthquakes and volcanoes); this wrath would not cloud our joy and song unto the Lord if sinners were to vanish from the earth, with the fervent wish for which, repeating the opening words of the psalm, the psalm concludes. *(Orig. p. 504)*

## Manner of Execution of the Psalm

For such content, the psalm merits that exceptionally solemn chanting, the like of which the Typikon appoints for only a few other psalms (the Polyeleos psalms, Psalm 136 [137 MT], Psalm 118 [119 MT]). The psalm, as indicated above, is begun by the superior or the ecclesiarch, who with the brethren chants the first half of verse 1: **"Bless the Lord, O my soul,"** and the refrain: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord."** "Then the second chanter of the right choir: **'O Lord my God,** **Thou art magnified exceedingly. Blessed art Thou, O Lord,'** softly, with harmonious voice, the rest of the brethren chanting along with them," that is, during this the rest of the brethren also chant softly along with the chanter (in the Greek this last remark is absent). Thus, the refrain **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord,"** taken from Psalm 118:12 [119:12 MT], is appointed here for the psalm and, it is assumed, ought to be appended unto each verse. But besides this refrain the Typikon presupposes other refrains for the present psalm as well, at least one more, as is shown by the subsequent rubric of the Typikon concerning the reading of the Prayers of Light by the priest, namely that this reading must begin "when they begin to chant: **'In wisdom hast Thou made them all'** and **'Glory to Thee, O Lord, Who hast made all things.'**" The first of these two verses constitutes the middle of verse 24 of the psalm, while the second expression is not found in the psalm; consequently, it is a refrain; yet the Typikon does not specify at which verse of the psalm this refrain replaces the preceding one, unless the latter remark is taken as such an indication, that is, if this refrain is not presupposed from verse 24 of the psalm. If we turn unto the tradition preserved in the practice of singing and in the musical books, we find here yet another refrain unto the psalm: **"Marvelous are Thy works, O Lord,"** which is attached unto verse 6 of the psalm: **"Upon the mountains shall the waters stand"** (entering into the singing of the psalm from this verse). The same tradition speaks of singing not the entire psalm, but only selected verses of it. The singing of the entire psalm is not explicitly stated in the Typikon either, but it is apparently presupposed both by the above-cited remark, "when they begin to chant," and by the fact that the reading of the 7 Prayers of Light, which requires considerable time, is appointed to begin at a specific moment in the singing of the psalm, prior unto which moment the priest is directed only to stand at his place.

Psalm 103 for the beginning of Vespers is not yet indicated in the well-known description of Sinai Vespers given by Abbots John and Sophronius (presumably of the 6th c.) in Nikon of the Black Mountain: here (Sunday) Vespers begins with **"Blessed is the man"** [^2046]. But according unto the Sinai Horologion of the 8th–9th c. and St. Theodore the Studite (†826), Vespers begins with Psalm 103 [^2047]. And a series of subsequent monuments of the 9th–10th cc.—the *Hypotyposis* (*Ὑποτύπωσις*) attributed unto St. Theodore the Studite [^2048] and the *Diatyposis* (*Διατύπωσις*) of St. Athanasius [^2049]—already concordantly indicate this psalm at the beginning of Ves- *(Orig. p. 505)* pers. As regards the manner of chanting it, in the "Canon of Antiphons (Refrains) for the Psalms of the Great Church of God," inscribed with the name of Patriarch Anthimus of Constantinople (6th c.), the refrain appointed for this psalm is: **"Have mercy (*οἰκτείρησον*) on me, O Lord"** [^2050]. The solemn singing of the psalm at the beginning of Vespers at the Vigil was introduced, of course, only by the Jerusalem Typika, the most ancient extant copies of which, such as the Georgian Shiomgvime and the Greek Sevastyanov of the 13th c., and the Greek Synodal of the 14th c., speak of singing the psalm in Tone 8 [^2051], whereas the most ancient Slavic [manuscripts] (14th c.) are silent regarding the tone [^2052]. Neither group indicates refrains for the psalm. Nor do the 16th-century manuscripts of the Typikon indicate them [^2053]. Yet all the most ancient Typika unanimously demand an elevation of the voice, and in general a more solemn singing, beginning from the middle of verse 28 of the psalm:

**"When Thou openest Thy hand"** (the description of the 6th day of creation and of Providence): "and when we arrive (*φθάσωμεν*) (Slav. 14th c.: 'after the verse is spoken by the canonarch, that is') at the verse: **'When Thou openest (*Ἀνοίξαντος*) Thy hand,'** the ecclesiarch makes a bow (*μετάνοιαν*) unto the superior, and the superior, or if he is not present, the ecclesiarch, lifts up the voice higher upon this verse (*ἀναφωνεῖ τὸν στίχον ὑψηλότερον*) (+ Shiomgvime and Synodal)" [^2054].

Unto this the Slavic [manuscripts] of the 14th c. add:

"and upon the conclusion of the psalm, both choirs having assembled together chant the verse: **'As Thy works have been magnified, Glory'**—the same tone (the same), and **'Both now'**—likewise. And they withdraw unto their places, and the first choir chants: **'alea alea'** (*alleluia*) **'glory to Thee, O God'**" [^2055].

Refrains unto the psalm are first indicated in ancient Horologia (*Chasoslovy*). Thus, in the Horologion of the Krakow edition of 1491, they are inserted in the text in cinnabar (which we replace with italics) after the following verses of the psalm:

"**'Bless the Lord, O my soul.'** Refrain: *'Blessed art Thou, O Lord...'* **'And His ministers a burning flame'** (v. 4). *'Marvelous are Thy works, O Lord...'* **'From the midst of the rocks shall they give voice'** (v. 12). *'Glory to Thee, O Lord, Who hast made all things...'* **'When Thou openest Thy hand, all things shall be filled with goodness'** (v. 28). *'Glory to Thee, O Lord, anene naana nea nene nayyinane* [^2056] *Who hast made all things...'* **'And the wicked, so that they be no more. Bless the Lord, O my soul'** [^2057] (v. 35, the last)."

The same refrains and at the same places *(Orig. p. 506)* of the psalm are also indicated by the present Old Believer Typikon, but it prescribes for singing not the entire psalm, but selected verses of it [^2058].

## Actions of the Priest during the Introductory Psalm

The singing of the introductory psalm, despite all its solemnity, is not accompanied by any ceremonies. Censing, as we have seen, must conclude prior unto it. On the contrary, from the beginning of its singing the priest, as it were, leaves off the performance of the service for a time: together with the paraecclesiarch who took part in the censing, having exited the sanctuary, they make before the Holy Doors—it is presupposed, having closed them beforehand—three bows (*μετάνοια*); then, turning back, they make a bow unto the superior and one unto each of the two choirs, and withdraw unto their places (*στασίδια*) [^2059]. But when they begin to chant **"In wisdom hast Thou made them all"** and **"Glory to Thee, O Lord, Who hast made all things,"** that is, verse 24 of the psalm (of all 35 verses) with its refrain, the priest approaches the Holy Doors again, and here in epitrachelion with uncovered head (*ἀσκεπής*) reads (*λέγει*) the Prayers of Light, which contain a supplication for all things needful for the evening and thereby answer unto the praise of the introductory psalm for the past day. These prayers are read before the Holy Doors because the Entrance into the sanctuary has not yet taken place. For this reason, in comparison with these prayers, the Prayer of the Entrance occupies a higher rank, and a yet higher one—the Prayer at the Bowing of Heads, which is read before the Holy Table.

Ancient Typika exhibit slight differences here from the present practice. The most ancient Greek [manuscripts] and the Shiomgvime speak of one bow by the priest unto the Holy Doors and one unto each choir (3 bows instead of the present 6); *(Orig. p. 507)* the most ancient Slavic has already 3 bows unto the Holy Doors (5 bows); neither mentions a bow unto the superior; 16th-century copies and the Old Believer [Typikon] agree with the present. More significant is the difference that the Greek and Shiomgvime appoint the reading of the Prayers of Light from **"When Thou openest Thy hand,"** that is, 4 verses of the psalm later than the present, from verse 28; but the most ancient Slavic (14th c.) and the Order (*Diataxis*) of Patriarch Philotheus are already like the present. The change was occasioned, perhaps, by the shortening of the chants. Copies of the 16th c. and the Old Believer [edition], instead of the present "in epitrachelion" (which is absent in all ancient [witnesses]), have: "and taking the epitrachelion and signing it with his hand crosswise and kissing it, he places it upon himself" [^2060]. This assumes the practice, observed even now in the East and in Greece, that the priest vests in the epitrachelion each time only for the duration of the prayers and sacred actions, while during the entire remaining time of the service he stands without it in the rank of the rest of the brethren; in view of this, the epitrachelion is hung on the front side of the iconostasis by the Holy Doors [^2061].

# THE PRAYERS OF LIGHT

The prayers read by the priest during the singing of the introductory psalm are termed "Prayers of Light," *εὐχαὶ τοῦ λυχνικοῦ* (*euchai tou lychnikou*), that is, prayers of the evening office (Vespers was called *τὸ λυχνικόν* / *to lychnikon*, "the Lucernarium" or "Office of the Lighting of Lamps," already in the 4th c.), since these are almost all the prayers of the priest at Vespers, and in antiquity they were distributed throughout various moments of this service. They are appointed in the sacred number of 7, which corresponds also unto the 7 days of creation and providence celebrated during their reading; at Matins, corresponding unto the greater length and importance of that service, analogous prayers are appointed likewise in a sacred number, but of 12. In their content, neither each of the Prayers of Light individually, nor, still less, their entire sequence, presents anything systematic. Nevertheless, each succeeding prayer, directing attention unto a new aspect of the divine essence, supplements in some measure the petitions of the preceding ones. The 1st, calling upon the divine mercy and longsuffering, these fundamental attributes of His, as an introductory prayer, asks first of all that He hear our supplication, direct us generally upon the path of God, and impart a joyful sense of the fear of God; the prayer has a concluding doxology identical with the exclamation of the Great Litany. The 2nd and 3rd prayers are of a penitential character, wherein one, moreover, asks for spiritual enlightenment and a sinless remainder of the day, while the other asks for the fulfillment of all our petitions that are full of hope in God, and for the granting unto us not only of fear before God (as in the 1st prayer), but also of love toward Him; the prayers conclude with the exclamations of the 2nd and 3rd litanies (the Little Litanies) of Vespers. The 4th prayer—of a joyful character—commemorating the angelic doxologies unto God, asks to unite with *(Orig. p. 508)* them our praise as well, now and in eternity; as its concluding doxology it has once again the exclamation of the Great Litany [^2062]. The 5th prayer, directing attention unto the Providence of God, which is unshaken by our sins, asks for preservation from them during the remainder of the day and throughout our whole life; it has a doxology nearly identical with the exclamation of the litany before the Canon at Matins and with the Liturgical exclamation before Communion. The 6th prayer, directing attention not only unto the Providence of God (cf. the 5th prayer), which testifieth unto the majesty, unsearchability, and goodness of God, but also unto the Kingdom promised unto us [^2063], once again (cf. the 2nd and 5th prayers) asks for a sinless remainder of the day. Exceptional in its content and length among the other Prayers of Light is the 7th. Directing our gaze toward the majesty, immortality, and light-bearing nature of God, and surveying the content not only of Vespers (expressions are borrowed from Psalms 103 and 140 [104 and 141 MT]), but also of Compline (there is an expression from Psalm 90 [91 MT] and the final prayer of Compline), it contains only a single petition for a sinless and blessed evening, night, and (already) morning.

The Prayers of Light, read at present during the introductory psalm, are more ancient than the use of this psalm at Vespers, and therefore they were originally attached not unto this psalm, but unto the so-called antiphons of Vespers, that is, unto psalms chanted by verses with special refrains, resembling the refrains unto our present Liturgical antiphons: **"Save us, O Son of God... through the prayers of the Theotokos,"** etc. In certain ancient Euchologia (ca. 13th c.) the Vesper prayers are entitled "Prayer of the 1st Antiphon," "Prayer of the 2nd Antiphon" [^2064]. Such titles are encountered even in copies of the 16th c. [^2065] In the most ancient Euchologia known at present (8th–10th cc.), however, the Vesper prayers are simply numbered [^2066], which perhaps indicates that already by that time they had been removed from their former locations and assigned unto a single moment of Vespers [^2067]. The simplest and, presumably, the most ancient practice for these prayers among known monuments—notwithstanding the comparatively late era of the manuscript (16th c.)—is represented, apparently, by the Georgian Euchologion of the Tiflis Ecclesiastical Museum, which indicates in the section entitled: *(Orig. p. 509)* "Sunday Prayers of the Antiphons and of Vespers, When the Priest Vests and a Vigil Occurs," the following order of Vesper prayers, significantly different from ours. Giving a detailed order of Vespers, this Euchologion does not mention the introductory psalm, but begins with the naming of the first three of our present prayers, calling them the prayers of the 1st, 2nd, and 3rd antiphons and appointing after each of them a little litany with the exclamation that serves as the conclusion of the prayer; thereupon, at various points in Vespers, it indicates 5 more prayers, and among them our present 7th prayer at **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** [^2068]. A Georgian manuscript of the Imperial Public Library No. 208 (16th c.), which gives the order of Vespers with slight differences from ours—although Vespers here has Psalm 103—indicates the same three prayers (the first three of our present ones) not at the psalm, but at the three antiphons of the Vesper kathisma, and besides them at various points of Vespers the same 5 additional prayers, and among them our present 7th prayer at **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"** [^2069]. Close unto this is the practice given by the *Sluzhebnik* in MS No. 518 of the Sophia Library of the St. Petersburg Academy, where of the Vesper prayers the three present ones are indicated at the beginning and the present 7th at **"Now lettest Thou"** [^2070]. Thus, the first 3 Prayers of Light from antiquity occupied their present position in the order of Vespers, namely, they were read at the very beginning of Vespers (at its initial 3 antiphons, before Psalm 103 was introduced here, and subsequently during this psalm).

Such a position these prayers hold immovably in all preserved monuments, whereas all the remaining prayers are arranged in different monuments in the most diverse order, and are not all indicated by all monuments [^2071]. These three prayers, consequently, constitute the most ancient nucleus of the Prayers of Light. Very soon this sacred number of theirs began to increase, mostly by drawing into their group prayers from other parts of Vespers. The *Sluzhebnik* of the 13th c. from the St. Petersburg Sophia Library No. 524 already has 4 prayers at the beginning of Vespers (the 4th being our present 6th) [^2072]. But, of course, uniformity in this regard could not exist in that era: fluctuation in the number of prayers continues down unto the 17th c. Nevertheless, it is characteristic that in the 14th c. the most widely accepted number of prayers, in Russia at least, was 6: Metropolitan Cyprian (1390–1405), in answer unto the question of Abbot Athanasius regarding the number of evening and morning prayers, replies: "at Vespers there are six prayers, the seventh is the entrance prayer, and the eighth is upon the completion of Vespers and after the exclamation" [^2073]. From this it was but one step unto the present practice with its 7 prayers in one group and two prayers at other places of Vespers. A similar practice, with slight differences not only in the arrangement of the prayers, but at times also in their composition, is represented by a series of monuments of the 15th–16th centuries, although the number of Vesper prayers in these monuments is still very diverse and *(Orig. p. 510)* reaches 9, 10, and 11 [^2074], but including herein also the prayers at other places of Vespers: at the Entrance, at the Augmented Litany, and at the Bowing of Heads; while in the group of prayers for the introductory psalm the majority of these monuments indicate either 8 or 7 [^2075]. Those having 8 add unto the present ones a prayer beginning with the words: **"Blessed art Thou, O Lord God Almighty, Who knowest the mind of man"** (*Благословен еси Господи Боже Вседержителю, сведый ум человечь*), which is present in many ancient Greek Euchologia beginning with the Euchologia of the 8th c. [^2076], wherein this prayer occupies mostly the 4th or 5th place and disrupts the agreement in the numbering of subsequent prayers with our present ones.
