In the number of 8 and with the indicated redundant prayer, the Prayers of Light are contained also in a series of the first printed editions of the *Sluzhebnik*, beginning with the Moscow edition of 1602 and the Striatyn edition of 1604, and ending with the Moscow edition of 1652. But in the *Sluzhebnik* of the Kyiv edition of 1629 by Metropolitan Peter Mohyla, regarding the prayer **"Blessed art Thou, O God Almighty, Who knowest the mind of man"** (the 5th), the following remark is made: "this prayer is not in the Greek from which this recension was corrected; read it if thou wilt." For the first time this prayer was omitted, and the Prayers of Light definitively assumed their present composition in the number of 7, in the Moscow *Sluzhebnik* of 1655. But in southern Russian editions down unto the end of the 18th c., the indicated prayer was retained with the above-cited remark of Metropolitan Peter Mohyla (it is present in the Chernihiv edition of 1797) [^2077].

# THE GREAT LITANY

## The Litany

*(Orig. p. 510)*
The song of praise unto God which Psalm 103 presents is not only accompanied and supplemented by the secret prayers of the priest, but is also replaced by the prayer of all the faithful. Such a prayer is the litany following the introductory psalm. The litany is a prayer of an entirely special character. It is calculated to tire the attention as little as possible, and to arouse it constantly. In view of this, a unified prayer is divided into a series of brief, distinct petitions, which are interrupted by the chanting of even *(Orig. p. 511)* more concise prayerful exclamations: **"Lord, have mercy"** (*Kyrie eleison*), **"Grant this, O Lord."** The name of this prayer, "litany," *ἐκτενή* (*ektenē*) [^2078]—an intense, diligent supplication—is, however, in Greek liturgical books applied only unto that which is termed among us the "Augmented Litany" (*sugubaya ekteniya*); litany in general is termed there *συναπτή* (*synaptē*, scil. *εὐχή*)—a connected or composite prayer. The name of litany was applied unto prayers of this kind because they represent especially fervent prayers offered up by all the faithful. With the purpose of drawing all into participation in them, they are intoned not by the priest—a person who by original custom was of advanced age ("presbyter")—but by the deacon; for which reason in ancient liturgical monuments the litany was termed *τὰ διακονικά* (*ta diakonika*), "diaconals" [^2079]. In view of the fact that the deacon is not a celebrant in the proper sense, the litany is composed not in properly prayerful expressions, but in expressions inviting unto prayer and indicating its objects. Yet from time to time (at the end of the Great Litany, in the final petition, and at the beginning of the Augmented and Petitional Litanies) this invitation unto prayer rises unto genuine prayer (**"Help us, save us..."**, **"Have mercy on us, O God..."**).

## The Great Litany: Its Character and Content

The first litany at the most important daily services is the Great Litany (*ἡ συναπτὴ μεγάλη* / *hē synaptē megalē*), which in antiquity was also termed *τὰ εἰρηνικά* (*ta eirēnika*), "peaceful" [petitions], that is, supplications (*αἰτήματα* / *aitēmata*; see Introductory Chapter, p. 345). From the three other kinds of litanies it is distinguished by the fullness of its content: not to speak of the Little Litany, which represents a simple abbreviation of the great one—whereas the Augmented Litany prays exclusively for persons, and the Petitional Litany for needs without distinction of persons, the Great Litany unites both supplications, so that the Augmented and Petitional are only a further unfolding of its content, for which reason it is placed at the very beginning of the service. Furthermore, from the other litanies it is distinguished by the sublimity and, as it were, mysteriousness of its content. Its supplication it begins not with any particular and everyday needs, even spiritual ones, but with that peace from above (*τῆς ἄνωθεν* / *tēs anōthen*), which the Apostle terms "surpassing all understanding" [^2080]. From these truly celestial heights the Great Litany in its 14 petitions (with the exclamation, 15) gradually descends unto circles closer and closer unto us: unto the world, unto the holy churches [^2081], their *(Orig. p. 512)* primates and ministers [^2082], unto the civil authority [^2083], our city (or monastery) and country and their needs, unto those who stand in greatest need of the help of God (**"For travelers by sea..."**—an enumeration in ascending order of the gravity of distress) [^2084], and only at the very end unto ourselves. The supplication concludes with a summons to turn for intercession in our needs, for which we have prayed, unto the saints, and especially unto the Mother of God, unto Whom are applied the same seven sublime titles that are applied unto Her in the liturgical exclamation **"Especially for our all-holy..."** (why, see below), to turn in sweet and tranquil hope for the fulfillment of the prayer. The conclusion of the litany is a doxology, wherein the glory of God is set forth both as the supreme ground for the fulfillment of our petition (as the glory of God is in general the foundation and goal of the world) [^2085] and which, as the supreme, angelic kind of prayer (see Introductory Chapter, p. 27), containing moreover the naming of the All-Holy Trinity (ibid., p. 17), the priest himself pronounces.

## History of the Great Litany: The Litany in First Clement

Already from the first century there has been preserved a prayer not only close in content unto the present Great Litany, but also termed *ἐκτενῆ τὴν δέησιν* (*ektenē tēn deēsin*). With such an "intense supplication" St. Clement, Bishop of Rome, counsels the Corinthian Christians to pray in his epistle written ca. 90–100, and adduces this supplication, taken, presumably, from the practice of the Roman Church:

"We ask (*ἀξιοῦμεν* / *axioumen*), O Lord, that Thou be our helper and protector; those of us in affliction *defend* [^2086], the humble *have mercy on*, the fallen raise up, unto those in need appear... [the infirm] *heal*, the wanderers of Thy people turn back, feed the hungry, ransom our prisoners, *raise up the sick*, comfort the fainthearted, that all the nations may know that Thou art God alone, and Jesus Christ Thy Servant, and we Thy people and the sheep of Thy pasture. Thou hast made manifest the everlasting constitution (*σύστασιν* / *systasin*) of the world through the works wrought (*διὰ τῶν ἐνεργουμένων* / *dia tōn energoumenōn*); Thou, O Lord, didst create the universe, faithful throughout all generations, righteous in judgments, marvelous in strength and majesty (cf. the exclamation), wise in creation and prudent in establishing that which hath been made, good in things visible and... unto those who trust in Thee; have mercy and compassion, forgive us our iniquities and unrighteousness and transgressions and shortcomings; reckon not every sin of Thy servants and handmaids, but cleanse us with the purifi*(Orig. p. 513)*cation of Thy truth and guide our steps to walk in holiness of heart and to do that which is good and well-pleasing before Thee and before our rulers (*ἀρχόντων* / *archontōn*). Yea, Lord, make Thy face to shine upon us for good in peace, that we may be shielded by Thy mighty hand and delivered from sin by Thy high arm, and deliver us from them that hate us unjustly. *Grant concord and peace unto us and unto all that dwell upon the earth*, as Thou didst give unto our fathers when they called upon Thee in faith and truth, to be obedient... and unto Thine all-virtuous (*παναρέτῳ* / *panaretō*) name. *Unto our rulers and governors (τοῖς τε ἄρχουσι καὶ ἡγουμένοις / tois te archousi kai hēgoumenois) upon earth Thou, O Lord, hast given the power of sovereignty through Thine awesome and ineffable might, that we, knowing the glory and honour given them by Thee, may submit ourselves unto them, in no way resisting Thy will; unto them, O Lord, grant health, peace, concord, and stability (εὐστάθειαν / eustatheian)*, that they may administer (*διέπειν* / *diepein*) the governance given them by Thee without stumbling; for Thou, O Lord, heavenly King of the ages, givest unto the sons of men glory and honour and power over that which is upon earth; do Thou, O Lord, direct their counsel according unto that which is good and well-pleasing in Thy sight, that administering in peace and gentleness the authority given them by Thee, they may find Thee merciful. Thou Who alone art able to do these things and far greater good with us, unto Thee do we make confession through the High Priest and Guardian of our souls, Jesus Christ, *through Whom be glory and majesty unto Thee, both now and unto all generations, and unto ages of ages. Amen*" [^2087].

## The Primary Source of the Great Litany

It is possible that this is a Eucharistic prayer;

the intercessory prayers of ancient liturgies recall it. Out of these latter prayers, which certain liturgies possessed prior unto the hallowing of the Gifts, and others after it, litanies arose. In later liturgies, both Eastern and Western, the intercessory Eucharistic prayer was pronounced solely by the priest. But the most ancient liturgies, presumably, drew the deacon into it as well. The deacon's exclamations at this prayer, which invited the people unto participation therein and announced for this purpose briefly the content of one or another of the most important parts of this prayer, gave rise unto the litanies. The manner and degree of this participation of the deacon, and following him the people, in the intercessory Eucharistic prayer were diverse in different liturgies. In the most ancient liturgies, if one regards as their representatives the liturgies of the Eastern culturally stationary Christian borderlands (Abyssinians, Copts, Persians, Syrians), this participation was very extensive. The deacon in his exclamations gave lengthy paraphrases of the priestly prayer (in an invitatory form), and the people responded unto these invitations unto prayer with entire prayers, rather than with brief exclamations alone, such as **"Lord, have mercy."**
*(Orig. p. 514)*
## The Litany in the Abyssinian Liturgy

Thus, in the Ethiopian (Abyssinian) Liturgy, after the part corresponding unto our Proskomedia and the initial exclamations of the priest,
"the deacon says: Stand up for prayer. Priest: Peace be unto all. People: And with thy spirit. D.: Stand up for prayer. Priest: Peace be unto all of you. P.: Lord, have mercy upon us. With thy spirit. The priest—a prayer analogous unto the following exclamation of the deacon and interrupted by an invitation of the priest himself: Pray.
> **Deacon:** "Ask and pray, that the Lord may have mercy upon us and spare us, and accept the prayer and supplication which is made for us by His saints, that, ever showing goodwill toward us, He may make us worthy of receiving and partaking of the blessed Mystery, and forgive us our sins. And all the people shall say thrice: Lord, have mercy. The priest—a prayer for those who have offered gifts. D.: Pray for those who have offered gifts. Priest—a prayer of similar content. After the Gospel, the deacon: Stand up for prayer. Priest: 'Peace" be unto all of you,' and he reads a prayer, whose petitions for various classes of the faithful or needs the deacon interrupts with exclamations: Pray for this Holy Church, one, Catholic and Apostolic, Orthodox in the Lord. People: Lord our God, grant us peace; Christ our King, have mercy upon us. D.: Pray for the archpastors, our Patriarch Abba N., the lord Archbishop of the great city of Alexandria, and our Metropolitan Abba N., and all Orthodox bishops, priests, and deacons. Pray for this Holy Church and our assembly therein. P.: Bless our assembly and preserve it in peace. After the Creed, the priest [recites] 'the prayer for perfect peace,' interrupted by the exclamation of the deacon: Pray for perfect peace and the mutual kiss [^2088] of the Apostles. Embrace one another; ye that do not communicate, depart... The priest continues the prayer, unto which the people respond: Christ our God, make us worthy to honor Thee with a holy and heavenly kiss, that we may glorify Thee with the Cherubim and Seraphim and cry aloud, saying: Holy... The priest—a brief prayer of thanksgiving content. Deac.: For our blessed and holy Patriarch N. and Metropolitan..., who in their prayers glorify Thee and give thanks unto Thee. Priest—a prayer with the commemoration of the saints and the faithful. People: Have mercy, O Lord, upon the souls of Thy servants who have eaten Thy Body and drunk Thy Blood and received rest in Thy faith" [^2089]."
*(Orig. p. 515)*
## The Litany in the Coptic Liturgy

As a further stage in the development of the litany one may recognize that form which the deacon's exclamations possess in the Coptic Liturgy attributed unto St. Cyril of Alexandria. Here, at the intercessory prayer before the hallowing of the Gifts, when the priest begins petitions for one or another class of the faithful or their needs, the deacon makes exclamations for them, after which the priest continues the prayer, preceding, interrupting, or concluding it with his **"Lord, have mercy."** The deacon's exclamations are such as these:
Pray for the peace of the one, Holy, Catholic, and Apostolic Church, for the salvation of peoples and the security of every place, and for the remission of our sins. Pray for our fathers and brethren. Pray for our fathers and brethren who travel. Pray for the temperature of the air and the fruits of the earth. Pray that Christ our God... (for the emperor). Pray for the fathers... (the departed archbishops). Pray for those who of their own means have made sacrifices and offerings. Pray for the life and prosperity of the Patriarch and our venerable father Archbishop Abba N., that Christ our God may preserve his life for many years and peaceful times and spare us. Pray for the rest of the Orthodox who are in all the earth, that Christ our God may be gracious unto them and have mercy on them and spare us. Pray for the security of this place and all places of our Orthodox hermit and monastic fathers and those who dwell in them, and for the security of the whole world, that Christ our God may preserve them from every evil and spare us. Pray for those standing here who participate with us in prayers, that Christ our God may preserve them and have mercy on them and spare us. Pray for all who have charged us to remember them in our prayers and petitions, that Christ our God may deliver them from every evil. Pray unto God with fear. Pray for this holy priestly assembly and for the entire order of Orthodox priests, that Christ our God may establish them in the Orthodox faith even unto their last breath. Pray for this assembly of ours and for every assembly of Orthodox peoples, that Christ our God may bless them and perfect them in peace and forgive us our sins [^2090].

## The Litany in the Syrian Liturgy

At a similar stage of development stand the deacon's exclamations in the Syrian Liturgy of the Apostle James, common unto the Melkites (Orthodox) and the Jacobites—and consequently having appeared prior unto the Monophysite heresy—and in the ancient Mozarabic (Southern Spanish) Liturgy.
In the former, after the part corresponding unto our Proskomedia and the exclamation of the priest **"Glory to the Father..."**, the deacon says: "For the tranquillity and peace of the whole world of believers in Christ from the ends even unto the ends of the universe, for the weak and the oppressed and suffering souls, for our fathers, brethren, and teachers, for the sins, transgressions, and offenses of us all, and for the faithful departed who have gone forth from us, with the offering of incense let us pray, O Lord." *(Orig. p. 516)*
The priest—a prayer of different, general content. A similar proclamation of the deacon occurs somewhat later. After the hallowing of the Gifts, the deacon says: Bless, master (*despota*). Let us pray and beseech the Lord our God at the present great and holy moment for our fathers and rulers... (that is, the Patriarch and bishops), let us pray unto the Lord. The priest—a prayer for them and the whole world. People: Amen. Deacon: Again and again we commemorate our faithful brethren, true Christians... (who have now asked to pray and are burdened with temptations and afflictions). The priest—a prayer with the response of the people: Amen. The deacon—a prayer for the sovereigns: Again and again we commemorate all faithful sovereigns, true Christians, who have erected and established the churches and monasteries of God in the four quarters of the earth, and the entire Christian commonwealth and the clergy and the faithful people, that they may prosper in virtues, let us pray unto the Lord. The priest—a prayer; the people—Amen. The deacon—commemoration of the saints: Again and again we commemorate... (the All-Holy Theotokos and the choirs of saints, with the naming of John the Baptist and Archdeacon Stephen)... for all of them let us pray unto the Lord. The priest—a prayer. The people—Amen. The deacon—commemoration of teachers: Again we commemorate before Thee, O Lord God, the teachers, interpreters of the undefiled faith... (namely, the departed among them), let us pray unto the Lord. The priest—a prayer. The people: Amen. The deacon—commemoration of the faithful departed: Again we commemorate... (with the ending): Therefore let us cry out and say: *Kyrie eleison* thrice. The priest—a prayer for the departed. People: Grant them rest, have mercy, and remit, O God, the sins... of us all... The priest—a prayer for the remission of sins and an unashamed end, with a doxology at the end. People: As it (Thy name) was and is unto generations of generations and unto the ages to come. Amen [^2091].

## The Litany in the Mozarabic Liturgy

In the Mozarabic Liturgy, something analogous unto the litany exists only on Holy Saturday (Holy Week in general preserves the greatest number of traces of ancient practice). Here, after each of the ten Old Testament readings (= paremias) a prayer is appointed according unto the following order:
After the 1st reading (Gen. 1–2), "the deacon says: For (*pro*) the feast of Pascha. Let us bend our knees (*flectamus genua*). Arise (*levate*)" [^2092]. With the title "Prayer" (*Oratio*) follows a brief prayer (of the priest), after which is the *Responsorium* (the response of the people): Amen; then the conclusion of the priestly prayer, like our exclamation, and again Amen. After the 2nd reading, the deacon says: For those who, being detained by diverse necessities, are unable to be present at Pascha. Let us bend our knees. Arise, etc. 3. For the priests and ministers. 4. For the unity of the Catholic faith. 5. For virgins (*virginibus*—according unto the priestly prayer: "as the glorious portion of Christ, in which the Catholic Church rejoiceth most of all"). 6. For those who *(Orig. p. 517)* do alms. 7. For travelers and those that sail by sea. 8. For the sick. 9. For penitents. 10. For the peace of the people and rulers [^2093].

## The Litany in the Liturgy of the Evangelist Mark

At a similar stage of development stand the deacon's petitions in the Coptic Liturgy of the Evangelist Mark, wherein after each of such petitions, having the form "Pray for such and such," follows a brief prayer of the priest. The petitions are the following:
"Pray for the living, for the sick, for the absent.—For the temperature of the air and the fruits of the earth, for the proper rising of the river waters (of the Nile), for favorable rains and crops.—For the health of men and beasts, for the good estate of the world and city,—for Christ-loving rulers. For captives, for the departed and those who make offering, for the afflicted, for the catechumens.—For the peace of the Holy, one, Catholic and Apostolic Orthodox Church.—For our Patriarch Pope [^2094], Father N., lord Archbishop of the great city of Alexandria. For this holy church and for our assemblies" [^2095].
The order of petitions here is the reverse of our present order—from bodily, particular, and most urgent needs unto spiritual and universal ones.

Yet Greek manuscripts of this liturgy correct this order, placing in the first place the petition for the peace of the Holy Church [^2096]. This liturgy, like the other Coptic ones, has the deacon's petitions after the hallowing of the Gifts.
Significantly more do the deacon's petitions in the most ancient Greek manuscript of the Liturgy of the Evangelist Mark, in the 11th-century Rossano Codex (in Calabria), recall our present litanies. Here the liturgy begins:
**"Peace be unto all,"** **"And to thy spirit."** Deacon: Pray (*προσεύξασθε* / *proseuxasthe*). People: **"Lord, have mercy"**—thrice. The priest—a prayer (of general content—thanksgiving for the help of God and a petition for it and for preservation from evil and sin), the end of which ("Through Whom and with Whom unto Thee be glory and dominion in the Holy Spirit") [is pronounced] aloud. People: Amen. Priest: **"Peace be unto all."** P.: **"And to thy spirit."** D.: Pray for the emperor. P.: **"Lord, have mercy"** thrice. The priest—a prayer. P.: Amen. Priest: **"Peace be unto all."** P.: **"And to thy spirit."** D.: Pray for the Pope and the bishop. P.: **"Lord, have mercy"** thrice. The priest—a prayer. Amen. **"Peace be unto all."** **"And to thy spirit."** D.: Stand up for prayer. P.: **"Lord, have mercy"** thrice. The Prayer of the Entrance. Amen. After the Entrance: D.: Unto prayer. Priest: **"Peace be unto all."** D.: Unto prayer (*Ἐπὶ προσευχήν* / *Epi proseuchēn*). P.: **"Lord, have mercy."** Priest—the prayer (of the Trisagion) with an exclamation. *(Orig. p. 518)* P.: Amen. After the Gospel, the deacon [intoneth] a litany (?), the priest—a prayer for diverse (bodily) needs. After the Creed, the deacon says: Stand up for prayer (*στάθητε* / *stathete*). Priest: **"Peace be unto all."** D.: Pray for those who bring offerings. Priest—a prayer for them [^2097].

## The Litany in the Nestorian Liturgy

Still closer unto our litanies are the litanies (expressly so called there) in the later recensions (yet generally very ancient) of the Mesopotamian-Persian Nestorian liturgies, whose most ancient recensions possess nothing at all corresponding unto our litanies (as among other liturgies is true only of the Roman and the Liturgy of the Apostle Peter [^2098]). Thus, the liturgy of the Malabar Christians (the Indian Nestorians) has two litanies: one after the Trisagion before the reading, the other after the hallowing of the Gifts; the first corresponds unto our Great and Augmented Litanies, the second unto the Petitional. The first:

"Deacon: Let us all stand uprightly and with joy and vigilance let us ask and say: Our Lord, have mercy on us. People: Our Lord, have mercy on us (the same response unto each of the twelve proclamations of the deacon). 2. Father of mercies and God of all comfort, we beseech Thee. 3. Our Savior, and the Giver of our salvation, and the Leader of all things, we beseech Thee. 4. For the peace and unity of the whole world and the good estate of all the Churches, we beseech Thee. 5. For the temperate balance of the air and season, the abundance of the fruits [of the earth], and of every ornament, we beseech Thee. 6. For our holy fathers, our Patriarch, the pastor of the whole Catholic Church, and the Bishop, that they may enjoy sound health, we beseech Thee. 7. Merciful God, Who in His love governeth all things, we beseech Thee. 8. Rich in mercy and abundant in goodwill, we beseech Thee. 9. Good Being and Giver of all gifts, we beseech Thee. 10. Glorious in heaven and exalted upon earth, we beseech Thee. 12. Immortal Nature and Dweller in the brightest light, we beseech Thee: save all, O Christ, Lord our God, by Thy grace, and multiply in us peace and love, and have mercy on us."
Thereupon follow the petitions of the deacon without response of the people, seventeen in number, beginning at times with the words "Let us pray," at times "Let us remember," "Let us make commemoration"; "Let us recall," "Pray ye," "For such and such," unto all of which together the people respond: Amen. These petitions, of which the first is "Let us pray, peace be with us," contain a prayer for hearing and mercy, for the Church, its everlasting peace, for bishops, the Patriarch, presbyters, deacons, the entire assembly; further, the "commemoration" of the "Most Blessed Virgin Mary, Mother of Christ and the Savior," with a prayer that the Spirit Who dwelt in Her may hallow us also; the commemoration of prophets, apostles, martyrs, confessors, with a prayer to imitate them; the commemoration of the "fathers" Nestorius, Diodore, Theodore, Ephrem, Abraham, Narses, and all others, with a prayer for the preservation of their teaching in the Church; further, the commemoration of the departed; a prayer for the country and state, for those who have fallen away from the faith, *(Orig. p. 519)* for the ailing, sick, and demon-possessed, for poor orphans, widows, the unfortunate and persecuted; and an invitation unto especially fervent prayer ("cry out from the whole heart...") for our sanctification; and in conclusion, a glorification of the mercy of God (corresponding unto our exclamation, yet pronounced by the deacon) [^2099].

## The Litany in the Armenian Liturgy

Already entirely close unto our litanies are the diaconal petitions in the Armenian Liturgy, attributed unto St. Gregory, the Illuminator of Armenia (4th c.). After several brief litanies (such a term is not employed) at the beginning of the liturgy, here, following immediately upon the Trisagion before the "psalm of the day" and the readings, there is appointed a litany replacing our Great and Augmented [Litanies], consisting of twelve petitions, with the response unto the first nine **"Lord, have mercy"**, unto the tenth **"Unto Thee, O Lord, let us commit ourselves"**, unto the eleventh **"Lord, have mercy"** thrice, and unto the twelfth a brief prayer of the priest for the acceptance of the prayer (corresponding unto the exclamation).

1. Again and again in peace let us pray unto the Lord. 2. For the peace of the whole world and the establishment of the Holy Church ("Let us pray unto the Lord" down unto the 9th petition). 3. For all holy and Orthodox bishops. 4. For our lord, the most holy Patriarch, for the health and salvation of his soul. 5. For our archbishop or bishop. 6. For the vartabeds (the episcopal council under the Catholicos), priests, deacons, subdeacons, and all the clergy of the Church. (7. Here for the sovereign and the reigning house our present petition is employed, but only among the Russian Armenians). 8. For the souls of the departed who have fallen asleep in the true and Orthodox faith in Christ. 9. Again for the unity of our true and holy faith. 10. Ourselves and one another let us commit unto the Lord God Almighty. 11. Have mercy upon us, O Lord our God, according unto Thy great mercy; let us all say with one accord. 12. Bless, master. The priest [recites] the prayer secretly [^2100].

## The Litany in the Ambrosian Liturgy

Closer even than this litany unto our Great Litany is the *prosphonesis* (proclamation) in the ancient rite of the Ambrosian Liturgy.

"Deacon: In accordance with the duty unto Divine peace and pardon (*Divinae pacis et indulgentiae munere*), imploring with the whole heart and the whole mind, we beseech Thee (*precamur te*). People: Lord, have mercy (*Domine miserere*, and so unto each petition). Deacon: For (*pro*) the Holy Catholic Church, which is here and dispersed throughout the whole world, we beseech Thee (so each petition concludes). For our Pope N. and our Pontiff (*pontifice*) N. and all their clergy, and all priests and ministers (*ministris*). For Thy servant N. the Emperor and Thy handmaid N. the Empress and all their army. For Thy servant N. our King and Prince (*duce*) and all his army. For the peace of the Churches, the calling of the gentiles, and the tranquillity of nations. For this city (*civitate*) and its preservation, and for all that dwell therein. For the temperate balance of the air (*aeris temperie*) and of the fruits (*fructuum*), and the fertility of the lands. For virgins, widows, orphans, prisoners, and penitents. For travelers, for those that sail by sea, *(Orig. p. 520)* in prisons, in bonds, in mines (*in metallis*), and in exile. For those who are held fast by diverse infirmities, who are tormented by unclean spirits. For those who in Thy Holy Church are bountiful in the fruits of mercy. Hear us in our every prayer and supplication, we beseech Thee. Let us all say. People: Lord, have mercy (*Domine miserere*). *Kyrie eleyson* thrice" [^2101].

## The Litany of the Testamentum and the Apostolic Constitutions

Yet in direct genetic dependence our litanies stand unto the diaconal prayers in the liturgies of the Syrian-Antiochene and Jerusalem recensions. The former are provided by the canonical-liturgical monuments of the 3rd century, the *Testamentum of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, and of the 4th–5th centuries, the *Apostolic Constitutions* (see concerning them the Introductory Chapter, pp. 70 et seq.). In both the one and the other such a diaconal prayer is appointed after the dismissal of the catechumens; in the second monument it is repeated also after the hallowing of the Gifts (the absence of a numeral in the second column signifies that the petition is found in the litany after the hallowing of the Gifts).

### Testamentum Domini

1. Let us pray unto the Lord God and our Savior Jesus Christ.
2. For the peace which is from heaven let us pray, that the Lord by His mercy may grant us peace.
3. For our faith let us pray, that the Lord may grant us unto the end to keep faithfully the faith which is in Him.
4. For concord and oneness of mind let us pray, that the Lord in oneness of mind may preserve our spirits.
5. For patience let us pray, that the Lord in all tribulations may grant patience unto the end.
*(Orig. p. 521)*
6. For the Apostles let us pray, that the Lord may grant us to be well-pleasing unto Him, even as they also were well-pleasing unto Him, and make us worthy of their inheritance.
7. For the holy prophets let us pray, that the Lord may number us with them.
8. For the holy confessors let us pray, that the Lord God may grant us with the same mind wherewith they ended their course to finish [our life].
9. For the bishop let us pray, that our Lord may preserve him long-lived in the faith, that rightly dividing the word of truth, he may preside over the Church in purity and without blemish.
10. For the presbyters let us pray, that the Lord may not take away from them the spirit of the presbyterate, and may grant them diligence and piety unto the end.
11. For the deacons let us pray, that the Lord may grant them to run their course blamelessly, to fulfill holiness, and may remember their labor and love.
12. For the presbyteresses let us pray, that the Lord may hear their supplication, and in perfection in the grace of the Spirit may preserve their hearts and help their labor.
13. For the subdeacons, readers, and deaconesses let us pray, that the Lord may grant them to receive their reward in patience.
14. For the faithful laity let us pray, that the Lord may grant them to keep the faith in perfection.
*(Orig. p. 522)*
15. For the catechumens let us pray, that the Lord may grant them to be worthy of the laver of remission and hallow them with the sign of holiness.
16. For the kingdom let us pray, that the Lord may grant it peace.
17. For the civil authorities let us pray, that the Lord may grant them understanding and His fear.
18. For the whole world let us pray, that the Lord may provide for each, granting unto each one that which is profitable.
19. For travelers and those that sail by sea let us pray, that the Lord may guide them with the right hand of mercy.
20. For those who endure persecutions let us pray, that the Lord may grant them patience and knowledge, and bestow upon them perfect labor.
21. For the departed who have passed away from the Church let us pray, that the Lord may grant them a place of rest.
*(Orig. p. 523)*

22. For those who have fallen let us pray, that the Lord may not remember their folly and may turn away His chastisement from them.
23. For ourselves likewise, all who stand in need of prayers, let us pray, that the Lord may shelter us, and keep us in a meek spirit.
24. Let us pray, let us beseech the Lord, that He may accept our prayers.
25. Let us arise in the Holy Spirit, that having become wise thereunto, we may grow in His grace, that in His name we may be glorified and upon the foundation of the Apostles be built up; and praying, let us beseech the Lord, that He may graciously accept our supplications [^2102].

*(Orig. p. 520)*
### Apostolic Constitutions

1. Let us pray unto God through His Christ; let us all with one accord pray unto God through His Christ.
2. For the peace and good estate of the world and the Holy Churches let us pray, that the God of all things may grant us His unceasing and inalienable peace, and keep us abiding in the fullness of virtue which is according unto godliness.
*(Orig. p. 521)*
3. For the Holy Catholic and Apostolic Church which is from the ends even unto the ends [of the earth] let us pray, that the Lord may preserve it unshaken and untossed by waves, and keep it until the end of the age founded upon the rock.
4. And for the holy diocese (*oblast'*) which is in this place let us pray, that the Lord of all things may account us worthy unstintingly to pursue His super-celestial hope and render unto Him the unceasing debt of supplication.
Let us commemorate the holy martyrs, that we may be accounted worthy to be partakers of their struggle.
5. For the whole episcopate under heaven, rightly dividing the word of Thy truth, let us pray; and for our bishop James and his parishes (*oblasti*) let us pray; for our bishop Clement and his parishes let us pray; for our bishop Evodius and his parishes let us pray; that the God of mercies may grant them unto His Holy Churches in health, honor, length of days, and bestow upon them an honorable old age in godliness and righteousness.
6. And for our presbyters let us pray, that the Lord may deliver them from every unseemly and evil deed, and grant them a presbyterate sound and honorable.
7. For the whole diaconate and ministry (*hypēresia*) in Christ let us pray, that the Lord may grant them a blameless ministry.
8. For readers, singers, virgins, widows, and orphans let us pray; for those who are in marriage and childbearing let us pray, that the Lord may have mercy upon them all.
9. For eunuchs who walk in holiness let us pray.
10. For those who are in continence and piety let us pray.
11. For those who bear fruit in the holy churches and give alms unto the poor let us pray; and for *(Orig. p. 522)* those who offer sacrifices and firstfruits unto the Lord our God let us pray, that the All-Good God may recompense them with His heavenly gifts, and grant them a hundredfold in the present world, and in that which is to come everlasting life, and bestow upon them eternal things instead of temporal, heavenly things instead of earthly.
12. For our newly enlightened brethren let us pray, that the Lord may confirm and strengthen them.
For kings and those that are in authority (*hyperochē*) let us pray, that they may be peaceably inclined toward us, that we may lead a quiet and tranquil life in all godliness and purity.
For the temperate balance of the air and the ripening of the fruits let us pray.
13. For our brethren that are in infirmity let us pray, that the Lord may deliver them from every sickness.
14. For travelers and those that sail by sea let us pray.
15. For those who are in the mines, in banishment, in prisons, and in bonds for the sake of the name of the Lord.
16. For those who labor in bitter servitude (*douleia*) let us pray.
17. For our enemies and those that hate us let us pray; for those who persecute us for the sake of the name of the Lord let us pray, that the Lord, having subdued their wrath, may scatter their fury against us.
18. For those who are outside and for the wandering let us pray, that the Lord may convert them.
19. Let us remember the infants of the Church, that the Lord, having perfected them in His fear, may bring them unto the measure of their stature.
For those who have fallen asleep in the faith let us pray.
*(Orig. p. 523)*
20. For one another let us pray, that the Lord by His grace may preserve and keep us unto the end, and deliver us from the evil one and from all the stumbling blocks of those that work iniquity, and shepherd us into His Heavenly Kingdom.
21. For every Christian soul let us pray.
22. Save us and raise us up, O God, by Thy mercy.
23. Let us arise [^2103]. Having prayed fervently, ourselves and one another let us commit unto the living God through His Christ [^2104].

Unto each petition the choir and the people, according unto the *Apostolic Constitutions*, respond **"Lord, have mercy"** [^2105].

## The Great Litany in the Liturgy of the Apostle James

In the proper sense, the first recension of the present Great Litany was the litany in the liturgy of the Jerusalem type, attributed unto the Apostle James—a liturgy in relation unto which the entire liturgy of the Asia Minor–Constantinopolitan recension (Basil the Great and John Chrysostom) is a simple abbreviation. Here the litany, it would seem, first received also its Greek name *συναπτή* (*synaptē*, already in 11th-century MSS), *καθολικὴ συναπτή* (*katholikē synaptē*) or simply *καθολική* (*katholikē*, 14th-century MSS). The litany corresponding unto our great one is here read in its full form after the kiss [of peace] before the Eucharistic prayer (anaphora), in an abbreviated form at the beginning of the liturgy, and in the number of several petitions with the petitions of the Augmented and Petitional Litanies before the Gospel and after the Gospel. In the most ancient Greek manuscript of the Liturgy of the Apostle James from the library of the University of Messina (10th c.) and in MS No. 1040 of the Sinai Library (11th c.), in the place of the first litany there is a lacuna. In its entirety in all four places of the liturgy the Great Litany is read by the manuscripts from the Basilian Monastery of Rossano (in Calabria, 11th c.) and Paris National Library No. 2509 (14th c.). The manuscript of the latter library No. 476 (14th c.) has only the opening words of the petitions, and for the litany after the kiss of peace gives only the beginning with a reference unto the earlier exposition. In its full scope (after the kiss of peace) the litany hath such a form (crosses prefixed denote petitions that enter also into the initial litany of the liturgy):

+ **"In peace let us pray unto the Lord. Save us, have mercy on us, be bountiful unto us** (Sinai MS: + **defend us**), **and preserve us, O God, by Thy grace.** + **For the peace from on high** *(Orig. p. 524)* **and the love of God toward mankind** (Sinai MS: + **oneness of mind**) **and the salvation of our souls, let us pray unto the Lord** (Paris MS No. 476 hath not this petition). + **For the peace of the whole world and the union of all the Holy Churches, let us pray unto the Lord. For this holy monastery** (the italics are absent in Paris MS No. 2509), **the Catholic and Apostolic Church which is from the ends of the earth even unto the ends thereof, let us pray unto the Lord.** (The Sinai MS instead of this petition hath: *For this holy monastery, Catholic and αποουσης (?), every city and countryside, and those who in Orthodox faith and piety of Christ dwell therein, for their peace and establishment, let us pray unto the Lord*—cf. below). + **For** **the salvation and protection of N., our most holy Patriarch** (in the initial litany the Rossano MS: *of our most venerable fathers N. and N., the most holy Patriarch*; the Paris [MS] names the names), **of all the clergy and the Christ-loving people, let us pray unto the Lord** (this petition is not in the litany after the kiss in the Sinai and Paris [MSS]). (+) [^2106] **For our most pious and God-crowned Orthodox sovereigns** (Messina: *For our most pious and Christ-loving sovereign*), **their entire court and army, for help from heaven, protection** (the italics are absent in Messina and Paris) **and victory for them, let us pray unto the Lord** (the petition is absent in Sinai). (+) [^2106] **For the holy city of Christ our God, and for this our reigning and God-named city, for every city and countryside, and for those who in Orthodox faith and the fear of God dwell therein, for their peace and establishment, let us pray unto the Lord** (the italics are absent in Paris; the first italicized phrase and "of God" are absent in Messina; the whole is absent in Sinai, but see above). **For those who bear fruit and do good works in the holy churches of God, who remember the poor, the widows and orphans, strangers and those in need, and for those who have charged us to remember them in prayers, let us pray unto the Lord** (in Messina in the margin, and the first participle is in the past tense: "who have borne fruit"). **For those who are in old age and infirmity, the sick, the suffering, those held fast by unclean spirits, for their speedy healing and salvation from God** (Sinai: *and for every Christian soul that is afflicted and oppressed, standing in need of God's mercy and help, for the healing of the ailing*), **let us pray unto the Lord** (the petition is absent in Messina). **For those who dwell in virginity and purity, in ascetic labor and honourable wedlock, for the holy fathers and brethren who labor in asceticism in the mountains and caves and dens of the earth, let us pray unto the Lord** (in Messina in the margin). **For travelers, seafarers, Christians living in foreign lands (*xeniteuontōn*—exiles/emigrants), and for our brethren that are in captivities and banishments, in prisons and bitter servitude, for the peaceful return of each unto his home with joy, let us pray unto the Lord** (absent in Messina). — **For our fathers and brethren who are present with us and pray together with us at this holy hour and at every season, for their diligence, labor, and zeal, let us pray unto the Lord** (the petition is absent in Messina, but instead thereof: *For Christians who have come and are coming to worship in these holy places of Christ, for the peaceful return of each of them shortly unto his own with joy*; in Sinai instead of the last two petitions before the petition for the aged and sick there is this: *For Christians who come to worship in these holy places of Christ , travelers, seafarers* [^2107], *exiles, and our brethren who are in capti*(Orig. p. 525)*vity, for the peaceful return of each of them unto his own*). **For every Christian soul that is afflicted and oppressed, standing in need of the mercy and help of God, for the turning back of the wandering, the health of the infirm, the deliverance of the captive, the repose of our fathers and brethren who have previously fallen asleep, let us pray unto the Lord** (before the italics is absent in Sinai, but see above; instead of the italics Messina hath: "fervently" (*ektenōs*), and before it the petition: "*For our ailing and laboring fathers and brethren, and those possessed by unclean spirits, for their speedy healing and salvation from God*"). + **For the remission of our sins and the pardon of our offenses, and that we may be delivered from all affliction, wrath, danger** (italics absent in Sinai) **and necessity, from the uprising of nations, let us pray unto the Lord. More fervently** (*ektenesteron*; absent in Messina and Sinai) **for the temperate balance of the air, peaceful rains, good dew** (italics absent in Messina), **an abundance of blessed** (Messina: *consecrated*) **fruits, the perfect beauty of the seasons, and for the crown of the year, let us pray unto the Lord.** (Only in Messina and Sinai: *For the commemoration* [Sinai: *and repose of all*] *of our holy* [Sinai: *and blessed*] *fathers, who from St. James the Apostle and Brother of the Lord and first Archbishop down unto* [a series of names differing in both MSS] *and the rest of our venerable fathers and brethren*). **That our supplication may be heard and well-pleasing before God, and that His rich mercies and bounties may be sent down upon us all, and that He may account all worthy of the Kingdom of Heaven, fervently** (Messina, Paris: *unto the Lord*) **let us pray** (the 1st and 2nd italics are absent in Paris; "fervently" is absent in Messina and Paris). + **Commemorating our all-holy, immaculate, most glorious, [(most)] blessed Lady, the Theotokos and Ever-Virgin Mary, [(the honorable bodiless Archangels)], the holy and blessed John the glorious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist, Stephen the First Deacon and Protomartyr, Moses, Aaron, Elijah, Elisha, Samuel, David, Daniel, the (holy) [divine, sacred, and glorious (Apostles)], (glorious) Prophets (and triumphantly victorious Martyrs), and all [with all] the saints and the righteous, that by their prayers and intercessions we may find mercy** (parentheses denote what is found only in the Messina MS; square brackets—in Sinai; italics—in Rossano and Paris; spaced type—in Rossano; for the initial litany instead of the names of the prophets after the Baptist: "the divine and all-praised Apostles, glorious Prophets, victorious Martyrs, and all the saints..."). **People: Lord, have mercy** thrice (absent in Messina and Sinai; in the initial litany of Rossano also after the 1st petition: "People: Lord, have mercy"; at the 4th litany the same [MS] and Paris No. 2509 at the end of the litany: "People: Unto Thee, O Lord"). The Sinai [MS] hath yet a petition for the offered Gifts, and after **"Let us stand aright"** directs the deacon standing on the right to read the diptychs of the living, giving two petitions: the 1st for the bishops with an enumeration of the names of the patriarchs, the 2nd for the rest of the clergy and Christians of diverse estates; the deacon standing on the left then reads the diptychs of the departed consisting of two petitions: the 1st for the saints with an enumeration of many names, beginning with the Mother of God, the 2nd for the departed Christians of diverse estates, beginning with the presbyters, with an enumeration of the names of the emperors; "and again the deacon on the right: *For the peace and good estate of the whole world and the union of all the Holy God's* *(Orig. p. 526)* *Orthodox Churches, and for those for whom each hath offered or hath in mind, and for the standing, Christ-loving people. People: And all and each*" [^2108].

## Ancient Variants of the Great Litany

Inasmuch as the Liturgies of Basil the Great and John Chrysostom were an abbreviation, it would seem, of the Jerusalem Liturgy of the Apostle James, so also the litanies therein were an abbreviation of the litany of the latter. In the Liturgies of Basil the Great and John Chrysostom the Great Litany appears in its present form from the most ancient among the complete manuscripts known today, the oldest of which do not, however, ascend earlier than the 11th century (8th–10th century manuscripts contain only priestly prayers). In comparison with the present text of the litany, manuscripts and early printed editions of the Sluzhebnik yield for the Great Litany only the following insignificant variant readings:
The 5th petition in Greek MSS of the 11th, and at times also 14th–16th c., begins: "For our bishop, the honorable presbyterate..."; in Greek MSS of the 12th c. and the majority of the 14th–15th c., in printed Greek, and in Slavic MSS: "For our archbishop, the honorable presbyterate..."; printed Slavic put here in the first place: "For the Patriarch", later ones: "For the Patriarch N...", still later: "For the Most Holy Governing Synod".
The 6th, 7th, and 8th petitions Greek MSS of the 11th c. do not have; from the 12th c. they appear in the form: "For our most pious and God-preserved (some: 'and Christ-loving') sovereigns, their entire court..."; so also in printed Greek, but later Greek frequently omit [them] (owing to Turkish rule); the most ancient Slavic MSS—14th c.: "For the orthodox prince, all his boyars, and his warriors"; somewhat later—15th c.: "For our pious and God-preserved princes (others: N)..."; or: "For the orthodox and God-preserved grand prince"; later still: "For the orthodox (others: and God-preserved) tsar and grand prince N"; so also the most ancient printed [editions]; later: + "and for his orthodox tsaritsa and grand duchess N, and for the orthodox tsarevnas"; "For our pious and God-preserved tsar N, and for the pious and God-preserved tsaritsa N, and for the noble tsarevich N, and for the noble tsarevnas N"; "For our sovereign the tsar and grand prince N, the sovereign tsaritsa and grand duchess N, our sovereign the tsarevich and grand prince"; still later in addition unto this: "for the most pious, most gentle, most autocratic, and God-preserved [emperor]... and for his most pious [empress]... and for the whole court...".
The 9th petition in the majority of Greek MSS of the 11th–17th c. and some Slavic of the 15th c.: "For this holy monastery and every city"; in some Greek MSS from the 15th c. and Slavic from the 13th c.: "For this city and every city"; in some Greek: "For the holy monastery or for the city"; in some Slavic: "If it be a monastery: For the holy monastery; but if it be in a city: For this city"; in others: "For this city and this holy monastery"; "For this city, if it be in a monastery: and for this holy monastery".
In the 12th petition "That we may be delivered", many MSS and printed editions after "wrath" have also "danger" (*kindynou*), besides "and necessity". After this petition 13th-century Georgian MSS have yet a petition: *(Orig. p. 527)* "And for all who stand in need of help from God, and for mercy upon them" (or "our souls").
The 13th and 14th petitions: **"Help us"** and **"Commemorating our all-holy"** are omitted by one Euchologion, presumably of the 12th–13th c., one of the 17th c., and the first Greek editions, placing also the exclamation of the Great Litany after the first Little Litany.
In the 14th petition (**"Commemorating our all-holy"**), "glorious" is found only in some 16th-century Greek MSS, printed Greek from 1838, and Slavic from 1655; some 12th-century Greek have before "with all the saints": "our father among the saints N" (the patron saint of the temple or the saint of the day?); Georgian MSS of the 13th and 17th c. have in this same place: "the holy Heavenly Hosts"; at the following Little Litany in this same place: "the holy glorious Prophet, Forerunner, and Baptist John", and at the following: "the holy and all-praised Apostles" [^2109].

## "Lord, Have Mercy" in the Litany

Inasmuch as the petitions of the litany are for the most part only an invitation unto prayer, the prayer itself in the litany is properly reduced unto the repetition of the concise **"Lord, have mercy."** Such a form of prayer cannot fail to appear poor. Yet scarcely could one find a more immediate and vivid expression for our fundamental and constant relationship unto God, from Whom man in every religion seeks above all mercy—help in needs and redemption from sins. Being so all-encompassing, this prayer formula is at the same time the simplest and most readily understood form of prayer for all, most suited unto believers of all stations, needs, and degrees of development. Without doubt, unto such merits of its content this prayerful exclamation oweth its widespread application and dissemination in Christian divine worship.

How much this prayer formula corresponds unto the fundamental religious needs of man is demonstrated by its use even in pagan religions. "Invoking God," says Epictetus, "we entreat him: Lord, have mercy (*Kyrie eleēson*)" [^2110]. In Virgil there is an address unto the gods: "have mercy upon me (*miserere mei*)", "have mercy." In the Old Testament this exclamation was heard in prayers almost as frequently as among us [^2111]. It is no wonder that in the Christian Church also we immediately encounter such a widespread application of it in divine worship [^2112] as it hath in the Jerusalem and Syrian Churches of the 4th–5th centuries, where the choir and people respond with it unto each petition of the litany, according unto the testimony of the 4th-century Pilgrim and the *Apostolic Constitutions* (see: Introductory Chapter, p. 142 and note 2 on that same page). It is remarkable, however, that the *Testamentum* *(Orig. p. 528)* *of Our Lord Jesus Christ*, likewise a monument of the Syrian Church, yet earlier than the *Apostolic Constitutions*, doth not speak of the response **"Lord, have mercy"** unto the petitions of its litany. In exactly the same manner, in the Liturgy of the Apostle James **"Lord, have mercy"** is appointed only at the conclusion of all the petitions with the rubric: "thrice." Nevertheless, this prayerful exclamation received ever broader dissemination not only throughout the whole East, where it is customary among the Syrians, Armenians, and Abyssinians (see Introductory Chapter, p. 299; above, p. 475, note), but also in the West, as is evident from the Ambrosian Liturgy and a series of other witnesses. According unto Blessed Augustine, it was used also among the Goths [^2113]. According unto later accounts, into the Roman Liturgy it was introduced by Pope St. Sylvester I (314–335) [^2114]. The Council of Vaison of 529 decrees: "Inasmuch as at the Apostolic See, as well as throughout all the Eastern and Italian provinces, there hath been introduced the sweet (*dulcis*) and exceedingly salutary custom of saying very frequently *Kyrie eleyson* with great feeling and compunction, it is pleasing unto us also that in all our churches there should be introduced this so salutary custom both for matins, and for masses, and for vespers" [^2115]. Pope Gregory the Great (590–604) in a letter unto John, Bishop of Syracuse, defending himself against reproaches that he had permitted certain innovations in divine worship in imitation of the Greeks, says: "*Kyrie eleyson* we neither have spoken nor do we speak as do the Greeks: among the Greeks all pronounce it together; whereas among us it is spoken by the clerics and responded unto by the people, and an equal number of times there is alternately spoken *Christe eleyson*, which among the Greeks is not pronounced at all" [^2116]. The capitularies of Charlemagne and Louis the Pious require that "Christians on Sundays, instead of standing at crossroads and in the streets and spending time in conversations, dances, and secular songs, should go unto the vigil and vespers, and walking both thither and back should sing their *Kyrie eleyson*"; likewise at funerals instead of diverse pagan rites, "that, if they know not the psalms, they should sing aloud *Kyrie eleyson, Christe eleyson*, men and women alternately" [^2117]. In Rome at the procession on the Feast of the Dormition the people sang antiphonally 300 times *Kyrie eleyson* and *Christe eleyson* [^2118].

### The Exclamation

The exclamations at the litanies, which were once the conclusions of the priestly prayers uttered before or after the litany, now—when such prayers are not appointed at the litanies or are uttered secretly—stand in connection with the petitions of the litany, indicating the foundation for their fulfillment now in the glory of God, now in His power, now in His goodness. The exclamation of the Great Litany points out such a foundation precisely in the glory of God, consequently, in the general perfection *(Orig. p. 529)* of the Divine essence, which evokes an involuntary veneration before Itself (thus, in comparison with the other exclamations, being the first at the services, it is distinguished by the universality of its content). At the same time it returns our thought from our needs and cares, with which the prayer of the litany was occupied, unto that glory of God which alone is the ultimate end of the world and of ourselves [^2119], and the sublime confession of which the Orthodox Church places at the head of all Her services in their opening exclamations.

### Development of the Exclamation

The exclamations at the litanies, as remarked above (see p. 462), possess a common origin with the Lesser Doxology, being, in the original form of the doxology "Unto Thee be glory unto the ages", an expansion of its second member "glory", whereas the present Lesser Doxology is an expansion of the first member "Unto Thee". Such an expansion is already provided upon the pages of the Apostolic Epistles. A one-member formula, besides that one: "Unto Him be dominion (*kratos*) unto the ages" [^2120]. Two-member formulae: "Honor and glory" (*timē kai doxa*), "Glory and dominion", "Glory and eternal dominion" [^2121]; later two-member formulae: "Glory and greatness" (*megalōsynē*), "Glory and power" (*dynamis*), "Glory and reverence" (*sebas*), "Glory and worship" (*proskynēsis*) [^2122]. Three-member formulae: "For Thine is the kingdom (*basileia*), the power, and the glory"; "Glory, honor, and reverence"; "Glory, reverence, and thanksgiving (*eucharistia*)" [^2123]. Four-member formulae: "Glory, greatness, dominion, and authority (*exousia*)"; "Blessing (*eulogia*) and honor and glory and dominion"; "Glory and greatness, dominion, honor"; "Glory, honor, dominion, greatness"; "Glory, honor, greatness, an everlasting throne (*thronos*)" [^2124]. Five-member formulae: "Glory, honor, dominion, and greatness, an everlasting throne"; "Glory, honor, praise (*ainos*), doxology (*doxologia*), thanksgiving"; "Glory, praise, magnificence (*megaloprepeia*), reverence, worship" [^2125]. A seven-member formula: "Blessing, and glory, and wisdom (*sophia*), and thanksgiving, and honor, and power, and might (*ischys*)" [^2126]. A further stage in the development of the exclamations, it would seem, is constituted by the glorification of the grace, mercy, and love toward mankind of God, which is not encountered in the Liturgy of the *Apostolic Constitutions* and is very common in the most ancient of the so-called "Apostolic Liturgies," *(Orig. p. 530)* the Liturgy of the Apostle James [^2127]. The formula "Glory and dominion" was especially customary among the Egyptians: the Liturgy of Mark hath it approximately 10 times, the Liturgy of James once, the *Apostolic Constitutions* once—yet not at the liturgy, but at the mealtime prayer—and the homilies of Chrysostom more frequently [^2128].

### The Great Litany at Vespers

The employment at Vespers and Matins of a prayer with such content as the Great Litany is based upon the well-known exhortation—expressed, moreover, with particular force (*parakalō*—"I beseech", I entreat)—of the Apostle Paul: "first of all that supplications, prayers, intercessions, and giving of thanks be made for all men: for kings, and for all that are in authority" [^2129]. "What doth this signify," asks St. John Chrysostom, "when the Apostle saith 'first of all'? It meaneth—at the daily assembly. The faithful know this, when morning and evening they offer their prayer for all men upon earth, for kings and all that are in authority, for the faithful" [^2130].

### Prayers for Peace and the Emperor at Ancient Vespers

Yet not from Chrysostom alone did there enter into custom among Christians a daily morning and evening prayer of such all-encompassing content, with the turning, moreover, of special attention therein unto persons in authority. Already in the Old Testament a special significance was attached unto prayer for civil authorities. According unto the testimony of the Prophet Baruch, the Babylonian Jews sent unto Jerusalem unto the High Priest a sum of money for sacrifices and prayer for King Nebuchadnezzar and his heir Belshazzar, "that their days may be upon earth as the days of heaven" [^2131]. According unto Josephus Flavius, in Jerusalem twice daily a sacrifice was offered for the Roman Caesar [^2132]. Unto the custom of daily, and moreover twice-daily, prayer for the whole world and for sovereigns the ancient Christian apologists appeal, for instance Tertullian (see Introductory Chapter, p. 84), in refutation of rumors concerning the misanthropy and unpatriotic character of Christians. St. Cyprian says that Christians "daily in the morning at morning worship and in the evening at evening worship pray for sovereigns" [^2133]. Against the Donatists, who had discarded prayer for kings and authorities, Optatus of Milevis says: "Entirely rightly doth Paul teach to pray for kings and for all authorities, even if the king were a pagan; all the more so if he *(Orig. p. 531)* be a Christian" [^2134] (the same thought is expressed by St. John Chrysostom in his homily upon the corresponding passage of 1 Timothy). With the adoption of Christianity by Constantine the Great, the names of the emperors began to be entered into the diptychs, consequently, to be commemorated at the liturgy before or after the hallowing of the Gifts; thus, the name of Constantine the Great was entered into the diptychs of the Constantinopolitan Church of the Holy Apostles built by him [^2135]; upon a column of the ancient Constantinopolitan Church of St. Laurence near the ambo were inscribed the names which the deacon read therefrom at the litany, and at the head of them stood the name of the emperor, and thereupon the bishop. Popes Felix III and Gelasius I (5th c.) state that the names of emperors were entered in the West, as in the East, into the diptychs [^2136]. When certain men "condemned the Emperor Anastasius as an adversary of the Council of Chalcedon, they excluded him from the sacred tablets" [^2137]. Maximus, Abbot of Chrysopolis (St. Maximus the Confessor, 7th c.), says against the Monothelites: "Among the sacred offerings upon the Holy Table, after the high priests, priests, and deacons, and the whole consecrated rank, there are commemorated with the laity the emperors, when the deacon saith: 'and those who have fallen asleep in the faith, Constantine, Constans, and the rest'; likewise he commemorates the living emperors after all the sacred persons" [^2138]. In the most ancient Roman sacramentaries—for example, that of Gregory the Great—in the prayer at the Canon of the Mass there is read: "*pro pontifice nostro N et pro rege nostro N*". Charlemagne at the Diet of Worms of 781 based the exemption of bishops and priests from military service upon the premise that "they must offer for the King and his army prayers, masses, and litanies" [^2139], and in his capitularies required that all priests "should offer constant prayers for the life and reign of our lord the Emperor, and the health of his sons and daughters" [^2140].

In the course of time, however, in the West there disappeared from the Canon of the Mass the commemoration of the king, perhaps with the appearance of heterodox monarchs in many states (or because the reading of the diptychs during the liturgy ceased altogether), for which reason Pope Pius V did not include this commemoration in his edition (1570) of the Missal (*Sluzhebnik*), reviewed and approved at the Council of Trent [^2141]. Nor is this commemoration present in the Canon of the present Latin Mass; nevertheless, upon royal anniversaries a special mass is celebrated for the king or queen, even should they be heterodox. Yet at the beginning of the liturgy, in the collect after the Gloria, *(Orig. p. 532)* as well as in a special Sunday and festival prayer, the sovereign is commemorated—in some countries alone, in others with his consort and family [^2142]—wherein the psalmic words are employed: "O Lord, save our King—or Emperor—N., and hear us in the day whensoever we call upon Thee" (Ps. 19:10 [LXX 19:10]).

The East, on the other hand, in this regard remained more faithful unto the Apostolic precept. In all Eastern liturgies there are petitions for the sovereign and civil authorities; only in the Coptic Liturgy of Basil the Great is this petition absent from the intercessory prayer after the hallowing of the Gifts, being present instead in the prayers of the liturgy prior unto its Canon; whereas in all the rest such a petition is found within the intercessory prayer, whether it was uttered after the hallowing of the Gifts (as in the Armenian Liturgy, in the Coptic of Gregory the Illuminator, in the Jerusalem Liturgy of the Apostle James, and in the Liturgies of Basil the Great and John Chrysostom), or immediately prior unto the hallowing of the Gifts (as in the Alexandrian Liturgy of the Evangelist Mark, in the Abyssinian, in the Coptic of St. Cyril of Alexandria, and in the Mesopotamian of the Apostles Addai and Mari) [^2143]. The omission of the petition for the sovereign and authorities in the intercessory prayer of certain liturgies caused this petition, in the Great Litany compiled from this prayer, to be placed after the petition for the clergy and the people. At present, petitions for the sovereign in litanies are omitted only in Turkey. Thus, in the *Hieratikon* of the Constantinople edition of 1895, at the Great Litanies of the Liturgy, Vespers, and Matins, there is set in place of the petition for the sovereign: "For pious and Orthodox Christians, let us pray unto the Lord." The petition for sovereigns is placed after the archbishop in brackets; in the Liturgy of Basil the Great it is absent. In the *Euchologion* of the Athens edition of 1902, in the Great Litany there is a petition for sovereigns, while in the Augmented Litany there is none.

## The Place of the Great Litany at Ancient Vespers

Inasmuch as Vespers and Matins borrowed their litanies from the Liturgy, at the former the Great Litany possessed precisely the same composition as at the latter. Yet not always at Vespers did the Great Litany, or the prayer corresponding unto it, occupy its present place—the very beginning of the service. Even at the Liturgy originally it stood not at the beginning, but in the middle—after the readings from Holy Scripture; so also in the *Apostolic Constitutions*; so also in the Liturgy of the Apostle James, where it hath its complete form after the Creed, while at the beginning of the Liturgy it stands in an abbreviated form. At the Vespers of the *Apostolic Constitutions* the above-cited litany hath its place after a series of litanies for the catechumens, the possessed, the candidates for illumination, and the penitents, immediately before the Litany of Supplication; at 4th-century Jerusalem Vespers—after the readings and the entrance of the bishop into the sanctuary (Introductory Chapter, pp. 136, 142). There are monuments even from the 16th century where Vespers begins with three antiphons with Little Litanies, and only after the prokeimenon hath a litany that represents the present Augmented Litany with an opening from the Great Litany, approximately in that form which the Augmented Litany hath in the Liturgy of the Apostle James (see Introductory Chapter, *(Orig. p. 533)* p. 377; see below, "The Augmented Litany"). Such, presumably, was also the case at the ancient Vespers of the Church of Constantinople, or the Chanted Rite (*Asmatike Akolouthia*); yet already under Symeon of Thessalonica (15th c.) even Chanted Vespers hath the Great Litany at the beginning. Vespers of the Studite-Jerusalem type received the Great Litany into its opening section, in all likelihood, much earlier: the Studite-Alexian Typikon of the 11th century presupposes it, it appears, in its present place.

### Who Pronounces the Great Litany at Vespers?

Although the litany is a diaconal prayer, nevertheless the present Typikon directs the priest to pronounce the Great Litany, as also the two following Little Litanies. And only the third Little Litany—after the 3rd antiphon of the Kathisma—is, according unto the Typikon, pronounced by the deacon. Having spoken of the reading of the Prayers of Light by the priest, the Typikon continues: "And when the psalm is finished, he saith the Great Litany: **In peace let us pray unto the Lord**, and after the litany the exclamation: **For unto Thee is due**." In this manner, according unto the mind of the Typikon, the participation of the deacon in the celebration of Vespers, which imparts unto the service a special solemnity, ought to begin only from **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Gospodi vozzvakh*), just as at Matins it begins from the Polyeleos or from the reading of the Gospel, if there be no Polyeleos (see below). In view of this, the initial censing at the All-Night Vigil likewise takes place without a deacon, whose duties are fulfilled by the paraecclesiarch. The requirement of such a late appearance of the deacon at Vespers emanates from the *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus (14th c.), wherein it is stated: "Upon the completion of the Prayers of Light, the priest says the Great Litany, and the deacon vests for the third antiphon of the Psalter and says the Little Litany." Yet this requirement is foreign unto ancient Greek and Slavic manuscripts of the Typikon, which assign all the litanies unto the deacon: "The Great Litany is by the deacon; and the priest exclaims: **'For unto Thee is due...'**, and at each antiphon (of the First Kathisma) he makes the Little Litany, and the priest exclaims" [^2144]. So also in the Georgian manuscript, and in the printed Greek editions [^2145]. Yet in later Slavic manuscripts and the Old Believer Typikon: "The priest or the deacon says the Great Litany" [^2146].

# "BLESSED IS THE MAN"

## The Kathisma at Vespers

After the Great Litany at Vespers there almost always followeth a Kathisma, which is omitted at Vespers on the Sundays and feast days themselves on account of fatigue from the vigil (Typikon, ch. 17 and September 15).

*(Orig. p. 534)*
With Saturday Vespers begins the weekly cycle of Kathismata, for which reason at this Vespers the First Kathisma is appointed, at Sunday Matins the 2nd and 3rd, and so forth. Although the selection of Kathismata for each day of the week, and even for the great feasts falling thereon, doth not correspond with the commemorations of that day, but followeth a simple turn of order—replacing thereby the singing of the entire Psalter within twenty-four hours, bequeathed by the ascetics—nevertheless scarcely could any other section of the Psalter be more suitable for Saturday-Sunday Vespers than the First Kathisma. Probably at the beginning of the Psalter, which was compiled after David by the collectors of his psalms and his imitators, the most poetic psalms were placed. Almost all the psalms of the First Kathisma (Psalms 1–8) admit of a Messianic application, foreshadowing under the image of the persecuted David the sufferings of the Savior. Certain of the psalms of this Kathisma, among other things on account of their singular loftiness, are taken as introductory psalms for Church services: the 3rd is the first in the morning Six Psalms; the 4th is the first at Great Compline; the 5th is the first at the First Hour; the 8th Psalm, concluding the First Kathisma, stands out among the rest by the loftiness of its poetry. Especially appropriate unto the present Vespers is the First Stasis (*Slava*) of the First Kathisma, containing Psalms 1–3, which stand in close connection one with another. "While the 1st Psalm praiseth the true servant of God, not determining whether this description is only ideal or whether in reality there existeth such an ever-green tree, and thereupon depicts the contrast unto him, without indicating the possibility and manner of salvation for those who walk along the false path unto destruction, the 2nd Psalm in expressions reminiscent of the 1st" [^2147] pointeth out in the invincible Anointed One of God and His dominion the sole salvation for the world; herein, unto the description given in the 2nd Psalm of the external activity of this Anointed One, in the 3rd Psalm there is added the depiction of His internal state. "The first three psalms of the Psalter," saith St. Symeon of Thessalonica, "refer preeminently unto the Lord; for the incarnate Word of God Himself was in truth the one blessed man—the nations rose up against Him—they that afflict Him were multiplied, His revilers and persecutors... But He—if He fell asleep by death, yet arose as from slumber" [^2148]. In the Roman Catholic Church Psalms 1–3 are employed alone out of the entire Psalter at Paschal Matins and are repeated at Matins of all eight days of the feast of Pascha [^2149].

## Manner of Execution of "Blessed is the Man"

It is no wonder if for such a Kathisma, and especially for its first antiphon, the Typikon appoints a particularly solemn execution. Passing over in silence the singing, or at least the melodic models, for all the Kathismata, the present Typikon indicates a chant tone only for this one and the 17th Kathisma: "Then we stichologize the Psalter in Tone 8, the First Kathisma, **Blessed is the man**, the first antiphon; the second and third antiphons we sing in the tone of the day." The present Kathisma is appointed, in this *(Orig. p. 535)* manner, to be sung in its diverse sections with diverse melodies, and the first antiphon in Tone 8—that same solemn tone in which the Introductory Psalm of Great Vespers is sung. Moreover, the first antiphon is sung with the refrain *Alleluia*, as are elsewhere only the Polyeleos psalms and sometimes the 17th Kathisma—a refrain employed among the ancient Hebrews at Pascha and the great feasts (see Introductory Chapter, p. 12) and forbidden among Roman Catholics during fasts. Concerning the refrain *Alleluia* unto the first antiphon of the First Kathisma, as also unto the Polyeleos psalms, the present Typikon and liturgical books do not speak, yet its use is founded upon musical tradition transmitted by neumatic and musical monuments. In Znamenny and Greek Chants *Alleluia* at **"Blessed is the man"** is appointed once, in Kievan Chant thrice [^2150].

## "Blessed is the Man" in Ancient Typika

Concerning the use of the First Kathisma at Sunday Vespers there is a witness from the 6th century (Introductory Chapter, p. 295), from a practice, however, where at the Sunday All-Night Vigil the entire Psalter was sung through (cf. at present at the conclusion of Matins Psalms 148–150). In an 8th-century Horologion according unto the rite of the Lavra of St. Sabbas, the First Kathisma is appointed at the beginning of all the services of the day as it were in the capacity of an independent office (ibid., p. 298). According unto the Studite-Alexian Typikon of the 11th–12th centuries, which presupposes this Kathisma, like all later Typika, at Sunday Vespers, for the 1st antiphon of the First Kathisma there existed a special chant melody of Tone 8, while its 2nd and 3rd Stases (*Slavy*) were sung in the tone occurring. As regards the refrain "Alleluia," it would seem that according unto this Typikon all Kathismata were sung with this refrain (Introductory Chapter, p. 365). Ancient manuscript copies of the Jerusalem Typikon speak concerning the execution of **"Blessed is the man"** in the following manner. A 13th-century Georgian manuscript: "We stichologize **Blessed is the man** in Tone 8; after (?) the 3rd Psalm we raise the voice a little."

According unto the Greek manuscript of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum, Sevastyanov Collection No. 491/35, 13th c., and Moscow Synodal Library No. 381, 13th–14th c.: "We stichologize **Blessed is the man** melodically (*meta melous*; No. 381: *idiomelōs*—idiomelon/self-toned) in Tone 8; at the second psalm we raise the voice (*anarrooumen*) a little" (No. 381: + "likewise also at the third"); thereupon the deacon makes the Little Litany; and the second and third antiphons in the tone of the day (No. 381: "the 2nd and 3rd antiphons according unto custom").

Slavic manuscript of the 14th century: "And we stichologize **Blessed is the man**; antiphon 1 we sing in the constant Tone 8, and the third psalm we sing a little higher; antiphons 2 and 3 in the present tone"; later manuscripts (15th–16th c.): "And we sing **Blessed is the man** with chant in Tone 8, and the other 2 Stases (*Slavy*) in the tone of the Octoechos" (the italics in certain 16th-c. manuscripts are absent) [^2151].

Old Believer Typikon: "We stichologize the Psalter in Tone 8. Rubric at Great Vespers as unto how many lines are sung of **Blessed is the man**, the 1st Stasis (*Slava*). The right choir begins: **Blessed is the man, alleluia**. Then the lesser right singer sings: **Who hath not walked in the counsel of the ungodly, alleluia**. Left [choir]: **And the way of the ungodly shall perish, alleluia**. Right: **Against the Lord and against His Christ, alleluia**. Left: **Blessed are all** *(Orig. p. 536)* **they that put their trust in Him, alleluia**. Right: **Arise, O Lord, save me, O my God, alleluia**. Left: **And Thy blessing is upon Thy people, alleluia**. Right side: **Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, alleluia**. **Both now**, left, **alleluia**. The right sings **alleluia** thrice. At the third psalm we raise [the melody] a little higher. The 2nd and 3rd Stases we sing in the tone of the day" [^2152]; according unto this Typikon, consequently, there are sung portions of the verses of Ps. 1:1 and 6 (the last verse), Ps. 2:2 and 12—the last [verse]. Ps. 3:8 and 9 (the two last [verses]), for the most part the conclusions of the verses, yet in Ps. 1:1 and Ps. 3:8 the first half of the verses (presumably on account of the length of these verses they were divided for singing into two parts, as also Ps. 2:12: **"Blessed are all they that put their trust in Him"**; the beginning of the chanted verse, perhaps, was proclaimed by the canonarch, and the choir only concluded the verse, as is done at present in the Kiev Caves Lavra). Yet the musical tradition of other chants for **"Blessed is the man"** (besides the Kievan Lavra chant) requires the singing of the entire verse. In comparison with the Old Believer Typikon, these chants do not have the verse **"Against the Lord and against His Christ"** and replace it with the 11th verse: **"Serve the Lord with fear"**; thus, from the 2nd psalm there are sung, as also from the 3rd, the two last verses, yet not entire.

# THE LITTLE LITANY AT THE VESPERAL KATHISMA

A special solemnity is imparted unto the First Kathisma likewise by the fact that after each Stasis (*Slava*) thereof a litany is appointed, whereas at Matins a litany is appointed only after an entire Kathisma, and at weekday Matins after a Kathisma there are no litanies at all. Such solemnity reminds of the origin of Vespers from the Liturgy and the agape meal, and constitutes a survival of the prayers and litanies at the initial antiphons of Chanted Vespers (from which the "little antiphons" at the conclusion of Vespers were distinguished—see Introductory Chapter, pp. 377 ff.). Litanies add prayer unto psalmic praise. For this purpose Little Litanies here suffice, which, being an abridgment of the recently uttered Great Litany, as it were merely resurrect its supplications in memory. Historically, the presence here of Little Litanies is explained by the prayers of the antiphons formerly situated at this place in Vespers, for which the litany served merely as an introduction in its 1st petition and a conclusion in its 2nd and 3rd petitions and exclamation, as is done at present at the Kneeling Prayers of Pentecost.
