The Little Litany repeated thrice throughout the First Kathisma is varied by its exclamation: at the 1st litany: **"For Thine is the might, and Thine is the kingdom and the power and the glory, of the Father..."**; at the 2nd: **"For Thou art a good God and lovest mankind, and unto Thee do we send up glory, unto the Father..."**; at the 3rd: **"For Thou art our God, a God that showeth mercy and saveth, and unto Thee do we send up glory..."** [^2153]. These exclamations all represent a gradual unfolding of the Divine attributes. If the exclamation of the Great Litany points indeterminately and generally unto the supreme worshipfulness of God (His majesty), *(Orig. p. 537)* then the second points unto His power and universal governance; the third unto His goodness and providence toward mankind; and the fourth unto the complete revelation of the Godhead in redemption.

## History of the Little Litany

The formula **"Again and again"** (*eti kai eti* / *paki i paki*) is found already in the *Apostolic Constitutions* (4th–5th c.) before the litany [^2154]. In the Liturgy of the Apostle James according unto the 11th-century Rossano Codex, before one of the opening prayers of the priest stands the proclamation of the deacon: **"Let us pray unto the Lord"**; before one of the subsequent prayers stands the deacon's exclamation: **"Again (*eti*) let us pray unto the Lord"** (at present among us such a formula is found in the petitions of the Augmented Litany, yet *eti* is there translated: "furthermore"); in the litany for the offered Gifts (after their hallowing) in this Liturgy, the first petition is: **"Again and again (*eti kai eti*) continually let us pray unto the Lord"**; the same occurs in the litany of thanksgiving after communion; in this manner, the proclamation **"Again and again"** appears only at the conclusion of the Liturgy; so likewise in the 14th-century copies of the same Liturgy, yet there the first diaconal proclamation is likewise: **"Again let us pray unto the Lord"** [^2155]. As we have seen (see above, p. 523), already the Liturgy of the Apostle James provides a litany corresponding unto our Great Litany, not always in one and the same scope, but at times in an abridged form; yet such an extensive abridgment thereof as is provided in the present Little Litany it knoweth not; nevertheless, the final litany in this Liturgy, that of thanksgiving after communion, consists of three petitions, like the present Little Litany. The most ancient formula of the Little Litany, apparently, began with **"Help us"** (*Zastupi* / *Antilabou*) (see Introductory Chapter, p. 377; cf. at the Vespers of Pentecost).

## Actions of the Clergy at the Vesperal Kathisma

Directing the priest to pronounce the Great Litany and the first two Little Litanies at Great Vespers, the Typikon assigns the final Little Litany at the Kathisma, before **"Lord, I have cried"**, to be pronounced by the deacon, perhaps as a token of its connection with **"Lord, I have cried"**, from which begins the participation of the deacon in the celebration of Vespers. "During the singing of the 3rd antiphon the deacon departs, and having made a bow unto the superior (asking thereby his blessing for participation in the service), enters the sanctuary; with him enters also the priest on duty; the deacon, taking his sticharion and orarion, receives a blessing from the priest and, kissing his right hand, vests in the sticharion according unto custom."

All manuscripts of the Jerusalem Typikon assign the Little Litanies, like the Great Litany, unto the deacon. The prescription of the present Typikon is taken from the *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus, where this is treated in greater detail:

"It is necessary to know that if the deacon does not come forth (*phorēsē* [does not vest]) at the beginning of Vespers, he vests during the singing of the 3rd antiphon, if there be a stichology; yet if there be none, during the singing of the Introductory Psalm, as hath been said. And he vests in this manner: he makes a bow unto the superior and enters by the side doors into the holy sanctuary; here he finds the priest standing, for he entered earlier; and having taken his sticharion, the deacon approaches the priest and says: 'Bless, *(Orig. p. 538)* Master, the sticharion with the orarion'; and the priest blesses it, saying: **'Blessed is our God always, now and ever and unto ages of ages.'** And having vested in this manner therein, the deacon, upon the conclusion of the stichology, goes forth and stands in the customary place and says the Little Litany" [^2156].

## Part One of Great Vespers in Historical Development

Both by its entire structure and by the solemnity of its execution, the beginning of Great Vespers strongly resembles Chanted Vespers, especially in its most ancient form, traces whereof, nevertheless, very few remain in its monuments of the 14th–16th centuries. Judging by these monuments, Vespers began with three antiphons (see Introductory Chapter, p. 377), each consisting of a single psalm sung throughout antiphonally with the refrain **"Alleluia"** or **"Glory to Thee, O God"**; these psalms, in all likelihood, were the 85th, at present the third psalm of the Ninth Hour; thereupon the 92nd Psalm, **"The Lord is King"** (*Gospod' votsarisya*), which hath at present provided the prokeimenon for Vespers; and finally—the 67th, **"Let God arise"** (*Da voskresnet Bog*) (see Introductory Chapter, p. 341), at present assigned only unto Paschal Vespers and Matins. Each antiphon had a priestly prayer and a Little Litany; whereas a lengthy litany, whether Great or Augmented, was, in all likelihood, uttered for the first time after the Entrance (see Introductory Chapter, p. 377). Behold, probably, that heritage which the Holy Sepulchre and Studite Typika received as the opening of Vespers (see Introductory Chapter, p. 357), and which they were obliged to rework in order to adapt it unto monastic divine worship, with its obligatory chanting through of the entire Psalter within a given period (see Introductory Chapter, pp. 189–190, 295). The result of such adaptation was the substitution, in place of the fixed psalms for the opening antiphons of Sunday Vespers, of the first section of the Psalter, while preserving both the former structure for the beginning of Vespers and the manner of chanting the psalms. And in place of the fixed "Sunday" psalms removed from the beginning of Vespers, there was introduced the fixed "evening" 103rd Psalm.

# "LORD, I HAVE CRIED"

After the Kathisma the Old Testament chants of Vespers are replaced by distinctively Christian ones: psalms give way unto stichera, and at the same time the fixed melodies of Vespers—for the Introductory Psalm and **"Blessed is the man"**—are replaced by alternating melodies, the tone of the Octoechos or the Menaion (in the strict sense this takes place when from the First Kathisma only its 1st antiphon is sung; if the entire Kathisma is sung, then already at its 2nd and 3rd antiphons the tone of the Octoechos begins). In view of this, upon the conclusion of the Kathisma with its litanies, the canonarch, whose duty it is to begin the most important chants, loudly announces this tone, namely the tone of the first stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**; consequently, on Sunday the *(Orig. p. 539)* recurring approaching tone of the Octoechos, and on feast days the tone of the first stichera from the Menaion, announcing it in the form: "The tone is such-and-such."

The 13th-century Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon and Slavic manuscripts do not mention such an announcement of the tone by the canonarch; yet according unto Greek manuscripts: "The monk appointed to canonarch, upon the conclusion of the stichology, proclaims the tone" [^2157].

## The Tones

Of the tones, whose application unto the service begins from this moment of the Vigil, there are eight, and each of them possesses its own musical coloring, difficult to define in words, just as in general the definition (interpretation) of this or that character of music is difficult. And this is all the more so in that the melodies themselves for a tone are not something immutably fixed, but have undergone and continue to undergo diverse modifications. Moreover, the melodies of one and the same tone are not identical for stichera, troparia, canons, and prokeimena. Nevertheless, the musical foundation across these diverse variations of a tone is even now one and the same, and hath been preserved more or less firmly throughout the centuries. Therefore a certain characterization of the tones is possible. Such a characterization was compiled by medieval Western theorists of church music for the Roman Catholic modes, and by virtue of the homogeneity of the musical structure of the Octoechos both among us and in the Western Church, founded upon the properties of the ancient Greek tetrachord, it is applicable unto our tones as well.

— The First Tone is simpler, more grave, and more majestic than the others; the Dorian mode, lying at its foundation, Plato and (pseudo-)Aristotle prefer unto others; it was employed for solemn, resounding hymns directed toward appeasing the anger of the deity, especially for hymns unto Apollo (*paean* / *paian* [Gr. ποαάν]) and at sacrificial libations (*spondē*); this musical mode was considered a guide unto a virtuous life; it was the favorite melody of the Arcadians and Lacedaemonians (according unto Polybius); according unto Athenaeus, it was practiced in the education of youths; Cassiodorus calls it the giver of chastity and producer of purity; the Pythagoreans animated themselves with it in the early morning for labor; Ptolemy, who assigns the eight melodies unto the eight heavenly spheres, compares the Dorian mode unto the sun: just as the sun dries up moisture and dispels darkness, so this mode dispels phlegm, sloth, sluggishness, sleep, sorrow, and confusion; it befitteth renowned men of rich gifts; it is sublime, devoid of luxury and licentiousness.

— At the foundation of the Second Tone lies the Lydian mode, which corresponds unto the sanguine temperament; it engenders meekness, benevolence, and pleasantness; it is delightful, breathes of pleasure, and was employed in dances; according unto Cassiodorus, it drives away superfluous anxieties and despair, and consoles the sorrowful; it is correlated with Jupiter.

— The Phrygian mode, lying at the foundation of the Third Tone, is compared unto the sea; it is stormy, rousing, provoking indignation; men were inspired by it unto battle; it is forceful and sharp, deeply piercing the soul; among poetic meters the anapest corresponds unto it; it contains large leaps in its melodic movement *(Orig. p. 540)* and suits the taste of impetuous, vehement, wrathful cholerics; it seeks harsh, martial words; Plato and Aristotle preferred it together with the Dorian mode above others, yet forbade its use unto youths in view of its passionate character.

— At the foundation of the Fourth Tone lies the Mixolydian mode, so named because it hath something in common with the Lydian mode (Tone 2); others call it Locrian (Julius Pollux); it exerts a twofold effect—now exciting unto joy, now suddenly inspiring sorrow; it was used by the ancients in tragedy because it inspired grief while having at the same time a certain measure of excitement and pleasantness; among the Pythagoreans it designated the harmony of the 7th and final heavenly sphere; by its wholeness and coherence it imparts a singular peace unto the soul; it is superior unto other modes by its gentle and pleasing modulations; unto those weighed down by worldly cares it inspires a longing for the heavenly, awakens the dulled mind, and more than other modes expresses the operation upon us of the grace of the Holy Spirit. — The other four tones are called "indirect" or "plagal" (*plagioi*) of the first four, representing toward them a certain antithesis (a negative pole).

Thus, the Fifth Tone hath at its foundation the Hypodorian mode, which, in contrast unto the Dorian, induced as it were slumber, for which reason the Pythagoreans employed it in the evening to assuage cares; it answers the taste of the listless, sorrowful, and unfortunate; it calms emotional agitations; Aristotle calls it majestic, steadfast, and grave, and compares its influence with the action upon the Earth of the Moon, the lowest planet, influencing humidity; it is a suppliant, somewhat weeping melody, full of entreaty for deliverance from calamity, disgrace, and bondage; it contains in itself something analogous unto paleness.

— The Sixth Tone hath at its foundation the Hypolydian mode, expressing feelings of piety, devotion, humanity, love, sorrow, and weeping; yet grief here is not suppliant, as in the preceding mode, but flows from love, devotion, and attachment (it was employed in prayers unto Venus); it stirred the soul and served as the language of the emotions; it was distinguished by a flowing and coherent progression of sounds.

— The Seventh Tone hath at its foundation the Hypophrygian mode, gentle, touching, pacifying, suppressing biliousness, soothing; unto it was ascribed even a certain flattery and deceptiveness, and it was suited unto Mercury; with it the Cretans and Lacedaemonians sounded the retreat from battle; it is suited unto words expressing exhortation, caress, and persuasion.

— The Hypomixolydian mode, corresponding unto the Eighth Tone, artificially added in order not to deprive the Mixolydian mode of its plagal counterpart, is likened unto the vault of heaven with its diversity of stars; it doth not express any single emotion, but is indifferent unto them; that which cannot be expressed by the other modes can be conveyed unto this one, in which respect it is akin unto Tone 1; it is leisurely pleasant and represents the immovability of future glory; it suits modest men endowed with a capacity for deep contemplation; it suits words concerning lofty matters, concerning the heavenly realm, and prayers for blessedness [^2158]; yet in general it is a melody worthy of its (final) *(Orig. p. 541)* place.

In the church tones the objectionable peculiarities of the Greek melodies found mitigation and transformation, being purified of everything sinful; only the general coloration remained the same. — As regards the number of the tones, eight could have been selected for it likewise on account of the symbolism of this number. It is regarded, according unto St. Gregory the Theologian and the writer calling himself Dionysius the Areopagite, as a symbol of eternity [^2159]. St. John of Damascus saw in the number seven the entirety of the present age, and in the number eight—the future state after the resurrection of the dead. "The divine worship of the Church, divided into or subsumed under the number eight, expresses in itself the thought that Christian life in time and in eternity consists in the perpetual glorification of the Lord, in eternal service unto Him" [^2160].

Concerning the adoption by the Church of Greek melodies for divine worship, witnesses exist already from the 3rd century (see Introductory Chapter, pp. 107–108); in the 4th–5th centuries there were no more than four melodies (ibid., pp. 160–161); unto Pope St. Gregory the Great (†604) in the West and St. John of Damascus (8th c.) in the East is attributed the introduction of the Octoechos [^2161] (ibid., pp. 334–335).

## The Psalms of "Lord, I Have Cried"

Under the title **"Lord, I have cried"** (*Kyrie ekekraxa* / *Gospodi vozzvakh*) are understood four psalms—headed by Ps. 140, **"Lord, I have cried"**; Ps. 141, **"With my voice unto the Lord have I cried"**; Ps. 129, **"Out of the depths have I cried unto Thee, O Lord"**; and Ps. 116, **"O praise the Lord, all ye nations"**. Of these psalms Ps. 140 is most suited unto the evening and its service, inasmuch as the singer therein entreats God to accept his prayer as an evening sacrifice; this petition, like the entire content of the psalm, shows that the psalm was sung by David, unto whom it is ascribed also in the Hebrew Bible, far from the Temple during one of his persecutions, for which reason the psalm in general contains a prayer for deliverance from enemies for the sake of the righteousness of the persecuted one. Homogeneous with it in content and circumstances of origin, Ps. 141 ("A contemplation of David; a prayer when he was in the cave") develops and intensifies this prayer (there: "Lord, I have cried unto Thee"—here: "with my voice unto the Lord have I cried", "I will pour out my supplication before Him"). The prayer of Ps. 141, in turn, is intensified in Ps. 129 (there: "with my voice... have I cried", here: "out of the depths have I cried", not simply "hear me", as in Ps. 140, or "attend unto my supplication", as in Ps. 141, but: "let Thine ears be attentive"). Unto Ps. 129 is joined the brief, two-verse Ps. 116, developing the final thought of Ps. 129: "For with the Lord there is mercy...": "For His mercy is confirmed upon us...". All these psalms, not to mention that they contain the thought of the replacement of the Old Testament sacrifice by a spiritual one, are applicable unto the Savior suffering and triumphing over His enemies, especially certain expressions, such as: **"Bring my soul out of prison"** (the grave and Hades)—the verse with which so fittingly begins the singing of the Sunday stichera; **"The righteous shall wait for me, until Thou shalt recompense me"** (the righteous *(Orig. p. 542)* in Hades waited to see how the work of Christ would end); **"I looked upon my right hand, and beheld, and there was none that would know me"** (the scattering of the Apostles during the sufferings of the Savior); **"Like a clod of earth is broken upon the ground"** (the rupture of the earth's crust during the earthquake).

Concerning the use of Ps. 140 at Vespers St. John Chrysostom speaks already (Introductory Chapter, p. 145). This psalm, in all likelihood, the *Apostolic Constitutions* (4th–5th c.) understand under the name of the "lucernarium" (*epilychnios*) psalm, beginning Vespers and exhausting its Old Testament material (ibid., p. 147). In the "Canon of Antiphons of the Psalms" attributed unto Patriarch Anthimus of Constantinople (6th c.), this psalm and the 85th have the antiphon: *kata lychnēs* ("from the lampstand") and together with the 12th psalm are called *lychnakoi*, as likewise in the 5th-century Alexandrian Codex of the Bible [^2162]. It is mentioned at Vespers by the most ancient Typika of the Great Church of Constantinople, and is present at Vespers in all Eastern rites and in all non-Orthodox rites of divine worship, excepting the Western, whereof the Roman rite hath all these psalms at Vespers once a week, the Ambrosian rite likewise, and on feast days always Ps. 129 (see Introductory Chapter, pp. 300, 301, 303). When there was at Vespers neither the 103rd Psalm nor the chanted antiphons, Ps. 140 was situated at its beginning; hence, perhaps, the assignment unto it of the censing which customarily began the service.

## The Initial Refrain

In view of the exceptional position which the psalms of **"Lord, I have cried"** occupy at Vespers, an especially solemn execution is assigned unto them. They are sung, similarly unto Ps. 103 and certain others, with special refrains, namely—at first with the refrain **"Hear me, O Lord"**, expressing the general thought of the psalm and composed from its words. This refrain is attached unto the verses of the psalm in that distinctive manner in which refrains are attached unto the so-called "antiphons" at the Liturgy. Namely—unto the first verse of the psalm the refrain is attached twice: the first time unto the incomplete verse, the second time unto the entire verse, whereby the opening words of the psalm are sung twice. Unto the second verse the refrain is attached once at the conclusion of the verse. The impression is produced that the chanter from fullness of feeling is as it were unable to utter the entire verse at once, and this is done by the other choir, beginning again the same verse from the start. For example, in the antiphons for Pascha from Ps. 65, instead of singing the 1st verse of this psalm with the refrain **"By the prayers of the Theotokos..."** in the following manner: "Shout with joy unto the Lord, all the earth; chant now unto His name, give glory unto His praise. By the prayers of the Theotokos, O Savior, save us", it is sung thus: "Shout with joy unto the Lord, all the earth. By the prayers of the Theotokos, O Savior, save us. And again (the second choir): Shout with joy unto the Lord, all the earth, (yet now with the addition of the remaining words of the verse:) chant now unto His name, give glory unto His praise. By the prayers of the Theotokos, O Savior, save us." In the same manner there is attached unto Ps. 140 its refrain **"Hear me, O Lord"**. There is sung: **"Lord, I have cried** *(Orig. p. 543)* **unto Thee, hear me"**, and the refrain: **"Hear me, O Lord"**; thereupon the 1st verse in full with its opening words already sung: **"Lord, I have cried unto Thee, hear me"**, etc., and the refrain: **"Hear me, O Lord"**; thereupon the 2nd verse now in a single delivery: **"Let my prayer be set forth..."**, etc., and the refrain **"Hear me, O Lord"**. The subsequent verses of the psalm, as also the subsequent psalms, are sung without a refrain.

The Studite-Alexian Typikon, certain manuscript copies of the Jerusalem Typikon—for example, Moscow Synodal Library No. 336/388 of the 16th century—and the Old Believer Typikon indicate the following refrains unto the psalms of **"Lord, I have cried"**: unto Ps. 140: **"Hear us, O Lord"** (according unto the MS of the Moscow Synodal Library: **"me"**); unto Ps. 141: **"I cried unto Thee, hear [me]"** (*Vozvakh Ti uslyshi*) (Studite according unto the Typography copy), or (Synodal MS) **"I cried unto Thee, hear me"**, or **"I cried unto Thee, O Lord, save me"** (Jerusalem), or the same without **"O Lord"** (Old Believer); unto Ps. 129: **"O God, Savior, have mercy"** (Studite Typography copy) or **"O Christ Savior, have mercy upon us"** (the rest) [^2163]. The second refrain is from Ps. 140:1 and represents an intensification of the first. The third refrain is a transition unto the stichera and, perhaps, the embryo thereof (so frequently do stichera end).

## Stichera

Upon the psalms of **"Lord, I have cried"** the Old Testament chant material of Vespers gradually passes into Christian: unto the final verses of these psalms church hymns are attached, and this alternate chanting signifies that the Old Testament accords with the New, according unto the word of Christ: "I came not to destroy the law, but to fulfill it" [^2164]. The church hymns attached in this manner unto the verses of the psalms received therefrom the designation of stichera—a genre of church hymns which by the Typikon is ranked below other genres of church hymns, such as the troparion, kontakion, exapostilarion (*svitilen*), hypakoē, and kathisma-hymn (*sidalen*), just as the chant melody of stichera is simpler than the melody of all the latter.

By stichera (*ta stichēra*, understanding *biblia*) among the Holy Fathers are not infrequently designated the poetic and didactic books of the Old Testament on account of their poetic meter [^2165]. In Greek Horologia so are called at times the Old Testament canticles—of Moses, Anna, and others. The designation "stichera" = little verse was most suited unto refrains taken from biblical psalms and canticles [^2166], and originally, perhaps, was applied only unto them: in the Holy Sepulchre Typikon of the 9th–11th centuries so are named the psalmic refrains unto the antiphons in the Passion service, for example: **"The rulers of the people"** (*Knyazi lyudstii*) [^2167].

*(Orig. p. 544)*
Refrains unto **"Lord, I have cried"** are mentioned already in the 6th–7th century in the well-known narrative concerning the visit of Sophronius and John Moschus unto Nilus of Sinai (Introductory Chapter, p. 295), yet they are here called troparia. In the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* (9th c.) the designation "sticheron" is applied unto the hymns at **"Lord, I have cried"**, at the Aposticha, and at the Praises, yet unto the first and the last not in all manuscripts of the *Hypotyposis* [^2168]. Even in the time of St. Symeon of Thessalonica (15th c.) this was not an exclusive or firmly established designation for the hymns attached unto the verses of the psalms, at least for the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**; these St. Symeon of Thessalonica designates as "hymns in idiomelic troparia (*hymnōn en tropariois idiomelois* [Gr. ὕμνων ἐν τροπαρίοις ἰδιομέλοις]), uttered together with the verses" [^2169] (perhaps by troparion is here understood the melody, the tone); the designation "sticheron" is applied by him only unto those at the Aposticha [^2170]. The word receives entirely its present application for the first time in the complete manuscripts of the Studite and Jerusalem Typika. — In their original form stichera were shorter than at present and in volume, presumably, equaled the verses of the psalms. According unto a Georgian manuscript reflecting the practice of the 6th–8th centuries, the sticheron unto St. Stephen was: **"Thou hast clothed thyself in holiness, O Stephen, archdeacon and protomartyr, companion of the Angels"** [^2171]. Such an appearance stichera still have in Chanted Vespers according unto Symeon of Thessalonica (Introductory Chapter, p. 342). At **"Lord, I have cried"** stichera not infrequently began with **"An evening sacrifice"** [^2172]: cf. the 1st Resurrection sticheron of Tone 1 and Tone 8 at **"Lord, I have cried"**.

## The Censing at "Lord, I Have Cried"

Both the content of the psalms of **"Lord, I have cried"** and the special solemnity of their execution demand that they be accompanied by censing. The censing at **"Lord, I have cried"** is performed by "the priest or the deacon"—the former, of course, when Vespers is served without a deacon. At Vespers outside the Vigil this is the first and only censing at this service. Of the other psalms, only the 118th is accompanied by censing.

The censing at **"Lord, I have cried"** the 13th-century Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon directs to be performed by the priest (although the litanies are pronounced by the deacon), yet all Greek and Slavic manuscripts direct it as in the present Typikon [^2173]. The *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus (14th c.) assigns it only unto the deacon, who receives a blessing from the priest with the words: "Bless, master, the censer"; the priest: **"Blessed is our God always, now and ever, and unto ages of ages"** [^2174] (an echo of the ancient beginning of Vespers with **"Lord, I have cried"**?).

*(Orig. p. 545)*

## The Number of Stichera

On Sunday the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** number 10, "for the sake of the perfection of this number," according unto St. Symeon of Thessalonica [^2175]. Besides Sunday, the same number of stichera and for the same reason is appointed at the Ascension and at the Vespers of the Sundays of Great Lent themselves (except Palm Sunday); in other instances 10 stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** occur on account of a concurrence of commemorations and an abundance of hymnographic material—thus on September 1 and at the Liturgies of the Presanctified Gifts. On the Twelve Great Feasts, excluding those always linked with Sunday—Palm Sunday and Pentecost—the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** are appointed for 8, including also at Pascha; so likewise for great saints; for lesser saints 6, and for small commemorations 3. In this manner, in the number of stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** Sunday surpasses the greatest feasts, notwithstanding that the Typikon in the number of these stichera clearly measures according unto the importance of the feast. If here a simple inconsistency does not obtain, then thereby, perhaps, the thought is instilled that Sunday is after all superior unto all other feasts in the event commemorated (before Pascha Vespers is still semi-lenten); moreover, a large number of stichera on Sundays was required by the almost invariable combination with them of the commemoration of a saint or another festal observance; with the normal number of stichera for commemorations of the latter kind being 3, there remain only 7 Resurrection stichera, one fewer than for great feasts.

The Western Studite Typika and the Evergetis Typikon had 8 stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** on Sunday: 4 Resurrection and 4 of the saint [^2176]; the Studite-Alexian Typikon had 9 [^2177], inasmuch as it tripled the 3 Resurrection stichera (if there was no commemoration of a great saint); the same occurs according unto the *Hypotyposis*, § 18, yet the passage is not read in all manuscripts; the Jerusalem Typikon from of old has 10 [^2178].

## The Composition of Stichera on Sunday

The customary composition of stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** is: 3 Resurrection stichera, 4 other Resurrection stichera called "Eastern" (*vostochny* / *anatolia*), and 3 from the Menaion. The first 3 Resurrection stichera, constituting in this manner a distinct group of stichera, are by an unknown author. To attribute them unto St. John of Damascus (8th c.), as is commonly done, is hardly possible in view of the fact that certain Western Studite Typika (the Typikon of San Nicola di Casole and others of the same recension), while ascribing the alphabetical stichera at the Aposticha unto the name of St. John of Damascus, the present stichera designate as "ancient" (*archaia* [Gr. ἀρχαῖα]) [^2179]. They are simpler in content than the Damascene stichera and do not contain his favorite thoughts. — Concerning the 4 "Eastern" *(Orig. p. 546)* stichera in each Sunday service at **"Lord, I have cried"**, one cannot say with certainty what their designation signifies and unto whom they belong. The Greek word *anatolika* [ἀνατολικά] can hardly be translated, as is done in Slavic books in the margins, as "Anatolian" [^2180] (this in Greek would be *Anatoliaka* [Ἀνατολιακά]); moreover, the name of the author in the titling of stichera is always expressed by the genitive case, and not by an adjective; therefore, although there was a hymnographer Anatolius unto whom belongs a series of stichera for certain feasts and saints, presumably the Abbot of Studios (9th c.), yet neither unto him [^2181], nor still less unto Patriarch Anatolius of Constantinople (5th c.) [^2182], in whose day such a genre of church hymnody did not yet exist, can the "Eastern" stichera be attributed; these are evidently anonymous stichera, designated thus presumably because they entered for the first time into the service in the eastern Jerusalem Typika and were unknown unto the most ancient Studite ones: they are mentioned, and immediately in the present quantity, for the first time by the Jerusalem Typika beginning with its most ancient manuscripts [^2183]. Of Western Typika only the Typika of the Italo-Sicilian recension contain them, whereas neither the Studite-Alexian nor the Evergetis Typikon contains them [^2184]. In comparison with the first, "ancient" Resurrection stichera, the "Eastern" ones are somewhat longer and more detailed in content. — After the 7 Resurrection stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** there are appointed 3 stichera from the Menaion. This is, so to speak, the normal composition of stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** of Sunday Vespers, yet at the same time perhaps the rarest. On the majority of Sundays of the year, besides the commemorations of one saint there is yet another commemoration: of another saint, of a feast, a forefeast, an afterfeast, or an Apodosis; even with the commemoration of a single saint this rubric is inapplicable if that commemoration is more solemn than usual, that is, if the saint is great, with a polyeleos, with great doxology, or of six verses; finally, on the Sundays of the Triodion there are no stichera from the Menaion at all. All these cases are provided for by the Typikon in subsequent chapters, and rubrics are given for them. There is not provided for, either here or subsequently, only that case which is perhaps the most frequent—namely, the coincidence with Sunday of the commemoration of two saints ("small"), of whom each possesses a distinct service. For this case one is obliged to be guided either by the rubrics of Chapter 2 of the Typikon, "Concerning a Saint Having a Vigil on Sunday" [^2185], inasmuch as a saint with a Vigil has a double quantity of stichera and troparia at the canon in comparison with the ordinary, or one may be guided by the rubric for September 1 if it fall on Sunday [^2186], wherein *(Orig. p. 547)* there are likewise 2 commemorations, although not of two small saints, and both commemorations are more solemn, or by the rubric for September 7 if it fall on Sunday, when there are likewise 2 commemorations, yet not both of saints. According unto all these rubrics alike, at **"Lord, I have cried"** it is necessary to sing 3 Resurrection stichera, 1 Eastern sticheron, 3 unto the one saint, and 3 unto the other. This case is directly provided for and such a rubric is given for it in the preface ("Brief Declaration" [*Izyavlenie vkratse*]) unto the General Menaion, a book unknown in the Greek Church, of very late origin (16th c.), with the indicated preface being of yet later date.

Typika of the Studite type having 8 stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** of Sunday Vespers, among which there were no "Eastern" ones, appointed the Resurrection stichera for 4 and unto the saint 4, with doubling of the former; those having Eastern stichera appointed: 3 Resurrection, 2 Eastern, and 3 unto the saint. The Studite-Alexian Typikon, having 9 stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**, did not allocate a place for stichera of the Menaion, excluding great saints, and tripled the 3 Resurrection stichera [^2187]. The Jerusalem Typika, beginning with the most ancient manuscripts, are unalterable on this point. That they in no manuscripts provide for two saints on Sunday testifies either that this point of the Typikon hath been preserved without change from the time when for each day of the month there existed no more than one service unto a saint, or that when there were two saints on Sunday in former times the service of one was omitted. It is remarkable that even the Chapters of Mark (*Markovy glavy*) of all recensions, while providing for all manner of concurrences with Sunday, do not speak of such a concurrence, whereas they speak, for example, of the concurrence with Sunday of a forefeast or afterfeast with two saints, directing then the omitting of the service of the second saint; they speak also of how to sing the troparia if on Sunday there be two saints with distinct troparia [^2188]; yet concerning the stichera and canon for this same case they contain no rubrics.

In the event that there is no Menaion in the church, in the Octoechos after the Eastern stichera there are printed for each Sunday Vespers 3 stichera unto the Most Holy Theotokos, the composition of Paul of Amorion, founder and Abbot of the Evergetis Monastery (†1054), who, perhaps, borrowed them from St. Ephrem the Syrian (Introductory Chapter, p. 174). These are stichera of penitential tone. Their tone only for the services of Tones 1 and 5 coincides with the tone of the Sunday; yet for the remaining services it is replaced by another, for the most part parallel, tone: in the service of Tone 2 the stichera of Paul are of Tone 6; in Tone 3—of Tone 7; in Tone 4—of Tone 8; in Tone 6—of Tone 3; in Tone 7—of Tone 2; in Tone 8—of Tone 4; this is, presumably, for variety and for complete correspondence with the stichera of the Menaion, the tone of which for the most part does not coincide with the Resurrection stichera. In view of that same variety and correspondence with the Menaion, the stichera of Paul, presumably, have likewise *prosomoia* (*podobny*), that is, they are executed unto a more beautiful and intricate melody than the ordinary tone melody. Their *prosomoia* are: Tone 1, **"Joy of the heavenly hosts"** (*Nebesnykh chinov*); Tone 6 (consequently, for the service of Tone 2, and so forth), **"Despairing"** (*Otchayannaya*); Tone 7, **"Today Judas watcheth"** (*Dnes' bdit Iuda*); Tone 8, **"O most glorious wonder"** (*O preslavnago chudese*); Tone 5, **"Rejoice"** (*Raduysya*); Tone 2, **"When from the Tree"** (*Egda ot dreva*); Tone 4, **"As one noble"** (*Yako doblja*).

*(Orig. p. 548)*
For the first time the stichera of Paul of Amorion appear, apparently, in the Slavic Octoechos published in Kiev in 1699. In the present Octoechos in Tone 1 there is a note concerning them: "Be it known that in Greek translations these stichera are not in the continuous text (*na ryadu*)." Nor does the Evergetis Typikon mention them.

## The Dogmatika

The most solemn stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** are sung with the refrain **"Glory to the Father..."**, wherein unto the first half of the refrain is joined the sticheron unto the saint if a sticheron with such a refrain is appointed for him (a *doxastikon* / *slavnik*); for the most part such a sticheron is appointed not unto the ordinary melody of the tone, but unto a special melody, and is called an *idiomelon* (*samoglasen*). Unto the second half of this refrain, unto **"Both now..."**, or unto the entire refrain if at **"Glory"** there is no sticheron unto the saint, is joined a hymn in honor of the Most Holy Theotokos, with Whose glorification each series of hymns in the Orthodox Church customarily concludes. The Theotokion concluding the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** of Sunday Vespers is always sung in the tone of the Sunday, notwithstanding the possible—and customarily avoided by the Typikon—discrepancy of such a tone with the preceding stichera, and in contrast unto the Aposticha stichera, which have a Theotokion always according unto the tone of the last sticheron, as well as in contrast unto the Praises stichera, which always have on Sunday one and the same Theotokion, consequently in one and the same tone (the 2nd). This is in view of the exceptional sublimity of these Theotokia, belonging unto St. John of Damascus, which by their entire aggregate present the complete doctrine concerning the most important of dogmas—the dogma of the Incarnation—and on that account are called "dogmas" or "Dogmatika". One can perceive a connection among all 8 Dogmatika according unto their content. "In the Dogmatikon of Tone 1 the unfolding of the dogma of the Incarnation begins with an indication of the universal glory of the Most Holy Virgin; thereby as it were is recalled the promise concerning the seed of the woman given unto the foreparents in Paradise and fulfilled in the Most Holy Virgin. In the Dogmatikon of Tone 2 is shown the relation of Old Testament types unto New Testament events. In the Dogmatikon of Tone 3 is shown the very birth according unto the flesh of the Lord our Jesus Christ, and the manner of this birth. Inasmuch as it is necessary to know the purpose of the Incarnation of the Son of God, this is unfolded in the Dogmatikon of Tone 4. Further, it is incomprehensible unto us how the Mother of God, being a Virgin, gave birth unto Christ and how after childbirth She remained a Virgin: this is brought somewhat nearer unto our understanding through the content of the Dogmatikon of Tone 5 (through certain Old Testament types). Inasmuch as we do not yet know in what manner in the person of Jesus Christ two natures are united, the Divine and the human, this is spoken of in the Dogmatikon of Tone 6, namely, that the two natures are unconfusedly and indivisibly united in the one Person of the God-Man. Nevertheless, despite all explanations, the Incarnation of God the Word is a mystery understood more by faith than by the inquiring intellect; for this reason in the Dogmatikon of Tone 7 it is stated that it was accomplished in a supernatural manner. In the Dogmatikon of Tone 8 the dogma concerning the Incarnation of God the Word is set forth in a positive and concise manner" [^2189].

*(Orig. p. 549)*

## The Distribution of Stichera Between the Choirs

Concerning the actual manner of singing the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"** the Typikon says nothing, yet it is understood of itself that they are sung by choirs alternately (*po likam*), and that before each sticheron the same choir sings also its refrain [^2190]. If the chanting is with a canonarch, then it is likewise understood of itself that before the stichera of the Menaion the canonarch announces their tone and *prosomoion*; if the tone of the Resurrection stichera coincides with that of the Menaion, he proclaims: "The same tone, *prosomoion* such-and-such" [^2191]. The last verse of the psalms, **"For His mercy is confirmed"**, with the last sticheron the Typikon directs both choirs to sing together—this in view of their timely convergence for the united singing of the Theotokion, during which the Entrance takes place and which therefore must be sung more solemnly than the other stichera. "At the final verse the choirs converge, signifying thereby both their mutual harmony and the union of the whole world through the Savior" [^2192]. At this same verse the priest is directed, having bowed unto the superior, to proceed (understood: from his *stasiad* / stall) into the sanctuary and vest for the Entrance (the deacon vests earlier—for the last Little Litany and the censing).

The above-mentioned 13th-century Georgian manuscript directs at **"For [His mercy] is confirmed"** that the priest with the deacon enter into the sanctuary and vest, and the choirs converge at **"Glory... Both now..."** and the Theotokion. The same is directed in Greek manuscripts, yet concerning the union of the choirs they state in general that at the Entrance they are already united. Slavic manuscripts speak of the vesting of the priest alone and of the union of the choirs at the 10th verse, **"For His mercy is confirmed upon us"**, wherein the Entrance begins with the *idiomelon*, if there be one. The *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus directs the priest to vest when they sing **"Glory... Both now..."** [^2193].

# THE ENTRANCE

## Its Meaning

The most important and sacred rite of Vespers is the Entrance (*eisodos* [Gr. εἴσοδος]). The very name of this rite fully indicates its essence. The sacred ministers now enter into the sanctuary and approach the Holy Table, evidently in order that their intercession for the faithful may be more powerful. Hitherto they entered into the sanctuary for brief periods through the side doors for necessary sacred actions; now they enter into it solemnly in order to remain there for prayer. Such *(Orig. p. 550)* a significance first and foremost the Entrance possesses likewise at the Liturgy, upon the foundation of which Vespers arose, at times replacing it: as there the priest enters into the sanctuary for the offering of the unbloody sacrifice, so here he enters for the offering of the rational sacrifice. From the Entrance the service acquires a more prayerful than laudatory character; from it begin the blessings of the priest; the service becomes more abundant in grace and bolder before God. "The Entrance is performed," says St. Symeon of Thessalonica, "for the imparting from the sanctuary of the grace of God and for the offering up of our prayer" [^2194]. The Entrance has also another, more mystical signification, linked, however, with that already indicated. It signifies "that the Only-begotten Son of God, having descended unto us from the heavenly spheres, ascended again and raised us unto heaven" [^2195]. Inasmuch as this was accomplished preeminently through the Incarnation of the Son of God, the Entrance signifies His Incarnation, and the Holy Doors [Royal Doors], like the impassable gate of the Prophet Ezekiel, the Most Holy Virgin (for which reason they are provided with an icon of the Annunciation) [^2196]. In this manner, the Entrance at Vespers expresses by action that which the Theotokion sung during it expresses by words. Action is more powerful than word, and the prophets, when their predictions mounted unto special intensity, replaced words by actions (the so-called "symbolic actions"). Therefore the mystery of the Incarnation does not content itself for its expression in divine worship with the words of a hymn, but seeks a more effectual expression, to a certain degree as it were being accomplished again through this action (as occurs with the death upon the Cross of the Savior in the Eucharist). Such an important significance the Entrance has at Vespers. It is in truth the holiest moment thereof.

## The Order of the Entrance

From this meaning and significance of the Entrance are explained all the particulars of its setting, which the Typikon in Chapter 2 indicates briefly, referring, evidently, unto the *Sluzhebnik* for the detailed order. According unto the Typikon, the priest during the singing of the verse **"For His mercy is confirmed upon us"**, that is, the last [verse] at **"Lord, I have cried"**, having bowed unto the superior, enters into the sanctuary and vests in the phelonion. Upon the pronouncing of **"Glory"**, the holy doors [Royal Doors] are opened, and the Entrance is made in the following order: in front are carried two candlesticks with candles—as a sign, of course, of the light of the teaching of Christ (two—either for greater solemnity in comparison with the initial censing, when the priest is preceded by a single candle, or, perhaps, as an indication of the two natures in Christ, as in the hierarch's dikirion); after them goes the deacon with the censer, by the incense whereof, according unto St. Symeon of Thessalonica, "is depicted the sweet-smelling soul and life *(Orig. p. 551)* of the Savior" [^2197]; and then goes the priest "plain" (*prost* / *haplous*), that is, with lowered hands—as a token of reverence (which is then required also of all by the exclamation: **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"** [*Sophia, orthoi!* / *Premudrost', prosti!*]), with lowered phelonion (meaning the ancient phelonion with the front portion reaching unto the feet)—of course, as a token of reverence in imitation of the Seraphim, who covered their feet with their wings [^2198]. The *Sluzhebnik* supplements these rubrics with the observation that at the Entrance "they proceed from the right side behind the Holy Table" and go forth through the north door; the latter as a token of the self-emptying (*kenosis* / humiliation) of the Son of God at the Incarnation.

Having gone forth from the sanctuary, the priest (further according unto the Typikon) takes his stand facing the holy doors [Royal Doors], while the deacon stands unto the right of him, somewhat obliquely; the deacon, having inclined slightly, holding his orarion with three fingers of his right hand, says quietly, yet so that the priest can hear: **"Let us pray unto the Lord."** The priest recites quietly the prayer **"Evening and morning and at midday"**, named in the *Sluzhebnik* "the Prayer of the Entrance". This prayer, in which there is an expression from the most important liturgical hymn **"We hymn Thee"**: "we praise, we bless, we give thanks, and we pray unto Thee" (significantly!) [^2199], repeats the supplications of the psalms at **"Lord, I have cried"** (as it were offering these supplications also from the priest), namely entreating God that our prayer may be directed unto Him as incense, and that our heart may not incline unto evil words and thoughts; it entreats further for deliverance from all that hunt after our souls; the prayer concludes with the doxology (termed "the exclamation") of the Great Litany: **"For unto Thee are due all glory, honor, and worship..."**, whereby it is expressed that a new independent part of Vespers begins, or that the latter properly begins from here, whereas up unto now there was preparation. The further rites of the Entrance the Typikon describes in the following manner. The deacon, having stood upright (*vosklonivsya*), says unto the priest, pointing toward the east (a region so rich in grace for a Christian) with the orarion, which he holds with three fingers of his right hand: **"Bless, master, the holy Entrance."** The priest blesses toward the east, saying: **"Blessed is the Entrance of Thy holy ones, O Lord, (the conclusion in the *Sluzhebnik* at the Liturgy:) always, now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen."** Thereby is expressed the assurance that in the Entrance there participate both the holy Angels, for which the priest directly prays in the prayer of the Liturgical Entrance, and the spirits of the righteous, inasmuch as it as it were repeats the Entrance of the Savior into heaven. Thereupon the deacon steps aside toward the superior, censes the icon at his place and the superior himself (asking thereby also of him a blessing upon the Entrance), and returns unto his former place, awaiting the end of the sticheron ("the verse"); upon the conclusion thereof he "enters into the midst", that is, approaches the center of the holy doors [Royal Doors] and, having signed a cross with the censer [^2200], as a token that by the Cross the doors of heaven are opened unto us, proclaims: **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"** (*Sophia, orthoi!* / *Premudrost', prosti!*), inviting thereby unto reverent standing in view of the sacred importance of the present moment, that is, of the Entrance, as is *(Orig. p. 552)* done also before the most important moments of the Liturgy—at the beginning of the Liturgy of the Faithful, before the "Canon" [Anaphora] of the Liturgy, and likewise before the dismissal of Vespers and Matins. (Unjustly is this proclamation considered preparatory unto the hymn **"O Joyful Light"** [*Svete tikhiy* / *Phōs hilaron*] or unto the prokeimenon: neither the one nor the other has place after the Entrance at the Liturgy, when the same exclamation is uttered; at weekday Vespers, when there is no Entrance, the exclamation is appointed neither in the Typikon nor in the *Sluzhebnik*).

After the proclamation, continues the Typikon, during the singing of **"O Joyful Light"**, the candle-bearers carrying the candles at the Entrance approach with them unto the holy doors [Royal Doors], the deacon enters into the sanctuary and censes the Holy Table (it is not said "round about"), while the priest, having bowed before the holy doors [Royal Doors] and kissed them, enters through them, after which the holy doors [Royal Doors] are closed. Upon entering into the sanctuary the priest, according unto the *Sluzhebnik*, having turned unto the west, stands with folded hands awaiting the conclusion of the prokeimenon, thereupon bows and departs unto his place—it is presumed, presumably, as is done in practice, that the priest stands during the singing of the prokeimenon at the High Place. By practice it is accepted that the priest at the Entrance kisses not the holy doors themselves, which are open, but their doorposts, or rather—the small icons placed upon the latter (the kissing of the doors themselves is preserved for hierarchical services). In exactly the same manner, by practice it is accepted to close the holy doors not immediately after the Entrance, but after the singing of the prokeimenon [^2201].

## Ancient Typika and the Greek Typikon Concerning the Entrance

In ancient manuscript copies of the Jerusalem Typikon the Vesperal Entrance is described more briefly than in the present Typikon, which borrows the order given by it with certain changes and additions from the *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus (14th c.). According unto the 13th-century Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon, at the words **"For His mercy is confirmed upon us"**:
"the priest with the deacon bow unto the superior, enter into the diaconicon and vest, and thereafter go forth preceded by a lighted candle, wherein all uncover their heads, both choirs unite and chant: **'Glory... Both now...'**, the Resurrection Theotokion in the tone to which they sang **'Lord, I have cried'**; at the Entrance the deacon proclaims: **'Wisdom! Stand upright!'**"

According unto 13th–14th-century Greek manuscripts:
"at the verse **'For [His mercy] is confirmed'** the priest and deacon depart and make a bow unto the superior or unto his place, as stated above, and having entered, vest in the sacred *(Orig. p. 553)* vestments in the diaconicon, and having entered into the temple (*en tō naō* [Gr. ἐν τῷ ναῷ]), make the Entrance (*eisodeuousi* [Gr. εἰσοδεύουσι]) with the censer, preceded by lamps (*lampadōn* [Gr. λαμπάδων]), while the brethren all uncover their heads, having united (later MSS: 'upon the uniting of the two choirs'), whereupon the deacon, drawing a cross with the censer, says: **'Wisdom! Stand upright!'**"

According unto Slavic manuscripts of the 14th–16th centuries:
"at the 10th verse both choirs unite and chant the verse **'For [His mercy] is confirmed'**; the priest and deacon make the customary bow unto the superior or unto his place, as has been said, and going into the sanctuary vest in the vestry in the priestly vestments (later MSS: 'vesture') and go forth unto the exit with the censer, candles going before (later MSS: 'the taper-bearer preceding with a lamp'). The monastics, each of them, uncover their heads, and we chant: **'Glory...'**, the idiomelon of the saint if there be one, and **'Both now...'**, the Theotokion of the current tone; yet if there be no idiomelon unto the saint: **'Glory... Both now...'**, the Theotokion of the current tone (later MSS: 'both choirs singing, and at the conclusion of the sticheron the Theotokion'); the deacon, having drawn a cross with the censer (later MSS: 'signs with the censer toward the Royal Doors cruciformly'), proclaims: **'O Gladsome Light, Wisdom!'** (later MSS: **'Wisdom! Stand upright!'**)."

According unto later manuscripts the order of the Entrance is set forth also by the Old Believer Typikon, with the following difference:
"upon the conclusion of the stichera and the Theotokion the deacon signs a cross with the censer before the Royal Doors cruciformly and, turning, censes the superior, yet if the superior be not present, he censes his place; and again he comes unto the Royal Doors, signing cruciformly with the censer, saying: **'Wisdom! Stand upright! O Gladsome Light'**, and we chant: **'Of the holy glory of the Immortal'**" [^2202].

According unto the *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus, after the censing at **"Lord, I have cried"**:
"the deacon, having returned, lays aside the censer and remains there; and when they chant **'Glory... Both now...'**, the priest enters and puts on the epitrachelion and phelonion, and the Entrance takes place: the deacon, having taken the censer, placed incense, and requested a blessing, as we have said (that is, as before the censing at **'Lord, I have cried'**), enters together with the priest through the north doors, the Holy Doors being opened, preceded by two readers with lamps (*lampadōn* [Gr. λαμπάδων]); behind them follows the deacon with the censer; the priest also comes forth, having a lowered (*kechalasmenon* [Gr. κεχαλασμένον]) phelonion, and they depart unto the customary place; here the readers set the candlesticks (*manoualia* [Gr. μανουάλια]) in the midst of the temple on both sides; and the priest stands directly opposite (*katantikry* [Gr. καταντικρύ]) the Holy Doors; the deacon also stands unto the right of the priest, somewhat obliquely (*ek plagiou* [Gr. ἐκ πλαγίου]), and bowing (*kypsas* [Gr. κύψας]) slightly, holding also his orarion with three fingers of his right hand, says secretly, so that only the priest may hear: **'Let us pray unto the Lord.'** And the priest says secretly this prayer: **'Evening and morning and at midday.'** And after the prayer they stand upright (*anistantai* [Gr. ἀνίστανται]), and the deacon says unto the priest, pointing simultaneously toward the east with the orarion, holding it with three fingers of his right hand: **'Bless, master, the holy Entrance.'** And the priest blesses toward the east, saying: **'Blessed is the Entrance of Thy holy ones, O Lord.'** Thereupon the deacon departs and censes the holy icon at the stall (*stasiad*) of the superior and the superior himself *(Orig. p. 554)* and again stands in the place where he stood previously, awaiting the end of the verse; and upon the conclusion thereof the deacon enters into the midst and, having drawn a cross with the censer, proclaims: **'Wisdom! Stand upright!'**... The readers, having taken the lamps again, proceed forward unto the Holy Doors; and the deacon, having entered within the holy altar [sanctuary], censes the Holy Table: the priest, having bowed before the Holy Doors and kissed them, enters, and the doors are closed" [^2203].

In the *Hieratikon* [*Hieratikon* / Gr. Ἱερατικόν] presently in use in the Greek Church, the Entrance is directed to be performed thus:
"the Little Entrance takes place preceded by taper-bearers, behind whom follow the deacon with the censer and the priest; when they come unto the midst of the temple opposite the Holy Table, they incline their heads, and when the deacon says: **'Let us pray unto the Lord'**, if a hierarch stands in the choir, he says secretly the prayer of the Entrance; yet if he be not present, the priest says it. The deacon: **'Bless, master, the holy Entrance.'** The hierarch, or in his absence the priest, blessing, says: **'Blessed is the Entrance...'** Then the deacon, having censed from where he stands the hierarch and the priest and the holy icons, proclaims: **'Wisdom! Stand upright!'** And censing, he enters into the sanctuary, and censes also the priest as he enters; in like manner the priest also, having inclined his head unto the hierarch or before the Holy Table, enters himself into the sanctuary through the Beautiful (*hōraias* [Gr. ὡραίας / Royal]) doors. The hierarch, or the priest standing in the choir, reads the evening thanksgiving: **'O Gladsome Light.'** If several priests perform the Entrance, they take a blessing (*kairos* / *kairon* [Gr. καιρόν]) from the hierarch before the *Doxastikon* and, entering into the sanctuary and kissing the Holy Gospel and the Holy Table, put on epitrachelia and phelonia; and during the singing of the Theotokion-*Doxastikon*, they go forth one after another and stand in a semicircle in the midst of the temple; upon the pronunciation by the deacon of **'Wisdom! Stand upright!'**, he, stepping aside, stands opposite the Holy Table in the rank of priests behind the last of them; the choir of priests sings slowly and reverently the evening thanksgiving, and at the words **'Having come to the setting of the sun'**, the deacon, censing the hierarch and the Despotic icons, enters into the sanctuary; and at the words: **'The Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit'**, the priests two by two, having inclined their heads before the Holy Table, enter, chanting together, into the sanctuary and, standing on both sides of the Holy Table, conclude the singing" [^2204].

## History of the Entrance

Already at the Jerusalem services of the 4th century in the Church of the Resurrection there was something corresponding unto the Entrance, namely, the entrance of the bishop behind the lattice (iconostasis) into the cave of the Tomb of the Lord, which replaced our altar [sanctuary], for prayer and the bringing forth thence of the blessing. Yet it is remarkable that such an entrance took place at all services there, even at the Hours, with the exception of Vespers alone, at which the bishop prays not behind the lattice, but before it (Introductory Chapter, pp. 140–142). This latter circumstance was, perhaps, because an entrance in the evening took place at the Liturgy, which in some places was still celebrated in the evening. When the Liturgy was everywhere transferred unto the morning, it was bound to transmit all the rites of its Entrance unto Vespers. All the particulars of the Vesperal Entrance are explained historically from the Liturgical entrances and their setting, especially in the Constantinopolitan Church *(Orig. p. 555)* of Hagia Sophia, the Typikon whereof influenced all other Typika. According unto the description of the treatise *On the Ceremonies of the Byzantine Court* (*De cerimoniis aulae Byzantinae*) of the 10th–11th centuries, the Little and Great Entrances at the Liturgy of great feasts in Hagia Sophia took place in the following manner. The patriarch, as well as the emperor, arrived at the Liturgy for the Little Entrance. The patriarch arrived earlier and awaited the emperor in the inner narthex (vestibule) with all the clergy; the patriarch held a cross, the archdeacon the Gospel, and the deacons censers and lamps; prior unto entering into the narthex the emperor in a special chamber of the outer narthex removed his crown (in token of reverence), in order to enter into the temple without it; having entered into the inner narthex, the emperor venerated the Gospel and the cross, the patriarch bowed unto the emperor and censed him, they kissed each other, and the emperor, taking the patriarch by the right hand, proceeded with him through the narthex unto its main doors, called the "Imperial Doors"; before them the patriarch read quietly the prayer of the Entrance; the emperor with a candle in his hand bowed thrice before the doors, and upon the blessing of the Entrance by the patriarch with the present words, during the singing of **"Come, let us worship"**, the emperor, having relinquished the candle, having venerated again the cross and the Gospel and taking the patriarch by the hand, entered with him into the temple and passed unto the solea, preceded by the clergy, the archdeacon with the Gospel, deacons with censers and lamps, and banners; the suite of the emperor entered into the temple through the side doors before the emperor and, as he passed through the temple, chanted *polychronion* (many years) unto him; the banners were set upon the solea. Having venerated the Holy Doors [Royal Doors], the patriarch with the words **"I will enter into Thy house..."** entered into the sanctuary; the emperor, however, taking the candle again, made a threefold bow before the Holy Doors and, having relinquished the candle, entered through the Holy Doors into the sanctuary, wherein the patriarch or hierarch drew the Holy Doors near unto him for kissing; having approached the Holy Table, the emperor kissed its covering raised for this purpose by the patriarch, took from one of the officials who had entered the sanctuary through the side doors the coverings or a chalice, which he brought as an obligatory gift at each such entrance into the temple, and set them upon the Holy Table, kissing the sacred objects situated upon the latter; then the emperor censed the Holy Table, going round about it with the patriarch; he censed also the other sacred treasures of the sanctuary, before which he previously bowed with a candle in his hand. After the censing, having bowed mutually with the patriarch and kissed him, the emperor withdrew into a special compartment of the temple—the *metatorion* (*mutatorium*), where he listened unto the Liturgy until the Great Entrance. Before the Great Entrance, in which, besides the emperor in the proper sense, or "the great [emperor]", there participated also he who bore the title of Caesar, or "the lesser emperor" (that is, the co-emperor crowned during the emperor's lifetime, or another imperial kinsman), it was reported unto the emperor that the time of the Entrance had arrived; he vested in a chlamys (which he removed after the Little Entrance) and, preceded by banners, proceeded along the right side of the temple toward its center, where the sacred ministers already stood with the Holy Gifts; unto the emperors, great and lesser, officials handed the candlesticks with lighted candles standing right there, customarily borne by readers at the entrances, and the emperors, performing now the duties of *depotatoi* (the lowest clerics, taper-bearers [^2205]), *(Orig. p. 556)* carried the candlesticks before the Holy Gifts from the ambo (in the center of the temple) unto the Holy Doors [Royal Doors], preceded by banners; at the Holy Doors the emperors handed the candlesticks unto court dignitaries, who set them upon the solea; the emperors took their stand on both sides of the Holy Doors, in which the patriarch stood and received the diskos [paten] and chalice from the archdeacon and the first priest who bore them; the latter, carrying the Holy Gifts past the emperors, said: **"May the Lord God remember your imperial realm in His Kingdom always..."**; and handing the sacred vessel unto the patriarch, they said: **"Thy high priesthood..."**; the patriarch, receiving the sacred vessel, prayed for the emperors and dignitaries; the emperors took their leave of the patriarch and withdrew into the *metatorion* until the kiss of peace at the Symbol of Faith [Creed] [^2206].

## The Distinction of the Vesperal Entrance from the Liturgical Entrances

Although the Vesperal Entrance was elaborated upon the foundation of the Liturgical entrances, yet it differs essentially from them in that it is performed without the Gospel (with the Gospel only when it is read at Vespers) and without the Gifts; by virtue of this the center of the Entrance is the priest himself. Unto him, depicting in himself Christ, whereas at the Liturgy Christ is represented by the Gospel or the Gifts, honor is rendered by the bearing before him of the censer and candle.

## Peculiarities of the Vesperal Entrance in Historical Development

The burning of incense was one of the accessories of royal processions in the East and in Byzantium [^2207]. In exactly the same manner was also the bearing before him of lamps. The latter in Byzantium took its origin from the carrying of torches before the Roman Augusti in processions. Before the Byzantine emperor during certain ceremonies a special official, the *lampadarios*, carried the *divamvoulon* (*dibamboulon*), a precious candlestick with a gilded lamp, the edges whereof were dyed with cinnabar. A similar candlestick, called the *monamvoulon* (*monobamboulon*) (in these words are contained the numbers 1, 2 with some other unknown word), was carried in Byzantium before the patriarch [^2208]. Before the Patriarch of Jerusalem in the 8th–9th centuries on solemn occasions walked 12 monks with candles [^2209]. A newly elected bishop in ancient Russia was escorted unto the tsar, the patriarch, and unto the cathedral with 12, 8, 6, or 4 candles, which were carried before him by special clerics—"flame-bearers" (*plamenniki*) or "fire-bearers" (*ognenniki*) [^2210]. According unto the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople, the Vesperal Entrance was preceded by three lamps [^2211].

*(Orig. p. 557)*
Unto Psalm 140 the Entrance was assigned because with this psalm in antiquity Vespers began. At Chanted Vespers the Entrance was performed at verse 8 of Psalm 140 [LXX 140:8]: "For unto Thee, O Lord, O Lord, are mine eyes" (Introductory Chapter, p. 342). Yet already the Studite Typika indicate the Entrance after the Theotokion at **"Lord, I have cried"** [^2212]. For this reason the present prayer of the Entrance has reference chiefly unto this psalm.

In the majority of ancient Euchologia this prayer is titled "the Entrance Prayer". Yet the Euchologion in MS No. 149 of the 15th century of the Mount Athos Pantokrator Library has the following Entrance prayer:
"Vouchsafe, O Christ God, that our entrance unto Thy sacrificial altar, being changed from all defilement, be accepted of Thee; having cleansed our hearts from an evil conscience, grant that our prayer may ascend as incense before Thee through the intercessions of Thine All-Pure Mother and of all Thy saints, for unto Thee is due..." [^2213].

According unto certain Euchologia, as a prayer for the Vesperal Entrance (evidently, in distinction from the Liturgical Entrance) there is appointed a brief verse, like the present blessing of the Entrance. Thus, in the 13th-century Georgian MS of the Imperial Public Library No. 208 the "Entrance prayer" is:
"Blessed is the coming of Thy holy glory, O Christ our God, always..."

In the *Sluzhebnik* of the Novgorod St. Sophia Library (at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy) No. 524 of the 13th century the prayer of the Entrance is the present one, yet the verse of blessing is:
"Blessed is the Entrance of Christ our true God" (an intensification of the thought of the present verse).

In the most important Russian cathedrals of the 15th–16th centuries, as the manuscripts of their *Chinovniki* [Hierarchical Service-Books] show, presumably under the influence of later Byzantine practice, the Vesperal Entrance, as well as the Matins Entrance at the Great Doxology still practiced at that time as a survival of Chanted services, were performed every Sunday with the participation not only of the entire cathedral clergy, for the most part very numerous, but also of the parish priests of the city, and even of visiting priests; yet already from the 16th century in Novgorod, Pskov, and even in Moscow the clergy began to feel burdened by the obligation to appear at the "processions" (*vykhody*) in the cathedral every Sunday; it was necessary to demand this of them under threat of a fine, as did, for example, Metropolitan Macarius in his charter unto Archbishop Serapion of Novgorod in 1551; under Patriarch Philaret even in the Moscow Dormition Cathedral it happened that "of necessity a single weekly priest walked" [^2214]. Besides other causes, this reduction of solemnity could have been influenced by the intensifying ascendancy of the Jerusalem Typikon, which supplanted in Russia the last remnants of the practice of the Great Church of Constantinople, with which practice the Studite Typikon, having grown up beside it, easily coexisted [^2215].

*(Orig. p. 558)*

# "O GLADSOME LIGHT" (*PHOS HILARON*)

## Content of the Hymn

After the stichera at **"Lord, I have cried"**, as it were in the capacity of a concluding sticheron, follows the hymn **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Svete tikhiy* / *Phōs hilaron*), termed in the Greek Horologion "the Lucernarium (*epilychnios* [printed *epilychnōs* / Gr. ἐπιλύχνως]) thanksgiving", uniting with simplicity an early Christian depth and power of feeling. The hymn contains in itself the glorification through Christ of the Holy Trinity and of Himself, evoked by the appearance of the evening light and by gratitude for having lived unto it. It falls into three parts so independent that they can be regarded as three distinct hymns.

1. **"O Gladsome Light"** (*Phōs hilaron* [Gr. Φῶς ἱλαρόν], in Greek it can also be the nominative of the predicate: "Thou, O Christ, art Light"; "gladsome" [gentle] in view of the evening) **"of the holy glory"** (intolerable for us sinners) **"of the Immortal"** (in contrast unto the setting of the sun and the self-emptying of Christ in His death upon the Cross) **"Heavenly Father, Holy, Blessed"** (whence cometh also visible light; two principal mutually linked attributes of divine life), **"O Jesus Christ"** (Christ as the Son of Man).
2. **"Having come unto the setting of the sun"** (having lived unto sunset), **"having beheld the evening light, we hymn"** (*hymnoumen* [Gr. ὑμνοῦμεν], in thanksgiving for this) **"the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, God"** [^2216]. (A Trinitarian hymn, after which we sing already "a hymn unto Christ as God" [^2217]:)
3. **"Worthy art Thou at all times"** (not in the evening alone) **"to be hymned with reverent voices"** (more fitting than ours; Greek *aisiois* / *aisiais* [Gr. αἰσίαις / printed αἰσίοας], blessed), **"O Son of God, Who givest life; for which cause the world"** (the thankful world) **"glorifieth Thee"** [^2218] (in certain MSS *heortazei* [Gr. ἑορτάζει]—keepeth festival unto Thee).

In this manner, the hymn continues the thoughts of the Theotokion (Dogmatikon) and depicts with words the silent actions of the Entrance.

## Origin of the Hymn

**"O Gladsome Light"**, alongside the Great Doxology and **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, is an ancient Christian hymn. It is cited in the Alexandrian *(Orig. p. 559)* Codex of the Bible of the 5th century. This is typical Christology of the 2nd–3rd centuries. Unto its antiquity testifies also the fact that it has lost the name of its author. It is significant that in this respect it shares the fate of several other very sublime hymns, such as, for example, besides the two indicated, certain troparia as well. Were not these hymns composed in a manner similar unto that of works of folk poetry, that is, were they not collective creations of the Church? [^2219] This supposition receives yet greater probability from the composite nature of certain of these hymns, as we have seen in **"O Gladsome Light"** (the same is true of the Great Doxology and **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**). For **"O Gladsome Light"** two authors are named: the present Greek Horologion inscribes this hymn: "an ancient creation (an allusion unto its ancient anonymity) or, as some say, of Athenogenes the Hieromartyr" (Bishop of Sebaste in Armenia, †311, or another), wherein reference is made (in a footnote): "St. Basil the Great, chapter 29, *On the Holy Spirit*." In the Slavic Horologion the hymn is attributed unto Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem (634–644), concerning which certain Greek Horologia make the remark: "of St. Athenogenes the Martyr, and not of Sophronius, Patriarch of Jerusalem, as some unjustly think; witness Basil the Great." In the time of Sophronius, in truth, the hymn was already in ecclesiastical use, as the Alexandrian Codex shows and the account of Sophronius himself concerning his visit unto Nilus of Sinai (see Introductory Chapter, p. 295). Yet the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople and the Chanted Office do not know this hymn (Introductory Chapter, p. 342). Unto St. Athenogenes the hymn is attributed, presumably, upon the foundation of the following words of Basil the Great: "Our fathers did not wish to receive in silence the grace of the evening light, but immediately upon its arrival offered thanksgiving. Although we cannot positively say who was the creator of those praises which we recite during the Lucernarium prayers, yet the people repeat the ancient voice, and unto none has it yet appeared that they utter blasphemy when they say: We praise (*ainoumen* [Gr. αἰνοῦμεν]) the Father, the Son, and the Holy Spirit, God. If anyone knew also the hymn of Athenogenes, which he, in place of a safeguarding remedy, left unto his disciples when he himself hastened *(Orig. p. 560)* already unto the holocaust, he would know also the mind of the martyrs concerning the Spirit" [^2220].

In this testimony, apparently, a distinction is made between the hymn with the words "We praise the Father, the Son...", that is, perhaps, **"O Gladsome Light"**, and the hymn of the Martyr Athenogenes mentioning the Holy Spirit [^2221].

## Manner of Execution

Concerning the manner of executing **"O Gladsome Light"**, the Typikon says: "and we chant", which fully corresponds unto the poetic and musical character of this "evening thanksgiving". Yet at weekday Vespers this hymn is read ("he says" [*glagolet*]), however, not by an ordinary reader, but by the superior himself (Chapter 9 of the Typikon), like other most important prayers (the prayers read by the superior are enumerated in Chapter 7 of the Typikon, note "Mark" [*zri*]).

## Ancient Typika Concerning "O Gladsome Light"

The Studite Typikon required **"O Gladsome Light"** to be sung *"vely"* (slowly and quietly?), as also the Six Psalms (concerning which in another place therein it is noted that it is sung or "spoken with a subtle and penitent voice"), as also the end of Matins, the Introductory Psalm at Vespers, **"Vouchsafe, O Lord"**, the **"Now lettest Thou"** [Canticle of Simeon], the Trisagion, and the troparion—in contrast unto **"The Lord is God"** and the Alleluia at Matins, which according unto the Studite Typikon were executed "with a shout and with chanting", "with a clear voice", "plainly" [^2222]. This was, presumably, among other reasons, in consequence of the unvarying repetition of the first class of hymns at every service. This class of singing, although it was performed by the entire brotherhood, was similar unto reading. Hence arose the vacillation of subsequent Typika and disputes in the Russian Church concerning whether one ought to chant or read these prayers, and in particular **"O Gladsome Light"**. Concerning the manner of executing the latter at the Vigil, ancient manuscript copies of the Jerusalem Typikon speak more indeterminately than the present Typikon. The 13th-century Georgian MS: "the people: **'O Gladsome Light'**"; 13th–16th-century Greek MSS and printed editions of the 16th–17th centuries: "and we: **'O Gladsome Light'**" [^2223]; Slavic manuscripts: according unto 13th-century *Sluzhebniki* of the St. Sophia Library at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy Nos. 518 and 524—the deacon: **"O Gladsome Light of the holy glory"**; the clergy: **"Of the Immortal Heavenly Father"** [^2224].

According unto the most ancient Slavic manuscript Typika: "the deacon, having drawn a cross with the censer, proclaims: **'O Gladsome Light, Wisdom'**; the appointed monk, while the priests enter, says: '... **Of the holy glory**'" [^2225]; according unto other MSS: "the deacon proclaims: *(Orig. p. 561)* **'Wisdom! Stand upright!'**; the appointed monk says: **'O Gladsome Light'**" [^2226]; according unto later ones the same, only "and we say: **'O Gladsome Light'**" [^2227]. The Old Believer Typikon: "the deacon: **'Wisdom! Stand upright! O Gladsome Light'**; and we chant: **'Of the holy glory of the Immortal'**" [^2228]. The custom of the deacon pronouncing, besides **"Wisdom! Stand upright!"** (or **"Wisdom!"** alone), before or after this also the beginning of the hymn **"O Gladsome Light"**, is thus, apparently, of Russian origin; yet the circumstance that in the 6th–8th centuries it was required that the most important hymns be intoned by the subdeacon, deacon, or even the priest (see Introductory Chapter, pp. 295–296, 307), a remnant whereof even now is the intoning of the Paschal heirmoi by the clergy, compels one to see in this custom a survival of profound antiquity preserved in the practice of the Russian Church, perhaps from the dominance of the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople. A similar survival, yet only from the Studite Typikon, was the custom of reading **"O Gladsome Light"**.

This custom evoked also disputes in the Russian Church. At the *Stoglav* Council [1551], Tsar Ivan the Terrible posed, among others, the following question: "For what reason in our realm in Moscow and in all the borders of Moscow, in cathedral and parish churches, except monasteries, at Sunday Vespers and at feast-day Vespers and for great saints, when an Entrance taketh place, do they not sing 'Holy Glory' (that is, **'O Gladsome Light'**), but speak it with a speaking voice, and at Matins on Sunday and on feasts do they not sing the Doxology, but just as on other simple days speak it with a speaking voice?" Unto this question the Council gave no separate reply, but in general decreed: "to perform church singing fully and according unto the order in all things" [^2229].

# THE VESPERAL PROKEIMENON

## Concept of the Prokeimenon

After the hymn **"O Gladsome Light"** there followeth at Vespers, not only festal but also weekday (excluding Lenten and sometimes memorial [requiem] Vespers), the prokeimenon.
