In view of this also, this partaking occurs at vigils only from September 1 unto March 25; at summer vigils, however, the blessed loaves are not tasted, but are eaten at the morrow's meal before other food (this is in view of the fact that the Vespers of the vigil, beginning after sunset, in summer, owing unto the brevity of the night, may end too late at night).
"And the blessed loaves have diverse gifts (*charismata* [Gr. χαρίσματα]), that is to say (i.e.), they stay (*pauei* [Gr. παύει]) burning heat (*pyreton* [Gr. πυреτόν], high fever) in those who drink them with water, and shaking ague (*phrikas* [Gr. φρίκας], chills/ague), and heal every infirmity (*malakian* [Gr. μαλακίαν], weakness) and every disease; and in addition unto these, they drive away mice (*sētas* [Gr. σῆτας], which signifies also 'moths') from crops (*gennēmatōn* [Gr. γεννημάτων], granary grains) and expel other noxious pests."

In the *Sluzhebnik* this notice is abridged:
"blessed bread is an aid against all evils, if it be received with faith",
and there is added a warning unto the priest, that he bless not the blessed substances a second time at another vigil, but distribute the bread unto the people and eat it himself at the table before other food, consume the wine with reverence, anoint with the oil at the end of Matins or put it into food, and sow or grind the wheat.

## Ancient Typika on the Blessing of Loaves

The Georgian MS:
"The cellarer breaks one of the blessed loaves and gives it unto the brethren, as well as a cup apiece of wine on account of fatigue, as this has been handed down unto us by the fathers; the brethren bow unto the sanctuary, unto the right and unto the left, and go forth from the church. From this time forth, in view of the communion of the Holy Mysteries, they must not drink water. Blessed bread hath manifold grace: specifically, when taken with water, it expels fever and heals every infirmity; it destroys also the worms harmful unto wheat."
Greek MSS and printed editions are as the present Typikon, only *(Orig. p. 612)* instead of "to taste anything"—"to drink water", and they lack "and expel other noxious pests", and sometimes instead of *gennēmatōn* [Gr. γεννημάτων]—*hōreiōn* [Gr. ὡρείων], "from granaries".
Slavic Typikon of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 328/383 of the 14th c.:
"they have diverse grace, they heal infirmities, and drunk with water it drives away the onset of diseases and heals all bodily debility; wheat and other fruits it delivers from noxious pests."
No. 678/386 of the 15th c. is as the present one. MS of the Kyiv Academy Museum Aa 194 of the 16th c.: "two cups apiece", and lacks "mice from crops they drive away".
The Greek printed *Euchologion* is as our *Sluzhebnik*, without the warning unto the priest.

The Moscow *Sluzhebniki* of 1602 and 1647: "to drink water or taste anything else", and they lack mention of the gifts.
In the *Sluzhebnik* of Peter Mohyla there is nothing even concerning the partaking. The Moscow [edition] of 1658 is in everything like the present *Sluzhebnik*.
The Old Believer Typikon is like ours [^2377].

## Historical Foundation of the Evening Blessing of Loaves and Wine

The prototype of this "meal", as has long since been observed by many, was the agape. At the latter the food was frequently as simple as that offered by the present Typikon for consumption at the vigil (Introductory Chapter, pp. 51–52, 75–77). Probably oil and wheat were also added unto the substances being blessed (and they were added, as we have seen, not without hesitation and not all at once) not without thought of the ancient agape, and likewise, probably under the influence of the very ancient practice of blessing oil. In the liturgical monuments of the 4th and neighboring centuries there are prayers for the blessing of water and oil, which were brought into the temple, apparently, alongside the bread and wine for the Eucharist, on which account prayers for their sanctification were placed following the order of the Liturgy. Such a place they occupy in the Syriac *Testament of our Lord Jesus Christ* (*Testamentum Domini Nostri Jesu Christi*), where they are cited with the note: "if the priest sanctifieth oil for the healing of those who suffer, then, placing its vessel before the altar, he saith with compunction"; the prayer beseeches God, Who hath granted us the Holy Spirit, Christ, Who hath sanctified us, made us wise, given us consciousness of sins, the power of His Spirit, the Healer, Who hath given unto the worthy the grace of healing, to send down upon the oil the fullness of His beneficent mercy, that it may relieve the laboring, heal the sick, and sanctify those who come unto faith; "this prayer is said also over water". The *Apostolic Constitutions* beseech the Lord of Sabaoth, Who hath given water for drinking and purification and oil to make the face cheerful, to sanctify these substances through Christ, to grant them "power effective for health, banishing diseases, driving away demons, and expelling every deceitful snare". The prayer in the Euchologion attributed unto Serapion, Bishop of Thmuis (4th c.), "concerning those who offer oil and water", "blessing" these substances "in the Name of Christ", likewise entreats for them "healing power", so that through the drinking of them and anointing with them "every burning heat (*pyretos* [Gr. πυρετός]), everything demonic, and every disease may be repelled" [^2378]. Mention of blessed loaves is made in the *Spiritual Meadow* [*Pratum Spirituale*]: Abba *(Orig. p. 613)* Sergius the Sinaite, having given such bread unto a lion lying upon the road and hindering his mules from passing, commanded him to get off the road, which the beast duly performed [^2379].
The second part of our Vespers, by its proximity unto the Liturgy, resembles the 2nd part (from the Entrance onward) of Chanted Vespers (Introductory Chapter, p. 342), only there the assimilation was unto the beginning of the Liturgy, whereas here it is unto the end.

# NON-ORTHODOX VESPERS (*Inoslavnye vecherni*)

Instituting a comparison of our Vespers according unto the themes of its hymns and prayers with non-Orthodox evening services, we find in the latter the following most significant differences (the points of agreement have been indicated in the exposition of the rite).

Armenian Vespers hath at the beginning Psalm 54:17–18 [LXX; Masoretic Ps. 55:16–17]: **"As for me, I cried unto God, and the Lord heard me; evening and morning and at noon will I tell and declare it, and He shall hear my voice"**, Psalm 85 [LXX; Masoretic 86] **"Bow down Thine ear, O Lord"**, Psalm 139 [LXX; Masoretic 140] **"Deliver me, O Lord"**, Psalm 120 [LXX; Masoretic 121] **"I have lifted up mine eyes"**, Psalm 90 [LXX; Masoretic 91] **"He that dwelleth in the help of the Most High"**, Psalm 122 [LXX; Masoretic 123] **"Unto Thee have I lifted up mine eyes"** (in our rite, at Daily Vespers), Psalm 53 [LXX; Masoretic 54] **"Save me, O God, in Thy name"** [^2380]; thus, all the psalms of our Sixth Hour, one of the Ninth Hour, and one from the Midnight Office entered into Armenian Vespers.

Coptic Vespers: Psalm 130 [LXX; Masoretic 131] **"Lord, my heart is not exalted"**, 131 [LXX; Masoretic 132] **"Remember, O Lord, David"**, 136 [LXX; Masoretic 137] **"By the waters of Babylon"**, 137 [LXX; Masoretic 138] **"I will give thanks unto Thee, O Lord"**, 145 [LXX; Masoretic 146] **"Praise the Lord, O my soul"**, 146 [LXX; Masoretic 147:1–11] **"Praise ye the Lord, for a psalm is good"**, 147 [LXX; Masoretic 147:12–20] **"Praise the Lord, O Jerusalem"**, the Gospel of Luke 2:25–30 on the Meeting of the Lord, the Creed [*Credo*], the 1st prayer with thanksgiving for the past day and with a petition to accept the evening doxology, to deliver from the snares of the evil one, and to grant a peaceful evening and night; the 2nd prayer for the forgiveness of the sins of the day, restful sleep, a guardian angel, and deliverance from evil and the torment of the devil [^2381].

Abyssinian [Ethiopian] Vespers: Psalm 117 [LXX; Masoretic 118] **"Give thanks unto the Lord"** and the "Songs of Ascents"—Psalms 119–128 [LXX; Masoretic 120–129] (**"Unto the Lord in mine affliction"**, in our rite the customary Kathisma at Daily Vespers); the Gospel of Mark 1:29–34 on the healing of Simon's mother-in-law and the evening healings of the Savior; **"Glory to God in the highest... goodwill"**; a petition for forgiveness through the prayers of the Theotokos; **"We worship Thee, O Christ, with Thy Good Father and the Holy Spirit, for Thou hast come and saved us"**; our 4 penitential stichera: **"I would fain blot out with tears"** [*Khotekh slezami*]; from the service of the Great Canon the stichera: **"My whole life"** [*Vse zhitie moe*], **"With the weight of heedlessness"** [*Tyazhestiyu nebrezheniya*], **"I have become an offense"** [*Bykh pretknovenie*]; our Theotokion **"Rejoice, O Pure One"** [*Raduisya Chistaya*]; **"It is good to give praise"**; penitential sessional hymns from the Psalter after the 17th Kathisma: **"I have sinned against Thee, O Savior"** [*Sogreshikh k Tebe Spase*], **"I cry unto Thee"** [*Zovu k Tebe*]; the Martyr's hymn [*martyrikon*] **"They who desired not earthly pleasures"** [*Izhe zemnyya slasti ne vozzhelevshe*]; the Theotokion **"O Virgin Theotokos Mary, preserve Thy flock"** [*Bogoroditse Devo Marie sokhrani stado Tvoe*]; penitential troparia: **"As the prodigal son"** [*Yako bludnyi syn*], **"I pray Thee like the publican"** [*Molyutisya yako mytar*]; a prayer unto the Lord Jesus with confession of the sins of the day and a petition for amendment, with the addition *(Orig. p. 614)* of a petition unto the saints and the Theotokos for intercession on our behalf; 2 prayers unto God the Father as the Creator of the day, with thanksgiving for the past day and a request for a peaceful night; a prayer for kings, resembling **"Establish, O God"**, and **"Thou Who at all times"** [^2382]. Thus the entire service is of a penitential character (Abyssinian Matins is of a more laudatory and supplicatory content).

Roman Vespers hath 5 consecutive psalms from among Psalms 109–147 [LXX; Masoretic 110–148], and thus Sunday Vespers hath Psalms 109–113 [LXX; Masoretic 110–114/115] with antiphons: **"The Lord said"** [*Dixit Dominus*] before Psalm 109, and **"The Lord said unto my Lord: Sit Thou at My right hand"** (v. 1) after it; for Psalm 110 [LXX; Masoretic 111], its v. 7: **"Faithful"**, **"Faithful are all His commandments, confirmed unto the age of the age"** [Lat. *Fidelia omnia mandata ejus: confirmata in saeculum saeculi*]; for Psalm 111 [LXX; Masoretic 112], v. 1: **"In His commandments"**, **"In His commandments he shall greatly delight"**; for Psalm 112 [LXX; Masoretic 113], v. 2: **"Blessed be the name of the Lord"**, **"Blessed be the name of the Lord from henceforth and for evermore"**; for Psalm 113 [LXX; Masoretic 114–115], v. 26 [v. 18]: **"We that live"**, **"We that live will bless the Lord"**; the *capitulum* (2 Cor. 1:3–4)—the glorification of God, the Father of Christ, for comfort in every affliction (probably the Resurrection is in view); the hymn *Lucis Creator* [^2383] unto God as the Creator of light and of day, which were created on this day of the week (the hymns for Vespers of each day glorify the work of creation of that day, on Monday—the creation of heaven, etc.; cf. in Jewish worship, Introductory Chapter, p. 11); the responsory: **"Let my prayer be set forth, O Lord, as incense before Thee"** (Ps. 140:2 [LXX; Masoretic 141:2]); the Canticle of the Theotokos, **"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** [*Magnificat*], with the **Glory to the Father** [*Gloria Patri*] [^2384].

Anglican Evensong begins with a verse of Holy Scripture on the power of repentance, followed by an exhortation unto the confession of sins, the confession itself repeated by all after the minister, the absolution from the minister consisting in his prayer for the granting of true repentance and the Holy Spirit and in the declaration of forgiveness by God unto the truly penitent, the Lord's Prayer said by all, with versicles and the Lesser Doxology, the reading of 2–4 appointed psalms, a reading from the Old Testament, the **"My soul doth magnify the Lord"** [*Magnificat*] or Psalm 97 [LXX; Masoretic 98] **"O sing unto the Lord a new song"** [*Cantate Domino*] with the Lesser Doxology, a reading from the Apostolic Epistles, Psalm 66 [LXX; Masoretic 67] **"God be merciful unto us"** [*Deus misereatur*] with the Lesser Doxology, the Apostles' or Athanasian Creed, the greeting **"The Lord be with you"**, **"Let us pray"**, **"Lord, have mercy"**, **"Christ, have mercy"**, the Lord's Prayer, suffrages, 3 Collects (general prayers)—the collect of the day, a collect for peace, and a collect for aid against all perils, prayers for the Sovereign, the clergy, and the people, and the Grace from 2 Cor. 13:13 [Masoretic 13:14]: **"The grace of our Lord Jesus Christ, and the love of God, and the fellowship of the Holy Spirit, be with you all. Amen"** [^2385]. *(Orig. p. 615)* Among Protestants the afternoon service consists of an opening hymn (at the choice of the pastor), a sermon with a brief concluding prayer, the **Our Father** and a Biblical blessing, a hymn, an intonation (a short versicle begun by the pastor and finished by the choir, for example: **"Blessed and praised be the name of the Lord, from this time forth and unto the ages"**), a collect according unto the day, a blessing at the altar (with the words of Numbers 6:24–26), and a concluding verse [^2386].

# THE BEGINNING OF MATINS (*Nachalo utreni*)

## Bell-Chime for Matins (*Zvon k utrene*)

Now begins the second and most important part of the Vigil—Matins [*utrenya*]. Its beginning is marked by a *peal of bells* [*zvonom*].

"After the Great Reading of the Acts of the Holy Apostles (or of the Epistles), the paraecclesiarch goes forth and strikes the great bell and the other bells."

It is not specified that he should strike first upon the one great bell and then upon all, as before the beginning of the Vigil, because this is not the blagovest (the initial tolling), which requires a special duration, but merely a "signal" [*znamenie*] of the beginning of Matins. Its duration is therefore completely unspecified.

### According to Ancient Typika (*Po drevnim ustavam*)

According unto the ancient recensions of the Jerusalem Typikon, at the beginning of Matins at the Vigil there was prescribed not only a bell-peal, but also a censing, and according unto certain Slavic copies of the Typikon, an exclamation as well; but the ringing was only on one large bell or semantron [*bilo*].

Georgian and Greek manuscripts and Greek printed editions:
"The candle-lighter [*kandilovzhigatel'*], having prepared the censer, enters and strikes the great [instrument]; and the priest censes."

Slavic manuscripts of the 14th century (Moscow Synodal Library Nos. 328/383 and 329/384):
"The kandilaptis makes a prostration unto the superior or unto his place, and departing, rings. Upon the completion thereof, the priest makes a prostration unto the superior, and having entered into the altar, takes the censer, places incense therein, and says the prayer of the censer; then he marks the Holy Table with the sign of the Cross with the censer, and proclaims: Blessed is Christ (No. 329 without 'Christ') our God always..."

Slavic manuscripts of the 15th and 16th centuries (for example, No. 678/386 and the Kyiv Theological Academy Museum) speak neither of censing nor of an exclamation, but concerning the ringing they add: "on the great wood and on the others, if there be any"; and so likewise...

...the Old Believer Typikon; concerning the ringing see also the Moscow editions of the Sluzhebnik of 1602 and 1647 (above, p. 610), where it is indicated in three installments.

## Initial Versicles of Matins (*Nachal'nye stikhi utreni*)

Matins of the Vigil begins with the angelic hymn at the Nativity of the Savior: **"Glory to God in the highest"** (Lk. 2:14), just as in a more expanded form it also concludes with it; this is, of course, in view of the fact that with the event *(Orig. p. 616)* that laid the foundation of our salvation—and which, moreover, occurred by night—and with its glorification it is natural to begin the cycle of daily services. In view of the exceptional importance of this brief hymn, which represents not a human composition, it is repeated three times in honor of the Holy Trinity. Having prefixed such a lofty hymn, the worshippers venture to begin their own praise also, and in the feeling of their own inadequacy for it, they ask for Divine assistance—again not in their own words, but in God-inspired words, though having already proceeded from human lips—with the verse of Psalm 50:17 [LXX; Masoretic 51:15]: **"O Lord, Thou shalt open my lips"** (Heb. *śəp̄ātay*, Gr. *χείλη*, lips) **"and my mouth"** (Heb. *pî*, Gr. *στόμα*, mouth) **"shall declare Thy praise."** The prayer here is expressed in the future tense of confidence. The verse was especially suited unto that era when the divine service was improvised. It is repeated twice, as it were for each choir. Constituting the beginning of the service, both versicles, however, must stand in the closest connection with its first section, which in liturgical services is always the psalms. Psalms in this case also begin the service, whereas the indicated versicles are regarded only as their initial refrain. This is expressed in that the versicles in execution are not separated from the Six Psalms that follow them, being recited in the same manner as the Six Psalms, and by the same person (see below).

### Their History (*Istoriya ikh*)

**"Glory to God in the highest"** was included from antiquity in the composition of the Liturgy. The Liturgy of the *Apostolic Constitutions* has this verse immediately before the Communion itself; our Liturgy and the Nestorian Liturgy attributed unto the Apostle Thaddaeus have it at the very beginning; the Roman Liturgy likewise has it in the opening part and in the form of the first section of our Great Doxology. Unto Matins the verse passed, perhaps, under the influence of the transfer of the Liturgy unto the morning and its union with Matins. At Matins it is mentioned in the oldest manuscript copies of the Jerusalem Typikon, but at weekday Matins, and not at Sunday Matins, where the Six Psalms is directly indicated [^2387]. — With the verse **"O Lord, Thou shalt open my lips,"** recited thrice,...

...St. Benedict prescribes beginning Matins; according unto the observation of the commentators on Benedict, this verse lifted the obligatory nighttime silence, for which reason it was customary with it to sign the mouth with the sign of the Cross [^2388]. And the present-day Roman Matins begins with it. With it likewise begins the Armenian Midnight Office (= Matins), with its recitation also thrice (Introductory Chapter, 299). The Lyonese Liturgy has it before the Gospel [^2389]. At Jerusalem Matins it appears in manuscripts simultaneously with the first verse, and both at once in the present manner of execution—that is, with the recitation of the first thrice and of the second twice—and in immediate connection with the Six Psalms, from which they were consequently never separated in manner of execution, that is, they were chanted in the same manner as the Six Psalms (see below).
*(Orig. p. 617)*

## The Plan of Matins (*Plan utreni*)

Our Matins, like the Roman Catholic service, visibly divides into four parts corresponding unto the four "watches" of the night, since the prototype of Matins was the ancient all-night vigil (*vigilia*), which on the eve of feasts occupied the entire night. These parts are:
1) The Six Psalms with the Great Ektenia and **"God is the Lord"**;
2) The Kathismata with the Blameless (*Amomoi*) or the Polyeleos and the Gospel;
3) The Canon;
4) The Praises (*Ainoi*) with the Doxology and the litanies.

### Part 1 of Matins (*1-ya chast' utreni*)

The first part of Matins, like the second, gradually elevates the worshippers from a sorrowful and penitential disposition—fundamental for a Christian—unto joy in God. Such an ascent in the first part of Matins has three stages: the Six Psalms, the Ektenia, and **"God is the Lord."** From a certain grief wherewith the first is suffused, the second—the Ektenia—transfers us into prayer of a supplicatory character, the hope aroused by which is already close unto the triumph breathing in **"God is the Lord."**

# THE SIX PSALMS (*Shestopsalmie* — *Hexapsalmos*)

This part opens—and with it, consequently, the whole of Matins—with the system of psalms known under the name of the Six Psalms (Gr. *ἑξάψαλμος*). Thus the introductory psalms at this service, in accordance with its length and its primary place among the daily services, are twice the normally accepted number of them for each service—3. The composition of the Six Psalms comprises:
— Ps. 3 **"Lord, why are they increased that trouble me?"** [*Gospodi, chto sya umnozhisha*],
— Ps. 37 [LXX; Masoretic 38] **"O Lord, rebuke me not in Thine anger"** [*Gospodi da ne yarostiyu*],
— Ps. 62 [LXX; Masoretic 63] **"O God, my God, unto Thee do I rise early"** [*Bozhe, Bozhe moy, k Tebe utrenyuyu*],
— Ps. 87 [LXX; Masoretic 88] **"O Lord God of my salvation"** [*Gospodi Bozhe spaseniya moyego*],
— Ps. 102 [LXX; Masoretic 103] **"Bless the Lord, O my soul"** [*Blagoslovi dushe moya Gospoda*],
— Ps. 142 [LXX; Masoretic 143] **"Lord, hear my prayer"** [*Gospodi uslyshi molitvu moyu*].

The psalms were selected, doubtless not without intention, from different parts of the Psalter evenly; by this they represent it in its entirety, as if to say that, properly speaking, one ought to recite it in its entirety, as the ascetics were wont to do by night. The psalms were chosen of homogeneous content and tone, predominant in the Psalter: namely, all of them depict the persecution of the righteous man by enemies and his steadfast hope in God, which only grows (cf. Ps. 3:8; 62:6 [LXX; Masoretic 3:7; 63:5]) with the increase of persecutions (cf. Ps. 3:2, 3; 37:7, 8 et seq.; 87:4, 5 [LXX; Masoretic 3:1, 2; 38:6, 7; 88:3, 4]) and in the end reaches jubilant resting in God (Ps. 102 [LXX; Masoretic 103]). All these psalms are superscribed with the name of David (in the Hebrew Bible as well), with the exception of 87, which is inscribed "unto the sons of Korah," and were sung by him, of course, during the persecution on the part of Saul (perhaps Ps. 62 [LXX; Masoretic 63]) or Absalom (Ps. 3; 142 [LXX; Masoretic 143]), reflecting in themselves the spiritual growth of the singer amidst these tribulations. Out of the multitude of psalms of similar content, precisely these were selected here also because in certain passages they have in view the night and morning (Ps. 3:6 [LXX; Masoretic 3:5]: **"I laid me down and slept; I awaked"**; Ps. 37:7 [LXX; Masoretic 38:6]: **"I went mourning all the day long,"** v. 13 [Masoretic 38:12]: **"imagined deceits all the day long"**; Ps. 62:1 [LXX; Masoretic 63:1]: **"unto Thee do I rise early,"** v. 7 [Masoretic 63:6]: **"I remembered Thee upon my bed, and meditated on Thee in the morning"**; *(Orig. p. 618)* Ps. 87:2 [LXX; Masoretic 88:1]: **"I have cried day and night before Thee,"** v. 10 [Masoretic 88:9]: **"I have stretched forth my hands unto Thee all the day,"** vv. 13, 14 [Masoretic 88:12, 13]: **"Shall Thy wonders be known in the dark? — But unto Thee have I cried, O Lord, and in the morning shall my prayer prevent Thee"**; Ps. 102:15 [LXX; Masoretic 103:15]: **"his days are as grass, as a flower of the field"**; Ps. 142:8 [LXX; Masoretic 143:8]: **"Cause me to hear Thy lovingkindness in the morning"**). Mournful psalms alternate with joyful ones, wherein for the former even-numbered places were naturally chosen. The psalmody material of the Six Psalms is somewhat multiplied; this was done 1) in that at the end of each psalm there is repeated its most characteristic...

...or most suitable passage for the morning service, to the extent of 1/2 to 2 1/2 verses, namely: Ps. 3:6 [LXX; Masoretic 3:5]; Ps. 37:22–23 [LXX; Masoretic 38:21–22] (the final verses); Ps. 62:7b–9 [LXX; Masoretic 63:6b–8]; Ps. 87:2–3 [LXX; Masoretic 88:1–2] (the opening verses); Ps. 102:22b [LXX; Masoretic 103:22b]; Ps. 142:1b–2a, 10b [LXX; Masoretic 143:1b–2a, 10b]. At the conclusion of the final psalm, the first of its two repeated passages is even pronounced twice (**"Hear me, O Lord, in Thy righteousness..."**). 2) Unto the psalmody material of the Six Psalms is appended the mixed Christian-Old Testament doxology customary in such cases (see above, pp. 468–469): **"Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, both now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, glory to Thee, O God** *(thrice)*; **Lord, have mercy** *(thrice)*; **Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, both now and ever, and unto ages of ages. Amen,"** which serves as the conclusion unto each triad of psalms, wherein at the second triad "Lord, have mercy" and the second "Glory... both now and ever..." are not said, in view of the immediately following ektenia, wherein these petitions are provided in an amplified measure.

## Its Origin (*Proiskhozhdenie ego*)

Prior unto the appearance of monastic typika, Matins in respect unto the quantity of psalms did not differ from Vespers: both in the *Apostolic Constitutions* have one psalm each, Matins having the 62nd (Introductory Chapter, pp. 135, 137); the same psalm is indicated for it in the treatise *On Virginity* [*De virginitate*] of Pseudo-Athanasius (4th–5th century) [^2390]. Under the influence of the ascetics who chanted the entire Psalter during the night, monasteries introduced the singing at Matins of 75, 60, 50, 30, 20, and 18 psalms; the Rule of Benedict and other Western rules reduced this number unto 12, basing themselves, doubtless, upon the very widespread ancient custom of chanting 12 psalms at a time, wherein the Rule of Benedict divided them into two groups of six, prefixing unto them Psalms 3 and 94; other rules (Western) reduced this number still further—unto six, five, and four psalms (Introductory Chapter, 189–190, 216, 301–313). The latter found application also in the Armenian Matins, wherein all the psalms of its 4-psalm group coincide with ours: 3, 62, 102, 142 (ibid., 299). And Choral Matins under Symeon of Thessalonica hath at the beginning Psalms 3, 62, and 133 (ibid., 345). The most ancient mentions of our Six Psalms are found in the well-known description of Sinai Matins of the 7th century, and in the *Hypotyposis* and *Diatyposis* (ibid., 295, 359).

## Manner of Execution (*Sposob ispolneniya*)

The Six Psalms with the verses preceding it—**"Glory to God in the highest"** and **"O Lord, Thou shalt open my lips"**—as the most important part of the service, the Typikon appoints to be read by the superior.

"And when the superior and all the brethren have arisen (from the reading), *(Orig. p. 619)* he begins: Amen (the response unto the concluding doxology of the reading?), Glory to God in the highest... (thrice); then he says: O Lord, Thou shalt open my lips... (twice). And he recites the Six Psalms in a quiet and gentle voice."

A certain lack of clarity in the phrasing here as unto who "begins" and "recites" the Six Psalms (perhaps intentional, = impersonal) is resolved in Chapters 7 and 9 of the Typikon and in the order of the first Monday of Great Lent, where it is directly stated: "and the superior says: Glory to God in the highest," etc.; and in the note unto Chapter 7 ("behold") in the enumeration of what is read by the superior, the Six Psalms is named. Thus, after a whole torrent of triumphant hymns, the Vigil now passes into a quiet, prayerful tone, which is so fitting for the beginning of a new service. This is the most minor-key part of the Vigil. Yet it is remarkable that here there are none of those rubrical remarks concerning a penitential disposition during the reading of the Six Psalms that are given in the typikon of weekday Matins (Chapter 9) and still more in the order of Great Lenten Matins (Monday of the First Week of the Forty Days).

## Execution in Antiquity (*Ispolnenie v drevnosti*)

Thanks unto the Six Psalms, as subsequently unto the kathismata, the beginning of our Matins in its tone corresponds fully unto the character of all ancient chanting, which was, like the Jewish synagogal singing, predominantly recitative (Introductory Chapter, 20, 155). In general, "in the early centuries, when the Blood of Christ shed for them still boiled in the veins of the faithful, the psalms were chanted with so moderate an inflection of the voice that the singing was more like reading than singing. A remnant of such chanting in the Western Church is singing *in directum*, which at times replaces antiphonal singing with voice modulations." For an especially long time such a character was retained by the chanting at the nocturnal service: according unto the rules of Isidore of Seville, the Nocturns were read, while Matins (*Laudes*) was sung, "that the delight of diversity might banish weariness" [^2391]. Thus, the Six Psalms in manner of execution is most faithful unto antiquity. However, such chanting for the Six Psalms is presupposed, as we shall see, only by the oldest Studite typika; whereas the Jerusalem typika initially, it appears, desired a more solemn chanting for it. In favor of this speaks the repetition, preserved to this day, of the most important passage from each psalm at its conclusion; this repetition is completely analogous unto the antiphon in Roman Catholic worship, with this difference, however, that the antiphon there not only concludes...

...the psalm, but is also prefixed unto it (in an abridged form). Since the Six Psalms arose already when almost everywhere the repetition of the antiphon after every verse of a psalm had been abandoned, this passage of the psalm repeated at its end was hardly intended for singing after every verse of the psalm, but played only such a role as the present Roman antiphon. In the *Life of St. Sabas* it is related that he once by night heard in the cell of a certain holy elder the singing (which proved to be miraculous) of psalms as if by a large congregation and with melodious execution (*metá mélous hēdyphōnou*) of one verse from a psalm (41:5 [LXX; Masoretic 42:4]), *(Orig. p. 620)* and thought that Matins (*kanōn*) was being celebrated [^2392]. The Studite Typikon says concerning the Six Psalms:

at the exclamation "Glory to the Holy": "the people, having said Amen, straightway begin to sing the 6 psalms; and they sing with compunction of heart, with fear, with all good order, not with shouting, but so voicing as to be scarcely heard (hardly audible), not overtaking one another in the psalm, but rendering these verses, and taking great care concerning this, that unto the conclusion of the 6 psalms they restrain stretching (stretching oneself, yawning) and coughing, and ever give heed that on the side they be in unison with the paranomarios, who stands in the midst of the church" [^2393] (that all conform in chanting with the paranomarios, who stands for this purpose in the midst of the church).

The communal chanting of the Six Psalms is presupposed also by Greek manuscript copies and printed editions of the Jerusalem Typikon, judging by the expression: "we begin the Six Psalms," which Slavic manuscripts replace already with "the superior begins" (14th-century manuscripts, but 15th- and 16th-century manuscripts add: "or the ecclesiarch"); (if Greek manuscripts concerning the reading of the prayers state that the priest reads them when "the superior begins Psalm 102," then here intoning is meant).
The *Diataxis* [*Chin*] of Patriarch Philotheus: "the superior or an appointed monk says the Six Psalms."
The Old Believer Typikon: "the abbot or ecclesiarch begins—in a gentle and quiet voice, and recites the hexapsalms in order" [^2394]. During the presence of Arseny Sukhanov in the East, the Six Psalms was read by the Patriarch [^2395].
— The repetition of the verses is noted in Slavic manuscript typika of the 14th century in accordance with the present Horologion, but after the 2nd and 5th psalms the verse is repeated twice [^2396]. This, like the present repetition twice of **"Hear me, O Lord, in Thy righteousness"** at the conclusion of the final psalm, must be a trace of the former chanting of the Six Psalms by two choirs. A trace of its chanting is likewise the present custom of chanting **"Glory to God in the highest"** and **"O Lord, Thou shalt open my lips,"** as well as the final **"Alleluia."**

The printed Greek Horologion after the 3 psalms has: **"Glory... both now... Alleluia** *(thrice)*" [^2397].
Early-printed Slavic Horologia, for example the Moscow edition of 1658 and the Old Believer editions, have: + **"Lord, have mercy** *(thrice)*, **Glory... both now..."**; and at the end of the 6 psalms: **"Hear me in Thy righteousness, O Lord, hear..."** and this verse once.
The Old Believer Typikon at the end: **"Glory... both now... Alleluia** *(twice)*, **and the clerics the 3rd Alleluia with singing."**

# THE MORNING PRAYERS (*Utrennie molitvy* — *Euchai Orthrinai*)

Not being content with their own prayer in the words of the Six Psalms, the faithful send unto prayer a grace-endowed intercessor for themselves—reminding one of the heavenly Intercessor for us before God—in the person of the priest, who *(Orig. p. 621)* during the Six Psalms, standing before the Royal Doors, offers our prayers in mysterious, silent colloquy with God. These secret prayers of the priest at Matins, in accordance with the greater length and importance of this service in comparison with Vespers, are more numerous than at the latter; yet their number is determined, as at Vespers, by the symbolic number 12, which rivals 7 in sacred significance. Most immediately, this number instills the thought that we would desire to spend in prayer all the hours of the night—a time especially conducive unto prayer and convenient for it—recalling that Matins arose out of the original all-night vigil (*vigilia*) on the eves of feasts.

Embracing all the needs of a Christian entering upon a new day, the morning prayers—more precisely, the prayers of Matins (Gr. *εὐχαὶ τοῦ ὄρθρου*)—are at the same time adapted unto the various parts of Matins, having been originally, like the evening prayers, intended for reading at different points of the service.

The 1st prayer, being introductory, thanking God for our awakening and for the present service, asks for Divine assistance in general and for the worthy celebration of divine worship; it concludes with the exclamation of the Great Ektenia. The 2nd and 3rd prayers, beginning with the words of the Canticle of the Prophet Isaiah, correspond in content unto this canticle, with whose verses "Alleluia" is sung at Lenten Matins (in place of **"God is the Lord"**).

More specifically, the 2nd prayer asks for instruction in working righteousness and holiness in the fear of God, that God may remember and hear all who pray with the priest by name, save them, bless and sanctify them, and grant peace unto the world, unto the Church, unto the priest, unto the sovereign, and unto all people (cf. the Great Ektenia and the Prayer behind the Ambo); the doxology (= exclamation) glorifies the name of God.

The 3rd prayer is for our instruction in God's righteousness, and for inner illumination (following the outer illumination of the preceding prayer) through the preservation within us of the seal of the Holy Spirit, which will bring in its train righteous action as well as a joyous forthcoming day; exclamation of the 1st Small Ektenia.

The 4th prayer asks that He accept our thanksgiving (offered hitherto) for sleep and awakening and vouchsafe us eternal blessings, wherein the prayer steps beyond the boundaries of those present and...

...embraces all the brethren on land, on sea, and everywhere; the exclamation (= at the morning Supplicatory Ektenia) glorifies the mercy of God.

The 5th prayer asks for the acceptance of our morning prayers (as the preceding prayer asked for the acceptance of morning thanksgiving), as incense, and that He bypass not with His help any one of those who keep vigil and sing; the exclamation (= of the ektenia after Ode 3 of the Canon) concludes the general glorification of God and begins a new series of exclamations.

The 6th prayer gives thanks already for the benefits of our whole life, and more specifically again for the past night, and asks that God vouchsafe us to sing and pray unto Him unceasingly, and remember "them that cry unto Him in the night" (consequently, those especially in need of help), crushing their invisible enemies; the exclamation (= after Ode 6 of the Canon) concludes the general glorification of the Kingdom and salvation of God.

The 7th prayer, repeating the former petitions for the acceptance of thanksgiving and instruction in His statutes, asks for instruction in worthy prayer for us and for the forgiveness of every sin; the exclamation "For Thine is the might, and Thine is the kingdom..." develops the first thought of the preceding exclamation and prepares for the next. *(Orig. p. 622)*

The 8th prayer develops the former petition for the acceptance of our prayer, enumerating its forms as well: supplications, confessions (perhaps an indication of the polyeleos psalms), nocturnal services—and asks for the granting of faith, hope, and love (the positive aspect of the negative good requested in the previous prayer—the forgiveness of sins), for the blessing of all our undertakings in the day now drawing nigh and the attainment thereof; the exclamation—with the glorification of the name and Kingdom of God, = at the Polyeleos.

The 9th prayer is for the worthy hearing of the Gospel, with the glorification of God as our illumination (having in view also the approaching dawn); it is identical with the Liturgy prayer.

The 10th prayer—of Psalm 50 [LXX; Masoretic 51]—adapts its petitions unto Christian needs (for example: "vouchsafe that there may be offered unto Thee a sacrifice of righteousness and an oblation upon Thy holy altars"), with the glorification of the mercy of God (= exclamation before the Canon, the development of the second thought in the exclamation of the 5th prayer).

The 11th prayer—of the Psalms of Praise (*Ainoi*)—asks the Creator of the Angels with special tenderness of heart (*milisi deyem*), attained through all the prayers, to accept our doxology (an anticipation of the next prayer), offered together with all the creatures of God; the exclamation (= after Ode 9 of the Canon) unites our prayer unto the angelic praise.

The 12th prayer—of the Great Doxology—repeating its thoughts, unites all the former petitions: for the forgiveness of sins, the acceptance of prayer, enlightenment, purification, and the fulfillment of the commandments ("walking becomingly as in the day"—the approaching...

dawn) and eternal life; the exclamation is a general glorification of God (a return unto the starting point).

### Their History (*Istoriya ikh*)

The morning prayers, like the evening prayers, were once distributed throughout the entire service. Yet the most ancient among the surviving Euchologia—such as, for example, the Barberini MS of the 8th–9th century, MS No. 226 of the Imperial Public Library (from the collection of Bishop Porphyrius) of the 8th–10th century, and the Cryptensis MS of Bessarion (*Bessarionis*) of ca. the 9th century, with which the Euchologion of the Paris National Library Coislin MS No. 213 of 1027 coincides regarding the prayers—simply number the morning prayers, indicating a place in the order of Matins only for the last three or four. What is important is that these Euchologia provide all our present-day prayers, excluding, however, the 9th, and in their present order, thereby allowing us to judge concerning the degree of their antiquity. The Cryptensis MS titles the 7th prayer "prayer of the Gospel," the 10th (there the 9th) "prayer of the 50th" (that is, of the psalm), the 11th (there the 10th) "prayer at the Praises" (*Ainoi*), the 12th (there unnumbered) "prayer or dismissal," and then the prayer of the bowing of heads; but before the last two, the Cryptensis and Coislin MSS have a prayer of the catechumens and two prayers of the faithful, with a note that they are read only on occasion (concerning these prayers and this rubric, see Introductory Chapter, p. 348). This latter circumstance, as well as the fact that in certain Euchologia—for example, MS No. 962 of the Sinai Library of the 11th–12th century—the first five prayers are titled "prayer of the first antiphon," "prayer of the 2nd antiphon," and so forth (the Euchologion of the same library No. 973 of 1153 and Patmos Library MS No. 105 of the 13th century title only the first three prayers thus; the Sinai Euchologion No. 958 of the 10th century titles only the 4th prayer thus; and Sinai MS No. 982 of the 13th century notes only concerning our present *(Orig. p. 623)* 10th prayer, there the 9th, "prayer of the antiphon, that is, of Ps. 50"),—these circumstances demonstrate that the morning prayers were originally adapted unto the Chanted Office (*asmatikos orthros*). When they were transferred unto Matins of the Studite-Jerusalem type, which had no antiphons at the beginning, it became necessary to distribute them among the constituent parts of this Matins; and the various Euchologia accomplish this each in its own way, such that one may say there are not even two that coincide in all respects.

Thus, the Georgian Euchologia—No. 208 of the Imperial Public Library and No. 450 of the Tiflis Church Museum, both of the 16th century, but bearing traces of very ancient practice—indicate after the Six Psalms, or at its last psalm (in the second Euchologion), our present 1st prayer (the prayers are not numbered): at the "kathisma" after the first "psalm" (perhaps an entire kathisma is called a "psalm") the 2nd prayer; after the second psalm the 3rd prayer; after the third psalm the 4th prayer, with the conclusions of the prayers being proclaimed as...

...exclamations after the litanies immediately following them (at the kathisma—small litanies); before the Gospel the 9th prayer; at Psalm 50—the 10th; after Ode 3 of the Canon—the 5th prayer; after Ode 6—the 6th; after Ode 7—the 7th; after Ode 8—the 8th, the prayer of fervent supplication; and after the Supplicatory Ektenia the "prayer of egress," that is, our present 12th prayer.

In Sinai Euchologion No. 973 of 1153: at the Great Ektenia the 1st prayer; after it the 2nd and 3rd; prayers 4–7 are cited with the rubric: "other prayers for (Gr. *διά*) the Polyeleos of Sunday in Holy Lent, when there is stichology"; after Psalm 50—the 10th prayer (there the 9th); after Ode 9—the 11th prayer; the "prayer of fervent supplication" at the Augmented Ektenia; after it the 12th prayer; and in its present place the prayer of the bowing of heads.

In the Euchologion of Patmos Library MS No. 105 of the 13th century: the 1st prayer at **"God is the Lord"**; after it the 2nd and 3rd; before the Gospel the 9th; at Psalm 50 the 10th; after (Gr. *ἀπό*) Ode 3 of the Canon the 4th; after Ode 6—the 5th; after Ode 9—the 11th (the conclusions of the prayers serve as the exclamations of the litanies); at **"Glory to God in the highest"**—the 12th; after the Supplicatory Ektenia the prayer of the bowing of heads; after the aposticha the "prayer of dismissal": **"O Lord, Creator** (Gr. *Δημιουργέ*) **of all..."** (with supplication for hearing, non-imputation of sins, pacification of life, and being counted worthy of the Kingdom of Heaven).

In the Sluzhebnik of the Sophia Library (at the St. Petersburg Theological Academy) MS No. 523 of the 14th century: at the Six Psalms the 1st prayer; at the kathismata the 2nd and 3rd; after Ode 3 of the Canon the 4th, 5th, and 6th; after Ode 6 the 7th and 8th; "when they chant *Have mercy on me, O God*"—the 10th; at the Praises (*Ainoi*) the 11th; after them and the Small Ektenia—the 12th (before the Gospel and the Augmented Ektenia).

Other monuments, although they do not provide a distribution of the prayers throughout the service, are nonetheless characterized by departures from the present and simultaneously most ancient order of the prayers, witnessing unto similar attempts to adapt the prayers of the Chanted Matins unto ordinary Matins: thus, MS No. 310 of the Moscow Synodal Library of the 16th century gives the following order: 1–5, 8, 10, 6, 7, 11; the Sluzhebnik of the same library No. 952/347 of the 14th century: 1–4, 10, 5, 6, 11; the *Taktikon* of Emperor John Cantacuzene of the 14th century (Greek MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 279), the Euchologia of the same library Nos. 280 and 281 of the 15th century, and Rumiantsev Museum MS No. 486 of the 16th century: 1–6, 10, 7, 8, 11, 12; Sinai MS No. 958 of the 10th century places 10 before 8. Other Euchologia achieve such an adaptation by a simpler route—by omitting certain prayers, predominantly those whose content and position made their assignment unto a specific moment of Matins difficult (as the above-named Euchologia likewise do); most often *(Orig. p. 624)* of all, in the vast majority of manuscripts, the 9th prayer is omitted, or placed outside the reckoning, or put last (an echo of the practice wherein the Gospel was read after the Great Doxology); Paris Euchologion No. 213 remarks concerning it that it "is not said in the Great Church, but in...

...the others, in which the Gospel is proclaimed after Ode 6 on great feasts"; at times prayers 7 are also omitted (see above and Sinai Euchologia Nos. 956 and 958 of the 10th century, No. 962 of the 11th–12th century, and the Eiliton-roll of the Athonite Xenophontos Library No. 161 of the 14th century), 8 (the same, excluding No. 958), 12 (see above and a series of Sophia Sluzhebniki of the 15th century, Nos. 530, 533, et al.), 11 (see above, an Eiliton-roll of the 9th century described by Bishop Porphyrius [^2398], and Athos Esphigmenou MS No. 208 of the 16th century), and 6 (Sinai Euchologion No. 962 of the 11th–12th century). In some manuscripts these omissions reach, therefore, up to four (in the last-mentioned Euchologion) and five prayers: thus, in Sophia Sluzhebniki No. 518 of the 13th century and No. 522 of the 14th century, prayers 4, 6, 7, 9, and 10 are lacking. And the Euchologia of Sinai No. 984 of the 15th century and Athens University No. 94 of 1542 contain only the first three prayers, prescribing that they be read at the Six Psalms.

Gradually and in various locales the recitation of the remaining prayers was also assigned unto the Six Psalms, and the number of such simultaneously read prayers increased from eight—since from the 9th onward the prayers bear the aforementioned titles assigning them unto other parts of the service ("at the Gospel," "at the 50th," "at the Praises," "at Glory to God in the highest"—thus in Rumiantsev Museum Euchologion No. 474 of the 16th century; in Sinai MS No. 961 of the 11th–12th century the 8th is also marked "before Ps. 50")—up to ten (thus in a series of Sophia Sluzhebniki of the 15th century, Nos. 538, 539, 540, 542, and Moscow Synodal Typography Library MS No. 130, where only the 11th and 12th prayers bear such titles: "at the Praises," "at Glory to God in the highest") and up to eleven (Metropolitan Cyprian: "at Matins 11 prayers, and the 12th prayer after *Praise the Lord from the heavens* at the bowing of heads" [^2399]). From this there was but one step unto our present-day practice with its 12 prayers at the Six Psalms (what was lacking, presumably, was the 9th prayer), represented in manuscripts from the 11th century: Euchologion of the Moscow Rumiantsev Museum Sevastianov Collection No. 474 of the 11th century, Athos Vatopedi No. 133/174 of the 14th century, Sinai No. 988 of the 15th century, Moscow Synodal Library No. 616/360 of the 16th century, etc. [^2400] and cf. below). As for printed Sluzhebniki, all Greek editions possess our present composition; of the Slavic, the Moscow editions of 1602 and 1647 lack the 9th, having consequently only 11 at the Six Psalms; the Sluzhebnik of Petro Mohyla of 1629 remarks concerning it that it is prescribed among the Greeks and leaves its recitation unto personal preference; from the Moscow edition of 1658 onward it is inserted, and the composition receives its present form.

### Their Recitation (*Chtenie ikh*)

The morning prayers are read by the priest in the same setting as the evening prayers, that is, before the Royal Doors, bareheaded, in the epitrachelion; "in some places also in the phelonion," adds the Typikon here, having in view, of course, the custom—canonized as early as the Stoglav Council—for secular priests *(Orig. p. 625)* to celebrate the whole of Matins, as of Vespers, in the phelonion. Such a setting of recitation, instilling the thought of repentance and our unworthiness,...

...recalls also the former practice of beginning Matins in the narthex. The reading of the prayers begins at the 4th psalm of the Six Psalms, **"O Lord God of my salvation"** (Ps. 87 [LXX; Masoretic 88]), evidently in order to afford the priest the possibility of hearing at least half of the Six Psalms.

### Ancient Typika on the Morning Prayers (*Drevnie ustavy ob utrennikh molitvakh*)

The Georgian manuscript does not mention the recitation of the prayers during the Six Psalms in the order of the Vigil, but speaks concerning this in the rubrics of weekday Matins (see there).

Greek manuscripts and the printed Greek Typikon (Jerusalem): "When the superior begins Psalm 102: **Bless the Lord, O my soul**, the priest himself says the prayers of Matins, standing uncovered before the Holy Doors"; so likewise the oldest Slavic; yet later Greek and Slavic manuscripts (Moscow Synodal Library Greek No. 381 and Slavic No. 332/385 of the end of the 14th century) prescribe beginning the prayers at the psalm **"O Lord God of my salvation,"** as at present. The *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus says the same, but does not mention the vestments.

The Old Believer Typikon: "Having taken upon himself the epitrachelion."

According unto the *Hieratikon*, the priest begins the reading of the prayers at the 1st psalm, reads before the Holy Table until the 4th, and then stands before the icon of the Savior, which he kisses in conclusion [^2401].

# THE GREAT LITANY AT MATINS (*Velikaya ekteniya na utrene*)

The Six Psalms is not so much a prayer as an outpouring of the feelings of the believer; the Great Ektenia following it, which stands in general at the beginning of all the most important services, constitutes already a defined, precise prayer, embracing the primary needs of a Christian. The Six Psalms at Matins, like the Introductory Psalm at Vespers, attunes the soul unto such prayer, awakening within it indefinite, yet all the more profound religious feelings; they prepare the way for the supplications of the Great Ektenia; at the Divine Liturgy there is no such preparation, because the faithful approach it having been sufficiently prepared by the whole cycle of the daily services, and especially by the Hours, and because in general they approach it with a greater elevation of spirit, which arises spontaneously from the consciousness of the importance of the impending Mystery.

The Typikon prescribes that the Great Ektenia at Matins, as at Vespers, be proclaimed by the priest, since the deacon appears only at the Polyeleos. The priest proclaims it before the Holy Doors, from that place where he read the morning prayers; and after its exclamation, the priest "having departed, stands in his own place," that is, together with the brethren, outside the altar, as at Vespers (see above, p. 533).

### According to Ancient Typika (*Po starym ustavam*)

The Georgian manuscript does not mention the ektenia.

Greek manuscripts and printed editions: "Then (the priest) says the ektenia and proclaims the exclamation."

So likewise the ancient Slavic manuscripts; later manuscripts and the Old Believer Typikon: "The priest or deacon performs the great diaconal service" [^2402].

According unto the *Hieratikon*, *(Orig. p. 626)* the choirs chant **"Lord, have mercy"** at this ektenia (which is proclaimed, like all things there, by the deacon) alternately [^2403].

# "GOD IS THE LORD" (*Bog Gospod'*)

Being a more joyful service than Vespers, being celebrated during the hours of Christ's Nativity and Resurrection, Matins, in place of Psalm 140 and the specifically evening psalms following it, possesses in their stead a general festive psalm in a far more solemn execution than those psalms, namely excerpts from Psalm 117 [LXX; Masoretic 118] under the title **"God is the Lord"** (Gr. *Θεὸς Κύριος*). Among the Hebrews, this psalm was designated for chanting on a certain great feast ("order the feast," v. 27), on the occasion of the manifestation unto the people of a great mercy from God, for which all Israel was bound to give thanks unto God, as for salvation from death and annihilation ("I shall not die, but live," v. 17). The well-known Paschal verse **"This is the day..."** is found in this psalm. Among the psalms, this is almost the most joyful, yielding in this regard perhaps only unto Psalm 67 [LXX; Masoretic 68]. Out of such a psalm is the hymn **"God is the Lord"** composed.

Moreover, from it the most powerful and characteristic verses were selected for this hymn, presenting in brief the content of the entire psalm. The principal among these five "selected" verses—**"God is the Lord and hath appeared unto us; blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord"**—is composed of two passages of the psalm arranged in reverse order (vv. 27a and 26), of which the first directly bears the meaning that the Lord (Yahweh) is the true God and that He has now revealed Himself unto us with special tangibility ("hath appeared," from the Heb. "hath illuminated," "hath shone forth"). With this is linked the fact that he who comes now, under such circumstances, in the name of the Lord is blessed ("in the name of the Lord" may also be referred unto "blessed"). The fact that these latter words were applied unto the Savior at His solemn Entry into Jerusalem, and that, according unto His words, with them they shall meet Him also at the Second Coming [^2404], all this points unto Him precisely as that "Coming One," Whose coming is equivalent unto the manifestation of God Himself and reveals God unto all.

Now the coming unto us of the Son of God, the manifestation of God in His flesh, according unto the teaching of the Apostles, possessed as it were three stages: the Incarnation, the Resurrection, and the future Coming [^2405]. The night inspires thought concerning each of these; each of them is commemorated in the night service as having been assigned unto the night (**"Glory to God in the highest,"** **"Behold, the Bridegroom"**). Yet at Sunday Matins the thought of the second, central "manifestation"—in the Resurrection—is most natural. Symeon of Thessalonica refers the verse unto the first and the last: "Well is it said in this hymn: **'God is the Lord and hath appeared unto us'**—the Word of God incarnate; **'blessed is He that cometh'**—He Himself as God in the flesh; **'in the name of the Lord'**—in the name of the Father and His own. And it is exceedingly fitting that by night...

...there is represented *(Orig. p. 627)* the Nativity—the manifestation of the Savior in the flesh, even as this occurred by night, and unto us who sit in darkness and the shadow of ignorance 'a great light hath shined,' according unto the words of Isaiah. Therefore do we also in this life, as in the night, await at midnight the coming of the Bridegroom of our souls, beloved by us and loving us" [^2406]. Unto the Resurrection the verses of the psalm accompanying **"God is the Lord"** are likewise most suited—excluding the verse **"O give thanks unto the Lord"** [Ps. 117:1], taken as the opening verse of the psalm: all of them depict the life of the Savior, full of persecutions (v. 11: "they compassed me about..."), accompanied by the consciousness that the death threatening from enemies would prove powerless over Him (v. 17: "I shall not die, but live...") and would entail the founding of the Church (vv. 22 and 23: "the stone which the builders rejected..."; cf. the verses to the evening prokeimenon).

### Ancient Use of Psalm 117 and "God is the Lord" (*Drevnee upotreblenie ps. 117 i "Bog Gospod'"*)

Psalm 117 [LXX; Masoretic 118] is an alleluiatic psalm (in the LXX) and was included among the Hebrews in the composition of the so-called "Hallel" (Pss. 112–117, Heb. 113–118; Introductory Chapter, p. 12), chanted at Passover, Pentecost, Tabernacles (Sukkot), and the Feast of Dedication (Hanukkah), but originally intended for Passover; occupying the final place in the Hallel, Psalm 117 entered into it later than the other psalms [^2407] and, apparently, was designated more for Tabernacles [^2408] than for Passover (moreover, in the Hebrew Bible it is not an alleluiatic psalm). Having presumably been sung by the Savior and the Apostles at the institution of the Eucharist, the psalm was suited for the Liturgy; and already the Liturgy of the *Apostolic Constitutions* takes from it the verse chanted today (vv. 26, 27a) as a preparatory verse for Communion (together with **"Glory to God in the highest"** and Hosanna) [^2409], as does likewise the Liturgy of Basil and Chrysostom (both without the transposition of the psalm's words); the Liturgy of St. James places the verse **"Blessed is He that cometh"** after the **"Holy, Holy,"** inserting before "that cometh" the words "Who came and" [^2410]. At Matins it is mentioned by the well-known 7th-century description of Sinai Matins, the *Hypotyposis*, and the *Diatyposis* (Introductory Chapter, pp. 295, 359). Yet the Chanted Matins (*asmatikos orthros*), even in the time of Symeon of Thessalonica, did not have **"God is the Lord."**

Judging from the fact that Psalm 117 in the LXX is an alleluiatic psalm—that in the Western Church the Alleluia is considered so specifically a Paschal and festive chant that it is not sung during fasts—and that among us the Alleluia constitutes a feature of the Lenten divine service, which has remained most faithful unto antiquity, one may think that **"God is the Lord"** was also once sung with Alleluia or replaced by it (cf. the content of the 2nd and 3rd morning prayers).

### Manner of Execution (*Obraz ispolneniya*)

In accordance with the greater significance of Matins in comparison with Vespers and the character of the hymn **"God is the Lord,"** it is chanted to the richest melody—the melody *(Orig. p. 628)* of the troparion, which serves as it were as its final refrain. More specifically concerning the chanting of **"God is the Lord,"** the Typikon in the present place states:

"And the appointed canonarch, who pronounces the prokeimena at Vespers, having made a bow unto the superior, proclaims: **God is the Lord** with its verses in the current Tone, and we chant the Sunday troparion."

This incomplete instruction is supplemented in other places. Chapter 9 of the Typikon, concerning the singing of the Alleluia that replaces **"God is the Lord"** and is executed according unto the same rubric, states:

"The canonarch, standing directly before the Holy Doors, pronounces **Alleluia** in the Tone of the Octoechos, reciting also these verses; and we chant the Triadica (*Troichny*); but if it be **God is the Lord**, we chant **God is the Lord** in the Tone of the troparion of the Saint with its verses, and we recite the troparion of the Saint." In the order of Matins for the First Monday of the Great Fast: "The appointed monk or priest recites **Alleluia** in the current Tone of the Octoechos with its verses. And after each verse the clerics chant **Alleluia** thrice."

The Sluzhebnik: "They begin to chant **God is the Lord** according unto the Tone of the troparion of the day; the verse... and **God is the Lord** is sung four times; then the troparion is recited... And while **God is the Lord** is being sung, the canonarch departs and stands in the midst of the temple bareheaded, and recites quietly (slowly?) the above-written verses; and he stands there until they begin the Theotokion; then he makes a bow in the place where he stands (toward the Holy Doors) and, having turned (unto the west), bows unto the choirs and departs. Thus does he do also when there is **Alleluia**."

All these rubrics presume, apparently, that the canonarch first chants **"God is the Lord"** to the Tone, and then chants its verses, whereupon unto each verse the choirs (alternately, which is why there are four verses) respond by chanting **"God is the Lord."** Therefore no proclamation of the Tone is required before **"God is the Lord"**: the canonarch demonstrates how to chant it. In practice, for the most part the verses with the initial **"God is the Lord"** are recited by the priest or deacon who proclaimed the ektenia, while **"God is the Lord"** is chanted four times [^2411].

### "God is the Lord" According to Ancient Typika (*"Bog Gospod'" po drevnim ustavam*)

According unto the well-known 7th-century description of Sinai Matins, **"God is the Lord"** was chanted by skilled chanters, and the presbyter began it (Introductory Chapter, pp. 295–296). The Studite-Alexian Typikon, contrasting **"God is the Lord"** as a joyful hymn with the Six Psalms with its penitential content, requires a corresponding distinction also in the chanting of the one and the other: whereas the Six Psalms is chanted "subdued" (*v'ly*, see above), "straightway on bright and festive days (when alone **God is the Lord** was sung according unto the Studite Typikon) we cry **God is the Lord** brightly and clearly, as having truly perceived the divine manifestation of light suddenly illuminating us, driving far away every cloud of mourning and dejection, and wondrously and brightly bestowing upon us serene joy, rejoicing in this and being unable to contain within ourselves the greatness of this ineffable gladness"; a similar manner of chanting is required by the Studite Typikon also for the **Alleluia** [^2412].

One of the Western Studite Typika (the Typikon of San Nicola di Casole, ch. 1) requires that the brethren stand during the chanting of **"God is the Lord,"** *(Orig. p. 629)* as at the Epistle and Gospel [^2413].

The Georgian manuscript of the Jerusalem Typikon does not indicate the manner of execution of **"God is the Lord"** in the order of the Vigil, but makes a note concerning this in the rubrics of weekday Matins (see there).

Greek manuscripts and printed editions: "The monk appointed from Vespers for the prokeimenon, having made the customary bow unto the superior, chants **God is the Lord**, and we chant the troparion..."

The oldest Slavic manuscripts: "The appointed monk, who chants the prokeimenon at Vespers... (having made a bow unto the superior or unto his place) chants **God is the Lord** in the current Tone, which... he invites with the verses **O give thanks** (etc.), and unto each verse the canonarch (or: monk) chants as refrain: **Blessed is He that cometh in the name of the Lord**. And the choirs after each verse chant **God is the Lord and hath appeared**, in the same Tone. Then again the monk: **God is the Lord and hath appeared**. And the Sunday troparion is recited by the chanters—."

Later manuscripts: "The appointed monk, who chants the prokeimenon at Vespers, having made a bow unto the superior, chants **God is the Lord** with its verses, and we chant the troparion."

So likewise the Old Believer Typikon, only instead of "chants" it has "pronounces."

The *Diataxis* of Patriarch Philotheus and the present-day Greek Euchologion: "**God is the Lord** is chanted" [^2414].

The Moscow Sluzhebniki of 1602 and 1647: "We chant **God is the Lord**; the verse: **O give thanks** (etc.). But if it be a fast, we chant **Alleluia**, reciting these verses."

The Sluzhebnik of Petro Mohyla: "And they begin to chant **God is the Lord** according unto custom; while the priest, standing in that same place, recites the customary verses after the singing of each choir and departs."

The Moscow Sluzhebnik of 1658 is like our present one.

The *Hieratikon*: "The choirs alternately chant **God is the Lord** four times in the current Tone" [^2415].

According unto the *Proskynitarion*, in the East (17th century) **"God is the Lord"** was chanted the first time by the patriarch or a choir, and then by the choirs in turn, while the verses were not recited [^2416].

## Troparia at "God is the Lord" (*Tropari na Bog Gospod'*)

Having transitioned from a sorrowful and penitential disposition unto a festive and joyful one, and from Old Testament sentiments unto that vivid premonition of salvation that is provided by the selection of passages from Psalm 117 [LXX; Masoretic 118], the hymns of Matins now pass over into direct Christian language. This is done through the appending of the troparion unto the psalm. At this moment the troparion receives its most solemn execution: even at weekday Matins it is sung twice, which is done at no other service, not even the Divine Liturgy; even if there are two troparia for commemorations equal in rank, here the first troparion is sung twice; this is primarily in view of the distribution of the singing between the two choirs. Since the troparion is here properly a refrain unto the psalm (as it was also according unto its original designation), and for a psalm or section of psalms the Lesser Doxology is considered an indispensable conclusion, another troparion (if there be one) and a Theotokion, or a Theotokion alone, is linked with the troparion by means of the latter—which Theotokion always...

...harmonizes in Tone (for symmetry) with the preceding troparion. Thus, if on Sunday—as *(Orig. p. 630)* is almost always the case—there occurs some commemoration with a troparion, the Theotokion is sung not in the Tone of the Sunday, but the Resurrection Theotokion (the so-called "first") is sung according to the Tone of the troparion of the saint. The Sunday Theotokion of the current Tone, remaining unsung because of this, is transferred unto the sessional hymns after the 1st Kathisma, replacing the Theotokion there—concerning which, indeed, the Typikon makes note already in Chapter 52. The same transfer, it goes without saying, must be made if a troparion is appointed in place of the Theotokion, as happens at the concurrence with Sunday of feasts of the Mother of God, forefeasts, afterfeasts, and certain other commemorations. In that same Chapter 52, it is noted that if on Sunday there be two saints, each with a distinct troparion, then the Sunday troparion is sung once, then the troparion to the 1st saint, **"Glory..."** (*Slava*)—to the other, **"Both now..."** (*I nyne*)—the Theotokion in the Tone of the last troparion.

### According to Ancient Typika (*Po drevnim ustavam*)

According unto the Studite (Alexian) Typikon as well, the Sunday troparion was sung twice and after it the Theotokion; but if a troparion to a saint was joined (which was done only for great saints), then it was sung once [^2417].

According unto the Evergetis Typikon, the troparion to the saint was, apparently, sung in place of the Theotokion.

It is noteworthy that in the Typikon of St. Nicholas of Casole (*Typikon Casulanum*) the troparion even at this place is called "dismissal" (*apolytic*) [^2418].

Of the Jerusalem Typika: the Georgian MS gives nothing; the Greek MSS prescribe: "We sing the troparion, doubling it; and at **Glory...** the troparion of the daily saint, if he be commemorated with a feast; but if not—the Theotokion of the tone, the 1st"; so likewise the printed Greek Typikon and Euchologion; the Slavic MSS and the Old Believer Typikon are like our present one, yet the oldest Slavic MSS add a rubric concerning the transfer of the Theotokion unto the kathisma.

In the East in the 17th century, troparia at Matins were sung, if they were not known by heart, with the assistance of a canonarch; **"Glory... Both now..."** was not sung, but was recited quickly, as in Russia as well [^2419].

### Sunday Troparia (*Voskresnye tropari*)

Replacing at certain services all other hymns, the troparion depicts in concise form the very essence of the celebrated event. This is likewise done by the Sunday troparia, sung at **"God is the Lord,"** at the Hours, and at the Divine Liturgy. Yet while some of them paint more a picture, the external side of the Resurrection (Tones 1, 4, 6), others...

...dwell upon its internal side; moreover, each successive troparion directs attention to ever different features of the event, drawing sufficient material for this from that sublime subject, so that not one of the troparia repeats the thoughts of another. The Theotokia to the troparia are dedicated predominantly to unfolding the mystery of the Incarnation of the Son of God, which became manifest from the time of His Resurrection, only occasionally dwelling upon His death and Resurrection (Tones 3, 6, 7, 8).

*(Orig. p. 631)*

### Their History (*Istoriya ikh*)

Judging from the fact that troparia are the most ancient part of festival services, known to that primary formation of divine worship represented also by the Typika of the Great Church of Constantinople of the 9th century, one might have expected that the Sunday troparia would be older than the stichera and canons, and that they appeared before St. John of Damascus; their anonymity likewise speaks in favor of this. Yet in surviving monuments they appear concurrently with the works of Sts. Cosmas and John of Damascus. Thus, together with certain of the latter works, they are indicated by a MS of the Jerusalem Patriarchal Library (No. 43 of the Monastery of the Holy Cross) containing the "Order of Passion and Paschal Week"; here they are placed as "sessional hymns" (*kathismata*) at the end of Vespers, after **"Now lettest Thou..."** (*Nyne otpushchaeshi*), beginning from the Vespers of Holy Saturday until Bright Friday, Tones 1–7 [^2420].

# THE PSALTER KATHISMATA AT MATINS (*Kafizmy utreni*)

With the troparion concludes the first, brief part of Matins, just as with it concludes Vespers and the whole of Matins (and the first part of the service of the Hour). The second part of Matins, like every service, begins with psalms and consists primarily of psalms and readings, interrupted only by litanies and a small number of hymns. For this abundance of psalms and readings Matins is indebted unto its nocturnal designation: by night, more than by day, prayer requires external support, which it finds in psalmody and edifying reading. Therefore Matins represents preeminently a service of psalms and readings. On the other hand, there has been transferred to Matins preeminently that part of divine worship which in antiquity consisted in the singing of the entire Psalter over the course of the daily cycle of services: the oldest rule concerning this distribution of psalms, the Sinaitic, assigns to Matins two-thirds of the entire Psalter—100 psalms, leaving for Vespers and the other services only one-third (Introductory Chapter, p. 218). Therefore in the present Typikon as well, out of the 20 Kathismata into which the Psalter is divided, the greater part falls upon Matins—two, and in certain periods of the year even three kathismata, whereas upon all the remaining services falls only one (at Vespers) or 3 kathismata for the entire daily cycle of the Hours (during Great Lent). Finally, of all the services, only at Matins does the Polyeleos occur, consisting of two full psalms. For this reason psalmody constitutes the most extensive and stable part of Matins; whereas for variable festive hymns (stichera, canons) the Typikon makes countless reductions in the psalmody of Vespers and the Hours, at Matins psalmody is never abbreviated, being retained even at Pascha at least as the Polyeleos at Matins of Bright Week (in the Greek Church) and as kathismata at its Vespers; psalmody at Matins is canceled only in exceptional cases: at the Matins of the great feasts (the Nativity of Christ, Theophany), when Great Compline (with its 6 psalms) precedes Matins and when it is joined with Vespers (at which a kathisma has already taken place); at the Matins of the first three days of Passion Week in view of the extraordinary abundance of readings (Gospels); and at the Matins of Holy Saturday for the sake of the Blameless (*Amomoi*, Psalm 118 [LXX; Masoretic 119], likewise a psalm). The completeness and stability of psalmody at Matins is all the more remarkable in that, judging by the content of the psalms, it is difficult to find suitable material in the Psalter for Matins: psalms possess for the most part an evening (penitential) character. In view of this, psalmody at Matins takes on more the character of a continuous, orderly reading of the entire Psalter ("regular kathismata") *(Orig. p. 632)* rather than a selection of psalms suited to the occasion (such a selection is made only for the beginning and end of Matins: the Six Psalms and the Praise Psalms). The Psalter at Matins is sung for the sake of its sacred text itself, which instills a religious disposition in general, as if to sanctify the beginning day by this divinely inspired word, as if to implore a blessing upon the impending day by holding in remembrance as many great divine truths as are scattered throughout the psalms. The Psalter is, as it were, laid as the foundation of the coming day, and is, as it were, confirmed by it.

### History of the Kathisma (*Istoriya kafizmy*)

*Kathisma* (Gr. κάθισμα) literally means "sitting." The word indicates that during this part of Matins one may sit. In the Greek Church to this day the parishioners sit at the beginning of the kathismata in the stalls (*stacidia*). Originally, however, they stood throughout the entire time of divine worship, so that standing (Gr. στάσις, *stasis*) was a constant characteristic of Christian worship; it was even considered the finest external expression of the essence of New Testament worship—the spirit of filial freedom before God, alien to servile fear; therefore the most ancient apostolic canon forbade kneeling not only on Sundays, but also on all days from Pascha until Pentecost, prescribing that on these days one pray unfailingly standing. Hence in the primary period of the development of the church order, which coincided with the greatest development of Christian enthusiasm (1st–3rd centuries) and proceeded without being under the predominant influence of monasticism (1st–4th centuries), the custom of sitting during psalmody could not have arisen. It appeared when in the services they began to strive to sing the entire Psalter within a single day and night or over a longer span. Cassian first mentions this custom in the 5th century (Introductory Chapter, p. 218), and the tone of justification in which he describes this custom of the Egyptian monks bears witness unto its novelty. Reports from the 6th–8th centuries, both...

...for the East and for the West, speak of sitting only during the (edifying) readings, and for the East standing is even emphasized during the singing of the entire Psalter at the nocturnal service: its sections in the well-known description of the Sinaitic Matins are called *staseis*, Gr. στάσις—standing, and it is stated that for their singing the monks stood up; and these sections (of 50 psalms each) according to their position at Matins correspond fully unto our kathismata. Standing during the kathismata is demanded also by the *Diatyposis* (see below, "Order of the Kathisma"; Introductory Chapter, pp. 295, 310). But transferred to the West, perhaps by Cassian, the custom of sitting during the psalms soon received wide dissemination there and passed over unto other parts of the service. In the East, by the 9th century there already exists the term *kathisma* (Gr. κάθισμα), which, however, is applied more, as among the Greeks today, to the hymns preceding the reading than to the sections of the Psalter, which are for the most part called *stichologiai* (Gr. αἱ στιχολογίαι [Orig. printed στιχολογίοα]), while the "Glories" of the kathismata are called *staseis* [^2421]; yet already in the *Hypotyposis* they are called *kathisma psalms* (Gr. κάθισμα ψαλμούς), and in the *Diatyposis* simply *kathisma* (Gr. κάθισμα) [^2422]. A trace of such a practice—sitting only during the readings and standing during the psalms of the kathismata—remains in the present Typikon as well: sessional hymns are appointed only after those kathismata which are followed by readings; thus, sessional hymns are not appointed after the kathismata of Vespers, which are not followed by readings; conversely, sessional hymns are appointed even without kathismata before readings, as, for example, after Ode 3 of the Canon.

### The Order of the Kathisma (*Chin kafizmy*)

The execution of the kathismata at Matins differs considerably from Vespers, both Great and daily. "The choir saith: **Lord, have mercy** (3). **Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit.** The reader: **Both now and ever, and unto the ages of ages**, and chanteth the kathisma of the Psalter" (*stikhologisuet kafismu Psaltira*). At Vespers, as we have seen, the kathisma is not preceded by **"Lord, have mercy,"** **"Glory... Both now..."**—this is because there the kathisma follows immediately after the Great Ektenia, where **"Lord, have mercy"** is repeated far more than 3 times, and where there is its own doxology in the exclamation, more extensive than this present lesser one. Concerning the division of the kathisma into parts, the Typikon nowhere speaks in detail, mentioning it only in passing in the order of Matins for the 1st Monday of Great Lent. In the Psalter with Order (*Psaltir' sledovannaya*), the kathisma is divided into three parts designated by the word "Glory" (*Slava*); this designation, unexplained in the liturgical books, is in practice considered equivalent to that doxology wherewith are divi- *(Orig. p. 633)* -ded the psalms of the Six Psalms, wherewith the psalms of the Hours conclude, and which consists of: **"Glory... Both now...; Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, glory to Thee, O God** (3); **Lord, have mercy** (3); **Glory... Both now..."** In practice, it is accepted at the...

...kathismata for the reader to recite the beginning of this doxology: **"Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit,"** the singers the middle, and the reader the end: **"Both now and ever, and unto the ages of ages"** (in the second lesser doxology) [^2423]. Such a division is made in order to link the kathisma more closely with prayerful invocation and to instill the thought that the reader and the choir vie with each other in glorifying God (they cannot wait for the end of the doxology). At the conclusion of the kathisma, if an ektenia follows it, at Sunday Matins and on other festive and semi-festive days, the doxology, now recited entirely by the reader, concludes (as is accepted by practice) with **"Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, glory to Thee, O God,"** since it is followed by the Little Ektenia, wherein there is both **"Lord, have mercy"** and an extensive doxology.
