If from Pentecost to Advent there are more than twenty-four weeks, then after the 23rd week readings are taken from the Sundays after Epiphany—the 6th, 5th, 4th, and 3rd—while on the final Sunday before Advent the readings of the 24th Sunday after Pentecost are read.

Protestants, with the exception of the Reformed, who leave the selection of readings to the discretion of the presiding minister, retained the Roman system of readings[^2784], moreover in its ancient form, that is, without the alterations introduced into it after the Reformation (Anglicans in places *(Orig. p. 769)* retained the readings of the Gallican rite which had prevailed in England). Variants: Easter Sunday in the Anglican Church: Col. 3:1–7; John 20:1–10; Trinity Sunday: Lutheran, Rom. 11:33–36; Anglican, Rev. 4:1–11; John 3:1–15; 2nd after Pentecost (there reckoned as the 1st after Trinity, etc.): 1 John 4:16 (7)–21; Luke 16:19–31; the readings of the 3rd and 4th Sundays = the 2nd and 3rd; 5th Sunday: Epistle = 4th, Gospel = 1st; 6th Sunday: Epistle = 5th, Gospel = 4th; 7th Sunday: Epistle = 6th, Gospel = 5th, and so forth up to the 24th Sunday (except the 16th, where Anglican: Gal. 6:11–18), where Anglican Epistle = 24th, Gospel = 23rd; 25th Sunday: Lutheran Epistle = 24th, Gospel = 23rd; Anglican: Jer. 23:5–8; John 6:5–14 (or the interpolated 6th Sunday after Epiphany, and then the 5th and 4th); 26th Sunday: Lutheran, 1 Thess. 4:13–18, Gospel = 24th; 27th Sunday: Lutheran, 2 Thess. 1:3–10, Matt. 25:31–46; 28th Sunday: Lutheran, 1 Thess. 5:1–11, Matt. 25:1–13; 1st Sunday of Advent: Matt. 21:1–9 [13]; 2nd Sunday of Advent: Luke 21:25–36; 3rd Sunday of Advent: 1 Cor. 4:1–5, Matt. 11:2–10; 4th Sunday of Advent: Phil. 4:4–7, John 1:19–28; Sunday after the Nativity of Christ:

Anglican, Matt. 1:18–25; 4th after Epiphany: Anglican, Rom. 13:1–7; 6th after Epiphany: Lutheran, 1 Pet. 1:16–21, Matt. 17:1–9; Anglican, 1 John 3:1–8, Matt. 24:23–31; 3rd of the Forty Days: Matt. 25:21–28; 6th: Anglican, Matt. 27:1–54.

The Roman system of readings (which differs from the Milanese and Mozarabic) was traced by medieval liturgists (Amalarius, Berno) to St. Jerome and Pope Damasus, an attribution occasioned by a remark in an epistle of the former[^2785]; Gregory of Tours (6th c.) says of the readings that they were *"sanctioned by the ancient canon"*[^2786]; yet in general the 6th–7th centuries in the West were merely a period of the initial formation of a fixed system of readings, as is evident from the conciliar decrees regulating this subject; thus, this is enacted by the Council of Braga in 563[^2787]; the Council of Toledo in 633, under pain of excommunication, mandates the reading of the Apocalypse during the period of Pentecost[^2788] (in all probability in view of the newly baptized, since the Apocalypse frequently speaks of washing in the Blood of Christ and of white robes). The dissemination, and perhaps also the completion, of the Roman lectionary system was fostered by the commission given by Charlemagne to Paul the Deacon (*Paulus Diaconus*) to compile the *Homiliarium*, that is, a collection of patristic homilies for feast days[^2789]. Complete ancient lectionary registers of Roman readings are: *Comes ab Albino ex Caroli imper. praecepto emendatus* (ed. a Thomasio, *Opp.* V, 297), *Capitularia Evangeliorum Spirense et Renaugiense* by Gerbert (*Monum. Veter. Liturg. Allem.* I, 418), *Comes* by Pamelius (*Lit. Lat.* II, 1), and *Comes Theotinchi* by Baluze (*Capitul. reg. Franc.* II, 1309)[^2790]. Not only manuscript monuments, but also printed liturgical books issued in diverse dioceses (Augsburg, Eichstätt) exhibited variations in the distribution of readings, which were definitively eliminated only by the Missal of Pius V in 1570[^2791].

Differences of the system of readings provided by these monuments from the present one: the 1st Sunday after Pentecost (subsequently Trinity Sunday) *(Orig. p. 770)* has Rev. 4:1–11 (= the present Anglican) and Acts 5:29–42 (in Pamelius), 1 Cor. 12:2–11, John 3:1–15 (= Anglican); the 2nd = the present Protestant; and thereafter as among the Lutherans up to the 25th Sunday; the 26th—Rom. 11:25–33, John 6:5–14; Advent as among the Lutherans and Anglicans; the Sundays before Septuagesima as at present, but there are only five Sundays after Epiphany, and for the 5th the Gospel is the present one (*Capitularia*) or Matt. 11:25–30 (Pamelius); from Septuagesima, as at present.

In the Western Church, therefore, the principle of continuous reading (*lectio continua*) of the New Testament is not maintained, nor was it ever maintained to such a degree as in the Eastern Church, frequently yielding to the principle of readings corresponding to the commemorations of the year (*lectio congrua sive propria*). Yet even in such seasons as Pentecost, the former principle is maintained as far as possible: the reading begins with the Acts and the Gospel of John according to ancient universal custom (*Tolkovy Typikon*, I, p. 183), wherein the latter, as with us, continues throughout the entire Pentecostarion, whereas the Acts is soon replaced (already on Bright Friday) by the Catholic Epistles; these latter conclude only after Pentecost, in the 1st–3rd Sundays following it; from the 4th Sunday after Pentecost the Pauline Epistles begin and proceed in order, interrupted on the 5th Sunday by a reading from 1 Peter, the reading of the Summer Ember Days (fast of the Four Seasons); the Gospels likewise follow in order, though in an order different from that of the Eastern Church: first Luke, with interruptions until the 16th Sunday, and thereafter without interruption Matthew (until Advent); the interruptions (on the 5th, 7th, and 14th Sundays from Matthew, and on the 6th and 11th from Mark) are explained by special commemorations: thus, on the 6th Sunday, Mark 8:1–9 was appointed perhaps in view of the harvest occurring at that time; on the 9th Sunday, Luke 19:41–48 is explained by the historical date of August 10—the destruction of Jerusalem. Beginning with the Sundays after Epiphany, a series of Pauline Epistles begins anew, in view of the ancient custom of beginning their reading at this point. The readings of the Forty Days (*Quadragesima*) are adapted to the ancient custom of catechizing during its days: the readings of the 1st–3rd weeks prepare for the rite of the renunciation of Satan and exorcism (the 3rd Sunday was termed the Sunday of Renunciation and Exorcism, *abrenuntiatio*, *exorcismus*), while the readings of the 4th–6th weeks prepare for the rite of adherence unto Christ (*addictio*, *sponsio*). Liturgists also perceive in the Roman system of readings the principle of two halves of the year: the winter, festive portion, the period of the bestowing of grace, and the summer, ordinary portion, the period of the assimilation of the latter: *semestre Domini et semestre ecclesiae*.[^2792]

*(Orig. p. 771)*

### The Armenian Lectionary System
The principle of continuous reading is most strictly maintained in the Armenian Church. Excepting feast days which have their own proper readings, and Sundays with special commemorations, such as Easter Sunday, the 2nd Sunday of Pentecost, and all the Sundays of the Forty Days, the readings here proceed in biblical order (with the omission of festal readings and, very rarely, of less important passages) on Sundays, Wednesdays, and Fridays, while during festal weeks (all the weeks of Pentecost and two after it, the week before the Dormition, and the fifteen days before the Theophany) readings occur every day, by virtue of which there fall upon Sundays not selected readings (of more prominent passages), but those that occur according to the regular sequence. The series of readings begins from Pascha with the Acts, and from Thomas Sunday with the Gospel of John, which books conclude at Pentecost; after it proceed all the Pauline Epistles (to the Romans—until the Dormition), concluding with the Pastoral Epistles (the Epistle to the Hebrews preceding them) before Septuagesima Sunday (the Catholic Epistles are not read); from Pentecost Matthew begins and proceeds until the 9th Sunday, Mark until the 6th Sunday after the Elevation of the Cross, Luke until the Theophany, and from it John 2–7 is repeated.[^2792]

### The Megalynarion: "It Is Truly Meet" (*Dostoyno*)
Following the Epistle and the Gospel, a further variable part of the Liturgy is formed by the hymn in honor of the Mother of God, chanted at Her commemoration after the consecration of the Holy Gifts, in response to the celebrant's exclamation: **"Especially for our most holy..."** (*Izryadno o Presvyatey...*). This hymn falls, consequently, upon the most sacred part of the Liturgy, occupied exclusively with prayers and praises unto God Himself, and predominantly unto God the Father. The introduction here of a hymn unto the Most Holy Theotokos testifies to the supreme degree of Her veneration by the Orthodox Church. Naturally, for the ordinary and Sunday Liturgy the most rapturous hymn was selected, confessing the Mother of God as higher than the Seraphim and the Cherubim: **"It is truly meet"** (*Dostoyno yest'*, Ἄξιόν ἐστιν). On the Great Twelve Feasts and their afterfeasts, this hymn is replaced by the 9th Heirmos of the Canon, as likewise dedicated to the Mother of God and fully corresponding to the hymn **"It is truly meet"**, which is also the 9th Heirmos of a Canon (of Great Friday) with a refrain prefixed. By this Heirmos, termed in such liturgical application the *Zadostoynik* (a term of the Slavic Typikon), the Liturgy in its most crucial part at the same time coordinates itself with the feast (which is why there are chanted as the *Zadostoynik* even such 9th Heirmoi as do not mention the Mother of God). At the Liturgy of St. Basil the Great (not falling upon a Great Twelve Feast or Great and Holy Week), **"It is truly meet"** is replaced by **"All of creation rejoiceth in thee"** (*O Tebe raduetsia*), a hymn which, if less ecstatic, is yet more profound. **"It is truly meet"** is Tone 6, while **"All of creation rejoiceth in thee"** is Tone 8, both possessing a special chant melody, though the former is also customarily chanted in Tone 8. **"It is truly meet"**, in addition to the Liturgy, concludes the chanting of the Canon at Matins and Compline and enters into the dismissal of the Typika (*Izobrazitel'nye*); **"All of creation rejoiceth in thee"** serves likewise as the Theotokion of the Sunday Sessional Hymn.

*(Orig. p. 772)*

#### History
In heterodox liturgies, both Eastern and Western, there is nothing corresponding to **"It is truly meet"**, despite the commemoration of the Most Holy Theotokos in the anaphoral prayer of all these liturgies (with the exception of the Nestorian), moreover in a form close to ours: *"especially"* (*izryadno*), *imprimis*.[^2793] But in all ancient Orthodox liturgies there is always a hymn unto the Most Holy Theotokos at this point: in the liturgies of St. Mark the Evangelist, of St. Peter the Apostle, and of St. James the Apostle (10th–14th c.), before the words **"Especially"**, immediately in the first two, and closely preceding in the last, the priest says: *“And remember, O Lord, the archangelic voice proclaiming: Hail, full of grace... blessed is the fruit.”*[^2794]

In one manuscript of the Liturgy of St. John Chrysostom: *“the choir chants: For (ὡς) it is truly and right to glorify thee, O Theotokos... while the choir chants this, the priest says: Hail, full of grace.”*

In certain manuscripts of the Liturgy of St. Basil the Great (13th c. and later), **"All of creation rejoiceth in thee"** is absent, and in its place:

*“then the priest prays, saying thus: Hail, full of grace, the Lord is with thee, etc.”*; in others, both are present.[^2795]

**"It is truly meet"** (*Dostoyno yest'*) was perhaps composed according to the model of **"It is meet"** (*Dostoyno*) occurring earlier at the Liturgy; regarding **"More honorable"** (*Chestneyshuyu*), see *Tolkovy Typikon*, II, pp. 289–290.

At present among the Greeks at the Chrysostom Liturgy:

*“The 1st choir chants harmoniously the Megalynarion (μεγαλυνάριον) of the Theotokos, **‘It is truly meet’**, in Tone 2”*;

at the Liturgy of St. Basil the Great:

*“The 1st choir simply recites (χύμα): **‘All of creation rejoiceth in thee’** down to ‘God before all ages’; the remainder of the troparion, however, slowly and with singing in Tone 1: ‘For He made thy womb a throne’, etc., unto the end.”*[^2796]

### The Communion Verse (*Kinonikon* / *Prichasten*)
The final variable part of the Liturgy is the Communion verse (*Kinonikon*, κοινωνικόν; Slavonic: *Prichasten*)—a verse, for the most part psalm-based, chanted during the communion of the sacred ministers within the altar. This communion, performed as a sign of special sacred mystery behind closed sanctuary doors and drawn curtain, constitutes the holiest moment of the Liturgy after the consecration (*transubstantiation*), demanding of the worshipers a profound inward recollectedness. The latter could not be attained through any prolonged hymn. What was needed here was precisely a single, concise and expressive verse with the refrain *Alleluia*, which marks all the most crucial and joyful moments of divine worship. The melody of the Kinonikon is directed toward this same end—slow, serene, and tenderly compunctious, in which echo the melodies of Great and Holy Week. (Such, at least, is the melody of the Kinonikon in the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra). The chanting of the Kinonikon may be divided between the two choirs—half a verse to each, which for the most part contains an independent clause (in the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, the 1st choir chants the Kinonikon, and the 2nd chants the *Alleluia*).

*(Orig. p. 773)*

The Communion verse of the Sunday Liturgy—Psalm 148:1: **“Praise the Lord from the heavens, praise Him in the heights”**—has here the same significance as the Praises (*Ainoi* / *Khvalitny*) at the end of Matins: in the consciousness of the inadequacy of our praise, at its conclusion we commit the work of praise unto the heavenly hosts. And the Resurrection of the Savior is pre-eminently such a deed for which the Lord can worthily be praised only in heaven. Moreover, in that earthly heaven which is the altar, during the Communion verse there takes place a sacrifice of praise worthy of the true heaven: the most intimate communion through the Eucharistic Gifts with Christ Himself, made possible through Christ's redemptive death (cf. the Paschal Kinonikon: **“Receive the Body of Christ”**). Aside from the Sunday, the Kinonikon **“Praise the Lord from the heavens”** belongs to two of the greatest feasts: the Nativity of Christ and Theophany at their principal Liturgy—the Liturgy of the Eve—as well as the Feast of the Circumcision, closely associated with the former, and the Church New Year (September 1).

If the Menaion saint has a Communion verse—and saints commemorated with Epistle and Gospel reading possess one—then after the Sunday verse his Communion verse is also chanted (*“and of the saint, if he have one”*), wherein the *Alleluia* is chanted only after the second Communion verse (by musical tradition).

#### History
The antiquity of the Communion verse is attested by its presence in all heterodox liturgies.

In the Roman Liturgy it is called precisely thus (*communio*) and consists of a verse, for the most part psalm-based, differing not only for different feast days, but changing also on Sundays—for example, on the 3rd Sunday after Pentecost, Psalm 17:3 [18:2]; this verse is read by the priest before the altar table with folded hands; on a solemn High Mass, however, it is chanted by the choir, and the ancient Roman Order (*Ordo Romanus*) says concerning its chanting:

*“As soon as the Pontiff (the Pope) begins the communion, immediately the schola begins the communion antiphon, and they chant until all the people have communicated; the Pontiff gives a signal that they should say the Gloria, and then, having repeated the verse, they cease.”*[^2797]

In the Mozarabic Liturgy, the Communion verse, rarely designated as such (*communio*), sometimes called *“for approaching”* (*ad accedendum*), usually (even on the Nativity of Christ) has the following composition:

*“The choir says: Taste and see that the Lord is good, alleluia (3). Verse: I will bless the Lord at all times, His praise shall continually be in my mouth. Priest: Alleluia (3). Verse: The Lord will redeem the souls of His servants, and none of them that trust in Him shall offend (Ps. 33:9, 2, 23 [34:8, 1, 22]). Priest: Alleluia (3). Glory... Both now... Priest: Alleluia.”*[^2798]

In the Nestorian Liturgy the Communion verse, here called the responsory, consists of two parts, separated by certain exclamations and actions of the sacred ministers; regarding the first part, in the oldest manuscript of this liturgy, attributed to the Apostles Addai and Mari, it is noted:

*“Deacon: Praise. And they recite the responsory”*;

in the contemporary Nestorian Liturgy at this point *(Orig. p. 774)* there are appointed such “antiphons”:

*“Deacon: Render praises unto God. Clergy: Praise unto Him in the church of the saints (Ps. 149:1) evermore, and the mercy of the Lord and His compassion be upon us unto ages of ages, amen”*;

the second part according to the ancient manuscript:

*“meanwhile the responsories are spoken: Brethren, receive the Body of the Son, crieth the Church, and drink His cup with faith in the house of the Kingdom. On feast days: Strengthen, O Lord, (..?) Daily: The Mysteries which we receive (..?)”*.[^2799]

In the Coptic Liturgy, Psalm 50 [51] serves as the Communion verse.[^2800]

Among ancient Orthodox liturgies, the Liturgy of St. Peter the Apostle, which in general is close to the Roman, has as its Communion verse the phrase spoken in the latter by the priest at the commingling of the bread and wine: *“O Lamb of God, that takest away the sin of the world, have mercy on us.”*[^2801]

In the manuscripts of the Alexandrian Liturgy of St. Mark the Evangelist, no mention is made of a Communion verse. In the Liturgy of St. James the Apostle, however, according to all its manuscripts (10th–14th c.), the Communion verse, preceded by the deacon's exclamation *“In the peace of Christ let us sing”*, is:

*“O taste and see that the Lord is good (Ps. 33:9 [34:8]). Alleluia.”*[^2802]

The Kinonikon **“Praise the Lord”** could have arisen from the chanted exclamation of the priest in the Liturgy of St. James after the fraction of the Lamb: *“Praise God in His saints”* (Ps. 150:1), or (according to another manuscript): *“Praise the Lord, all ye nations”* (Ps. 116:1 [117:1]).

In antiquity, apparently, the Communion verse chanted during the communion of the clergy was repeated also during the communion of the laity: in an 11th–12th-century manuscript of the Apostol (the Muravyov manuscript) of the Moscow Theological Academy Library, on Meatfare Sunday:

*“Kinonikon: **‘Rejoice (in the Lord, O ye righteous)’** the small; and when the holy communion begins, **‘Rejoice’** double and **‘Let our mouths be filled’**.”*[^2803]

At present among the Greeks:

*“The leader of the 2nd choir (the Lampadarios) chants (the Kinonikon) slowly and melodically (ἀργῶς καὶ μετὰ μέλους) in the tone in which the Cherubic Hymn was chanted”*, that is, *“in the principal (κύριον) tone of the day.”*[^2804]

### The Order of the Panagia (*Chin o Panagii*)

#### Meaning and Content of the Order
The essence of the Order of the Panagia consists in this: that from the church upon the conclusion of the Liturgy, the prosphora from which the particle in honor of the Mother of God was extracted at the Liturgy is carried forth by all the brethren with sacred songs into the monastic refectory (*trapeza*); there it is placed upon a special vessel, and at the conclusion of the meal, with the glorification of the Holy Trinity and prayer to the Most Holy Theotokos, the prosphora is elevated (raised up) above Their icons, and the brethren partake of it. The meaning of the rite, evidently, is vividly to represent the presence at the meal of God Himself and of the Most Holy Theotokos. Such a significance of the rite is indicated also by the tradition concerning its origin *(Orig. p. 775)* recorded in the Sequenced Psalter (*Sledovannaya Psaltir'*; discussed below). According to St. Symeon of Thessalonica, *“a portion of bread we offer daily unto our One God existing in Trinity in the name of the Mother of God, because through her divine childbearing we have come to know the Holy Trinity, and because she bare for us the Living Bread.”*[^2805] The immediate objective of the rite is so closely to unite the refectory meal with the just-concluded Liturgy that both should appear as a single divine service and the former should communicate its grace unto the latter. Thanks to the Order of the Panagia, indeed, the monastic dinner is transformed into a veritable divine service of the type of the Typika (*Izobrazitel'nye*) and Compline, with Kontakion and Zadostoynik in place of a Canon (and on Pascha even with an entire Ode of the Canon).

**"Panagia"** (παναγία—*“All-Holy”*), or *“Most Holy”* (*Sequenced Psalter*, fol. 135v), is a title customarily applied to the Mother of God, but in the Order of the Panagia—or, as it is more fully titled, *“On the Elevation of the Panagia”* (*Sequenced Psalter*, fol. 136)—this appellation is applied to the prosphora from which at the Liturgy the particle was extracted in honor of the Most Holy Theotokos. This prosphora is, therefore, the most sacred after that from which the Lamb was extracted, and which, as the most sacred of all, is consumed not in the refectory after taking food as is the panagia, but in the church itself prior to any food (*antidoron*).

The not inconsiderable hymnody and ceremonial rites of the Order of the Panagia, which is celebrated, as its rubric indicates, only in monasteries on all days (and not solely on Sundays, although placed in the chapter on the Sunday service), can be divided into three parts:

1) The blessing of the refectory meal;
2) The elevation of the panagia;

3) The thanksgiving for the meal.

— Aside from the present place, the Typikon also touches upon the Order of the Panagia in Chapter 35, *“On Food and Drink”*, introducing certain supplements to the present exposition.

The rite opens, as does every church service, with a psalm. In accordance with the brevity of the rite and akin to Vespers, it possesses a single introductory psalm, namely Psalm 144 [145]: **“I will exalt Thee, my God”**. The psalm (alphabetical) presents an ecstatic praise unto God, unto His greatness as well as His goodness, especially outpoured upon them that call upon Him; it is taken here especially for verses 15–16: *“The eyes of all look toward Thee in hope...”* The psalm does not have **“Come, let us worship”** before it, by reason of connection and analogy with the Liturgy. The brethren all *“recite”* (*glagolyut*) the psalm; consequently, they chant it in recitative, as is done in the Solovki and other monasteries.[^2806] The psalm is chanted along the way from the church to the refectory; consequently, its chanting begins in the church immediately following the dismissal of the Liturgy and concludes in the refectory. The brethren walk two by two, preceded by the superior. Who carries the panagia and in what manner is not indicated either here or in Chapter 35 of the Typikon; yet in the Paschal Order of the Panagia, where it is replaced by the *Artos*, the latter is carried by the deacon upon a *panagiarion* (a proskomide vessel bearing an image of the Mother of God). In certain monasteries, for example in the Moscow Gethsemane Skete, the *“Most Pure”* (*Prechistaya*) prosphora, which during the Liturgy stands with the diskos or a dish of similar construction *(Orig. p. 776)* upon the High Place, is carried in front by a hieromonk, behind whom the brethren walk two by two in their monastic mantles.[^2807] According to Chapter 35 of the Typikon, the carrying of the panagia is accompanied by the striking of the semantron (*bilo*) or bell, which imparts a special solemnity to this procession and at the same time serves as the tolling (*blagovest*) for the refectory meal, which, thanks to the Order of the Panagia and the patristic reading, constitutes a genuine church service. The psalm is chanted with such calculation as to end it upon entering the refectory: *“And having arrived at the refectory and the psalm being finished, we recite (that is, in the same manner as the psalm—we chant in recitative) the refectory prayer: Our Father.”* The prayer is introduced here not only because, as the chief Christian prayer, it is necessary at every service, but also on account of its fourth petition; it is not omitted even in the Paschal Order of the Panagia, though it is absent at the evening meal. To the prayer is joined the blessing of the refectory meal, preceded by the usual introduction: **“Glory... Both now... Lord, have mercy (3). Bless.”** (see above, p. 719). The superior or priest (probably in the absence of the superior)[^2808] pronounces: **“Christ our God, bless the food and drink of Thy servants...”**, etc. (see in the *Sequenced Psalter*, whence it is evident that the final *“Amen”* of this blessing is likewise pronounced by him), blessing, as goes without saying, the table. *“And each one sits...”*

*“...down in his own place according to rank,”* says Chapter 35, *“with reverence and silence”*—with reverence, because the refectory meal here is the same as a divine service; with silence, also in view of the fact that during the meal a reading takes place. Regarding the reading, nothing is said in Chapter 2 of the Typikon, but in Chapter 35 the order of reading is also provided: *“the reader immediately (as soon as the brethren sit down) begins the preface of the reading which he intendeth to read”*, that is, the reader pronounces the title of the reading in the form, for example: *“The Life (or: The Passion) of the Holy Martyr N., bless, father.”* *“The superior or the priest of the day, blessing, saith: ‘Through the prayers of him whose reading this is...’”*, that is: *“Through the prayers of the holy martyr (or: ‘of our venerable father’) N., Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us.”* What is to be read in the refectory on ordinary Sundays and weekdays the Typikon does not specify either here (in Chapters 2 and 35) or anywhere else; only for certain feasts does it give such an indication—for example, on December 25 in the refectory *“we read the homily of Chrysostom whereof the beginning is: Anciently the patriarchs.”* By established practice it is customary to read the Lives of the Saints in the refectory, yet not from the *Prolog*, from which they are read after the 6th Ode, but from the *Chet'i-Minei* (Menologia), where the Lives are more extensive. And this is undoubtedly an ancient practice, only not recorded in the written Typikon. It is more fitting in the refectory to read the Life of the saint of the following day, in order to prepare for the forthcoming service unto him, and in view of the fact that the liturgical day concludes with the Liturgy (cf. the rubric of Bright Saturday concerning the Ninth Hour and the closing of the Holy Doors). During the meal the panagia in the panagiarion *“stands in an arranged place”*, that is, upon an analogion in front of the tables beneath the icons or the Holy Doors (if the meal takes place in the church). Here also must lie upon an analogion the icons of the Most Holy Trinity and the Most Holy Theotokos, necessary for the rite of elevation.

*(Orig. p. 777)*

Begun with prayer, the meal is likewise punctuated by recurring prayer, although very brief. Before each course of the dinner (*“at each serving of that which is offered”*), *“the superior strikes the kandya or bell, and when all have arisen, the server (the principal among those serving at dinner, that is, the cellarer) saith: ‘Lord, bless.’ The superior: ‘Glory to Thee, Christ God, our hope, glory to Thee’”* (Chapter 35 of the Typikon)—that is, each course is preceded by the same thanksgiving, only briefer, with which the dinner began and with which each church service customarily concludes. The reader does not interrupt the reading for these exclamations. Upon the conclusion of the meal, the reader stands at the end of the table and, turning toward the superior with his hands crossed upon his breast, proclaims aloud: *“Holy fathers, forgive me a sinner”*, bowing to the ground. The superior imparts unto him a blessing. This is the rite of forgiveness for errors in the reading.

The elevation of the panagia itself is performed after the eating, upon the conclusion of dinner. Consequently, the elevation is preceded by a brief thanksgiving for the meal (the full thanksgiving occurs after the elevation), which forms the transition to the rite of elevation:

*“After the meal, he that celebrateth the ministry (the priest of the day) saith the verse: ‘Through the prayers of our holy fathers, Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us.’ And we: ‘Amen.’”*

This is the blessing for thanksgiving and for the elevation of the panagia in place of **“Blessed is our God...”** (cf. at the beginning of morning and evening prayers), serving also as the signal to arise from the table.

*“And having arisen they recite (all recite together): ‘Blessed is God, Who hath mercy upon us and nourisheth us from our youth...’”*—a prayer unto God the Father, glorifying God for nourishing us and all creation, and asking for joy, contentment in all things, and an abundance of virtue (in full in the *Sequenced Psalter* in the Order of the Panagia); and **“Glory to Thee, O Lord, glory to Thee, O Holy One, glory to Thee, O King”**—another prayer unto the Holy Trinity, glorifying Him for bestowing upon us food unto gladness and asking Him to fill us with the Holy Spirit that we may not be put to shame at the Dread Judgment (in full, ibid.). These two prayers conclude with the petition for a blessing upon the elevation itself, which constitutes the solemn conclusion of the meal, in the usual form: **“Glory... Both now... Lord, have mercy (3). Bless.”** The requested blessing is imparted not by words, but by the rite itself. By whom the elevation is performed is not specified in Chapter 2 of the Typikon, and is apparently left open by the expression: *“he that is about to elevate the Most Holy”*; Chapter 35 of the Typikon assigns this to the deacon (*“here however we have the custom that the deacon performeth these things”*—cf. the exposition of the rite on Bright Saturday), evidently as the person who, according to the original concept of this order, is a servant of tables (Acts 6:2); in the Paschal rite the corresponding action is entrusted to the cellarer.

In view of the importance of the forthcoming sacred action, he who is about to perform it asks forgiveness (like the priest before celebrating the Liturgy and communicating) in the words customary for such occasions: *“‘Bless, holy fathers, forgive me a sinner’; and we: ‘God forgive thee and have mercy on thee.’”* A preparation necessary for the forthcoming exalted ministry—the offering of sacred sustenance unto exalted invisible Guests. Having cleansed himself *(Orig. p. 778)* through the forgiveness of offenses from men and sins from God, he who elevates the panagia proceeds to the very action of the elevation.

*“And taking the portion (the prosphora) with the outermost fingers of his hands* (with the thumb and little finger, and with the remaining fingers, consequently, making a canopy over the prosphora, though in the exposition of the rite on Bright Saturday: *‘with three fingers of both hands’*) *he elevateth it slightly (raiseth it a little) above the icon of the Holy Trinity, saying with a loud voice: ‘Great is the name’*,” not daring to utter the Name itself, which is then done by *“the superior or the priest of the day: ‘Of the Holy Trinity.’ And transferring it above the icon of the Mother of God, he signeth it crosswise (not simply raising it as before, but cruciformly), saying: ‘Most Holy Theotokos, help us.’ And we (not the superior or the priest, as on that occasion): ‘Through her intercessions, O God, have mercy on us and save us.’”*

And since the rite has the most immediate relation unto the Mother of God, constituting an offering unto her (for unto God the most sacred sacrifice of the Eucharist has already been offered), there follow next prayers unto her alone. All recite together (*“we recite”*, as previously with the thanksgiving prayers, in contrast to the following *“we chant”*): **“All generations call thee blessed...”** (*Blazhim Tya vsi rodi...*). This is a joyful hymn unto the Theotokos, praising her in the name of all generations of mankind for containing the Uncontainable One and for her constant prayer on our behalf (*“day and night”*—not without reference to midday), which consolidates the civic order (which likewise secures our sustenance) (the hymn serves as the Theotokion to the troparia for the departed at the Midnight Office, where its tone is also indicated: Tone 2). Then there is chanted (the first chanting in the Order of the Panagia) the most customary hymn in honor of the Theotokos, **“It is truly meet...”** (concerning the replacement of this hymn by a Zadostoynik in the Order of the Panagia on feast days and afterfeasts nothing is indicated anywhere, yet during the Paschal season it is replaced by the entire 9th Ode of the Paschal Canon). The brethren partake of the panagia. *“And after all have communicated, the superior or the priest saith: ‘For the many prayers of our Most Pure Lady the Theotokos.’”* This exclamation serves as the blessing upon the third part of the Order of the Panagia now beginning—the thanksgiving for the meal—and as its link with the second part dedicated exclusively to the Mother of God, for which reason the response to this exclamation (*“we however”*, that is, all recite) is the previous: *“Through her intercessions, O God, have mercy on us and save us.”*

Further, preceded by the verse: *“The Lord is merciful and compassionate; He hath given food unto them that fear Him”* (Ps. 110:5 [111:5]), which as it were replaces here the introductory **“Come, let us worship”** before the psalm (cf. the antiphon before the psalm in the Western Church) and expresses the general content of the thanksgiving for the meal that is to follow, there follows Psalm 121 [122]: **“I was glad when they said unto me”**, which is introductory to this part of the rite, portraying the prosperity (*“abundance within thy towers”*) of Jerusalem (the spiritual—that is, the Church), issuing from the visitation of the temple of God. Following the psalm, the order of thanksgiving for the meal, conforming to the type of the briefest services (the Inter-Hours, etc.), has the Trisagion and, following **“Our Father”**, troparia (not designated as such here, and indeed receiving no designation whatsoever). Among the troparia, first of all *“is said”* (recited by all), as is noted, moreover, concerning the subsequent troparia, **“We thank Thee, Christ our God”**, which contains, in addition to thanksgiving for satiety, a petition for the Heavenly Kingdom and for the *(Orig. p. 779)* co-abiding of Christ here with us; the second half of the troparion, **“(Yet) as Thou didst come into the midst of Thy disciples...”**, constitutes the Hypakoe of St. Thomas Sunday, Tone 6. At **“Glory... Both now...”**, if it be a “Dominical” (= Twelve Great)[^2809] feast, its kontakion [is chanted] (at brief services, such as the Typika, of the festal hymns only the kontakion is appointed); on other days (excluding the Afterfeast of Pascha, when **“Having anticipated the morning”** [*Predvarivshiya utro*] and **“Though Thou didst descend into the tomb”** [*Ashche i vo grob*] [are said]), the troparion common to hierarchs and venerable fathers, as the patrons of the monastery, **“God of our fathers...”** (Tone 4), is said at the *Glory*, and at *Both now*—the one common to all saints and the Theotokos: **“Through the intercessions, O Lord, of all the saints and the Theotokos...”** (Such invariance of the troparia in the Order of the Panagia for all days of the year, excluding the Twelve Great Feasts, recalls the similar invariance at the Midnight Office, which does not abandon its customary troparia even for days with a Polyeleos). With these specified troparia concludes the third part of the Order of the Panagia—the thanksgiving for the meal—and together with it this entire rite. Following the troparia comes the dismissal. The dismissal here, naturally, must be of the small dismissal type; yet even the small dismissal here possesses an abbreviated and modified form. Namely, without the exclamation of the priest **“Glory to Thee, Christ God...”**, there is pronounced (by all, as is everything preceding): **“Lord, have mercy (3). Bless”** (the preparatory *Glory... Both now...* was already between the troparia). The priest, in place of **“May Christ our true God...”**, says: **“Blessed is God Who hath mercy upon us and nourisheth us...”**

#### History of the Order of the Panagia
The prayerful sanctification of the monastic meal attains its culmination in the “Order of the Panagia”.

Ecclesiastical tradition attributes directly apostolic antiquity unto this rite. This tradition is placed in the *Sequenced Psalter* immediately following the exposition of the rite, but it also enters as an integral component into that narrative concerning the Dormition of the Most Holy Theotokos which is provided by the *Chet'i-Minei* (Menologia). According to this tradition, when the Apostles, following the descent of the Holy Spirit upon them and prior to their departure to preach in diverse lands, lived together, they were accustomed at the midday meal to leave an unoccupied place at table for Christ, placing there a head-cushion with a fragment of bread (*ukrukh*). Upon the conclusion of dinner and after the prayer of thanksgiving, they elevated this bread fragment with the words: **“Glory to Thee, our God, glory to Thee. Glory to the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit. Great is the name of the Holy Trinity. Lord Jesus Christ, help us”** (replacing the two final exclamations during the Paschal days with **“Christ is risen”**). This rite the Apostles performed also following their parting from one another—each one separately. Gathered miraculously for the translation of the Mother of God and having performed Her burial, on the third day they were sitting together at the refectory table. When after dinner they, elevating according to custom the bread fragment in remembrance of Christ, pronounced: **“Great is the name...”**, they beheld in the air the Most Holy Theotokos, surrounded by Angels and promising to abide with them always; involuntarily the Apostles then exclaimed instead of *(Orig. p. 780)* **“Lord Jesus Christ, help us”**—**“Most Holy Theotokos, help us.”** Having departed following this unto the tomb of the Mother of God and having opened it, the Apostles did not find Her most pure body there, and became convinced that She had been taken up into heaven unto Her Divine Son.[^2810]

The prayerful blessing of the meal the Christian Church could have inherited from the Old Testament—Jewish—tradition. What form it had in the latter can be judged in part by the rites of late Judaism (ritual being generally stable): at an ordinary meal, composed, however, of not fewer than three persons, the head of the family or the most honored person recites the formula of blessing over the bread, slices and distributes the pieces unto his fellow-diners; a portion of the bread remains until the conclusion of the meal as a symbol of the presence of God; in like manner also the wine is blessed, wherein the chalice is lifted above the table; over each separate course blessings are recited.[^2811] The Christian agape meals, especially when they were not combined with the Eucharist, without doubt gave birth to many rites of the Order of the Panagia.[^2812] It is remarkable that the most important of the prayers of this rite in nearly their present form are provided by monuments of the 4th century: in St. John Chrysostom and in the work of Pseudo-Athanasius, *On Virginity*. It is precisely here that there is given as the prayer before dinner the prayer: **“Blessed is God Who hath mercy upon us and nourisheth us”**, only in Chrysostom it is in the singular, without *“Who hath mercy”* and *“worship”*, and in Athanasius without *“ages”*. The prayer **“Glory to Thee, O Lord”** is found only in Chrysostom without differences from the present text.[^2813]

With the emergence of monasteries, the refectory meal within them immediately received an especially prayerful setting and was regarded as a brief church service. In the Pachomian monasteries this service consisted of a psalm and a prayer, sometimes of several psalms and prayers.[^2814]

The oldest monument of the Studite Typikon, the *Hypotyposis*, says concerning the meal: *“When the brethren go to the morning meal, upon their lips is a verse (from a psalm, of course); they sit at tables by nines. The taxiarchs perform the service at the table decently, without noise. There is also a reading, at which the brethren sit during winter in head-coverings (koukoullia / kuvuklia) upon their heads. The sign, moreover, of the end of this reading is, at the last course, the sound of spoons cast together by all into the dish. In like manner also for the mixing (of wine) and for the courses there is (a signal) by a stroke.”*

According to the *Diatyposis*, *(Orig. p. 781)* beyond this: *“the brethren go unto the refectory at the sound of the bell... with a verse upon their lips, and likewise when they arise (from the table), until they reach the narthex, in order to perform thanksgiving for that which they have received. There is also a reading by appointment of the ecclesiarch, who also takes care that that which they did not have time to finish reading in church should not be neglected,”*[^2815] that is, for the refectory there was its own cycle of readings and, in addition, at it were completed the readings appointed for the daily services that were not finished in the church.[^2816]

A further stage in the development of the Studite refectory rite in surviving monuments may be recognized in the order provided by the Synaxarion of the Mount Athos Iviron Monastery in a Georgian manuscript of the early 12th century. Here, first of all, is the most ancient brief notice concerning the refectory meal: *“The brethren enter into the refectory, having upon their lips a song, and seat themselves without dispute at the refectory tables by nine men. During the eating there is a quiet reading of the Paterikon; upon the conclusion of the eating, however, recognized by the clatter of the spoons gathered together, an instruction.”* Immediately following this, undoubtedly recorded at a later date, is a complex refectory order:

*“Upon the conclusion of the Liturgy the leaders of the choir (the singers) enter into the diaconicon unto the presbyter (who celebrated), whom the ecclesiarch (as head of the singers and their representative) greets according to rank. The refectorian enters and inquires whether they are free (whether the Liturgy has ended). Having learned this, he departs and rings the small bells. The presbyter and the brethren gather in the narthex; the presbyter pronounces: **‘Glory to Thee, Christ our God, glory to Thee’**; all harmoniously and compunctiously begin the psalm: **‘I will exalt Thee, my God’**, and proceed into the refectory. Following the blessing (of the table) they seat themselves by nine men at the table without dispute and noise. When all have sat down, the refectorian, having bowed unto the superior and received from him a blessing, brings the reader. When the reader names the title of the reading, the refectorian proclaims aloud: ‘Lord, bless. Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us, amen.’ We all repeat quietly the same; in like manner also the other exclamations the brethren repeat after the refectorian. Before each course the refectorian says: ‘Lord Jesus Christ.’”*

*“The overseer walks through the refectory and reminds the brethren of silence. Before the collecting of the spoons the refectorian says: ‘Lord Jesus Christ’; the reader approaches the superior and, having received a blessing, begins to collect the cups, for upon his duty lies the washing of them. When the brethren (finish the diakonia ‘service’, that is, the course) and by the will of God are satisfied, the refectorian says: ‘Lord Jesus Christ...’ and, having placed before the superior a woven basket, proclaims: ‘Lord, bless.’ All say: **‘Blessed art Thou, O Lord, Who hast satisfied us... Glory to Thee, O Lord, glory to Thee...’** and lower into the basket the bread fragments remaining upon the table. When the refectorian elevates the Theotokos (the panagia), all arise and begin: **‘Merciful and compassionate...’** (Ps. 110:5 [111:5]), **‘I was glad when they said unto me...’** (Ps. 121 [122]), **‘Holy God...’ ‘Our Father...’ ‘Lord, have mercy’** (12), **‘Bless.’**”*[^2817]

*(Orig. p. 782)*

In the complete Studite typika we find already an Order of the Panagia not far removed from the present one. In the oldest of the complete manuscripts of the Studite-Alexian Typikon (12th–13th c.) it is stated thus concerning the refectory meal: Following the Liturgy, or on fast days following the Ninth Hour and the Beatitudes and after *“receiving the blessing of the brethren”*:

*“They strike then the semantron thrice, and straightway they come unto the refectory, having in their mouths Psalm 144: **‘I will exalt Thee, my God’**, chanting it.” “And the priest who served proceeds before all, and near him goes the hegumen. And when the priest draws near the steps that lead unto the upper table, he stands below such steps, on the right side, looking eastward, and saying this prayer secretly to himself: **‘Lord our God, heavenly and life-creating Bread’**, look for it in the Euchologion. And when the hegumen has entered, he bows; and when he has entered and stood in his place, and when the aforesaid psalm is finished, then upon the 1st and 2nd table the priest, signing the saving sign of the cross, adds the exclamation of the aforesaid prayer; and the brethren having said amen, the hegumen sits down and after him the rest. And when all have sat down, the reader makes the beginning of the reading. And the priest who served, standing upright, blesses, saying thus: ‘Blessed is our God always, now and ever, and unto the ages’; and the brethren having said amen, he that serves the refectory first, whom they indeed call the senior, bids all to keep silence. And upon the silence the reader begins to read.”* They bring in the first course—*“cooked broth”* (*varivo*); the senior proclaims aloud and *“in full voice: ‘Lord, bless; pray’*; the brethren arise; the priest who served blesses the food: *‘Christ God, through the prayers of our fathers, bless our food and drink, now and ever...’*; the brethren, having said amen, sit down; *‘and upon whatever food the hegumen lays his hand, then all the others also begin to eat.’* Unto the hegumen they present a small spoon (*lzhytsyu*), by a stroke of which he gives the sign at table for the change of courses and for the blessing of them. Having taken the small spoon, the hegumen strikes with it, giving the signal to distribute the wine; following the strike the senior proclaims: *‘Lord, bless’*, without *‘pray’*; unto the hegumen approaches the cellarer-custodian (*kutnik*, supervisor of the storeroom) and *‘having received a prayer from him, he goes around with a two-handled cup and gives wine into each one's cup’*; behind him go others with warm water (*ukrop*) and ladle unto each. Such a passing around of wine or ‘ladling’ (*pocherpanie*) occurs thrice during the dinner: following the bringing in of the *varivo* (the liquid dish), following the bringing in of the *sochivo* (porridge/boiled wheat), and following the eating thereof; for each ladling a sign is given by the hegumen with a strike of the spoon. At the first ladling the brethren arise and, holding their cups, extend them from their places unto the hegumen for a blessing; at the remaining ladlings each blesses his own drink with the sign of the cross over it. In the absence of the hegumen, the sign by the stroke of the spoon and the blessing is given by the economos (steward); yet if the latter possesses not holy orders, the blessing is given by the senior or the priest who served; in the hegumen’s seat no one sits. Upon the eating of the first course, the senior (of those serving the refectory) *‘bids all the brethren to keep silence’*, and the second course—*sochivo*—is brought in; the senior says: *‘Lord, bless; pray’*; all arise, *‘and that which is set forth is blessed not by him that blessed first, but by another priest, reciting the aforesaid prayer (“Christ God, through the prayers of our fathers bless the food...”), which is said not only at the beginning over the broth, but also over the other foods.’* If *(Orig. p. 783)* there be several courses, this entire rite of blessing is performed over each. Upon the conclusion of the last ladling, the senior sets at the edge of the first (the hegumen's) table a special dish and strikes upon it thrice with a large spoon, and immediately the reader ceases reading; another empty dish is set by the cellarer upon the lower table; the brethren place their spoons into these dishes, and now begins the rite corresponding to the ‘Order of the Elevation of the Panagia’, which may be termed the ‘elevation of the bread fragments’ (*ukrukhi*). The hegumen pronounces the verse: **‘Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us’**; all repeat this verse. The hegumen places upon the dish the bread fragment remaining with him, saying: **‘Lord, bless.’** The senior begins with a loud voice: **‘Blessed is God Who nourisheth us’**, and the others chant with him this prayer, placing their bread fragments upon the dish. These fragments are designated for distribution by the cellarer unto the poor, and it is forbidden to offer them unto the brethren at the next meal. Unto the aforementioned prayer the priest who served joins, making a cross over the dish, another prayer as well: **‘Christ God, replenish the remnants of Thy servants and have mercy on us, for Thou art holy, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages.’** Following the *‘Amen’*, the senior (of those serving the refectory), having bowed (unto the hegumen) at the edge of the table and pronounced with a loud voice: *‘Bless, pray for me’*, unto which the hegumen quietly responds: *‘God save thee’*, taking the dish with the bread fragments, makes a cross with it, saying with a loud voice: **‘Great is the name’**; all respond: **‘Of the Holy and Consubstantial Trinity; may It preserve us all, amen.’** The hegumen: *‘May the Lord remember all spiritual fathers and our brethren’*; the brethren: *‘Amen.’* At the sign of the hegumen the senior begins with a loud voice: **‘The Lord is merciful and compassionate’** (Ps. 110:5 [111:5]); all arise and chant further. The priest who served: *‘For all things we give thanks unto the Lord.’* The brethren: *‘Lord, have mercy’* thrice. The priest: *‘Above all we give thanks unto the Father and to the Son and to the Holy Spirit, now and ever, and unto the ages...’* The brethren: *‘Amen’*, and they begin Psalm 121 [122]: **‘I was glad when they said unto me’**, which they chant as they walk before the hegumen from the refectory, joining also Psalm 83 [84]: **‘How beloved are Thy dwellings.’** The procession from the refectory is directed into the *predbozhnitsya* (the narthex), where the priest, having stood before the Holy Doors, makes the prayer: **‘Unto Thee, the true Lover of mankind, O God, we sinners...’** *‘Upon the conclusion of the prayer, when we have said Glory, there takes place the dismissal of the aforesaid prayer by the priest.’* Following the *‘Amen’*, the priest and the brethren make three prostrations. The priest, having turned, says: *‘Bless, holy ones.’* The brethren fall upon their knees, saying: *‘Bless, father.’* The priest: *‘Christ God, through the prayers of the Most Holy Theotokos and of the holy Forerunner (the patron saint of the temple) and of all the saints, have mercy on us and save our souls.’* Following the *‘Amen’*, each goes unto his own cell.[^2818]

Almost literally identical with this refectory order is the rite provided by the Typikon of the Constantinople Pantokrator Monastery of 1136 AD (in a manuscript dating only from the 18th c.). The difference consists in the following: They departed unto the refectory, having received the antidoron, after a three-fold stroke upon the wooden semantron (*drevo*). The priest recited secretly to himself the same prayer, which however is cited here in full: **“Lord my God, life-creating Bread, true Food of the whole world, Who directest our present *(Orig. p. 784)* life and hast promised unto us communion of the future, do Thou Thyself bless our food and drink and vouchsafe us without condemnation to partake of them, who praise and give thanks unto the Giver of all good gifts”**; then the priest, making a cross over the table, proclaims the conclusion of the prayer: **“For blessed and glorified is Thy most honorable and majestic name.”** The signal for the change of courses is given by striking upon the table with a small wooden mallet. In the exclamation *“(Great is the name) of the Holy, Consubstantial”*, there is the addition *“and Life-Creating”*. Following the elevation of the bread fragments the hegumen blesses all; there is chanted **“Merciful and compassionate”**, Psalms 121 [122] and 83 [84], the priest recites the prayer; the remainder found in the Studite-Alexian Typikon is absent here.[^2819]

In the surviving Greek monuments of the Jerusalem Typikon there is no refectory order.

In Slavic manuscripts (14th–15th centuries) this order is similar to the Studite-Alexian, but instead of the elevation of the bread fragments there is already the elevation of the panagia according to the present rite, with slight variations. The difference of the general refectory order from the Studite-Alexian consists in the following:

*“Following the dismissal of the Liturgy the priest who served goes forth, and after him follows the hegumen and the rest of the brethren through the same doors, reciting Psalm 144 [145]. And through other doors let no one go forth; and they walk each one by one, even as they sit at table; they converse not among themselves at all; nor do they walk two abreast.”* The 1st and 2nd tables are blessed not at the exclamation of the prayer **“Lord our God, heavenly and life-creating Bread”**, but at the immediately subjoined prayer (the present one): **“Christ God, bless the food...”** Before the rite of blessing the wine it is noted: *“And when there is consolation”*, *“they drink each his cup, saying: ‘Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us, amen’”* (nothing is said of signing the cup with the sign of the cross).

*“And after dinner the hegumen takes the bread of the All-Holy Theotokos and places it upon the dish and signs it with a cross with his hand, if he is a priest. And straightway he strikes, and the reader ceases, and arising the hegumen says: ‘Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us.’ The brethren: ‘Glory... Both now...’ The hegumen: ‘Blessed is God Who hath mercy... Glory to Thee, O Lord, glory to Thee, O King, glory to Thee, O Holy One... Glory... Both now... Lord, have mercy (3).’ He that is about to elevate, deacon or reader or cellarer or whosoever of the brethren [says]: ‘Bless me...’ They answer: ‘God save thee.’ And lifting the bread he says: ‘O great is the name.’ The brethren: ‘Of the All-Holy Trinity.’ And straightway he, signing a cross over the panagia with the bread, says: ‘All-Holy Theotokos,[^2820] help us.’ And we say: ‘Through her intercessions’ (in later manuscripts: ‘All generations call thee blessed’). Then they take the bread of the All-Holy [Theotokos], saying: ‘Thy womb became...’[^2821] And straightway all, having arisen from the table, say: **‘The Lord is merciful and compassionate’**, Psalm 121 [122], we recite it unto the end, walking toward the church; then Psalm 83 [84], Trisagion; following **‘Our Father’**, on Sunday the Hypakoe; if it be of an illustrious saint—the kontakion; on another day troparia, Tone 6: **‘As Thou didst come into the midst of Thy disciples... Glory... Both now... Through the intercessions, O Lord, of all the saints... Lord, have mercy (3).’** The priest: **‘Unto Thee, the true Lover of mankind, we sinners and Thine unworthy servants offer praise, having been satisfied with Thy rich bounties; together with earthly goods, make us partakers also of Thy heavenly *(Orig. p. 785)* gifts, O Christ God, through the intercessions of the Holy Theotokos and of all Thy saints, now and ever...’** The priest: **‘Blessed is God Who hath mercy...’** The hegumen: *‘God forgive and have mercy on them that have served us.’* And the brethren bow unto the ground. And we go unto our cells.”*[^2822]`

In later manuscripts, of the 16th century, the Order of the Panagia is mentioned in the refectory order, and the latter is given in the briefest form: in agreement with the ancient manuscripts, the order of procession unto the refectory and seating therein is indicated; then:

*“the reader straightway begins the preface of the reading which he intends to read; then [the priest] blesses with a verse that which is proposed to read; and at each service of what is offered (at the serving of each course) [they] say: ‘Glory to Thee, Christ God, our hope, glory to Thee’”*;

concerning the asking of forgiveness by the reader it is spoken as in the present Typikon, Chapter 35, only with the added note concerning the duty of the reader to wash the dishes.[^2823]

The early printed typika and the Old Believer Typikon in Chapter 53 provide the same order as in the manuscripts of the 14th–15th centuries, with the following differences:

Following the prayer: **“Lord our God, heavenly, life-creating Bread...”**, *“the priest, taking out the bread of the Most Pure [Theotokos], says the troparion: **‘Today is the salvation...’** [*Dnes' spaseniyu*] and, having placed the particle upon the palm face upward and cutting the particle cruciformly with a knife, he places it upon the panagiarion and sets it in its place; the table being prepared and upon it the appointed food, warm bread and salt and drink having already been brought.”* Following the blessing of the reading and the bringing in of the broth (*varivo*), the cellarer and the *oinochoos* (that is to say, the cupbearer), having received a blessing from the hegumen, present unto him *“broth in a vessel which is upon a dish”*, and the second—kvass in a cup; unto the brethren there is likewise distributed a cup of kvass each; *“and if it be a Dominical Feast, or if from a certain Christ-lover (a donation should be made), then two cups of kvass (strong ale), but if there be no feast, then rye kvass”* (wine is not mentioned here, yet in the synaxarion portion it is mentioned repeatedly). Upon the first strike with the spoon or upon the *kandya*, preceded by the exclamation of the “senior”: *“Lord bless; pray”*, the presiding priest says: **“Our Father, Glory... Both now... Lord, have mercy (2). Lord, bless”**; the hegumen: **“Christ God, bless the food”**; the reader: *“Amen.”* In the absence of the hegumen, that which is appointed for him is performed by the “chief of the church” or the “prior, that is to say, the builder (*stroitel’*)” or the “first priest, or he that served”. *“The hegumen strikes the kandya and the reader ceases; then, standing before the icon, he makes three prostrations and asks forgiveness of the superior. And when they arise from the table, the senior, that is to say the cellarer, or the refectorian proclaims with a loud voice: ‘Through the prayers of our holy fathers, Lord Jesus Christ, Son of God, have mercy on us.’ And straightway the hegumen strikes the kandya, and takes the bread of the Most Holy Theotokos, and gives it unto the deacon, and he holds it. And arising the hegumen says: ‘Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us.’ The clerics, however, say: ‘Amen. Glory... Both now... Lord, have mercy (2). Lord, bless: Blessed is God Who hath mercy upon us and nourisheth us...’”*, and further as at present.

He that elevates asks forgiveness of the hegumen: *“Forgive me, holy father, and bless, *(Orig. p. 786)* whereinsoever I have sinned in word and deed and thought and in all my senses.”* The hegumen: *“By His grace may God forgive and have mercy on us all.”* The deacon, elevating, removes his hood (*koukoulion*). *“Of the Holy Trinity”*, says the hegumen. *“Most Holy Lady Theotokos, help us.”* *“And the clerics say: ‘Through her intercessions...’, then ‘All generations call thee blessed...’ written in the Midnight Office. And after this the clerics chant: ‘All generations call thee blessed, O Virgin Theotokos, most blessed and immaculate Mother of our God; thee, O Theotokos, do all generations call blessed; for thou dost pray for us unto Christ our God’; then **‘It is truly meet’**; but if it be a Dominical Feast, we chant the Heirmos of the 9th Ode of the feast; then the hegumen says: **‘The Lord is merciful and compassionate; He hath given food unto them that fear Him’**; the same also the clerics recite. And the hegumen breaks the holy bread and distributes it unto the brethren. And the clerics recite the Trisagion; following **‘Our Father’**, if it is Sunday, the Hypakoe of the tone of the day is said; but if it is a Dominical Feast, we say instead of the Hypakoe the kontakion of the feast or of a great saint who has a Polyeleos.”* On ordinary days the troparia are as among us: following **“Lord, bless”**, the prayer **“Unto Thee, the true Lover of mankind...”** The hegumen imparts the dismissal, and following the response of the brethren *“Amen”*—*“God forgive...”*[^2824]

As the testimonies of Blessed Symeon of Thessalonica and Mark of Ephesus demonstrate, in Greece in the 15th century there existed an Order of the Panagia which was, in all probability, entirely identical with the present one. Symeon of Thessalonica mentions in it **“Our Father”**, the prayer **“Glory to Thee, O Holy One, glory to Thee, O King...”**, four exclamations **“Great is the name”**, etc., the hymn **“All generations call thee blessed...”**, and **“It is truly meet”**. This rite had there even a broader application than at present: it was celebrated not only at monastic meals, but by many priests also during the Liturgy following **“Especially concerning the Most Holy...”**[^2825] either constantly or at the request of certain persons. Blessed Symeon *(Orig. p. 787)* of Thessalonica says concerning himself that he *“established that in cathedral churches this mentioned rite should be celebrated daily, namely, that the priest at every Matins at the end of the 9th Ode should elevate this bread.”* There was elevated in Greece not the entire prosphora, but a three-sided particle (in honor of the Holy Trinity) extracted from it. At the monastic table a lamp was placed before the vessel containing the panagia. The elevation was performed by the reader who read during the refectory meal.[^2826]

The order of the refectory meal and the elevation of the panagia among the Greeks is described also by Arseny Sukhanov in his *Proskynitarion* (17th c.). Upon the conclusion of the Liturgy they bring into the refectory the “bread of the Mother of God”, and a “simple elder” or a priest simply extracts a particle from it; when the patriarch, having rested from the Liturgy[^2827] in his cell, comes into the refectory and sits down, the priest of the week strikes the *kandya* and says **“Our Father”**; the patriarch blesses the table while seated. He sits at a separate small table, and dishes are served unto him by deacons, and wine by archdeacons, who in his presence do not sit at table, but dine afterward.

*“And when it is time to drink, the archdeacon fills the vessel, and the weekly priest strikes the kandia, and then all arise, and the reader ceases reading. And the archdeacon says: **‘Through the prayers of our holy master, Lord Jesus Christ our God, have mercy on us.’** And all say: ‘Amen.’ The patriarch, having received the vessel, says unto all: **‘Evlogite pateres’** [Εὐλογεῖτε, πατέρες, ‘Bless, fathers’] and drinks; all the rest, standing, say: **‘Through the prayers of our holy master...’**, then **‘Ton despotin’** [Τὸν δεσπότην], and make a slight bow. And when he has drunk, all sit down; and whoever wishes to drink pours a cup of wine from his vessel and, setting it down, says unto the patriarch with a clear voice: **‘Evlogison despota’** [Εὐλόγησον, δέσποτα, ‘Bless, master’], while the patriarch signs with his hand, saying: **‘O Theos’** [Ὁ Θεός, ‘God’], and having drunk standing, he sits down; and thus all drink the first cup, being blessed, standing; but when a second, and a third, and a fourth whoever wishes, they drink sitting and without a blessing.”* If the patriarch be not present, then *“they receive a blessing from the weekly priest and drink sitting. And when they have finished eating, the patriarch orders the kandia to be struck, and the reader, having ceased, says: **‘Di' evkhon’** [Δι' εὐχῶν, ‘Through the prayers’], and having approached, bows unto the patriarch seeking forgiveness; and the patriarch gives him a cup of wine and sets a small slice of bread upon the cup. Then again he strikes the kandia; afterward the refectorian, having taken a basket, says with a clear voice: **‘Through the prayers of our holy master...’**, but if the patriarch be not present, then: **‘Through the prayers of our holy fathers...’**, and he goes unto the patriarch and says (in translation from the Greek): ‘Bless, *(Orig. p. 788)* master, the remnants of the fragments’; and the patriarch from his table puts into the basket a portion of bread and says: **‘Christ God, bless the remnants of the fragments and make them an abundance for this holy monastery, for Thou art holy always...’**”* The refectorian goes about with the basket and collects the fragments (*ukrukhi*), saying: “Bless, fathers”, and they answer him: *“O Theos synkhore ke eleisise”* [Ὁ Θεὸς συγχωρήσοι καὶ ἐлеήσοι σε, ‘May God forgive and have mercy on thee’]. Upon the stroke upon the kandia all arise, except the patriarch, and say: **“Blessed is God Who hath mercy... Glory to Thee, O Lord... Glory... Both now...”** The deacon or monk elevates the bread, raising it from the dish, saying quietly: **“Great is the name.”** The patriarch, having arisen, answers: **“Of the Holy Trinity.”** The other two exclamations the ecclesiarch and the brethren pronounce. At **“It is truly meet”** [*Dostoyno*], the patriarch, and after him all, break off a small piece from the bread presented by the ecclesiarch upon the panagiarion, while the refectorian, following behind, censes at each one the held crumb of bread. Having consumed the bread, they wash it down with wine—the patriarch from one cup, and the others from two other cups passed from one to another. The ecclesiarch and the refectorian ask forgiveness from the patriarch with a bow; he signs them with his hand, saying: “God forgive and have mercy.” Next [follow] **“Merciful and compassionate...”**, the Trisagion, the troparion or kontakion, **“Lord, have mercy”** (2), **“Bless, Lord”**; the patriarch [pronounces]: **“Blessed is God Who hath mercy...”**, **“Ton despotin...”** The ecclesiarch, refectorian, cooks, and servers, having exited the refectory immediately after seeking forgiveness from the patriarch (prior to **“Merciful and compassionate...”**), fall upon the ground at the patriarch’s exit, saying: “Forgive me, master”, unto which he responds: “May God forgive and have mercy upon you”; they continue to lie upon the ground during the exit of the entire brotherhood, saying unto each one departing: “Bless, fathers”, unto which the one passing responds: “May God forgive and have mercy.”[^2828]

In completely identical fashion the rite of forgiveness following the meal is performed unto this day on Mount Athos.

The titles placed above the Order of the Panagia and distinct prayers of the rite in certain manuscripts demonstrate that it was performed outside monasteries as well, on the following occasions: upon someone’s entrance into service or office, or upon embarking on a journey, particularly by water.[^2829] This rite was likewise performed at the Byzantine court after dinner. According to the description of Pseudo-Kodinos (14th century), *“after the dishes are cleared from the table, the domestikos brings the bread upon the panagiarion; the emperor arises; the first of those present at table, having received the panagiarion, sets it upon the table, and having elevated the bread, hands it unto the domestikos, and the latter unto the emperor; as soon as the emperor brings the bread unto his lips, all loudly chant unto him: **‘Many years’**.”*[^2830]

*(Orig. p. 789)*

Casting a single glance over the entire development of the order of the monastic meal, one cannot fail to note in its history, as the most characteristic phenomena, certain particularities. Even prior to Christianity, the necessity of prayerful blessing of the meal was recognized. The most important of the refectory prayers in its present form was already known to the 4th century. The agape, and following it monasticism, imparted unto the meal a genuine liturgical character. The origin of the Order of the Panagia itself, which currently constitutes the focal point of the refectory meal, is hidden in the depths of history. Yet the circumstance that it is unknown to the Studite Typikon widely diffused throughout the Greek East—possessing here in its stead the elevation of the bread fragments (*ukrukhi*)—this circumstance compels one to presume that this order appeared for the first time in the Jerusalem Typikon and could have originated within the bosom of the Jerusalem Church at a very early date. As soon as the Mother of God received in the Church all Her glory and honor, there must have arisen the idea of a certain eucharist in Her name as well. In order to distinguish this eucharist more sharply from the true one, the elevation is entrusted unto a deacon and a simple monk (among the Greeks even unto a reader). Remarkable is the similarity of the order of the meal in the Studite and Jerusalem Typika, reaching at times literal identity in everything except this detail (the elevation of the bread fragments instead of the panagia), which is, to be sure, the most important. It is very characteristic that the Studite Typikon commemorates the Mother of God only at the evening meal. It is remarkable that the Studite Typikon lacks the Lord’s Prayer at the beginning of the meal, *(Orig. p. 790)* replacing it with another prayer, which naturally yielded its place later unto the greatest of prayers, which so fittingly suits the meal by its fourth petition.

Hymns in honor of the Mother of God gradually increase in number. Later typika have from ancient times attempted to omit the concluding psalms, the result of which in the present Typikon is the disappearance of Psalm 83 [84]. In compensation for this, these typika exhibit a tendency toward multiplying the number of brief prayer formulas. Later typika restrict the participation of the brethren in favor of the superior and generally complicate the rite excessively (the Greeks and the Old Believers).

The venerable antiquity of the rite, demonstrating how continuously it was considered an indispensable component of every piously festive meal, might plead—alongside its indisputable compunction—for its greater practical application at present and for the desirability of its dissemination beyond monastery walls. Yet even within the latter, it appears, it is not everywhere observed.

*(Orig. p. 791)*
