[^1614]: Concerning the beginning of monasticism on Athos there is no reliable information; Athonite traditions trace the emergence of monasteries here as far back as pagan times (Emperor Caracalla, 211–217 AD) or at least unto the flourishing of Egyptian-Palestinian asceticism; the Arab devastations of Athos circa 670 AD and subsequently circa 830 do not permit us to say anything certain concerning Athos prior unto the 9th century, although the foundation of nearly all present Athonite monasteries traces its origin back unto this most ancient period. The first historically attested Athonite hermit ('hesychast') was St. Peter (who lived on Athos, 681–734 AD); during the era of iconoclasm many monks sought refuge here; St. Euthymius (circa 840 AD) restored monasticism on Athos after the second Arab devastation; his disciples established the first cenobium on Athos—Vatopedi, and John Kolobos built the first stone monastery on the isthmus at Hierissos and obtained from Emperor Basil the Macedonian in 872 AD a chrysobull whereby Athos was granted unto the exclusive possession of monks. But thereupon enmity arose between the cenobites and anchorites; the latter separated and established in Karyes their own administration ('Protat') headed by the Protos. After a new Saracen devastation circa the middle of the 10th century, monasticism on Athos was restored by St. Athanasius, who founded the Great Lavra on Athos with donations from his friend Emperor Nikephoros Phokas. Following a complaint of the anchorites against the predominance of the cenobitic life, alien unto ancient Athos, Emperor John Tzimiskes by his Typikon (*τυπικόν* or *tragos*) of 971 AD recognized equal rights for both modes of ascetic life on Athos. Unto this period belong the first reliable accounts concerning the majority of present Athonite monasteries, such as Iveron (founded by Georgians), Docheiariou or Daphne, Panteleimon or Thessalonian, Esphigmenou (founded by inhabitants of the Thessalian village of Sphigou), Chilandar (named after the founder's surname), Zographou, founded by the Greek George the Iconographer (in Greek *zōgraphos*), Koutloumousiou (after the founder's name), Xeropotamou ('dry torrent'), and Dionysiou, founded by Alexios Komnenos in 1118 [or later by Alexios III in 1374] at the request of Dionysius who asceticized here. Emperor Constantine Monomachos by his Typikon of 1046 forbade Athos commercial relations with laity. From this time onward the present strict order became established on Athos (absolute exclusion of women). Alexios Komnenos in 1090 recognized Athos as independent of the Metropolitan of Thessalonica and subject solely unto its own Protos. In the 11th century Bulgarian monks appeared on Athos, settling the Zographou Monastery; in the 12th century Serbian monks (headed by Prince Stefan-Simeon Nemanja and his son St. Sabbas), unto whom Chilandar was granted; and Russian monks, unto whom was given first the Monastery of Xylourgou, and in 1169 also St. Panteleimon ('Rossikon'). The majority of Athonite monasteries are dedicated unto the Most Holy Theotokos; there are also churches of the Forerunner, Chrysostom, and Nicholas. There was on Athos (in the 10th century) likewise a Latin monastery with the Rule of St. Benedict—Karakallou (after the surname of the founder). (Bishop Porphyrius Uspensky, *Istoriia Afona* [History of Athos], Kyiv, 1876, *passim*; Sokolov, I., *Sostoianie monashestva v Vizantiiskoi tserkvi s pol. IX v. do nach. XIII v.* [The State of Monasticism in the Byzantine Church from the Mid-9th to the Early 13th Century], Kazan, 1894, pp. 214 ff.).

A., *Opisanie liturgicheskikh rukopisei*, Vol. I: *Τυπικά*, p. 238, from manuscripts of the 16th century (Athos-Iveron Library No. 754) and even of the 19th century, which nevertheless represent copies from 11th-century codices, perhaps even from the autographs of St. Athanasius (preserved in the skeuophylakion of the Lavra of St. Athanasius and shown unto no one), against which they were collated in Meyer's edition (Dmitrievsky, *ibid.*, p. XXXIII).

[^1616]: The first and most ancient manuscript is preserved in the Sinai Library in a separate gathering detached from a Gospel Book, lacking the beginning (the Triodion commences from Ascension) and the end (terminating on August 6); the second is in the same library appended unto Gospel Book No. 150, complete, but only for the major days. Its distinction in the synaxarion from the Typikon of the Great Church, apart from the order (the Triodion comes first): no patriarchal celebration is presupposed; there are no commemorations of church dedications or earthquakes (except October 26). In all probability it was utilized in a diocese subject unto the Patriarch of Constantinople. Judging by the mention of a church of Elijah, whither a litany took place on the 2nd Sunday after Pascha (according unto the Constantinopolitan Typikon on that day the litany was unto Chalkoprateia), one might suppose that it was used on Sinai, where a church of Elijah existed. Yet it is more probable that the Kanonarion is of Southern Italian or Sicilian origin, because it contains Western and Eastern commemorations according unto the dates of Western calendars (May 8: 'Archangels Michael and Gabriel—Apparition on Mount Gargano'). In the earlier copy the latest commemoration is that of Theodore the Studite; in the later, that of Paul the New († 784 AD) (Archbishop Sergius, *Polny mesiatseslov Vostoka* [Complete Menology of the East], Vol. I, p. 145). Published in Russian translation by Archimandrite Antonin, *Drevnii kanonar' Sinaiskoi biblioteki* [The Ancient Kanonarion of the Sinai Library], Kyiv, 1874; in the original Greek by Dmitrievsky, A. A., *Opisanie liturgicheskikh rukopisei*, Vol. I: *Τυπικά*, p. 172.

[^1617]: The Chronicle states under the year 1051 that St. Theodosius, upon the multiplication of the brethren in his monastery, 'began to seek the monastic rule, and there was found then Michael, a monk of the Studion Monastery, who had come from the Greeks with Metropolitan George; and he began to seek from him the rule of the Studite monks, and having obtained it from him, transcribed it, and instituted in his monastery how to chant the monastic chants, and how to make prostrations, and to read the readings, and the standing in church, and the entire church order, the sitting at table, and what to eat on which days, all according unto the rule'; and from the Caves Monastery 'all monasteries took over the rule' (*Povest' vremennykh let* according unto the Laurentian Codex, ed. Archaeographic Commission, St. Petersburg, 1872, p. 156). But according unto the *Life of St. Theodosius* composed by Nestor, Theodosius 'sent one of the brethren unto Constantinople unto Ephrem the Eunuch, that he might send unto him the entire Typikon of the Studion Monastery copied in full', which took place circa 1062 AD (*Zhitie*, ed. O. Bodiansky in *Chteniia v Obshchestve istorii i drevnostei rossiiskikh*, 1858, fol. 111v). These conflicting accounts are reconciled by the supposition that the monk Michael possessed an incomplete copy of the Typikon, perhaps the *Hypotyposis*, for which reason ten years later St. Theodosius felt the need for a complete text ('the entire'). — Prior unto the appearance of the Studite Typikon and thereafter, until the Mongol-Tatar invasion, in cathedral and parish churches in Rus' it is thought that clergy were guided by the Typikon of the Great Church of Constantinople. The Council of Vladimir of 1274 and that of Constantinople of 1276 establish the existence in the Russian Church of certain customs of the Great Church, such as the celebration of the Proskomedia (*proskomisanie*) by a deacon (in all likelihood, such may have been the most ancient custom in general), the celebration of the Presanctified Liturgy on Cheesefare Wednesday and Friday and on Great Friday, the reading of the Gospel by the hierarch four times a year (the 1st Gospel of the Passion, at the Paschal Liturgy and Vespers, and at the litany of September 1), and the Elevation of the Cross with the peculiarities of the Great Church: some of these customs are affirmed by the councils, while others are abolished (Pavlov, A. S., *Russkaia istoricheskaia biblioteka*, St. Petersburg, 1880, Vol. VI, Nos. 6, 12), yet all persisted in places until the 15th and even 17th century, especially in the Novgorod lands, which encompassed the entire north of Rus'. Furthermore, in comparatively late manuscripts of the 14th–15th centuries there has been preserved the translation of entire offices of the Great Church into the Slavonic tongue, such as the Order of the Washing of the Holy Table on Great Thursday, the Order of the New Year (Indiction) on September 1, and the litany according unto the Typikon of the Great Church. Unto the same testify the Slavonic manuscripts of the Asmatika (refrains unto psalms in the Sung Office, for example, *Tin ikumenin* = *Vselennuiu* ['The world']), the phrase in ancient Typika 'chanting at Trithekte' indicating the existence of this office, and finally even a fragment of the Typikon of the Great Church in the Slavonic translation of Archbishop Clement of Novgorod († 1299) in the Moscow Khludov Library (Popov, A., *Pribavlenie k opisaniiu rukopisei Khludovskoi biblioteki*, Moscow, 1875, p. 117), and the like. See concerning this in greater detail and for citations in the work being printed by Archpriest M. Lisitsyn, *Pervonachal'nyi slaviano-russkii Tipikon* [The Original Slavonic-Russian Typikon], St. Petersburg, 1911 [1910], where the author indicates also another fragment of the Slavonic translation of the Typikon of the Great Church in Popov's description, p. 117, designated a Triodion.

[^1618]: The most ancient manuscripts of the Studite-Alexis Typikon: 1) In MS Moscow Synodal (Typography) Library No. 285/142/1206 of the 11th–12th century, lacking the beginning (Meatfare Sunday) and the end, containing only the Triodion Typikon, and instead of a Menology (which may, however, have been torn off) a Kontakionarion, in places noted with musical neumes, for the entire year; 2) nearly complete (from the Sunday of the Prodigal Son) and full (with the entire Menology and an extensive disciplinary section) in MS Moscow Synodal Library No. 330/380 of the 12th–13th century, of a more comprehensive redaction than the first; closer unto the Typikon of the Great Church than the first (in the commemorations of the Sundays of Great Lent), consequently no less ancient, although containing more commemorations (by 12); then 3) former St. Sophia Novgorod Library (now preserved in the St. Petersburg Theological Academy) No. 1136, in all likelihood of the 13th century—containing only the Triodion from Meatfare Vespers and the Menology through January 17; 4) Moscow Synodal (Typography) Library No. 144/1236; 5) Moscow Synodal Library No. 333/381, written in 1398 AD, without the disciplinary section; 6) No. 905/382 of the 15th century. All these manuscripts, beginning with No. 330, are nearly literally identical with one another, clearly transcribed from a single exemplar, though the later ones occasionally present slight alterations of specifically Studite practice (for example, omitting mention of the Lenten Liturgy on all days of the fast, observing with less solemnity the commemoration of St. Theodore on November 11, designating him 'father' rather than 'our father'). There exist also several fragments of the Studite-Alexis Typikon (for instance, in the miscellany of the former St. Cyril of Belozersk Library [in the St. Petersburg Theological Academy] No. 275 and others).

[^1619]: The Monastery of Grottaferrata and its Typikon long defended their independence from their mighty neighbour. The friends of the first hegumen, Nilus, could not persuade him even to visit Rome and its holy places. Hegumen Bartholomew, although maintaining friendly relations with Popes John XIX and Benedict IX and even participating in the Lateran Council of 1044, nevertheless oversaw the writing of Menaia that strictly preserve Eastern traditions and diverge from the later Grottaferrata Typikon. Only Hegumen Blasius is styled by Pope Martin IV as his vassal; in view of such new relations with Rome there was undertaken by this hegumen a renewal (*ἀνακαινίσθη*) of the Grottaferrata Typikon; it is readily apparent wherein it consisted: on November 1 it is prescribed to celebrate All Saints; on great feasts a Latin litany is appointed, and at the Liturgy a 'combined Greek and Latin order'; during Great Lent a daily Presanctified Liturgy is recommended in view of the custom of the Roman Church to celebrate a full Liturgy daily; on the Exaltation and during the Nativity Fast (Philip's Fast) cheese and eggs are permitted; in the litanies the Pope is commemorated with the title 'our most honorable and holy father *ho deina* [N.]', Latin terminology is introduced, etc. The Typikon has been preserved in a manuscript contemporary with Blasius bearing the date 1300 [1299/1300 AD] in the monastery library No. A. α. VII [A. II. 7]. Described by Toscani, Th., *Ad Typica Graecorum*, Rome, 1864; supplementary unto this description in Dmitrievsky, A. A., *Opisanie liturgicheskikh rukopisei*, Vol. I: *Τυπικά*, pp. 899 ff.

[^1663]: A native of Constantinople, Nikon was obliged to retire from the Rhaithou Monastery, where he had tonsured as a monk, on account of the dissatisfaction of the brethren, unto the Black Mountain Monastery; following its devastation first by the Turks in 1085, and later by the Crusaders in 1098, he returned unto Rhaithou. He is renowned as the author of the *Pandects* ('Compendium'), a work of canonical content, and the *Taktikon* ('Rule'), of liturgical and monastic-disciplinary character, among other writings. His works in Greek have not yet been published (they are preserved in manuscripts of the Sinai Library), with the exception of fragments (in Pitra and others); the *Pandects* and *Taktikon* enjoyed great veneration in ancient Russia and provided much material for the *Kormchaya Kniga* (Nomocanon). They were printed in Slavonic at Ostroh [printed: Otroge] in 1645, Pochaiv in 1795, and Moscow in the Edinoverie Typography in 1889. Mansvetov, I. D., *Tserkovny ustav*, pp. 187 ff.; Golubinsky, E. E., *Istoriya russkoy tserkvi*, Vol. I, Part 1, p. 748.

[^1675]: The most ancient witness of the Hagiorite Typikon following the *Diatyposis* of St. Athanasius (excerpts from which are repeatedly cited also by Nikon of the Black Mountain) still in its purely Studite form may be recognized in the Georgian 'Great Synaxarion,' translated for the Iviron Lavra by its dean (vicar hegumen, *kathegoumenos* / καθηγούμενος) George the Hagiorite (Mtatsmindeli) [printed: *Itatsmindeli*] in 1038–1042, which was utilized, as is evident from its contents, in other Athonite monasteries as well, and in all probability in the Lavra of St. Athanasius, upon which Iviron was dependent; this Synaxarion is close unto the *Hypotyposis*, *Diatyposis*, and the excerpts from the Hagiorite Typikon in Nikon (who likewise designates this Typikon a Synaxarion); it is a ktetorial typikon of Studite type (there are no all-night vigils; the number of kathismata is identical; festal antiphons at Matins), yet with local peculiarities (fasting regimen, Georgian commemorations). (The Synaxarion in Russian translation from manuscripts contemporary with St. George—Tiflis Ecclesiastical Museum MSS Nos. 193 and 222—is published in Archpriest Kekelidze, *Liturgicheskie gruzinskie pamyatniki*, pp. 228–272). From the 13th century complete Jerusalem Typika appear upon Mount Athos as well. The Typikon given by St. Sava of Serbia († 1237) unto the Hilandar Monastery upon Mount Athos refers for divine worship unto a certain 'Synaxarion,' perhaps that whose 14th-century manuscript is preserved at present in the Hilandar Library (MS No. 66/70)—of purely Jerusalem type (Dmitrievsky, A. A., 'Drevneyshiy Khilandarskiy Sinaksar po ustavu Ierusalimskomu,' *Trudy Kievskoy Dukhovnoy Akademii*, 1905, Vol. II, p. 473), just as it itself represents a mixture of Jerusalem practices (vigils) with local customs (fasting regimen). (The Hilandar Typikon from a manuscript contemporary with St. Sava was published by Bishop Demetrius, *Tipik Hilandarski*, Belgrade, 1898). Even after the introduction of the Jerusalem Typikon in the Athonite monasteries, previous and local customs continued to be maintained; for this reason this introduction did not extinguish the distinctive Hagiorite Typikon, but merely imparted unto it a Jerusalem coloring, as is evident from the very titles of its surviving manuscripts (none of which have been published). Thus the Greek Vatican Library MS *Codex Palatinus* No. 101 of 1474 is entitled: 'Typikon of the Lavra of St. Sabas and of the Lavra of St. Athanasius the Athonite'; in the same library, MS No. 38 of 1423: 'Typikon of the Holy and Great Monastery of St. Athanasius upon Mount Athos'; in the 1336 Typikon of the Laurentian Library in Florence, MS No. 15, there are 'Chapters of the Most Celebrated Ecclesiastical Ordinance of the Holy Mountain.' The most important Athonite monasteries possess at present written texts of their Typikon (of Jerusalem type); thus the Lavra of St. Athanasius in 15th–16th century manuscripts; the Pantokrator Monastery in a 15th-century manuscript. The ordinances of the Dionysiou Monastery were recorded in 1624 by its hieromonk Ignatius, and this record enjoyed great authority—copies thereof exist in many Athonite monasteries; thus for the St. Panteleimon Monastery there was made (in its library there is an 18th-century manuscript) a revised copy from the Dionysiou Typikon under the title: 'Accurate Typikon of the Ecclesiastical Office, Collected from St. Sabas and Diverse Others'; here, besides the Athanasian Typikon, references occur unto the Athonite Typika of the 'Right Choir,' of the 'Left Choir,' and the 'Great Typikon of the Adrianopolitan.' From the Dionysiou Typikon a copy was likewise made in 1875 for the Iviron Monastery under the title: 'Abridged Typikon in Conjunction with Local Custom' (all unpublished and unresearched). Yet unto this day, as ever, the Holy Mountain follows in divine worship unwritten traditions more than written texts; for this reason divine worship here is guided not so much by the Typikon as by the *typikaris* (a most honorable personage in the monastery), and in difficult cases by a council of *typikareis* (Dmitrievsky, A. A., 'Svyatogorskiy [afonskiy] Tipikon,' *Rukovodstvo dlya selskikh pastyrey*, 1897, Nos. 1, 3, 4, 5).

[^1698]: The repeated **"Lord, have mercy"** originally, in all probability, was repeated thrice, then 12 times, a trace of which remains at present at the conclusion of Lenten services and in Typika of the Studite recension; subsequently it could be increased unto 30, and then unto 40 times (in non-Chalcedonian Eastern churches even unto 60 and 100; thus among the Armenians, see above, p. 333); a trace of all these forms of practice is provided by the Horologion of the Moscow Synodal Typography Library MS No. 77/150/1223 of the 15th century, where at the First Hour **"Lord, have mercy"** is appointed 30 times, at the Third 40, and at the Ninth 12 times (fols. 20 and 38); in the Studite Typika for ordinary Hours 40 times, and for the Royal Hours 30 times (Typikon of the Moscow Typography Library MS No. 185/142/1206, fols. 20v and 7v); occasionally such a distinction is made: in Great Lent 50 times, in the Nativity (St. Philip's) and Apostles' (Sts. Peter and Paul's) Fasts 40 times, and on ordinary days 30 times (Horologion of the Imperial Public Library MS Q. I No. 67 of the 15th–16th [printed: XV–XII] centuries, fol. 154v); at the inter-hours in the majority of manuscripts 30 times (see below). Distinctive in the Ethiopian Horologion of the 14th century: 41 or 51 times: Turayev, B. A., *Chasoslov efiopskoy tserkvi*, pp. 39, 49, and elsewhere.

[^1717]: On Fridays of all fasts according unto this Typikon, in place of Compline, a special service was appointed: *hē presbeia* (ἡ πρεσβεία, intercession, supplication; cf. *preces* in Western offices), consisting of two parts: the first, after the exclamation **“Blessed is the Kingdom”** and the Great Litany, consisted of three pairs of Theotokia (with an intercalary **“Glory... Both now...”** proclaimed by the deacon within each pair), separated by Little Litanies; the second part was analogous unto the present Moleben, consisting of Psalm 112 [113], **“God is the Lord,”** a troparion, and a canon unto the Mother of God with the customary inter-ode responses, after which followed the Trisagion, after the **“Our Father”** a troparion, and a litany (augmented). The service was celebrated in white vestments. Dmitrievsky, *Typika*, pp. 874–877.

[^1755]: Such are, for example, appended unto the Gospel of the Jerusalem Library of the 9th century; appended unto the Apostolos of the St. Petersburg Imperial Public Library MS No. 57 of the 9th–10th century; appended unto the Gospel of the Laurentian Library in Florence of the 10th century; Odessa Museum MS of the 10th century; Museum of the Kyiv Theological Academy MS No. 708 of the 10th century (from the Nizhyn church); Paris Coislin Library MS No. 205 of the 10th–11th century. All of these, like the Constantinopolitan of the 8th century, do not have commemorations for all days of the year, and have few venerables (e.g. the Odessa manuscript); among them the Coislin manuscript is especially archaic, perhaps derived from a witness of the 7th–8th century: it lacks the Entry of the Theotokos, the Synaxis of the Theotokos on December 26, the Veneration of the Chains of St. Peter, St. Mark, St. Jeremiah, Martyr Procopius, etc.

[^1756]: Thus commemorations for all days are found in the aforementioned Jerusalem manuscript of the 10th century; appended unto the Callipolitan (Gallipoli) Gospel and Paris National Library (BNF) MS No. 79 of the 10th century; Moscow Synodal Library MS No. 43 of the year 1055; and of the Cryptaferrata (Grottaferrata) Monastery, styled the *Eklogadion* of the 11th century. Yet the majority of Menologia of the 11th century and some of the 12th, and even of the 13th century, still lack commemorations for all days of the year; among these, for instance, the Menologion appended unto the famous Ostromir Gospel of the 11th century, appended unto the Greek New Testament of the Laurentian Library in Florence MS No. 27 of the 12th century, appended unto the Slavic Apostolos of the Slepche Monastery (near Prilep) of the 12th century, appended unto the Glagolitic Gospel of the Zographou Monastery of the 12th–13th century, and appended unto the Slavic Gospel of the Reims Library of the 13th century.

[^1785]: In the ancient Psalters (for example, one from the library of the Monastery of Xeropotamou on Mount Athos), the 'refrains' (*pripevy*) unto the chosen psalms—designated here as the 'work of Kyr Philotheus' and taking the place of the present-day Megalynaria (*velichaniya*)—have the following form: for the Nativity of the Most Holy Theotokos, Entry, and Annunciation: **"Rejoice, O full of grace, Mary, the Lord is with Thee; alleluia"** (*"Радуйся обрадованная Марие, Господь с Тобою, аллилуиа"*); for the Exaltation: **"Thou hast given a banner unto them that fear Thee, that they may flee from before the face of the bow: Thy Cross, O Christ God"** (*"Дал еси знамение боящимся Тебе еже убежати от лица лука крест Твой Христе Боже"*, LXX Ps 59:6); for the Apostle John the Theologian: **"Come, all ye, let us praise the son of thunder, John, the virgin, the confidant of Christ"** (*"Приидите вси сына громова восхвалим Иоанна, девственника, Христова наперсника"*); for the Great Martyr Demetrius: **"Come, ye lovers of the martyrs, let us praise Demetrius the Myrrh-gusher, zealous follower of the Savior"** (*"Приидите мучениколюбцы, восхвалим мироточного Димитрия, ревнителя Спасова"*); for St. Chrysostom: **"Come, all ye in unison, let us praise John Chrysostom, the universal teacher"** (*"Приидите вси согласно восхвалим Иоанна Златоуста, общаго учителя"*); for the Apostle Andrew: **"Come, all ye in unison, let us praise Andrew the First-called, the kinsman of Peter"** (*"Приидите все согласно восхвалим Андрея первозванного, Петрова сродника"*); for St. Sabbas: **"Come, all ye in unison, let us praise Sabbas the All-consecrated, the boast of the Cappadocians"** (*"Приидите вси согласно восхвалим Савву всеосвященного, Каппадоков похвалу"*); for St. Nicholas: **"Come, all ye earthborn, let us praise the hierarch Nicholas, instructor of the people of Myra"** (*"Приидите вси земнороднии восхвалим иерарха Николая, миряном наставника"*); for the Martyr Eustratius and his companions: **"Come, let us praise Eustratius and Auxentius, Eugenius and Mardarius, and glorious Orestes"** (*"Приидите Евстратия, Авксентия восхвалим, Евгения и Мардария и Ореста славного"*); for the Nativity of Christ: **"Come, with the angelic choirs let us cry aloud: Glory to God in the highest, born in a cave"** (*"Приидите с ангельскими лики возгласим: слава в вышних Богу, рожденному в вертепе"*); for Basil the Great: **"Come, all ye earthborn, let us praise Basil the Great, the boast of the Caesareans"** (*"Приидите все земленороднии в восхвалим Василия Великого кесареом похвалу"*); for Theophany: **"My Jesus is baptized by a servant in the river Jordan, illuminating all creation"** (*"Крещается Иисус мой от раба в Иорданстей реце просвещая всю тварь"*); for St. Theodosius (as also for St. Euthymius and St. Sabbas of Serbia): **"Come, all ye in unison, let us praise Theodosius the Cenobiarch, instructor of monks"** (*"Приидите вси согласно восхвалим Феодосия общежителя, иноком наставника"*); for Athanasius of Alexandria: **"Come, all ye in unison, let us praise great Athanasius, the glory of the Alexandrians"** (*"Приидите вси согласно восхвалим великаго Афанасия, александром славу"*); for Gregory the Theologian: **"Come, let us praise the depth of wisdom, the second confidant"** (*"Приидите, премудрости глубину возхвалим, второго наперсника"*); for the Three Hierarchs: **"Come, let us praise Basil, Gregory, and John Chrysostom, the champions of the Trinity"** (*"Приидите Василия, Григория восхвалим и Иоанна Златоустаго, Троицы поборники"*); on Meatfare Sunday: **"Turn back, O Lord, the captivity of our souls, and plant Thy fear within our hearts, O Planter of good things; alleluia"** (*"Возврати, Господи, пленение душ наших и страх Твой всади в сердца наша, Насадителю благих, аллилуиа"*); on Sunday of the Veneration of the Precious Cross: **"Thy Cross we adore, O Master..."** (*"Кресту Твоему покланяемся Владыко…"*, cf. LXX Ps 98:5); on Palm Sunday: **"Come, let us also, like the children, offer faith unto God as palm branches, and love as boughs"** (*"Приидите и мы яко отроцы принесем веру яко ваиа Богу, любовь же яко ветви"*); for St. George: **"Come, ye lovers of the martyrs, let us praise George the Victorious, the boast of the Cappadocians"** (*"Приидите мучениколюбцы, восхвалим победоносца Георгия, каппадоком похвалу"*); for Ascension: **"God is gone up with a shout, the Lord with the sound of a trumpet, to save the image of Adam"** (*"Взыде Бог в воскликновении Господь во гласе трубне, еже спасти образ адамов"*, LXX Ps 46:6); for the Nativity of John the Forerunner: **"Let us all in unison praise John the Baptist, the friend of the Bridegroom"** (*"Вси согласно восхвалим Иоанна Крестителя, друга Женихова"*); for the Apostles Peter and Paul: **"Let us praise the citizens of the Jerusalem on high, Peter and Paul, disciples of Christ"** (*"Вышняго Иерусалима гражданы восхвалим Петра и Павла, ученики Христовы"*); for St. Athanasius of Athos: **"Come, all ye in unison, let us praise Athanasius of Athos, the glory of monastics"** (*"Приидите все согласно восхвалим афонскаго Афанасия, инокующим славу"*); for the Transfiguration: **"My Jesus and Lord is transfigured upon Mount Tabor, having manifested His glory"** (*"Преобразуется Иисус мой и Господь на горе Фаворстей, показав славу свою"*); for the Dormition: **"[Thy choir] offers unto Thee a departure hymn, O Mary, for Thou hast translated from earthly unto eternal mansions"** (*"Песнь ти исходную приношает Марие, приставибося от земленых к вечным обителем"*); for the Beheading: **"Come, all ye, let us praise the friend of the Bridegroom, the reprover of Herod, John the Forerunner"** (*"Приидите вси Женихова друга восхвалим, Иродова обличителя, Предтечу Иоанна"*); after the Megalynaria: **"Glory to the Father... Glory to Thee, O Holy Trinity; glory to Thee, Father, Son, and Holy Spirit; Holy Trinity, glory to Thee"** (*"Слава Отцу… Слава Ти Троице Святая, слава Ти Отце и Сыне ио Святым Духом, Троице Святая, слава Тебе"*), **"Both now and ever... Rejoice, O full of grace, Mary, the Lord is with Thee, and for Thy sake with us. Alleluia, alleluia, alleluia, glory to Thee, O God"** (*"И ныне и присно… Радуйся, обрадованная Марие, Господь с Тобою, и Тебе ради с нами. Алиилуиа 3, слава Тебе Боже"*). These refrains are also significant in that they demonstrate which feasts were regarded as the most important. In the printed Serbian Menaion of 1536, unto these refrains are added refrains for Pentecost: **"Glory to Thee, O Trinity: Father, Word [printed: *Лове*], and Holy Spirit; glory to Thee, O God"** (*"Слава Ти Троице, Отче и Лове и Душе Святый, слава Тебе Боже"*), six refrains unto the Mother of God at the Polyeleos, appended alternately unto the verses of Psalm 134 [LXX 134], and refrains for the 9th Ode. (Archimandrite Antonin [Kapustin], *Zametki poklonnika sv. Gory* [Notes of a Pilgrim to the Holy Mountain], Kyiv, 1864, p. 252). In the Kraków edition Horologion of 1491, there are cited in one place two Megalynaria for each feast—one differing from the present-day one, and the other identical with the present (fol. 270v ff.); in another place (fol. 163v), only the present-day ones are given.

[^1806]: The extent unto which this Typikon was implemented in the Athonite Iviron Lavra even prior unto the appearance there of a complete copy of it, under St. Euthymius, its second hegumen († 1012 AD), is evident from the life of the latter, compiled by his successor and translator of the described *Synaxarion*, Gregory Mtatsmindeli [the Hagiorite]. According unto the biographer, Euthymius stood in church without leaning upon a staff and without leaning against the wall. The brethren standing by the wall were likewise forbidden to lean against it. The younger brethren stood in the middle of the church in two or three rows, reverently, with hands lowered; when appointed, they sat upon their benches, which likewise stood in the middle of the church in two or three rows. Euthymius appointed two God-fearing *epitropoi*-overseers, one senior, and the other junior, subordinate unto the first. The junior *epitropos* was sent through the cells and brought unto church any brother who remained in his cell. If a brother did not arrive for the Six Psalms, Euthymius judged him according unto the rules of the father (Theodore) in the following manner: he did not punish one who labored much by day and had no time to sleep—his daytime labors were imputed unto him as an ascetic struggle of prayer. But those having leisure or performing petty tasks, as well as priests, deacons, and readers, he subjected unto such punishment: he compelled the younger to make 100 prostrations before the altar, while the elderly and infirm he deprived that day of wine and food. During the service, the senior *epitropos* stood at the doors and inquired of any departing brother concerning the reason for his exit; if no essential need was apparent, he did not permit him to leave; but in case of genuine necessity, he let him out only upon condition that he return immediately. In the event that the one who exited was late, he was subjected unto a rebuke; and if he was late a second time, on that day he was not admitted into the refectory, but was kept upon dry bread or sentenced unto 100 prostrations. Unto those laboring untiringly, the holy father permitted leaving the church after the Six Psalms to rest, but with the obligation to return by the second bell ringing. Unto the weak among the brethren, he allowed standing in the narthex and leaning upon a staff, and unto the sick even to sit. Younger brethren conversing, laughing, or taking each other by the hand were immediately reproved; and if caught a second time, they were reported unto the holy father, who judged them strictly. One guilty of quarreling or fighting was brought unto the cell of the holy father, who commanded him to lie upon the ground; the guilty brother, having made a bow, lay down; one of the brethren held him by the head, another by the feet, and a third struck him over his cassock with 30, 40, or 60 blows of a belt. If anyone interceded for the one being punished, he was subjected unto the very same punishment. Those punished, kneeling, bowed before the holy father and with tears in their eyes begged his forgiveness. Thereafter they lay upon the ground and remained in such a posture for two or three weeks (?). From time to time the holy father came unto them and comforted them in word and deed; unto the same he urged other monastic officials. The executor of the punishment likewise comforted the punished brother and presented him with a cassock, or a scapular, or some other necessary item. The punished regarded the punishment they endured as though they had suffered it from the hands of Christ Himself. Above all, the holy father took care that no one should give false testimony or witness in any matter without knowing its circumstances; whoever was convicted of this he expelled from the monastery. The blessed father provided the brethren with everything, down unto needle and thread, and thereby deprived all of an occasion to sell or acquire anything without his command; a brother could not transfer his property unto another without the consent of the holy father. If anyone transgressed the will of the holy father and acquired clothing or anything valuable, he strictly rebuked him. We have seen more than once how he burned in the monastic enclosure a scapular, clothing, or a klobuk (*koukoulion*). Frequently he said unto the brethren: "The saints denied themselves even water. Is it not sufficient for us to take food twice a day, and that in abundance—with wine and various dishes?" Therefore, if anyone bought wine and oil, the entire purchase was poured into the refuse pit. Kekelidze, *Liturgicheskie gruzinskie pamyatniki* [Liturgical Georgian Monuments], pp. 305 ff., 478 ff.

St. Sergius, founder of the Holy Trinity Lavra, likewise was not ashamed of any labor, neither cooking nor shoemaking, and worked for two; his special tasks were the milling of flour for prosphora and baking them, rolling candles, and cooking kolyva (Golubinsky, E. [^1817]: Dmitrievsky, *Τυπικά*, pp. 671, 678. In the Typikon of Empress Irene this order of election develops into a very intricate rite. Upon three identical parchments was written the prayer: "O our Master Jesus Christ, through the intercessions of our all-immaculate Lady the Mother of God Full of Grace, reveal unto us sinners whether Thou deemest worthy of governance over us our sister [Name]"; the parchments, sealed by the patroness of the monastery, were placed upon the holy table for the duration of the Vigil and the Divine Liturgy. Immediately following the Divine Liturgy, the Trisagion is chanted and the troparia: **"Have mercy on us, O Lord..."** (*Pomiluy nas, Gospodi...*); **"Glory..."**, **"O Lord, look down from heaven and behold..."** (*Gospodi, prizri s nebese i vizhd...*); **"Both now..."**, **"O Only-Begotten, Consubstantial..."** (*Yedinorodne, Yedinosushchne...*). The priest (fully vested) intones the Insistent Litany, unto which he appends the petition: "Furthermore we pray that the Lord will show us one worthy of governance over us"; the sisters chant: "Lord, have mercy" thirty times with fifteen prostrations, lifting up their hands with the prayer: "O God Who knowest the heart, reveal unto us sinners one worthy of governance over us." The priest, having made three prostrations before the holy table with the same prayer, takes one of the parchments, and following verification of the seal, the woman who sealed it opens it; the elected nun, after three prostrations, takes from a special place before the sanctuary the Typikon and the staff, stands in the abbess's stall, is greeted by all, glory is sent up unto God, and the customary dismissal is given by the priest (Typikon of Empress Irene, ch. 11; Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, vol. 127).

[^1835]: Plutarch, *De virtute*; Pape, W., *Griechisch-Deutsches Handwörterbuch*, Braunschweig, 1880, pp. 1162, 262. Later, the word *typos* (τύπος) was assigned the meaning of an edict, a law; the word already possesses such a meaning in Philostratus († 240) and the 5th-century ecclesiastical historian Socrates (Sophocles, E., *Greek Lexicon of the Roman and Byzantine Periods*, New York–Leipzig, 1888, p. 1099); yet *typos* with this meaning does not form the adjective *typikos* (τυπικός) in any author; among ancient Christian writers (Clement of Alexandria, Origen, Basil the Great) this adjective signifies "symbolic," "prefigurative" (see *ibid.*). The root meaning of the word cannot entirely vanish in all instances of its usage; and if *typos* sometimes denotes a law or rule, it is of a special character; thus, in Gregory Nazianzen it is used in relation to the Symbol of Faith [the Creed]; in Justinian it signifies the Divine Law (for citations see Sophocles); Emperor Constans designated his well-known confessional edict by this term [*Typos*]. But a religious law or rule differs substantially from every other kind, and its distinctiveness is well expressed by the basic meaning of the word *typos*. More precisely than "rule" [*ustav*], *typikon* (τυπικόν) could be translated as "ordinal" [*chinovnik*], Lat. *ordinarium* (thus translated by Toscani, *Ad typica graecorum*, Romae, 1864, p. 5).

[^1836]: The word *diatyposis* (διατύπωσις) is first used in ecclesiastical literature by the *Apostolic Constitutions* (4th–early 5th c.) applied, seemingly, to ecclesiastical constitution in general or, more immediately, to the rites of ordination and the Liturgy (*Apostolic Constitutions*, VIII, 3).

The Russian expression "vo vsya tyazhkaya" [ringing all the heavy bells/strikes] is not used in Greek (Kazansky, P., *O prizyve k bogosluzheniyu v vostochnoy Tserkvi* [On the Summoning to Divine Service in the Eastern Church] // *Trudy pervogo arkheologicheskogo syezda v Moskve 1869 g.*, Moscow, 1871, p. 313).

[^1855]: Archimandrite Antonin (Kapustin) recounts concerning the bell-chime for the All-Night Vigil in the Athonite St. Panteleimon Monastery (Rossikon): "They struck the great 'semantron' [*bilo*] in the bell-tower; they beat upon it at first slowly, then swiftly and briskly with rising and falling of pitches, with their playful permutation, with a rapid transition from lower to higher and vice versa, or by slowly modulating them through semitones with gradual fading to complete cessation, and with an unexpected resurrection to new vivacity and vigor. Such tolling or beating was renewed three times after pauses for the rest of the 'artist,' as the Greeks called the ringer, visibly moved by his art; and each time he allowed them to hear new tone combinations, diverse from the first strike of the mallet to the last. This music continued for half an hour" (*Zametki poklonnika Svyatoy Gory* [Notes of a Pilgrim to the Holy Mountain], Kyiv, 1864, p. 29).

[^1859]: By the word *kōdōn* (κώδων) the LXX designates the bells on the vesture of the High Priest (Exod 28:34). Presently among the Greeks *kōdōn* denotes a small bell of about 3 pounds in weight; a larger one is called *kampanon* (κάμπανον). On Athos, *kōdōn* designates the altar bell in the shape of an inverted bowl with a small striker above; this bell is struck at the conclusion of the Proskomedia, and at this signal the brethren, standing each in his place, having removed their klobuks and bowed low, commemorate their relatives, the living and the reposed, while the priest in the altar extracts particles; at the Liturgy of the Presanctified Gifts, at the signal of this bell they fall prostrate during the transfer of the Holy Gifts, and then at a new signal they rise. The word "kandiya" does not exist in the Greek language, neither ancient nor modern (Kazansky, P., *O prizyve k bogosluzheniyu v vostochnoy Tserkvi* [On the Summoning to Divine Service in the Eastern Church] // *Trudy pervogo arkheologicheskogo syezda v Moskve 1869 g.*, Moscow, 1871, p. 316).

[^1860]: According to Allatius, Michael Psellos said in an oration to Emperor Constantine Monomakhos (1042–1054): "The sacred *kōdōn* shall awaken thee, and thou shalt prostrate thyself upon the sacred dais" (*Graeciae orthodoxae scriptores*, Romae, 1652, VII, 3). According to Pachymeres, upon the return to his see of Patriarch Joseph I of Constantinople (in 1282), he entered the patriarchate amidst the ringing of numerous church *kōdōnes* (κωδώνων) (*Michael Paleologus...*, VII, 3). According to Eustathius, Metropolitan of Thessalonica, the Crusaders who captured Thessalonica were always agitated by the sounds of semantra, but remained calm upon hearing the sounds of "great *kōdōnes*" summoning to psalmody at the Church of St. Demetrius, evidently because these latter sounds were familiar to them (*De Thessalonica a Latinis capta* // Migne, *Patrologia Graeca*, Vol. 136, col. 121).

[^1874]: Thus, the Liturgy of the Apostle James has the following beginning (that which is found in its earliest 11th-century Rossano manuscript is printed in italics, and in later ones in ordinary type): *Deacon: Let us pray to the Lord. People: Lord, have mercy.* Priest: In the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit, now and ever, and unto the ages of ages. Amen. *Deacon: Let us stand aright. In peace let us pray to the Lord. Priest, a prayer: Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit...* and 2 more prayers. *Deacon: Master, give the blessing. Priest, a prayer...* etc. (Petrovsky, A., *Apostolskie liturgii vostochnoy Tserkvi* [Apostolic Liturgies of the Eastern Church], St. Petersburg, 1897, Appendix, pp. 1–3). The Liturgy of the Evangelist Mark, used from antiquity in the Alexandrian Church, begins according to the Rossano Codex: Deacon: Stand for prayer. Priest: Peace to all. People: And to thy spirit. Deacon: Pray. People: Lord, have mercy. Priest, 1st prayer (Swainson, C. A., *The Greek Liturgies*, Cambridge, 1884, pp. 2–3). But in its more ancient redaction (in Renaudot, *Liturgiarum Orientalium Collectio*, Paris, 1716, II, 184) it begins with three prayers of the priest, to each of which the people respond Amen; then the Deacon: Give the peace. Priest: The grace... be with you all, etc. The Liturgy of the Mesopotamian Church, attributed to the Apostle Thaddaeus—a Nestorian liturgy, but in its ancient core (printed here in italics) originating before the Nestorian heresy and, in any case, not later than the 7th c.—begins: *In the Name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Glory to God in the highest, and on earth peace, good will among men, now and ever...* Choir: *Amen and Our Father.* Priest, bowing his head, makes the exclamation: *Glory to the Father, and to the Son, and to the Holy Spirit, now...* Choir: *Amen.* Deacon: *Pray. Peace be with you.* Priest, a prayer (Petrovsky, A., *Apost. lit.*, p. 61).

[^1927]: The Raskolniks [Old Believers] in this refrain pronounce *Alleluia* twice, replacing the third *Alleluia* with what is, in their opinion, its equivalent: **"Glory to Thee, O God."** Such a manner of chanting *Alleluia* in this refrain was prescribed by the Stoglav Council (1551), which designated the custom of tripling the *Alleluia* a "Latin heresy" (the Latins, according to the Council, "do not glorify the Trinity, but quadruple It," which the Council apparently deduced in some fashion from the *Filioque*). The Council appealed in defense of the twofold *Alleluia* to the *Life of St. Euphrosynus of Pskov* (†1481), to whom the Most Holy Theotokos Herself "revealed and forbade concerning the threefold *Alleluia*, commanding Orthodox Christians to say the twofold *Alleluia*" (*Stoglav*, ch. 42 / ed. D. Kozhanchikov, St. Petersburg, 1863, p. 148). In this *Life*, composed shortly before the Council, it is recounted moreover that St. Euphrosynus was in great sorrow concerning the mystery of the most holy *Alleluia* (that is, whether one ought to double or triple it) and, failing to find an answer to this in Russia, undertook a journey to Greece, where from a conversation with Patriarch Joseph and from the practice of the Hagia Sophia Cathedral and all the monasteries he became convinced of the necessity of doubling the *Alleluia* and introduced this custom into his monastery, on account of which he was denounced and persecuted by the people of Pskov headed by the Priest Job. The question of the *Alleluia* occupied other church figures of that era as well; even prior to St. Euphrosynus, St. Photius, Metropolitan of Moscow, in response to an inquiry from the people of Pskov on this point, expressed himself in an epistle of 1419 in favor of the threefold *Alleluia*; Bishop Gennadius of Novgorod did likewise in 1491. Consequently, in the 15th century the question was disputed, and ground for dispute was provided by diversity not only in practice, but also in liturgical books themselves. Whereas in some Greek and Slavic manuscripts of the 13th–16th centuries it was indicated to triple the *Alleluia* (for example, the Horologia of the Rumyantsev Museum, Sevastyanov Collection Nos. 496–497 of the 13th–16th c., the *Ordinance on Chanting the Great Compline [Mephemon]* in MS of the St. Sophia Library of the St. Petersburg Academy No. 1264); in others it was indicated to double it (for example, Slavic Typika of the Moscow Synodal Library Nos. 383 and 384 of the 14th–15th c., Potrebnik No. 259 of the 16th c.). Not only in Russia, but also in the East there was no uniformity in this regard, as witnessed by the observations of so impartial an observer in this matter as the monk Arseny Sukhanov in his *Proskynitarion* (*Pravoslavny Palestinsky Sbornik*, Vol. VII, fasc. 3, St. Petersburg, 1889, pp. 44, 205, 225). The presiding hierarch of the Stoglav Council himself, Metropolitan Macarius, in his *Great Menion Reader* (*Chet'yi Minei*) denounces those who double the *Alleluia* and symbolically grounds its threefold nature (April, fol. 816), on which basis scholars even suspect in the decree of the Stoglav Council, as well as in the remarks of the *Proskynitarion* concerning the twofold *Alleluia*, a later interpolation. (Concerning all this, see: Macarius, Metropolitan, *Istoriya russkoy Tserkvi* [History of the Russian Church], St. Petersburg, 1868, Vol. VIII, pp. 131ff.; Odintsov, N., *Poryadok obshchestvennago i chastnago bogosluzheniya v drevney Rossii do XVI v.* [The Order of Public and Private Worship in Ancient Russia up to the 16th Century], St. Petersburg, 1881, pp. 243–249; Dmitrievsky, A., "Bogosluzhenie v russkoy Tserkvi v pervye pyat' vekov" [Divine Service in the Russian Church in the First Five Centuries], in *Pravoslavny Sobesednik*, 1882, VII–VIII, pp. 359–362; Nikolsky, K., Archpriest, *Posobie k izucheniyu ustava bogosluzheniya pravoslavnoy tserkvi* [Manual for the Study of the Typikon of Divine Worship of the Orthodox Church], 7th ed., St. Petersburg, 1907, pp. 178–179). Originally and for a long period the *Alleluia*, following the example of the Old Testament church, was chanted, of course, neither twice nor thrice, but once; so it was in the 3rd century, according to the testimony of the *Testamentum* and Tertullian (see Introductory Chapter, p. 108). The dogma of the Trinity, brought to the forefront in theology by the heresies of the 3rd century, compelled Christians to make it the primary subject of their confession; hence, presumably, the extensive application of the number 3 in subsequent worship (the three-psalm group, the three-antiphon structure); hence could easily arise the tripling of the *Alleluia*. But direct witnesses to such a manner of chanting the *Alleluia* prior to the 13th century are lacking; on the contrary, wherever the chanting of the *Alleluia* is discussed, it is presented as if it were uttered once (Cassian, *De institutis coenobiorum*, II, 11; Horologion of the Sinai Library No. 863, 8th c.). Judging from the fact that in the Catholic Church the *Alleluia* is chanted once, twice, and thrice (*Missale Romanum*, Campidonae, 1823, p. 255; *Breviarium*, pp. 22, 29, and others), one may suppose that this threefold manner of its chanting existed. With three antiphons, on the first antiphon the *Alleluia* could be chanted once, on the second twice, and on the third thrice; thus in the order of monastic burial according to MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 396 of the 13th–14th c. (Dmitrievsky, A., *ibid.*). The single *Alleluia* is preserved among us in Psalm 136 and at the Liturgy. In the Ethiopian Horologion after the psalms our current refrain apparently possesses its simplest and most ancient form: "*Alleluia*. Glory to the Lord," 3 times (Turayev, B., *Chasoslov efiopskoy tserkvi*, p. 63).

[^1951]: In the Roman Catholic Church the Hours contain all the component parts of our Hours, but in a different order. As with us, the Hours there all possess a single scheme, excluding Prime (the First Hour), which also among us in antiquity differed in structure from the other Hours, as is evident from the Sinai Horologion of the 8th–9th c., concerning which discussion will follow in the explanation of Chapter II of the Typikon. Following the usual beginning in the Roman Catholic Hours there follows a hymn, proper to each Hour, corresponding to our troparion, ending with *Alleluia* (on Sunday) or another refrain, an "antiphon" (on weekdays). Next follow three sections from Psalm 118 [LXX 118 / MT 119] (which is divided among all the Hours into 11 sections; two of them are read at Prime together with other psalms, and three at each of the remaining Hours without other psalms); these three sections of Psalm 118 at each of the Roman Catholic Hours impart to it the same three-psalm type that our Hours possess (Psalm 118 was chosen for the Hours, presumably, because it speaks of ceaseless meditation upon the Law of God, of glorifying God seven times a day, and the like). After the three sections of Psalm 118, ending with *Alleluia* or another antiphon, there follow two brief excerpts (*capitula*) from the New and Old Testaments (from the Epistles and the Prophets) with concluding refrains (*responsoria*), occasionally changing according to feasts (corresponding to our "verse of the Hour," as well as to paremias and prokeimena). After these *capitula* follows *Kyrie eleison, Christe eleison, Kyrie eleison* (corresponding to our "Lord, have mercy" 40 times) and the *Pater noster* ["Our Father"], again with responsories (the first of which consists of the final words of the Lord's Prayer: "and lead us not into temptation...", corresponding to our exclamation). Then follows the collect/prayer proper to the day (among us, to the Hour), which is preceded and concluded by exclamatory responsories: "The Lord be with you" (*Dominus vobiscum*), with the response: "And with thy spirit. Let us pray (*Oremus*)." After the prayer there is likewise a responsory: "Let us bless the Lord (*Benedicamus Domino*)." The exclamation "The Lord be with you," which is also pronounced by a deacon officiating at the Hours in the absence of a priest, and even in his presence with his permission, is replaced, if a lector reads the Hours, by another: "O Lord, hear my prayer, and let my cry come unto Thee" (*Breviarium Romanum*, pp. 52, 62, 43ff., 24ff.). These responsories surrounding the concluding prayer of the Hour clearly correspond to our priestly exclamation after the Prayer "Thou Who at all times." This is the Roman order of the Hours; the Ambrosian (Milanese) and Mozarabic orders are somewhat longer (Seredinsky, T., Priest, *O bogosluzhenii zapadnoy tserkvi* [On the Divine Worship of the Western Church], St. Petersburg, 1849, Article 2, p. 6). The proximity of the Roman Catholic Hours to our order of the Hours clearly bears witness, of course, to the fact that the order of the Hours in its fundamental structure was formed both there and here during the period of living fraternal communion between the two Churches. Closely related to both the Roman Catholic and Orthodox orders of the Hours are the Hours of the Eastern Monophysites, for example, the Copts. According to the ancient Horologion of the Copts, the order of the Hour consists of an introductory troparion (cf. the hymn of the Hour among the Roman Catholics), 12 psalms (a vestige of the "Order of the 12 Psalms"), a Gospel reading corresponding to the commemoration of the Hour (cf. *capitula* and paremias), troparia with verses and Theotokia identical to our first troparia, a verse of the Hour identical to ours, other troparia largely coinciding with our second troparia (after the Trisagion), the Symbol of Faith [Creed], the Trisagion with "Our Father," and a concluding prayer proper to the Hour (Archimandrite Porphyrius, *Doctrine, Divine Service... of the Copts*, pp. 57ff.). Still closer to our order are the Hours according to the Ethiopian Horologion of the Coptic Church (14th c.): after the usual beginning, 12 psalms, the Gospel, our troparia of the Hour and Theotokia, the verse of the Hour, the Trisagion, *Alleluia*, troparia largely coinciding with our troparia after the Trisagion, the Creed, *Kyrie eleison* 41 times, a brief penitential prayer beginning "Holy, Holy, Holy...", a dismissal troparion, the prayer "Thou Who at all times," *Kyrie eleison* 41 times, and a prayer of blessing common to all the Hours—with the invocation of a succession of saints by name, similar to our litany prayer **"Save, O God, Thy people"** (Turayev, B., *Chasoslov efiopskoy tserkvi*, pp. 47ff., 33ff., 39ff.). In both Horologia there is a special office similar to the conclusion of our Matins and the First Hour; but this office is not called an Hour.

[^1955]: Duhm, B. *Die Psalmen erklärt*. Tübingen, 1899, p. 213. Previously, on the basis of v. 10: "look upon the face of Thine anointed [Christ]," this psalm was referred to David's yearning for the temple during his flight from Absalom; but by "anointed" [*christ*] the psalmist could also have understood the superior of the temple or any king as the supreme guardian of the temple.

[^1956]: Obscure expressions in the psalm: "For the sparrow [bird]" [Ps. 83:4 / MT 84:3], literally from the Hebrew "even the bird," that is, just like a bird. "Blessed is the man whose help is in Thee" [v. 6 / MT 5], whom God helps on the pilgrimage to the temple, which is especially arduous from the lands of the diaspora. "He hath set ascents in his heart," that is, he undertakes the journey to the temple across both mountains and "into the vale of tears [weeping]" [v. 7 / MT 6]—a valley of weeping on account of its barrenness and perils, "unto the place which He hath appointed," keeping ever before him the longed-for goal of the pilgrimage; but from the Hebrew: "they (those journeying to Jerusalem) make it (the valley of weeping) a place of springs"—God miraculously sends them water. "For the lawgiver shall give blessings" [v. 8 / MT 7]: God, Who prescribed in the Law such pilgrimages to the temple (three times a year), blesses these pilgrims (from the Hebrew: "the early rain also covereth it—the valley—with blessings"), and they "shall go from strength to strength," that is, during the arduous pilgrimage their vigor will continually increase, whereas with ordinary travelers the opposite occurs. In relation to the crucified Christ, the vale of weeping is earthly life with its sufferings and death, through which He elevated His human nature unto heaven.

[^1957]: Gunkel, H. *Ausgewählte Psalmen*. Göttingen, 1904, p. 133. This author, as well as Duhm cited above, are rationalists, but this did not prevent them from providing an excellent explanation of the present psalms, as well as certain others.

[^1964]: In the Coptic and Ethiopian Horologia at the Ninth Hour there are appointed Psalms 95–115 (omitting 112 in the first Horologion and 113 in the second), the Gospel of Luke 9:10–17 (on the feeding of the 5,000—a connection with the agape feast?), our troparion and Theotokion after the Psalms, but between them at "Glory" an additional special one, containing a prayer for worthy communion (connection with the agape feast?); among the troparia after the Trisagion—the second is different from ours, but likewise concerning the thief; the prayer is different, but of the same content (Turayev, B. *Chasoslov efiopskoy tserkvi*, pp. 63ff.; Bishop Porphyrius Uspensky, *Verouchenie, bogosluzhenie... koptov*, pp. 66ff.).—At the Roman Catholic None (Ninth Hour), the hymn entreats God, as the steadfast strength of all things (*rerum Deus tenax vigor*), abiding motionless within Himself and determining the succession of the hours of daylight by consecutive declines, to grant light at the evening (of life), from which our life might never depart, but that holy death might be followed by eternal glory as a reward; then three assigned sections of Psalm 118 [LXX 118 / MT 119]; the antiphon to them on weekdays (in place of the Sunday *Alleluia*) is "Look upon me" (*Aspice in me*); the *capitulum* is 1 Cor. 6:20 ("For ye are bought with a price: therefore glorify God..."); the responsories to it on Sunday: "I cried with my whole heart; hear me, O Lord"; "I will search out Thy statutes"; "Cleanse Thou me from secret faults, O Lord, and spare Thy servant from the sins of others"; on weekdays: "Deliver me (according to the Vulgate: 'redeem me', *redime*), O Lord, and have mercy on me"; "My foot hath stood in uprightness"; "From my secret faults..."; another *capitulum*, Isa. 14:1: "Her time is near to come, and her days shall not be prolonged, for the Lord will have mercy on Jacob, and will yet choose Israel"; responsories to it: "Upon thee, Jerusalem, the Lord shall arise, and His glory shall be seen upon thee"; "Come, O Lord, and do not tarry"; "Forgive the transgressions of Thy people." Thus the Roman Catholic service of the Ninth Hour does not directly commemorate the sacred events of this hour and in content differs little from the services of the Third and Sixth Hours (as we shall see).

In accordance with this, on Mount Athos the introductory psalm at the Vigil, according to the description of Archimandrite Antonin Kapustin (from 1859), is executed in the following manner: "The reading of the introductory psalm began rapidly, seemingly presaging a very swift course of the service. But at the midpoint of verse 28 of the psalm the reading ceased. There began what chanters call the *anoixantaria* (*ἀνοιξαντάρια*), that is, the remaining words of the verse and the remaining verses of the psalm, chanted by both choirs alternately. The first choir, or rather the chanter (*psaltēs*) of the first choir, began to intone the words: 'When Thou openest (*ἀνοίξαντος*) Thy hand...' etc., and he concluded the psalm two hours later. After each verse the singers alternated, standing afterward, drenched in sweat, in the rank of refrain-chanters" (*Zametki poklonnika sv. gory* [Notes of a Pilgrim to the Holy Mountain]. [^2088]: By this light is shed upon the original meaning of the first petitions of the Great Litany: these were petitions for that peace which is requisite for the offering of the Eucharist, and whose outward expression was the kiss of peace prior unto this offering. In the Persian-Nestorian Liturgy attributed unto the Apostle Thaddaeus, before the prayer for the hallowing of the Gifts, the deacon says: "In your minds pray for peace with us"; before communion: "Let us pray for our peace among ourselves"; after communion—the same (*Sobranie drevnikh liturgiy* [Collection of Ancient Liturgies], St. Petersburg, 1874–1878, IV, pp. 22, 30, 36). In the Liturgy of Nestorius at the beginning of its "canon," the deacon says: "Let us pray for our peace among ourselves" (ibid., p. 47). In the Gallican and Mozarabic Liturgies, instead of this, the priest or deacon says: "Offer peace unto one another." The choir responds: "My peace I give unto you" thrice with the refrain of the lesser doxology, and then the priest says: "Give the kiss of love and peace, that ye may be prepared for the Holy Mysteries of God" (ibid., IV, pp. 106, 144).

Deacon: In peace let us pray unto the Lord. Choir: Lord, have mercy.
D.: Let us pray for the peace of the whole world, for the good estate and union of the Holy Churches of God. Ch.: Lord, have mercy.
D.: Let us pray unto the Lord for the pastors of the Church, bishops, deacons, for all the clergy and all the Christian people. Ch.: Lord, have mercy.
D.: Let us pray unto the Lord for sovereigns and all that are in authority, that they may execute the work of their governance in righteousness and love. Ch.: Christ, have mercy.
D.: Let us pray unto the Lord, that He may grant us a temperate balance of the air and an abundance of the fruits of the earth. Ch.: Christ, have mercy.
D.: Let us pray for the salvation of travelers, the sick, prisoners, and all that suffer. Ch.: Christ, have mercy.
D.: Let us pray unto the Lord for the preservation of peace among all nations. Ch.: Lord, have mercy.
D.: Let us pray unto the Lord, that He may deliver us from every evil, spiritual or temporal. Ch.: Lord, have mercy.
D.: Let us pray unto the Lord, that He may forgive our transgressions and account us worthy to live holily and receive everlasting life. Ch.: Lord, have mercy.
Thereupon follows a prayer (*collectio*) with the response of the choir: Amen (*Sobranie drevnikh liturgiy*, IV, p. 97).

[^2201]: In greater detail, with additions unto the Typikon and *Sluzhebnik* produced by general and local practice, the rite of the Entrance is set forth in the *Order of Matins, Vespers, and Midnight Office* [*Posledovanie utreni, vecherni i polunoshchnitsy*], edition of the Kiev Caves Lavra, 1861, 1884. According unto this *Order*, the deacon before the Entrance censes the Holy Table round about, and the priest kisses the Holy Table; upon departing through the north door they proceed behind the ambo; when they halt, the deacon censes the holy icons and the priest, takes the censer in his left hand and the orarion in his right, and requests a blessing upon the Entrance; unto the blessing of the Entrance by the priest the deacon replies: "Amen", censes again the priest and the choirs and, having taken his stand in the Royal Doors, awaits the conclusion of the Theotokion; upon entering into the sanctuary, the deacon censes the Holy Table and the High Place, while the priest kisses the Holy Table and takes his stand at the High Place unto the right of the Holy Table facing west; the deacon goes forth again through the Royal Doors, censes the people, and upon returning into the sanctuary censes the front side of the Holy Table and the priest, after which he takes his stand at the High Place unto the left of the Holy Table; here he stands with the priest until the end of the prokeimenon, making exclamations unto it.

[^2215]: In the Roman Catholic Church even now there is something analogous unto our entrances, and in certain ancient orders of the Latin Liturgy there was an entrance entirely according unto our order. Thus, at the Gallican Liturgy at the very beginning after the "Introit", at the Canticle of Zechariah, "the priest, representing Christ coming into the world, appeareth before the congregation, preceded by the deacon bearing the Gospel and ministers bearing lamps, in token of the evangelical light brought by Jesus Christ into the world." In exactly the same manner at this Liturgy there are transferred from the side altar unto the main altar by the deacon the paten (*patena*) with the bread, and by the priest the chalice with the wine before the consecration of the Gifts (*Collection of Ancient Liturgies* [*Sobranie drevnikh liturgiy*], Vol. IV, p. 102). In the present Roman order of the Mass, unto our Little Entrance corresponds at the beginning thereof the so-called *introitus* ("entrance"), consisting of an antiphon and psalm, appointed for each feast, during which the priest, after censing the altar, approacheth from its right side unto the center with hands folded upon his breast, having previously made a bow of the head unto the cross. Unto the Great Entrance in the Roman Catholic Mass corresponds the transference before the Mass of the chalice and other Eucharistic vessels from the sacristy unto the altar, preceded by a cleric with the Missal unto the ringing of a bell.

[^2257]: In ancient monuments it was termed simply "litany" (*ektenēs* [Gr. ἐκτενής]), whereas the Great Litany was termed *synaptē* [Gr. συναπτή], and the Litany of Fervent Supplication [Litany of Petition] *aitēseis* [Gr. αἰτήσεις] (petitions). So, for example, in the Evergetis Typikon (A. Dmitrievsky, *Typika* [*Typika* / Gr. Τυπικά], p. 607). The designation *ektenēs* is correctly translated into Slavonic as "fervent prayer" [*prilezhnoe molenie*]; at the Liturgy of the Evangelist Mark, before the words of institution concerning the Body the deacon proclaims: *ekteinate* [Gr. ἐκτείνατε] ("pray earnestly"), and before the words concerning the Blood: *eti ekteinate* [Gr. ἔτι ἐκτείνατε] ("pray yet more earnestly") (C. A. Swainson, *The Greek Liturgies*, p. 52).

[^2260]: *Kopiaō* [Gr. κοπιάω]—to labor unto exhaustion (Matt. 6:28). Thus were called the gravediggers [fossarii / kopiatēs], of whom Constantine the Great constituted a special corporation, exempt from taxes and subject unto ecclesiastical authority, consequently, a certain order of clergy. It is scarcely probable that they are meant here and placed prior unto the singers because they stood higher than them (Veniamin (Krasnopevkov-Rumovsky), Archbishop, *Novaya Skrizhal'* [The New Tablet], in 4 parts, St. Petersburg, 1858, p. 26); rather, here are meant the manual laborers of the monastery, and they are placed higher than the singers on account of the arduousness of their service.

[^2264]: The petition "for those who bear fruit", not encountered in earlier monuments of the Augmented Litany, arose from a special litany—the "prayer of fruit-bearing" (*euchē karpophorias* [Gr. εὐχὴ καρποφορίας]), appointed in the Liturgy of the Apostle James after the Our Father and "Holy Things unto the holy" (later manuscripts of the Liturgy of the Apostle James, Paris 14th c., no longer possess this litany) and containing a supplication for "those who have borne fruit" (*karpophorēsantōn* [Gr. καρποφορησάντων]), wherein are meant those who brought bread and wine for the Eucharist (in antiquity, perhaps, also other provisions for the agape). This litany contained 1–3 petitions—for the archbishop, clergy, and people (Messina, Rossano, and Sinai MSS) and together with or in place of this (Paris 14th c.) for help unto all the afflicted ("for every suffering soul", or the like) and the repose of the departed, and thereafter or between these petitions (in the Messina, Sinai MSS, and the Holy Sepulchre *Order of Passion and Paschal Week* of the 9th–12th c.) also a petition for those who brought fruits in such forms: "For those who have brought fruit-offerings on this day, that they may receive defense, forgiveness, and communion of eternal life, having finished [their course] ineffably (?), let us pray" (Jerusalem Order); "Furthermore for the salvation and remission of sins of our brother who hath offered" (Messina); "For the health, salvation, and remission of sins of the servants of God N. and N., who have borne fruit on this day" (Sinai) (Swainson, *The Greek Liturgies*, 312; Dmitrievsky, A., *Bogosluzhenie strastnoy i paskhalnoy sedmitsy v Ierusalime IX–X v.*, 30, 284).

Λιτή] in Homer, although it still signifieth also an ordinary request (*Odyssey*, XI, 34), yet *litai* [Gr. λιταί] with him are personified penitential prayers, daughters of Zeus, following after the wicked goddess *Atē* [Gr. Ἄτη] and making amends for her ruinous deeds (*Iliad*, IX, 502 [printed 52]); among the classics, however (Pindar, the tragedians), the word has only a religious meaning; later there appears the synonymous word *litaneia* [Gr. λιτανεία], used of prayer in the Septuagint (2 Macc. 2:16; 5:5; 10:16; Dionysius of Halicarnassus, 1st c., and others); of a religious procession *litaneia* appears for the first time in the 4th century in John Chrysostom and Basil the Great; *litē*, presumably, for the first time in the 6th century, and among the Greeks it becomes predominant in this sense (Theodore the Reader, 6th c.; *Spiritual Meadow* [*Pratum Spirituale*]), whereas among the Latins the second term [*litania*] does so. For detailed citations: Pape, *Griechisch-Deutsches Handwörterbuch*, II, 1, 54; Sophocles, *Greek Lexicon*, 716.

[^2373]: The Liturgical Apostle has, in addition to the division into chapters and pericopes [*zachalá*], special sections numbering 72, in the margins before which are placed indications of the days of the week: "Sunday", "Monday"... This division was made for cell reading, as is explained in the MS of the Moscow Synodal Library No. 51. Into these sections are inserted also the "narratives" [*skazaniya*] concerning the origin of the epistles. To use this division for the present readings (Nikolsky, K., Archpriest, *Posobie k izucheniyu ustava bogosluzheniya* [Manual for the Study of the Typikon of Divine Worship], 230) is impossible, if only in view of the discrepancy between the number of sections and the Sunday vigils at which such readings are appointed, which number fewer than 50.

[^2436]: In the Kyiv-Pechersk Lavra, by tradition, presumably from the dominance of the Studite Typikon and other recensions of the Octoechos, they sing different Sunday Theotokia compared with those placed in the present Octoechos. Here they are. Tone 1 after Kathisma 2: "Having conceived unconsumed the Divine fire and given birth without seed unto the Fountain of life, the Lord, O full of grace, Theotokos, save them that magnify thee." Tone 2 after Kathisma 2: "Concealed from the laws of nature, thou hast united virginity unto Divine childbearing; for thou alone hast given birth unto Him Who was begotten of the Father before thee without mother, therefore thee, O Theotokos, do we magnify." Tone 3 after Kathisma 1: model (*podoben*), like the sessional hymn, **"Today the Virgin"** (*Deva dnes'*): "The heavenly hosts rejoiced with love and the earthly trembled with fear, when the most pure voice came upon thee, O Theotokos; for a single triumph shone forth for both, when it delivered the first-formed from death." Tone 4 after Kathisma 1: "Thee do we magnify, O Theotokos, crying aloud: Thou art the mountain wherefrom ineffably was cut a stone, which shattered the gates of Hades." Tone 5 after Kathisma 1: "A wondrous miracle of conception and an ineffable manner of birth was made known in thee, O Pure Virgin; it astonisheth my mind and terrifieth my thought; thy glory, O Theotokos, is spread abroad unto all, for the salvation of our souls." In Tones 4 and 5 the Theotokia of the 1st Kathisma are transferred unto the 2nd. In Tones 6 and 7 the customary Theotokia are transposed. Tone 8 after Kathisma 1: "Rejoice, thou that through the Angel receivedst the joy of the world; rejoice, thou that didst bear thy Creator and Lord; rejoice, thou that wast vouchsafed to be the Mother of God." **"All of creation rejoiceth in thee"** (*O Tebe raduetsya*) is model (*podoben*) to the 1st sessional hymn. After each kathisma there is one sessional hymn, sung once: for Tones 1–6 the present 1st and 2nd after the 1st Kathisma; for Tone 7 the first after the 1st and 2nd Kathismata, but transposed; for Tone 8 the same without transposition (*Notny Obikhod of the Kyiv-Pechersk Dormition Lavra*, Part 1: *All-Night Vigil, Score*, Kyiv, 1910, pp. 104ff.).

May God kindle in our hearts the fire of His love. 7. May the Gospel reading be unto us salvation and defense. 8. May divine assistance abide always with us. 9. [^2473]: In other liturgies the exclamations preparatory unto the Gospel received even greater development than among us. Thus, in the present Abyssinian Liturgy the priest says: "The holy Gospel, the word of the Son of God, preached and proclaimed by N"; the people: "Glory to Thee ever, O Christ our Lord and God" and Psalm 80:2, 3 [LXX; Masoretic 81:1, 2]; after the Gospel: "Cherubim and Seraphim send up glory unto Him. Holy, Holy..." (Bishop Porphyrius Uspensky, *The Christian East. The Divine Services of the Abyssinians*, 60). In the Coptic Liturgy, after a twofold prayer of the Gospel, the second with the exclamation "Let us pray for the holy Gospel," Deacon: "Arise." Priest: "In the Name of God." Deacon: "Bless, master." Priest: "The beginning of the holy Gospel according to N." The interpreter (reader?) of the Gospel: "Stand with fear of God [and hear the holy Gospel] of our Lord and God." After the Gospel, a silent prayer (Bishop Porphyrius Uspensky, *Doctrinal Teaching, Divine Services... of the Copts*, 128). In the Nestorian Liturgy of the Apostles Addai and Mari, likewise after 2 prayers: "Deacon: Prepare yourselves for the hearing of the holy Gospel. Priest: Peace be with you. People: With thee and with thy spirit. After the proclamation whence the Gospel is taken, Deacon: Glory to Christ our God. After the Gospel he says: Glory to Christ our God, let us commit ourselves and one another unto the Father, and unto the Son, and unto the Holy Spirit." In a later recension of the same Liturgy: "Priest: Peace to all. Deacon: To thee and to thy spirit. The clergy [sing] a chant unto the four Evangelists concerning the worthy hearing of the Gospel. Priest: The holy Gospel of our Lord Jesus Christ. Reading from St. N. After the Gospel the clergy sing: Glory to Christ our Master" (Petrovsky, A., *The Apostolic Liturgies of the Eastern Church*, 65, 66).

[^2537]: Regarding the doubling of stichera and troparia, the general rule is that a stanza appointed to be doubled must be chanted twice in succession, and not repeated subsequently; this is required by the antiphonal character of liturgical chanting in general.

[^2538]: The fundamental rule of this combination is that the entire kanon of Sunday Matins must not increase beyond 14, that is, that each of its odes must contain no more than 14 troparia including the heirmos. How consistently and strictly the Typikon enforces this principle of combining other kanons with the Sunday kanon is shown by the circumstance that even when a Great Feast of the Theotokos having a kanon to 16 coincides with Sunday, Sunday Matins does not increase its kanon by a single verse, and the festal kanon for this reason is halved and chanted only to 8. It is as though the number 14—this doubled sacred 7 (7 troparia for each choir)—constitutes an inviolable prerogative for the kanon of Sunday Matins.

[^2622]: *Euchologion*, 37; *Typikon*, 3; *Hieratikon*, 33; *Old Believer Typikon*, 9 (17). In correspondence with the inter-ode interval of Odes 3 and 6, a reading would be required after the exapostilarion. But it is absent, presumably in order not to interrupt the unbroken stream of hymnody in this portion of Matins, where the solemnity of the divine service reaches its apex. Moreover, the readings of Matins increase in their importance and compunction in the course of its progression: first the commentary on the Epistle, then on the Gospel, then the *Margarita* (the finest works of the greatest Father [St. John Chrysostom]), and finally the Prolog (frequently replacing the entire service of a saint); here an even superior reading would be required; such could be only Sacred Scripture itself (cf. the conclusion of Vespers); in antiquity here there was indeed a Gospel reading (as also at Roman Catholic Matins). As a replacement for a reading here serves the "Catechesis" [Oglashenie] after Matins.
